By far the best game on Steam at the time of writing. A gripping storyline, flawless voice acting and infinite replay value.
The protagonists attempt to survive in a dystopian society, where a mysterious seemingly immortal figure known only as The Farmer holds them hostage at Ground Zero of a biology experiment gone wrong. This experiment, presumably performed by The Farmer, has created a race of super Suidae, which now run rampant at The Farm.
One of many theories to explain how all of this came to be, is that the game is biblical in nature. The Farmer represents the son of god himself. He is the shepherd and our heroes are His flock. This is made obvious by the way The Farmer is visually represented - impaled to the wall of a barn. This is a clear reference to the crucifixion of christ and as He was born in a barn, it also serves as a symbol of rebirth. This explains the borderline divine abilities of The Farmer: He survives for months, despite being impaled to a wall with a pitchfork. He can open and close doors with his mind. He can conjure up weapons and ammo. He is impervious to both bullets and explosives. He sees and knows everything that happens on The Farm.
It is theorised that the protagonists are undergoing purification in purgatory. They seek to eradicate their sins, which are represented by the swine, with help from their lord and saviour The Farmer. There are certain collectibles in the game, which can only be reached by dying to the swine. This means that The Farmer rewards martyrdom. We must learn from these brave warriors and seek to rid ourselves of sin in their wake. This game has shown me the way through the valley of darkness and helped me see the light. It is never too late to embrace the guidance of The Farmer. We must repent.

FlatOut 2 is an absolute get! I can't recommend it enough!
I was dying for a new racing game to play and happened to have a few bucks in my Steam wallet from selling cards and on a whim bought it for a mere $2.49! Which was an out right steal for this game. If I had known how fun this was I would of gotten it sooner, its regular $10 asking price is still a steal for this!
Fun:
• Slamming into people feels nice, heavy and like you're really doing some damage to'em.
• It has variety in spades. Be it flinging your driver across water, through burning hoops or for playing poker. Demolition derbies, short simple circuit tracks and the varied longer race courses, theres a lot here.
• The sound design is astoundingly good. It has probably the best tire squeals I've ever heard in a racing game. Most games have 1 long squeal which sounds more like the car is doing a burn out than struggling to maintain grip. In this it has a nice stutter to it, like it really is struggling and about to give. You can hear rocks knocking around your wheel well and under your car on the dirt tracks, something I notice games overlook a bit.
• The cars are a great. With a heavy focus on muscle cars for the most part, which is great cause I lost my taste for racing games when they suddenly became mostly about nasty little rice burners (looking at you Need for Speed.). Only about 1~2 cars handled bit squirrely- *coughSpeedevilcough* -and the real only customization to the cars is being able to pick a color.
• The AI actually will crash and wreck without you around, and the follow the same rules you are ei. getting hung up on random track debris and not taking turns perfectly all the time! They maintain a nice difficulty without ever truly being fustrating. Though I'm sure Sofia Martinez will be on your list of people you want dead.
• It. has. Cheat codes.
Meh:
• The soundtrack is just well.. meh. At no point will there ever not be a guitar or drum playing. It tends to get a little grating to listen to near constant noise. Overall its not the worst soundtrack I've ever heard but its nothing I'd listen to outside of the game.
Flaws:
• Only real flaw I can think of is that the menus would not work with my controller.
• Also you really don't get anything for 100%ing it. Quite the shame, least its a fun 100% to get.
Only thing I wish it had was weather and the abilitly to mirror and reverse the tracks.
In the end you should just get it. GET IT NOW!

Edge of Space is a Terraria but sci-fi effort in the same vein as the more popular Starbound, even going as far as to include Terraria crossover content, which was one of the selling points of the game for me. It is also one of the most tedious and uninteresting games I've ever played. The basic gameplay loops are completely uninspired and dull. Terraria has wonderfully satisfying Metroidvania progression that makes slowly mining the world in order to acquire better gear and be able to defeat more difficult enemies an absolute joy to play. In the strictest sense, it's a very repetitive game, but it all feels so good that it's wonderfully engrossing. Edge of Space achieves none of that. It's a grind that just feels like a grind, and even in 1.0 is still a bit toward the wonky side, particularly the jumping mechanics.
I have issues with Starbound and it also misses some of what made Terraria work, but it at least feels like there's potential there, and even still in beta it is a lot more fun than this. Edge of Space needs fundamental design overhaul and the 1.0 release really is just polishing a game that never actually worked on the most basic level. One thing I can say for it is that I don't think the graphics are as bad as some other people are making them out to be. Don't get me wrong, they're certainly not great, but I don't think they're intolerable. In a very fun game, they'd probably be fine. Unfortunately this is not a game that plays well.

Outlast is a first-person survival horror video game developed and published by Red Barrels. The game revolves around a freelance investigative journalist, Miles Upshur, who decides to investigate the abandoned Mount Massive Asylum, released for PC on September 4, 2013 and on February 4, 2014 for PlayStation 4.
The game takes place in Mount Massive Asylum and your main objective is to escape the hospital alive and show to world what horrors takes place there.
The protagonist, reporter Miles Upshur, is incapable of combat, except for scripted sequences allowing him to shove enemies out of his way, like the fight with Richard Trager. Miles carriers his notebook and camcorder to film and wrote his horrific experience in the asylum.
The gameplay is ballanced, the only way to escape from chasing enemies is to hide in dark places, under beds or inside staff lockers, but intelligent enemies can search under beds or the lockers. An other advantage of the player is parkour, which helps him to move fast, slowing the enemy, by jumping over beds, tables or crawl in narrow areas. The camcorder helps you with the night vision. Once activated, the player can see through dark but in the same time, it consume the battery.
The game is powered by Unreal Engine, which always means good graphics. The game is so detailed that you can see small lines in fingerprints and in the same time, VERY disturbing with the corpses and organs. Every patient have something scary about it appearence and the entire asylum is well made and detailed.
The music is amazing and fretting when you're chased or searched. The story is great and scary, I will not say too much about it because this is a spoiler free review.
Overall, it's a fair horror, honest and direct as a punch in the belly that makes few places, but they do well. It does not break barriers but is made with responsibility for gender rules with total irreverence for the player more susceptible. I don't recommand this game for the faint of heart, but if you want and think you can finish a horror game, then sure, play it, but it's your responsability.
PERSONAL RATE: 8.50/10

General Muttonchops, esteemed and then dishonored general before the campaign of '68 now found himself on a small steamboat. They had been sailing the unforgiving zee now for a month or so. They had begun to run disturbingly low on rations and supplies a few days ago. They spotted an island a day ago.
That brings us to today. The good ex-general had led his men to the island, in hopes of getting supplies in exchange for money. What they found was quite different. Two representatives had awaited them. A guinea pig in medieval platemail, and a rat in less appealing wear. Turns out both representated two factions at war. The General, being a sensible man, pledged his loyalty, zailor's lives, and, of course, guns, to the guinea pigs in a heartbeat. He met with the king, they talked, and Muttonchops swiftly led his technolagically superior vessal aganist the rats, bombarding them from sea. When he and his guinea pig comrades stormed the beach, sabres drawn, they had found rat corpses, and a rat child mourning over the severed corpse of presumably parent. The child was later on enslaved.

To be honest, I wouldn't even pirate it. Playing the game for around 24 hours is more than enough publicity for this game's current quality. It also has a big homage to L4D with every intro having a random script of chat for a moment before starting the match with your camera panning into the back of your character's head. July 2016. I guess Evolve has lost it's appeal. Based on what I understand, it's on its last legs. The number of players has dropped to 157 and was temporarily boosted to 24,000 after it went Free To Play. It has become crap after knowing that you grind your way to victory.
I suspect a Pay To Win model will come in assuming the player numbers return. Currently, you just grind Silver. Lots of Silver. E.g. 5500 for a new character. Changed my review to Negative.
PROS
1. Interesting Concept
Pretty fun to have a 4 man kill 1 monster game. I loved the part where the hunters talk shop in the carrier and the way they enter the battleground by skydiving and landing with their jet packs.
CONS
1. Graphics intensive
I could not get the game to run reasonably smooth for a fun game. I don't want the quality of graphics to drop but, hopefully, someone manages to code a easier to render game or graphic cards fall in price so much that every gamer gets a smooth and decent game.
2. Gameplay explainations
They do not explain the game well enough before you enter combat. The Assault's (Markov) lightning gun only works at close range and doesn't trigger unless an enemy comes within range. At the beginning, I thought my system wasn't working since the lightning gun didn't fire.
3a. Repetitive Gameplay
Over and over again, it's either toss a grenade, shoot, mine, bomb or beam. Kind of boring.
1. Reverse Hunt
Now the Hunters start off in a weakend state and with limited abilities. Their equipment is wrecked and they need to restock. The Hunters have a headstart and there are small ammunition and upgrade caches all over the map. Special OP weapons will be unlocked in this mode. Once they restock and level up, it's killing time.
A weakend Stage 3 Monster is now hunting them and appears later. A Monster using smell would be hunting human prey.
2. Monster vs Monster
I would like to play a game of Monster Vs Monster. I know that certain Monsters would be OP in a 1v1 match but I would like to see some variety. E.g. In Goliath vs Wraith, Wraith would lose as it's not a fighter type. Skills like Abduction would be useless.
There is a story behind this. All the captured Monsters have now been put into a battle royale situation by a clandestine organisation who has been paying for the Monsters. The Monsters are caught in a dome that gradually shrinks over time, forcing the Monsters towards each other.
3. Pack Leader Monster
Seems kind of unfair that it's always 1 vs 4. How about a Monster that summons more allies as it levels up? At Level 3, it would have a whole AI pack to fight with. One of its skills could be converting Tyrants over to its side.

Batman - The Telltale Series is Batman, as a Telltale series. No false advertising here. Telltale means you'll get an adventure with choices in dialogue and action, mixed with some sequences of quick time events. There's no inventory, and there are a few "puzzles" that aren't worthy of the name and just there to add flavor (gotta keep those detective skills up). If you have experience playing any of the Arkham games, it's a bit like the detective sequences in those, only even simpler. Expect no great intellectual challenges here, just a laid back story experience where you get to make a choice every now and then.
If you have experience with Telltale games, you'll know by now that the games are much better at presenting the illusion of choice rather than actual choice, and this one is no different. In fact, there's only one major branch in the story (in the sense that events are substantially different), but it's a branch of the form "does X happen before Y, or Y before X", so they quickly meet up again. Every other choice you make at best has a
effect on how the main events unfold, but those main events will always unfold. For every "X will remember this", you can't tell if "remembering" means they'll act any differently, but they probably won't. Initially, the game seems to be setting up an intriguing dilemma of "who do you trust with your secrets", implying that you have to pick a side, but this never really goes anywhere. Characters may express approval or disapproval of how you've been doing things, but beyond some initial dialogue they won't act any differently. Choice, yes. Consequences, not really. Of course, this only becomes really noticeable if you replay the game, and replaying the game also means redoing all the fixed sequences, which a bit of a chore. You would replay this once out of curiosity, but no more than that.
The lack of real choice doesn't mean you end up with a bad story. The story starts off strong, gets a twist in the middle that plays nicely on your preconceived notions of what's going to happen (if you already know your Batman lore) and then unfortunately dips at the end with a lackluster conclusion followed by an almost obligatory cliffhanger/sequel hook. The confrontation with the main villain at the end, in particular, feels like it could have been much more than what we get. There was a rich opportunity to draw on the parallels between Batman and the villain, but nothing is really done with this, so that you're only left with a QTE sequence as they duke it out in fisticuffs. Overall, the story suffers from the same problem a lot of Batman stories do: as you progress you get the uncomfortable feeling that the villains aren't all that wrong, and Batman isn't all that right -- which is good if you explore that as a theme, but the game doesn't do that (nor does it really have room to do that, given its format). It's nice that you get to choose your "style" of Batman, but the lack of real consequences ultimately makes that a lot less interesting than it could have been. There's a lot of room for choice even with a relatively fixed character like Batman, and I'd love to see a game that really tries. This isn't it.
Graphically, the game looks fine, but with noticeable frame rate drops that absolutely have no business being there when running on the kind of hardware I ran it on (16 GB RAM, SSD, GTX 1070). Fortunately this only happened to me on scene transitions and not (noticeably) during action scenes, so gameplay wasn't affected, but even so -- when your cel-shaded adventure game has worse performance than
, you know you're doing something wrong. (For that matter, when your
is ultimately less engaging than that of
, you're doing something wrong.) The music is fine, if unremarkable (it doesn't feature any of the old Batman themes, but then I didn't expect it to). The voice acting is excellent all around.
If you're a Batman fan and you're not averse to the Telltale brand of semi-interactive fiction, this is worth getting on a sale -- not at full price. If you're not a Batman fan, I wouldn't recommend this on its own merits at all. I'm giving it a thumb's up because I feel I got my money's worth, but I can't shake the feeling that it could have been much more, and I doubt I'll be picking up the sequel any time soon.

Having spent a significant amount of time playing Tropico 4, there is something very off-putting about Tropico 5. In Tropico 4, one would always start fresh with each campaign mission. In Tropico 5, the island is carried over between missions. There are benefits to this, but it changes the way the player plays the game. There are buildings the player might want to put near the coast that aren't available until later missions, but it's quite likely the coast will already be well developed by the time those buildings can be built. This forces the player to build akwardly, with future additions in mind, to demolish what are in many cases expensive buildings to make room for new ones, or to simply learn to live with a less-than-ideal situation that will penalize them moving forward.
Many of the interface changes between 4 and 5 seem to make it more difficult to access information rather than easier. There seem to be fewer useful overlays and the overlay can be very difficult to read. Some buildings or building upgrades have an effective radius that can't be viewed, leaving the player guessing. It's still very difficult to easily see what areas are being served by which service buildings. The interface changed from 4 to 5, but that really seems to be the extent of it. It wasn't improved in any significant way. It's just different.
There are good points to the new game as well. Features I would be excited about if the rest of the game didn't feel clumsy. The introduction of research, upgrades and building managers are all interesting features. Greater variety in the military is also very interesting, though the military itself is clumsy to use and combat can be rather infuriating. There are some clever additions made in this iteration that might see better development in a sequel.
The core gameplay of Tropico is still there, so some may enjoy this. First time players may not find as much fault with the game. Personally, i'll hold out hope that (the likely inevitably sequel) Tropico 6 will fine tune things and simply be a better game on whole.

By far the best game on Steam at the time of writing. A gripping storyline, flawless voice acting and infinite replay value.
The protagonists attempt to survive in a dystopian society, where a mysterious seemingly immortal figure known only as The Farmer holds them hostage at Ground Zero of a biology experiment gone wrong. This experiment, presumably performed by The Farmer, has created a race of super Suidae, which now run rampant at The Farm.
One of many theories to explain how all of this came to be, is that the game is biblical in nature. The Farmer represents the son of god himself. He is the shepherd and our heroes are His flock. This is made obvious by the way The Farmer is visually represented - impaled to the wall of a barn. This is a clear reference to the crucifixion of christ and as He was born in a barn, it also serves as a symbol of rebirth. This explains the borderline divine abilities of The Farmer: He survives for months, despite being impaled to a wall with a pitchfork. He can open and close doors with his mind. He can conjure up weapons and ammo. He is impervious to both bullets and explosives. He sees and knows everything that happens on The Farm.
It is theorised that the protagonists are undergoing purification in purgatory. They seek to eradicate their sins, which are represented by the swine, with help from their lord and saviour The Farmer. There are certain collectibles in the game, which can only be reached by dying to the swine. This means that The Farmer rewards martyrdom. We must learn from these brave warriors and seek to rid ourselves of sin in their wake. This game has shown me the way through the valley of darkness and helped me see the light. It is never too late to embrace the guidance of The Farmer. We must repent.

I'm a little bit disappointed in some of the recent negative
of this title.
While I can understand and certainly respect some of the feedback provided by those who have written thought out and critical evaluations of Sunless Sea it seems a lot of those who rate it down do so for the wrong reasons. Or, at least, went in with the wrong expectations treating this title as something it is not.
A lot of the complaints seem to be about the reward -- or lack of -- for undertaking voyages and how they get very little for sailing from one side of the map to another. This seems to me the polar opposite of what you should expect when getting into this title. Too many people place value on in-game assets as a form of entertainment as opposed to the experience you're supposed to get out of it by way of narrative and exploration. This narrative, the exploration and enjoyment of the game come from exploring and reading new and different adventures or stories as you progress instead of monetary rewards for simply traveling far and wide with the purpose of simply upgrading your ship. This title's emphasis is about taking the time to invest yourself in it's atmosphere, lore, the denizens of the unterzee and the harshness of the game's universe which should have been plain to see from the very first line in the game's description;
In Sunless Sea the idea of upgrading your ship isn't necessarily to have the biggest and most effective ship or loadout in the game but to have enough to keep you going from one adventure to the next with a little spare to keep you afloat and maybe upgrade further down the line. You will die, it's expected, and you're supposed to continue from where your previous captain died as a fresh and more experienced person in the game world. To rate it down simply because you did not get enough to survive and found it hard to upgrade completely misses the point and makes most of these negative reviews moot. Is it a bad game because someone got into it for the wrong reasons? No, not at all. It's akin to getting into a first person shooter somewhat like Call of Duty yet expecting a non-linear, open world realistic military shooter. It just isn't that type of game and reviews of such are more subjective as opposed to objective; needless to say subjectivism in
isn't exactly what you should be basing your final conclusion on.
The game itself is well presented, well written and it's tough. It's meant to be tough and unforgiving as it adds to the atmosphere, the feeling of loss when you undertake long voyages and are forced to lose crew members you've invested time in. It results in the player making harsh decisions they won't soon forget and make them think twice in the future when they choose specific routes or options in who they side with, what they decide to do on moral grounds or financial grounds. Have your character fall in love, feel that loss when the time invested in such an affair is ripped away from the player through neglect or the death of said interest or the character themselves. It's all part of the experience and that's the kind of experience you should expect when getting into Sunless Sea.
I highly recommend this title as it does what it sets out to do, doing so extremely well, and can have players lose countless hours in it's universe and become deeply invested. However, don't enter the Unterzee expecting anything other than a tough experience which forces you to learn from your mistakes. Expect an adventure of well written stories littered throughout the game world and the high possibility of having to start over again with the experience of your mistakes from a previous life.
Objectively this is a great game. Subjectively this is not a game for everyone. Make sure you research this title before you go in and know what to expect. Afterall, you wouldn't buy Stellaris if you really wanted a game like Civilization or Endless Legend.

Evolve is a Sci Fi shooter trying to surpass the cooperation concept of the Left 4 Dead franchise. Following a Merc-Hunter crew that chases huge monsters and underlines the "Hunters become the hunted."
CHARACTERS/ROLES: Something that must be said, is that this game is very brutal and unforgiving for newcomers, if you are one of those competitive people who stuff video games into their life, prepare for a red forehead from facepalming and a lot of leadership and teaching (and raging), microphone is a must. Being that its a role based team of hunters, when new players pick a role that is crucial, such as Trapper or Medic, they will sabotage your game and pull you down with them. In order of importance, in MY opinion, it goes like this.
Trapper > Medic > Assault > Support
Trapper is the most important because skilled monster players will avoid you like ninjas, tracking has a sharp learning curve and involves more then just chasing big blue footprints; Daisy cuts you some slack if you are new to the role and will let you contribute to the team, without actually contributing to the team; meaning if you suck and cant track a poodle. Daisy will at least revive teammates on your behalf.
Medic is more than just self explanatory; Val, the tier one medic, has a crucial ability of tranqing the monster, allowing the medic to make up for a mediocre trapper. And of course is crucial to keeping the crew alive.
Assault is the main damage dealer, but is more forgiving because a badass Trapper or a good Support can compensate for him.
Support is the least important, but still essential to the team, aerial strikes and counteracting monster rushes on the Medic and Trapper so the team can keep up the good fight. And catching the team when they are losing makes the Support essentially a fallback role.
There is some witty banter and situational shout outs which make the characters interesting and alive, you won't hunt the monster in absolute silence, tactical callouts and jokes from superb voice actors make the crew likeable. The character tier system in the game make it self explanatory that Tier 2 characters require a much better skill level to play the second character effectively, Tier 3 in comparison to Tier 2 is still easier, as the abilities are so fluid, that you can both attack and support your team.
The Tier 3 characters are absolutely boss, Abe is by far my favorite character. Characters are set up in tiers of their typical teams, easily summed up with
Tier 1: Team Cohesion and selfless abilities. Focus of drawing out fight and countering with precise attacks. (Orbital strikes, Energy shield, Med gun, Mines, Harpoon traps)
Tier 2: Survivalist and DPS abilities, synchronized attacks and harrassing the monster. (Lazarus Device, Harpoon Gun, UAV, Sentry turrets)
Tier 3: 100% Combat oriented Team, 90% of abilities are intended for use during engagements and hot pursuits. (Healing grenades, Tracking Darts, Adrenaline rush, Stasis Grenades)
GAMEPLAY: The maps are very big and very alive, wildlife will hunt and flee as well as feed and migrate, the game is visually stunning and very immersive. Gunplay is fun and satisfying. Good Monster players can make the Monster role seem insanely easy. Noobs will get caught by hostile wildlife and ignore you when it catches you after you free them. Noobs will also successfully trap a whole four players; all of them your teammates! Playing your role effectively will give you tense moments of action and fun, adreniboners will be common in this game, there is an obvious balancing issue that needs to be addressed with the
Tier 3 monster the "Wraith," as it can spam the decoy ability too effectively whilst taking no damage and delivering full damage to Hunters, not only that, but any HUD icon signaling the monsters whereabouts that the Trapper placed on it with Griffin or Abe is directly on the Decoy. However, the Monster is the most important player in the game being that unskilled players won't even make it fun for the Hunters.
MONSTER: This needs it's own section because I can't compliment the monsters voice acting or background. I must say it is very worthwhile to go hard out into the role of monster. Stealthing isn't the only way to eliminate Hunters, rather than stealth I prefer to leave my tracks deliberately, going right through dens of hostile wildlife and jumping over rivers with Tyrants (Alien Alligators) sitting at the bottom, without a competent Medic or Trapper as I stated above, as the Monster you will absolutely stomp the Hunters. knowing how to outrun and trick the Hunters is key, at one point without even engaging them until stage 3; I killed two hunters with two Tyrants. Daisy is like a pumpil on your butt and makes Monster challenging, as she will make sure to avoid you and not plunge herself into danger to revive teammates, you will find Hunters using every strike they have after you stomp the Trapper and Medic.
Val is a solid 10/10; absolutely delicous, Markov is a tough 7/10; but the vodka adds nice flavor to the meat, I am a fan of delicous dark meat Maggie with a Daisy side was a good 8/10, Hank's beard gets stuck in your teeth; 5/10.
The Wraith, is an absolute badass; between it's stalking and strategic attacks, it's a serious change of pace from the Goliath, the most accurate way to sum it up is it's basically a floating ninja that teleports. My very first game as Wraith was way easier then the Goliath or the Kraken, rather then accurate ranged attacks or just rampaging through a hail of gunfire you instead trick the hunters into leaving a huge opening. I did so using a decoy while attacking the relay, my decoy went left after the lone support, the Hunters grouped up on the opposite side of the room firing at it, the Support jetpack dodged into his team, one supernova attack forcing them into the corner, and they all died at the same time. I win.
4/10
+ Characters well written with superb voice actors
+ World well designed with a living environment
+ Core concept of Teamwork surpasses Left 4 Dead
+ Monster gameplay is tense and fun
+ Satisfying gunplay and action
+ PVE rewards Hunters and Monsters
- Unforgiving for new players
- Matchmaking system matches new players with veterans
- Balancing issues
- Pay to win

Judging by the alpha content, this game does not justify an AAA price tag. And I'm not talking about the bugs the alpha obviously has...
The idea is fantastic, the execution lackluster. Basically every match plays out the same way: Either the monster hides for long enough to reach level 3 and dominate - or the hunters catch it prior to that and kill it. Rinse and repeat over and over again.
The monster gameplay feels satisfying with a lot of force behind every attack. But animations also feel rather clunky at times. Hunter gameplay varies greatly from role to role, hovever you're basically playing a two-trick pony which gets repetitive rather quickly. The skills of the hunters supplement each other nicely and it might be a lot of fun in a group of friends, but playing with friends doesn't work in this alpha so I can't say whether that is true and in uncoordinated groups the enjoyment is limited.
What I think the game lacks is a third party to make things more interesting. Merely monster vs. hunters over and over again is not enough. If there was a third party fighting for their own goals and against both the monster and the hunters (think of Giants: Citizen Kabuto or Alien vs. Predator multiplayer) this would add a lot more unpredictability to the experience. As far as I can tell there will be two variants of each of the hunters classes and two diffrent monster types to play at launch. This is not enough for 50 USD/EUR or whichever currency you happen to pay with. Wait for DLC to add variety to the game and pick it all up on a sale with a hefty discount and you will get good value for this game.

Overall there is not much to say about Half Life: Blue Shift. It's not a bad game but it's not good compared to Opposing Force and Half Life. And even that for the most part is just for show, though I never tried it, I did miss an odd QTE and for the most part, I didn’t effect the action one bit, only once did I die from a missed QTE and that was in the final boss fight and I was left thinking, why did I just die from that glancing hit, compared to all the other brutal battering my character as suffered throughout the game, in the actual story of the game?! All the QTE seems to do is build a finishing move at the end of the fight, but the fight would end anyway and would finishing move look any different if I hadn’t built up enough “Bat” power? Maybe something I might have to utube….
Time I think for Telltale to put some more effort into its gameplay as well as its stories.
Anyway, as for the story of this game, its good and I really enjoyed it, some moments catching me by surprise, however a complaint for all games like this, your given choices to pick but due to the limits of actual games these days, they don’t really effect the story of the game, the same things are going to happen, just certain elements are going to change.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the second expansion pack for Half-Life. You play as Black Mesa security guard Barney Calhoun and it’s a parallel story with Half-Life but short. It’s not that good and I’ll explain why. If you remember from my previous review, Half-Life: Opposing Force featured a decent amount of new content for Half-Life. Now this game is like the opposite were there is no new weapons, NPCs, or weapons but instead just a new 90 to 120 minute campaign just slapped onto the original Half-Life game. However this game does feature the new HD pack, where it basically takes existing models, weapons, and weapon sounds and replaces them with newer, better looking ones. This addon also can be used with the original Half-Life and expansion Opposing Force but that’s really not a big deal for this review. I also noticed that the HD models have washed out looking textures on them for some reason compared to when using them in other Half-Life games. As for the gameplay and everything, it’s really the exact same game but with recycled textures and new maps for the single-player campaign (no multiplayer included). For 2001 this game was just bland by this point especially with titles like Halo hitting the XBOX back in the day. However if you can pick-up this game cheap on steam then get it because it’s certainly not a bad game but nice to play through Half-Life again with a new campaign.

This game will have you jumping from the first minute you start playing, to the last, even when you half expect a Zombie to be hidden in a bathroom waiting for you to open a door, it still shocks you, with its gripping yet gory soundtrack, to the way they lunge towards you from the darkness.

FlatOut 2 is now available for many years. It is racing game which handles a good balance between simulation and arcade and players who prefer either of the genres still will admit that it is an excellent fit.
The game is playable on multiplayer and has several different types of single player modes. The most important is naturally the career mode. It contains thoughout its progress all other modes in a well mixed compilation.
One cannot choose a difficulty, however the game has a very fair difficulty development which never gets unfair, but is mostly challenging. There are three types of car classes. Each has its own event plan and you have to beat all the events of one class to unlock the next one. The cars of every new class are harder to handle since they are getting faster and faster. Within the classes there is a development of the difficulty too because in each class you unlock better cars which raise the difficulty for the above stated reason.
You can choose between four car types. There is the light small one with a good acceleration. The big and heavy one favourable for crashing. The normal inbetween which is balanced. The fast type which you usually unlock in each class after a few races. Specially the first three types have have different types of gameplay according to their strengths and weaknesses wherefore you have a different gaming experience in each of them. Each car can be also performance tuned with various parts which you can buy (visually the cars don't change).
The career consists of trophies which consist of normal races. But there are also (Destruction) Derbies where your main challenge is to survive as long as possible while crashing other cars and gaining points to win the competition. Moreover the career has every now and then fun events which gameplay bases on launching your driver through the front window in different games which are generally based on different real world sports.
You have seven opponents throughout the game which have their own names and portraits and each of them has his own an unique style of driving and usage of car types. The opponents are getting better with further progress in the game as you do. It is also worth to mention that your competitors in the races don't react any different to bots than to you.
The tracks you drive on are very various and are always well mixed when compilated in trophies. There are no parts which repeat unnecessarily which is a reason why the gaming experience is till the very end so much fun.
Very much in the game is about crashing other cars. You get star ratings for each crash which results in higher income. It is possible to wreck your opponents totally which upmost important in derbies. Also your nitro charges with crashing into opponents as well as into evironmental objects. Specially towards the ending of the game it gets a strategic character to gain nitro. The fun events are often really challenging and if you beat them you still have the urge to beat highscores.
But FlatOut 2 is still a racing game. If you don't want to crash you don't have to. This counts for the trophies. In derbies and fun events you obviously have a different main task.
Another point that has a huge impact on the gaming experience is the tracklist (music) that is played in the races. It fits perfectly and it emphasizes the characteristics of the game strongly.
The best way to play this game is with friends with in local network. You can create tournaments with all the different tracks and events you like and it has because of its competitiveness a similar multiplayer experience like Mario Kart.
Since the game is not very expensive anymore and appears often on sales I warmly and highly recommend this game for everyone who is at least slightly interested in racing games.

This is an honest review of Red Orchestra 2: Heroes or Stalingrad
This is one of my favorite games of all time. The smooth combat, and the immersive enviornments really make this game stand out above the other World War II games out there. This game may be a few years old, but it still looks great despite it's age. Pros:
-Smooth gameplay
-Realistic
-Large maps
-Bullet drop (makes snipers even more fun)
-Class limit (so there isn't 30 MKB's on one team)
-64 player servers
-Realistic gore
-Bandaging system
-Realistic LMG's (You replace the barrel when it becomes too hot. Prevent's LMG spam)
-Tanks
Cons:
-Low player base
-Difficult to do well (Players familiar with other shooters may have trouble getting used to the game)
-Rising storm isn't really worth it
FINAL VERDICT:
This is a fun game to play by yourself, or with your friends. The community isn't bad, but it isn't all good either. I would definitely recommend this game to anybody interested in World War II, or anybody who is looking for a realistic shooter to have fun with

I played the game during the free weekend, and I have some problems deciding should I recommend it. I really enjoyed it, but I probably won't buy it. And much of my enjoyment came from the fact that I had the game for a limited time only.

The atmosphere of the game is great. The zee is dark and full of terrors, many weird adventures await those foolish enough to live the life of a zailor. Discovering all those strange lands, hoping to find a friendly port, being engaged in the story... really well done. All this is accompanied with really great music.
The game is very slow - battles and action are rare, most of the game is reading or watching your boat sail to the next port. Often you have to return to Fallen London for supplies if you don't want to die due to lack of food or fuel - this also slows your exploration down. You must find a balance between being safe and exploring. And in some way, I found this slowness a nice thing.
I must mention, that the first playthrough was very confusing - finding a list of current quest takes some time, many conditions of events are described in a complicated way. It takes some time to get used to.
I knew I had the game only for a weekend, so I didn't bother with the "main quest" - I wasn't even sure what was my main quest. I simply explored, I didn't feel forced to grind for money, stats etc. If I had lost my most successful captain, well, that would be probably the end of my free weekend. I'm not sure if I would decide to start again. There was one or two situations when my crew almost fell into complete madness during way back to Fallen London. And I found that exciting, not being sure if it's the end of the adventure. But I think my approach would be completely different if I had bought the game and felt more forced to complete it - starting again would be more frustrating.
In the end, I think I recommend the game, it's an interesting experience. But I think I've finished mine, at least for now. Maybe some day I'll buy the game. But that may be different type of playing and I suspect it may be worse.

Looks like I got this game on July 9, 2013. Today the game came out of Early Access as v.1.0, and unfortunately, the game is still rather hard to digest.
When I first played, the game had a few graphical issues, and it looked like it could have needed something like an editor to an author. Fine, I could always go back to it - though at this point I was beginning to regret buying this. At this point (and a couple subsequent playthroughs), I felt the game was not intuitive, unfriendly to beginners, and rather difficult for a game where you literally build your character to advance. Gathering materials? The laser pick was extremely weak and could not be as easily manipulated as Starbound's (as much as I don't like comparing, especially to Starbound). I took a long time gathering enough supplies (after dying a few times, some from mobs in the starting area and some from falling off the edge of the map) to make anything. Also, while the game no longer has the difficulty (sort of...) and the 10 free respawn limit, those things severely discouraged me from doing anything. So I waited.
Today, I opened the game with no expectations of things and found myself facing similar issues from the first time I played. The UI needs a lot of work - this doesn't look at all like a modern game with a futuristic setting - the dialog boxes look like just hastily placed rectangles and fonts (I spotted some serif fonts...) look like they were not even picked with intent. Some of the tips need editing in syntax and grammar, and overall, the game feels very much like a beta still. I wasn't pleased by the "tutorial" either, since the first thing I saw was a codex full of unnecessary text.
Nothing in the game has struck me as intuitive so far, even regarding the gathering of materials. I got the DLC items and the pick is marginally stronger than the starting one, and while it's got a wider beam (3 tiles wide), the width becomes useless because the pick target cannot be directly chosen - so if you just dig downward, for example, in the same direction, you just end up with a 1 tile wide chasm, walls either damaged or already "healed" to normal. Everything seems so grindy already - I know that games won't have you start off with good gear ready to kill bosses, but in the first quest of the tutorial, each one of those enemies (although they do no damage) took many hits to die. I don't see any fun in spending minutes killing common mobs (because face it, you're gonna attract aggro for all those missed attacks and some of those enemies move too fast with the starting rifle) and then spending minutes gathering.
I'm going to pass. Sorry, I tried, but more than 2 years did not give sufficient progress for me to enjoy this - too grindy and too unpolished.

This game is emotionally exhausting. When it's your first world and you spawn in the middle of a forest and all you can pick up are sticks, things really seem to suck. Then you find your first shelter and you feel your entire being go "...YES."
You slowly learn the controls: How to check your overall state, how to keep track of calorie intake and burn, and how to keep wildlife at bay. Not to mention walking, crouching, moving things around to keep your home clean and organized.
This game forces you to use your knowledge of survival and how animals react to certain things. Those random facts stored in the back of your brain finally become useful!
Once you find an area where there are shelters, fishing holes, and plenty of game, you settle down and the days start to pass by. Things are going to be alright! Then your food supply runs low. You have to make every single shot on that bow or rifle count, because your ammo is also running low. That's how you get your food. Your medical supply runs low. Your clothes wear thin. You have to pack and leave home to find more supplies.
Never take anything for granted; the slightest things can get you killed. And once they do, it's heartbreak because you grew attached to your world and can't go back and fix it like in other games.
This game has me playing non-stop for hours, and I 10/10 would reccommend it. It's by far the most complex survival game I've ever played, and it definitely deserves more attention than it gets. I learn more about it every time I play.

...is a decision-based story-driven adventure. In a Gotham city still unsure what to do about the presence of a masked vigilante known as the Batman, billionaire Bruce Wayne is faced with seeing his friends, family legacy and everything he holds dear crumble around him with the rise of a new threat to the city.
Much like other Telltale games, there is little gameplay, it's all about decision-making. During conversations, these decisions are dialog choices you have a limited time to pick from, influencing the outcome of conversations and future events, as well as your relationship with the characters you're interacting with (which may also influence the outcome of future conversations or events). Action scenes are QuickTime events, with some influencing the outcome of the encounter, others being immediate win/lose scenarios, and others that build up a meter you need to achieve a minimum of by the end of the encounter.
The story is set in its own version of the Batman universe, starting in the early days of the bat where the police are very conflicted about the presence of the vigilante while regular mobsters and corruption still litter a pre-supervillain Gotham City, including an ambitious district attorney Harvey Dent, or a recently appointed lieutenant James Gordon. This adaptation borrows from comic books, the Animated Series, the Gotham TV series and other sources while still being its own product.
As usual, Telltale does a great character-focused game, everyone having layered personalities with motivations of their own, and the choices you make really do change the information you get and how events unfold. Sure, at its core, there is a specific story being told you cannot diverge from, but the way it is told depends on your decisions. Whose side will you pick? Who will you save? Do you go as Bruce Wayne or as Batman? This allows you to go beyond dialog choices into choosing what part of the story you get to see, and what part you don't, encouraging replayability.
While some may worry about yet another origin story, this adaptation feels fresh enough to rediscover beloved characters and antagonists while remaining true to the essence of Batman. The series will obviously develop a continuity of its own, and I can't help but wonder how many of the decisions you make (such as
) will carry over to the following seasons.
While cel-shaded 3D graphics do give the it sort of a comic book feel, the textures and lighting effect are far superior to
. Characters have good facial animation conveying the emotions they feel in what they say. The voice acting is also top notch and suits the characters as much as the tone the game should have.
This game is a lot more about Bruce Wayne than it is about Batman, so people going in hoping to see their favorite dark knight may feel disappointed. While there are Batman segments with their own dialog or action choices, most of it is QuickTime events, with the occasional detective "figure what clues go together" you can't fail, if only due to being able to do trial and errors until you get the desired series of combination for the story to progress.
There are a lot of character interactions that don't seem to have any effect on the game. Right until the game's ending you still get "This person will remember that" notifications in situations where it really won't change anything for the rest of the game, some of which I have serious doubts actually will carry over to future seasons.
While I haven't experienced any of the bugs or crashes other people have made mention of, the framerate drop that's been reported by some is indeed apparant, even to those who have powerful gaming PCs.
I enjoyed this new take on the Batman that will unfold into a supervillan-filled Gotham, and am really, really looking forward to playing
. Centered on the man behind the mask, rarely has a game or series focused on Bruce Wayne as a normal human, rather than a playboy façade hiding a tourmented Batman. You should probably avoid it if you can't stand QuickTime events, are looking for action, or simply don't care much about the Batman mythos. Otherwise, it's a high recommendation!

The controls for this game are abysmal. I can't enjoy any of the nice ideas in this game because I'm fighting the controls the whole time.
- Flying a fighting plane -> sounds fun -> because of bad controls it's nearly impossible to hit anything and because after missing the whole time you are so focused to hit at least one thing you make one mistake and end up driving the plane into the ground
- Using the grapling hook -> sounds fun -> because of bad targetting half the time the hook doesn't land where you want it wich ends up draining your time and nerves if you have luck and killing you if you don't have luck
- Flying a gunship -> sounds fun -> 50% of the time this is legit fun / 50% of the time you can't hit your target because gunships seem to not have the ability to shoot down in a steeper angle than 15°, except when enemies are attacking you with them while you're on the ground, in these cases they can shoot you at nearly all angles
The above examples are the ones that really drove me mad, but there are many things that made my experience impossible to enjoy:
- Cars are pretty useless in this game and only a gimmick, the only ones that I really used where the cars with mounted guns, but these have very limited use because you can't shoot and drive at the same time. That means you drive to a location, then you go to the gun, then you aim and shoot, then you go back to the drivers seat and go to a new location, it gets tedious very fast.
- Much of the terrain isn't built for traversing by foot. Now could come the argument:"But you have the grappling hook, you can get everywhere with that." And that is true, but that means if you want up a small ledge that is just a little to high for your jump you have to go through the all the tedious animations of the grappling hook only to cover a distance of the length of your ingame leg and you face the possibility that the bad targetting will interfere wich will make you waste even more of your time.
- Explosions killing you even though you're sitting inside a still intact tank.
- Weapon drops vanishing after a few seconds.
- If many weapons lie close to eatchother it's practically impossible to specifically change only your small or only your big weapon while in a fire fight.
- That you can't look up what you're still missing to get a specific town/base to 100% is really annoying because as it is you can never be sure if you're missing something you need to destroy or a hidden crate.
- The high prices for anything in the black market while you don't have a steady income.
- The waiting time for extractions to other locations by the black market helicopter. And it is a waiting time, not a loading time, because the further away the location is the longer it takes.
And then there are some things that didn't have to be in the game, but they could've made the game better:
- After completing a base you should get a list with the vehicles you can get from there.
- Strongholds should generate a steady income or at least an infinite ammount of paying jobs.
- The blackmarket shouldn't need to be manually summoned by placing a beacon and waiting a (short) loading screen before you can interact with the blackmarket menu followed by a 2nd loading screen, instead you should be able to get to the blackmarket menu directly from your PDA and you only get a loading screen after you choose something.
There are more things but these suffice. In summary I like the idea of the game, I hate what they made out of the idea. Some problems are probably because of technical limitations, but they are still problems.
And the game just has some things in it that are just incomprehensible to me. They market the game as over the top but then they make it pretty hard or at least time consuming to aquire the means to do anything over the top or they actually have something in the game that just lends itself to be really over the top and cool, but because of the way they put it in the game it looses all the "coolness".
For example the fighting planes, they could be so fun, just drowing a base in fire, but because their controls are so bad you won't be able to even hit the base until you crash into it.
To me this game is a big time waster without any pay off after investing said time.

Gameplay wise, controls similar to contra/metal slug esque games. The focus is on boss fights with no check points or continues during said fights, only three hits (can be modified via shop) and it's back to the start.
Art style is obviously a big attraction here, however the gameplay isn't anything too new or exciting. It's also not a terribly long game, however it's a game I feel you can pick up again after some time has past to quickly run through it again.
Like old arcade games, the two player doesn't change the flow too much and is just there to enjoy playing with another person (local only).
Things I nitpicked
-The audio fits the theme very well, but sometimes the low quality/mono-esque sound effects bother me.
-Inability to turn off film grain.
-Because the game consist of boss fights it's hard to tell how effective different weapons/EX moves/Supers are from eachother.
-Parry requirement for better score. In most cases I'd rather dodge and avoid having to readjust from the parry's short hop. Trying to go for sudden parry's can result in damage due to tight timing of jumping twice and you only have 3 hitpoints. Parrying should be reflective in time or card usage since it rewards players with an ex card that should speed up fights if those moves are even better than regular attacks. The fact that you're required to parry with it's own space on the results makes me feel it's a detriment to parry and not rewarding gameplay wise. But hey at the end of the day it's just a letter that doesn't do anything.

The first thing you immediately notice when starting up Guru Games' Medusa's Labyrinth is how stunningly beautiful this game looks. Ultra settings can require a lot of resources from your end (I am not sure if this is a matter of optimisation, though) - this is something that usually only AAA games do.
Once you finished your marvelling just outside the ancient temple your journey continues within. The admiration stops here and is replaced by the constant fear of something (perhaps a Medusa?) lurking somewhere in the ancient corridors. Using headphones or turning the volume up a lot is a must here; a torchlight can certainly ease the terror but your bow with only 3 arrows will not do so, at all.
Then, when you finally know who you're up against, a chase ensues and continues until it abruptly ends. And this is the only issue Medusa's Labyrinth has - it is unfinished. The 60-minute or so story seems to be polished enough but how amazing it would be to see the story through till its very end. Especially since the notes scattered across the temple give you some background information but only to increase your curiosity and desire for more.
I do not know that of all the 150,000 downloads how many players purchased the DLC content to provide financial support but I sincerely hope Guru Games will get it so that they create a 10-hour long campaign to finish the tale.

What is Half Life: blue shift
Half life: blue shift is a standalone expansion pack for Half Life. Half life: blue shift was originally meant to be part of the Dreamcast version of Half life just like how Decay is for the PlayStation 2 version but unfortunately before the production of the Dreamcast version began Sega announced that they would be discontinuing the Dreamcast, so Gearbox ported Blue shift over to the PC. Half life: blue shift also was the first expansion to include the HD content which was meant to be for the Dreamcast version originally. What the HD content did was that it replaced things such as the MP5 for a higher quality assault rifle and it replaced some NPC models as well, in my opinion i don't really like the HD models so i have turned them off in the options menu.
The story
In Half life: blue shift you play as a security guard called Barney Calhoun who was later used has a main character in Half Life 2. Before the Black Mesa incident Barneys job was to protect the equipment and personnel within area 3 of Black Mesa but when the incident happens your main goal is to escape the facility.
The pros of Half life: blue shift
- Good story that fills in the gap of the Half life story line
- The game has some very good level design
- The AI was very good for its time and still is since they react to different thing such as if you wait near a door the marines will throw in grenades
- You have to interact with NPC's in order to progress through game, this is good because your not just opening doors like you did in the original Half life
- There are decent puzzles and they evenly spaced out in the game
- The game is very enjoyable including the combat even though enemy's can seem like they can take several rounds in the head
What is bad about Half life: blue shift
- One of the most obvious things is that nothing new was really added to the game such as weapons, enemy's etcetera
- The game is very short only taking me around 3 hours to complete and that was without doing the tutorial section of  the game
- I found that the game was easy even though i was playing on hard
- some times i got stuck on the environment such as in between boxes or on the walls located in Xen
Overall Half life: Blue shift is a very good game but does have a few issues but they don't affect the game too much since the game is very enjoyable, also even though the game is very short it is also very cheap so you do get what you pay for. I do recommend getting this game if you like any Half life game or just generally like old school first person shooters like doom, but if that is the case then you would of most likely would of played a Half life game.

-Easily the shortest entry in the Half-Life series, even shorter than Half-Life 2: Episode 1 (and I play games at a snail's pace).
-Not much new content in general when compared to Opposing Force. No new weapons, enemies, etc. I mean, there's a new character, so I guess that's something...
-
-There's a REALLY annoying bug where, if you die and respawn by clicking one of the mouse buttons, your weapon will constantly fire off until you click the mouse button again. I'm not sure if there's a fix for this or even if it's just me, but just be wary of that.
Out of all of the entries in the Half-Life franchise, this is probably the least impactful. In fact, I'm willing to bet there have been mods for Half-Life that both continue the story in its own way and left more of an impact to the player. That being said though, this expansion isn't bad by any means. Just not quite as good as other games in the series.
If you want this game, I'd recommend buying one of the Half-Life complete packs if you don't have a large number of the other entries. You'll get the other entries and save money overall in the process.

Half Life Blue Shift is an expansion pack that takes place during the events of the first Half Life. This time around we play as a security guard called Barney Calhoun. He is mute and plays exactly the same as our last protagonist Gordon. If it wasn't for people calling you by your name you would have no clue you are supposed to be a completely different character.  The same goes for the levels, enemies and weapons. There is zero new enemies or weapons, in fact there are less weapons in this game. Levels themselves are very much like base Half Life, nothing special but definitely of the quality same quality and takes a bigger focus on action. A slight nick-pick I have is that the melee weapon is still a crowbar like the engineer Gordon  instead of a baton that would be far more suited toward a security officer.
The first thing you will notice starting up the game is that the user interface is now blue instead of orange like the main game. It is probably done to remind you that you are a security officer but has no other effects. The main change is that you no longer refill your “armor” via the wall mounted H.E.V system since you do not have that suit. Instead you scavenge around for usable security armor sets to refill your armor count. One big difference is that unlike the main game this now has a few unique npcs with their own personalities and motives instead of the original's endless army of generic clone npcs. You will also catch a few glimpses of Gordon Freeman from time to time but will never interact with him.
Blue Shift is an expansion pack that plays it very close to home. It has very few changes from the base game and adds nothing new other than a few characters. This is a pretty safe dlc to skip as nothing very important happens story wise. It is more of a four hour adventure for those seeking more of that Half Life experience. In that regard it is a pretty solid dlc if you do not mind the lack of anything new to see. So if you fit that description you will find your fix here but for everyone else this is a by the books dlc that can easily be passed on if you had your fill of Half Life with the base game.

I'm gonna break this down to 3 parts for ya. My reaction, my thoughts, and my conclusion.
First My reaction:
This is gonna be a long one. First of, not what Iw as expecting. Anyone expecting? Please raise a hand, cause I need to sit on the faaaar side of the room. Cause this is beyond my expectations.
Here I was thinking, "hey, it's the same guy who made Stanley Parable. I love that game!"
And soon it turns into "What did I just walk into... Maybe there's something here. Something I'm not looking at. Maybe it's gonna be a twist of some sort"
And ends in, "There is no twist. There is, but that... was part of the story. This was it. Did any choice I made I matter? What did I just play? It can't seriously end like this right?"
Alrightio, now that that's out of my system. Seriously, what the fricken hay! (tricking to keep this clean... and here I thought it was out of my system.)
My Thoughts:
Firstly, it's not like Stanely Parable... at all. Like at all. Like take any idea you have of that game.... you got it right? In your hands?.... Good.... Throw it straight into the trash.
Good. Now that I got your attention. This is different. This is you riding a boat in a journey of one persons relationship with another human being, and at the end of the boat ride, you gotta ask yourself, did this actually happen? Is this for real? I don't have an answer, and maybe I'll find out in the future.
This game is about you walking through the time lapse of games made by a person, and trying to etch into a person's perspective, their art, and mind. And which each step you take, you go down a road of one view, delving deeper into what this person thought, only to realise in the end, it was all for a twist.
Yeah I spoiled part of the game. It all leads to a twist. But it deludes you every step of the way, like there wouldn't be one, or if there was, it would be that all of this is a trick.
It's one heck of a psychological ride. Don't say I didn't warn you. Cause I did right here. Can't take that back
Stick on the ride, cause in the end, you'll feel like you need someone to talk to. Cause it's about art. The true nature of art. And no, that's not actually what the game tells you. Just my interpretation of it.
My Conclusion
Surprisingly, this had a lot more positive reviews than I expected. I came here thinking that this, would be mixed. Like who would seriously go into this game knowing what you'd get into?  But in the end, this game gets you to think.
Think about how you interact with people, people you might be a fan off, or interested in. People who you learn about, not by your conversations, but people who you know through their work, their creatations, their art.
This is not some happy game. But if I have to say, pretty damn interesting one. If you had to ask me, get it, if you like this kind of thing. The psychology behind this is what makes people like it. If you don't, then stay away.

1. Scare Factor – 8.5/10
Let's go over the biggest draw of FNAF right now:
Is FNAF scary? Yes.
Will it leave you a screaming wreck? Probably not.
Do not believe the claim that FNAF only jump-scares you if you lose. There are jumpscares sprinkled throughout, including when you lose. If you play it, you'll know what I mean. That, though, isn't really what makes the game work: What makes it work is that it essentially winds you up like a spring to the point of breaking, and you have no idea whether or not that will pay off via a jumpscare.
There's one issue, however, and it's the same problem Alien: Isolation had, in that it begins to get rote over time. A jumpscare, no matter how well executed, is only scary the first few times; after a while, it becomes irritating. It doesn't help that the game gets very hard later on, with the result having less and less to do with your actions and more and more with the RNG. Ergo, you will likely die a lot, and fear will quickly be replaced by frustration.
2. Gameplay – 6.5/10
The basic gameplay of FNAF is fairly simple. Essentially, watch the security cameras to be tipped off as to when an animatronic is drawing close, and slam the doors on either side of you shut when one is. The trick here is that you have a limited amount of power, which drains continuously. What doesn't help is that literally everything you do drains power. Check the cameras? Drains power. Flick the door lights? Drains power. Have a door closed? Drains power. Foxy pounding on your door? You guessed it.
Overall, the gameplay isn't anything groundbreaking, but it does its job well enough, holding the game up with solid, easy to learn mechanics. The more subtle nuances of the game aren't really explained, but the mind will probably pick up on them (particularly audio cues).
As mentioned before, however, all is not well within the gameplay, and it has to do with the massive difficulty spike of the fifth night.
The first four nights will reward your knowledge of the systems of the game well,  allowing you to conserve power. It will also help you immensely if you can exploit  the way the game works (If you see Pirate Cove is empty, for example, slam the door shut *before* looking at the West Hall camera).
It's Night 5 and 6, however, where the game starts to unravel. Suddenly, skilled play isn't rewarded nearly as much as simply being lucky. Bonnie or Chica showed up at the door? Better hope they leave sometime in the next five bloody minutes. Better hope Foxy doesn't decide to charge you three times, draining a larger chunk of your power every time. Better hope Freddy doesn't decide to cross the level in ten seconds and then stand outside your door for the rest of the night.
Custom Night's now-famous "4/20" mode (AKA: You set all the animatronics to their maximum difficulty) is almost entirely luck-based, and you'll only be able to beat this mode when the AI decides it'll let you win. For an idea of how long that can take, put it this way: Famous Let's Play Youtuber Markiplier took seven hours to beat it. I will readily admit, I've never done it, mainly because I lack the patience and time required to do so.
Sound Design – 9.5/10
I'll admit, if there's one thing FNAF nails almost perfectly, it's the sound design. Every animatronic has its own noises, from Foxy's humming to Freddy's deep laughter. Audio cues, such as footsteps and the clattering of dishes, allows one to (mostly) avoid looking at the security cameras. In fact, these audio cues become absolutely essential to surviving Nights 5 and 6 (along with a great deal of luck). The only issue I take with the sound design is the fact there's no real way to tell the difference between the footsteps of Chica and Bonnie, which would add a nice element of skill to the game (not having to flick both hallway lights to find out which side it's coming from, if any).
Story – 7.5/10
The story of FNAF is, to put it mildly, difficult to pick up on. I'm all for allowing a player to decide how much story they want in a game, but I think FNAF swings a bit too far in the “We will not tell you the whole story” bit. I get what it was going for – You're a night guard at a place where someone got their frontal lobe bitten off by an animatronic, the animatronics want you dead, stay alive till 6:00. Nice and simple, but it tries and, in some ways, fails to emulate the storytelling style games such as Metroid Prime use. If you pay attention to things such as the shifting newspaper clippings on the walls, you can find yourself in a far bigger story, all tracing back to when... (*******SPOILER ALERT*******)
five children went missing in Freddy Fazbear's Pizza.
(********END SPOILERS*******)
There's one major issue, though: That requires you take your focus off the animatronics who are trying to kill you. Since doing bloody well anything in this game drains power, shutting both doors and looking through the security cameras will suck away your power at an incredible speed. Considering that, from what I've seen, the newspaper clippings only really start to change later in the week, this basically means you will need to take screenshots, and even then, it's completely random when those clippings will show.
Overall, for all of its issues in execution, it's quite a good story being told here, even with quite a few things being left open to interpretation. What is unfortunate, however, is that to truly understand the full tale, you'll need to buy the two sequels.

Good Lord this game is phenomenal. Even though it's still in an ALPHA stage of development I've spent a LOT of time in it, and I'll absolutely be spending a lot more. I'd never played a survival game before (thought I've watched a fair number of them played), and I was hooked within the first half hour of gameplay. Apparently for experienced players there are some issues that need to be resolved yet later in the game, but that's to be expected since it is so early on in its development. On that note I feel like I should mention that the developers steadfastly put out 2 updates each month, so you can really see that the game IS actually in development. It's great.
Finally, as far as the gameplay goes, it seems pretty darn well polished for an alpha game, and the few issues I've encountered are things that will almost certainly be rectified by the time the game comes out in full. It is ABSOLUTELY worth the $20, and I feel that getting it on sale for $10 was ridiculous--I feel like I should give the devs the other $10 just to support them making this game. TL;DR

Sunless Sea is a lovecraftian rogue-lite, RPG, exploration game which is set in the same universe of "Fallen London", the browser game, where everything wants to kill you, including yourself. It's rather difficult to compare it to any other game as it appears to be the first of its kind, all other games that were similar such as "A House of Many Doors" were inspired by Sunless sea. It's got a beautiful yet unsettling artstyle that builds a world much bigger than what you may have originally though.
Let me just make this abundantly clear from the start of this review, this game is NOT fun, and it wasn't built to be either. It moves incredibly slowly, you have to manage 3 different bars to stay alive, and every enemy you encounter is either as fast, or faster than your ship, with devastating attacks and very long ranges. You will most definitely have to run from every enemy you have the displeasure of finding, and you will most definitely find your death to the hands of such creatures, but fighting was never the point of this game. The pacing and difficult nature of the game was created to be jarringly slow, as the darkness and loneliness of the underzee envelopes you. But the game is never intense or scary, and never seeks to invoke such emotion, instead every creature and infact every building you encounter is frankly disturbing, the slow pace of your ship serves not to hinder you, but to slowly reveal the underzees horrors, evoking a feeling of discovery, and disgust whenever you find a new port.
Now, you may be thinking "Themeing is all well and good, but if the game is not fun, then what's the point? Well it's the exploration and story of the game. Every single port in the game has a story to be told, some filled with adventure, and others that reveal the dark underbelly of the fallen world. At the start of the game you choose who you were in your past life, and who you will be in the future. Are you a street-urchin(pun intended) rising from rags to riches? Or a veteran looking to write your name in the history books(or atleast have a shantee written about you) as "The Captain who charted the zee"? Sail the dark waters and find your glory, explore the deep, hidden world of these lovecraftian horrors, and maybe even anger the gods of the zee in the process.

This is the point of the review where I say all the negatives of this game, and while these cons do make the game incredibly frustrating and infuriating, just remember that I think this game is amazing and you should definitely go buy it right now.
OK, on to the bad bits. You may have just read the description of this game and found the word "Rogue-Like" and "Frequent deaths". This, I had found, to be an absolutely terrible idea for a game as detailed in story as this one. You have to die atleast 5 times before you chew into the meat of this game's story. You may think of youself as a patient person, but I had to play 30 hours of this game before I actually got into the story, and I had died about 15 times. I could excuse this play time if I hadn't had to die and restart right from the beginning with nothing except for what you started with (you can choose to take some things from your previous captain, but I chose not to do so 'cause I found that that was basically cheating, but after the 10th run I realised I had to do so to stay alive).

Secondly, some stories have a quick pace to them, but require you to travel back and forth across the whole map, I'm not going to spoil it, but I'm just going to say that it involved monkeys. Throughout that whole port's story, I had to go from the main island(Fallen London), all the way to the island at the other side of the map, then continously go back and forth between islands, just to complete one quest.
Thirdly, the grind, it's the worst thing, it makes the game literally unplayable. OK, I lied, there isn't a grind, but I couldn't think of a better way of bringing up this subject matter. If you play this game, and you start grinding, stop, you're doing it wrong. Never should you ever have to go back and forth in a single port collecting the same items then selling it to another port for money, it ruins the game's pacing and makes the underzee a chore. If you're low on funds, adventure out to new ports in the area, their stories will most likely reward you kindly.

It seems like a lot of people have bought this game assuming it was a naval combat simulator, or a naval trading simulator. I have around 60 hours in the game, most of it not on this steam account, so I want to make sure you know what you might be getting into.
Let me try to avert these expectations. This is a glorified text adventure game, and I mean glorified in a non-sarcastic way. It really is glorious how the graphics and sounds accompanying the text can add to it. It's a novel that unfolds as you play. The sailing mechanics are quite fun (Except for the grind, more on that later), but they are NOT the main draw. The main draw is the incredibly pretty prose.
Losing can be fun in this game, but unlike what the description seems to be pushing a little to far, the main draw is also not the difficulty. It is exploration. Do you like the idea of exploring a town where no one has a permanent identity? Do you like the idea of sailing off the edge of the map to an abstract fever dream? Would you have fun learning about a city where people willingly give up certain emotions, and then deciding whether to join them?
Sunless Sea is not about the sea. It's about the atmosphere, and it's about the feeling of learning secrets of the world around you. It's about being able to look back and think on how many stories you've seen, and the pride you can feel having learned so many things. The combat and trading is to supplement this.
Now, there is one problem with this game I wholeheartedly agree with! The grind. Oh lord the grind. Take my advice. Make sure you have self control, get cheat engine, and when you think to yourself "Oh my god this trade rout is so boring I want to go to that one island but I don't have the money and it sucks. I'm gonna do something else and not touch this game.", you cheat in the fuel you need. The grind has a deadly effect on the playability of this game.
You will think "I'm taking a break", and then when you see the game in your library, you will think "That takes so much investment to get what I want, there are other games that respect my time more."
And then you will never play it again. That happened to me. I got the game, put 7 hours in it, and then I kept meaning to get back to it but never did until a year and a half later. Then I got cheat engine, and used it just slightly to get past that point where I was frustrated to quitting, and it swiftly became one of my favorite games. Ever.
