I'll be frank I was a little hesitant to try out this particular Telltale series, because recent entries have been inconsistent (I'm looking at YOU Game of Thrones).  However a friend recommended it, and having had good memories from some of their older games. I figured I'd give the game a chance.  Having played it, I can see why some consider it a polarizing game.
The biggest thing that Telltale presents in this entry that differentiates itself from the others is the balancing of the personas of Batman and Bruce Wayne. There are a few cool moments where you get to choose which one to use to deal with a given situation.  Other than that it is a fairly by-the-numbers Telltale game.  Nothing really separates it in terms of narrative, plot, or characters.
Telltale avoids the pratfall of repeating well-known Batman backstories by having some artistic license with established lore.  I'll admit I was a fan of a couple of these flourishes (the less cartoony Penguin was one), but ultimately Telltale does little with these treads.  It's hard to go into details without going into spoilers, but let's just say about halfway through the game a lot of details are revealed to Bruce/Batman.  It's a great moment, but I personally don't think there's an effective payoff for it.  I think there should have been a decision for Telltale to decide whether to create a cohesive story throughout 5 episodes or relying on a villain-of-the-week formula.  By choosing the in-between, no side character really gets time to be fleshed out nor does the plot stand well on its own.
Gameplay-wise, the game feels light on content.  Clocking at around 8 hours cummulatively,  this is the shortest telltale game I've ever played.  Each episode boils down to a variant of dealing with the prior episode's finale, going to the batcave, investigating, and punching things.  Don't get me wrong, I loved this formula in the Arkham series, but Rocksteady had more resources to make each thing feel intuitive.  Telltale has.... a kind of linking tool on interactive objects.   Admittedly it is cool to use when doing detective work, but it feels a bit tacked on for fight scenes.  The dialogue, which usually shines in talky games, is pretty meh.  Granted the Batman series is not known for deep dialogue, but it seems odd a company like Telltale wouldn't have had put more time in this aspect.  Story and dialogue is usually their bread-and-butter.
Also worth mentioning, as other reviewers have noted the game does not seem to be optimized.  My rig had no problems running the past games as well as current-gen PC games.   There are numerous occasions where animations lag or the lip syncing is off.  It was not bad enough for me to stop playing, but it can be noticable.
In the end I have to say that at recommendation will probably hinge on whether you find something memorable about the game.  I have just played it recently and I'm struggling to think of a moment where I said, "This is definitely the best way to tell this story."  With season 2 launching recently we'll just have to see if the series will evolve.

so first of all, this is based on how well the game did in what it was trying to do. Its a story that you become a part of, making choices and getting emotionally involved in, its not a typical "game".  Its not trying to be a "game",  So it is unfair to  grade it as such.
This is the First Telltale series ive played, and I adored it. I am an avid gamer, and was never interested in these types of games because i felt they werent real games. But i saw this one on sale for like $6, and as a longtime batman fan, I picked it up.  looking back, now that ive experieced it, i would gladly have paid full price. It pulls you in to the story, as any good film would, but then it places you in the drivers seat, and makes you make the hard choices that we so often criticize movie characters for doing.
ALso i have to say, this is BY FAR my favorite iteration of Batman and the universe that ive seen on a screen yet.  obviously the fact that i got to make all of batmans choices makes me biased, but i really actually loved they way telltale did my favorite superhero here.  Refreshing.
Now obviously, in the end, the general story has to come out mostly the same, but its the way you get there, and in what state that changes.   as someone who has always valued the small details that immerse you in a story, and the character of the relationships in them, this game really hit the spot.  I tend to get emotionally involved in the story, and this game just totally used that in me.  The choices i was making really actually affected my emotions toward the story, sometimes feeling confident in my decision, while sometimes feeling immediate regret, that stuck with me through the story.  I found myself at the edge of my seat in many moments, and i felt i really stepped into Bruce Waynes shoes.  You really feel like you have control over WHO Bruce is and why he does what he does.
As far as the glitches and bugs everyone seems to be complaining about, I didnt experience a single one, and my pc isnt even that great.
Well done, Telltale.  Ill be grabbing your other titles asap.

I was able to score LIMBO for free during a special promotion here on Steam. The only reason why I decided against recommending this game is because I don't believe it's worth anything more than five dollars, honestly. Wait for another sale/special promotion or just have a dumb friend/family member buy it for you, tbh.
I want to say that the most frustrating part of this game is the limited control scheme. Players move the Boy with the arrow keys and interact with various objects using the CTRL key, and there is no way to rebind the keys to a more familiar configuration. Also, there's no crouching/ducking (the DOWN arrow key is used only for descending ladders, ropes, and ledges), and you jump using the UP arrow key (which was very annoying).
From a game design standpoint, having a limited amount of controls is a very clever way to add difficulty to a video game, especially one as simple as LIMBO.
From a player standpoint, however, it would have been so much easier to rebind the keys to ones I'd be more comfortable pressing in conjunction with one another (for example, instead of jumping with the UP arrow key, I would move it to ALT or the spacebar). This was a constant source of irritation, but that's just a small personal gripe.
Now, my biggest grievance with this game are the puzzles. The puzzles in LIMBO are not exactly difficult to solve―they just require precise timing and a
of patience. You
. a grizzly death. Often.
I would say the only thing that prevented me from quitting the game altogether was the fact that it was so short to complete, so I tried my best to power through it (in between my fits of impatient rage, lol).
On a lighter note, I do think that the music in LIMBO was very pretty, and it did help to set the mood. There's also a certain sound effect when a certain platform lowers that sounds just like an obelisk raising in Gauntlet: Legends. It made me very happy.
I won't spoil it, but even though I see people decide against recommending this game due to its ending, that is the main thing that made me think, "wow. That was actually kind of worth it." The ending isn't by any means award-winning, but it did take my breath away and left me feeling all floaty―even made me smile―due to the way it was presented. And that, my friends, is art.

So often nowadays it's become harder and harder no matter what for games to really make me feel something and for me to lose myself in them, totally immersed. Precious few pieces of work have been able to do this recently and video games above all else were once my one real escape. The Beginner's Guide seemed to make up for all the [lost] time, all the dulled emotions, all the lack of concentration and feeling that I needed or even wanted to go on. To see how much further down the rabbit hole I could go. To explore. To learn.
Really, (and it may or may not have been the intent (I may be attributing meaning like Davy where there wasn't any but...) really, it was because I saw myself so clearly in the past, present and future in Coda and Davy. As someone with the pretense of being a creative, introspective and maybe even intelligent person that constantly needs to find a reason - any reason for the way things are, as Davy did; to solve the problem, to fix myself, this game hit home like a freight train. It also spoke so clearly about the feelings I have felt and continue to feel about a dear friend of mine who killed himself: maybe if I'd done something better or differently I could have helped him? Sometimes, there are no solutions like with the themes of mental illness that this game deals with; there are no magic bullets. Sometimes the best thing you can do to move on...is to let go, and stop fixating on the idea that you can solve it, even after it's passed. It wasn't the first thing that's made me realise this...but it was one of the most beautiful and poignant reminders of this truth and I can't thank you enough for it.
Like with Davy and Coda, being part of the experience that this game created in just 97 minutes made me feel far less alone, and I'm not scared or ashamed to admit that.
Thank you.

(Played during free weekend)
-I found the sailing to be very slow paced; it felt like it was wasting my time.
-The stories did not interest me. Stuff happened, but there was no emotional investment, no significant conflict, nor any excitement or tension.
-Events/choices were arbitrary; you either need to try everything and memorize the results, pick at random and treat it like an adventure story (with you in the back seat), or look up the results to see which one is actually useful to you.
-Money making system seems poor (it's difficult to get enough money to keep going in the beginning). The main mission early on is gathering data from other docks - these missions do not pay for themselves unless you manage to gather multiple at a time (hard if you're low on money/fuel/supplies, like you are at the beginning).
-Starter ship seems to be one of the best ships. "Upgrading" costs a fortune and requires more fuel/supplies for the same distance (as the "upgraded" ships tend to be heavier and require more crew to function).
-Combat is extremely simplistic (just aim and fire; follow from behind if possible to minimize incoming damage). Killing enemy ships usually doesn't give you many resources (usually not worth the fuel, supplies, and damage you've spent/taken). Strangely, I once fought a ship that was apparently not hostile (there was no obvious difference between that ship and any other - I only found out I was pirating a friendly ship when it was mentioned by one of the crew in the follow-up "story"), and this ship had plenty of fuel and supplies. Why didn't any other ship have fuel/supplies?
-(Minor) I ended up dying by trying to sail off the edge of the map (doing so led to an okay outcome on a different edge), which forced me into an event where I had a 98% chance of dying and losing almost everything. With no warning that that's what was going to happen, it felt unfair.
I saw someone suggest that it was more fun to cheat in the supplies you need (you can modify the autosave to give yourself plenty of money). After a few hours of playing normally, I tried this to see what other content was in the game. When I found that the best ship in the entire game was barely any better than what I had started with (and consumed around 2x as many resources and - even with the best engines - still didn't move faster than the starter ship), it was quite a disappointment. Sure I could engage harder enemies (which occur further out from the starting area), but this only changed the scale of the numbers involved.
As I hinted above, I think this game is best enjoyed by pretending that the main character is in control (since the choices are pretty much down to "which one sounds the most interesting/valuable" unless you look them up). Even so, the resulting plot is not likely to be very interesting.
If you thoroughly enjoy Fallen London's story telling and resource gathering system (it's a free online game by the same company, so check it out), then you'll probably enjoy this game too - it's essentially more of the same (but without any restrictions on how much you can play). Otherwise, I do not recommend this game.

Outlast is an outstanding and perfect example of what a horror game should really be. Even if you play it again a few times you still will feel uneasy and on constant alert. Every corner you turn you are filled with fear if there'll be an enemy or any general insane patient running lose in the asylum that could pose a threat. The story is fantastic if you actually pay attention to it by reading all of the documents that you find.
If you've played it excessively, you may feel you've seen it all with this game and have become resistant to the crippling terror that you previously experienced. If you want to feel it again, insane difficulty is avaliable and it will bring back that anxiety that you've experienced your first time playing. Well, maybe even more. But you'd have to take it seriously and actually have the will to beat the game on that difficulty. The idea of dying and starting at the very beginning again without the comfort of checkpoints (as well as low health) definitely will make you more tense.
The game doesn't really fall short with anything, my only complaint is that sometimes enemies can be fooled a little too easily, taking away some of that horror factor. But that is rather small of an issue in my opinion.
I've never played a horror game better than Outlast, and I sure can't wait for the second to come out.

This game is pretty bad. Probably one of Telltales worst. Had I paid 23 euros for it then I would be furious.
The writing is atrocious. The plot just feels very contrived. Batman is probably the biggest moron in Gotham. He notices his friend, Harvey Dent, break down because of his tragic accident. Instead of accompanying him to a psychiatrist or something, he does nothing about it. There are several investigation scenes where Batman sounds like a child trying to put two and two together. Very early on, Batman learns the identity of some of the major villains, but despite this he won't go after them right away and lets them casually gain more power in Gotham. There are tons of inconsistencies and it's hard to tell whether or not this because of the choices featured in the game. In the second episode, Catwoman betrays the main villain by teaming up with Batman and ♥♥♥♥ing up their attack during the debate. In the next episode, we see Catwoman and the main villain working together as if nothing ever happened. Some of the choices don't seem to have the right consequences. In the first episode, I showed my non-violent approach while interrogating a goon. In the next scene, Alfred would scold me for beating a man half to death even though the worst I did was apply pressure to the criminals arm which is unskippable.
This game tries to sell itself as a reimagining of the Dark Knight, but it just falls flat on its face. Batmans parents being criminals doesn't work, because after the second episode he stops caring. There's no moral dilemma, just one line about how his whole superhero career is based on a lie and that's it. After that it's pretty much forgotten. Penguins reimagining as a scummy, thin Australian man doesn't work. Bruce knows he's part of a terrorist group and has vast knowledge over his criminal records yet somehow Cobblepot gets his hands on Wayne Enterprises. His eccentric attitude doesn't fit in at all so the board appointing him as CEO makes very little sense whatsoever. It’s true that he faked his resumé, but how did nobody realize this? The main villain is a reimagined sort of famous character as well and it’s as stupid as it sounds. It’s like having the villain of a Superman-story be Jimmy Olsen. Their motivation is shallow and comes out of nowhere. Some of their actions are pretty stupid too like how the villain for some reason returns to a crime scene where the two dead bodies of their adoptive parents were discovered one episode earlier. This is probably because the writers wanted Batman to get to that place so they could develop the main villain more, but couldn’t figure out how to get him there.
There game is also a technical mess. The framerate dips a lot for seemingly no reason. There are several parts in the game where I the game ran but still had just a black screen with the subtitles running. In some parts, the camera would focus on the wrong thing, zoom out making certain objects appear that shouldn't be there and some models would just disappear.
The entire game just feels generic. There are no meaningful additions to The Walking Dead Formula. It feels very cookie cutter despite trying to sell itself as something that has never been done before in the Batman universe. Combat still feels clunky and awkward just like it did in the Walking Dead. The music is especially forgettable, compared to other Batman or Telltale games. There's maybe one or two meaningful choices in the entire game. My verdict? Avoid it like I avoid social interactions.

This is the one, kids.
An endless, explorable open world with 4 unique ecosystems to discover (city, desert, icy mountains, jungle).
Fun, mindless gunplay and enormous explosions out of a Stallone or Schwarzenegeer flick from the 80's.
A ridiculous story with unbelieveable characters that totally clowns the major petrol-controlling superpowers of the world (USA in particular takes it on the chin as a butt of the jokes).  Yet Rico is an honorable and Chaos-loving individual with a clear motivation... to blow stuff up more!
The controls are solid on controller or M/KB and customizable.  Vehicle control is superb and extemely variable between the over 105+ unique cars, boats and planes you can operate in the open world.
The side missions are very entertaining and should be played through in their entirety.  You will get many more flavors out of the game doing every single Faction side mission as many of them contain unique and fun objectives and mechanics not seen elsewhere in JC2, including the main plot missions.  Where else can you be contracted to drag a statue head of Baby Panay back to a rich guy's mansion after pulling down said statue with a Razorback tank and grappling hook?
If you are debating between JC2 and JC3... this is the game you want.  Perfect controls and endless gameplay, over 100 hours to consider getting to 100% explored and/or 100% achievements.  Highest recommendation for an open world action game.  10/10

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the last standalone expansion for Half-Life and the last game to take place at Black Mesa. (Decay doesn't count and Black Mesa is a remake of the original Half-Life) You play as Barney Calhoun, a security guard who is trying to survive the events of Black Mesa (See Half-Life & HL: Opposing Force). Personally, I find this game the weakest of all the Half-Life games.
Pros:
-Great to introduce Barney Calhoun as you'll meet him later in Half-Life 2
-Same pros as Half-Life (Great gameplay, great level detail, etc.)
Cons:
-Same weapons used by the great Gordon Freeman (Crowbar and everything) no new weapons like Opposing Force
-Relatively boring story
-Rarely any new enemies unlike Opposing Force
-No Half-Life 3
Overall, this game is OK its not the best Half-Life game. (7.5/10) I recommend this game if your a BIG Half-Life fan, or you want to learn more about Barney before the events of Half-Life 2. However, there is really nothing else to it. I felt that Gearbox could've done a better job with this expansion (See my review of Opposing Force to see what Gearbox can really do).

From one of the old 'big dogs' of Playstation Home, Four Kings is a solid casino title, with a lot to offer, but a fair few minor flaws.  I haven't tested every single title, but after spending a chunk of time on several, I can say the following:
Pros:
A good set of titles that all function well; poker is of course only as good as the players you get, but all the basic functionality and pomp is here, combined with the daily tasks and tier increases that made PS Home attractive for folks like me.  It is, in essence, a wide array of gambling options with level ups and leveling bonuses.  That's kind of awesome.
Regular influx of chips.  Playing for free long-term is entirely possible due to getting a decent chunk of chips for free from a number of resources (daily super slots, daily/weekly tasks for more chips, 250 chips every 15 minutes in game), which keeps the title from feeling locked off to any reasonable extent.
Looks great.  Not Skyrim-with-a-million-graphics-mods great, but there's obviously been a lot of work to make the Four Kings look interesting, like the kind of place you could go for a vacation.
Cons
Lack of counter of autoplay.  This is a minor quibble but it does frustrate.  I like to play the machine game 'Instant Keno', and it's a bit annoying that when I select the autoplay option that until it gets to the final play, I have no visual indicator how many runs I have left.
Wasted space.  I love the nightclub and the apartment!  They look great, and again bring me back to what I liked about Playstation Home.  Except, they have no purpose at present.  The nightclub has the same music as the rest of the game.  The DJ booth, the bars, all have no interactivity.  The apartment is arguably worse, in that while it looks lovely, there's no way to interact with anything in this allegedly personal space, not even the televisions that look for all the world like they SHOULD be interactive.  I don't want these spaces excized, mind you; it helps to separate the title from generic casino titles in a similar vein, but all of the above needs SOME measure of interaction.  Mini-games, additional places to spend chips/RP/etc, looping videos, new music, I don't care what.  But for it to be lacking all of that makes it little more than window dressing.
Limited spending options.  At present, chips let you play games, winning gives you RP, which can be used to buy a SMALL handful of avatar items, and if you earn X amount in a single month, you get VIP access for a month.  And... that's it.  Can't upgrade your apartment, avatar options are super limited, no special entertainment options for expending RP, etc, etc.  I hope this changes, as there's a lot of room here for enhancement of the overall experience beyond the casino games (which, again, work great and are decently diverse).
Overall, the game is a recommend.  Yes, it has flaws, and I hope to see the title expand a LOT.  But what is there right now is a complete gambling title with solid gameplay in a good environment with countless options for snagging more chips for free and getting your fix on for the day.  And for an entry price of free, it's hard not to say give it a shot.

Very fun racing game! I used to have this years ago on my PS2, but I don't play that anymore. I finally decided to get it for my computer, and it's just like I remember: plenty of crashing and destruction!
It's better than FlatOut 1 in the fact that there are better/more cars to choose from, and the same with tracks, but not with free roam. In the first FlatOut, you were able to go backwards on tracks and drive around the area. You sadly cannot on this game, but the racing is still fun nonetheless.
As for the demolition derbies, they are also plenty of fun. It's nice when a game isn't too easy, so I do like the fact that there is a contact timer of about 44 seconds, meaning you have to smash into someone at some point. The AI is also certainly smarter than the first FlatOut, thus adding to the difficulty of derbies and races. It only has 3 more derby arenas than the first one, for a total of 6, so there certainly could have been a few more arenas.
Lastly, you can't forget the minigames! There are oddities such as Royal Flush, Baseball, Bowling, and a few others where you have to fling yourself out of the car. These are pretty entertaining, especially with friends. It can get slightly monotonous by yourself though.
All in all, this is still lots of fun for a game made in 2006!

Is it worth $60? Probably, but it is in alpha, so it's gonna get even better, making that $60 worth every bit.

Since reviews aren't just opinion meters and-
Oh, they are.
Well here's a breakdown anyway:
The art is quite good, but I can't look past the animations, which I personally don't much like. They seem slightly unnatural somehow, as if forced or overacted.
The music is okay, and at times reminds of a certain game that parallels EoS a lot.
Then again, there isn't a whole lot of it yet, so I can't be sure.
One thing I quite like is how the game is actually somewhat intuitive. I mean it has all that arbitrary stuff where you go through the tiers of equipment and unlock things that you would realistically have beforehand, but I can overlook that since it's an industry standard, no matter how dumb it is.
The tutorial goes through the mechanics and controls at lightspeed. Something that's great for someone like I, who plays games like Xonotic, but would be really damn hard for anyone who isn't used to learning new controls extremely quickly. The rest of the game seems to just leave you to do what you want after the tutorial, which is good and bad, depending on how you look at it.
As usual, sandbox style progression using "tech", and unlocks of new gear.
There isn't much emphasis on building, possibly because there's not really much need, and possibly because the small hotbar and needing to manually stock it with stuff all the time is a nightmare, at least coming from games like Starbound which allowed you to place things by picking them up in the inventory. A small issue I have with it, but I'm sure many people would feel the same.
The map is automatically smoothed by making every top corner (tiles y-1 and x±1 are air) 45°. Not a great feature, since building with this in mind can be very annoying.
There are too many bugs to go into. I'm hoping this is because it's still in EA.
The map generation algorithm is pretty basic. Very similar to Starbound, but less to explore for lack of content so far. out of the few worlds I've looked at, all are the same flattish top island with other small islands above and below. It's a little like an extremely dense asteroid belt. It's not incredible.
Overall, this seems kind of interesting, but not so much so that a person who just bought the Weekly Bundle would give it a good review.
I don't recommend the game, but I don't recommend not playing it either. It's one of those things where you just don't quite know how it'll turn out.

Good Lord this game is phenomenal. Even though it's still in an ALPHA stage of development I've spent a LOT of time in it, and I'll absolutely be spending a lot more. I'd never played a survival game before (thought I've watched a fair number of them played), and I was hooked within the first half hour of gameplay. I would ABSOLUTELY recomment this game for beginning survival game players (since that's what I am). Apparently for experienced players there are some issues that need to be resolved yet later in the game, but that's to be expected since it is so early on in its development. On that note I feel like I should mention that the developers steadfastly put out 2 updates each month, so you can really see that the game IS actually in development. It's great.
Finally, as far as the gameplay goes, it seems pretty darn well polished for an alpha game, and the few issues I've encountered are things that will almost certainly be rectified by the time the game comes out in full. It is ABSOLUTELY worth the $20, and I feel that getting it on sale for $10 was ridiculous--I feel like I should give the devs the other $10 just to support them making this game. It's been a joy so far (in case you couldn't tell by this review), and I can't wait to see how it continues to develop.
TL;DR
Do yourself a favor and get this game--it's worth it.

I liked Tropico 3, bought Tropico 4 and LOVE it.   I didn't think Kalypso/Haemimont could screw Tropico 5 up.  They did.  The game has far less content than Tropico 4 did on release day.  This is so you can buy content later as DLC!
The economy controls are dumbed down.    Rent, wages, and all other economic factors are frustratingly simplified and broad.
Shipping was a bit of an annoyance in Tropico 4,  goods could stack at docks faster than it could be shipped.   In Tropico 5, that has been remedied (sort of) but the new way of shipping goods is an annoying, island clogging, minutiae-filled chore that makes me long for T4's flawed but ultimately less annoying shipping system.
T4's troops worked automatically and you had no control over them.  In T5, you do have control.  A good thing, right?  Wrong.  The troops controls are clunky and unresponsive.  Another chore, not fun.
Rebels in Tropico 4 would appear if you were doing things wrong or didn't have enough jobs.   There was a reason (and cure) to having rebels on your island.  In Tropico 5,  you have rebels for no reason.  Your island could be a perfect paradise, but huge rebel attacks will still occur.  The Developers have admitted the rebels are arbitrary and for no reason other than some lame excuse about it being an upstart island with political turmoil; it just (and does, often) happens.
In Tropico 4, you could be a benevolent ruler, or a brutal Tyrant, which is what Tropico was all about.   In Tropico 5, you are an impotent and weak  governor that can only survive by doing your best in hopes of  pleasing the fickle masses to desperately stay in power.
Then there is DLC.  Tropico 4, when it came out, was quickly buried in DLC. BUT!  The first several DLC were handy, useful DLC.  The DLC had VERY useful buildings, cool decorator pieces, a mission, and outfit.   Over time though, the Tropico 4 DLC became cheap, useless cash grabs.   This crappy DLC content continued on into Tropico 5.  All the DLC in Tropico 5 is pointless and adds nothing interesting.  Not only that, but a few skilled gamers actually found large chunks and entirely complete, usuable DLC in the RELEASE DAY game files.  Which the Devs tried to patch out and B.S. away.
In Hindsight, you could offer me Tropico 5 for free, and i'd decline the offer.  Tropico 4 is superior in nearly every way.  With Tropico 4 being available on Steam, there is absolutely no point, reason, or need to buy Tropico 5.
This really, for me, is a bummer.  This isn't some game I saw, tried, and didn't like.  I LOVE Tropico 4.  I WANTED to see this game succeed.   Kalypso/Haemimont are the little guys in the gaming industry.  But when they got greedy and released a content-weak game and put that content (that isn't that great to begin with) in DLC, they sold their integrity to nickel-and-dime their customers.
I was dissapointed when  Kalypso started rushing out several shoddy DLC at the end of Tropico 4's run.  Now, with Tropico 5,  Kalypso/Haemimont are no longer on my radar, I don't care about their games.
That's okay.  I still have Tropico 4.
EDIT:  Some people have posted below with some very good arguments about where my review may be wrong.  I still feel my review stands, but if you are truly looking into whether you should spend your money on this game or not, it wouldn't hurt in reading the comments below for some very valid responses that may change your mind.

This was a great game for the Half-Life series.  For those of you who have high expectations from modern shooters, then you would be unsurprisingly dissapointed because of your adjusted standards.  This game was made with the original gold source engine back in the early 2000's in which it is apparent to what the engine can and cannot do.
The game.
The game can be beaten in a time span of 2.5 to 3.5 hours and it includes the Hazard Course as a tutorial (recommended for adjusting settings before diving into the game.)  It is not long but it is an official story for Barney Calhoun during the Black Mesa Incident.  The gameplay is the same as Half-Life's gameplay except that there is a body armor mechanic that replaces the HEV suit.  The biggest problem in regards to HL: Blue Shift is the Gold Source engine's AI pathfinding issues.  AI characters (NPC's) will only follow you for a certain distance and have trouble going around corners thus making key NPC's frustrating to work with sometimes.  Also, there is no long-jump module.  Out of the 24 times that I've completed this game on the original disc, there were no notable bugs and/or glitches except for a spinning giblet that clips through the wall.

Having played every title in the series from the very first Tropico, I must admit that Tropico 5 brings very little new features or points of interest to the table. The revised combat system was somewhat interesting, but general streamlining of features and loss of micromanagerial opportunities turned me sour towards the fifth title in the series.
Some thoughts:
- Loss of variety in how you run your tyrannical/benevolent island paradise. From the get go, you're under the heel of the provincial goverment, under whom you serve as the governor of Tropico. Fairly easy, but extremely limited options.
- Research tree and allocation seems pointless. Extremely limited options and techs available. Some can be unlocked via tasks as rewards, but it seems an unlikely hurdle to overcome while managing your people.
- Sadly, you are beholden to the majority population. The people make mandates of you, instead of the other way around. I always preferred ruling with a tyrannical fist for the first few decades, consolidating my power, before going from communism to good ol' fashioned capitalism and upping happiness to a 100. Sadly, you cannot really choose your path as much as in the previous titles, due to the 'Era & Tech' system they implemented.
- Radio commentary is not particularly funny or interesting.
- I do like the trade import/export agreement options, which allow for a much more detailed plan for your trading strategy. However, you cannot pursue all resources, but rather randomly generated contracts, which may or may not be relevant to your wealth and interests.
- Lack of building options. Most likely added in due time with DLC, albeit I've always been against this sort of slow cash milking structures in games.
- Money just seems to be pouring in, non-stop. I may be good with the game economics due to my extensive playtime in the earlier titles, but I never had to plan ahead, conserve my wealth and make tough tactical decisions with the budget.
- Rebels have been buffed, for better or worse. Oddly enough, the game seems to run in constant Rebel Yell mode, and those pesky pineapple farmers are going to be armed to the teeth if you let your guard down.
Final verdict:
You're honestly better off with Tropico 4. It sports a much wider range of features, options and fewer restrictions in how you conduct and build Tropico to be the shining gem of the island nations. Tropico 5 might be worth looking into at some point, but I personally found the limitations issued at each point vexing.

Morphopolis is a gorgeous P&C game bringing you through the life of a bug that morphs into other forms as it completes its journey. Where that journey goes exactly, is not really known, but you will point and click your way through several beautifully designed levels, finding hidden objects to unlock puzzles and continue onto the next stage.
The music is rather relaxing and don't get old too quickly but after a long while, you may just want to mute it and play your own music instead.
The puzzles aren't too hard but will require a bit of your brain to solve.
My biggest gripe is control. As you are controlling your little critter around, sometimes it gets confused or locks up and goes back and forth back and forth cause it doesn't really know what you want. Instead of pointing and clicking and your creature going there, you have to hold it, and not al paths are self-evident.
The game moves at a very slow pace, so if you're not in a realxed mood, don't bother to play it or you might get frustrated with the slow speed. Personally I think the game has no replay value, but for such a cheap game, did you really expect any?
Overall 6/10 - Get it on sale for an interesting mix of art, music and puzzles.

Rarely does a game make me look at others and consider my own opinions in a new light by jump starting some critical faculties that I wouldn't otherwise use for video games. At least not unless I'm prompted. The Beginner's Guide walks you through the familiar, and then eventually the bizarre, holding your hand with a simple experience that introduces the idea of experiencing a video game as a work of art.
While the narrative is simple enough, it's told in a synthesis of deisgn with a few touchstones that demonstrate how the interactive can colour an experience. You don't just wonder about the narrator, but about yourself as a player, and what it means to be in a game world.
I don't know how helpful it is to get bogged down in whether or not this game is showing us a true story (if you want my guess, you aren't getting it), but instead I'm going to try and use the tools I built through this game to look at other similarly abstract works, and maybe a few that are completely different.
In essence, this game is a tutorial for video games as art. That's if you believe titles are the best signposts. And maybe they aren't.

This is definitely amongst the best options in the survival genre today and my personal favorite, i just cant stop playing it (every time i dies i tell myself im done, only to come back five minutes later). You've done a great thing with the atmosphere and gameplay and, given that this is alpha, i'll give my input to see if it can get even better.
The high spots:
-Single player. Nuff said.
-Very immersive and nerve-racking, the basic needs have been done really well
-Different items are elaborate enough to force you to really decide which you need the most
-Great landscape and object design/art, a proof of concept for simple, yet effective and charming
-Obviously the lack of zombies, the focus on actual survival is very refreshing
-So much fun.
Issues/Suggestions:
-Lack of variety. Even though the items in the game are nicely done, they soon become repetitive and the wonder of finding new and particularly useful things is lost.
-Punishing. I dont mean this in a sense that the game is overall too hard, its hard enough which makes it challenging, but sometimes unexpected events lead to a bitter sense of unfairness, for example: The first time i left mysterious valley through the ravine pass i didnt kniw where to go, so i tried to go down the mountain-side, i found a place that sloped down and all was well when suddenly... i dropped 20cm and died. yup... you could have at least have made it impossible to go there, or have made it possible to go down... this just made me feel cheated, like i should have been able to live. another one is the moments the game saves, which sometimes makes it impossible to survive, once i was at full everything and then after harvesting a deer was at 4% health because of the cold, if it were really immersive my character would have just stopped a long time before (and no, the cancel button is not good enough).
-Crafting. This isnt as much criticism as it is a suggestion. I think that crafting is a great idea but lacks implementation. you can only make a handful of items and most of them require cured things, which means youll only use it quite a few days in. I think it needs serious expansion, and maybe some items could even be crafted without a workbench (like the fishing line for christ` sake).
-Lack of visual feedback for worn items. I like the fact that this is first person, but seriously. You cant tell at all what youre even wearing unless you look at your inventory and see whats equipped. I think itd be really nice to have on the condition menu, instead of a naked body, your actual character (one of the two on your promo video) and then you could showcase the different items youre wearing, how cool would it be to see your own wolf jacket? you could even make different models depending on the characters condition...
-The map soon becomes memorized, im not really going to hold a grudge because of this or expect much change because i realise it takes a lot of time and effort to build landscapes, especially large ones, but just know that it would be really cool to have a more massive map.
Overall: Bloody amazing game, cant wait for it to be finished. Youve done an amazing job and i hope to see it develop further and be finished. 100% recomend.

Banished is, overall, a great city simulator--it's very easy to wile away hours just hanging out, expanding, and reaching that population sweet spot. I experienced no bugs in my playthrough, but it did take several failed cities to really understand the mechanics of the game.
At the end of the day though, reaching that population sweet spot is the only real "bug" the game has. The game's population model is predicated on *growth* instead of *sustainability*, so even if you get to a point where your settlement is consistently generating a food surplus and everyone is in good health, you *will* run into a population decline problem. The only way to avoid this is to keep building more houses, so that people will start new families. So, if you reach the end-game where you've successfully built a full, self-sustaining community that occupies all the free space on a map, *you will still fail.*

Project Zomboid is one of those few gems that is released every 5-7 years, where should I begin this review?
Let's start with the concept of the game. The whole idea of PZ is to survive as long as possible, there are no objectives,  no end goal, just survive. Now this may sound easy, but in a world full of zombies constantly out to get whatever they smell/hear/see this can become rather challenging. We all know what zombies are and do, they are dead corpses that were reanimated by some sort of virus or disease and now out to infect everything in sight. And if you're an avid zombie hunter, then this game may sound like just another game with zombies in it, it's not.
Let's get to the actual gameplay elements;
Crafting: You can literally build what ever type of base you want, now this is by far one of the coolest features, you can wall off entire city blocks if you wanted to. (that would require quite a bit of resources though, I'll get to that in a minute) You can build doors, floors, walls, bars, stairs, and light posts among other things. You can craft weapons, or repair ones you've broken, you can add modifications to said weapons too! Got a baseball bat, some nails, and a hammer? Create a spiked baseball bat that deals pretty significant damage and does it in style too.
Barricading: This should probably go in the crafting section, but whatever. Barricading is something most of us zombie hunters have wanted to do for some time now, and sure some zombie games do have it, but Project Zomboid executes it brilliantly, the resources required for barricading are pretty rare depending on how lucky you are and what type of settings you selected before you started your game. (only in Sandbox mode can you select said options) You can barricade windows and doors, which not only helps keep the creeping zeds at bay, but also makes it so they can't see you through said windows, which is really cool. (you can also put sheets up to block outsiders from looking into your safehouse)
Scavenging: This has been a part of modern zombie games for quite some time now, however this game does do one of the more realistic approches to it, food that you scavenge must be kept in a fridge or else it will spoil and make you sick if you attempt to eat it. Items that you need for crafting/barricading are pretty rare and thus valuable when found. You really need to pick and choose only the stuff you'll need at that moment when scavenging because you can only carry so much before becoming over encumbered, and don't forget you can always come back for whatever you can not bring with you at that time. There is another cool option about this, you can carry two bags with you at a time (this would require you to equip one bag in the secondary slot, and a big/normal, hiking/school bag equiped on your back) which gives you plenty of more space along with weight reductions applied from the bag(s) you have equiped at the time.
Moodles: These are moodlets that pop up every now and then to tell you what your character is feeling/thinking, think The Sims, it's just like that. These can range anywhere from being tired, to getting cold, you'll want to keep a close eye on these. Most are not that important, however they're are some that do require your attention and you'll want to be on the lookout for such as, exhaustion, starving, getting sick, getting cold, getting wet, (when it rains) bleeding, and being in pain. A couple tips. 1) You'll want to avoid going out looting/killing during a storm because you'll get wet and will have an increased chance of becoming sick which could be the death of you if you don't take things easy. (killing zombies, running) 2) Lay down every now and then, you're not superman, your character needs sleep just as much as you do. 3) Make sure to always carry bandages/bandaids on you, in case you need to break open a window or patch up a wound, these are a necessity.
Skills: This is a really fun feature in the game, you will develope skills according to how you play overtime. Do you like sneaking around avoiding the undead masses? Or do you like running in swinging hand over foot? either way will get you XP in these skills, which in time will unlock skill points that you can assign to your favorite most used abilities. Remember though, this is not carried over to multiple characters, if your character dies, all the abilities you've unlocked die with them.
Farming: This is a pretty cool feature, it requires quite a few resources that may or may not be tricky to find depending on where you are and what options you've chose before starting the game. I'm not too experienced in this aspect as of the time of this review, however I do know that it is a great food source after the power/water has went out. You can grow your own crops inside your safe zone, or where ever, it really doesn't matter as long as you have the right materials you need, you can start your own little Farmville. (without being bombarded with 53,721 requests from people you barely know. I'm looking at you, Facebook)
Distracting: You can distract the zombies with a few different methods, distracting a group of zombies could end up saving your life for another day. If you've got some gasoline handy and a few matches/lighter you could light up a near by house distracting the horde of undead while you easily sneak by and loot the otherwise damn near impossible house/building with ease. If you're playing with a friend(s) you can distract zombies while your friend goes in and loots the place dry by shouting at them, this will make your life a little bit harder though depending on how many of them there actually are, and Vice versa. Alams in houses can provide a quick distraction, if you're quick enough that is. Break a window or force it open in certain homes and you'll hear an alarm buzz for about 20-30 seconds, if you're quick enough to get out you can easily evade the on coming hordes making it easier to loot the outer area around the house you just sounded off, however this could very well be the end of your life if you get caught up in an oncoming group of zeds.
Weapons: As with most zombie games, this game is based on melee/close quarter combat, there are guns available, however they're pretty rare, most are found in the cities and or gun stores, but of course those areas are hard to get to and loot without proper means, meaning you'll be doing most of your killing with a good ol' baseball bat/crowbar/golfclub, which is by no means a bad choice. (well except maybe the golfclub, you'd be better off fighting them with a toothbrush) The baseball bat has pretty decent durability, and is great against zombies, you can kill most zeds with a couple blows from a baseball bat, same with the crowbar, the better more rarer melee weapons such as the Axe and Sledgehammer are great too, however they're mostly located in the city areas, consider yourself lucky if you find one in the suburbs. Guns are great for clearing out areas, just make sure that you have enough ammo on you, because once you pull that trigger, it's on, that's like a dinnerbell to the infected.
Be SMART: This game is heavily focused on realism, this isn't a game where you're an overpowered solider that cannot be killed, you can and probably will be killed quite a bit starting out. Only RUN when needed. Don't be a glutton and eat everything in sight, you may need that for another day. If you think it's a bad idea, then it is, and you shouldn't do it. And one last thing, STAY AWARE OF YOUR SURROUNDINGS AT ALL TIMES.
Those are the main features of the game as of 4/20/2014 (Yea I know what day it is har har har)
I'd like to add in that you will NEED to think before you act if you want to survive efficiently, this game is about your experience in the zombie apocalypse, what would you do in this situation if it actually happened? That's up to you, however, don't be careless, or else you will not survive for long.

Basically, go play this game. But don't play it on Hard. You won't miss out on gameplay and will enjoy the story more.

This is a welcoming, Eye-Spy kind of game, set in a colouful and beautiful reimagining of the insect world. It is very attractive, fun, but it has a few annoying aspects.
It has a very attractive art style, which appears to be hand-drawn, and is very colourful. This art style is very calming, and is accompanied by nice, atmosphereic music. The colour palette used is very outlandish and unique, which gives the feeling of an almost alien world, this lines up well with the oddities of the insect world.
Morphopolis is not only very beautiful, but it is quite enjoyable. The gameplay is that of the Eye-Spy concept, of needing to find objects, on a list, that appear to blend in with the environment or that are crowded by a whole lot of other objects. This is a very calming gameplay mechanic, which is well used in the game, especially because the objects you need to find blend in well with the evironment, making it a slight challenge to find, but not too hard, just enough to be relaxing. This game mechanic not only helps the game to be relaxing, but it also compliments the colourful art in the game, as it makes you observe and appreciate the background art more. The gameplay is not just Eye-Spy, but is also various puzzles, these puzzles range in difficulty, they are all possible though, and if confusion sets in, it only takes a few minutes to figure out what exactly you need to do, and if you can not work it out, it's easy enough to just click spam everything until it is solved.
There are a few annoying things about this game, that are deal-breakers for some. The insects in your control move slowly, mainly because they are insects, and the game requires you to move to different screens back and forth, which can be tedious, but if you were an optimist, you could say it helps you to relax and appreciate the art more? The game has some very vague insturctions, which can ake progressing hard. The game does have a hint system, but the hint system can't help with everything. It is suggested that you have a walkthrough handy, just in case you are unsure what to do next, as it might happen.
Morphopolis is very worth buying. It is quite short, but it is an experience that is worthwhile. Worthwhile for it's art style, for it's gameplay, and for its achievements.

Cuphead is not an easy game, but most of its difficulty lies in RNG and controls that aren't as tight as they need to be. Does this make Cuphead a bad game? No. Some people can get past those things. I stopped wanting to play it after about 8 hours, 6 of which were retries.
In terms of skill needed to succeed this game isn't as hard as, say, Super C or Contra SS, but again, RNG mainly and not quite up to snuff controls make it harder than it should be.
I was managing to get through the game decently well though, until the robot. Everything about its design is completely infuriatingly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. From the random enemy patterns locking you into taking damage, to the fact that everything takes about 2x as much damage to kill as it should, to the foreground blocking vision from necessary hazards. It represents a ridiculous difficulty spike in a poor way.
I don't think this game needs an easy mode, I think it needs to be tuned better in general. Slight tweaks here and there would have made this game best in its genre. Up there with the greats like Contra, and Metal Slug. As it is though, it's sort of middle of the pack at best.
The presentation is top notch though, so go watch a Let's Play of it. It's a treat!

I really don't understand what people love so much about this game.  I guess I might as well explain why I don't like LIMBO then, eh?
It has an incredibly boring art style and it has no music worth listening to.  You would think that game developers would at least try to please the player's eyes and ears, right?  I thought that too, until I saw endless black and grey blurry crap all over my screen and started listening to this game's "music."  The music is just your run-of-the-mill dark ambient sounds, and the black and grey art style gets old really quick.  At many parts of the game, you're just strolling around slowly (VERY SLOWLY), and you have nothing to look at but the boring forest/factory areas.  The only good part about the art direction is the heavy use of parallax scrolling, and the fact that distant and close-up objects are blurred out and relatively easy to distinguish from the ground and walls that you can interact with.
This game is way too slow as well.  Many great games allow the player to determine the pace of their own gameplay, one great example being the original Super Mario Bros.; you can play Mario slowly, or you can pick up the pace and deal with a higher level of risk.  With this game, you are forced to move around at the pace of a snail and MANY parts of the game are merely the task of walking to the right or left for a very long time.  This coupled with the boring atmosphere leads to even more boredom.
Another problem with this game is the fact that it is entirely based on trial and error.  Many puzzles (I'm looking at you, pressure plate + smashy blocks puzzle) aren't solvable until you try them multiple times.  Thankfully, the errors don't lead to a game over screen and a bunch of waiting around until you can get into the game again.  All you have to do is watch the nameless boy die, then you can go back to your last checkpoint (which are everywhere).  Despite the fact that deaths don't send you back a significant amount, every time that I was trial-and-error'd I rolled my eyes, groaned, and showed all other signs of frustration.
[SPOILER ALERT!!!]
I'll be discussing the lackluster plot in the following paragraphs, so if you'd like to experience it yourself then you probably shouldn't read this.
The primary character in Limbo is a nameless boy who awakens in the middle of a forest.  While walking around in the forest, he encounters many dangers.  At one point during his journey, he encounters a female character who abruptly vanishes before he can reach her.  After this, the forest eventually gives way to a crumbling city environment, and then a factory setting.  On completion of the final puzzle, the boy is thrown through a pane of glass and back into the forest (in slow motion which takes AGES to watch). He walks a short distance until he again encounters the girl again.  The end.
After the game ends, the player is sent back to the main menu and should realize that the boy and girl are both dead, since the exact same setting is presented, but instead of the boy and girl there are two lumps on the ground with flies buzzing all around them.
From the title, we can assume the characters were dead all along.  Nobody saw that coming, right?  Oh wait...  Anyone who knew anything about the word "Limbo" saw it coming.
[SPOILERS OVER!!!]
One redeeming quality of this game is that it actually has a couple of good puzzles.  Some puzzles are creative and difficult.  However, this is overshadowed by the large collection of bad puzzles in the mix.  Most puzzles are trial and error puzzles that are not fun at all.  Some puzzles are hard just because there is some gameplay element that was not explained very well.
I acknowledge that this game is (initially) charming and interesting, but it seems so long and is so boring that I just can't recommend this game for anyone, unless that person is a hipster who likes to think he's cool because he can understand art.

Review after the free weekend:
Unfortunately, this game is basically impossible to complete without a walkthrough or magical knowledge of game events and locations - e.g. you can get a quest from the Admiral to go to location X, with no hint whatsoever as to where location X might be, or you might get a quest to drop off 12 colonists in another location that might well take you hours to find.

Similarly, levelling up officers requires you to scroll and click for every single point (you could just keep the window open so you don't have to scroll back down after each click, but nah - we gotta waste all of the player's time!).
Also, someone should tell the developers that resolution also applies to windows (i.e. 1920x1080 should not be a tiny window in the center of my 1920x1080 screen).

This is a fantastic, immersive game for those seeking story, atmosphere, exploration, and gloomy Victorian cosmic mystery. If you're looking for fast-paced naval combat, fast travel, or anything like that... look elsewhere.
When enjoying this game, DO:
- Gaze ponderously outside your window at the rainy day or snowstorm outside
- Keep a notebook of hints and events that occur during your travels
- Brew up a few cups of tea
- Enjoy in a dimly-lit room, quiet save for the moody soundtrack
Do NOT:
- Check your phone while your boat sets sail from port to port
- Expect to fully uncover the lore after your first captain
- Expect a screen to pop up announcing you've "beat" the game
- Turn down the game music and listen to "Jack Jams" on Spotify instead
Despite the game's simple graphics and interface, I've spend far more time playing this than any other indie game simply because the lore is so well-hidden and elegantly obfuscated. And although you should definitely aim to "get into the mood" for at least your first several experiences, it's an easy game to fire up and play for 30 minutes between homework assignments, before cooking dinner, etc. etc.
Highly recommended, but know what you're getting.

I first played AudioSurf in 2010 and immediately loved it, the idea that you could put any song from your music library into a game and it would generate a track for you to weave your way through collecting coloured blocks.

On the subject of age, i'd say it looks pretty good for something that is almost 10 years old and it plays very nicely too, keeping a consistent, stable framerate on Windows 10.
I have always found myself coming back to this game again and again, wanting to beat the highest scores on some of my favourite songs, and new songs I find from time to time and it never fails to disappoint, with the gameplay never wearing old with there being a theoretically infinite library of levels for you to choose from, provided you have the song's file of course.
Compared to AudioSurf 2, i'd say it's neither better nor worse, but a good point for 2 is that it can be a bit more challenging on slower songs, and it has Steam Workshop of course.
I highly recommend this game, over the years I have sank a fair few hours into it, and I absoloutely love it, it is easily in my top 10 favourite games of all time.

Outlast is a first person survival horror game that has completely revitalized the genre. While other similar games such as Amnesia are psychologicaly disturbing to the player, Outlast has the immediate effect of scaring your wits out, as your only option is to run away from the pshyco freaks that are trying to murder you and slice you with various weapons.
Outlast is one of the most popular games for a reason, as its unique horror scenario in a horror psychiatric hospital (a horror fanatic's wet dream) is perfectly well crafted, and leads to a riveting story. While the story is very linear and does not let you explore the hospital at your own will, the charm of the story and its various characters make the entire experience worthwhile. Some of the characters throughout both the original game and the DLC will make you remember their names in awe, as you remember their intense moments of horror and shock all well as some of their most popular lines of dialogue.
Outlast and the WhistleBlower DLC is one of the greatest combination of any video game to date, and I would like to congratulate Red Barrels on their wonderfull work.

As a long-time fan of Batman, I found Telltale's take to be a unique and interesting take on the Dark Knight's mythos.
Unlike some of other Telltale's licensed properties which find ways to either take place on the outskirts of canon with new characters in the universe ('The Walking Dead' and 'Game of Thrones') or serve as prequels ('Wolf Along Us'), 'Batman' is a complete reboot of the comic's story and its character. This allows them to take some pretty daring risks with sacred canon (who were Batman's parents really?) as well as some bold reinventions of classic characters (the Penguin is almost unrecognizable from any prior version of the character). As such the story feels bold and refreshing.
One disappointment is, like many Telltale games at this point, there's not a lot of chances for the story to diverge based on your choices. At one point you are given the option to make a change that completely turns a familiar character's predestined path from the comics. There were numerous opportunities to take this character in a different direction but the story changes very little regardless.
Despite this I give the game a solid recommendation. Telltale could have played it safe and done something very familiar with the franchise of Batman but they took some risks and came out with a story that's worth checking out.

I really don't understand what people love so much about this game.  I guess I might as well explain why I don't like LIMBO then, eh?
It has an incredibly boring art style and it has no music worth listening to.  You would think that game developers would at least try to please the player's eyes and ears, right?  I thought that too, until I saw endless black and grey blurry crap all over my screen and started listening to this game's "music."  The music is just your run-of-the-mill dark ambient sounds, and the black and grey art style gets old really quick.  At many parts of the game, you're just strolling around slowly (VERY SLOWLY), and you have nothing to look at but the boring forest/factory areas.  The only good part about the art direction is the heavy use of parallax scrolling, and the fact that distant and close-up objects are blurred out and relatively easy to distinguish from the ground and walls that you can interact with.
This game is way too slow as well.  Many great games allow the player to determine the pace of their own gameplay, one great example being the original Super Mario Bros.; you can play Mario slowly, or you can pick up the pace and deal with a higher level of risk.  With this game, you are forced to move around at the pace of a snail and MANY parts of the game are merely the task of walking to the right or left for a very long time.  This coupled with the boring atmosphere leads to even more boredom.
Another problem with this game is the fact that it is entirely based on trial and error.  Many puzzles (I'm looking at you, pressure plate + smashy blocks puzzle) aren't solvable until you try them multiple times.  Thankfully, the errors don't lead to a game over screen and a bunch of waiting around until you can get into the game again.  All you have to do is watch the nameless boy die, then you can go back to your last checkpoint (which are everywhere).  Despite the fact that deaths don't send you back a significant amount, every time that I was trial-and-error'd I rolled my eyes, groaned, and showed all other signs of frustration.
[SPOILER ALERT!!!]
I'll be discussing the lackluster plot in the following paragraphs, so if you'd like to experience it yourself then you probably shouldn't read this.
The primary character in Limbo is a nameless boy who awakens in the middle of a forest.  While walking around in the forest, he encounters many dangers.  At one point during his journey, he encounters a female character who abruptly vanishes before he can reach her.  After this, the forest eventually gives way to a crumbling city environment, and then a factory setting.  On completion of the final puzzle, the boy is thrown through a pane of glass and back into the forest (in slow motion which takes AGES to watch). He walks a short distance until he again encounters the girl again.  The end.
After the game ends, the player is sent back to the main menu and should realize that the boy and girl are both dead, since the exact same setting is presented, but instead of the boy and girl there are two lumps on the ground with flies buzzing all around them.
From the title, we can assume the characters were dead all along.  Nobody saw that coming, right?  Oh wait...  Anyone who knew anything about the word "Limbo" saw it coming.
[SPOILERS OVER!!!]
One redeeming quality of this game is that it actually has a couple of good puzzles.  Some puzzles are creative and difficult.  However, this is overshadowed by the large collection of bad puzzles in the mix.  Most puzzles are trial and error puzzles that are not fun at all.  Some puzzles are hard just because there is some gameplay element that was not explained very well.
I acknowledge that this game is (initially) charming and interesting, but it seems so long and is so boring that I just can't recommend this game for anyone, unless that person is a hipster who likes to think he's cool because he can understand art.

Cuphead is a wonderfully packaged classic cartoon-themed game designed to be unforgivably challenging and aesthetically pleasing.  The game that bears the closest resemblance to this one in my mind is Contra (NES), as there are multiple weapons, bosses, and sidescrolling.
Pros
+excellent gameplay mechanics (dodge, parry, tight controls, super abilities, unique equipment combinations)
+variation between bosses in attack patterns, the environments, and the boss phases
+well produced soundtrack that fits the theme closely
+hand drawn animations (yes, look for the production video on YouTube on how they did it)
+several unlockables and secrets
Cons
-Not for you if you are a newcomer to games that require quick reaction time, recognizing video/audio cues, or finding patterns
-Not for you if you don't have a controller
-Not for you if you lose your cool with trial and error (see above point if you break your controller)
-Not for you if you have any reasonable doubt that $20 is too much for this game given the above and your relative interest in playing this game
Bottom line (TL;DR)
This game is tough but well made and personally gratifying.  You'll look back at the end and think of the challenges you overcame, and (maybe) want do it all again for expert mode!

I'd like to start by talking about a common horror trope: the jump scare. A lot of horror fans are put off by it, and if done poorly, many can see it coming from a mile away. While many could say jump scares are Five Nights at Freddy's big gimmick, there's also a lot of tension in the game regardless. Is there someone waiting outside my door? The door's closed. Are they still there? Am I checking on Foxy enough? Too much? Chica is in the corner camera, should I close the door or check elsewhere? But most importantly of all, will I be able to get through the whole night before I run out of power and Freddy gets me?
What makes FnaF work is in its simplicity. You can't leave the room. All you have are your cameras, the two doors, and their lights, essentially making you a sitting duck. A night will last you about 8.5 minutes, so it's easy to pick up and play. The animatronics are sufficiently creepy, and the dim and flickering lighting creates an unsettling mood. There's also quite a bit of lore if you know where to look *coughgametheorycough*.
Certainly worth $5.

The game is extremely promising but the way its parameters are currently tuned is off and makes it hard to enjoy. Here's a typical example of what's wrong with this game: wake up in the morning, fully warm and rested, eat a hot deer steak, drink half a gallon of water and head outside. All four bars maxed out and the day is sunny and warm. You're thinking - great, I should be able to do a 5 hour hike, work for a while and get home several hours before nightfall. Well, think again. Not 5 hours into the hike, the character is suffering from hypothermia, exhaustion and thirst. By midnight he's on the brink of death from hunger, thirst, exhaustion and cold. It's laughable really.
It's obvious that the developers of this game have never spent any serious time outdoors and have no idea what human beings are capable of surviving. People have survived Siberian gulags and then trekked back to Europe in extreme weather and with little to no food. People have moved to unexplored continents with far less than what the protagonist in this game has, had their crops completely fail and still managed to survive long harsh winters. But in this game, a few hours of walking outside brings you to the brink of death, as if you were walking on the surface of Mars or something.
On a more positive side, the game mechanics are really nice and realistic in emulating the actions you have to take to survive. The cell shaded graphics are pleasing and the way the weather randomly changes makes for a very cool effect. If the developers would take some hints and make this a bit more realistic in terms of what the character can endure, that would be great. I understand that the game is still in Early Access, so the negative nature of this review is probably temporary and I'll be willing to amend it once the game is officially released and all the issues are fixed.

Let's get the really bad things out of the way first. This is by far the buggiest Telltale game I have played (and I have played and finished pretty much all of them) and there are still quite severe graphical gliches and other bugs. One time the camera got stuck on Batman in an awkward pose when the sound from the scene it was suposed to cut to played out (restarting from the last save did not fix it). Peoples heads sometimes turn in an angle that almost give Regan from The Excorcist a run for her money. This week it crashed in the climax of the second episode for me and then forced a 12 GB update. When the update was finished the savefile was seamingly gone (during  the update, they created a new folder for all the save data, and didn't, move your savefile). It was fixable, but then they did the same thing the next day (when they tried to hot fix the update i assume) forcing you to again fix it. This is almost laughably incompetent by a company like Telltale that should know what they are doing when they have used the same engine and playstyle for the last 4 years. It's not a dealbreaker for me, I still love their games overall, but they sure make it hard to defend them sometimes. I would not judge anyone who ripped the game to shreads for the above thou, since that shouldn't be an issue with games that's a year old.
With all that said, this is still a good game if you like Telltales style. If you don't you probably not reading this anyway since you should know what their strengths and weaknesses are, and this game is no difference. There are "choices" and some scenes are entirely different depending on where you choose to go, or if you go as Batman or Bruce. But the real consequenses are mostly minor changes in how people treat or trust you. If you accept that that's what Telltale mean with "the story is tailored to your choices" and don't expect entirely different games with multiple endings, you will probably be satisfied with how different the game plays out.
They manage to find a good balance between playing as Bruce and Batman. The story is overall good even if it takes a very drastic change on some characters, but for the most part it's well handled. It's kind of refreshing to see a new take on Batman, that isn't Frank Miller drivel. The only problem I have is that the main Villain is kind of weak and in the end makes very little sense in their abilities. This makes it so that it doesn't really stick the landing, even if the first episodes are really good. In the end it's better than Game of Thrones, but not as good as The Wolf Among us or Tales from the Broderlands. You will enjoy it if you like Telltales other games.

Following below is my original review, to see my experience from when I was active.
Now noted, I played Terraria a few months ago, did some multiplayer with a few friends, and got bored of it. It has been a few months since I last touched it.
Going into this game, I was launched into the tutorial, and got a far better grasp of the basic mechanics than I did when I first got thrown into Terraria. While both do not require special placement for materials and such, this game gave a different emphasis that yes, even dirt is an important resource.
I think that's what really got me into this game. Every resource you mine actually has a use, and you don't have to dump piles of dirt into a chest so it doesn't clutter your inventory. You actually need dirt now.
Another thing that gives this game an edge against other games in this genre is the fact that you get decent ranged weapons through the tutorial. Normally you get a junk sword and all ranged weapons run on limited ammunition. Here, there's infinite ammo and it serves you well enough until you can research better schematics later on. I think that's important.
Finally, I just like the overall look. The background, the creatures, and your character all have a pleasing look that also saves resources so it doesn't eat up the GPU. It has an art style that branches off just enough where it doesn't look too foreign, but still has its own identity.
All in all, good game. If you get it on sale, you got a really good deal.

There are billboard missions you can take to get more rare stuff (is it the only way?) like aluminium or uranium, they are simple and seem buggy. For example, having two missions to collect 50 dirt immediately completes both if you have 49+ dirt in your inventory, and collect just one more piece of dirt.
When you play the tutorials where you need to shoot humanoid training dummies, it becomes immediately apparent that the hit boxes are... let's just say, you have to hit them in a certain spot, their legs for example are completely off the hit box boundary.
If you have neither played Terraria, or the Terraria 1.3 update, I'd recommend that instead, or keeping an eye on Starbound. Survival.  Straight out.  There's no one out there but you and the animals.  The game tracks your hunger, thirst, body temp, medical ailments(sickness/injury) and calorie intake and usage.  Failing to manage all of these correctly will result in the death of you.
Inventory.  This is your mini game to keep you occupied while trying to defrost your tootsies.  Clothes, food, water,  weapons and miscellaneous supplies all have a purpose and must be maintained to survive successfully.
Animals.  They're out there and so are you.  These towns are only big enough for one sheriff so show them who's boss.  But be warned.  A failed skirmish with a hostile animal can result in fatal injuries.
The environment.  This is the star of the show.  It will stop at nothing to kill you with its sudden storms, blistering winds or vast wilderness where one wrong turn could cost you more than just time.  I was in fog so thick I literally didn't know which way to go and I ended up getting lost.
For a survival game this is top of its class.  Don't let the art style throw you off.  This is the most realistic survival game to date.  No game makes you feel the desperation of scavenging like this one.  Just hoping to find something to eat or drink.  The relief of finding shelter just before nightfall to keep from freezing to death.  The fear of running in to a small pack of wolves as they feast on a dead animal carcass.  Or the absolute dread when night has fallen and you have inefficient supplies to make a fire.
How long can you survive?

Medusa's labyrinth is a first person stealth game set in mythical ancient greece, that is clunky, short and slow to get going. Having said that....when it does get going it's pretty effective at being intense, and making the most of a basic setup.
It's only an hour or so long, and is more of a proof of concept than a full on game  - which I think the creators have admitted to (?) and it's free anyway.....If they do make a complete go of this they've certainly got a lot right here.
It sets up a foreboding atmosphere in the first half an hour, as you wander deeper into a very dark temple / catacomb area, with little happening except for a few nicely paced jumpy events to unsettle you. There's some well written notes that you find lying about that build up the experience quite well as they give a bit of backstory, and lessen what would otherwise be a little bit boring.
But you'll soon find out that the place you're in isn't deserted, and the occupants are none too friendly, or human for that matter.....You have a torch and a bow, though these don't help much as (a) the bow is only for distracting enemy, and (b) torches burn out, and also even with the brightness turned upto full this is a dark game with your light not extending very far. It also gives away your position, meaning you have to chuck it away and move through the darkness if you want to avoid getting your head bashed in.
It's at this point that the slow build up really pays off, and the last half of the "game" is fairly nerve wracking.
I think they've got the atmosphere nailed, and it controls reasonably well (I got stuck behind some scenery once), has good AI, sound effects and decent graphics. Whether or not a full game traipsing through dingy almost pitch black environments would be as interesting, or sustainable, is up for debate. But this is a freebie, and quite spooky, so if you like to be put on edge you could do worse than check this out.
