To start: I used to add a much longer header to these reviews, but since it made reviews too long to submit from time to time, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery. Also, this review will be written with respect to Half-Life and Opposing Force, so there are spoilers ahead for those two.
Gameplay: Half-Life 1 had some interesting things, Opposing Force had the same interesting things but with even more interesting things. Blue Shift has less things in it than even Half-Life 1. Calling this an expansion pack is, to be quite frank, something of an insult to Opposing Force. You don't even get all of the human arsenal, let alone ANY the alien arsenal. Enemy design has gone back as well; you fight a total of six different types of enemies throughout this "expansion" pack. There aren't even any bosses!  Level design is... well, it's alright. Nothing too impressive, but nothing really worth slandering. The big kicker is the fact that I beat it in just over two hours, not even dying once on Normal Mode (apart from a not so good platforming section). It feels like something of a fan project as opposed to the quite frankly stellar performance put forward in making Opposing Force. This was two years later, so there really was no excuse. 5/10.
Story: Well, maybe the story makes up for it? Not really. You're a security guard, some things happen and you exit Black Mesa. No intrigue whatsoever; hell, the G-Man makes one appearance. That's it. Definitely another disappointment. 4/10.
Graphics: Yet another step back from Opposing Force. Even after just having beaten it, I'm struggling to remember anything about the Black Mesa complex's area design apart from the final "area" of the game. You go to Xen which is neat and all, but again; it just feels like more of the same. It's just as technically adept as Opposing Force, so I don't really have any complaints there. It's just that the area design feels so damn lackluster. 3/5.
Sound: There's a couple of songs for the OST which are relatively intense and used for all of ten seconds, leaving you feel kinda unfulfilled. Voice acting is just alright now that there's no G-Man, and the sound design is pretty much on the same level as Opposing Force. 3/5.
Overall scores are: 5/4/3/3; cumulative score of 5.0/10. Out of the "main" Half-Life 1 series, play Half-Life 1 and Opposing Force. If you really wanna see what this one is about, just watch a speedrun. It'll save you an hour and a half and about $5. Really, really lackluster.

Cartoonish art style is the best way to describe this game. It is obvious to see it is drawn by hand with these lucid and fantasy colors. It is a perfect interpretation of what is like being on drugs. It's not my cup of tea, but it definitely has an unique art style.
Soundtrack is relaxing, just as it should. You can tell it is here they drew a lot of inspiration from Tiny Bang Story, which is one my favorite soundtracks of all time. Beautiful piano medleys throughout the whole game.
It is definitely not as good as the more mainstream point-and-click adventure games, but it never claims to be. It is a fun and short game, which all fans of these types of game should experience. The price is definitely worth it too.

Morphopolis is a very artsy game.  Beautiful and colorful and a little surreal.
At it's core it's a hidden object puzzle game where you find objects and then use them on other objects. Sometimes this initiates a puzzle that you have to complete.
Some objects in the environment you need to click on to initiate the ability to go on an object hunt which was a little annoying, though not unfair. Just remember if it looks important click on it once to see if it pops up that it wants something.
The game barely has any instructions and mostly you're just on your own.  But despite the lack of any prompts that tell you what to do the game doesn't just leave you hanging as the puzzles do make enough sense that one should be able to piece together what you need to do. I only have problems with one puzzle that I needed to look up how to do it.
Morphopolis feels like it was designed to play on a tablet, phone, or any sort of touch screen as the controls are 'click & hold' or 'click & drag' oriented. Though this did not really subtract from the game for me.
The game is short (I beat it in about 2 hours) and does not really have any replay value but I still say buy it if you got a couple of extra dollars available. It's a nice little game to waste some time on and it's dang pretty to look at.
P.S. You'll 100% the game on your first play-though probably.

Project Zomboid in itself is a good game. It really is. The community is helpful, the developers are descriptive in updates, and the Wiki is an offical Wiki, not some Wiki(a). (If you don't know what I mean, I mean the Wiki site is in the format of Wikipedia, not like the Wikia site, which is different.) I also see this as a game that won't die off in a year or so. Build 25 added 3D models, (although I wish you could turn them off :P) soon other survivors will be (RE)added, and multiplayer is finally thawed from the closed beta state.
There are a few problems, however.
The game is INCREDIBLY hard after surviving for a few weeks or so, even without Zombies, the game would be quite hard still. Now difficulty is not a bad thing, at all, it's more of a blessing. When you mess up, it really feels like it was your fault, not the games. If you leave an oven on overnight, your house will burn down and you might have to jump a window.
Back to the real problems:
Even if you have the best graphic card in the world, I'd think this game would still lag a little bit. It needs to be optimised a smidge more, but it's most definitely not unplayable.
SCHOOLS ARE THE WORST PLACE. DO NOT ENTER.
The price tag. While this game is good, it's not quite worth 15 dollars yet. It's still in Beta/Alpha, I can't tell, there are a lot of alpha problems and beta graphics. The audio option is only in Build 25, and while the music is good at first, it can get very repetitive very quickly. Game, I'm cooking food, not fighting the night itself.
I've noticed no bugs suprisingly, just heard about them
RANDOM QUESTION: IS IT A HORROR GAME? NO. It's like DayZ, or 7 Days to Die, but like Don't Starve.
Final Score: 7.8/10, buy it, but realize it's not done.

I had overslept. My peaceful trek into the wilderness to harvest small game had taken a horrific turn. Blood pouring from my head and infection setting in, I stumbled back to the shack, the only respite in this desolate wilderness I cared to call home. I no longer cared about the hunger that tore at my abdomen. I had made a miscalculation, and that error would prove to be fatal.
I stammered through the door and took what little medicine I had. Whoever had lived here before me had left a few menial supplies. I could think of nothing but the disease festering in my open wounds. I laid down to rest... Surely in a few hours the antibiotics would take hold. I had come too far to die from an invisible enemy.
I lurched awake. I had overslept. Not even embers glowed in my woodstove. The cold had crept in during the night and enveloped me in my slumber. My body was completely numb. I looked around my shack but could see nothing. My heartbeat throbbed in my ears, strong and rythmic. Something was wrong.
I stumbled through the shack. My vision was blurred, I could barely stand... My traps... In my panic I had forgotten to empty my traps. I was starving.
Panic once again siezed me. I burst from my shack, shuffling into the pounding blizzard. I had to make it to my traps, I had to get food. I disappeared into the wilderness, viciously clawing through the snow. Hypothermia had set in.
Then I was lost, completely void of all sense of direction. The blizzard hung like a screen over my eyes. I looked around desperately, trying to recognize whatever I could. I had walked this path many times. I crawled a few more feet. Then I understood. This was it.
I could hear wolves in the distance, their growls lost beneath my own heartbeat... I had overslept. I sat down in the frigid snow and let the hunger take me.

So, I played this game a really long time ago because of the several recomendations I read, about it being an indie gaming jewel and the narrative being compelling and enticing. and I did not exactly enjoy it. Now It showed up as free to play for the weekend, so I wanted to give it another chance to find out whether or not the rough edges had been sanded, and my veredict is... it is EXACTLY the same game I played almost two years ago, down to the pixel. I am certain it has its niche of people that will love it, but for me, this one's a definite no because:
-Just as I remember, the game moves at a snail's pace, and literally any and everything in the zee moves faster than your starter ship. There is no fast travel to locations you already charted, no auto-pilot and no way to speed up time, so about 50% of your gaming experience is spent staring at the screen while your ship moves as fast as a slug on sandpaper
-The tutorial is barely there, and it's the total absolute bare minimum an unpaid intern on his first day should do to be called a tutorial. The game has a metric♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of knowledge to learn, and it is tossed at you all at once, with barely any explaining.
-The death mechanic is not exactly well implemented, dying sets you back way too often, and it more often than not, be due to circumstances you had no way to avoid. Back when I first played this almost 2 years ago, a lifeberg popped out of nowhere right in front of me: faster, harder, sturdier and stronger than me by several orders of magnitude and an attack on sight behavior. I could not outrun it, I could not fight it. Almost two years later, the experience repeats itself, and I was not in some far away bereft land, Ihad barely traveled a couple nautical miles away from London and an unbeatable enemy was already there.
All in all, game feels slow, plays slow, explains little and gives even less after a long time playing it, and honestly a game that requires a 10 hour grind before you get to the good part is plain and simply not for me. I'm all for roguelikes and perma-death mechanics, but when it takes you 30 hours just to get back to where you were at, after dying because of randomness, it does not feel engaging, it's just a grind. Imma just uninstall and find something else, because even with the discount, the game is simply not my cup of tea, would probably gift it again should I receive it for free.

On the whole this is a pretty great game. I sunk tons of hours into it and got lost in building my city. It is a little annoying to try and figure out all the rules of the game on your own, as the descriptions of certain items are misleading. Looking up a guide is a good thing to do before you start, because a good start can really make a difference. Luckily I had a friend that had been playing already, so I was able to get tips from him, but for new players it can be hard. Also there are frustrating times in the game, especially when populations start to crash. You could be fine one minute and have a ton of excess resources, but be running out of everything the next minute, so keeping a watch on firewood and food is extremely important. Also the randomness of harvests can be annoying, as I once had a year where all my farms produced nothing, which made my food levels deplete and population starve, which was really annoying. Other things like that can be very annoying, which is this games downfall.
But on the whole, playing this game is enjoyable. It has its faults and problems, but it is fun. It can be super challenging, but that just makes overcoming those challenges all the more rewarding.

This game is atmopspheric and unforgiving. EVERYTHING wants to kill you. Sometimes it gets so lonley, you'll be desperate for the fear of a wildlife attack.
Please know going into this game, it asks A LOT from you. To be attentive, to invest time, consideration, and to gamble a bit. Also, you will spend a lot of time literally standing/sleeping/walking, trying not to die. I hope you like spending time indoors in the dark. You really do get out what you put in. If you want, you can survive for a couple weeks barely moving, sleeping your life away... but eventually you have to go find more food, or light a fire.
The Long Dark has high highs and low lows. I'm re-writing this review on a high - have always rated it as a "buy" though.
You have to watch everything. The cold, the wind, the light, the dampness, enemy wildlife, small and steep drops, carrying space, food and water allotment.
The negatives I used to have for this game are gone. They fixed a lot of the glitches, so now if you're injured or die... it's more natural, not something bogus.
To finish this up... sometimes everything can be going perfect. Full health, warm, fixed clothes, water, weapons, gear, sleep, suns out, no wind, clear roads...... and then fog rolls in and you lose your bearings. You realize you're low on tinder. You went out too far and nights coming. Or the wind is picking up. Or there's wildlife. Hell, maybe you misstep cause you're not paying attention.
Like I said. Unforgiving. But beautiful. Fulfilling. Haunting. Challenging.
EDIT: Oh, and if you're Canadian... you may have been fortunate/unfortunate enough to experience some of it IRL. Like when checking the temp as -20, you think "cold, but we can tough it out." Then it hits -40 and windchill? You know to get the eff inside.

This was a very interesting game to play and it would be (if it's not already) a great game to keep however some pros and cons are to be presented:
Pros:
-Great story and diffrent little stories and it allows you to see into the daily lives of the denizens of the ocean (however this is just once, however the little side-quest is a nice touch)
-huge map to explore with diffrent islands to visit each with a diffrent personality
-It does have a nice sort of satisfaction if you do manage to win... or lose... if you manage to do a lot
Cons:
-Exploring can become repitative and eventually boring you will be tearing your hair out because oh no you just died and guess what? if your playing on the harder mode, you have to repeat everything all over again (although it is a point they make about frequent deaths... it's still pretty annoying, and ppersonally is not exactly fun to do)
-Money can be a real b**** to get as you would have to go back and fourth...slowly... to each port to earn a reliable and steady income.
-If you are not into reading then this IS NOT THE GAME FOR YOU, it has a crapton of text to read (optional if you already seen it)
-money will evaporate very quickly unless you're super lucky and receive enough money to improve the chances of earning more.
-The rewards you get for completing quests as they are very poor and would require you to actually lose money and resources overall, so just doing the repitative motion of gathering ship reports would be more reliable and actually more profitable than doing quests, espically the ones that require you to go to far off places.
In conclusion, this is a game meant for peple who like grinding, reading, frequent deaths and diffculty, and going to and fro diffrent places. Although the story(if you manage to do enough) is pretty good and deep. Although I do hope in the future they do improve the game play and reward system a bit, i would say without the cons this is a very good game.

Ever wanted to play System Shock 2 but were afraid that your friends would laugh at you for playing a game with such ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics? Well, then Bioshock is for you!
Play as Jack, the human equivalent of a pickle jar dressed up in an ugly sweater. Do what no rational person would ever do and ride a bathosphere into the dark below from an ominous, cult-like lighthouse in the middle of the Atlantic after surviving an improbable and unreasonably catastrophic plane crash. Try to piece together the puzzle that is the plot of the game as you are guided by foreshadow-the-character into a surprise twist ending. Feel the helplessness and claustrophobia around you as you scavenge the gruesome remains of the Von Braun's crew for ammunition and sustainance. Wait, which game is this again?
Bioshock features breathtaking combat where the player chooses between using steampunk airsoft guns or deadly jazz hands on deranged and drugged-up psychopaths. Experience exciting mechanics, such as the plumber hacking minigame. Search every trash can, bathroom stall, and decrepit wardrobe for your next EVE (read: heroin) fix. Choose from a variety of gear and equipment to approach every unique situation... or just machine gun everything to death after hustling every vending machine on the map for all of their machine gun ammo.
Widely recognized as "revolutionary" or "genre-defining" by "video game veterans", Bioshock suffers from a widespread case of "pretty good, but way overhyped." If you've always dreamed of visiting an underwater metropolis built by objectivist loonies, then this game is probably worth a gander.

HI,
I have never written a review for a steam game before, but i feel that this little gem deserves my support.
what is this game: A ZOMBIE APOCALYSPE SURVIVAL SIMULATOR. this game is about casual joes and casual janes left behind in a city full of zombies, you try to survive in (depending on game mode) as long as you can. its almost inevitable that you'll die, so you're basically playing the STORY OF HOW YOU DIED. you WILL perish, and even if so, you can rejoin the world you just played in with a new casual person, while having available all the progress that the previous character has made; and will probalby run into your zombiefied former char.
Players who dont care about a "great" story (which in my opinion is still to be invented for cpu-games) and/or feel that sprite graphics are charismatic will find him/herself enjoying this game A LOT! btw: even though the graphics are (in comparison) greatly outdated, you get used to them in a blink (i LOVE them!!!) and its the combination of the amtosphere and the gruesome sounds that scare me more than any other super-high-def game is supposed to be shocking you.
controls are simple and great and complicated at the same time. micromanagement of your stash can get a bit of a drag, but if you stick to a (your) system, all is good and it makes perfect sense! combat is damn good fun and will leave you quite shoked sometimes how carelessly you can massaker a family of five in their house, just for a bag of chips and some dogfood ;)
crafting is great and necessary, you'll be able to skill you character with it. the multitude of hazards are amazing, even just peeping through a curtained window can cost you your dear neck!
for me the most complete and most intelligent zombie game out there, while still in alpha!!! try the demo and if you like it please pay the ridiculously cheap €14.- (with the date of this review). it is well worth every cent!!! the community in this game is very nice, helpful and mature so if you would like to contribute, there's much to do and everyone will assist.
If you (after having seen hollywood zombie films) think you could survive in a so much smarter way than the protagonists, get this game and try out how long you can make it! I DARE YOU!!!

What I got was a narrated walking simulator, and not even a good one (like Dear Esther). The premise is that Dave (the developer) is releasing this compilation of unreleased games created by his estranged friend, which strongly intimates that this is a true story. However, the stronger links between the games and the signature off-the-wall style of Dave's development of The Stanley Parable are littered throughout ALL of the so-called "unfinished games", which suggests that it's all him.
The narrated story was interesting, but I couldn't help but feel that this was a cheap take on what he's done before. It's not an indie darling - it's a so-so walking sim with a decent first-person audio narrative.

TL;DR: fun game, has a lot of gameplay and UI/UX issues, get it in a sale.
I'm not sure I like the game, but it sure is addictive. It's addictive in the same sense that most unforgiving games with permadeath are: that drive to give it another shot, see if a different approach may yield better results, applying what little we learned in this round to hopefully do better in the next one. In this regard, it reminds me a lot of FTL.
The graphics are adequate and help create a fitting atmosphere. Some elements are just so-so, e.g. the vortices or what I assume represents bad weather, and the ships are merely adequate. But these small blemishes can be easily overlooked. The sound and music are also very fitting, and it appears the music reacts to both your location and present situation. Every port and their surrounding area seems to have its own soundscape. I probably should pay more attention to the sound, but I'm one of those people who automatically blocks out the music on a conscious level, although it still helps set the mood.
But the one thing every reviewer agrees on: this game is merciless, and there's a certain learning curve. While I don't mind permadeath per se, in this game, it clashes with the narrative elements. Every time you die, you start over with a new captain. The legacy mechanic allows you to retain some stats/belongings from the previous captain, but every storyline they participated in is reset. They can receive the same quests, or enlist the same officers, but the stories play out the exact same way, word for word, *from the very beginning*. And this is where the game falls a bit short for me: it wants to be two conflicting things at once. It wants to be a narrative-driven game, but because it also wants to be a merciless permadeath game, it forces you to reread paragraphs and paragraphs of narrative. So after a short while, you develop this habit of just skipping or skimming it, at which point you start to wonder why it's there to begin with since you no longer even bother reading the new text.
On to the UI. Let me start by saying I'm a couch player, so I need to enlargen the UI elements and fonts to make this game playable on the TV from 10ft away. I think it's very commendable that the authors put these options in there, although the lack of controller support is puzzling since the game would lend itself so well to being played with a controller. However, some elements could've been better. The buttons in the main menu offer too little contrast. Especially from a distance, without UI scaling. And the flow through the ingame screens lacks, well, flow... In your Gazetteer (book that serves as the ingame menu), many pages are redundant. There's this button after visiting a place "Back to the city". Clicking it, rather than taking you to the "City" menu, just shows you a page telling you that you can just click "London" at the right edge of the screen. The harbourmaster's summary of your "action items" in the form of a list of messages contains no clickable items and disappears until your next visit when dismissed. After interacting with one of your officers, you're taken back to an unrelated screen devoid of any information or relevance, rather than back to the Officers screen from where you came. All in all, the gazetteer is a jumbled mess. There are even parts of the game where it simply states that to unlock a certain interaction, a certain status "must be !", as if someone forgot to put in the template variable that will be filled in with the actual value. It's little things like this that give the game an unpolished and unfinished look.
And then there's the gameplay. It's easy to get hooked on this game, if you're the kind of person who enjoys starting over and devising ever better strategies. But some things are just boring busywork. You're supposed to report back on ports you visited, but doing so requires you to write these reports in the first place. This requires you to actually click a button when docked, nested in one of the menu items. This is a redundant gameplay element, a piece of senseless busywork. It's not like there's this situation developing at these ports, and every time you visit, the story progresses and you learn new details. The text is more along the lines of "these fishermen play their cards close to their chest and reply mostly with evasive answers, but after a while you manage to piece together enough clues to write your report". Every port has its own variation, but every time you visit the same port it's the exact same text. Filing these reports separately upon returning to London is even more tedious. And it's not the only instance of busywork in this game: the only way to obtain news is to go to your lodging and explicitly click "read the paper". These things should not require user interaction, if they have a place in the game at all.
And then there's the "everything is an item" mechanic. You can collect secrets, but it's abstract. You just receive an item called "Secret". You can have multiple, and they can be used/traded. This leads to ridiculous scenarios such as you learning a secret from an NPC, which becomes a "Secret" inventory item, which you then spend on the Cladery Heir in the form of "revealing something about your past" in order to improve your Hearts stat by 1. And literally everything in this game suffers from this illogical mechanic: read the paper in London, and you have one "News" item which several ports are interested in. But if you use it at one port, it's gone and can no longer be used at another. Secrets, news, ... are not modeled as knowledge, but as consumables which are stored in your inventory.
In summary:
Despite its shortcomings, the game is still quite addictive. Whether I find it enjoyable is something I haven't fully decided yet. Some issues with the game are easy to ignore, e.g. the "everything is an item" mechanic, while weird and illogical, is just something you have to accept and get used to. But the game suffers from a schizofrenic undecisiveness about what it wants to be: some parts (the secrets, the tales of terror, ...) are so abstract and devoid of detail, whereas other parts such as the quests drown in narrative. And this narrative clashes with the "fail often and restart from zero" approach to progression, which leads to repitition, causing the player to ignore or skim the narrative entirely.
Would I recommend it? Sure, it has enough good elements to keep things interesting. But not at full retail. It's simply too unpolished and even unfinished to justify the asking price. Especially compared to other games that cost less (e.g. FTL), and are more polished and more focused in their gameplay elements.

Excellent survival game...even for ALPHA / EA.  Puts survival and open-map genre onto a whole new level.  It's unique, it's tough, it's got depth and struggle.  It will test your skills and abilities.  Every decision you make needs to be calculated, thought out ahead of time and executed with precision timing which depends on time of day, health, hunger, thirst, supplies, weather, local resources, food supply and storage and much more.
- You start on a map of your choosing and all maps are connected together so you can travel across a vast area.  The maps are also open map and doesn't constraint the player to a single pathway, you're free to explore the area in its entirety and not forced to take paths.
- Good balance between a game and realism.  Loot can be make it out alive today or die tomorrow and is very random giving replay value pretty high and intense gameplay throughout.
- Optimizations are improving.  Haven't played for a couple months and had to play on low settings.  Came back and put settings on medium with bigger resolution and got better performance now than I did couple months ago.  So great job on optimization and for lower end computers!
- Ability to use your surroundings is becoming more available to players.  For example, you can break down shelving, crates, chairs for materials.
-
The only NPC you encounter are wildlife, some people may like this, some people may not.
I personally wouldn't mind finding other NPC considering it is a area that is habitable and not a area that is abandoned so seeing other people would not be a big thing. They can give you tips on upcoming weather conditions, tips on random loots spot, trade offers, maybe even gather quests for unique loot only available by doing those quests...maybe that is more of a "story mode" feature which isn't available in ALPHA.  As for breaking the 'survival' aspect of it with NPC, I do not think so because these are winter cabins people goto for vacations.  It is a area that is habitable and not a area that is abandonned so seeing other people would not be a big thing.  So right from the get go you being "dropped" into this habitable place alone and seeing not a soul is kind of awkward to say the least.
- One thing that quirks me though is you cannot see out of windows when you enter a small cabin.  Looking out the window to see the weather or if any wolves are outside would be nice without actually having to exit the cabin to check.
- Although the buildings are not randomly placed, after a few runs you know where to go for buildings and those "hotspots" for certain items reducing replay value somewhat.  Most players will develop a pretty static run meaning their path of travel on the same maps will be identical for each session or game (straight from one building or loot spot to the next).
- Not really a con but personal preference.  No third person view.  I like looking at my character as I play, see the clothing you put on, backpack, how ragged your clothes are.  The more worse the condition the clothing is you could make it look tattered and ripped up on the character.

I do recommend this game to anyone interested in this type of story driven action adventure, but especially to those who are fans of the Telltale stories in general.

This is an excellent game.  Right now it is only in Sandbox Mode, but the Sandbox is very good, and the world the devs have created is beautiful.  There are currently 5 interlocking maps, and together they comprise a massive world.  The object is pure survival- you spawn randomly in the Canadian wilderness with a backpack and a bedroll, and you have to brave the elements and wild animals.  The scenery, especially the weather and sky, is beautiful and really immerses you in the experience.  They are still tweaking the details, but the devs are very receptive to feedback, and each update has been a good step forward.  Buy it now, no need to wait for the Story Mode, which is coming soon.  The only fair criticism of the game as it is is that it is a true survival game - the point is to try to go as long as you can, and in the Sandbox Mode there is no way to "win."  Make your own goals and see how you do! 10/10

Wow !! Where do I begin ?
Arguably the best $11 I have ever spent on computer gaming ever !!
Any game that can suck 255+ hours out of me in the last 40 days must be something special and in my opinion The Long Dark is just that. Its not perfect by any stretch but let me be clear on this...it's Pro's vastly outweigh its Con's.
I'll explain my opinion, Sandbox Voyageur 200+ days:
Pro's:
Highly addictive game play that MAKES you want to keep playing.
Very challanging but fair
The smallest accomplishments feel huge because your game is on the line the whole time....love Permadeath.
So far, 5 great regions each with its own Pro's and Con's
Great job on the weather, lighting, ambiance etc
Tools, equipment, food etc all very intuitive and easy to use menu(s)
So it's simple and clean and alot of fun and should be in everyone's Steam Library.
Now for the Con's...and please take this in the spirit in which it is intended...I love this game and only want to see it improve since I will be playing it even more once the divorce goes through (way too many late nights)
Con's:
No auto-Walk...at least I can't find it. Burning out my hands on those long treks.
Wind, wind, and more wind....and almost always in my face no matter which direction I go. Makes for some long returns to base and god help you if you are loaded down.
Graphics get screwy every now and then, good thing I am not "sensitive to the effect".
Food, matches etc going bad I think needs to be tweeked. I can live with the current rate that food goes bad but matches going bad really bugs me. There are more than enough of them in the game...thats not the point.
Spraining my wrist while walking. Really? Like I said before, these are all minor things but I hate forced/contrived hardships.
5 great regions so far yes...but I need more...much more. After 200 plus days I have nothing new to do, I am super stocked on everything, 100 + arrows and ammo, staging areas in each region, even been to the summit several times and cleaned it out. I want to keep discovering !!
Again I am incredibly happy with my purchase. Here are a few things I think would keep me playing if not playing more.
Suggestions:
More things to do: Kill a fox, make a warmer hat and scarf from it or how about a moose, very tough to take down but lots of meat 40kgs, and the hide can be used to make a larger backpack with a slightly increased weight allowance. You show a shovel on the Main screen but I have yet to see one in game. Make it accessible if it isn't already so we can dig a survival fort in a snow bank, and give us candles as well. An axe and the ability to chop down trees with those logs weighing alot but lasting a really long time on the fire. I personally don't want to go the route of being able to build my own log cabin but I wouldn't mind being able to repair existing ones (new regions perhaps) to a certain level(warmer).
In terms of regions: Sea Side Ship Yard, Valley of the Frozen, Farmland Acres, Fishing Village, Mining Town.
That's all. Buy this game. You won't regret it. Developers like this should be supported. Hopefully they continue to release content and keep us hooked.

It's nice to look at, dripping with atmosphere and even a bit eerie thought with health packs, super powers and bullets galore it's not scary and death is little more then an inconvenience with the vital chambers running free of charge. Still this one of the few shooters that gives the player the freedom to do things their way, do you hack the security systems into booby-traps, doge your way them or just blow them up? Do you go in guns blazing or sneak around taking down targets one by one? Sadly it also uses the mortal choice gimmick that's become so popular in games following Fable without really expanding on it's potential so you end up with the same old Good ending vs Bad ending with no gray area, which just comes off as a bit lazy.
My second gripe is lack of an inventory screen, few things are more annoying then being loaded down with guns and not knowing how many bullets each one actually has without going though them one by one which is an even bigger hassle then you throw in the special ammo each gun has as well. Why do we have special ammo again? I already have a list of super powers latterly at my finger trips so throwing in magic bullets just seems like overkill. Odds are most players are just going to pick their favorite plasmids/guns and never bother with the rest. Most of which are to situational to be of any real use (Call Big Daddy, Enrage).
Despite all the gripes though Bioshock is still a very good game, the story is shallow but the game play is solid. It has its minor annoyances like Dumb AI and Sound spam but still avoids the really awful ones such as QTEs. All and all it reminds me of the old school shooters where the idea was to shoot bad guys and have fun, not force you to watch an interactive movie while the game basically plays it self. Its good to see developers still know how to make a decent shooter.

Audiosurf converts any music in your pc in an obstacle course to be traversed with a variety of ships with distinct powers and gameplay styles.
+The idea, while not outrageously original, is really cool and nicely executed. Literally whatever music you dump into the game will become a track with its difficulty based on the speed, complexity and flow of the song. It's really fun to play this game to one of your favorite songs, and even a barebone experience without any gameplay variations is nice.
+3 tiers of difficulty and various different ships with equally different mechanics, that range from a simple, straightforward ride to enjoy the music and the track to score-busting abilities that greatly change the pace of the game in favor of a more proper "game" experience compared to the simpler, "experience"-style base ship. There's even the co-op ship!
+Those obsessed with leaderboards will of course find a whole lot of them here.
+It's cheap, it's small, it runs on a toaster and is perfect for short sessions too, while still having a hardcore appeal thanks to its more elaborate ships and higher difficulties.
-It's a simple game with a simple concept and it does that and nothing more, so you'd better make sure it fits your style.
-Visually the game looks... kind of nice, hypnotizing and trippy with its disco colors and feel, but it's quite basic on this side. Audiosurf 2, which is out by the way, has much more flair and options, if you want a more complete experience, but it's also significantly more expensive and has quite some useless fluff in it, so some people still favor this game over its sequel.
-Not all tracks make for great... tracks (forgive me). Slow music (i.e. some jazz, ballads, romantic songs etc) will produce slow, boring circuits with nearly no difficulty. Beware of the opposite end of the spectrum, since songs with a high bpm can instead turn into extremely difficult tracks.
Audiosurf is a classic example of a very simple game that, depending on your personal liking, can have as much longevity as is the music you can feed it. You can like this game because it is a good offer for record hunters, or because it's an entertaining way to interact with your music beyond just listening to it. If you think that's the case, the bunch of euros this game costs are surely worth it.

The most entertaining multiplayer fps so far that has just the right amount of realism (this review is based on 'Realism' -mode of the game). Getting shot gets you killed (or disabled which is the same as killed in game terms) most of the time, depending on the weapon you get shot with: higher caliber weapons drop you with more certainty while pistols require more accuracy. Getting shot in the head or the heart (yes, the game lets you know where you were hit) kills anyone instantly. If you get lucky enough to survive a shot, you must spend a few seconds bandaging the wound or you will bleed out and die (yeah, not very realistic but very entertaining and exciting gamewise!). Also, sometimes you survive being shot for the few moments it takes you to bleed out from a serious wound that you cannot bandage: your screen starts to go black and you can no longer move, aim, reload or switch weapons. You can empty your current weapon in the general direction of the enemy sometimes getting lucky enough to hit them. Heroic effort, that! Nothing can save you from dying in this state, however.
The game simulates suppression by turning the screen gradually black and white while a loud thumping of your own heart can be heard. This indicates your soldier panicking in the midst of an artillery barrage (which causes the most suppression in the shortest amount of time), getting shot at (bullets hitting near you gradually make you panic) and finally fellow soldiers getting hit and dying near you. In game terms, you aim is lowered by the additional weapon sway and the screen effects make it harder (not impossible, just more difficult) to aim accurately.
The two sides (US and Imperial Japanese) are balanced in a way that - despite their numerous differences - offer a different experience in gameplay. Both sides have a set of limited roles ranging from the single team leader, several squad leaders, machine gunners, assault troops, snipers and an indefinite amount of riflemen up to the team size of 32 players. In addition the US get flamethrowers, and engineers carrying trench guns, while the Imperial Japanese have 'Knee-mortar' -soldiers.
Also the technology of the time is - to my knowledge - displayed accurately: the US soldiers are equipped with semi-automatic weapons (M1) most of the time while the Imperial japanese troops have to make do with their bolt action rifles (Type 38, Type 99). In some maps, like Guadalcanal, the US troops have bolt-action rifles (Springfield) as well since the M1-Garands had not yet been delivered to them (as is historically accurate). All in all, the US have more firepower at their disposal at any given time.
In return, the Imperial Japanese troops have bayonets from the beginning (which the US soldiers lack until upgraded) and they can banzai charge - resulting in higher suppression resistance - causing suppression in the enemy the more soldiers are joined in the charge - and the ability to withstand more hits than usual (headshots and shots through the heart kill instantly, as normally). The US troops suffer from suppression more easily than the Imperial Japanese troops. Japanese officers also get katanas, which are a cool way of disposing opponents.
In terms of weaponry, the Imperial Japanese soldiers can use their grenades as booby traps: 2 can be in place at the most by a single soldier at any given time. If you plant a third, the first one disappears. Yeah, again not very realistic but it balances the game. The booby traps can be seen plainly if placed on an open terrain with no vegetation and they can be detonated by shots, grenades or artillery fire. US soldiers walking over or very near one detonate it and most often die instantly while the Imperial Japanese soldiers can walk over them without triggering them. An US soldeir can, however shoot at a booby trap to detonate it in the face of any enemy soldiers (there's actually an achievement for this!).  The knee-mortar (as inaccurately named by US troops of the time; some poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s actually tried firing it from their knee, often  breaking their thighbone as a result) is basically a grenade launcher which must be setup prior firing. It can be deadly in accurate hands but is often a cause of accidental team kills among new players trying it, don't get discouraged if this happens and remember to apologize for team kills! A knee-mortar soldier gets 5 grenades to shoot at respawn, which can be replenished once at a single supply point like any other ammunition.
The flamethrower that the US  have, is a weapon feared by many Imperial Japanese players. A mere touch of its flames will kill you almost instantly and the flames fill a bunker quickly and completely leaving nothing alive inside. In contrast, the fuel runs out rather quickly, the range is limited,  and the US soldier carrying it is perhaps the most targeted soldier among enemy troops.
Both sides' team leaders must coordinate with their squad leaders to bring down artillery fire on, or near the enemy. This mostly acts as an area denial behind capture points so that the defending or attacking players are denied access to secure it. Soldiers finding themselves inside a barrage must get out of there quickly or get killed by the blasts: the game mechanic of artillery kills anyone inside the area over time. If you're very lucky, you can survive for a few seconds to run into safety.
The game has a honor system with ranks starting from 0 (new players) and ending in 100 - the highest rank available. The honor rank is account based and it is shown on a 'kill list' rotating on the upper right corner of the display (who killed who, how and where the shot it if a vulnerable spot) whenever you die or kill an opponent. You never know where the shot came from (unless you actually saw it your field of vision) as the camera locks instanly as you are killed so you can not look around to spot the enemy while dead.
The individual roles on a side (rifleman, machinegunner, squad leader etc.) get experience (team points) points based on performance in battle: staying near you squad leader or team leader grants you extra team points whenever you kill someone or help capture an objective (which in itself grants several points). Also extra points are awarded for killing someone FROM the object zone and even more if the TARGET was in the object zone as well. Normally, you get 2 ream points from a kill and -2 for a team kill.
A team kill can be forgiven by a player by saying 'np' in the public chat (the 'np' is not shown in actual chat) which removes the penalty from the player who caused it. It is generally polite to apologize for team kills and forgive them if the player causing it apologized. Sometimes you can guess with almost certainty that a team kill was an accident. Sometimes you just make the mistake of running into an area where someone just said they'd throw a grenade at or the team leader announced that the artillery barrage would strike in: in these cases you should own your mistake and 'np' immediately, especially in the case of team leader's artillery barrage which could result in numerous team kill penalties quickly. If you get enough team kills, whether accidental or not, you get kicked from the match and can't rejoin until the map changes.
Respawns in the game are periodic (a rotation of 16 seconds, I think) simulating waves of reinforcements arriving. The team leader has a limited ability (with a cooldown period) to instantly respawn all dead players. Both teams have a set number of tickets which dwindle as players keep dying. If the tickets reach zero, spawn protection is disabled and no more respawns can take place. Maps are also time limited and failure by the attacking team to capture an objective will eventually result in a lockdown period of 3 minutes during which they must capture the point or lose despite the time left on the map's time counter.

***DIsclaimer***
I purchased this game upon release into early access.  At that time, many of the advertisements were compairing this game to Terraria, hence the nature of my review
I had a lot of hope for this game.

Let me preface this by saying I love Terraria.  I played a ton of it with friends and by myself back when it was first launched, and again with all the updates with my girlfriend.  I went from thinking it was a 2D Minecraft rip off to a great game that reminds me a bit of your old school games (Ghost and Goblins comes to mind with the new Expert mode)

Terraria had its charm in the exploration.  You died, a lot.  You learned from said deaths.  You learned different materials make different items.  You fail a lot, in funny and unexpected ways (i.e. Farming Wall of Flesh, then realizing that I had been equipping my armor in the social slot).  The exploration was in both the world itself, and the mechanics.  They gave you nothing, said "Here is the world, have fun" and that was it.

Edge of Space forgets that.  I start a new character, and I am inundated with tutorials as if I was a toddler.  The game literally stops everything to tell you to right click to pick up an item from a chest, including a video.  I am all for tutorials done right, but this one is just patronizing.

The UI is just trash.  I have a character menu, inventory, tech, ect.  They are all small enough to fit on the screen all at once, yet they are their own movable UIs with wasted space.  Not to mention if I want to craft something to equip, I may have to go through three different menus for it.  This developer took a huge step backwards in design.

The character control is also a problem.  It just feels slow and unresponsive.  I felt like I was on a server lagging in single player (and with the rig I have, this game should not give me any delays whatsoever).  The feel of everything was just off too.  Mining is aiming a laser at a rock and waiting.  Terraria did it right, because you would hear the clanking as you mined, making it feel like you were doing something.

Lastly is the performance.  It felt like it was running at 30, because I was getting that same blurriness I would get at lower frame rates.  The game however has a FPS counter that was staying at a solid 60.  I pulled up the Steam FPS counter, and low and behold, while it did stay around 60, it would very occasionally dip, but the in game FPS counter stayed at 60.  I have a feeling that this counter is not accurate, and the developer has static text up there, but I will not say 100%.

I will end with this, Have I been harsh on this game, comparing it to Terraria?  Yes, very much so.  They have marketed it as the spiritual successor to Terraria, and thus started the comparison.  Sadly, it fell very short of the mark they were aiming for.
I wish to put this into the actual review itself, since this actually has me hopeful about the future of this game.  From the head developer in the comments from this review "Thank you for your review, i think there rae some valid points we are trying to address. At the same time the game is meant to feel different."  The developer actully listens top criticism in a positive way, which could make this game potentially great in the future.

Short but oh-so-sweet. This is my personal favorite of the expansions (I haven't played Decay). Opposing Force is legendary but in my opinion it tried to do too much and suffered because of it.
Blue Shift, on the other hand, feels more like "vanilla" Half-Life; all the standard weapons (with the exception of the crossbow) are here, as well as all the standard enemies. Yet it still manages to find ways of making the chaos of Black Mesa feel fresh with brilliant level design and lots of neat little scripted sequences; puzzles are clever and obtuse upon first encountering them, but will have you slapping your forehead when you figure them out. Gearbox had two previous games to zero in on what works and what doesn't.
The level design is also seemless and true to the setting and story. (It even starts with a homage to the famous tram ride from the original.) Blue Shift features the best Xen level in the trilogy; while there is some platforming to be found, a trek down a spooky alien steam wrought with waterfalls and deadly fauna plays like something out of Lovecraft.
Lastly, Barney is just a likeable hero. After surviving the resonance cascade and the ensuing aftermath, the story moves forward with your attempt to rescue and subsequently assist a group of scientists in escaping the facility. This turns out to be a very difficult task with many twists and turns. While no traditional boss fight is present, the final area of the game involves a nail-bitingly climactic battle against a vengeful military.
It is also worth mentioning that Blue Shift is the only game in the entire series with
Cons? The usual Half-Life faire: the gunplay, while tense, is hindered by the ridiculous enemy AI and pathfinding; unless they are standing still they are almost impossible to hit, making grenades, rockets and shotgun shells integral to survival. The crosshair is practically invisible at higher resolutions and requires a patch to turn it back to its native blue. I also didn't like the inclusion of Gearbox music, i.e. the soundtrack from Opposing Force, which is terrible for the most part, yet cryptically the game is almost devoid of ambient noise. I will say that the new voice acting was a nice touch, featuring most of the original cast (plus a new character I won't spoil.)
It's also worth nothing that this was the first playthrough where I realized I like the original models better than the HD ones (at least the weapons) and switched them off halfway through.

Half Life 1 was a fantastic first person shooting game released somewhere around 1999. This Blue Shift is the second rather dull expansion pack for Half Life 1. To be blunt, the first expansion Opposing Force is better, because it offers more guns, new gameplay mechanics and a lot of new monsters. Blue Shift however offers nothing new except new levels that will take you under 4 hours to complete the first time around.
Blue Shift takes you through Black Mesa and Xen once again when everything goes wrong and aliens invade. You start the expansion riding the tram to work (just like Half Life 1) after taking an optional training course that is literally the same training course from Half Life 1.
The gameplay is more challenging than the original game in both good and bad ways. The good way is the game shows off its artificial intelligence by pitting you... Barney Calhoun, a blue shift security guard at Black Mesa, against hundreds of marines sent into the Black Mesa facility. Usually you fight 10 marines at a time in wide open areas. The enemies will scatter when you throw grenades, run away from you, try to flank you and fan out so you're not shooting enemies like dominoes.
The negative ways that the expansion is challenging comes from several dark areas with dozens of head crabs jumping at you around every turn. It feels cheap compared to Half Life 1 and Opposing Force.
There are a few shining lights for this expansion and that is rescuing scientists, although it's not much of a rescue, because any of them can die and it doesn't matter. The expansion also dabbles in having an important character Dr. Rosenburg that you will rescue and he will guide you to the end of the expansion. Guide you as in briefly tell you what to do through believable voice acting.

My first review on Steam, I wish it could be more positive, but I am tired of spending money to discover low quality lurking behind these overly positive reviews.
What can I say, this game has been done many times before, and in much better ways.  The time in development (in my opinion) should have seen "Edge of Space" in a much more polished state than it currently is, considering the 2D style of the game.  *For the record, I understand the nature of "Early Access", but I do not believe that games should forever exist in a state of early access simply to justify financial or developmental limitations.  Having said that; open world, 2D scrolling, space exploration, voxel-based laser mining, crafting matrix, etc....   we've seen this song and dance play out again and again with the expectation that, maybe this time, something new and refreshing will find us.  Well, for me at least, it did not with Edge of Space.  I could have overlooked the poorly rendered and seemingly unrelated intro clip, a clunky tutorial that introduced an even clunkier UI, and even the low-res character, enemy, and background models.  What I couldn't overlook, however, were the poor aiming/targeting/tracking mechanics of the various starter (and presumably all) weapons and tools.  Proper hit detection, field of effect, and cursor-reticle alignment are so critical to a game like this, that to experience immediate frustration and difficulty utilizing said tools told me most of what I needed to know about Edge of Space.  I know, I didn't even play for a full hour, but let me be clear: This is a Starbound, and thus, a Terraria clone.  Unfortunately, it doesn't even rise to the level of quality those games possess, not to mention the lack of charm.  I appreciate the seemingly responsive nature of the developers, and the consistent development blog updates, but this one seems to have hit a creative wall both visually, and technically.  Sorry for the detraction, but I will be placing this game on the back burner for now.

Wow !! Where do I begin ?
Arguably the best $11 I have ever spent on computer gaming ever !!
Any game that can suck 255+ hours out of me in the last 40 days must be something special and in my opinion The Long Dark is just that. Its not perfect by any stretch but let me be clear on this...it's Pro's vastly outweigh its Con's.
I'll explain my opinion, Sandbox Voyageur 200+ days:
Pro's:
Highly addictive game play that MAKES you want to keep playing.
Very challanging but fair
The smallest accomplishments feel huge because your game is on the line the whole time....love Permadeath.
So far, 5 great regions each with its own Pro's and Con's
Great job on the weather, lighting, ambiance etc
Tools, equipment, food etc all very intuitive and easy to use menu(s)
So it's simple and clean and alot of fun and should be in everyone's Steam Library.
Now for the Con's...and please take this in the spirit in which it is intended...I love this game and only want to see it improve since I will be playing it even more once the divorce goes through (way too many late nights)
Con's:
No auto-Walk...at least I can't find it. Burning out my hands on those long treks.
Wind, wind, and more wind....and almost always in my face no matter which direction I go. Makes for some long returns to base and god help you if you are loaded down.
Graphics get screwy every now and then, good thing I am not "sensitive to the effect".
Food, matches etc going bad I think needs to be tweeked. I can live with the current rate that food goes bad but matches going bad really bugs me. There are more than enough of them in the game...thats not the point.
Spraining my wrist while walking. Really? Like I said before, these are all minor things but I hate forced/contrived hardships.
5 great regions so far yes...but I need more...much more. After 200 plus days I have nothing new to do, I am super stocked on everything, 100 + arrows and ammo, staging areas in each region, even been to the summit several times and cleaned it out. I want to keep discovering !!
Again I am incredibly happy with my purchase. Here are a few things I think would keep me playing if not playing more.
Suggestions:
More things to do: Kill a fox, make a warmer hat and scarf from it or how about a moose, very tough to take down but lots of meat 40kgs, and the hide can be used to make a larger backpack with a slightly increased weight allowance. You show a shovel on the Main screen but I have yet to see one in game. Make it accessible if it isn't already so we can dig a survival fort in a snow bank, and give us candles as well. An axe and the ability to chop down trees with those logs weighing alot but lasting a really long time on the fire. I personally don't want to go the route of being able to build my own log cabin but I wouldn't mind being able to repair existing ones (new regions perhaps) to a certain level(warmer).
In terms of regions: Sea Side Ship Yard, Valley of the Frozen, Farmland Acres, Fishing Village, Mining Town.
That's all. Buy this game. You won't regret it. Developers like this should be supported. Hopefully they continue to release content and keep us hooked.

Telltale once again proves that they're fantastic at story-telling within a more cinematic video game style, along a cartoony style. The Wolf Among Us is still the best one in my opinion, but Batman - The Telltale Series (a very good name for it) comes very close. I have already finished this game on PS4 but since the PC version was so cheap, I thought why not. The game runs much better than it did when it first came out (I played the first episode for free back in November and it was worse than right now).
The dialogue is very well written, definitely. The dialogue options are great and sometimes, it was just what I was thinking. I have gotten quite sick and tired of hearing the same voice in many big games (ahem Troy Baker - as the Batman this time (he played the Joker in Batman Arkham Origins) and I do wish he voiced the Joker instead of Batman in this game, or both really. I don't have a problem with Batman's voice, but it's just so... Troy Baker-y. Hopefully you can get where I'm coming from. I mean, take Saints Row IV and Infamous Second Son for instance. They both have the same voice actors, it's like playing the same game. But regardless, it would be great to hear Troy Baker as the Joker in this game though, and sadly that wasn't the case. Troy Baker very very nicely imitates Mark Hamill's voice. While not as good, it is probably the best alternative.
The plot twists in this game are very shocking. Just when you think that was it, oh no... the entire story is incredibly interesting and the shocks just keep on coming. The ending of episode 5 did leave a sour taste in my mouth, and I felt very dissatisfyed with my choice. Though it's rather disappointing to see that most of the choices you make during the game make a very small difference to the story. I'd rather not spoil, so you do something and whichever way you do, people still have a bad reaction to it. This happened twice just in episode 1! (I'd have to count all the other times.) Please, if you come into this game, come in with no knowledge whatsoever. Do what you want to do. Even if it may seem like a wrong choice, it will probably be more interesting to the story.
I did encounter some bugs, and the graphics aren't great. The game consists of quick time events but overall this game is more of an animated movie than anything else. There are some detective scenes and some scenes where you get to explore a bit like in the other Telltale games. These felt boring and more like filler. Even the planning for fights seem way too long for the short action scene they will provide.
Though let's be serious, the whole story was great. It was a very good cinematic experience (you MUST remember, I already played the whole game - all 5 episodes - even if I may [CURRENTLY] have low hours in it).
If you are a Batman fan like I am, this game is a must own. And even for anyone who likes great stories, this game is well written, the music is great, and it overall surprised me often.
9/10 Must own.

and its free credit policy!
is one of the few simulation titles on Steam worth keeping an eye on. All in all,
is a fairly decent casino simulation that not only has room to grow, but counts with a dedicated development team willing to listen to feedback and improve over it. Grab your friends and get ready for a good relaxing time as you dive into the most economical harmless Vegas ever!

After putting about a literal day's time into this game, I'm disappointed.  Not because of the intriguing worldbuilding and writing surrounding in-game lore, but because of how much wasted potential there is and how much the game works against itself.  Some people will say this is a "niche" game and if you don't fall into that niche, you won't like it.  I don't think that's true; I like parts of this game because they work (largely the worldbuilding)—I don't like other parts because, well, they don't.
Many of the game mechanics are designed to make the world feel brutal and difficult.  The game sells itself or has been sold by players as a roguelike of sorts, which is all well and good, but consider that it takes you days of play-time to acquire something that feels like completion and then the game expects you to do it all over again.  Oh, your map changes.  Islands are not where they once were.  You can look forward to updated or changed stories and new things to disc—no wait, no you can't.  You put days into this game on one "successful" character and then are expected to retire or kill him and do it all over again in a world that is ENTIRELY the same except that islands have moved around.  Why would you ever want that?
The saddest part about the difficulty and ultimate end-game is that the worldbuilding and lore is where this game shines, but players are actively dissuaded from exploring it in a way that makes for a fun game.  Then when they finally pull it off, there's nothing waiting for them at the end except an expectation that they'll slog through the exact same thing all over again.
And then there's the lingering question of how to make money in this game or the lack of ship variety.  There are at most two or three good ways to do it (selling sunlight/red honey/coffee) and piracy is right out (you just sank an enormous enemy dreadnaught? well, we're feeling generous today—have 1 fuel).  Many of the relatively few ship options are completely irrelevant and NONE of the interesting factional ships are available to the player at all despite the ability to side with these factions through narrative.  There is only a single ship available that is designed for hauling goods and then the return on that goods hauling is nonsensical (+/- 2-3 "echoes" per item).
And finally I just want to note that what is by far the most (and probably only) interesting ship in the game, the Cladery Heart, lacks a vital forward gun slot.  This makes the crazy around-the-world quest to get it silly because it's instatly invalidated in serious ship-to-ship combat by the same ship you'll always end up sailing in whether you like it or not—the Eschatologue dreadnaught.  That is, if you want to spend a couple hours making money selling sunlight.  You know, the only real way to do it.  Whoops.
I'm glad I only spent $5 on this (thanks trading cards!) because that's about how much of the game is actually working for itself.  $5 in worldbuilding.

It's difficult to sum this up in one sentence but I will try: it attempts, and does a good job at, drawing your primal fears.
Darkness.
Big creepy crawlies.
Unknown.
Tight spaces.
LIMBO is a minimalistic, 2D puzzle platformer, in which you control a nameless boy through environments which are, to put it lightly,

There is no exposition, no dialogue and very little information; the story is left up to you to piece it together.
The art style is minimal, with absolutely no colour whatsoever. For the most part you can distinguish items you can interact with. Key word is "most".
Even the sound design is minimal, yet impeccable. Headphones ABSOLUTELY RECOMMENDED.
Controls are the bare essentials: jump and climb on ropes or ladders, move left and right, drop or descend from ropes or ladders, and a general interaction button with which you can push or pull items, or trigger mechanisms. It's physics based, so momentum and angle are taken into account when traversing terrain, as well as how fast or heavy things must be to kill you, and you will die a lot. No wonder the devs called it "trial and death".
My playthrough, which was completing the main levels, took around 2 hours, but several achievements reward exploration in certain areas, and there might be a hidden level I've missed, so that's probably going to bring the playtime up a bit.
The regular price tag makes it a bit difficult to justify the purchase, as although it is an experience, it doesn't offer enough longevity I feel. Grab it on sale, or for free until the special offer ends.

First off, this game is amazing even though I haven't played it recently so I don't understand why there are bad reviews. I hardly ever write a review but I felt this game is worth my time reviewing. With all the new updates, I am actually going to set out some free time to play it again. In fact, I enjoyed this game even before all the big updates and patches were made (wipes included).
It is similar to Terraria in the aspect of genre but uniquely different in terms of content.
Edge of Space speaks for itself what it's about (almost). You are an alien thrown into an unknown "world". Whether it was a planet or on an asteroid, even I'm not quite sure. Everyone complains it's hard to grasp but there is a tutorial at the beginning which I happened to accidentally skipped. Even so, I didn't find the game entirely hard to follow if you know the basics: collect materials, build a house/base, kill monsters, etc. Not to mention all the cool pets and mounts you can create. Come on...a laser to collect materials and space guns?! Jet packs to fly! It really sticks to the sci-fi feel. Oh, I would also like to add I love how smooth the movements are in this game.
The challenge is in figuring how everything works and the satisfaction when you do.
Since last time that I played, the only thing I really would complain about is how each character was bounded to certain worlds if they were made in multiplayer/single player. You can't select any character to load into a world if that character wasn't made in that particular world. Some materials that can be collected in single player were unable to be gathered in multiplayer (but before I stopped playing this issue was already fixed). There weren't as many boss fights as I would like and their drops weren't always anything special. Overall, when I stopped playing I was merely waiting for more content to be released.
I've seen a lot of reviews comparing this to Terraria and Starbound. If you like those games more then play those games instead of comparing it to this one. Why? Because if this game was exactly like Terraria then...that defeats the purpose of making a uniquely different 2D Sandbox game. Also, if you hop into the game for less than an hour and deem that it's awful then you're not even giving the game a chance.
I would also like to repeat that this game is in EARLY ACCESS. There will be bugs and the sort so if you don't want a game that's in DEVELOPMENT, I would advise you to wait if you have no patience for an unfinished game rather than buy it and give it a bad review because it has a lot of potential.

Telltale once again proves that they're fantastic at story-telling within a more cinematic video game style, along a cartoony style. The Wolf Among Us is still the best one in my opinion, but Batman - The Telltale Series (a very good name for it) comes very close. I have already finished this game on PS4 but since the PC version was so cheap, I thought why not. The game runs much better than it did when it first came out (I played the first episode for free back in November and it was worse than right now).
The dialogue is very well written, definitely. The dialogue options are great and sometimes, it was just what I was thinking. I have gotten quite sick and tired of hearing the same voice in many big games (ahem Troy Baker - as the Batman this time (he played the Joker in Batman Arkham Origins) and I do wish he voiced the Joker instead of Batman in this game, or both really. I don't have a problem with Batman's voice, but it's just so... Troy Baker-y. Hopefully you can get where I'm coming from. I mean, take Saints Row IV and Infamous Second Son for instance. They both have the same voice actors, it's like playing the same game. But regardless, it would be great to hear Troy Baker as the Joker in this game though, and sadly that wasn't the case. Troy Baker very very nicely imitates Mark Hamill's voice. While not as good, it is probably the best alternative.
The plot twists in this game are very shocking. Just when you think that was it, oh no... the entire story is incredibly interesting and the shocks just keep on coming. The ending of episode 5 did leave a sour taste in my mouth, and I felt very dissatisfyed with my choice. Though it's rather disappointing to see that most of the choices you make during the game make a very small difference to the story. I'd rather not spoil, so you do something and whichever way you do, people still have a bad reaction to it. This happened twice just in episode 1! (I'd have to count all the other times.) Please, if you come into this game, come in with no knowledge whatsoever. Do what you want to do. Even if it may seem like a wrong choice, it will probably be more interesting to the story.
I did encounter some bugs, and the graphics aren't great. The game consists of quick time events but overall this game is more of an animated movie than anything else. There are some detective scenes and some scenes where you get to explore a bit like in the other Telltale games. These felt boring and more like filler. Even the planning for fights seem way too long for the short action scene they will provide.
Though let's be serious, the whole story was great. It was a very good cinematic experience (you MUST remember, I already played the whole game - all 5 episodes - even if I may [CURRENTLY] have low hours in it).
If you are a Batman fan like I am, this game is a must own. And even for anyone who likes great stories, this game is well written, the music is great, and it overall surprised me often.
9/10 Must own.

Cuphead is a breath of fresh air ironically for something that is baised on the 1930's. I personally loved every moment the game had to offer and was constanly blown away by the level of quality throughout the entire game. The art in this game is beautiful; every character is unique and has personality to match. The little details are what make this game great, like watching the frames when a boss transforms into its next menacing stage. I used to watch old cartoons from what this game is baised on with my dad, and the about of love and respect that was put in shines through.  I was so giddy with joy as a watched a flying waffle explode on my screen or a mermaid turn into medusa and turn me to stone. Also I could just watch Cuphead bounce up and down all day. The gameplay is simply brilliant to say the least. The controls are tight and I never expirienced any form of input lag or frame drops. The closest thing I can relate Cuphead to is classic megaman, exept of running a stage and facing a boss, you face ridiculous over the top bosses on thier own and do the running bit as a another stage. This game is not easy, which is super refreshing in a market where I feel thats games have been boiled down to simple waste on time. With Cuphead whenever I beat a boss or passed a stage I felt a great sense of accomplishment that I haven't had from a game in a long time. Half the fun of the game is getting frustrated with a boss, and harnessing your skills to learn the patterns and timings to succeed. All of the games mechanics were used to thier full, for instance there is a flying mechanic that was introduced early on that was consistantly used throughout. There are also a great number of costumizations that you can make to Cuphead like secondary fires, special moves, and abilities that I felt enhanced the game and let me play with my own style. Overall, Cuphead is a genius game that is well worth the small price of $20. Thank you MDHR for doing what you did with this game, it was well worth the wait and I look forward to future projects.

short: It's The Good♥♥♥♥♥♥My Dudes (story mode isn't out yet but the sandbox is neat as heck)
long: A very interesting take on the survival early-access genre that's been sweeping across Steam the last few years, swapping out a focus on crafting and combat for a style that focuses more on resource management and general survival skills. With a unique setting that forces the player to be constantly planning ahead, you're very rarely on easy ground. Even something as simple as trying to get firewood needs to be thought through, with exposure to the harsh sub-arctic elements being a constant drain on your abilities, not helped by the near constant presence of wolves. While this becomes less of a factor later on, as the difficulty plateaus and players become complacent in their means and abilities (a problem with open-world survival games as a genre), the presence of permadeath and the ease that one mistakes slides into many mistakes can keep players on their toes even as their time in the sandbox enters in-game weeks. The tense and desolate atmosphere helps accomplish this as well, with a mostly silent soundtrack that focuses more on the sounds of the world around you. Borrowing from games such as Minecraft, the music kicks in at random and for short bursts, which can accentuate an otherwise normal in-game moment. When the ambience isn't being drowned out by the sounds of a crackling campfire or the harsh winds of a blizzard, it helps ground the player as a solitary figure inside of a vast landscape.
basically it's a very neat experience and while it's very much a Survival Game, it manages to nail the atmosphere and setting in a way that sets it apart from the crowd. combined with gameplay mechanics that work semi-realisticly (it's still very gamey, what ya gonna do) and maintain an appropriate level of stress on your resources, it takes the Survival genre places I'm surprised nobody had executed this well before.

The Beginner's Guide is interesting and fascinating in lots of ways and, frankly, it is more than just game.
So, here is the list of advantages:
I wouldn't say, that everyone must try it, because some like action games, some like FPS and this is totally fine. But if you enjoyed Stanley Parable or, for instance, Portal (i know these games are way different, but, trust me, they definetely have something in common), you should try it.

I bought this game right before multiplayer came out. Ever since I started playing it, my experience has been positive. At first, you don't think the game is very in-depth, but you will soon relize there is a lot to learn in this post-apocolyptic world. With such simple graphics - which I've found to be very smooth - this game has so much to do that you will never find yourself sitting in one spot wondering what you should do next. Your character has these status bubbles called "moodles" that let you know when your character is hungry, angry, afraid, thirsty, tired, etc. and how each moodle effects your characters ability to function. A nice thing about the moodles is that if your character has a neutral moodle, it doesn't show up, so you can focus on the moodles that are negatively effecting you and the rare positive effects of a moodle. Gameplay is phenomenal and I'm still learning things I can do within the game. I've been playing multiplayer ever since it has came out and I have only had an enjoyable time doing so.
CUSTOMER SERVICE:
This game has one of the best teams behind it. They work with the community to fix every bug, while still making additions to the game constantly. I reported a problem I was having, to be responded to that same day by a developer who set this problem to committed and has already had it fixed for the next build, which went out less than a week later. The only bad thing that I've noticed is navigating the main website and their forums.
ADDITIONAL FEATURES:
They have free map building tools, which I haven't tried, so I cannot comment much on them. As well, I believe they have free modding tools. I haven't had experience with them, either.
SHOULD YOU BUY THIS GAME?
Games I can compare this to: Sims and minecraft. It has the open-world building aspect like minecraft, but has more in-depth emotions like the Sims. The "moodles" are a lot easy to handle than the Sims, becuase, in this game, the moodles aren't constantly seeking your attention. If you ever wanted to see how successful you'd be in a zombie apocolypse, this is the game for you.
