57h played during the Big Alpha week-end, I haven't had that much fun and so few sleep since TitanFall beta and that says a lot because it was so new GameplayWise on so many levels, Evolve made me feel the same.
Beside the first day which was very hectic with 1h wait time per game average, this is probably the most achieved Alpha I have ever played (and I played a lot of them) and to be honest it felt more like an open beta stage very close to release, so huge congratulations to the whole team and thank you for the reactive patch that finally allowed us to play almost normally on saturday.
I could write probably 5 pages about the good sides and the small problems that still remains but im too lazy for that so I will only mention a few:
- I would love to be able to make a private lobby so me and my friends could play together versus one of us being the Monster but im sure it's already planed because you certainly don't want to make the same mistake TitanFall did at release and seriously compromised it's player base.

Project Zomboid is currently still in development, which is truly amazing, because the game right now conveys a extremely playable version even if it’s only in Beta. The game is being worked on and further development updates are being released to give the players more content to play around with. Updates are very consistent and nearly always add more content to the game (unless it’s a bug fix update which are also frequent).
If you’re the type of person that enjoys a completely realistic and immersive, zombie apocalyptic experience, where every character has a different to story to tell, with every play through. Then Project Zomboid is for YOU.

So I'm giving this... "game"?... a thumbs up, which translates to a recommendation. But I'm not 100% confident in my recommendation. It's just that I cannot in good conscience give it a thumbs down. And I suspect that most people who've played all the way through it might understand what I mean, but I can't explain it to anyone who hasn't "played" it yet without somehow ruining the experience. And that, really, is all this is, is an experience.
It's not really a game in the usual sense of the term, even though technically it is, to some degree, nothing but game, plus narration. The primary purpose of the game is to listen to the narration, so without sound (or without listening) it will be a pointless exercise and I would advise against it. There are some (okay, several) "slow" bits that, narratively, have to be, but it might try your patience. If you're looking for a fast-paced time, there are hundreds, perhaps thousands of games better suited than this one.
It reminded me of The Stanley Parable in that it is sort of a commentary on the world of game design and game-playing, as well as a game that's not about the game, per se. I should also warn that this game isn't as amusing or whimsical as The Stanley Parable. I think I laughed a few times during The Stanley Parable, where as partway through this game I felt uncomfortable. Which I think was the goal.
So... a very qualified thumbs up, and just know that it's first and foremost a story that relies heavily on the medium of gaming and player interaction. (And no, watching a YouTube walkthrough of this will probably not do anything for you. You need to be immersed in the scenarios for the full effect. It adds to the realism. Trust me on this, at least.)
On a more superficial note, I doubt I'd have been happy paying full price for it. If you pay (via a sale)the cost of a Redbox rental or an Amazon movie streaming, that sounds about right.

I can't remember what I expected from this game before buying it.  I think I was looking at a typical hack and slash game.  A friend recommended it, so I gave it a go.  I'm glad I did.
An hour into the game, I still wasn't sure what I was playing.  I liked the passage of time, the needing to eat and drink, and finding better weapons, but that was barely scratching the surface.
I learned to build new objects (by learn, I mean I figured out that I could do it...  you don't need to find plans, or anything, as the game just lets you know what you need after you find a hammer).  I thought I was doing well, and was a little worried that this game was going to end up being Farmville with zombies...  then the power and water went out, and I was left unable to cook food easily.  Without power, there's no refrigeration, and perishables will rot.  Now, it's a battle for survival not just against zombies, but against time, and your own biology.  Hunger and thirst are as dangerous as any biter.  The rain which was an inconvenience before is now essential, and it doesn't come along often enough for my liking.
If you're on the fence about this game, just pick it up.  Farmville, it ain't.

It's difficult to sum this up in one sentence but I will try: it attempts, and does a good job at, drawing your primal fears.
Darkness.
Big creepy crawlies.
Unknown.
Tight spaces.
LIMBO is a minimalistic, 2D puzzle platformer, in which you control a nameless boy through environments which are, to put it lightly,

There is no exposition, no dialogue and very little information; the story is left up to you to piece it together.
The art style is minimal, with absolutely no colour whatsoever. For the most part you can distinguish items you can interact with. Key word is "most".
Even the sound design is minimal, yet impeccable. Headphones ABSOLUTELY RECOMMENDED.
Controls are the bare essentials: jump and climb on ropes or ladders, move left and right, drop or descend from ropes or ladders, and a general interaction button with which you can push or pull items, or trigger mechanisms. It's physics based, so momentum and angle are taken into account when traversing terrain, as well as how fast or heavy things must be to kill you, and you will die a lot. No wonder the devs called it "trial and death".
My playthrough, which was completing the main levels, took around 2 hours, but several achievements reward exploration in certain areas, and there might be a hidden level I've missed, so that's probably going to bring the playtime up a bit.
The regular price tag makes it a bit difficult to justify the purchase, as although it is an experience, it doesn't offer enough longevity I feel. Grab it on sale, or for free until the special offer ends.

A beatifully drawn game with an equally beautiful soundtrack. I can recommend Morphoplis if you are looking for a serene experience of clicking hidden objects and solving puzzles. It is let down somewhat by the slow and clunky movement in the game, but given how simple the gameplay is, I can excuse it. The first time I played it though, I couldn't work out even the basic movement, which is essentially point in a particular direction and hold down the mouse button.
There are only certain paths you can follow through the foliage, and it's soon obvious where these paths are. The learning curve of working out what on earth you are supposed to be doing in this garden somehow adds to the dreamlike quality of the scenery, and there are no textual or spoken cues to stop you thinking like an insect interacting in its natural environment.
You should come to Morphopolis with a relaxed frame of mind, because otherwise you could get easily frustrated. It's the gaming equivalent of getting in touch with nature and living among the flowers. It is a very short, casual game, but leaves its mark on you, showing what else games can be than blood-thirsty war games.

If you enjoy the Battlefield series but wish it were based in WWII, this is your game. This game is immersive and intense--from the crack of a sniper in the distance to the creaks of an enemy tank's tracks. I highly recommend this game, even at the retail price; if you can get it on sale, all the better.
Overall, this game is a rich and rewarding FPS with a lot of replayability. Pick it up and enjoy!

Pros:
-It really makes you have to plan ahead and really think about the needs of your village.
-Relaxing. It does get a bit stressful keeping up with food and housing, but you can slow down time or pause to think it through.
-Smooth UI. You can pull windows, the map and whatnot and move them around the screen to see what you want to see. A rare trait nowadays with these sorts of games.
-Good AI. Your workers take roads when available, go to the nearest storage spot and take the shortest path. Now I have seen one glitch when my worker wandered halfway across the map but a quick restart fixed it.
Cons:
-It is very very easy to screw up and everyone dies and you have to restart. I've never been one to shy away from an unforgiving game but it just gets sad after awhile. It took me about 5 villages just to get started, finding new needs that I didn't consider.
-People hog houses. I love the aspect of families living in houses and having children that eventually move out. But if I have 9 houses and 18 old people that can't have children anymore, they die and their children are already too old to have children and everyone dies of old age. I've played with boarding houses but my population grows too fast and can't keep up with food. Those three things alone have killed off every single one of my villages within one year. Cascade effect that you cant stop.
-You pretty much need workshop mods to last more that a few years.
Overall I love this game. It's hard and makes you think. It takes a lot of work to keep your village going but it's satisfying to see it grow.

In the early hours of the morning, the Jungle is asleep.
Slowly, the light steadily comes forth from above, shadows of a thousand leaves and branches filters through, the morning mist creeping everywhere. The smell of wet grass lingers, the vegitation thick and entwined at everything. There are no animals but the occasional bird, chirping in the distance beyond the vastness of the Jungle.
The scene is idyllic and peaceful. In another time, in another place, it would had been welcoming.
But in a time of war, never was the phrase "the Fog of War" aptly realized in a Jungle enviroment such as this; with every rustle of a leaf and snap of a branch caused by the Enemy, every bush, thicket and tree hiding the Enemy, every imaginary figure in the mist and shadowy unknown, the Enemy.
Far from your mind is the idea that Death can come for you suddenly at any moment. So cautiously you approach the Jungle at the arms ready, your comrades walking beside you in the same cautious manner, the Bayonets on their weapons gleaming occasionally from what little sunlight penetrates through from the vegitation above. Your ears hear everything as you walk, from the beating sound of your heart, the slight clanking of helmets and equipment to the mouthless nervous breathing of your friends. Yet you can barely see what's ahead of you, the thick Jungle swallowing you with each step you take.
Suddenly you hear a sound that startles you, like a small stick being waved through the air sharply. You look around, trying to look for the source as you continue on. It happens again, this time going past your head.
You realize its a bullet snapping by and instinctively you aim at the mist infront of you and fire a round off. Everyone around you is jolted by the shot and pauses, but before anybody can say something you hear the unsheathing of steel in the mist beyond. Then you see figures in the mist running towards you, Bayonets at the ready.
"BAANNZAIIII!" they scream in one bloodcurdling voice .
In the hunderds they come for you, suddenly appearing through the foilage, charging at you blindly. No time to think or speak, only time to react to the oncoming frenzy. You fire at the figures here and there, dodgin a Bayonet thrust meant for you and returning it with fatality for the reciever. Sounds of flesh being gorged and penetarated, human voices both friend and foe screaming, gagging, moaning. The smell of blood and cordite now hanging in the air.
Then you find yourself running through a war torn village along with everyone else, shooting, killing, stabbing Japanese soldiers here and there where ever you find them. Death comes in every direction and in every form and manner that Modern War can provide. A Flamethrower next to you engulfs figures in Napalm along with a house they were in, the burning men screaming in their language, their voices filled with agony as they try to put out the flames desperately and in vain. To your right, a machine gun crew sets up position and fires away, tracer rounds ripping through bodies, huts, and the Jungle nearby, suppressing a rival machine crew from firing at your direction.
Explosions occasionally go off here and there. Grenades, mortars, heavy artillery. Your ears begin to ring from the symphony of all these sounds going off together then by random occurance. The whizz and snap of bullets begins to deafen you. Cover to cover, you aim and shoot then you continue onwards along with your comrades. Enemies who drop down on the first shot get shot again and again for good measure.
This blood lust continues on for 30 minutes, but for you and for everyone who was there it continues Forever. With each Death you create and witness, your mind subconsiously etches it in your memory.
By the end of the day, the area is filled with corpses and every manner of tool for warfare scattered and abandoned. The sickly stench of death now permeates across the air, the Jungle humidty fast at work decomposing the bodies of both Friend and Foe alike. Whatever these corpses once were, you acknowledge that they met Death bravely and without hesitation.
And through it all, you wonder how you made it through. But you have no time to think. The match is over, and the game begins again with a new round.

Really wanted to love this and be able to recommend it but I'm afraid I can't.  However if season 2 is a belter you'll probably need to play this first.  And in fairness it's not that bad, it just has some major flaws and appears really buggy, even a whole year on.  Which is a shame as Telltale is a studio I have a lot of time for.
I know a lot of people will complain that choices don't matter, and the major story milestones are set in stone.  That's fine for me.  What I can't forgive is where there are instances of obvious ignoring of my choices and the application of the opposite of what I choose just to keep the story on rails e.g. I specifically did not tell vicki vale a suspect's name, and then later on in the game t says I did.  Or when Gordon calls Batman a hero in one scene and then threatens to lock him up the next with no obvious cause inbetween.  Why give me the choice in the first place if it's going to be stamped on later?  Or they'll show a scene that will be in an upcoming episode which never comes to be.  Now I could accept that if I had played the game as they were releasing each episode one at a time but I'm playing this long after all episiodes were out!  Also the dialogue can be a bit odd at times, with tone and attitude of characters shifting all over the place, and conversations seeming quite unnatural.  They should have taken the time to ensure the quality was there, and instead it all looks rather rushed and amateurish.
The game also suffers some major technical problems.  Whole scenes will play out with only audio and a black screen, or frozen on a weird graphical oddity.  Sound effects don't tie in with actions.  Sound effects can be missing.  Lip sync can be all over the place.  Recurring stuttering.  An odd freeze on the last frame of scenes before it cuts away elsewhere.  This all seemed to get worse as I went on with Episode 5 being borderline unplayable.
The scene pacing was a bit too fast for me as well.  I'm more used to the more recent batman films, the gotham series, and the recent batman games, and the game flits from scene to scene with barely time to gather your breath, and some plot points really stretch the limits of believable logic at times.
What the game has to be commended for though is that the QTEs, a bane in most other types of games, actually work quiet well here.  Also, the story itself, barring some minor points, as a whole is rather pleasing.  They have not been afraid to play around in the lore of the Batman universe, and change some things about, the majority of which I can't say for fear of spoilers.  I liked fact they had gone and done things like given Penguin an English accent and actually made it make sense within the story.
So all in all, it's a rather unfortunate affair.  If you love telltale and you love batman you will get some enjoyment from this.    But there are better telltale games and better batman games out there.  If you want to get into telltale, go elsewhere, check out the Wolf Among Us, or The Walking Dead.  And if you want Batman check out any of the Batman Arkham games.

Wow !! Where do I begin ?
Arguably the best $11 I have ever spent on computer gaming ever !!
Any game that can suck 255+ hours out of me in the last 40 days must be something special and in my opinion The Long Dark is just that. Its not perfect by any stretch but let me be clear on this...it's Pro's vastly outweigh its Con's.
I'll explain my opinion, Sandbox Voyageur 200+ days:
Pro's:
Highly addictive game play that MAKES you want to keep playing.
Very challanging but fair
The smallest accomplishments feel huge because your game is on the line the whole time....love Permadeath.
So far, 5 great regions each with its own Pro's and Con's
Great job on the weather, lighting, ambiance etc
Tools, equipment, food etc all very intuitive and easy to use menu(s)
So it's simple and clean and alot of fun and should be in everyone's Steam Library.
Now for the Con's...and please take this in the spirit in which it is intended...I love this game and only want to see it improve since I will be playing it even more once the divorce goes through (way too many late nights)
Con's:
No auto-Walk...at least I can't find it. Burning out my hands on those long treks.
Wind, wind, and more wind....and almost always in my face no matter which direction I go. Makes for some long returns to base and god help you if you are loaded down.
Graphics get screwy every now and then, good thing I am not "sensitive to the effect".
Food, matches etc going bad I think needs to be tweeked. I can live with the current rate that food goes bad but matches going bad really bugs me. There are more than enough of them in the game...thats not the point.
Spraining my wrist while walking. Really? Like I said before, these are all minor things but I hate forced/contrived hardships.
5 great regions so far yes...but I need more...much more. After 200 plus days I have nothing new to do, I am super stocked on everything, 100 + arrows and ammo, staging areas in each region, even been to the summit several times and cleaned it out. I want to keep discovering !!
Again I am incredibly happy with my purchase. Here are a few things I think would keep me playing if not playing more.
Suggestions:
More things to do: Kill a fox, make a warmer hat and scarf from it or how about a moose, very tough to take down but lots of meat 40kgs, and the hide can be used to make a larger backpack with a slightly increased weight allowance. You show a shovel on the Main screen but I have yet to see one in game. Make it accessible if it isn't already so we can dig a survival fort in a snow bank, and give us candles as well. An axe and the ability to chop down trees with those logs weighing alot but lasting a really long time on the fire. I personally don't want to go the route of being able to build my own log cabin but I wouldn't mind being able to repair existing ones (new regions perhaps) to a certain level(warmer).
In terms of regions: Sea Side Ship Yard, Valley of the Frozen, Farmland Acres, Fishing Village, Mining Town.
That's all. Buy this game. You won't regret it. Developers like this should be supported. Hopefully they continue to release content and keep us hooked.

This isn't just a good game, it's a literal work of art. Every character and environment is designed with care and in a style that is obviously unique. It's one thing to compliment it but this should be seen as a standard for effort in the game industry. The flashy high end graphics of AAA titles are nice, but nothing can beat pure unadulturated creativity. It's inspiring in all honesty.
The controls (controller) are insanely smooth. I've seen a few bad reviews rip on the games control set up but to me, and what seems to be the majority, it felt like butter the second I started moving. It's so intuitive that, like many have said, you can't blame your failures on anything but yourself. They go where you move them and unfortunately sometimes the situation is too overwhelming for your feeble mind, so you're obligated to try over and over and over until you succeed. It's very addictive. The controls are set up so that your thumbs can hold down the fire button while still being able to access A,B and Y with just a roll of the finger, allowing you to focus more on your surroundings while still engaging the boss and other objects.
The random patterns are a huge focal point. You are not put into a situation where you are remembering a specific pattern. You're forced to know which movements are required for which enemy/attack, react to the pattern changes as fast as possible and blend it all together to dodge in a nice flow. Switching between weapons and saving friends or parrying intensifies the situations.
Level variety is rewarding as the controls stay familiar, but are utilized differently. Example, rather than trigger a quick dash, as a plane, holding Y (dash) will allow you to shrink and travel faster around the screen. Along with engaging the enemy, switching between the fly modes to squeeze through gaps is very gratifying and intense.
Although these are a few important aspects, the main point is that the game is fun and addicting. It's beyond worth the $20. This is a game where you crawl through each level, one attack at a time, having to restart and perfect your response time. It's not failing at all, you're learning through trial and error, which is ignored in todays newer games. You will play for hours and have to just cut it off to return the next day, refreshed and ready to jump back in and chip away some more. It's hard to hate failing since everytime you do so you're rewarded with more of the awesome soundtrack and opportunities to see more and more detail of the levels, when you're not dodging for your life. Every time you play you learn to appreciate the effort put in more and more.
This was a labor of love from a small team that has shown new gamers how good games like this were and still can be. Games that some of us remember grinding through as children on SNES and Gameboy. You should honestly allow yourself to love everything about this experience because when you look back, you'll appreciate moments like this where real game enthusiasts deliver something sincerely from them to you. It may be hard to look back on games like Super Mario Bros 2 or 3 and understand why they were so popular but it was because of gameplay like this that can transcend the evolution of gaming graphics and horsepower, relying on pure enjoyment.

Ever want to be a leader of your own nation? With it's own set of rules, laws, and regulations? plus the ideological factor that drives your nation so?
Then this game is for you!
I had a blast while playing this game and you will too! There is a lot to do in this game, which can make time fly fast which is nice. Like in Sid Meier's Civilzation V you have to keep an eye out on your happiness, and your production level! Too litte, and your nation will starve of resources and rebel against you, Too much, and you will have constant invasions by the outside world. You need to find the right balance, plus make sure you choose your edicts wisely, pick the wrong ones too early and you will be at a disadvantage, pick the right ones in the right point in time might just help in your favor, or not depending upon whether or not you choose to upgrade your armies and defenses.
You can 'customize' your dictator, with outfits, looks, first name and last name. However, the first name is randomly generated so that's the downside to that. Plus you can upgrade your 'dynasty' members to be better, which is highly advise. Another downside is that it's not like Crusaders Kings where you can marry someone and have a child, it's randomly generated with a look, and the only thing you can customize is the outfit itself.
The locations are very well done, each island offers a unqiue spin on how you want to build your nation. If you pick a tiny island you have limited resources to build your country, If you have a huge island you have endless opportunity to build whatever it is you want to build. Like real life you must geographical plan out where you put your buildings and roads, plus your defenses and what not. The last you want is have a full fledge invasion, and your military defenses is sub-par, plus your guard tower locations are out of whack.
The music in this game while it's fun to listen too, It can get a bit repetitive so becareful there.
I am honestly surprised there is no mod workshop for this game, i can see the potential in what kind of mods this game can produce. Lastly, the achievements are easy to earn. And the tutorial is really simple and easy to understand.
If you want in-depth nation building then this game is for you. Recommend!

Pros:
-The levels are open ended and encourage exploration- which you don't mind doing, because every aspect of the enviroments are densely detailed and gorgeously rendered. The enviroments in themelves tell a part of the story.
-The sound design is incredible- the ambient noise of Rapture does very well to immerse you in the experience. And while not all of the music is catchy (aside from some fantastic old jazz), it certainly adds to the ambiance.
-The gameplay is beautifully crafted. The shooting is nice and responsive, the enemies are smart and the plasmids are awesome. There are plenty of ways to interact with the enviroment during combat, and it rewards experimentation.
-Tons of customization options allow the player to tailer the game towards their desired playstyle. With a little tweaking of the plasmids, you can even make Bioshock into a stealth game (not kidding- I've done it)
-Above all: an amaingly crafted storyline with memorable characters and a mind-blowing plot twist. Every single aspect of this game works to emphasize the narrative and make it more believable- from the mechanics and enviroments to the way that voice-overs are presented. Don't look the plot of this game up- you don't want to ruin it for yourself.
-Big Daddies are seriously the coolest enemy in any game.
Cons:
-The game is sold as a survival-horror title, although it really isn't all that scary. The atomosphere is incredible, and it deffinitely has horror elements, but it isn't terrifying.
-The ending is pretty lackluster, which is kind of a downer after the spectacular story.
Overall:
Despite it's flaws, I can most assuredly say that this game is my favorite of all time. This game changed how I looked at games as a medium for art and storytelling. I hope that whoever reads this can get the same sort of experience out of it that I did. It's not perfect, but I love it to death.

This is a review of the Big Alpha for Evolve, because the game isnt listed as Early Access, I figured I would say this first just in case people didn't know about the Alpha.  The game as it stands, in Alpha state, is pretty solid, you have 2 monsters, with a third one that hasnt been shown yet, and 8 hunters in the alpha, with more to come in the finished product.  In order to get the other monster/hunters, you only start with one of each, you have to finish challenges for the class, like do so much damage with your ablilites and whatnot.  Its a cool setup, character masteries and things are awesome.  The gameplay is fun on both sides, monster and hunter. Audiosurf is the ideal game for anyone and everyone looking for a game that incorporates music into a fun and intriguing 3D platform. In short, the object of the game involves uploading an mp3 (or WMA) file from your computer as a playable track is layed out following the beat of the tune. Once the rendering is complete you are given a choice as to which ship you would like to obtain as you 'ride' the song you chose.  I've found it to be quite relaxing especially with some of the easier puzzled vehicles such as Mono and Pointman as you can really focus more on the music while having to maintian the simple task of avoiding grey bars and filling up meters. Would I recommend this game? Well, as others have said there are some viable flaws that may or may not affect the gameplay such as
A) Only being able to play songs downloaded onto your computer
B) No mods
C) Most people have moved onto Audiosurf 2 (which, that being said has it's own if not MORE flaws)
If these things don't particurally pertain to you or even with the few cons you are willing to bypass for the amazing gameplay then Audiosurf is a great game for you.

In the early hours of the morning, the Jungle is asleep.
Slowly, the light steadily comes forth from above, shadows of a thousand leaves and branches filters through, the morning mist creeping everywhere. The smell of wet grass lingers, the vegitation thick and entwined at everything. There are no animals but the occasional bird, chirping in the distance beyond the vastness of the Jungle.
The scene is idyllic and peaceful. In another time, in another place, it would had been welcoming.
But in a time of war, never was the phrase "the Fog of War" aptly realized in a Jungle enviroment such as this; with every rustle of a leaf and snap of a branch caused by the Enemy, every bush, thicket and tree hiding the Enemy, every imaginary figure in the mist and shadowy unknown, the Enemy.
Far from your mind is the idea that Death can come for you suddenly at any moment. So cautiously you approach the Jungle at the arms ready, your comrades walking beside you in the same cautious manner, the Bayonets on their weapons gleaming occasionally from what little sunlight penetrates through from the vegitation above. Your ears hear everything as you walk, from the beating sound of your heart, the slight clanking of helmets and equipment to the mouthless nervous breathing of your friends. Yet you can barely see what's ahead of you, the thick Jungle swallowing you with each step you take.
Suddenly you hear a sound that startles you, like a small stick being waved through the air sharply. You look around, trying to look for the source as you continue on. It happens again, this time going past your head.
You realize its a bullet snapping by and instinctively you aim at the mist infront of you and fire a round off. Everyone around you is jolted by the shot and pauses, but before anybody can say something you hear the unsheathing of steel in the mist beyond. Then you see figures in the mist running towards you, Bayonets at the ready.
"BAANNZAIIII!" they scream in one bloodcurdling voice .
In the hunderds they come for you, suddenly appearing through the foilage, charging at you blindly. No time to think or speak, only time to react to the oncoming frenzy. You fire at the figures here and there, dodgin a Bayonet thrust meant for you and returning it with fatality for the reciever. Sounds of flesh being gorged and penetarated, human voices both friend and foe screaming, gagging, moaning. The smell of blood and cordite now hanging in the air.
Then you find yourself running through a war torn village along with everyone else, shooting, killing, stabbing Japanese soldiers here and there where ever you find them. Death comes in every direction and in every form and manner that Modern War can provide. A Flamethrower next to you engulfs figures in Napalm along with a house they were in, the burning men screaming in their language, their voices filled with agony as they try to put out the flames desperately and in vain. To your right, a machine gun crew sets up position and fires away, tracer rounds ripping through bodies, huts, and the Jungle nearby, suppressing a rival machine crew from firing at your direction.
Explosions occasionally go off here and there. Grenades, mortars, heavy artillery. Your ears begin to ring from the symphony of all these sounds going off together then by random occurance. The whizz and snap of bullets begins to deafen you. Cover to cover, you aim and shoot then you continue onwards along with your comrades. Enemies who drop down on the first shot get shot again and again for good measure.
This blood lust continues on for 30 minutes, but for you and for everyone who was there it continues Forever. With each Death you create and witness, your mind subconsiously etches it in your memory.
By the end of the day, the area is filled with corpses and every manner of tool for warfare scattered and abandoned. The sickly stench of death now permeates across the air, the Jungle humidty fast at work decomposing the bodies of both Friend and Foe alike. Whatever these corpses once were, you acknowledge that they met Death bravely and without hesitation.
And through it all, you wonder how you made it through. But you have no time to think. The match is over, and the game begins again with a new round.

I figured I'd write a review about the one who started it all since FnAF3 is out to the public. I personally just love this game, for many reasons. One, because of its concept: Here you are, some little night guard at a pizza place, right? Not too scary, just a bunch of old animatronics, some microwave pizza and a guy telling you everything is going to be fine... why would he do that, right? Prepare to have every childhood Chuck E. Cheese memory scarred forever with the eternal burning question, "Are YOU ready for Freddy?" As every heart-pounding, tension weighed second is filled with the horror and dread of a band of killer cursed animatronics with you as their pawn, limited power, a camera, and two blast doors with the worst power upkeep in history. But as if this were not bad enough, you've been hired for 5 nights of this maddening torture. ON MINIMUM WAGE? NOW WE'RE TALKING! But there's one more animatronic they don't want you to know about. He's alot like our idle, with a certain golden sheen... Which, again, raises the question:
Are you ready... for Freddy? But, really, the aspect of this game might seem cheesy, for some people, mainly because the only real threat is mainly the expecting jump scares, which do get kind of cheesy after a while, but it really does have a frightening atmosphere and a nice back story which has been slowly uncovered in the last three games. All of this strange happening starts at the original Fred-bear's Family Diner, where we only have one animatronic: Fred-bear, or just Freddy. In some of the FnAF2 Mini-games, there is one that is believed to be depicted as the first restaurant, with Freddy giving out cake to the children. A child watches through the establishments sole window as the children are offered cake by their idol. But as it goes on, Freddy seems to grow helpless and slow, more and more unable to move; the children begin crying when they do not receive their cake, and just outside, a man pulls up towards the window. Freddy comes to a standstill and is forced to watch as the child outside the window is murdered by a stranger, and without hesitation, simply ups and leaves without consideration for his wretched deed. This, is what begins the mystery of Freddy Fazbear's Pizza.

Half-Life: Blue Shift Review
The bad news is that Blue Shift, the actual game, doesn't amount to much on its own terms. The good news is that the revamped graphics and inclusion of Opposing Force make the retail package a lot more worthwhile.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the second official retail expansion to Valve Software's groundbreaking 1998 first-person shooter. It's worth noting that Half-Life's publisher, Sierra Studios, has used the Half-Life brand name on many other products, including refurbished "Platinum" and "Game of the Year" editions of the original game, and has also helped promote (and sell) fan-made Half-Life mods, including last year's Gunman Chronicles and the extremely popular multiplayer mod Counter-Strike. Blue Shift was developed by Gearbox Software, the same team that brought you the excellent 1999 Half-Life expansion, Opposing Force, in which you play as one of the commandos sent in to ventilate Gordon Freeman, the protagonist of the original game. Blue Shift itself was originally developed as supplemental content for Half-Life for the Sega Dreamcast, but unfortunately, that console was discontinued earlier this year. Thus, plans for the release of Half-Life for the Dreamcast changed, which is why Blue Shift has now been made available for the PC. In North America, Blue Shift also comes bundled with Opposing Force--and you don't need the original Half-Life to play either of these. For good measure, Blue Shift also includes the Half-Life High Definition pack, which refurbishes some of the graphics throughout Half-Life and makes the entire game look a little newer. The bad news is that Blue Shift, the actual game, doesn't amount to much on its own terms. The good news is that the revamped graphics and the inclusion of Opposing Force make the retail package a lot more worthwhile.
The high definition pack noticeably enhances some of Half-Life's graphics.
It takes much more effort to put Half-Life: Blue Shift into proper context with all the preceding Half-Life products than it does to actually finish the game. It's not that the game is easy so much that it's extremely short--it'll take you between four and 10 hours to see everything in Blue Shift. You are put in the role of one of Half-Life's stalwart, levelheaded security personnel, whom you'd run into from time to time in the original game, as well as in Opposing Force. Barney Calhoun, your character in Blue Shift, supposedly doesn't have the same academic background as Gordon Freeman, nor does he have the military training of Corporal Adrian Shephard, the protagonist of Opposing Force. In the context of the game, none of this really comes across--Barney runs extremely quickly (just like Gordon and Adrian) and can suffer an inordinate amount of damage (just like Gordon and Adrian). This makes sense in Half-Life, where you are protected by a state-of-the-art environment suit, as well as in Opposing Force, where you are a highly trained soldier. In Blue Shift, it's a stretch, and the only time you get the sense that you're actually supposed to be a down-to-earth security guard is in an early sequence in which you have to get your sidearm and pick up your security vest and helmet. Like in Half-Life and Opposing Force, your character never actually says a word during the course of Blue Shift. In Half-Life, this helps immerse you into the game. In Blue Shift, it's too bad, since the main appeal of Half-Life's security guards comes from their numerous, wry one-liners and other banter.
Like Opposing Force, Blue Shift takes place during the same time frame as Half-Life. You start out heading in to work just as you would any other day, but things quickly go awry in the Black Mesa Research Facility. It's suddenly under siege, and as a member of its security force, you're tasked with defending the facility's scientists from aliens and also from government soldiers, who have come to do you in. In practice, you'll traverse the same sorts of dangerous levels that are found in the original game and Opposing Force. During the course of Blue Shift, you might catch a couple of clever references to both Opposing Force and the original game. These, along with a few other in-jokes, make for the most enjoyable parts of Blue Shift. The rest of it consists of a few fairly straightforward firefights, an obligatory jaunt to Xen (Half-Life's perennial parallel universe), and several jumping puzzles that manage to be just clever enough instead of annoying. There are no new challenges to be found, it's all over very quickly, and there isn't much point in revisiting the levels.
Blue Shift's weapons may look different, but the difference is only skin-deep.
However, you may find that once you've installed the High Definition pack, Blue Shift gives good reason to revisit the original Half-Life (as well as Opposing Force). This graphical enhancement increases the size of most of the texture maps found in the game and its expansion and also improves some of the 3D character models--you'll quickly notice that the scientists, security guards, and government soldiers all look more lifelike. The High Definition pack also changes all the weapon models from Half-Life. The most jarring of these changes is that Half-Life's terrific submachine gun has now been replaced by a full-on assault rifle that's functionally identical but looks a lot heftier and sounds even louder when it fires. Half-Life is almost three years old, so all of these graphical enhancements are helpful, though they still don't make Half-Life look like a new game--nor are many of the changes themselves very noticeable. Furthermore, these enhancements are entirely superficial--Half-Life will still play the same as before.
If you buy just one Half-Life-branded game besides Half-Life itself, then that game should be Blue Shift. You can always get Counter-Strike as a free download, and Opposing Force comes packaged with Blue Shift anyway. Don't be misled by the fact that Blue Shift doesn't require Half-Life: If for some terrible reason you don't actually have the original, then owning it should be your first priority. Besides, Blue Shift is actually best suited for those who own and enjoy the original Half-Life. These players will quickly find that Half-Life remains extremely enjoyable today and that the enhanced graphical touches in Blue Shift's High Definition pack make it fun to revisit some of the original game's incredible scenes for the umpteenth time. Otherwise, Blue Shift is a great value if you've never tried Opposing Force--an expansion pack that originally retailed for $10 more than Blue Shift's $30 retail price. However, if you've finished Opposing Force and already spent plenty of time with the original game, you'll find that Blue Shift doesn't have a lot to offer. It's much too short, and it has no multiplayer features--therefore, it won't satisfy your craving for more of the intense action that made Half-Life so remarkable. You can get a $10 rebate for Blue Shift if you've already bought Opposing Force, but that still doesn't make the underachieving Blue Shift worthwhile on its own.

As I’m sure you can see I have only played about an hour of Edge of Space before I uninstalled it and asked for a refund. I cannot claim to know almost anything about the game itself in terms of if it has storyline, how good the mechanics are later on in the game or what kind of a sandbox it is. I’m simply writing about my experience with it and what I should have done to avoid this.
Personally what I didn’t like about the game which is unfortunate for the developers was the introduction. The thing that really allows you to make your first impressions (excluding the tutorial of course), sum up what your experience with this game is going to be like, how everything works etc. I had no problem with the tutorial. I very much enjoyed the general mechanics of the game. I liked how it works, I also could get used to the overall ‘look’ of the game and how it varies from Terraria’s cute pixels. However as soon as I started the actual game itself it all went down-hill.
When I spawned I was confused. “Where was I?”, “What was going on?” I was hoping for some kind of guide (yes, like in Terraria. *sigh) to help me however I was instead met by a distressed, flying, talking shark who after saving politely asked me to make him a toothbrush out of uranium or something. Now, I DO NOT like the addition of quests and things like that on a sandbox. (And again it’s my fault for not watching or reading any reviews) so I was annoyed that I had been restricted already so soon into the game. I like having freedom in a game however a clock timing me down to gather materials to make a toothbrush was very annoying to say the least. However this not what annoyed me, no what annoyed me was the fact that I could not find any Uranium anywhere. So I decided to screw the quest thing and do what I had bought the game for. Explore a new alien world, and have no idea what to expect. However I soon fell off a cliff and almost died. Then I fell off another cliff. And another. And another. It was only then that I realised I must have spawned on the top part of the picture in the Menu of the game where there are many floating islands. I didn’t like this at all as I felt I was restricted to the area island where my spawn was. It didn’t feel like one big map for me to explore, rather different areas I would have to go to as the game progressed. So I decided I would go as far as possible and see if I could find a dungeon or something. After mining things from pretty far away from the spawn point I was told I had a full inventory. So I moved some stuff into the bin last of which was a block of ice which after being deleted I thought nothing off. However when I looked back into my hot-bar, my mining laser had been replaced by this ice. And as there don’t seem to be any instructions beyond the simple things shown in the tutorial I had no idea how to get my mining laser back into my hotbar. The UI was extremely confusing and I was rapidly losing my patience with it. I then killed myself again and spawned back to pod only to realise random things in my inventory were now ice. On top of all of this you cannot move anywhere in the map without being constantly attacked by flying jellyfish and millions of little ‘wolf things’ on the floor that are much faster than you meaning they start to accumulate faster than you can seem to kill them. All this just seemed rather unprofessional and I still had no idea what the hell was going on and why a flying, talking shark needed uranium for his toothbrush. The gameplay was not at all what was displayed in the second trailer and the story so far involved a talking shark. Was he to be my guide??? I just wanted to get to the building, exploring and killing bosses part. I suppose it's maybe just not that sort of game.
It’s not that the game was ‘bad’ as such it’s just that I believe the trailers were a bit misleading within the fact that one shows a Terraria like style of gameplay where your character is free to build and explore and the other shows a very interesting backstory that looked pretty prominent and seemed like something you would progressively learn about throughout the game through recruiting NPC’s, slaying bosses etc. None of this was in the introduction.
It’s entirely my fault that I neglected to look into the game before I bought it. In all honesty I am basically one of those people who just wanted a ‘Terraria in space’ thing. I should have watched other people play it before I blindly went in and bought it. The main two reasons I bought it Edge of Space over Starbound was A) It was £5 cheaper or so, ( ͡ᵔ ͜ʖ ͡ᵔ ) :D and B) I know the lead developer is a friend of Redigit and had permission to use some Terraria bosses (which makes my Terraria in space fantasy even more realistic) and must mean it will have some Terraria qualities. I know that the game is still in Early Access so is obviously far from perfect, but I just expected better.
I suppose the whole point of Early Access is so that people can post their constructive criticism and the developers take it into account. So maybe I will purchase the game again when it’s properly released. I just wish the game had a little more freedom from the start, coincidently just like Terraria does (*another sigh) and not have a random quest to make a toothbrush for a shark out of uranium. Either way, make sure you WATCH GAMEPLAY for Edge of Space before you buy it because it can be different from what it seems. (I'm no proffesional, I just wanted to get my opinions out there!)
Thanks for reading!!!
*Edit: Just thought I would say that Steam did promtly give me a refund for my purchase within about 2 hours.

I feel it best to write this review after I just died in the game and logged nearly 31 days survived.
Heres' how it ended...
I ventured far from my base in order to find a gun and level the playing field. I traveled to Desolation point and spent several days there and finally located a forge, bow, and gun. By the time I had them all I had enough cured hides to craft eveything I needed to become the hunter once I returned to my base in Coastal Highway...but I never made it back.
After deciding on final gear and strategically leaving resources at the processing plant, the ship, and the lighthouse i finally set out. I killed a deer, two wolves and snagged a rabbit as well. Food was no issue but I got sloppy with my water. I had enough had I not made one critical error. Traveling through the broken highway A storm came and I sought shelter at a nearby cave. Deciding to wait it out I checked my warmth and it was at the warmest. The arrow while in the cave showed it was increasing so i bedded down for the night to wait it out. When I awoke I was at 17% and I had hypothermia. I immediately try to build a fire but realize I have no tinder...Coupled with I'm thirsty and low on water now. I go through the mine trying to find where I left tinder, nope none here and i'm encumbered so I unload a ton of gear in order to give myself a chance to make it. I begin traveling back to the lighthouse after drinking the last of my water. I must start a fire to get water, then I can purify it and survive.
On the way to the lighthouse I'm exhausted and my % continues to lower because of my exhaustion and thirst. I make it to the lighthouse and find no tinderplugs..I swore they were here, they must be in the ship. I begin traveling to the ship where they are not to be found so it must be in the processing plant. Darkness has fallen and I begin traveling to the plant hoping I don't die of exhaustion or thirst on the way. Success...I make it there unscathed and find my tinderplugs. I go outside and start a fire, melt snow, and boil it. I have overcome my hunger and I'm still warm. I go back inside to get sleep in order to rest and begin healing knowing tomorrow I'll have to make more water but I'll have no exhaustion and Day on my side...ok...just use my bedroll...um...where is my bedroll?
I realize I dropped my bedroll in my panic at the mine. I knew time was of the essence and just dropped a ton of stuff not realizing I dropped the roll aswell. I have 7% health...I have to make it to a bed so I venture back out...at night. I wobble with blurred vision toward the ships direction only to hear growling. I try to locate it to fire at it but to no avail, He pounces me and bites...I bleed out.
The game is amazing. Best survival game I've ever played. I wager its better than the ones I haven't played. The immersion is what is top notch though. I played on the middle difficulty and found the game challenging and fun. I was invested and took note of each detail. I boasted when I survived a bear attack and my first bout of hypothermia from falling through ice. I felt my heart race as I played shadow avoiding wolves or when I was a track star trying to outrun them to the next doorway. I held hope that each location I explored held a bow or gun I could use to hunt for food and defend myself with instead of hope for another box of crackers or soda. I felt as though I was living the game and as designers thats what we strive to achieve for gamers.
Thank you Devs, great work and I look forward to more of it.

This game has a lot to offer. Do you like "The Matrix"? This game plays sort of like those movies.
You'll slow down time, weave to dodge a bullet, jump at a guy, shoot him in the face, turn around to see a guy behind you, throw your gun at him to disarm him, grab his katana and kill him with it, throw the katana at another guy, teleport into him, killing, grabbing your katana mid-air from your previous throw, and slash down a fourth guy, only to have a fifth guy blindside you and kill you. And then you do it again, only different but equally bad♥♥♥♥♥
While the story may be pretty short (about 2-3 hours), it's actually an interesting experience, and there's always secrets to find in the campaign levels so there's a reason to come back and play it more.
The real meat lies in the Endless Modes. This is where the arcady replayability really shines through. Endless Mode is where you play through arena-like levels with enemies rushing at you. There are different win conditions for each mode, such as "how many can you kill in 60 real seconds" or "how fast can you kill 20 enemies" or simply just survive and kill as many guys as possible before being killed. It's the hallmark of a good game if you keep playing just because it's fun, and that's what this is for me.
There are also challenge modes that let you play through the main game again but with different modifiers, such as katana only, or no guns but punches 1-shot. There are also speedrun modes if that's your thing.
Also the obligatory, "this is the most innovative shooter I've played in years". But really, it's a good game.

After just a few minutes of playing this what looked like a, and don't hate me for this, "bad game", I was completely blown away by how good the gameplay itself was. Survival here isn't as easy as other survival simulators such as Minecraft, Terraria and Don't Starve, and because I became pretty good at those games and surviving, nothing prepared me for the challenges of Project Zomboid, which made it really interesting, fun and challenging.
The aim of the game is not to survive as long as you can, but actually to just to delay the inevitable fact that you are going to die one way or another. The ways you could die range from being mutilated by a horde to a simple everyday sickness, and even though this doesn't sound really great, it makes the game really interesting and special.
If anyone is looking for a game to play and test your knowledge on survival, Project Zomboid is one well worth the challenge...

One of the first games I ever bought on Steam, and still one of my favorites, as well as one that I still come back to every so often. I tend to think of it more as an interactive visualizer than a game, but that's not say it lacks gameplay. A pleasing variety of game modes offer just about any difficulty level you'd like, from a laid-back, casual experience that doesn't require a lot of thought to an ultra-hardcore race that requires catlike reflexes as you struggle toward achieving a global high score.
The core game mechanics are simple (but are heavily remixed across the different modes), which is desirable in this sort of game. Without a doubt, this game's main selling point is the fact that you can plug in any songs you have MP3s for (among a few other, listed filetypes), and the game will generate technicolor rollercoasters unique to each track.
Bottom line: Audiosurf is great for virtually anyone who falls into that section of the Venn diagram between music lovers and gamers. (Also, it has a sequel, but as an owner of both, I tend to stick with this one. That's not a strong preference, and they're essentially two versions of the same game, but it's something to consider.)

**Written during Alpha Stage**
57h played during the Big Alpha week-end, I haven't had that much fun and so few sleep since TitanFall beta and that says a lot because it was so new GameplayWise on so many levels, Evolve made me feel the same.
Beside the first day which was very hectic with 1h wait time per game average, this is probably the most achieved Alpha I have ever played (and I played a lot of them) and to be honest it felt more like an open beta stage very close to release, so huge congratulations to the whole team and thank you for the reactive patch that finally allowed us to play almost normally on saturday.
I could write probably 5 pages about the good sides and the small problems that still remains but im too lazy for that so I will only mention a few:
- I would love to be able to make a private lobby so me and my friends could play together versus one of us being the Monster but im sure it's already planed because you certainly don't want to make the same mistake TitanFall did at release and seriously compromised it's player base.
- Please get rid of the never ending and multiple loading stages, and if one of the player can't load the game after 30s he should start as AI till he's loaded and replace the AI. People with low end computers should lower their graphic settings or suffer the consequences. The ones with appropriate settings shouldn't suffer waiting 5mn for some 2005 laptop.
- Game balance is overall really nice, so don't listen to the whinny hords that just need more practice and strategy with the monster and teamplay with the hunters. Only the Kraken seem a legit debate, because if it gets to stage 2, in the hands of a decent player it's really powerfull, so I'd get rid of the "homing" part of those missiles it can spamm and let the player skill only be involved here. Morphopolis is a very interesting, and unique game that takes place in the world of insects. There are very few games of this variety. At first glance you might think that this is just an artificial life simulator type of game (Examples of such games are Simlife, Simant, and Spore). But, you would be wrong. Because this is actually a 2D, point and click game with puzzles (LOTS of them to say the least). You start the game off by playing as a caterpillar, and you must help the caterpillar create a cocoon in order to proceed to the next level. Don't start thinking that you'll play as a caterpillar in every level, there actually are other insects in this game you can play as later on. Don't worry, I won't give away the names of the other insects or describe their appearances (assuming you're a gamer who likes surprises). There are puzzles in every level of Morphopolis. A puzzle can be accessed by collecting a certain amount of items (Sticks, berries, pollen, etc.). Some puzzles are easily solved in a matter of minutes, while others will have you leaning your head against your hand wondering how on earth you can find a solution to the current puzzle. The artwork in this game is absolutely beautiful. But the animation is somewhat cheap (Seems like the kind of animation you'd see in a Newgrounds game). Now as for the soundtrack, it's very atmospheric, and fits the game like a glove. The only complaint I have with this game is that it's too short! I managed to complete this game in a single day (I'm not kidding). Partly because the puzzles in this game are very similar to puzzles I've seen in other games. Now if you're a casual gamer, then chances are you're probably going to be playing this game much longer then I would. Overall, Morphopolis is a very well designed game that I wish could have a sequel or an expansion pack. If you like Professor Layton or any other puzzle game in general, give this one a try.
It's great fun! Trial & Error is sometimes needed, but it's never frustrating as there are enough checkpoints.

When I bought this game I was well read up on the mixed opinions and figured it was worth the risk; the pros seemed worth it as someone who really enjoyed atmospheric Lovecraftian stuff.
I do believe there are some strong elements to this: the actual text and the stuff you can come across in your discoveries can be really memorable, and the base premise remains enticing.
Unfortunately, it's weighed down by an incredibly tedius and grind heavy game. I made a similar complaint with Darkest Dungeon that the grind holds back some of the enjoyment, but I believe that game is able to still stand strong on it's gameplay, presentation and graphics/music. I can't say the same here.
...Yes, I've only played about 2.6 hours. Having said that, most of those 2.6 hours were spent just steering the boat in a direction, hoping to come across something interesting or supplies. I would come across things just tantalizing enough to get excited, believing something big was on the way or I might be thrust into some new adventure. Usually I just wound up starving to death at sea and some cannibalism. Not nearly as exciting as horrific as you'd want to belive.
Right now the game is free to play, and you can get it on sale for 6.50. You might be able to have better fortune than I had for that kind of deal, but for the baseline 19$ I paid for it, having some kind of enjoyment in the first two hours is pretty important.
So in short
PROS:
+ Unique setting
+ Good writing and worldbuilding can stir you to excitement when finding a new location, if for a moment
+Lovecraftian, I'm a sucker for that sort of thing
CONS:
- Slow, way too slow. I'm not looking to prosper and win or anything, but I'm hoping to at least have a gripping descent into death and insanity before my legacy turns to ash and my boat sinks
- Grindy. You 'inheret' some of the findings and fortune from any previous, unfortunate members of your family upon a death, and the game seems to put a lot of emphasis on this. Grinding is bad.
- Paltry assests. The art for this game is painfully underwhelming, to the point where some otherwise disturbing happenings are lessend by some mediocre renditions- more than that, apparently a lot of it is recycled from some of their previous titles. That's just weak- music and visuals can be a make or break element in a game banking on atmosphere and forging a narrative, and should be given some serious handling.
-Maybe it's just because I never got past the early stage of the game where I'm essentially just some sap in a dingy with a pea shooter strapped to the back, but the combat is incredibly tedius, a mishmash of real time aiming and manuevering coupled with timed button pressing. Even when something is happening, it's still just not that compelling.
FINAL VERDICT: I dunno. I want to believe there's some merit to be found in this after toughing out the cons, but I wasn't able to find it and after several hours in I was starting to feel mostly disappointed more than anything. I think this is worth trying since it's currently free for a few days and you can buy it on sale for 6.50... But don't buy it for more than that, and not before you try it for yourself.
Having said that, I can't reccomend it under any other circumstance.

This is one of the most realistic games I've ever played. When you're getting shot at or arty'd by the opposing teams commander it makes you really feel like your getting arty'd or shot at. Squad leaders mark artillery and have to stay alive as a mobile spawn point, throw smoke for attacks, etc, otherwise that is when the other team that has their team in order will murder you. My only frustration with this game is that this game goes on sale so often that many newbies get a hold of this game, which is fine. Nothing worse than having a dumb new commander or SL that are lollygagging around while your team gets bombarded by the other well organized team. I welcome all people to try this game, but know how to play before you come into such a well structured team-realism game before you go buy it and think its just about blowing heads off. Batman - The Telltale Series is a game which consists of five episodes in which you control Bruce Wayne/Batman as he fights crime in Gotham in an original Batman story. Gameplay consists of choosing dialogue options and making tough moral decisions, interspersed with quicktime event combat, and detective sections where you connect pieces of evidence together.
I am a big Telltale fan and thoroughly enjoyed their take on Batman. It was fresh and not afraid to make big changes to the usual lore, while still staying true to Batman's roots. Of course the usual criticism of Telltale - that the choices don't
matter despite their protestations - could still be argued here, but Telltale has improved since the days of season 1 of The Walking Dead in making choices have actual consequences.
Batman seems to take a different approach to the choice-based narrative too, there are still the usual moral choices where neither answer is correct, but Batman also includes choices of whether to be Bruce Wayne or Batman in certain situations. I greatly appreciated this as Batman games are almost always 100% geared around being Batman, for good reason I'll admit, so it was refreshing to have more of a focus on both aspects of Bruce Wayne. This gameplay choice also feeds in to the narrative which isn't afraid to explore the age old Batman question of which persona is really the mask - and your decisions can actually construct a narrative which leans towards either answer. There are also gameplay segments where you are forced to choose between one situation or another which adds replayability as Batman cannot be in two places at once.
I had some performance issues while playing this game - for example I died a few times because the qte button prompt never appeared - but my laptop is quite low-performance so I blame that mostly on my hardware rather than the game. I still managed to enjoy and complete the game despite this, but if you aren't sure about your computer specs and want this game then maybe wait for a sale before buying it.
Overall I would say that if you are already a Telltale fan then definitely buy this because it's another great game.
If you have yet to play a Telltale game then I would still recommend this, but only if you are someone who enjoys narrative-focused games as that is its main appeal. The only gameplay relies heavily on qtes so if you think that will turn you off then maybe this game isn't for you. If you still really aren't sure then there are plenty of let's plays on youtube you can have a quick look at to see if this is the sort of game you would enjoy or not, that's what convinced me to get the game for myself.
If you are planning on buying the sequel "Batman: The Enemy Within" and are wondering whether or not to get this as well I would recommend buying it but it isn't necessary. The Walking Dead seasons 2 and 3 don't require playing the previous season(s) to be enjoyed but doing so does give you a greater connection to the characters.
DISCLAIMER - I bought this game as part of Humble Bundle's Telltale bundle which drastically reduced its price

Banished is a fantastic game. It's difficult, but not because of it's complex learning curve (like some games -- looking at you DF). It teaches you everything you need to know in one of the best ways i've ever seen. And then subjects you to harsh winters, natural disasters, and the ever challenging balancing act of population growth divided by needs and hunger.
The only downside, one i've heard in other reivews, is that the game lacks a reason to go back to the old save files. 9 times out of 10 i'll just make a new town, because while I enjoyed the hell out of working on my previous town, there is no real incentive outside of achievements to loading up an old, longer save. Games like civ are different in this way, because (different genre, but bear with me) they allow you goals to strive for. Space, cultural victory, etc. In this game, you're just trying to see how long you can survive against the elements -- and your own planning. But you can do that at any point in the game, you don't have to put 50 hours into a single town. The difficulties don't really change. You're trying to solve the same puzzle.
Overall, like I said, a PHENOMENAL game. And created by one guy. Support him, love his game, and try the mods. I don't play them often, but one person said the popular mods add 20x the content the base game comes with. And the base game comes with A LOT.

Funny story, actually. I bought this thinking it was Starbound, and was horribly disappointing. I have no idea what build I was getting into.
What I got into was pretty much "build a base with a couple of buildings as a home-base, upgrade your characters and build armor and weapons, then kill the like 20 or so different enemies in the game."
I mean the way to progress your character was to get little data-chips that would increase your xp.
It was cute, but it took waaaay too long to progress, and when you did a lot of the time it felt like half of your progress was for very little.
Now it's been a while, there's a pretty clear line between enemies that act as a faction that alert each other and gang up on you(can get really tedious at times, but as long as this is a beta that's all good) whereas there's other wildlife enemies where some'll be more aggressive, but less factional in that they communicate with others of it kind, and then other creatures doesn't really care that much, but gets mad or scared if you attack them.
Base construction used to have a power generator and a command center's CPU-distribution as their main sources of power for the base equipment. Now they have Command Centers that power parts of bases, but command centers will conflict with each other, so you'll either have bases build into segments, or bases placed in completely different edges of the map, still connected by the Command Centers as one can teleport from one CC to another.
There's the separation between Phase-type weaponry (that doesn't use ammunition) that does less damage than projectile-based weaponry(which does use ammunition), there's signs that they'll end up giving us energy-based weaponry as well.
Game's also got a few vehicles, as of patch 0.4458 we have the Zephyr, decent hp, medium speed vehicle, pretty large, would guess about 6x7 blocks-size or so? There's also a Thunderbird, which I haven't tried, but it's supposed to be more armored, but slower. Other than these mechanical vehicles there's mounts: A crab, a jumpy raptor, a fast raptor and a net with captured jellyfish that works like a hoverbike. Jellyfishbikes have very little fuel, but are way faster than traveling by foot, never tried mounts as I was worried their lack of ability to fly or hover would make it hard to traverse in any useful terrain, as there's not much to gain by scouting the surface, unless you're on-foot killing enemies for loot and XP.
Hope to see the ability to equip and upgrade vehicles and/or mounts with different types of weapons/mining equipment in the future(choosing between phase, projectile and energy, potentially even one additional weapon slot in specific cases would add interesting layers into the vehicles section I think) Definitely hope to see refueling stations/refueling kits in the future as some vehicles are way to expensive to have them permanently expire after traveling a short distance, not to mention that giving the vehicle retrievability until it's destroyed could justify increasing costs of vehicles, and giving it said weapon/armor upgrades as mentioned earlier.
Not sure what the devs have in mind in terms of npc's or vending machines, but so far this game is intriguing.
The different AI behaviors are also interesting in terms of there being completely passive AI, passive-aggresive AI, faction aggressive AI's and some that will camouflage themselves rather than attack you for survival.
Nature yielding multiple resources as well giving different elements like sap, bark, the leaves and seeds, which affects what players can do in terms of crafting. It's half interesting due to different categories of crafting materials (Inorganic(processsed)/raw, minerals/chemicals/organic etc) but I also halfway feel like plants and gems end up kind of taking up a little bit much inventory space, as much as I adore the complexity. It works, but with a limited amount of inventory space it's definitely tough if you're going solo. Which also makes the swarmy enemy spawns a bit tough to deal with. Haven't tried playing with friends yet, so would say this'd be way more fun multiplayer.
All in all, in its current state I think that if you wish to roll solo and only go for weapons and armor upgrades I think the game'll last a few days. If you're going for exploration, building bases, upgrading yourself and essentially minmaxing on everything on your own it'll be worth everything from 1 week and up depending on how fast you are with these kinds of games and how much time you have to play it. I'm thinking 15+ hours a day being super efficient and lucky with weapon stats(Because weapons' stats are semi-RNG. Dmg per shot, in-game gun visuals, accuracy, crit rate, Ammo cap, MAYBE reloading time, and refire rate/rounds per second). Although it's a bit buggy and pretty slow in its current state, its simple "complexity" in crafting and although the devs(and their resources) are in charge of how much they can do with it I think it has sick potential, even if they end up sticking with the content they have right now, although more stuff's always beyond appreciated.

I bought this game in the Humble Telltale bundle. I have finished 3 out of 5 episodes, and so far I've really enjoyed this game. I have had a *few* issues, and they're mostly technical:
- Some lag, but nothing game-breaking.
- When I first was playing the game, if I set it to the correct resolution for my laptop (1920x1080), the ingame cursor wouldn't cover the whole screen, like there was an invisible boundary I couldn't move the cursor past. This was solved with going to Program Files (x86) > Steam > steamapps > common > Batman The Telltale Series, then right-clicking on Batman_win8.exe, selecting "Properties", going to the "Compatibility" tab, and checking "Override high DPI scaling behavior."
- The past two times I've tried opening the game it opened in a weird windowed mode that was shifted a little down and to the right on my screen. This was solved by closing the game and opening it again.
Additionally, the usage of letter keys AND arrow keys AND the mouse in QTEs has been a bit awkward because I don't have three hands. However, it has just now occurred to me that I can probably use WASD instead of the arrow keys, and that would probably fix that problem.

What can I say about Outlast?
Nothing...
Lest I bring up horrible memories of intense running and hiding under beds from cannibals, grooms, and hulking beef monsters. You may have to be a squeamish sissy like me who detests the dark to really be immersed in it.
Outlast has you explore a disgusting "asylum" to expose a corporation's unethical practices regarding treatment of it's patients and Variants.
It has a neat story, some interesting antagonists that you may love to hate, or actually fall in love with (ask the fangirls of the Groom- don't look him up just play the DLC and you'll know).
Creepy scenes that make you cringe and scream, especially in the DLC. Outlast sports spiffy textures, and is very well optimized (at least for me on Windows 10).
Great ambience and mood. You loathe going into the dark but know in your frantic head you can't continue unless you explore there where the buses don't run. The music does help to create intensity.
Two problems I have: It's somewhat short- I played it on the second highest difficulty and wasn't trying to speedrun it to almost blast through it.
And the ending to the main game left much to be desired.
Otherwise it's a solid horror experience to play by yourself or with some timid friends. Don't play it on Normal or even Hard. Your character holds too many batteries and can survive getting beat with blunt objects like they are tissues. Bump up the difficulty to Nightmare or Insane for a true experience. And read some of the "Classified" documents and just absorb the world.
P.S. Yes DLC is good. Very good. Give Red Barrels your money. You have too much disposable income anyways.

This game has a reliance on cheap and ineffectual horror tropes.
Jumpscares only startle people if they don't expect it coming. Horror is more than jump scares, it's anticipation and both well timed delivery and denial. Outlast isn't scary at all, it's jumpscares are predictible and dated. Jumpscares themselves have always been weak, at least to me. At least in my opnion, true horror is something that is patient, careful and slow to execute. The faster something happens the weaker the effect. Ultimately an ideal horror writer would want your own imagination to become your worst enemy. The environment is there to facilitate your own dread manifesting things that are not there. But your tension makes even the simplest thing seem magnitudes worse. I studied horror in literature, traditional art mediums, interactive (like games) and cinema when I was in university and I can say that I've got at least an academic understanding of the nature of horror.
As a game, outlast is functional (It's solid, easy to tweak, never crashes, has good load times and mecanically is fantastic!) if very, very tired. I've been trying to play through it to the end but...it's agonizingly boring. It delivers too much on what you expect to happen, the environment is stale (A "haunted" asylum? *sigh*). I really, really want to enjoy good horror but what most developers and writers consider to be horror is actually just shock. What is truly scary is unknown, ambiguity and mystery. When you don't know what is pursuing you, when you feel something lurking around the corner. Something that darts by, out of sight, barely noticed. In a game many horror elements would need to be in places where you could easily miss them and if you do, well...you missed them. If they are geared to deliver in a place where you're sure to see them, they don't have any effect such as a window or a door that you're reaching for.
At least in my opnion, for something to be genuinely scary, it needs to create an atmosphere that is terrifying FAR beyond any scary entity (ghost, monster, demon, maniac, etc.). I should be more afraid to "be there" than I am afraid anything that's dangerous. If I'm terrified of the environment than anything that happens (or better yet "doesn't" happen, part of the anticipation) will be significantly more intense. Horror and fear is an art that is not well practiced by movies and games. In the end, for me anyway, this game is more an exercise in "beating" it. Defeating the game at it's own game. I don't need weapons to defeat maniacs, only patience to evade or outlast (hah) them.
As a final note, if you think I may be rushing, I'm not. I like to take my time in a game, to appreciate every detail that went into it's design. Especially in a horror, I want to get immersed to make the scares more personal but this game is so painfully predictible and it's lack of any actual scary content or supernatural forces makes it no scarier than walking down a crowded street in a metropolis at noon (which for agoraphobics is scary, so I'll give it that). I spend a lot of time looking around and the enemies are something I casually dodge around while still idly exploring "chase" scenes. It's like the whole game moves in slow motion.
Let's hope the second one actually makes a game about ghosts and scary stuff. Real monsters, not just maniacs.
