All of these issues though, are not nearly as bad as people make them out to be. You never HAVE to buy chips in order to play. You are generously given chips frequently. Every 15 minutes you get 250. Logging in for the first time grants you 1000, and 500 for each subsequent day you log in. And finally, doing daily and weekly tasks, gives you chips. Trust me, you should have plenty of enough chips to start playing anything except for maybe Poker.
As for bugs, I personally have only encountered one. It's slightly annoying to join a table, only to freeze and be unable to do anything. That being said, that was literally only the first day of me playing. I haven't had that problem at all since.
People complaining about "Dealers dealing to nonexistent people" are probably just having internet troubles. Now, the only REAL issue, is the lack of tables. There's tons of slot machines and plenty of seats in Bingo, but there's a huge issue with Blackjack and Poker tables being full constantly.
I fully recommend this game for people that don't want to spend money on actually going to the Casino. It's a casual casino experience, and it's great at being that.

Audiosurf is an arcade game in which you’re controlling a rocket-like vehicle moving through a track generated by the music that you choose. Your objective is to collect as many orbs as possible to get a high score and get on top of the leaderboard for the song that you’re playing.
The art style is simplistic, with the track and some details (like stars, circles, stripes and other various shapes in the background) being one color on the black background. The color changes in tact with the music, and shifts dynamically from green through yellow to red and back, which really does look nice while playing. Technically, this is an indie game and has no kind of super graphical features. It doesn’t need them either. It does run smooth in full HD, which is important.
There is no story or characters in case you wonder. This is an arcade game, the only goal of it is pure fun and achieving a high score. And it’s good at that! Depending on the mode that you choose, you’re either collecting single colored bricks while avoiding grey blocks on the way that break your point streak, or try to collect as many different-colored blocks as you can while arranging them in a matching order, Tetris style. If you don’t manage to match them before you hit next blocks, you lose your streak and your points. There are various modes, each with specific quirks to the gameplay, and a few difficulty levels, which introduce more colors to match and remove the side of the track on which you can “rest” to avoid overfilling the block-bar. The easiest modes allow you to enjoy the music while chilling, the hardest will test your skill.
The main feature of this game is that you can load your own music to play “on”. You choose it from the folder on your PC and the game creates a track that corresponds with the pace of the song you’re playing. It works great with everything, from pop through rap to heavy metal. To be honest, it’s not that different regardless of the music genre, but it makes a custom track for each song and is fun as hell.
That must be the most important thing about this game. It’s FUN! For a moment, you can just forget everything, play your favorite music and focus on it as the track adapts to the changes in the pace of the song, while controlling a rocket and moving blocks like in Tetris, everything on a hypnotic and pulsing background. It sounds chaotic, but believe me, it’s entertaining! If you like music a lot you should really try this out, just to experience the songs in a bit different way than before!
There are leaderboards, both for your friends, regional and global, for each song that was played on Audiosurf. If you want to get on top of that leaderboard and master that one song, go ahead. It’s easy to learn, hard to master. And enjoyable at that.
I really like this game, as I had a lot of fun playing it. HOWEVER, there is one big problem with it now… Audiosurf 2 is out, and even better. I give this game a thumb up, because I sincerely think it deserves it, but if you have not played it yet, I recommend trying out the second one instead. As an older arcade game, there is just no reason to come back to this one when a better version is out. For the time when it was released and value on its own, I still must give Audiosurf a high score. It earned it fairly.

There's a section in this game where the narrator relates a conversation he had with another game developer about whether or not games need to be "playable". As in, could you expect a reasonable person to actually sit down and do what is required to progress through the game?
The Beginner's Guide is a two hour narration of a man's psychoanalysis of his friend, of himself, and of the video games he's made. As Games As Art criticism, it's a fine piece of work, though a little on-the-nose. So much direct explanation and analysis is explicitly stated that it doesn't give you much left over to actually think about and puzzle out yourself. The story shines brightest when the narrator discusses his relationship between him and his friend, and while it occasionally gets a little overwrought, overall it is well-written and enjoyable.
Back to that original question, though - the narrator says he believes that games need to be playable, but the irony is that The Beginner's Guide is not a playable game. You don't *do* anything. You're not playing a game, even in the artsy modern "this is an experience, not an arcade game, pleb" sense. People deride games like this using the pejorative "walking simulator", but games with that label have you do more than go from point A to point B. You take in a world, you absorb ambience, you meet and talk with personalities. You
with people and things, that's the key; and that's what The Beginner's Guide lacks.
I've said it before and I'll say it again; fit the medium to the message, or the message to the medium, but don't mismatch them and get angry when people don't like your square peg in a round hole. This would have been a great movie, but it's a mediocre game, so I don't recommend it.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the second and final expansion for the original Half-Life and was developed by Gearbox Software (the same developers for the first expansion Opposing Force) and published by Valve. A fairly short but decent expansion which gives us yet another perspective to the entire Black Mesa Incident from a different character.
This time the player takes on the role of Barney Calhoun, a security officer employed at the Black Mesa Research Facility and the man who has helped Gordon Freeman out of so many sticky and difficult situations. The game starts out with Barney Calhoun carrying out his duties and then being caught up in the Black Mesa Incident which, like Opposing Force, cleverly coincides with the original Half-Life’s storyline.
What Gearbox Software does well is maintaining the atmosphere and world of the original Half-Life while providing the experience through the eyes of someone else who was involved in the story of the original Half-Life. For me, Blue Shift felt like the final game in the Penumbra series (Penumbra: Requiem) as it ends the first Half-Life game’s storyline in a fairly chilled and relaxing way without forcing the player to battle an end boss whilst providing a few situations where a puzzle needs to be solved.
The core gameplay is the same as it is for Half-Life and Opposing Force with the weapons and other items not really changing which isn’t necessarily a bad thing. The health system is also the same with some slight changes as those that were in Opposing Force. Since security officers do not wear HEV suits, they cannot make use of any HEV suit charger units that are located around the facility. Instead the player must pick up security officer issued body armour vests and helmets to replenish their armour protection. Something that I’ve noticed about Blue Shift is that you will find an enormous amount of first aid packs around each chapter and this makes the game less challenging. The player’s flashlight seems to have been designed differently with the way light is dispersed in dark places which felt a lot more realistic.
Structurally, the game is chaptered like the previous games and provides a fun, linear storyline that will keep you engaged and wanting to find out more. Barney Calhoun does not encounter any of the alien creatures of Race X as Adrian Shepherd did in Opposing Force, but does encounter hostility from the marines and the traditional Xen alien creatures.
Overall, there is not much more that could be said about Half-Life: Blue Shift. It provides a new and interesting perspective to the storyline which leaves a lot of questions and few answers. For those who want to return to the events of the Black Mesa Incident and see the situation unfold from a different viewpoint then I highly recommend Blue Shift. I personally found it a joy to play and think it is just as good as Opposing Force.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is a first-person action game by Gearbox Software and Valve and serves as the third official expansion to the Half-Life franchise.  Unlike Half-Life or Half-Life: Opposing Force, Blue Shift does not introduce new game mechanics; rather, it offers a new type of narrative storytelling through constant interactions with an NPC character (i.e., Dr. Rosenberg).
In this game, you step into the shoes of Black Mesa Security Guard and Clone Template Barney Calhoun, a man whose normal routine of offering beers and guarding doors is shattered with a catastrophic accident that opens the facility to an alien invasion and U.S. Military intervention (a direct result of Dr. Freeman's experiment from the first game).  As Barney Calhoun, you try to survive the alien invasion, protect the survivors, and escape the now doomed Black Mesa Research Facility.
+ Good story (NO SPOILERS) that serves as the 'final link' that connects every story (Half-Life, Half-Life: Opposing Force and Half-Life: Decay) of the Black Mesa Incident together.
+ Constant interaction with an NPC that is essential to the plot rather than for opening doors
+ The first game in the franchise to introduce 'HD' content during its time
+ Intense action as can be expected from a Half-Life game
+ Satisfying puzzles
+ Adaptive enemy AI, especially with the soldiers
+ Great level design
+ Barney can kill dangerous aliens and highly trained military soldiers wearing only a flak vest and an almost transparent plastic helmet as protection (He would be perfect in the Warhammer 40,000 universe as an Imperial Guardsman).
- VERY SHORT and possibly the shortest game I ever played with only 3 hours of playtime on Hard Mode and Training Tutorial
- Existence of bugs despite being 14 years old (Particularly a bug where you're unable to move)
- No new weapons, enemy, or gameplay mechanics.
- Most weapons from the first game were removed
- Relatively easy (even on hard mode) as compared to the other games.  In my opinion, it is because acquiring 'armor' and health kits are a lot easier.
Story and lore wise, Blue Shift is GOOD but other than that, it does not offer any new content aside from the new player perspective of the overall Half-Life Lore.  In my opinion, Blue Shift is not an expansion but more of a DLC (downloadable content) than anything else, which is not a bad thing by the way, especially one with a good story and fun action sequences.
So do you buy Blue Shift?  YES but DO NOT BUY Blue Shift alone! Instead, purchase

What can I say about Outlast?
Nothing...
Lest I bring up horrible memories of intense running and hiding under beds from cannibals, grooms, and hulking beef monsters. You may have to be a squeamish sissy like me who detests the dark to really be immersed in it.
Outlast has you explore a disgusting "asylum" to expose a corporation's unethical practices regarding treatment of it's patients and Variants.
It has a neat story, some interesting antagonists that you may love to hate, or actually fall in love with (ask the fangirls of the Groom- don't look him up just play the DLC and you'll know).
Creepy scenes that make you cringe and scream, especially in the DLC. Outlast sports spiffy textures, and is very well optimized (at least for me on Windows 10).
Great ambience and mood. You loathe going into the dark but know in your frantic head you can't continue unless you explore there where the buses don't run. The music does help to create intensity.
Two problems I have: It's somewhat short- I played it on the second highest difficulty and wasn't trying to speedrun it to almost blast through it.
And the ending to the main game left much to be desired.
Otherwise it's a solid horror experience to play by yourself or with some timid friends. Don't play it on Normal or even Hard. Your character holds too many batteries and can survive getting beat with blunt objects like they are tissues. Bump up the difficulty to Nightmare or Insane for a true experience. And read some of the "Classified" documents and just absorb the world.
P.S. Yes DLC is good. Very good. Give Red Barrels your money. You have too much disposable income anyways.

I bought this game in the Humble Telltale bundle. I have finished 3 out of 5 episodes, and so far I've really enjoyed this game. I have had a *few* issues, and they're mostly technical:
- Some lag, but nothing game-breaking.
- When I first was playing the game, if I set it to the correct resolution for my laptop (1920x1080), the ingame cursor wouldn't cover the whole screen, like there was an invisible boundary I couldn't move the cursor past. This was solved with going to Program Files (x86) > Steam > steamapps > common > Batman The Telltale Series, then right-clicking on Batman_win8.exe, selecting "Properties", going to the "Compatibility" tab, and checking "Override high DPI scaling behavior."
- The past two times I've tried opening the game it opened in a weird windowed mode that was shifted a little down and to the right on my screen. This was solved by closing the game and opening it again.
Additionally, the usage of letter keys AND arrow keys AND the mouse in QTEs has been a bit awkward because I don't have three hands. However, it has just now occurred to me that I can probably use WASD instead of the arrow keys, and that would probably fix that problem.

Sadly, I simply can't recommend this game. Telltale seem to be stuck on their "formula" and, frankly, that formula gets stale. They don't really improve anything with each title...on the contrary, their games seem to get worse and more boring and repetitive with every instalment. While Batman's story is not bad and has a few twists and turns, ultimately the game can't do such a character justice.
Graphics:
Telltale still uses the same engine from several years ago...they try and polish it with every title, but ultimately it was outdated then and now just looks horrible. Animation quality is as stiff as a young man's boner when seeing a naked woman for the first time. Textures are grainy and really terrible. There's even texture pop-in...and the "black line of Telltale" is once again part of it as well (it's basically a black line that can be seen in many scenes, stretching trhoughout the screen...simple graphics bug, but still not fixed). When the people try to react to something they look comical instead of showing real emotions. It's 2017, people. You need to up your game. And my god, how arrogant or stupid can you be to put the EXACT same character model right next to each other in at least one certain scene? 6 times!!!!!!! Is this Batman: The Clone Wars?
Sound:
Voice acting is pretty decent, the conversations flow into one another, so that's all good. Generally sound effects are ok, but sometimes sound seems to cut out for no reason...i.e. a sound effect is just not playing.
Performance:
Oh my, this is one of the main reasons to not recommend this game. It runs like absolute (bat♥♥♥♥♥♥ The loading times are long (I once even waited a minute or so), and every action and scene needs to be loaded when that action occurs, causing a hiccup almost every time. That means the already stiff animations are even rougher, because during a fight the game will just stutter repeatedly. This is, frankly, unacceptable. There's also no way to skip certain cutscenes or "last time on", scenes which have the same dreadful stuttering...again, I waited about 30 seconds until the next scene played out in Episode 5's "last time on"...unacceptable.
Gameplay:
It's quicktime events. Really that's almost all there is to it. And if you're not doing those, you'll be "investigating" crime scenes (like 5 in the game or so...1 for each episode), which means looking at each circle and then making some very easy connections like "gun casings connect to killed officer"...meh. It's a bit like in the Arkham games, only worse, because there is no actual effort involved. Another new gameplay "feature" is the possiblity to take out enemies in different ways at certain times...but again, this just means selecting whether you want to kick or punch someone mostly. And then there's the much marketed "Batman vs. Wayne" choices...of which there are a total of THREE in the game...and one is just for the epilogue. And none of those choices affect the game's story at all. You might read different newspaper articles, but who cares? Batman was definitely not the correct character to use for this style of game...sorry, it's ♥♥♥♥ing boring. There's no tension. No fear of failure. Just randomly press the buttons shown on screen and never make a choice and you'll get the same outcome as everyone else.
Story:
The meat of the game...I'd say it's decent. They tried something very original here and I can respect that, even though I'm not on board with everything. They used familiar characters and gave them a different background and development. Whether or not the choice of enemies is good is up to you to decide, but I found it a bit "lacking" to be honest. There are just too many gaps to make the villain believable...
Choices:
Oh yes, the much touted choices...it seems they're getting worse with every instalment as well. I remember in the first Walking Dead there were a lot of choices that were also tracked at the end of each episode...gradually those choices became less and less and ultimately we all know that no matter what choices we make the episodes play out almost in exactly the same way. Spoilers below:
In any case, you can't reason with people, you can't convince them (not) to do something. I know that is the Telltale formula, but like I said, it gets old and in the case of Batman it doesn't really work so well. Does it matter what the public or police think about Batman? No, not really. You may get some different dialogue from time to time, but there are no hidden scenes or missions. Something that is desperately needed to reinvigorate this type of game. Heck, it's barely 8 hours long...and most of that is just watching cutscenes. Give me multiple paths to finish the game. Stop building "series", or if you do, make it so that my choices affect the next game in the series. Let me convince someone to get them on my side. Give me more gameplay options, not just quick time events. Then you can do so much more with the choices...disappointing.
I avoided this series for quite some time but came to enjoy the story more than the bland gameplay mechanics.

I bought this over a year ago and while interesting and fun then it is _WAY_ more fun now and only getting better. I'm a hardcore zombie fan (watched many movies, played many games, read books, etc.) and this game is a top notch zombie experience: hunger, thirst, fear, tension, permadeath, etc. I get tense playing this game without even realizing it. Even as it stands it's an interesting, tough challenge, but new features like underground environments, hunting, vehicles, etc. will only make it that much better. One of my favourite features about this game is that the permadeath takes the focus off grinding on a character for years and puts the focus back on the fun of the game. You're _going_ to die, so don't stress about levels too much. My second favourite feature is the persistent "sandbox" mode where anything you build stays around for your next character. Have a farm started? It'll still be there. Have a stash somewhere? Your next character can find it. It's a compelling storyline in itself and I imagine could make for a decent short story compendium.
I judge games on whether I get at least one hour per dollar I pay for the game and Project Zomboid has achieved that several times over already.

Cuphead only recently came to my attention, so for I game I hadn't heard anything of, I was suprised when I saw how much buzz was floating around it. To avoid spoilers, I bought the game blind without reading too much or watching any gameplay, so I could see for myself firsthand.
The first thing that struck me right away was the art design. The person who was in charge of art direction should get an award for how good the attention to detail is at recreating the retro cartoon look and feel for this game. From the character models, to their animations and sounds, it is literally the most fully realized art direction I've ever seen in a game. Even the slightly scratchy screen overlay with the mixture of super saturated and faded colours is genius.
Touted as run and gun game, I feel that couldn't be any more accurate to describe the gameplay. Levels play like side-scrolling shooters and it absolutely gave me a Super Nintendo vibe of game like Mega Man and Contra. And like those games, there's♥♥♥♥♥♥onscreen happening everywhere at all times, with bullets flying, bombs exploding, enemies popping out of other enemies... Needless to say, the game is brutally difficult. And to make things even more difficult, the player has very few lives in each level, and there are no checkpoints so if you die, it's back to the start. A "simple" mode is offered for players who find the difficulty too much, but what's too bad is that the simple mode limits the players experience in boss battles by cutting the battle short, so they will only end up seeing about half of the boss battle. That said, this is probably the fairest way the devs could have dealt with the difficulty question, because a player who wants to just cruise through the game can do so on simple, but a player who defeats the game on harder difficulty gets the reward of seeing all the extra cool boss stuff.
The gameplay and controls are silky smooth, though I did encounter a few unusual glitches in my time playing. One of the most endearing things about the game is the wonderful inclusion of a local two player coop, just like the good old SNES. This game was begging for a local coop and it works fantastically. I found I enjoyed the game infinitely more whilst playing with a mate, I think maybe because the difficulty is significantly reduced to a more manageable level, but also dying constantly felt less less like a relentless struggle and more like a hilarious challenge with a friend. Furthermore, two playing player allows for the opportunity for a last chance revive if your friend is killed, which made tons of sense to me in terms of the games balancing, so for that reason I would definitely recommend this game with multiplayer in mind. And on that note, it kind of blows my mind that Cuphead doesn't have an online multiplayer option to play with a stranger or even a friend on another computer. I really, really hope this is something that gets added in the future. In the meantime, there is a workaround you can use if have an Nvidia card and GeForce Experience.
$20 felt expensive for this game when I first saw it because it looked so simple, but there really is so much fun to be had that a $20 value actually seems like a great price to me now. This is one of those games that if you are of a certain age like me and have fond memories as a kid, playing your Super Nintendo and getting wrecked over and over again until you somehow beat that game, then I think Cuphead is going to really appeal to you. It's like a game you loved from your childhood, wrapped in a fresh coat of paint.

10/10 I would drink from Cuphead's cup.
No really though, it's a superb game. Think of it as a gauntlet of intense, multi-phase boss battles with MegaMan-esque run 'n gun stages sprinkled in between. Movement and shooting controls are responsive, tight, and precise as Cuphead (and Mugman) navigate through the run 'n gun stages and dance with death like a star in the crazy boss battles. The game's controls are also fully re-mappable so if you're used to certain actions being on certain buttons, you're more than welcome to do so.
The game is challenging and you will die a lot as the name of the game is trial-and-error but there's a certain level of satisfaction that comes with learning the ins and outs of each stage. The quick and snappy death-to-revival phase makes said learning phase relatively painless, save for the player's tolerance for dying over and over again. Once you've mastered a stage and blast through it like a speedrunner on crack, seeing that BRAVO! or KNOCKOUT! will certainly make you feel like a big damn hero.
The game's main attraction, however, comes from the game's art and sound direction which is the most charming love letter to 1920s~1930s cartoons that you'll ever find on this side of media. Just knowing how much detail and effort was put into each frame of animation (and believe me -- there are hundreds, if not thousands, for each boss alone) will make you appreciate how gorgeous the game looks and sounds in action. Between the fluidity of the animation, the squashy, stretchy, rubbery goodness, and the roaring horns of the game's jazzy big-band soundtrack, you'll quickly find yourself engrossed in the experience.
Cuphead is not without its pitfalls, though, as certain bosses can often make you feel like you're dying "cheap" deaths with bits and bullets just thrown seemingly for the sake of having more stuff on the screen to be afraid of. The run 'n gun stages also start to feel like an afterthought as you progress through the game. I would also cite the art style as a divisive one. If you're no fan at all of that kind of animation or, for some reason, have an aversion to it, you're probably not going to appreciate it -- and I feel like the art style is a major factor in what makes Cuphead stand out from the crowd.
Cuphead is also relatively short and the main story can be completed within 4 to 8 hours depending on how much you feel like getting good. Personally, I didn't get good and just enjoyed the ride. :3
Overall, I absolutely recommend this game, sale or no sale. It's well worth the $20 for just the game, not at all including the audio-visual feast you're about to be purchasing. Also buy the soundtrack, yeah?

At best, these kinds of puzzles add very little to a game, but at worst, like here, they add a completely unnecesary level of boredome and frustration.
I'm all for "difficult" games like Dark Souls, but this game should have stuck the relaxing formula of other hidden object games.

This game has a reliance on cheap and ineffectual horror tropes.
Jumpscares only startle people if they don't expect it coming. Horror is more than jump scares, it's anticipation and both well timed delivery and denial. Outlast isn't scary at all, it's jumpscares are predictible and dated. Jumpscares themselves have always been weak, at least to me. At least in my opnion, true horror is something that is patient, careful and slow to execute. The faster something happens the weaker the effect. Ultimately an ideal horror writer would want your own imagination to become your worst enemy. The environment is there to facilitate your own dread manifesting things that are not there. But your tension makes even the simplest thing seem magnitudes worse. I studied horror in literature, traditional art mediums, interactive (like games) and cinema when I was in university and I can say that I've got at least an academic understanding of the nature of horror.
As a game, outlast is functional (It's solid, easy to tweak, never crashes, has good load times and mecanically is fantastic!) if very, very tired. I've been trying to play through it to the end but...it's agonizingly boring. It delivers too much on what you expect to happen, the environment is stale (A "haunted" asylum? *sigh*). I really, really want to enjoy good horror but what most developers and writers consider to be horror is actually just shock. What is truly scary is unknown, ambiguity and mystery. When you don't know what is pursuing you, when you feel something lurking around the corner. Something that darts by, out of sight, barely noticed. In a game many horror elements would need to be in places where you could easily miss them and if you do, well...you missed them. If they are geared to deliver in a place where you're sure to see them, they don't have any effect such as a window or a door that you're reaching for.
At least in my opnion, for something to be genuinely scary, it needs to create an atmosphere that is terrifying FAR beyond any scary entity (ghost, monster, demon, maniac, etc.). I should be more afraid to "be there" than I am afraid anything that's dangerous. If I'm terrified of the environment than anything that happens (or better yet "doesn't" happen, part of the anticipation) will be significantly more intense. Horror and fear is an art that is not well practiced by movies and games. In the end, for me anyway, this game is more an exercise in "beating" it. Defeating the game at it's own game. I don't need weapons to defeat maniacs, only patience to evade or outlast (hah) them.
As a final note, if you think I may be rushing, I'm not. I like to take my time in a game, to appreciate every detail that went into it's design. Especially in a horror, I want to get immersed to make the scares more personal but this game is so painfully predictible and it's lack of any actual scary content or supernatural forces makes it no scarier than walking down a crowded street in a metropolis at noon (which for agoraphobics is scary, so I'll give it that). I spend a lot of time looking around and the enemies are something I casually dodge around while still idly exploring "chase" scenes. It's like the whole game moves in slow motion.
Let's hope the second one actually makes a game about ghosts and scary stuff. Real monsters, not just maniacs.

I've never played a TellTale game before, and so far I've only made it through two episodes of this one. I waited awhile to play it since there were so many complaints about performance; I wanted to give the devs enough time to work out the kinks.
I have to say, I'm hooked. There are definitely some noticeable glitches and oddities (one scene in particular Bruce had his head on backwards while talking to someone, which was pretty funny), but for me personally, nothing that really interfered with the game. I have the settings maxed out and apart from some hitches here and there, the game runs fine. I have a decent computer, so perhaps that makes a difference.
This isn't so much a Batman game as it is a Bruce Wayne game. Most tellings of his story focus heavily on the Bat, but in this game you are navigating politics and dealing with people with your wits, which is an interesting and fun challenge. The voice-acting is very well-done, and the game is just, honestly, quite tense. Although I don't regret any of my choices so far, I'm very curious how things would have played out had I made different decisions.
The tough thing is it's difficult to call this a game. It's quick-time events and dialogue choices. That said, for what it is, I think they do a good job. You have limited time to make any of your choices, which adds an overarching tension to everything. The Batman scenes, although well done, are only about as good as quick-time scenes can be, but they're still enjoyable enough. However the Bruce Wayne scenes steal the show. The story so far is well-written and enjoyable. Although there have been so many versions of the Batman story told, this doesn't feel like the same-old-same-old.
I would recommend this with the caveat that this is NOT a typical Batman game, and feels very very different from the ones in recent years where you run around playing as Batman. This is a story, plain and simple. If you enjoy well-told, tense stories, and don't have a potato-computer, pick this up.

This being my first Telltale game I was not sure whether I would enjoy it or not... and after finishing this game, I'm still not sure.
:
-
If you are a fan of Batman and/or superheroes in general you will most likely enjoy the story. The main character is ofcourse Batman, but the story centers just as much on Bruce Wayne, the man behind the mask. Classic as well as original (as far as I know) allies and villains make an appearance as Batman tries to keep Gotham safe.
-
My favorite character by far.
:
-
I'm not a big fan of neither point-and-click games nor quick-time events, which make up 90% of the gameplay. The quick-time events do not punish your for pressing the wrong button, and I honestly would probably have enjoyed the game more if there was no gameplay at all and it was more like a movie just with some choices you had to make along the way.
-
This is of course a matter of taste, but I didn't really enjoy the cel-shaded style (which it seems Telltale uses for most of their games). Catwoman did still look good though, and I did get more used to the art style after a while.
-
You can't skip the previews at the end or the summaries at the beginning of episodes. This can get a bit annoying when you jump straight from one episode to the next. If you stop playing between two save points you will also have to replay most of if without being able to skip the cutscenes that you've already seen.
-
To avoid spoilers I won't mention any names
, but there was especially one character that I thought sounded a bit off.
Despite of all the negatives mentioned above I still ended up enjoying the game, at least enough to make me want to play the sequel (as long as it has Catwoman in it), as well as try out some of the other Telltale games.
I recommend this game to fans of Batman and/or Telltale games, but you might want to wait for a sale.

You can have 95% of your population gathering food right next to a warehouse and they'll still go into starvation mode.  You'll start a new game and think you have it all figured out, just to have it happen again a couple of hours later.  This seems to have more to do with how the resources are being delivered between locations when levels get low... A vicious cycle occurs where too little food gets picked up/delivered and is consumed as soon as it is available.
Laborers specifically need lots of work.  If they need to clear trees and rocks from a new building, instead of checking if the new location actually needs those resources... they'll bust their butt moving all the logs and stone to the stockpile just to haul it all back.
Also, many buildings have a radius where villagers will look to forage, hunt, etc.  Move one of these buildings too close or too far from town, and either resources aren't found quickly enough or they take too long to deliver.  It would be helpful if the AI either knew to ignore areas where the resource can't be found or if instead of a radius around the building, the player can select/de-select land within the effective radius.

I'm a fan of Tropico 3 and 4 (have never played 1 and 2 before) and I have to say that Tropico 5 is very different from both of them. I used to rate this game negative due to the fact that I expected it to be a sequel to 4, but it turns out fairly different from 4 (I played it during a free weekend and didn't like it as much). However, this summer sales I decided to give it another go as I read reviews about "Don't play it expecting a sequel to 4 mindset" kind of stuff. And I have to say without it I really did enjoy the game as a whole.
What I like:
1. More interesting gameplay: World War, Cold War that kind of era stuff.
2. Better trading system: like you can select to trade with other countries.
3. Combat: I'm not too sure why some people disliked it but I feel it is better? Like you can see the health of the enemies instead of just hoping that it dies after a period of time (in Tropico 4).
4. Exploration: I thought it was pretty cool but I kind of think it is missing out on something...like it doesn't enhance the gameplay as much.
5. Research Points: Unlocking stuff is something, I feel, that makes the game have progression.
What I dislike:
1. Salary adjustment: Really? Budget that increases in blocks?
2. Continuing off the island: I prefer building from scratch and then customise it in any way I wanted it to rather than to continue off from what buildings I left off with.
3. Crown: It is not really a game mechanic but it is legit re-tarded (Steam censor). An example is charging for real-estate and reimburses you. I don't know if the game devs trying to simulate real-world govts but it is really pointless.
What I'm love-hating:
1. Plantation: Tropico 4's plant it on places that are more fertile. You don't know if you should build something on it or just let it be. In 5 an area of land is set for the farmers to grow crops, even though the land might not be fertile.
I'm not too sure about the satirical stuff in both 3, 4 and 5 as I'm a gamer who enjoys the mechanics rather than the storyline(s) for city-building games.
I'm currently only 3h in so these are like my 2-cents worth of opinion of the game. I would still prefer 4 over 5 as the dislike-point-2 was kinda a deal-breaker when comparing both games.

Hands up all those who, at least once in their life, did not want to make there own game (MeMeMeMe!). Well, go grab you Cobolt and C++, now you can program to your hearts content with GamersGoMakers by gnifrebel Games (Try say that three times fast with a mouth full of pixels!).
Game Play
Pick from one of three decades (80s, 90s and 2000s) to start in, with three difficulty levels (easy medium or hard). Pick whether you are a Guy or Gal, and customise them in you favourite colours (Guys in pink, Gals in Black me thinks) then it’s time to hit the keyboards.
You start off in your bedroom at your mums. Depending on the decade you have picked, choose your favourite Computer or Console Everything is renamed in comical style but you have no problem guessing who or what they are indicating. Then aim your Ascii sights on a genre, you only have a few to pick from at the start but more open up later. Again it will depend on the decade.
After you start R.S.Iing your poor little finger through your first game, you will have more choices to Python your way through, do you want great sound and crap graphics or do levels plague your every thought, but you can’t give a stuff about AI.
Then its onto deciding if you want story and plot or just more violence, sex and Barry Manalow. Once that’s done, you get to run your eye over the packaging choices you have and finally you get to over price your Ruby on Rails rip off.
Now you can sit back and wait for the moolah to pour in……. in your dreams princes! Wake up and smell the stench of Critics’ reviews, get some more training, research new techs (OMG beautiful Monochrome and 8bit audio!). Get out of the bedroom (And away from your mums nagging) and rent or buy an office, hire staff, get you♥♥♥♥♥♥to those E3s, PAXs, or CeBITs. Above all, Javascript till your hands fall off and get that next big thing out there.
Everything Else
For those in the know, GamersGoMakers is too similar to Game Dev Tycoon and one can be forgiven for sneezing RIP OFF!  Honestly, in doing a little searching, I too thought the same. Have never played GDT so I can not comment on the similarities.
What I do know, GamersGoMakers is a bloody good game management sim, the graphics are nice and simple 2.5D as well as the music and sound effects, all are done right, to the right ambiance.
BUT! GamersGoMakers is harsh and unforgiving, just like DinkC. It is too easy go into debt, the starter budget, even on easy is frugal. The Reviewers page is out of touch with itself, you can get six thumbs up and one down but will get a very low rating and at times just the opposite will happen. That low review will send you to the wall, literally. And the 90 day game life is a little unrealistic and dose not give you a chance to financially recover, even with a best seller game. Easy is more like hard, Medium is extreme and Hard is Nightmare on Javascript Street.  A sandbox mode would be a nice added feature.
When all is said and programmed, I keep coming back to this game, it is harsh but addictive. Simply brilliant and yet frustrating at the same time. This game will be my all time favourite Indie so far and if your as sim maniac as me, you must get this game, your SecondLife will not be complete without it. DASL out man!

Very pleased with the alpha; good fun on both sides, had close fights throughout and solid enough seeming balance the characters play differently enough to keep them fresh, the first day was rough with server issues but thats to be expected. Stealth seems very strong and can be frustrating for the hunters but with a good team it has a good back and forth flow though either side can get decimated within a few seconds of bad play. Average games sit at the 10-15 minute mark. Some can be over far too quickly if the monster is caught out early.
I'd say a microphone is essential theres enough basic tools to get across your intentions; Q - to mark points of interest and map markers for anything more important. Without a mic I see you struggling on the Human side.
I only played a couple of games as the monster so the majority of my experience was human side with atleast one friend, I enjoyed both but obviously tackling some hulking monstrosity with your pals is great. Hoping the further additions to the game are equally good and that the end game balance with all the perks bumped up is still fair.
Also some form of private lobby allowing friends to play all 5 roles would be apreciated, even if it removed class progression to remove exploiting the system. I've not been keen on the E-sport competitive focus the games been getting marketed as but if it means it remains well balanced and tense as the alpha has been I'll apreciate it. Frankly I'm not into the levelling up system as it forces play thats not neccesarily beneficial for the team just so you can unlock something extra, it also puts walls between the content you may want to access earlier. Though as previously stated my main worry is that the level gap will negatively affect the gameplay, reloading at 10% speed increase doesnt seem that big of a deal 30% does if the final level is 150% speed that could drastically affect how things play out and the other perks look to have similar increases. I'm rambling on... I've got high hopes for it and I've enjoyed what I've played, I hope that experience isnt going to be damaged by the implementation of an abitrary levelling system just to keep people playing. For all I know that may just be Alpha padding though it seems well implemented.

LIMBO is not a good game. It is not a great game. It's an alright game that molds quickly when left out too long.
The graphics are pretty interesting, and are the game's main gimmick in terms of bringing new ideas to the world of Platformers.
The setting starts out beautifully, the dark and morbid forest full of disturbing atmosphere straight out of Dark Souls, but then quickly falls apart about halfway through. Once you leave the forest, the entirety of the rest of the game is in a disgustingly boring industrial factory-esque area that leaves pretty much anything the game had going for it behind in the dust, changing the mood of the game pretty dramatically in a way that I can't say I enjoyed whatsoever. It's pretty much just straight puzzles, a box-moving gravity-flipping gauntlet of nonstop boring puzzles, without any of the flavor the early levels had.
There is no story. Any. At all. If you expect anything more than "go to the right" you'll be disappointed. This is a great game for illiterate gamers, since there is no reading proficiency needed to enjoy the non-existant plot.
The puzzles are usually pretty simple, but I'll admit got me stumped once or twice, so there's still some challenge in it. My major complaint about the level design is that the primary source of difficulty comes from the slow and clunky movement of the child, given there are many many challenges that revolve around you moving very quickly and even at your fastest may only make it by a thin margin.
All in all,
If this game's second half hadn't been such a terrible turn of scenery, atmosphere, and gameplay, this game could have gotten a reccomendation from me. The opening sections were so much fun. But seriously though everything past the forest is just hot garbage, and I don't want anyone to have to play through that again unless they're stuck in a twelve hour flight layover and forgot any other source of entertainment to bring with them besides a laptop and this game on it. It's that bad.

Five Nights is a very scary game, I'll give it that. Having to leave doors open and expose yourself to danger in order to survive is also a pretty clever mechanic for a horror game.
My problems with it boil down to two huge things though:
1) It's not a good kind of scary. Sure, jump scares are scary but it never really feels fair or interesting. It could just be my taste, but being scared by something in that manner is a lazy way to do anything. Horror is something much easier to achieve than terror, but much less effective. I found that after losing a few times I stopped being scared altogether since it just struck me as a fail-state. Terror is a much more lasting and effective means of scaring the player which Five Nights focuses much less on, at least that's what I found.
2) The gameplay itself is boring. This is probably my biggest problem with the game. It's just not fun to play! It turns out shuffling through screens over and over again gets dull really fast. Even if the payoff is the suspense of not knowing where things are, it hardly even tries to feel engaging about the process, because it just wants you in there for the jump scare.
All in all it feels like it's got the potential if it didn't just seem like a way to drum scares up out of people. Think of it like that jumpscare maze game: Funny to watch someone play, scary to try playing, but boring as heck to play yourself.

While the game prides itself on its atmosphere, which it does very well, the graphics are well done, and no, they aren't photorealitic graphics, and doesn't need to be. The atmospheric music plays in appropriate situations, like if you are out at night, or if your health is low, and so on. Each area has it's own theme and difficulty level, and there is something unique to explore in every zone. The weather effects and the sky are always beautiful even if you are freezing to death you can't help but marvel at it. But games aren't made to be pretty and be looked at.
The biggest problem that many players will tell you are the wolves. As video gamers we know developers and programmers have to take certian liberties for the sake of gameplay, and we know video game versions of animals are more aggressive than thier material world counterparts. The problem is the game can't make up it's mind what kind of wolves they want in the game; wolves have a very wide and unreasonable aggro range; so at certain points its possible to completely avoid them, even if you are willing to take very large detours (which waste time causing you to freeze to death or worse), and once aware of your presence will continue to follow you regardless of how you shake them; the only thing that's guarunteed to work are flares, and the wolf is usually back not 15 seconds later. If there are multiple wolves the first one will reaggro the instant the second one is flared, which means the engine cannot handle aggro mechanics with multiple wolves in it. Scenarios where multiple wolves are handled independently, removing wolves feel as a pack animal. You can leave bait for a wolf and it will stop what it's doing (even eating a fresh venison deer it just killed not five seconds ago to eat a rotting rabbit carcass you left rotting on the floor in whatever shelter you were holed up at). If you leave a piece of meat when multiple wolves are out and if you observe this from a distance, you can see the way the wolves act like computer AI as each of halt thier normal behavior when they get in range of the meat and slowly walks toward it.
The game can't even make up its mind how it wants the wolves to act; most wolves patrol an area they when they spawn and do a usual stalk you when you get into aggro radius and walk toward you as you move away from them. Run away from them and they chase after you. Even if you stand still, the wolf will appear after a period of time and then run up and attack you and you have to do a quick-time event where you tap the left mouse button to fill up a meter to fight it off. If you have something that can be used as a melee weapon, say an axe or a knife, you get a bonus on how fast the meter fills. During the even the wolf can do one of three things: do a random injury that depletes your condition (your health), inflict a bleeding effect which is always accompanied by an infectious disease, and tearing your clothing, which in turn reduces your tolerance to the elements. The longer it takes you to fight off the wolf, the more Bad Stuff it can do to you. Each of these things can be dealt with using your survival supplies; bandages, antiseptic, sewing kits and cloth. All of this seems fair if not for two things: wolves can sometimes spawn over a hill or otherwise outside your visibility range and rush to attack you immediately, and this can happen right after another wolf or bear attack, giving a player no chance to defend themselves. The other problem is that wolves have an very, very big aggro radius and can aggro through walls and other obstacles. Even in the starter area, there is no way to avoid and encounter and certain areas must be avoided completely making you take huge detours which increase your exposure and use up supplies and aren't gaurnteed not to have wolves either. I also have a problem when I try to shoot a wolf with a bow or gun, the wolf "arcs" as it runs toward you.
Even being aware of your surroundings isn't guarenteed to avoid a wolf battle; in a game that functions on atmosphere, using your ears to detect animals doesn't help. The growl of a wolf, the snort of a bear, or even the gallop of a deer all come from a direction other than the animal who made it. I lost count of the number of times number of times that I heard a wolf growl, only to look around confused as the wolf closed in on me. Everything about the wolves make it clear that they are designed to be Video Game Enemy #21378 that is simply there to kill you, and it completely destroys the immersion and atmosphere the game is trying to create. There are even wolves placed right near several popular shelter spots; I have been attacked right outside Jackrabbits and Misanthropes trying to start a fire outside and most of my deaths have been right outside Camp Office, Trapper's, the Barn, and other popular spots.
The final issue is with the difficulties. Playing at a high level difficulty should be a challenging yet rewarding experience. Because the major selling point in this game is immersion, playing at the Stalker level is a constant stress test and gives the player little time to appreciate the wonder of the world around him, as video game enemies are around every corner. While this may be appropriate for zombie apocalypse games like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, it's not very immersive if we have to look over our shoulder, and check every hallway and room for traps like your in an AD&D Giaxian dungeon. The game has asbosulely no idea what "punishment" is; punishment is when a player does something he should not, inflicting a penalty at random or even for things players should be doing just makes the player hate himself and develop bitterness and resentment for what he should be interacting wit instead of developing respect for it. Pilgrim on the other hand allows the character to walk through the woodlands unmolested, if the players explores everything on Pilgrim, the entire experience of playing on Stalker is ruined as the player as already seen every location. Without atmosphere and exploration, the game as nothing to offer but generic video game enemies dressed like wolves.
While I can appreicate the permadeath nature of the game, most permadeath games at least leave youwith the consolation that you had something to show for your efforts. NetHack has a scoring system and a a "bones level" where your character's remains can be looted by you or another player. Diablo III has the ability to archive your character. The Long Dark has none of that; it has a journal in which you can write entries in which you can write whatever you want in it and tell your character's story. Once the game hands you one of it's cheap deaths, your character's journal and all its development is wiped away forever, as if it never existed. When a permadeath erases all your characters accomplishments and development, its mark on the world is just as meaningless as if you would infinitely respawn without penalty. A videogame world should be one where a player has the opportunity to make some kind of impact on its world or have some kind of control. Because the game is so punishing, the player becomes less and less invested as time goes on, and incentive to utilise the journal becomes less and less. No one wants to write the same story over and over again if it's going to be erased.
The Long Dark is a game that tries to create what is a survival horror without the zombies, and while I can give it huge amounts of suspension of disbelief it time and time again pulls me out of the immersive state it creates. Simply posting "we took liberties with wildlife" at the beginning doesn't mean that you can pull whatever stunt you want and say "because video game". Fantasy worlds don't need to be realistic, they need to be believable. The Long Dark as it stands is far from believable.

After 7 hours of gameplay I can happily say that I enjoyed my time spent in this game and it's replay value is quite high... however! This game is certainly not short of apparent flaws that can leave an ill feeling for someone seeking any sort of challenge in this game! Let's just jump in headfirst with the combat system shall we. Without hesitaion I can say that this games quick time/combat system could be mastered within 1 minute by anyone with a few brain sells and an age above 6! Not a huge problem for someone who is after a strict story based experience but for those who are seaking the same challenges faced in the amazing game "Tales from the Borderlands", it is! It is overwhelmingly easy to go the entire game without dying once... in fact the only time I did die was when I thought the arrow was wanting me to go up instead of down. My own mistake presented more of a challenge. With this being said I do not take many points off as the game was still extremely enjoyable as easy as it was! This leads me to my next point. When the game says in text before every episode that the story will be tailored to the choices you make, you damn well makle sure Telltale that is actually what happens becuase never once did my choices in this game have real consiquences and it seemed as though the game tailored before hand and not with my choices. A great example of this is Officer Gordan. Almost every thing you say this man is met with text saying "He will remember that", the only problem, it is never brought up again EVER! It is almost as if it is implying that Gordan will dwell on this later in private and I should be conserned for... no real... reason! This game lacks the quick thinking and decision making skills that games like "The Wolf Among Us" and "Tales from the Borderlands" often times required which in my opinion is what Telltale's games are all about, because without these what is the point in making decision other than to appeal to the characters in game!
Overall I do not hate this game nor do I even dislike it! I really enjoyed this game and I really love where they took the traditional Batman story we know and love! Telltale stuck to their mature rating on this with realistic violence and adult scenarios that do not cater to a young audience and really compliments the city that is Gotham and the dark nature of Batman. Unlike the games rocky start, I did not experience any major performance issues other than minimal stuttering between transitions which quickly wen't away! If you are debating on whether or not to buy this, I would say it depends. If you are okay with minimal effort and a very story based experience then do buy this. If you are looking for a challenge and a good balnce of gameplay and story then maybe look elsewhere as it may not meet your expectations!
Thanks for reading and hopefuly I helped with your decision!

I'm a fan of Tropico 3 and 4 (have never played 1 and 2 before) and I have to say that Tropico 5 is very different from both of them. I used to rate this game negative due to the fact that I expected it to be a sequel to 4, but it turns out fairly different from 4 (I played it during a free weekend and didn't like it as much). However, this summer sales I decided to give it another go as I read reviews about "Don't play it expecting a sequel to 4 mindset" kind of stuff. And I have to say without it I really did enjoy the game as a whole.
What I like:
1. More interesting gameplay: World War, Cold War that kind of era stuff.
2. Better trading system: like you can select to trade with other countries.
3. Combat: I'm not too sure why some people disliked it but I feel it is better? Like you can see the health of the enemies instead of just hoping that it dies after a period of time (in Tropico 4).
4. Exploration: I thought it was pretty cool but I kind of think it is missing out on something...like it doesn't enhance the gameplay as much.
5. Research Points: Unlocking stuff is something, I feel, that makes the game have progression.
What I dislike:
1. Salary adjustment: Really? Budget that increases in blocks?
2. Continuing off the island: I prefer building from scratch and then customise it in any way I wanted it to rather than to continue off from what buildings I left off with.
3. Crown: It is not really a game mechanic but it is legit re-tarded (Steam censor). An example is charging for real-estate and reimburses you. I don't know if the game devs trying to simulate real-world govts but it is really pointless.
What I'm love-hating:
1. Plantation: Tropico 4's plant it on places that are more fertile. You don't know if you should build something on it or just let it be. In 5 an area of land is set for the farmers to grow crops, even though the land might not be fertile.
I'm not too sure about the satirical stuff in both 3, 4 and 5 as I'm a gamer who enjoys the mechanics rather than the storyline(s) for city-building games.
I'm currently only 3h in so these are like my 2-cents worth of opinion of the game. I would still prefer 4 over 5 as the dislike-point-2 was kinda a deal-breaker when comparing both games.

I would recommend Banished to anyone, who enjoys economic micro-management and creative city building. It reminds me a lot of Anno 1404 (aka Dawn of Discovery) and Stronghold. If you enjoy these games you will probably also enjoy Banished and find it quite addictive.
Unlike Anno and Stronghold, Banished doesn't have any conflict or war. You are the only player on the map, there are no pesky AI opponents. The aim is to guide your people through the year without starvation, expanding your settlement without overextending, and keeping paths between homes, jobs, and food stores at an optimal level. In addition, you can certainly also try to make your settlement visually appealing. It's an open-ended game, so if you prefer set objectives, it may not be for you, although you can always try to get all achievements or make up your own. Banished is susceptibly simple, yet allows for a lot of variety and creativity.
The graphics or look of the game is simple, yet somehow elegant.  Buildings, landscape, and people look "quaint" for lack of a better word, but not too cartoonish, and fit well together. Nothing is jarring, and I especially like the seasonal changes and weather effects. If you desire more variety, there are a large number of custom assets for Banished on the Steam Workshop.
I have played the game for 40+ hours, mostly on slow speeds, and I am now the proud mayor of a village with 300+ souls. At various points throughout, I thought I had "made" it, and the village would run itself from now on. Boy was I wrong. A tornado ripped through town, dysentery broke out, crop yields varied from year to year, and growing the population without causing starvation, lack of tools or convoluted logistics, proved to be an ongoing challenge. I have played a variety of economic city builders that after the initial "hump" were extremely easy to manage and growing population was boringly easy, Banished so far was much more of a challenge.
It's my first playthrough, so I can't really comment on the replay value of the game, but my guess is that the game has enough inbuilt variety (maps, difficulties, random events) and room for my own creativity, that I will play it again and again. I can also see myself trying different strategies (e.g. fishing village, minimal forest resources, trading economy) during future playtroughs. The large number of mods and assets on the Steam Workshop probably helps with replay value as well.
I have read a few very negative reviews, but I honestly think whether you like or dislike Banished depends more on which style of game you enjoy than the game itself. Banished is certainly a very well thought out economic city builder.

GamersGoMakers is a Game Development Tycoon in similar vein to Game Dev Tycoon, Mad Games Tycoon, etc. Players will get their starting position in either the 80s', 90s', or 2000s', as they develop a wide variety of games in order to grow their studio and improve in game quality. Though it is very similar to other games, GamersGoMakers boasts different systems and more complex gameplay.
GamersGoMakers, for what it's worth, is highly addictive for me and some others, but for a bad reason I'll get into later. The ideas here are amazing, and with a little more time and effort could make for a much more competent and better-made game. Some of these ideas work - some don't. The addition of storytelling mechanics, more in-depth reviews, as well as community reviews are appreciated, even if flawed a little. This game also has a wide variety of platforms for your virtual self and team to develop on, which is also impressive. Licenses are an interesting idea, and while they could have added more, they're not terribly done. The development systems are quite interesting when they're not executed poorly, and the ability to get more features to help improve your games quality are interesting - not too well executed, but interesting, nonetheless.
This is where I begin to feel bad for GGM. For as cool as it's ideas are, the execution is very finicky. I'll go over them one by one, so hold on to your seats.
1) The Rating Board
This is a cool idea on paper but ends up being one of the worst executed parts of this game. Depending on the level of content (based on 3 categories) you put in your game, you can get an E-M ratings from a mock ESRB. Then again, the ESRB is actually an American rating system, with places like the UK having boards like PEGI in their place... surprise, those other boards are nowhere to be found in this game! That's a nitpick, sure, but if you're going to go for realism, then it should be hard to make that mistake.
Another issue I have with this is that it doesn't really work too well. When I imagine a rating board in these types of games, I imagine a system to put more than just 3 things in that only shows you the results later on and is completely randomized based on your choices. Another surprise: that's not here either. You'll always know what rating your games will get, which takes any possible tension from this system out of the way.
Ratings can affect many things, but the way this is handled is inconsistent and sloppy. If your games have an Adults Only rating, there's a 90% chance your game will get banned almost everywhere. If you're thinking about this logically, then you should realize rather quickly that there was no point in adding this rating to begin with. Your games can also be banned for having an M-Rated dose of Sexual Content in them... even though those same people can let other games by you with the same content slide without pain.
The trick to getting good sales is to have a good balance of violence, sexual content, and language. You can hire a producer to do this for you, but producers in this game are almost completely pointless as they'll either shoot for the highest rating and get your game banned, or they'll do exactly what you were about to do, with the same results. I'm going to be honest here: I lied when I said that any of those 3 things can effect your sales. They don't, actually. However, even if this were true, the game only vaguely hints at it and nothing more.
2) Awards
A good idea, but there's very little to it. I'll tell you this: there are only 3 awards you can get for a game in this game. The first is a Game of the Month, then a Game of the Year, and finally Bestselling Game of the Year. This sounds good on paper, but the stakes are never raised, so once you realize a pattern that works, you can abuse it, and if your fanbase is big enough, you have a pretty high chance of getting both a Game of the Month and Game of the Year. It just gets boring after a while, and that's sad.
3) Employees
Having employees is not new to the tycoon genre, nor is it new this type of sub-genre. This said the way this game handles this time mechanic is just sad. As your studio grows bigger, you can move to more offices and buy rooms for new employees like designers and developers. The effect they have on quality is very little, with the best additions being the marketing manager, lab assistants (as they get you cool, new stuff). The only way for your employees to get experience, though, is through training. I once did a playthrough where none of my employees were above rank 5, and none of them had any specialties to them. Then I did another run where I spent time training them to ensure specialties. Can you guess what the difference between those two runs were? That's right!
4) Non-Critic reviews
Another good idea with mostly lackluster execution. I like the fact that the average score is always lower than the critic's score, but this said, the reviews themselves aren't particularly interesting or helpful. Chuck Norris jokes died a long time ago, and this game came out in 2014.
5) Critic reviews
This game is buggy... very buggy at times. It's easy to click on something that's not supposed to be there and then get an error message telling you to report it to an email address that's probably been long abandoned. None of these bugs are funnier, however than the review ones. I once had a critic say that my Point n' Click adventure game had a good combat system... a point that's reserved for action games.
And, even without those silly bugs, there are a few inconsistencies, too. Like, for example I make an adventure game about students and school, and the reviewer then proceeds to tell me that my imaginary game has dungeons in it.... suuuuuuuure. Also, typos. This game has lots of them, and it hurts every time.
6) Staff Day
Here's something I only got on 1 run: staff day. I believe you get this ability if your studio is both a AAA one and has over 15 million fans. If you're lucky and patient enough to get to this point, then you'll quickly realize what I realized: Staff Day is almost meaningless. Basically, the staff plays the game to find out things that need to be improved. The issue is that there are only 3 options to choose from, and for the most part, they're not helpful. I once had an MMORPG, and I was told the gameplay sucked. Fine, but there's no option to improve that, and it could have been handy considering the game was panned for poor gameplay.
7) Game Engines
There is no point in making game engines in GGM. Why? Simple! While in games like Game Dev Tycoon there was time to build and utilize an engine before you had to improve it, here you get research opportunities fairly often, and even if there's a gap, it's probably taken up either by you waiting for the engine to be finished, or you waiting for the first game to use it to be complete. This sucks.
8) Game development
In Game Dev Tycoon and the such, there was allot to hold your attention while you were making a game. Not so much here, though. It's easy for me to doze off in a podcast while I'm playing this because so little holds my attention... and I generally dislike podcasts!
9) User Interface (UI)
The UI in this game is, without a doubt, clunky. Sometimes, you'll be given boxes with a check mark and a red X. Both do the same thing, but this is never communicated to the player so, even if it was necessary, they'd never know.
Also, let me not forget to tell you this: This game is abandoned! The dev will never do another update again... and it costs 10 bucks.

As quite a lot of people have mentioned, Bioshock has not aged well. The games does work on Windows 7 64 bit (the os I ran it on) but I had to do a bit of tweaking to get it stable, for instance, I had to run it in Dx9 mode. With Vsync on the game suffers from frequent slowdowns and stutter (with i5 3570k and hd7950) and if you have the mouse sensitivity on low, the in game menus are near impossible to navigate. Turning off Vsync will alleviate these problems but you will get a lot of screen tearing.
The game itself is an interesting idea but suffers from a poor user interface, the environments all look pretty much the same and the objectives are mostly 'kill something and collect items from corpse'. This involves lots of random searching for enemies in the hope they might hold the item you need. You can also 'hack' certain things in the game (security systems, vending machines etc) but the hacking game is so annoying that I didnt bother for the entire game, I just used the auto hacking tool.
Overall, the game was fairly enjoyable in spite of all the flaws, this was helped by the interesting story and freaky characters. If you can put up with all the flaws I am sure you will get some enjoyment out of this but as a full price release I cannot recommend it.

PROJECT ZOMBOID
This game is very unique from the millions of apocalyptic games. First of all its a simulator, There aren't a lot of great simulators for the apocalypse. Well most of them aren't still in EARLY development, Most of them are released as they are and don't update as frequently and have new content, but Project Zomboid does. New patches release adding new mechanics, bug fixes, customization, and so much more thats just one of the greatest aspects of Project Zomboid.
Once you launch Project Zomboid you're greeted with an amazing soundtrack. If you don't believe me launch it for yourself! At the main menu you're shown these catigories " Mods, Survival, Sandbox, Laststand " and in the background it shows a heartwarming illustration of what appears to be a man hugging his sick wife. In these catigories you can play Survival, Sandbox or Laststand.
SURVIVAL. In survival you get to choose the two maps created so far, make your character and traits your character has and what their career was before the apocalypse struck.
SANDBOX. In sandbox you get the choice to make the world how you'd like it to be. You can change the way zombies see, hear, and smell. You can change how often loot spawns, the season you start in, how long the water and electricity will shut off etc. . .
LASTSTAND. In laststand you instantly spawn in a house with a crate carrying weapons to defend yourself. You takedown the hordes until they break in and take you down. There is a timer so you can see how long you survived which makes it fun to challenge yourself or brag to your friends!
For the price Project Zomboid is right now I would call it a steal! 15 US dollars for a game as it is now plus all the updates and patches coming, this Indie game could definitly go for more. You can't beat the fact it goes on sale every now and then for even less!

One of the more contentious games I've played. When I first played it, I didn't really enjoy it and gave up halfway through. However, years later, I'm doing my fourth playthrough of the game...
It does a lot of things right. Rapture is one of, if not the best setting that a video game has had to date. Rapture feels like a real place, a living and breathing entity that you get to explore piece by piece. Following the quest arrow is discouraged here; take your time to soak in the atmosphere. The story has one hell of a twist in it, one of the most surprising I've encountered to date. The RPG elements are well-done, and I daresay that this was one of the last games to let you actually carry your entire arsenal on your back, along with having multiple types of ammo for each weapon, some customization in the form of improving your weapons, plasmids that act as stats boosters or spells, and the ability to hack turrets, cameras, or helicopter bots to join your side. The game feels like a weird mixture of late 90's FPS games and the mid 2000's.
On the other hand... well, a lot of things go wrong. The gunplay is horrendous; the wrench is actually the best weapon in the game, which is really silly. You can totally ignore every single weapon except for electric ammo on certain weapons when it's time for a Big Daddy. The story falls apart after the twist, and the ending is one of the most unsatisfying conclusions I've ever witnessed. The game totally drags on after that twist as well, as by that time you are incredibly powerful and can tear through most enemies without any problems. The game is also not introducing new mechanics during this period, so it feels like one endless grind up until the end. It's almost not even worth sticking through to the end, just because of how stale it gets. When people talk about modern FPS games being too short, I point them to the latter half of Bioshock. Death is utterly inconsequential, and you can just die over and over and over again with no penalty.
Luckily, Rapture saves the game. The whole underwater city oozes with atmosphere. It has kept me coming back every few years to dive back in... but I have only honestly finished the game once. I can't bring myself to play much more when my character has robots of death following him, a wrench that launches you across the room, and tons of cash for first aid.
If you see it on sale for cheap, it's totally worth checking out. It holds up seven years later, although it is a bit rough around the edges.

If you're looking for an authentic "zombie survival" experience, then look no further.
No other zombie survival game that I have played (and I have played many) imbues the same level of depth and emotion as this game does. Threats are all around you, and you will not survive, but the real question is how far will you make it? Thirst,  hunger, sleep deprivation, heat, cold, depression, boredom, sickness, infection, and of course: Zombies. The choices you make will determine how long you will  last, leading to some difficult decision making. The game does a fantastic job of portraying a zombie apocalypse in all it's horror and darkness.
The zombies are "proper" zombies. That being, slow, shambling, and non-superhuman undead as portrayed in Max Brook's "Zombie Survival Guide" and "World War Z" (The BOOK not the movie!). The threat of infection is real. One scratch is all it takes unless you're lucky. And if you've been bitten, it's game over no matter how much you try and fight it; what's left is how you choose to spend the last few days of you're life. It'll make you think twice before courageously taking on a small horde of zombies with your baseball bat.
Simply by playing the game, you are creating your own story for your character. It's a dynamic world full of zombies and you get to decide what you want to do and what your priorities are. There is lengthy character progression through a skill system, making you're character all the more precious as you invest more time into them. The longer you're alive, the more you'll want to survive.
The game is still in Alpha, so it's considered incomplete by the developers, meaning there are many more features to come.
I can't wait to see what they add to this game as time goes on. It already feels like a complete experience, so anything new they put in can only add to it.
This game is worth every penny. Something that I have a lot of difficulty saying about many other games.

I would definetly recomend this game to any person who enjoys a realistic WW2 shooter. It is real enough to immerse you with its great sound, music, and gameplay. However it is gamey enough for those who are new can easily pick it but with a steep learning curb in some areas. The multiplayer is the majority of where your time will be spent and thankfully for the most part, the community is really good. There are competitive and casual servers and plenty of maps that can be downloaded and play on with a server that supports that map. This game is by far my favorite realism shooter (speaking of which, the realism mode is what you need to play in order to truely experience what this game brings to the table). Be warned however, in this game, people do not run around with MP-40's and go rambo, you will be most likely be armed with a Kar98 or a Mosin Nagat Rifle, luckily, the riflemen class is very satisfying and should be your first step in this game. As you level up your character, he gains passive buffs, they are not game breaking at all, in fact, they make you a more attractive target in some instances. Weapons can be level up to 50, at certain levels (0,25,50) you get either attachments such a bayonet (most common attachment) a better scope (usually for the marksmen class) or different types of magazines such as the PPSH-41. Again, I would highly recomend this game to anyone who appreciates WW2 and a good shooter. The reasons listed above are only just a taste of what this has to offer. I can say without a doubt, that I got my money's worth out of this realism WW2 FPS.
