It is not bad but I think the negatives overweight the positives. It is pretty simple game and one of the major constantly used feature: map is bugged and does not properly reveal the black parts as you explore the world is something I would not expect. The fights are really bad. First time I was able to kill 3x times stronger pirates by simply keep behind them I felt proud, the 10th battle in this way I didn't felt any pride any more, because it was not my brilliance, it was just pure stupidity of the AI. And the biggest issue, it get monotonous very fast in like 2 hours of gameplay. You just travel from port to port and move things around. The only way you can die is to start a fight and not flee if it get bad. The game might be better for someone who is interested in the story and reading the dozens of pages of dialog, but for someone who is more interested in the game mechanics and just want to get a sandbox and create his own story, it is in a way empty game. The world is pretty small and often when you pick one choice it is not clear what will happen, you see what it will cost but you don't see the gain. Example: you buy some animal for 500, you go to university and sell them the animal, you get 100. You don't know how much they pay before you click the button and then there is no way back. This is not about your skill, about reading dialogs, about taking risk, this is just wrong design.

Cuphead only recently came to my attention, so for I game I hadn't heard anything of, I was suprised when I saw how much buzz was floating around it. To avoid spoilers, I bought the game blind without reading too much or watching any gameplay, so I could see for myself firsthand.
The first thing that struck me right away was the art design. The person who was in charge of art direction should get an award for how good the attention to detail is at recreating the retro cartoon look and feel for this game. From the character models, to their animations and sounds, it is literally the most fully realized art direction I've ever seen in a game. Even the slightly scratchy screen overlay with the mixture of super saturated and faded colours is genius.
Touted as run and gun game, I feel that couldn't be any more accurate to describe the gameplay. Levels play like side-scrolling shooters and it absolutely gave me a Super Nintendo vibe of game like Mega Man and Contra. And like those games, there's♥♥♥♥♥♥onscreen happening everywhere at all times, with bullets flying, bombs exploding, enemies popping out of other enemies... Needless to say, the game is brutally difficult. And to make things even more difficult, the player has very few lives in each level, and there are no checkpoints so if you die, it's back to the start. A "simple" mode is offered for players who find the difficulty too much, but what's too bad is that the simple mode limits the players experience in boss battles by cutting the battle short, so they will only end up seeing about half of the boss battle. That said, this is probably the fairest way the devs could have dealt with the difficulty question, because a player who wants to just cruise through the game can do so on simple, but a player who defeats the game on harder difficulty gets the reward of seeing all the extra cool boss stuff.
The gameplay and controls are silky smooth, though I did encounter a few unusual glitches in my time playing. One of the most endearing things about the game is the wonderful inclusion of a local two player coop, just like the good old SNES. This game was begging for a local coop and it works fantastically. I found I enjoyed the game infinitely more whilst playing with a mate, I think maybe because the difficulty is significantly reduced to a more manageable level, but also dying constantly felt less less like a relentless struggle and more like a hilarious challenge with a friend. Furthermore, two playing player allows for the opportunity for a last chance revive if your friend is killed, which made tons of sense to me in terms of the games balancing, so for that reason I would definitely recommend this game with multiplayer in mind. And on that note, it kind of blows my mind that Cuphead doesn't have an online multiplayer option to play with a stranger or even a friend on another computer. I really, really hope this is something that gets added in the future. In the meantime, there is a workaround you can use if have an Nvidia card and GeForce Experience.
$20 felt expensive for this game when I first saw it because it looked so simple, but there really is so much fun to be had that a $20 value actually seems like a great price to me now. This is one of those games that if you are of a certain age like me and have fond memories as a kid, playing your Super Nintendo and getting wrecked over and over again until you somehow beat that game, then I think Cuphead is going to really appeal to you. It's like a game you loved from your childhood, wrapped in a fresh coat of paint.

10/10 I would drink from Cuphead's cup.
No really though, it's a superb game. Think of it as a gauntlet of intense, multi-phase boss battles with MegaMan-esque run 'n gun stages sprinkled in between. Movement and shooting controls are responsive, tight, and precise as Cuphead (and Mugman) navigate through the run 'n gun stages and dance with death like a star in the crazy boss battles. The game's controls are also fully re-mappable so if you're used to certain actions being on certain buttons, you're more than welcome to do so.
The game is challenging and you will die a lot as the name of the game is trial-and-error but there's a certain level of satisfaction that comes with learning the ins and outs of each stage. The quick and snappy death-to-revival phase makes said learning phase relatively painless, save for the player's tolerance for dying over and over again. Once you've mastered a stage and blast through it like a speedrunner on crack, seeing that BRAVO! or KNOCKOUT! will certainly make you feel like a big damn hero.
The game's main attraction, however, comes from the game's art and sound direction which is the most charming love letter to 1920s~1930s cartoons that you'll ever find on this side of media. Just knowing how much detail and effort was put into each frame of animation (and believe me -- there are hundreds, if not thousands, for each boss alone) will make you appreciate how gorgeous the game looks and sounds in action. Between the fluidity of the animation, the squashy, stretchy, rubbery goodness, and the roaring horns of the game's jazzy big-band soundtrack, you'll quickly find yourself engrossed in the experience.
Cuphead is not without its pitfalls, though, as certain bosses can often make you feel like you're dying "cheap" deaths with bits and bullets just thrown seemingly for the sake of having more stuff on the screen to be afraid of. The run 'n gun stages also start to feel like an afterthought as you progress through the game. I would also cite the art style as a divisive one. If you're no fan at all of that kind of animation or, for some reason, have an aversion to it, you're probably not going to appreciate it -- and I feel like the art style is a major factor in what makes Cuphead stand out from the crowd.
Cuphead is also relatively short and the main story can be completed within 4 to 8 hours depending on how much you feel like getting good. Personally, I didn't get good and just enjoyed the ride. :3
Overall, I absolutely recommend this game, sale or no sale. It's well worth the $20 for just the game, not at all including the audio-visual feast you're about to be purchasing. Also buy the soundtrack, yeah?

Will I ever be warm again...... This game has been described as an immersive, thoughtful exporation- survival experience.
I will take the term immersive first- To me before this game it meant i might get into the character, and the ambiance of the terrain, maybe feel a twinge of regret after getting to my level 100 whatever and achieving the goal of this or that.  What the word doesn't tell you is that when your freezing, starving, lost in a blizzard, heart pounding, completely wore out and dehydrated that the howl of the wolf and the russle of his paws in the snow will come very close to making you **** you pants IRL just as you come around a rock outcriopping and make out the outline of a cabin with a canadian flag waving in the wind and your heart truelly skips a beat because you just might make it through the first night. I'm serious, if this game doesn't suck you in ith the artwork, the detail, the raw need to survive and spit you out the other side usually dead, then youre not alive!!
Thoughtful, Every aspect of survival is intertwined in this game, you need water but to get it you need to make a fire, but to make a fire you need wood, all of this burns energy  while out in the cold getting colder. But you also need food and don't forget the pesky wolf that was on your heals on your way inside. So you say to yourself, I have a bedroll, might as well sleep a while...but if your freezing and still cold then its lights out- Basically if you dont plan every move deliberatly and successfully you will die, They say in the description that every decision is life or death, in truth you have about 2 mistakes in a row maximum before your untimely demise.
Are there some issues with the game, Sure, it's alpha but I have seen games that are twice as far along not half as good, and most of the issues are minor.. And the devs are all over getting them fixed actively
If your looking for the cookie cutter, run of the mill survival this is not for you- if your looking for a more mature gaming experience where you get to immerse yourself in a very detailed and beautiful as it is brutal world, this game is a must.

Guru Games have done well in creating short but jarring mini-adventure into a catacomb of ancient Greece, which, play time notwithstanding, does well in creating a foreboding atmosphere. The setting is unique and would provide many opportunities to draw on the myths of an ancient civilisation to create an interesting horror adventure. but to make the experience truly unique would require more than re-iteration of mechanics used in other, more iconic titles.
The length of the game leaves me wondering what could be;
Medusa herself,
is one of many creatures that would provide unique gameplay opportunities. Her myth dictates any who look upon her face are cast in stone. Perhaps the player is forced to locate her relative position using a reflective surface - a broken shield, a repurposed brazier or metal lamp to avoid being caught.
The game has the foundations and setting of something that could be truly amazing and I hope Guru Games decide to develop this further, flesh out the story and introduce some unique and unsettling enemies. Until then this is a nice little experience while we wait.

Without a decent, new iteration of SimCity for me to play, I've been looking high and low for new city simulator games in order to scratch that particular itch. I spent a large chunk of time a few years ago playing Cities XL, but never got around to reviewing it (maybe I'll post a retro-review in the future). Cities XL has so far been the best of the bunch and has a very wide scope, but it's developer has folded, and the game has never truly felt complete.
...
The primary gimmick of the Tropico series is that the player isn't a mayor (as most city simulators claim); instead, you play as a dictator who is granted governorship of a small Caribean island-nation by a European power. It's basically a Cuba-simulator. At the start of a game, you must create a dictator avatar, and that character can have children and heirs in order to maintain your dynasty. From a meta standpoint, this gives much greater justification for the breadth of power that the player has over the development of the city. But this dictatorial theme isn't just a gimmick; the game actually does use it for gameplay purposes.
...
Because of the subject matter, it is a good thing that this game's tone remains very tongue-in-cheek. It doesn't really take anything seriously, so you don't have to feel too bad about repressing your citizens or killing dissenters in order to bolster your approval rating. This is good, because a more serious approach would probably make the game too dour to be fun.
...
The novel concept makes this series worth trying out for someone who needs a diversion from mainstream city-building and strategy games. Tropico 5 is competent enough to be more than just a novelty game, and the little world that it creates is very alive and organic. It's limited scope, however, can railroad the player a bit, and so this game definitely won't monopolize my time in the way that SimCity 4 did years ago.

Health packs go quickly, and if you want to use Plasmids (powers with varying effects both unique and traditional) and have ammunition then exploration is an absolute must. The great part is that it never feels like a chore, I actually feel like a guy whose looking around in desperation for something to help him survive in the hell hole know as Rapture. Patterns will come out and this makes them a little too easy to prepare for, though this very well could be a tactic by the devs to give you a "heads up" and make sure you won't die. All in all, this game is great, and you should GET IT.

This is a review based on the free weekend a while back:
The scenes are still burned into my memory..... We were drifting slowly towards London's harbor but had run out of food half-way along the journey. With what little fuel we had left we could not afford to hunt for food, not if we expected to reach London. Slowly, the food stores ran out. Then the hunger came. Increasingly often, the crew came to me, their captain, begging for food. But what could I give them? At first I managed to console them with words of courage, but that doesn't fill bellies. As the days passed I could see them wither away, their gaunt faces haunting my dreams, their desperate moans tormenting my waking hours.
We were 4 days away from our destination when it happened: Our helmsman died.
He tasted horrible, but the rest of us arrived in London alive.
I can see it before my mind's eye, even though this was all told in text events.
That paragraph captures the essence of this game. The actual game play is really simple and easy, and frankly I am very glad for that. The events are the real challenge of the game. You will never have the stats to get through ALL events, and you never really know if you even WANT to. This is not a game you play for the high score, you play it for the experience.

I wish there was a "conditionally recommend this game" option, because it's not for everyone.  If you're an impatient player and you like to rush through early content or you instantly go to walkthroughs to speed up your gaming experience, I would not suggest this game at all.  If you hate games that throw a wall of text at you because you don't like games that treat the experience like a "novel-in-a-game", don't play this game.  Lastly, if you prefer a very linear storyline and you're incredibly obsessive-compulsive about always choosing the "best option", I don't recommend it.  This game is incredibly slow paced with a very lengthy "early game" and it is "Story Rich", meaning it has highly descriptive paragraphs of text for the majority of the dialogue interactions.  The dialogue is also highly divergent, you'll generally have two or three different options to choose from when confronted with a decision.  There is no voice acting, so if you just skip through all the dialogue hoping to listen rather than read, you'll be completely lost.  There also isn't a lot of direct action, most of the "action" takes place in the dialogue, the actual navigation of the map is the only place where action occurs and it's highly repetitive.  The Zubmariner DLC looks to provide a little variety in that area, but the requirements to build a Zubmarine are far out of your reach as a starting player, so you won't get into the DLC very early.  This isn't a "bad" game, but there are a lot of aspects that will test your patience, especially if you're new to the game.  Save yourself the hassle and buy something else if these are major setbacks for you in terms of gameplay enjoyment.
On the positive side, the game has a great atmosphere for those that like everything dark and spooky.  The dialogue will be highly enjoyable if you're a gamer that prefers games with a deep story.  This game is a "Choose-Your-Own-Adventure" type game in terms of the storyline.  The fact that the interactions offer so many different options offers very high replay value.  This seems to be geared towards a certain style of play that actually fully embraces the idea that you're probably going to die before you actually finish your quest.  Dying and starting a new captain gives you a chance to try different story options the next time.  You could play the game all the way through with your original captain, but that will probably require you to play in "Merciful Mode" where you can manually save/reload.  Be warned, though, you can't get some of the achievements by playing that way, since a few of them are based around dying repeatedly.
The designer's intent for the game is for you to play the game by establishing a "lineage" and writing a will for your heir in case you die at sea.  You can also purchase a home and start saving "heirlooms" as a nest-egg that your heir can sell to start off with some extra money.  Unfortunately, when you die, you lose all map progress (with one exception if you decide to continue as a certain class) and the entire story resets.  For most of the story options, your choices are final, so if you did something "wrong" or want to try a different option, you'll have to get your current captain killed to reset the story and start fresh with new options.
You have the ability to inherit stats from your previous captain, but one drawback is that you can only inherit 50% of one stat per captain, so if you're trying to min/max to start a new captain with the highest stats possible every time you die, it's more advantageous to continuously spend points on the same stat and pick the same inheritance type than to spread your points around or to try a different inheritance type each time you die.  Starting base-stat points and bonuses from officers or equipment don't count, so if you're not choosing the most intuitive options when boosting stats or choosing an inheritance type, it's possible to go through five captains without inheriting a single thing.  Unfortunately, without putting points into multiple other stats, you'll fail a large portion of the interactions, as different interactions will check different stats, depending on the challenge.
Finally, a large portion of the game involves random events, usually bad ones which have a very real potential of being fatal.  These are very difficult to avoid unless you play the game as slowly and cautiously as possible.  For example, to avoid being obliterated by a large sea monster you're unprepared to deal with, you might have to push the engines full throttle.  Pushing the engines reduces fuel levels even faster and has a chance of causing an explosion.  Explosions always damage the boat and will kill crew members if you fail the interaction check.  If your crew capacity drops below 50%, the engines run at reduced speeds (by varying amounts based on the number of remaining crew).  If your crew capacity reaches zero, your ship sinks and you die.
So in the above scenario, you could die by not fleeing fast enough and being killed by a sea monster or enemy ship.  If you had already suffered previous crew losses, you'd already be running at reduced speeds and you would have to push the engines just to be fast enough to escape, but you could die by pushing the engines, causing an explosion, failing the check and losing your remaining crew. If your boat already had significant hull damage, you could die by pushing the engines to escape, passing the check but the guaranteed damage from the explosion reducing hull integrity to zero.  You could survive the failed check but have capacity drop below 50%, slowing your engine speeds and allowing the sea monster to catch up and destroy you (or putting you within range of torpedo fire).
You could even come out of all of that unscathed, without an explosion.  However, if your fuel was low and you were far out at sea, burning that extra fuel might push you to run out of gas before you make it to a safe port.  You could decide just to sink right then and there or you could try to wait it out.  Your Terror would continue to rise and eventually that could lead to a mutiny, with the ensuing violence killing you if you fail the check.  You could even run out of fuel but make it to a safe port, only to find the port does not sell fuel or supplies.  You could sacrifice your remaining supplies for extra fuel, but face hunger.  You could remain in port and watch helplessly as your crew continues to eat the remaining supplies.  Either way, you'd reach hunger levels that could initiate mutiny.  You could succeed in the check, surviving at the expense of killing all the mutineers, which would eventually reduce crew to zero, killing you.  So many ways to die...all because you tried to avoid being eaten by a sea monster.
If you're really prone to rage-quitting, I'd HIGHLY SUGGEST that you lose out on an achievement and play with the option to manually save/load rather than playing off a single autosave.  To illustrate how unforgiving this game can be in its default mode, I'll illustrate with an example.  I lost a captain due to fuel shortages from saving 7,000 Echoes to upgrade to a new boat but not having any money to pay for extra crew to run the engine at full speed for a pick-up job for the Blind Bruiser that he'd kill me for not completing in one trip.  My heir inherited 50% of my Veils stat.  Didn't inherit the boat, but inherited 50% of my money (which was now at a measly 9 Echoes).  10-15 hours of earning 7,000 Echoes all down the drain.  Oh well, that's life at zea...

I found this game while searching for a city building game without having to deal with other tribes and the normal fighting part that so many games have, but something that was not just another Sim City clone, there are plenty enough of them. Banished ticked all the boxes for me. The game itself I found a little tough to start with, it has a pretty steep learning curve and unlike most games of this style, if you get something wrong very early on, you very VERY quickly find yourself without any inhabitants due to them dieing of starvation or cold, so pressing the pause button right at the start and planning your village is essential, otherwise the only other option is to start over, which I had to do a fair few times. The thing I found most annoying about the game is the weather, I found it made the screen a little difficult to see clearly quite often, that and some of the map seeds are frustratingly bad to play, it took a good few start overs to find a map that suited what I wanted to do. Other than that, I have had hours of fun playing this game so far, albeit in the easiest settings, using valleys and without disasters and that kind of thing. I love the mods that are available, especially the medievil pack, which gives you extra buildings and resources to give you much more scope for your village and which also makes it a lot easier to keep your villages alive. Getting the balance right for all the resources you need is a fun challange in this game and it is really satisfying once you crack it and your villages finally get to live long and healthy lives, because once you've done that, you get much more freedom to start designing your village how you want it. I've not managed to get any of the achievements for this game yet, but that's something to help keep the interest going and something else to push for. Big thumbs up from me, well worth a play.

If you enjoy building up a city to have everyone die of starvation and freezing cold within 40 years, then this is your game. Although some people have reached 900+ citizens, I don't study how the game mechanics work. As a result, within 40 years, out of nowhere, my citizens kill themselves due to "a-lack-of-food" and "freezing-cold". This game's fault is with the starvation problem---once one citizen dies of starvation, the rest will follow swiftly despite a food surplus. And even if your city's population doesn't change, the amount of food your citizens consume constantly grows. For example, my most recent city housed ~300 citizens and a storage of 12,000 lbs of food. Two years later only about 30 citizens were born, but now I've hit a starvation period. Why the game doesn't have the citizens ration their food is beyond me. I've addressed this issue to the 'Banished' community before and I took their advice of lowering commute times and resource barns to/fro a citizens workplace. This however, didn't help as I still went for about 40 years before and uncontrollable starvation period that wiped my city---despite having a plethora of farms and other food production centres. If the game's community comes out with a food multiplier, then buy this game. Nevertheless, this game requires too much trial and error to figure out how the game's mechanics work to succeed. I just don't have that kind of patience to play an indie game that requires me to keep restarting because of some bull****.

First of all I liked Game Dev Tycoon alot.
So after reading the reviews here I choose to buy GamersGoMakers.
The first thing you notice is that it seems like a complete rip-off of GDT. Thats partly true. But the developers did add a few new twists to the game. Unfortunatly those new twists are bad implemented or just an illusion of impact.
In this whole type of game it's natural to have randomness as a keyelement of the game. Though in GamersGoMakers it's the only element.
You don't have the feeling of development as you had in GDT. Here you'll always make games with  scores of 50-70% and so you're bound to keep doing Publishing Contracts to grow. Publishing contracts will give you an income of 600k and producing an 70% Title without publisher will give you about 30-50k.
That makes no sense. How does the publisher make any money with the 60% games I've developed for them for 600k.?
I've created about 40 games and all 40 were about 50-70% and one game got a 90%. Tough it seemed really random as I used the exact same settings as the game before that got 70%.
Short: The game gives a big illusion of complexity and choice and after a while you get behind it and realise it's just pure dice rolling of the PC. That + the really bad UI leads to a boring game.
I sinked about 60 hours into Game Dev Tycoon and I easily get hooked by these types of games, but GamersGoMakers is a bad Tycoon game.

Those prioritizing receiving their money's worth will want to characterize this as an arcade game, something you either play rounds after one another or off and on over years, with unrivaled focus on this mechanic.
The story can be enjoyable. If the idea of The Matrix creepypasta appeals to you then you will likely enjoy the plot. There are no real characters, just a narrator that addresses the player directly, It relies on themes and archetypes to get itself across rather than interpersonal conflict. The campaign outside of the plot though will satisfy you as it is exactly the sequence of separate, distilled, action movie vignettes most players would expect.
Genre wise, potential buyers should stress the action part of action puzzler. Outside of one specific mode time, in fact, does move on when you're still. I believe the developers intend this game to be played by nurturing reaction and instinct, at least at first. You will gradually learn to pull off more elaborate moves within this restriction but don't have infinite planning time. If you're picturing yourself doing physics and geometry calculations you'll benefit by think you'll be like Captain America doing shield throws instead. Remember strategy games are typically top down whereas this is first person so, for example, you don't know your own hitbox but what you pick up with intuition.
A mild critique is that the environments all have an urban feel, likely to reinforce sterility and contrast against the only living beings. They are all excellent. But I had not known swords were a weapon prior to playing and found myself wanting a forest, or a foot bridge over a river, or a field of blades. It's something you should know going in though. Guns are the main attraction but you'll have your shootout in a club, not in a western saloon.

is a very rare type of game subgenre within the horror genre that the developer wanted to convey. It is not that it is scary by any means, but through a very vivid and creepy soundtrack, the environment becomes an enthralling trudging through Greek mythology. Yes, the game is very short and can be completed within one sitting at around thirty minutes depending on skill. However, if you want to take in the environment, read all the notes left along the way, which are divided into parts, until the whole story invested into Greek culture is explained, it can take around one hour. While I do not expect this game to rise in popularity on the charts of top free-to-play games, I would recommend this game for anyone who has a very thorough and loving appreciation for Greek mythology and ancient civilizations, especially Roman civilization.
One of the primary features of
that stands out is its immersive sound design. It is as if you can hear the groans, coughing, and sickness among the people that came before, and although you never encounter human characters in the game nor does the story ever reveal if they died somehow by later discovering Medusa, the notes we find along the way depict a traveler’s thoughts. In fact, the traveler’s mother and father who sent this girl named Aloyna to the temple to become an oracle- one who is a person of wisdom as either a priest or priestess for whom advice and counsel was always sought because they were supposed to be the wisest of all people when it came to knowledge of the natural world. We see more of this theme of oracles that occurs readily in Plato’s famous book Euthyphro, which depicts the dialogue of events and people in Socrates life right before his trial took place. This was when Socrates was seventy years old in the year 399 BCE (cf. p.47,
, Reeve & Miller).
Miletus condemned Socrates in the trial based of impiety. It was not just the distinction between pious and impious acts of moral ethics that was the topic of discussion during Socrates time, but a discussion that ran rampant in the idea that Euthyphro, who was a wise scribe at the time, was believed to have corrupted the youth. He despised anyone who may have taught a philosophy that was seen by the community as deceptive and not something that was taught to them. This is interesting because in Greek culture, much like a priest in monism is ordained for their teachings, oracles must affirm in polytheism that any individual’s teachings are regulatory in the bounds not of opinion but of human interest.  On the other hand, in

A lot of people have been saying "Beat story in ~2.6 hours - not worth $25 but fun game nonetheless." and "This game is innovative yes, but it fails badly on the price to length ratio: I completed the game in less than 2 hours."
To these people, I say phooey. This game IS worth the $25 and let me tell you why with one word: Challenges
The story is short and sweet, and it is quite fun. The story is maybe only worth five or ten bucks, add in the endless mode and you've easily got a $15 game. But the last $10 is provided by the Challenges; different game modes that have you play through the campaign with added modifiers.
These challenges are usually challenging, (as the name suggests) and force you to really break the habits you develop during the campaign. They are the real game, offering far more unique content than the campaign or endless mode, and they are what i've spent the majority of my time in SUPERHOT on. They change a lot of things, and severely alter the battlefield dynamic, causing you to play in ways you'd never considered or expected. Even though they all have you play through the same campaign, the difference in playstyle and the experiences you have are staggering, so much so that I'd almost go so far as to describe each one as being it's own campaign.
These modifiers range from the difficulty-increasing Hard and Impossible modes, to the slightly more fun and unique ones, like the katana-only or ghost modes. Then, there's the outright ridiculous ones, like the FUNFUNFUN challenge and the recent halloween cahllenge, which were great for a laugh.

If you want a $25 campaign to play through once, don't buy this game for full price, wait for a sale. If you want a $25 game that you are willing to put a little time into for a complete experience, DO get this game, you won't regret it, and I would challenge anyone who does want to invest time in this game to 100% it for a complete experience; Do ALL the challenges, beat the campaign, unlock ALL the endless levels, get every achievement, and you're bound to have a good time.

"If you look at a tree, you might have a hard time imagining how something so tall and strong could be turned into something as thin and weak as a sheet of paper. The process begins with the raw wood, which is made up of fibers called "cellulose."The cellulose fibers are stuck together with a natural glue called "lignin." When the lignin is removed and the cellulose fibers are separated and reorganized, paper can be made.It's also possible to make paper from a variety of other types of plant fibers, such as cotton, flax, bamboo, and hemp. For example, cotton fibers are often used to make the paper that money is printed on. The overwhelming majority (about 95 percent) of the raw material used to make paper, though, comes from trees.To make paper from trees, the raw wood must first be turned into "pulp." Wood pulp is a watery “soup" of cellulose wood fibers, lignin, water, and the chemicals used during the pulping process.Wood can be turned to pulp in a couple of different ways. Mechanical pulping involves using machines to grind wood chips into pulp.The resulting pulp retains most of its lignin, though. The short fibers created by grinding leads to weak paper most suitable for newsprint, phone books, or other types of low-strength papers.The more commonly used method is chemical pulping, also known as “kraft." Chemicals are used to separate lignin from the cellulose fibers, leaving a pulp mixture that can make stronger papers.Depending on what type of paper is desired, the pulp mixture might need to be bleached to create whiter paper. Papermakers use a variety of chemicals to bleach pulp to the color they want.Once the pulp is ready, it is then used to make paper in a process that is quite similar (in the basics) to the process first used by the ancient Chinese more than 1,900 years ago. Because the pulp mixture is so watery (sometimes as much as 99 percent water!), the cellulose fibers need to be separated from the watery mixture.Huge machines spray the pulp mixture onto moving mesh screens to make a layered mat. The mat of pulp then goes through several processes to remove water and dry it out.Finally, the mat is run through heated rollers to squeeze out any remaining water and compress it into one continuous roll of paper that can be up to 30 feet wide.When the paper has the desired thickness, it may be colored or coated with special chemicals to give it a special texture, extra strength, or water resistance. As a last step, the paper rolls are cut to size and packaged for shipping to other facilities for additional processing to turn it into all sorts of specialized papers."

Edge of Space pits you against the environment as you progress downward as opposed to side by side.   You gradualy start to encounter bigger badder challanges that not only require you to be well prepaired equiptment wise, but it also requires you to bring more advanced tools.
The versatility in Edge of Space's tools seperates it from alot of other sandbox games because you can choose to have a longer, less powerful range, or a shorter more powerful version of your tools.   This gives you options to work with.
The armor sets also differnt from other games in the aspect that they are not necissarly combat focused.   Instead of Ranger, Mage, Melee, you get  Builder, Explorer, Fighter.  Each armor catering to a particular task rather then a weapon role.  All items are created from crafting data of a specific sub catagory in crafting, so you can specialize and focus on one area at a time rather then pooling all of your science (aka accumulative xp pool ) into everything at once.

What a strange game.
Perhaps it's a good sign that over the course of playing The Beginner's Guide, I developed multiple interpretations of what it's trying to say.
The Beginner's Guide is the story of two indie game developers and the relationship they share over the course of a dozen or so developed games. One developer walks you through the other's games, one at a time, explaining what he thinks each game is trying to "convey." They are all walking simulators, and at times, you get the pretentious cringe of trying too hard to feel meaningful.
My first major takeaway is that The Beginner's Guide exists to help you think about games differently. It is obviously *for* "games as art." Games that are less about gameplay and more about message. It's here to walk you through how to view these types of entertainment in a way that does not prioritize completion rates and collectibles and action. It's like an art teacher teaching you how to appreciate art.
But that is only one of the game's many messages. The Beginner's Guide has a lot to say about a lot of different things, and some of them may not even necessarily make sense to you. There's things in here that I suspect may only be relevant to other game developer types. About the sort of... mental needs you build up. The attachments to certain ideals you have.
I'm not entirely sure I understand all of what The Beginner's Guide is trying to communicate, but... well. It impacted me just the same, in ways I didn't even feel prepared for. The feelings this game conjured in me lasted for days.
Maybe that's mission accomplished.

What can I say about this early access gem. I guess to start it is one of the most complete EA titles I have owned and it still has a whole new mode (story mode) that has yet to come out.  It is also an EA title with very very few bugs.  in fact in almost 200 hours of play I have only found one, and I got it about 5 times. While leaving a building I drop through the map. This game is also the purest survival game I own with other titles like Savage Lands, The Forest and 7D2D. This game can also be very rewarding to us as customers too. The sense of satisfaction you get from surviving an encounter you think you will not is very rewarding indeed. You earn your life, you earn one more day, one more place to sleep at night or wait out a storm. Every day is a fight to survive, against the elements, against the wild animals and even against your own instinct. This is pure survival at its finest. This game is a steal at EA pricing and is easily worth full retail of a finished game. I wish there was a "conditionally recommend this game" option, because it's not for everyone.  If you're an impatient player and you like to rush through early content or you instantly go to walkthroughs to speed up your gaming experience, I would not suggest this game at all.  If you hate games that throw a wall of text at you because you don't like games that treat the experience like a "novel-in-a-game", don't play this game.  Lastly, if you prefer a very linear storyline and you're incredibly obsessive-compulsive about always choosing the "best option", I don't recommend it.  This game is incredibly slow paced with a very lengthy "early game" and it is "Story Rich", meaning it has highly descriptive paragraphs of text for the majority of the dialogue interactions.  The dialogue is also highly divergent, you'll generally have two or three different options to choose from when confronted with a decision.  There is no voice acting, so if you just skip through all the dialogue hoping to listen rather than read, you'll be completely lost.  There also isn't a lot of direct action, most of the "action" takes place in the dialogue, the actual navigation of the map is the only place where action occurs and it's highly repetitive.  The Zubmariner DLC looks to provide a little variety in that area, but the requirements to build a Zubmarine are far out of your reach as a starting player, so you won't get into the DLC very early.  This isn't a "bad" game, but there are a lot of aspects that will test your patience, especially if you're new to the game.  Save yourself the hassle and buy something else if these are major setbacks for you in terms of gameplay enjoyment.
On the positive side, the game has a great atmosphere for those that like everything dark and spooky.  The dialogue will be highly enjoyable if you're a gamer that prefers games with a deep story.  This game is a "Choose-Your-Own-Adventure" type game in terms of the storyline.  The fact that the interactions offer so many different options offers very high replay value.  This seems to be geared towards a certain style of play that actually fully embraces the idea that you're probably going to die before you actually finish your quest.  Dying and starting a new captain gives you a chance to try different story options the next time.  You could play the game all the way through with your original captain, but that will probably require you to play in "Merciful Mode" where you can manually save/reload.  Be warned, though, you can't get some of the achievements by playing that way, since a few of them are based around dying repeatedly.
The designer's intent for the game is for you to play the game by establishing a "lineage" and writing a will for your heir in case you die at sea.  You can also purchase a home and start saving "heirlooms" as a nest-egg that your heir can sell to start off with some extra money.  Unfortunately, when you die, you lose all map progress (with one exception if you decide to continue as a certain class) and the entire story resets.  For most of the story options, your choices are final, so if you did something "wrong" or want to try a different option, you'll have to get your current captain killed to reset the story and start fresh with new options.
You have the ability to inherit stats from your previous captain, but one drawback is that you can only inherit 50% of one stat per captain, so if you're trying to min/max to start a new captain with the highest stats possible every time you die, it's more advantageous to continuously spend points on the same stat and pick the same inheritance type than to spread your points around or to try a different inheritance type each time you die.  Starting base-stat points and bonuses from officers or equipment don't count, so if you're not choosing the most intuitive options when boosting stats or choosing an inheritance type, it's possible to go through five captains without inheriting a single thing.  Unfortunately, without putting points into multiple other stats, you'll fail a large portion of the interactions, as different interactions will check different stats, depending on the challenge.
Finally, a large portion of the game involves random events, usually bad ones which have a very real potential of being fatal.  These are very difficult to avoid unless you play the game as slowly and cautiously as possible.  For example, to avoid being obliterated by a large sea monster you're unprepared to deal with, you might have to push the engines full throttle.  Pushing the engines reduces fuel levels even faster and has a chance of causing an explosion.  Explosions always damage the boat and will kill crew members if you fail the interaction check.  If your crew capacity drops below 50%, the engines run at reduced speeds (by varying amounts based on the number of remaining crew).  If your crew capacity reaches zero, your ship sinks and you die.
So in the above scenario, you could die by not fleeing fast enough and being killed by a sea monster or enemy ship.  If you had already suffered previous crew losses, you'd already be running at reduced speeds and you would have to push the engines just to be fast enough to escape, but you could die by pushing the engines, causing an explosion, failing the check and losing your remaining crew. If your boat already had significant hull damage, you could die by pushing the engines to escape, passing the check but the guaranteed damage from the explosion reducing hull integrity to zero.  You could survive the failed check but have capacity drop below 50%, slowing your engine speeds and allowing the sea monster to catch up and destroy you (or putting you within range of torpedo fire).
You could even come out of all of that unscathed, without an explosion.  However, if your fuel was low and you were far out at sea, burning that extra fuel might push you to run out of gas before you make it to a safe port.  You could decide just to sink right then and there or you could try to wait it out.  Your Terror would continue to rise and eventually that could lead to a mutiny, with the ensuing violence killing you if you fail the check.  You could even run out of fuel but make it to a safe port, only to find the port does not sell fuel or supplies.  You could sacrifice your remaining supplies for extra fuel, but face hunger.  You could remain in port and watch helplessly as your crew continues to eat the remaining supplies.  Either way, you'd reach hunger levels that could initiate mutiny.  You could succeed in the check, surviving at the expense of killing all the mutineers, which would eventually reduce crew to zero, killing you.  So many ways to die...all because you tried to avoid being eaten by a sea monster.
If you're really prone to rage-quitting, I'd HIGHLY SUGGEST that you lose out on an achievement and play with the option to manually save/load rather than playing off a single autosave.  To illustrate how unforgiving this game can be in its default mode, I'll illustrate with an example.  I lost a captain due to fuel shortages from saving 7,000 Echoes to upgrade to a new boat but not having any money to pay for extra crew to run the engine at full speed for a pick-up job for the Blind Bruiser that he'd kill me for not completing in one trip.  My heir inherited 50% of my Veils stat.  Didn't inherit the boat, but inherited 50% of my money (which was now at a measly 9 Echoes).  10-15 hours of earning 7,000 Echoes all down the drain.  Oh well, that's life at zea...

Why the negative review? The game is perfect, isn't it?
Yes and No.
I have beaten the game and gotten the vast majority of achievements so why would I do that if I didn't like the game?
There is a lot to love about Cuphead but I don't see anyone pointing out its faults. So that's what I'll do.
I'm just going to skip over the part where the game is visually and audibly stunning and get into the cons. I'm sure these cons have the potential to ruin the game for some people. That is the only reason why I'm doing this.
Con 1: The game is really a compilation of boss battles. Each boss battle is unique and cool. However a lot of the times bosses will have seemingly random moves that make no sense. Moves that you would only know about through trial and error. If you want to get the best score, you can't take damage at all which makes the game very grueling at times as you constantly open menu and restart because a random shark jumped behind you and took up half the screen instantly.
Con 2: The items in this game are not balanced. Some are useful 90% of the time while others are good on paper but awful in practice (this doesn't apply to gun types really. there are only two useless guns but they are fun to use anyway. )
This includes one passive that if removed from the game I'm sure it would be impossible. (the smoke grenade, which makes you invincible when you dash allowing you to just teleport past enemies)
There isn't a lot of variety in items to begin with, so this just makes it feel like you only have 2 - 3 choices ever.
Con 3 : I feel like the game would be funner for everyone if the first few levels were easier. I'm not saying they aren't relatively easy, but to a new player it can be a frustrating experience and if it were easier it would make the transition a lot smoother. Something we can all learn from Super Meat Boy is that if you make a game that relies on being challenging, then you need to start the player off slowly.
Con 4: Building on what I mentioned before, Cuphead relies on being challenging because the game itself is not very long. If you don't worry about stats or getting perfect score the game can be completed in no time. This means it is really only made for the type of player that always tries to beat their own score, which is not everyone.
Con 5: Hitboxes and determining what object will hurt you and what won't can be really confusing. Usually you can tell because the game consists of the background, platform, obstacles that don't hurt you, and everything else that does hurt you. This is similar to my first Con that this creates a sort of artificial difficulty and encourages trial and error. However this is more due to the nature of the game's art style and outlining, which is usually consistent and not a problem.
That's really it. The game is fantastic in every other way, however these problems need to be noticed. A score wouldn't do it justice.

Several buildings and elements were very blatantly missing from the game (as they had been in previous installments) meaning they would be bound up for a few bucks to be sold back to me in this new and exciting way! The decisions taken by the developers and publishers to withhold game data (literally, look it up) to sell access to it later for $5-$20 a piece, however, sets terrible precedent for the industry, and on a person to person level is just plain rude. The Tropico series has been a masterpiece in its uniquely deep yet lighthearted take on the genre, and to see the creators ignoring their fan base and wasting everyone's time with frivolous money-grabbing DLCs has seen this release step into the spotlight for "How to Make Money and Disappoint Everyone." I hope things turn around, though money I'd imagine speaks far louder than even the most abrasive criticism.
TL;DR: Don't waste your money on this and the guaranteed Sims-sized-load of expansions and DLCs. If you've played Tropico 4, you may enjoy it's more linear cartoony atmosphere, but you'll be back playing Tropico 4 again in a month. If you haven't played Tropico 4, GO PLAY IT RIGHT NOW.

TLDR: It's a brilliant city builder with loads of charm.
I have been a fan of the Tropico games for a long time and I have to say I like this one the best.
The Negatives: Let's get the negative out of the way. It's another Tropico game, some would say that's a good thing, others would not. Built up your island, update to a new era, build it up again. The formula has not changed much over the years.
1) The DLC, while the DLC isn't necessary it adds a few new buildings, missions and usually one outfit. This seems like their selling off some of the content piecemeal and most of the DLC buildings don't add anything too interesting.
2) The character customization is really lacking. After several titles under their belt I would have hoped the character customization would have been better. Male, female, a dozen outfits, a dozen colors, a dozen trim colors, a dozen hairstyles, etc. While this in theory seems like a lot of content, it's not really because half of the clothing options are absurd. Do you really want an astronaut with a clown nose and a Napoleon hat? Didn't think so.
The Positives: The game is just oozing with charm. The characters, the storyline, the feeling of going back to the island after being away for so long is just exciting. If you love city builders with production chains you'll like this.
1) The music is as good as it's always been. It really pulls you into the world that you create.
2) The interactions are very interesting. Given the opportunity to send an heir off to college do you send them to Russia or the US, or do you send the off to a no-name school. Will they cause trouble, will they stay and never come back? There is a lot of variety to the missions.
3) The game has never looked better. It's a gorgeous game to look at. I sometimes enjoy just letting the game run on standard speed and watch my little Tropicans go about their daily lives.

BioShock is a great game. I wouldn't play it a second time, but I still recommend it. Great price, too. Get the bundle.

Telltale specialises in adventure video games. These are generally easy to complete and by doing a walkthrough we usually acquire all achievements possible. The emphasis is on story immersion: there are lots of cutscenes and during dialogues the option we pick can have consequences in the story later on. QTEs (quick times events) are common but not very difficult. Our inventory (if there's any) is always kept to a minimum during the game. The games' graphics are acceptable but they are nowhere near those of the AAA games out there.
It is nice to see how the company goes from one franchise to another. Their take on Batman is perhaps the most ambitious ever as it is a very unique take on the franchise we all know. Since it is easy to spoil the story here I am only going to say the creators picked the early days of Batman to serve as the basis of the story. Gordon is not yet commissioner, Harvey Dent is running for mayor and Batman is seen more of a caped villain than a hero. Remembering how Thomas and Martha Wayne died plays the most important part here.
Since some of the previous games included a lot of gore and violence we can expect the same here. As Batman beats up the enemy henchmen there is a lot of blood during the fisticuffs. And here comes an interesting part of the game: we can decide to severely beat up some thugs or even torture our enemy during an interrogation scene. You may like Alfred, Batman's ever loyal butler but you can harshly respond to him and even reprimand him for his opinion. It is an interesting concept since we can become some sort of bad Batman here. In certain parts of the game we can decide either to visit someone disguised as Batman or turn up as Bruce Wayne - picking the bat always makes it easier to intimidate. We also need to decide who to save in key moments - here both people will be saved but picking somebody first can be crucial.
There is always something new in a Telltale game as much as these games are pretty much identical in terms of gameplay. In Batman we often do crime scene investigations. We find evidence and we have to connect the relevant items to one another. I also like how the tech Batman uses can help us plan, in advance, how to take down thugs in an area. We regularly visit our Bat computer to be able to check on the news of Gotham, read the codex (that includes info on the NPCs of the game) and complete some easy puzzles so that the story can advance.
The graphics, as usual, are rather simple but they serve their purpose. It was strange for me to see the game stutter and have glitches for the very same reason. I can see they always have some new upcoming games so the guys must be working hard on a new project but regardless of the time constraints you have you need to make sure proper optimisation is done before the release.
There are some videos under the extras menu where Kinda Funny founder Greg Miller talks with the creators as well as the voice actors of the game. This is pretty informative and interesting, something I hope will be included in future games, too. Alternatively, they could include some making-of recordings; I'd be happy to see such videos.
Batman is a high-quality adventure game and perhaps Telltale's best to date. It is an excellent - and very ambitious - take on the DC comic we all know. It has a great story, a surprisingly exciting villain and all the production values (voice acting, music) are well placed. I hope the optimisation will not be an issue in the future and that they will keep focusing on the very thing they do well: storytelling.

"If you look at a tree, you might have a hard time imagining how something so tall and strong could be turned into something as thin and weak as a sheet of paper. The process begins with the raw wood, which is made up of fibers called "cellulose."The cellulose fibers are stuck together with a natural glue called "lignin." When the lignin is removed and the cellulose fibers are separated and reorganized, paper can be made.It's also possible to make paper from a variety of other types of plant fibers, such as cotton, flax, bamboo, and hemp. For example, cotton fibers are often used to make the paper that money is printed on. The overwhelming majority (about 95 percent) of the raw material used to make paper, though, comes from trees.To make paper from trees, the raw wood must first be turned into "pulp." Wood pulp is a watery “soup" of cellulose wood fibers, lignin, water, and the chemicals used during the pulping process.Wood can be turned to pulp in a couple of different ways. Mechanical pulping involves using machines to grind wood chips into pulp.The resulting pulp retains most of its lignin, though. The short fibers created by grinding leads to weak paper most suitable for newsprint, phone books, or other types of low-strength papers.The more commonly used method is chemical pulping, also known as “kraft." Chemicals are used to separate lignin from the cellulose fibers, leaving a pulp mixture that can make stronger papers.Depending on what type of paper is desired, the pulp mixture might need to be bleached to create whiter paper. Papermakers use a variety of chemicals to bleach pulp to the color they want.Once the pulp is ready, it is then used to make paper in a process that is quite similar (in the basics) to the process first used by the ancient Chinese more than 1,900 years ago. Because the pulp mixture is so watery (sometimes as much as 99 percent water!), the cellulose fibers need to be separated from the watery mixture.Huge machines spray the pulp mixture onto moving mesh screens to make a layered mat. The mat of pulp then goes through several processes to remove water and dry it out.Finally, the mat is run through heated rollers to squeeze out any remaining water and compress it into one continuous roll of paper that can be up to 30 feet wide.When the paper has the desired thickness, it may be colored or coated with special chemicals to give it a special texture, extra strength, or water resistance. As a last step, the paper rolls are cut to size and packaged for shipping to other facilities for additional processing to turn it into all sorts of specialized papers."

From the get-go, Outlast is one of the best-looking and sounding survival horror games to date. Everything from the dynamic lighting to a fantastic soundscape work together to keep you on edge every second of the experience. On both PC and PS4, I dreaded entering any new areas or opening any closed doors for fear of what lurked in the dark unknown. Little details that are often forgotten in games, like leaving a trail of bloody footprints after stepping through a pool of blood, really help sell the illusion that Mount Massive is an actual place.
But for as great as the world looks, the character models are represented with a bit less fidelity. They're not bad per se, but certain enemies that appear terrifying from a distance lose quite a bit of their terror when viewed up-close. You'll also notice quite a bit of enemy repetition during the latter half of the campaign. That being said, you'll probably be too busy running away like a maniac to notice most of the time.
You're ostensibly powerless in Outlast, meaning that your main tools for survival are running and hiding. Barreling down a hallway with a beast right on your heels, bursting through a series of doors when you have no idea what's on the other side, and eventually finding a closet to hide in and evade your pursuer provides a fantastic and terrifying thrill. And once enemies begin tearing apart rooms and opening closets in search of you – yep, you can imagine just how nerve-wracking this game gets.
Your guardian angel in Outlast comes in the form of a camera with a night-vision setting. Much of the asylum is bathed in darkness, so you'll be viewing a lot of the world through a bright-green lens. This helps create a great sense of tension, which is heightened by the fact that the camera runs on batteries that need to be found throughout the environment. Outlast forces you to be conservative with your resources, as running out of juice in a particularly dark area forced me to have to reload a prior save file and replay a good chunk of a level. This punishment seemed severe at the time, but ultimately acted as a lesson in how careful planning was essential in order to survive in this world.
Where Outlast bogs down a bit is when it tries to shoehorn typical game design elements into the horror experience. Slowly making your way through a dank basement crawling with enemies is great – but having to activate three generators in order to restore power to the area? Not so much. While I'm not against the "find three things" structure of many games, its place in Outlast had a tendency to momentarily pull me out of the experience and squash tension.
Also, the fact that your character has no way of defending himself means that if you're discovered and cornered by one of your pursuers, you're probably going to have to restart that section. I found myself dying in specific encounters multiple times until I memorized the level layout and enemy patterns. That's not terribly out of the ordinary for a stealth game, but Outlast's strength is in its well-paced horror, and repetition dulls that power. Instead of being terrified, I was simply annoyed that I had to keep dying in order to figure out how to solve certain environmental puzzles.
Thankfully these moments were far outnumbered by long stretches of tense, satisfying exploration which rewards you with a well-written and unsettling story. Diligent searching reveals numerous notes and diaries that help flesh out tragic tales of mental patients tortured by villainous scientists, and that provides a surprising bit of heart to this bloody tale. It's also one of those horror games that works both when you're playing it alone in the dark, as well as having a group of people gather around the television and experience the scares together.

The Verdict

Outlast can stand proudly as a unique and terrifying survival horror game. Unlike many modern horror games, it remembers that the most frightening monsters are those that you can't kill, but have to flee from, and it creates an outstandingly creepy atmosphere that rendered me defenseless against its many well-paced jump scares. Annoying design choices and forced moments of repetition have a bad habit of spoiling the mood, but between them is an experience that's scary as all hell.

This game is in early access, and is a review of the current build.
Pros:
Beatufiully atmospheric, with great pastel-like graphics. There were some spots where I just stood outside and stared at the scenery for a few minutes.
Wolves and Bears are deadly. Although a healthy survivor with some good equipment can fight off a wolf, bears can bring anyone very close to death and are not to be trifled with. However, killing an animal will provide you with enough meat to survive for a significant amount of time.
No minimap. Instead of breaking the immersion by having some magical compass on your screen, the player is forced to remember the maps and what direction they've been headed in. Footprints can help you navigate backwards, but are quickly covered in a blizzard.
Blizzards look beautiful and are incredibly dangerous. Low visibility, erased footprints and freezing temperatures can quickly kill even a highly equiped survivor.
The weather follows patterns, and as you play the game you become able to guess when a blizzard might be coming or when it might be a calm day.
Permadeath greatly increases the stakes. If you were able to save, even at checkpoints, it would be easy to take massive risks and potentially reap the rewards without consequences. Permadeath means that you are forced to play like you are actually stranded in the wilderness and carefully consider your options. And if real life catches up to you, there is a perfectly functioning pause button.
The game is realistic. There are no zombies or supernatural creatures trying to kill you, it's just an ordinary person stranded in Canada after a geomagnetic disaster knocks out power and screws up the weather.
Mixed:
Small maps. It is possible to explore an entire map within a few days, and easy to memorize the entire map. However, your walking speed is realistically slow and a larger map might mean that you spend hours getting from place to place.
Low carry weight. After collecting an arsenal of tools, weapons, food and drink, you have very little room for loot. On the other hand, this forces you to carefully consider what you really need to survive and is a realistic carry weight. In addition, being overencumbered only tires you out a little faster. A good cup of joe quickly solves the issue.
The story mode is currently in production, but not released. Without it you are merely surviving in the maps for as long as possible, which can eventually get a little boring. It also isn't very fun to not have some higher goal to strive for against the backdrop of surviving.
Cons:
The human faces on the frozen corpses are downright silly. Nothing breaks the immersion of feeling all alone in a ruined world like seeing a cartoon stick figure face on a corpse. Since no face really would fit into the art style, I would advise keeping the faces covered in frost or eaten off by the crows.
Rabbits and dear don't have a very good A.I. In tight areas, they can get turned around and run right next to you or get stuck rather than fleeing.
Limited crafting. You can only craft a handful of things in the game, some of which seem like they should be obvious. I believe that you should be able to craft things to maintain your tools and weapons on any workbench.
Finite resources make it so no matter how careful you are, you eventually run out of raw materials. The primary one is metal, which is plentiful in the world but not infinite. In addition, you would eventually be forced down into just crawling through the bushes in furs searching for things to shoot with the bow.
In conclusion, I greatly enjoy playing this game and recommend it to anyone who is interested in a challenging and immersive survival experience. Here's hoping for a quick release of story mode!

I'm going to start this review by telling you not to read anything beyond this first paragraph until you play it. What I will say here is that this is best played with zero knowledge of its content beforehand, beyond a smattering of people saying "this is worth playing, you should play this". I'm going to recommend the same: Take an hour and half out of your day, and make sure you play it all in a single sitting with no other distractions. Avoid any Youtube videos and online discussions regarding this game until you've played it yourself, or the full effect will be lost of you, and ringing that particular bell will spoil any experience you might ever have had with it.
Now, onwards to anything that even hints at its content - though I'm still avoiding spoilers. It makes for a short review, but I think it's important.
Ready? Okay then.
This is less a game, and more of an emotional narrative experience. It really needs to be experienced from the perspective of the player to have its full effect as you follow its story, so don't think you're going . I'd love to write more, but I know that even having warned you in the first paragraph not to read further, chances are a few of you have skipped ahead and are reading this anyway, and I still don't want to risk spoiling anything for you. This is one of those games that is affected by a Heisenberg's uncertainty principle of sorts, as its intended effect would be ruined by revealing even the smallest piece of it.
From a critical perspective, if you're looking for a sequel to The Stanley Parable, this isn't the game for you, as this is NOT a comedy piece. Additionally, this is a far more linear experience than most; there's very little replay value - though I really recommend a second playthrough, since a lot of the context behind the narrative changes once you know how things play out. For the asking price though, I think it might be a little too much: I personally grabbed this in the Humble Bundle, but if you missed it, I suggest waiting for it to go on sale.
But despite this criticism, I still definitely recommend picking it up for at least a single playthrough.

The game is fantastically well written and ridiculously creative with its worldbuilding. If you are into unique settings and love to explore worlds with tons of lore, this is definitely the game for that. As an important note, however, that is more or less the only real value to the game, and there isn't much else noteworthy between the blocks of text. While difficult, this game is genuinly refreshing. Unlike the likes of Sim City and Tropico, this game focuses further on how weather effects your villagers, how much of every resource you have, and death. Personally, there was a massive learning curve. My villagers died constantly, and I'd have to much of one thing, and then bam! The winter has come and everyone freezes to death. The music and art of this game is more or less basic. You will hear the same song in a constant loop, and the sound effects are OK, not annoying but not the greatest. The art is simple, but it fits the tone of the game. Everything is clear and the interface is very easy to understand and maniupluate. My only gripe is sometimes things will get in the way, and things will close without notice. There are steam workshops available for this game, which I have not tried, but I am pleased to see that they allow that.
If there was a scale, I'd give this game a 7/10. If they improved the music, the graphics, and maybe added a bit more depth into it, it would be as popular as the other games of its kind.Pick this up when there is a sale, it is not expensive, and enjoy!

Telltale had its ups and downs, but after they announced Batman I was incredibly excited by what Telltale could do to one of my favorite super heroes of all time and boy did they deliver.
Story wise the game follows more on Bruce Wayne than Batman and what happens to him when the caped crusader takes control of his life. It follows on how broken both of them are in ways and it's interesting seeing what happens to Bruce Wayne when Batman takes control.
The first episode delivers on the thrills and exciting action you would expect from a Batman game. Also, the game has some puzzle solving, where you have to put together details to solve a crime which was very fun.
Graphically the game looks alright. Telltales comic book style translates well for Batman and gives it a decent look which translated both well for The Wolf Among Us and Tales from the Borderlands.
Audio is strange, I had a few times where in the action scenes the sound would cut off, but overall it's pretty good.
Now for a few negatives I had. The story is a bit weak, but it's still enjoyable. Hopefully, the other episodes are better.
Overall Batman Telltale Series is a great title and is worth it purchasing at full price.
Episode 1 Rating 8.5/10
Episode 2 Review:
Episode 2 Picks up almost as soon as Episode 1 wraps and again follows on Bruce Wayne more than Batman.
We start to learn that Bruce's parents weren't the people we were lead to believe they were and we start digging deeper to find out the past of Bruce's parents.
So as Stated at the start of the review this again follows more on Bruce than Batman and how he copes with all the things crashing down on him while people accuse of being a criminal like his parents and it's really interesting.
This episode, unlike the first one, has even less Batman segments until the very end, which is rather disappointing since I really wanted to see a lot more of Batman kicking♥♥♥♥♥
In the end, I can say this telltale series is still really strong and I can't wait to play through the other episodes.
Episode 2 Rating: 8.5/10
Episode 3 Review:
Episode 3 also begins right after Episode 2 wraps up and Batman now has to investigate what the Children of Arkham are planning for Gotham after he finds out that they stole a bunch of chemicals that could kill a lot of people.
Episode 3 is so far not as good as the previous episodes as the story kinda falls flat and both Bruce Wayne and Batman don't really feel like the character, especially Bruce Wayne who acts like a different person entirely from the first two episodes.
The action is again once you play as Batman, but this is the least you play as Batman which is again sad and I really think it should have a lot bigger emphasis on Batman, but Bruce Wayne again takes the reigns.
Overall this episode isn't really that good, but the plot twist at the end of the episode is what saves this from being straight up bad.
Episode 3 Final Rating 6/10
Episode 4 Review WARNING SLIGHT SPOILERS:
Episode 4 begins after Episode 3 and Bruce Wayne is placed in Arkham Asylum. With everything crashing down and Lady Arkham's plans coming together and Penguin taking over his life Bruce has to make difficult choices to save the day and any cost.
Episode 4 is rather good as it finally passes the spotlight to Batman which two great scenes and this episode is rather dark in content as the drug that injected Bruce at the end of Episode 3 shows his darker side emerging.
Also, Episode 4 has a great, but rather a small cameo from the clown prince of crime himself JOKER. He steals every scene he's in and it's absolutely great and I really want him to appear in the final episode or in Season 2 if that ever happens.
In the end, this penultimate episode is great and I can't wait to see how everything wraps up in the final Episode.
Episode 4 Final Rating: 7/10
Episode 5 Review:
Episode 5 begins as soon as 4 wraps up after the events leading up to the ending of episode 4 Gotham is turned into a war zone between factions and as Batman/Bruce Wayne you have to make tough choices to save the day.
This Episode is great, but it has one massive problem, which I will talk about later.
First of all the episode has great action scenes as Batman, where you kick major♥♥♥♥♥ This episode also has great segments for Bruce which up to this point I felt he was quite boring and his best segments sort of bland. This episode founds a great mixture of both of them showing everything you want to see out of both of them.
Story wise it wraps up almost every loose end, but this is where my problem comes up. The ending is a big middle finger if you hoped for a satisfying conclusion and it ends in the generic telltale way where there's a cliffhanger and it's probably never gonna get resolved like Tales from the Borderlands, Minecraft and The Wolf Among Us.
Episode 5 Rating 8/10
So now I'll go over the entire season:
Overall the season is good. The characters and story are interesting enough to warrant a couple of playthroughs. Batman is bad♥♥♥♥♥and Bruce is interesting enough you want to see how he deals with being Batman.
Is it the best telltale game? Hell no. It's probably the best telltale game since Tales from the Borderlands. Hopefully if Telltale make season 2 it won't have a cliffhanger ending.
Final Season 1 Rating: 8/10

+ Batman and Bruce Wayne are both fantastic characters

+ Graphically looks great
+ Joker
Cons:

I'd have to describe this as "a pretty poor game". That is to say, "it's pretty", and "it's a poor game". I picked it up dirt cheap because my never-plays-computer-games girlfriend (and I) enjoyed Machinariam and The Tiny Bang Story, the advertised equivalents, but aside from the nice art style there was no comparison. She lost interest in under ten minutes, and I only persevered because I didn't want to waste my 20 cents...
It's nice-looking, searching out the grubs and beetles to collect is about as entertaining as finding the goals in any other such game, and the occasional puzzles you unlock are adequate (though few), but the pointless requirement to click-and-hold on invisible paths to compel the insect to transition between screens was surely intended to draw out a game that could otherwise be finished in half the time. Naturally, you have to page back-and-forth to trigger new requests to satisfy, but making me wait doing nothing with the mouse button pressed was an annoyance. It didn't help that on my ageing PC the game often ran like a three-legged dog with terminal asthma; I finished it in 2 hours, but it could have been 30 minutes.
This is five levels of hide-and-seek that offers no reward for the ultimate completion: beat the last puzzle, it just goes back to the level-selection screen and that's it. Literally no indicator that you've finished the game, other than the absence of a Number 6 to click on. Not even a pretty picture, and given that the art is this thing's only selling point that just seems lazy. It feels like something that was made by a team who watched games being played without ever playing one themselves. Nice art is not enough, not nearly.
