Holy standstills! It's Telltale's Batman - the Stop Motion series!
So I guess by now everyone knows Telltale's shtick: make interactive movies in which you can alter minor dialogues and actions. You can either get along with it or don't, that's pretty much up to personal taste. I for one like most of them, given I don't play them too close to one another.
The Batman series by Telltale is just what you would expect gameplay-wise, but sadly it's hindered by a lot of smaller and bigger issues that keep this game from being en par with their best titles such as the first The Walking Dead or Tales from the Borderlands.
Let's get to the story first, since that's why anyone plays these games.
Telltale changes much of the common Batman lore, which in itself is a good thing. You'll see things and characters you probably know well, but they are not exactly like you've come to know them, so there's a freshness to most of it. It starts out with an already established Batman, so you won't have to suffer to yet another origin telling here, yet it does not feature any villains yet. I assume so far Bats has been fighting common crooks and climbed the occasional tree to save an old lady's kitty. We are getting introduced to the villains one by one, with the occasional surprise in here.
Without going into spoilers, all in all it's a servicable to entertaining story.
Unfortunately there's not much other really positive stuff to say about it, so I'll start with the nitpicking now. And prepare yourself, it's gonna be quite a list.
The writing:
Telltale switches and jumbles the creative staff (director and writers) for pretty much every single episode. And it does show. This is nothing like Rocksteady's Arkham series, where they hired an actual Batman writer (Bat-veteran Paul Dini). You'll have to make do with whoever was available at the Telltale office at the time, it seems. This results in some lack of consistency in overall quality.
Every so often you'll have to be brave and face clichéd sentences like "You did the best in an impossible situation." or whatever they had left lying around at the bottom of their text asset box.
And since we're playing a detective story when we play as Batman, there really shouldn't be logical errors in there where one visits a scene as Bruce Wayne, then goes back to the Batcave wearing the Batsuit, or putting a mobile phone into the Batcomputer to retrieve data which already got completely uploaded to it when the phone was found. Most of the crime scenes where you have to connect clues are so blatantly obvious that it's actually insulting to have a clever fellow like Batman running around connecting dots and wondering what happened, when even the dumbest of us have figured out the "mystery" at first glance.
The musical score:
You remember those epic soundtracks we've had for Batman since Danny Elfman? Sorry mate, nothing to see... I mean hear here, move on.
Voice acting:
While all involved do a fine job, I can't fathom why they didn't at least try and get
famous voice actors. At the very least give us Kevin Conroy as Batman. And Mark Hamill would probably work for next to nothing just to do the Joker once again.
Instead we get the usual suspects we know from Telltale: Troy Baker, good old Dave Fennoy, and so on.
I did appreciate Laura Bailey as Catwoman though, just because it's Laura Bailey.
Having said that, this is really a very minor subjective nitpick. As said, all involved do a good job.
Design and character choices:
This is probably the most unoriginal Penguin depiction you'll ever see; really, they could have replaced him with just about any other character, established or not, and it wouldn't have changed the story one bit. He's just some bloke with a stubbly beard and an accent. If he wouldn't be wearing a vaguely penguin-shaped mask at one point for no reason really other than to hide his real face, there would be no connection at all.
Gotham itself, which you'd think would be the most important part next to the characters, is just ... some city. Alright, the Arkham Asylum silhouette looks fine, but the rest could've just been any other city.
Graphics:
This is where it really lacks any Batman feel. Sure, the Batman costume itself is fine, but other than that?
Textures are low quality, sub par compared to any other Telltale game, let alone modern games in general.
The cell shading I would actually consider broken. Many of the lines just stop in between, the thickness in regard to distance is all over the place, and sometimes there's even completely disjointed lines crossing half or even the complete screen with no connection to anything; simply some ugly glitches they couldn't be bothered to remove apparently.
Character models in crowds tend to repeat themselves. In particular there's a scene with a crowd at the end that not only repeated some models up to five to six times, they were sometimes even standing directly next to each other. That's just plain lazy.
At one point I was inspecting a graffiti on a blank wall.
And the list could go on.
Performance:
I've never had any performance issues with other Telltale games. I did with this one, and looking at the forums, I'm not the only one. Low framerates, up to the game outright stuttering or freezing, especially during action scenes and QTEs, is something that I experienced throughout the whole game.
In conclusion:
A mediocre to okay game by Telltale standards, which I would still recommend. But sadly it gets dragged down a lot by the above mentioned issues. Get it if you are a hardcore Telltale or Batman fan, otherwise I'd say there's better Telltale games out there.

I got this game along with some other games from a humble bundle. Since it was the only game in the bundle I knew, I made a direct walkthrough right after the purchase.
Expecting it to be a "Stanley Parable-like" experience, I spent a long time finding gags in the early game, until I realized that there was actually no achievement system for this game.
---- Some Personal Ideas of the Game(Spoiler Alert)------
At first the game turned out to be a collection of interesting yet absurd thoughts presented in the form of unmature, under-developed games. The concepts were interesting, full of unruly imagination. But soon the games show a strong sense of loneliness. Coda, the creator of these games, seems to be keep illustrating his fear of being alone. And then suddenly "the machine" stopped. Coda wanted to make it move, but ended up having no choice but destroying everything that once he enjoyed.  I could feel the despair from the other side of the screen.
-----------------------------------------------------------
I am deeply impressed by the gloomy atomsphere the game created, especially in the second half. I don't really think I have fully understood the entire game. Maybe I would give it a second shot in the future. But not in a short time, since it takes time for me to recover, from the feeling of helplessness the game brought me.
Definitely different from Stanley Parable. Less funny but much more thoughtfulness.

Professional Preview (Italian):
Abstract translated in English:
Edge of Space is a promising heir to the 2D sanbox legacy initiated by Terraria, which introduces deep changes in one of the fundamentals of the genre: the crafting system. Having to invest your hard earned experience points in developing every single Research branch to discover their advanced recipes is both an incentive to explore the world in solo play and specialize your character in multiplayer games. There are bugs here and there, but the developers are actively supporting the game through continous patch deploying. We can't wait to see what new features will be introduced in the next updates: we'd like to see a compass that aims to your last bound cryopod or a geological probe to see what resources can be found in the area.
Commento in Italiano:
Edge of Space è un promettente erede della tradizione sandbox bidimensionale iniziata da Terraria, che introduce novità incisive in una delle meccaniche principali del genere, il crafting. La necessità di sviluppare i singoli campi di ricerca, investendo i punti esperienza ottenuti interagendo con l’ambiente, per scoprire le ricette più avanzate, aggiunge un incentivo a procedere nelle partite in solitaria e, allo stesso tempo, permette una maggiore personalizzazione dell’esperienza di gioco in multiplayer. I bug non mancano, ma le continue patch pubblicate dallo sviluppatore mitigano in parte la situazione, oltre a introdurre nuovi elementi di gameplay. Non ci resta che vedere quali altre feature verranno introdotte nei prossimi aggiornamenti: magari una bussola che punti verso la propria criocapsula o una sonda geologica per mappare le risorse presenti nell’area circostante.

Batman - The Telltale Series is an enjoyable but still disappointing season of the telltale lineup. It has a great story with some impressive plot twists in it. Telltale found a good balance between telling the story of Bruce Wayne and Batman. Most characters are well developed and illustrated. However besides the story telling the game leaves a lot to be desired. Frequent FPS drops left me annoyed and frustrated. And mediocre facial expressions and voice actiong on some characters left me confused and lost. The minutes long recaps between episodes are really annoying as they are not skippable. Not much was to be expected gameplay wise. Just some quick time events and sherlock holmes clue finding. The choices you made did feel impactful and were very immersive.
In the end this 7-8 hour long game is worth getting if you are looking for a relaxed interactive movie. Even more if you are fan the Batman universe. However if you are expecting a lot of mechanical gameplay, you will be left disappointed.

I was curious of the other Game Management games out there. I started out with Game Dev Tycoon (Throughly enjoyed that game with 200+ hours), then I tried Game Tycoon (Which is absolutely dreadful, don't waste your time and money. You're better off wiping your butt than spending it), I tried GameBiz 3 (Enjoyed it for its gameplay but hated it for its extremely poor UI and sales restrictions), and I played Game Dev Story on iOS (Which is great for on the go. I enjoyed it for its simulation, but not very much for its management and lack of interaction). So one day, I came upon this game and I decided to give this a shot.
Pros:
-Very detailed! I like how they really invested into what goes into a game; such as system design, content design, sound design, game writing, network, ect. The list goes on.
-Game Reviews appear like actual reviews.
-You can create your own Casing! This is honestly my favorite part of the game, hands down. None of the other Game Dev games ever did this!
-Competitors; more specifically they affect you in so many factors such as affecting your game releases, console releases, ect. You can even buy them out and have them develop their own projects but still receive an income or you can have them help you out in your own projects!
-More indef development. You can have voice actors, stunt devils, and so much more!
-This game has a lot of humor! The names of the actors are reversed in such a great fashon!
-Sales Charts are detailed and give you great statistics.
-You can choose your starting location! With each starting location, you get seperate perks!
-You can choose your own price! This should already be a given to any GD game!
Cons:
-If you do poorly in the game, the reviews will just tell you "You should focus on so and so more," It doesn't give you a plus minus system like GDT does. What makes it even worse, is that when you develop another game of the same genre, it doesn't tell you what was something you weren't suppose to do, you have to pull up another menu to do so.
-The UI is very much confusing and requires so many menus to open for information. If you wish to replace another employee you have to basically write down the levels of each employee and what they are good in. It should automatically tell you this instead of menu hopping.
-Graphics are very uninspiring. Everything is basically a still image.
-The notifications takes up about 1/5th of your screen. It doesn't need to be that big. Whats worse is that if you wish to look a previous notification, you are bombarded by what other notifications of irrevent games from irrevent companies. You also can't go back very far in time.
-Upgrading and researching are such a time consuming waste. You can't unlock the publishing office until the early 2010s. To make this seem even more terrible, you can't unlock your hardware lab until the 7th gen (X360, PS3, WII), around 2004-7ish. You can't make a retro console. The game won't even tell you if you can even research more technology due to the bombardment of the nofications.
-Buying new offices are basically the same as the last bullet point, half of the stuff you wish to create are locked off until the later 2000s.
-Early game start is virtually impossible unless you know what you're doing. There are no wiki's or any source of information from what I looked on the internet about what makes a game good. I had to revert to the steam forums for an JPG about what you invest your points in.
-Custom Consoles sell COMPLETELY POORLY! It took until my forth console to even get to a 10% marketshare whereas my competitors are at 25-35%. Which also makes no sense, the marketshare exceeds 100%, how is that even possible!?
-By later game, around 2000s, it slows down tremendously and begins to feel repeatitive.
-Genre and game selection is confusing. You can pick an Action Genre but you have to pick a sub-Genre. EX: Action-Beat em Up. Then you create a story with it. Then those stories are locked for the genre specific game. If I wanted to create a Military Action RPG, I can't. I can only use Military FPS.
-------------------------------------------
Final Verdict: Better than Game Tycoon at least!

Finally got around to finishing this tonight, it really is worth all the hype and acclaim it has received since 2007. Even though I only played through it this week, it still had a lot of jaw dropping moments, great atmosphere and one of the most vibrant and interesting worlds to explore in gaming.
Rapture is a haunting and beutifal city with a tortured but fascinating past. The mutterings, screams and genral dialouge uttered by the Splicers adds a real element of mystery and creepiness to everything, and the 30's-50's music that plays on radios in game further adds to the story of a once grand, fallen city, while also introducing a new genaration to some truely great music!!!
The ''plasmid'' system is a great addition to the game and has inspired several other games since, including Dishonered! Plasmids allow for a nice change from gunplay, which while fun, sometimes fails to satisfy. Choosing two plasmids to survive at a time adds some nice stratergy to the gameplay. It also stops the game feeling like it is too full of bullet sponges.
The story has one of the most genuinely great twists in gaming, one I can honestly say I did NOT see coming, yet it didn't feel forced. The ingame audio logs are all worth listening too (unfortunely, background noise sometimes interfers with these and that is a problem) and add only more intriuge about Rapture's history.
I attempted to play this back in July, but for whatever reason, it didn't grab me. I picked it up again this week, and couldn't put it down until I finished. For whatever reason, I complety misjudged this game, I really reccomend you play this masterpeice.

No OK for real now. Reminder tho: this is more like a personal experience than a decent review. I start with an unimportant intro, followed by a complete ♥♥♥♥♥torm of words about my own experience with the game, but at the end I sum up some pros and cons. So if you’re not really into reading a lot of unimportant but straight-out-of-the-heart commentary, you can directly scroll down to the summary.
I bought Outlast during the Steam sales last October (Halloween and stuff) and I was so excited to play the game, just because of the trailer. So when I finally jumped into it - together with a friend sitting next to me ofc - I was very excited and curious. Sadly, after the 2nd jump scare (no spoilers, there is more than one jump scare in the game) my friend and I screamed like two little ♥♥♥♥♥es and I turned off the game, without playing it for a couple of months.
After a few months, I restarted, accompanied with two more friends, hoping we would outlast a bit longer, but now I got stuck in the 1st "hide mission", you know, those objectives when you need to sneak around without getting detected or else your head will be ripped off.. So yeah, I had a bad start playing this game. BUT: one summer day, in my attic during a great storm, I finally found the man - or woman, no sexist here - in myself and completed Outlast in just a few hours.
The thing I loved the most about Outlast was its ambience. Sure, there are a bunch of jump scares and all that, but what made the horror in this piece of art was for me everything else: the environment, the music, the NPC's, but let’s start with the gameplay. I got used to playing “the vulnerable victim who can't fight back"-thing, since I played Slender and Amnesia and all that, but this game took it to a whole new level. First of all: THE ♥♥♥♥ING HANDCAMERA! It's such an amazing idea, and was executed very well. (NOTE: remember to put on your camera after a cut scene, because sometimes that doesn't happen automatically and then you forget recording and the game won't add notes to your journal.) Second: the parkour. Although sometimes a bit unrealistic ("Oh no, I'm followed by murderers, let me just wrench myself between these racks and they'll stop following me") it was really amazing to know that you have a force - your agility - to outsmart your pursuers. Technically, it also worked very smoothly. I don't have a gaming laptop, so I couldn't play it on high settings - which I recommend, ambient feeling, y'know - but it almost never lagged or glitched or whatever. As said, the true horror of Outlast isn't in the jump scares, but in things like the environment. I remember myself thinking "Oh really, an asylum? How original", but boy oh boy original it was.
!!!MINOR SPOILER ALERT!!!
Although it all started very cliché, with the crazy people and stuff, you'll learn after a while that there is something MORE to it, and with more I mean supernatural... That's what I actually kinda disliked about the game, since I am not a big fan of supernatural stuff
ENDING OF SPOILER ALERT
But then again, how amazing is a game when you get to love it, even though you're not a fan of the storyline?
I also deeply recommend playing The Whistleblower DLC since it gives a lot more information about the storyline, which is a bit unclear after completing the normal game.
To sum up (for all the lazy people who did not read my interesting opinion)
PRO:
- the gameplay (camera, parkour, hide and sneak)
- the music
- the NPC's (they are REALLY ♥♥♥♥ed up, I can tell you that. They are also very memorable. There won’t pass a day without you thinking about Chris Walker, Trager, Wernicke and – ofc – Eddie “The Groom” Gluskin. They were given so much personality! )
- the ambience and environment (especially the truly disgusting parts, they make Outlast Outlast)
CON:
- the unrealistic aspect of pursuers stopping to pursue you after you wrench yourself between racks
- the story (my humble opinion, one of the main aspects of the story is something I don't like)
- THE MOANING!!! For real, let me explain this quickly. Although it adds a lot of tension, hearing your character moan and his breath trembling, it got kind of annoying after a few hours. On the bright side, the game doesn't take more than a few hours, so that's fine.

I would say if you want to get more of a single player experience with a zombie survival game then this is the game you want to get. There are a multitude of ways to customise your game before you play. From the type of game, time, character settings, traits, zombie movement and amount etc. Never one game will be the same. As to how this game plays, it is not a walk in the park. This game is true survival at heart and you can't be complacent and the more risks you take, the more likely you are to die. Some ways I have died have been from not clearing a house before looting, getting cornered by a horde inside a house and also outside, eating rotten vegetable, getting sick from being out in the rain too much, falling off the stairs (early beta), not making sure a zombie on the ground is dead, walking through a forest and then suddenly getting set on by a horde, leaving the lights on or window open for visibility, getting shot by an npc (early beta), attacking a zombie on the road only to attact more further down it, burning the house down by leaving the oven on. Longest I've lived for was 10 days.

At this stage, not many people may like it as it is. The developers are still working on getting a lot of things in the game. They have lots of features planned to be implemented which are currently not present at the moment. The game is not done and there is still a lot to add.
Another thing:
Just because it's a randomly generated, 2D scrolling, sci-fi themed, mining, crafting, and building based game; it doesn't mean it's a clone of that game. It has many different mechanics and the devs took a different approach to the genre. Don't compare the two.
My final note is this: If you want a fun terraria-like space game, you can go with either Starbound, Signs of life, or this game, Edge of space. Whichever you choose, don't compare it with/to the others two. I've only played Edge of Space, and I've loved it.
However, if you don't like to playing unfinished games, I recommend you not to buy it; or at least not right now. It's up to each one's preferences.

Edge of Space is in no way enjoyable in its current state. It is repetitive, bland and pointlessly grindy.
There is no joy of exploration because there is hardly anything to see. 3 Biomes with the same mechanics just reskins and renames of previous resources. And a handful of pre-built dungeons instances that you can travel to, and are awful.
The combat is terrible, there are only 3 weapons that just get reskinned over and over again. And worse, they are so horribly imbalanced that you use the rifle for 95% of combat, the mortar for cheesey splash-damage-through-walls tactics on the other 5% and the carbine is completely pointless as a crappier version of the rifle.
The mechanics are clunky. You can't run down sloped tiles and jump, even though the dungeons are designed with downward sloping jumps in them. Hit detection is dodgey, enemies in certain positions can be invulnerable to direct fire because terrain hit boxes seem to register before enemy ones so your shot somehow ends up blocked by the wall behind them.
The enemies are dull. There's like 16 all told, and half of them are just reskins of the same run-at-player-bump-to-damage design with bigger numbers.
The design is darn well♥♥♥♥♥backwards sometimes too, for example:
In the dungeon where all your digging and wall placement tools are disabled, the enemies ghost through walls. But out in the sandbox where you can cheese the mechanics, enemies are blocked by walls. Why, in the one place where you can be guaranteed the enemy NPCs can't be path blocked would you put in the world's most annoying terrain ignoring floating enemies?
You have to unlock higher tier crafting by spending experience on generic tech level up consumables and using them, and the amount of unspent experience you can have at any time is capped. So you have to stop every 5 minutes and craft more tech consumables through the laggy crafting menu or start losing out on experience. Why the heck would you try to half♥♥♥♥♥it through the existing crafting UI rather than give it its own UI to spend experience directly? And even more why the heck would you cap it? Especially cap it so low you have to stop and spend it about 20 times to level up even one tier at later levels.
The whole game is extrodinarily grindy. Everything of value beyond the starter tiers requires converting hundreds of hundreds of junk tiles into a general purpose crafting material (Carbon fibre and super coolant). When enemy specific drops -are- needed, the same enemies drop like 10 different types of item, of which you only need the 1, so you have to farm enemies for 10x longer before you can craft one of anything. And unlocking new crafting tiers takes waaaay longer than it takes to get bored of the last reskin you unlocked hours ago.
And that's why I can't recomend this game even with furter development planned. Hardly any of the updates are exciting or ingenuitive, just more reskins called content. The design choices make no sense. And every system currently in place is poorly implemented. I have not one piece evidence the devs are capable of polish or exciting design in all these gigabytes of early access game.
They can make lots of hi-res sprites though. So there's that.

So, the story had some cool ideas, some bad, ultimately why is this a negative reveiw? The detective scenes were kinda boring, especially the first couple. Some scenes just Hiccup and we have no fix. An issue that really, really bothered me was during the final climactic scene, the game suddenly crashed. Fix your bugs telltale. There was alot of plot that seemed so generic and uninspired. Areas I would have liked to see were left unexplored, the villains motivations in the game were poor at best, and incredibly random in some areas. There's also a major inconsistency with the plot:
Overall it's another one-way telltale game. Your decisions don't affect the plot at all, you can't make any real meaningful choices. All you really have here is a generic plot from the batman universe with a beautiful presentation. Even with this presentation however, it has bugs, graphical studdering, which further mar it away from being something wonderful.

I have sunk so much of my life into this game. It's a happy medium between creativity and strategy. You have to allocate your resources properly so you can build your dream fantasy settlement while also meeting the demands of an ever-growing town. The game will also turn the tables on you from time to time, so even in ideal conditions you have to be ready for anything. For instance, natural disasters like fires and tornadoes won't do much to a small, young town because there isn't much to there be destroyed, but they can level entire cities and wipe out your stocked resources. The most interesting part to me is watching the town evolve over time from a few shacks in a vast forest to sprawing farmlands and urban centers. The Banished workshop also offers some incredible mods that add all kinds of producation chains, terrain options, decorations and more. I never get bored! Definitely recommend.

This game is odd, but in a good way.
I can't tell what it's trying to be; whether it's a child's game, with dark, underlying themes, or whether it's an adventure into a mystical world just below normal human perception. But whatever it is, it's incredible. The puzzles were mostly easy (with the exception of the trickier final puzzle) and the gameplay was point and click, which searching aspects. But this, for me, was less of a game, and more of an experience. The art was absolutely awesome, and gave the world a unique and intriguing twist I haven't seen in a story game before.
Should you buy it? That depends. If you're the kind of person who sits down for five minutes, leaves, and comes back, don't buy this. But if you like to take your time, and involve yourself in a game, this story without words would appeal to you like no other.
The soundtrack made me just sit down and listen to the music, while the screen displayed just a menu, for about five minutes before starting the game. Each environment gave me a new sense of accomplishment, and I just look back on it and smile. That is, until I play it again.
It is a short game, but it will change you.

Morphopolis is an atmospheric game where you partially control an insect in an environment, collecting specific items by clicking on them, somewhat reminiscient of those old I Spy games. I certainly had a bit of a nostalgia hard-on while playing this game, full disclaimer on that one.
I'd certainly say Morphopolis is quite therapeutic (unless you hate bugs), it has calming music, a vibrant environment that somehow feels huge, empty, and filled to the brim at the same time through its artistic use of the whole bug-world. There are plenty of times where you'll feel like the game is moving way too slow, and you will be stumped heavily on a puzzle or two here and there, perhaps to a point of rage, but in the end it makes you feel more accomplished. There even is a noticable progression between levels which gives you an air on familiarity in a new, strange environment.
In the end, the game doesn't take too long to beat. But the apprehension and depiction of the whole game makes it feel longer, it gives you a feeling of being accomplished and completed. It's not a wonderful, 10/10 game, but for someone who's willing to take the time and mild frustration to complete the game, it can be a nice gaming/art experience.

I definitely recommend this game, though not as emphatically as I would like to.
The writing and aesthetic are spectacular, but after awhile the game's rogue-like nature, which didn't initially bother me, became a turn off. Every time you die and restart your adventure the game world, to an extent, reshuffles all of the locations, but none of the story lines tied to these locations change. Story threads that were incomplete upon your previous death, especially those further across the world, can require a good amount of time/effort to get back into assuming you don't die again before reaching their starting point, and again assuming you don't die before completing them on your second, third, fourth, etc pass. After awhile I found myself wishing for a rogue-less option twhere I could explore the world and enjoy the writing, without having to restart completely from scratch after a death.
TL;DR: This is a great game, but I found myself eventually wishing it was less rogue-like and more story driven RPG, or at least offered that as an option.

Morphopolis isn't the most challenging game I've played, nor is it the most interesting "story" wise, but I really enjoyed the art style and the overall feel. The music playing throughout was excellent and very pleasant to listen to. It varies with each level but sounds like one cohesive series.
It IS a slow paced game, with 5 levels taking about 2 hours, but I still liked this, as it allowed me to really soak in the artistry and look a everything in detail. That being said, there were times I was sighing at the slowness of the insect I was controlling when I went up a plant for the 4th time. You will have to crawl back and forth between areas often.
There isn't a proper tutorial and without word prompting, it was initially difficult to understand what the game wanted me to do. There was also no indication of what my insect character's "powers" were so I got stuck a few times and wasted time going between spots looking for things that I could not see without using said "powers" I discovered these abilities entirely by accident. Note that this could just be my fault and not the game's. This was my first game of this genre since the 90's and maybe I just required a little more hand-holding than most for the beginning.
Adjust expectations before starting this game and I think anyone who likes puzzle games will thoroughly enjoy Morphopolis. If you expect action and puzzles that really get you scratching your head for 30 minutes each, you will likely be disappointed!
Would have loved 10 levels instead of 5 so I could spend a little more time in this world, but for a quarter (yes, just 25 cents!) I definitely got my money's worth!

The most realistic, unforgiving WW2 game out there. No crosshairs, no "Killcam", and no ammo counter. You have to physically open the rifle bolt or handgun slide to roughly check how many bullets are left. There is bullet drop and bullets will penetrate through objects and walls. You can manually select between automatic and semi auto fire. You can also adjust iron sights for distance and the iron sights actually move. If you get shot you have to stop and bandage or you will bleed out and die. Most of the time though one bullet is all it takes for you to die instantly. You hear your player breathing when you aim down your sights and the sights go up and down slightly in sync with your breathing, until you hold your breath. Some servers also do not show teammates names above their heads so you have to visualy make sure it is an enemy by their clothing. All servers always have friendly fire on. This game is not for people who get frustrated with realistic fps games. This game relies very very heavily on teamwork, so much more than in say any of the Battlefield games. If you love realistic WW2 games though then this is the game for you.

GamersGoMakers (GGM) is a step up from Game Dev Tycoon (GDT) - with only having a look at the screenshots you could legitimately think that it would be its direct successor. However GGM's complexity surpasses GDT's own - there's much more to do and much more to consider, wrapped up in mechanics not following the known paradigm in many details.
Direct competition (which you can buy out later on to let them either continue developing their own games or support you with yours in certain aspects), detailed and helpful reviews, boni depending on where your company is founded, a lot of different room types like sound and motion capture studios and a lot of other differences and improvements indicate how much thought the devs put into their game.
The UI however doesn't live up to the expectations. So many things are happening all the time that it is either not able to summarize everything in a well arranged way or it makes it a chore to actually get things done - want to train your employees? Open the staff window, click employee, click train, close window to do other stuff, wait, open window again, click next training option, rince, repeat. Finally everything trained? Don't worry, the game will throw several new training options for half of your about 14 emploess at you a minute later. A training queue for example would be a welcome addition.
Also, the difficulty seems to be a bit unbalanced. The game is way too easy at the lowest setting, while the next level already gives you something to gnaw on your finger nails. Note: I don't mean the game is too difficult in the normal settings, I just think that the gap between easy and normal is too big - figuratively spoken you're thrown into cold water and almost nothing can prepare you for what the game suddenly has up its sleeves (I'm looking at you, 1985+ reviews D:).
However these are flaws or issues I can perfectly live with. GamersGoMakers is a game that really surprised me with its quality. If you like this kind of games, go for it - you won't be disappointed!

If you are new to Game Developer sims, I would recommend you take a look at Game Dev Story or Game Dev Tycoon first, this game is more in depth and not a game that I would recommend to a newcomer to this, like I wouldnt recommend a newcomer to RPGs to start off with a game like Baldur's Gate.
However, if you enjoy these types of games already, you might be wondering if GamersGoMakers is worth buying in spite of its goofy name and its obvious similarities to Game Dev Tycoon? Yes, if you love GDT you will love this, especially if you are craving more from GDT and didnt find it in depth enough. Also if you found GDT to be pretty annoying in the late game when the performance can chug or that the game's feedback on how to make your games better to be lacking, you will find plenty to like here. That said, GGM does have one fairly significant flaw, and that is the UI.
The UI is actually pretty nice as far as being simple and easy to figure out, but it does have some issues that take a while to get used to. It took me a couple hours of play before I really got it down, and I still on occassion have an issue with some tasks like assigning developers. Also, I dont particularly care for the graphics style of this (or GDT for this matter) and was hoping that this wasn't so similar to GDT in the graphics front. I realize it may be too late for them to change it now without having to do a drastic overhaul of some elements of the game, but I do find the graphics to be pretty dull and boring to look at. That said, this game is a rock solid sim, it works very well and has enough of a challenge and randomness to it to keep me coming back, I can see myself playing this for a LONG while (like I did with GDT and GDS).

Disclaimer:  This is an early access title, so as always, buyer beware.  It may or may not make it to the finish line, but from what I've experienced over a few years development cycle with this game, it's team is nothing if not dedicated and focused on the goal of pushing this game to release, so I'm fairly confident it will be released, just not as hastily as other titles.
The question to be answered, is whether or not this game is worth buying right now.  While it's in the same sandbox genre as popular (and depending on who you ask, infamous) titles such as terraria, minecraft, and starbound, the graphical style sets it apart fairly decisively.  It's not super high-res, but the cartoonish yet realistically proportioned characters are a nice change from the pixelized Devs-Don't-Give-A-Damn you sometimes see.  What can I say, some people like pixels, others don't.  For my part, I do like pixels.  Anyway, see the screenshots for a good idea of the art style.  At the very least, the art style is consistent throughout the game as far as I've seen.
The devs have taken an interesting direction in the way of progression, in that every action you take, whether it be killing monsters, felling alien vegetation, or just digging up some mud, nets you experience that can be spent toward research in the area of your interest.  It's an interesting component that I suppose promotes cooperation and teaming up with other players who can fill the gaps in your research to help fully kit out your base.  Materials aren't enough to build all that you need, you actually need the experience and research level to create equipment and objects, unlike terraria and starbound where you only need touch a component to know how to put it together.
The alien environments don't take the typical planetoidal approach to world generation, and instead you find your avatar cast adrift on a sea of floating islands, which you can hop from one to the next with a handy jetpack, which you get from playing through the tutorial at the very beginning of the game.  It's necessary to build a suit of armor with exposure protection in order to delve deeper into the world's depths, so progression is a multi-pronged challenge as you have to gather experience and then spend it correctly in order to build a base and equip yourself for the dangers you'll find in the lower levels of the planet.
There's not much else for me to say about this title, but if you're still on the fence after hearing all of this, know that the game is still in development, and in order to expedite the process your characters and worlds may be wiped.  So bear that in mind if it's a factor in your decision.
For my part, I bought it at 20 dollars a while back, and like where the game is going.  I trust this dev team enough to get the job done eventually, and really look forward to when it's finished.  If you have the money to spare and want to put it to a project, and this one sounds good based on all you've heard, great.  Honestly, this either is your cup of tea or isn't, and that's okay.  I will say that it's my cup of tea, and an interesting and very different entrant to the 2d sandbox genre.  I don't regret buying the game.

Blue shift is, practically, any decrease in wavelength. Oh, wait, it is also the expansion pack (the 2nd one) for the critically acclaimed game Half Life! And this one was also developed by Gearbox. Interestingly, it came more than a year after Opposing Force, the 1st expansion pack, and while that one packed a punch, Blue Shift did not really offer anything new.
So, there is no real new content here: no new weapons, enemies or new music. But! It is Half Life! And also, you control Barney! The security officer who was bashing the door when you were riding the train with Gordon in the base game.
And this is why I liked in Opposing Force, as well. How the new protagonist's story was connected to that of Gordon. You could see a familiar locale in the distance (when in the helicopter in the beginning) or the aforementioned example of the security guard.
In any case, while Blue Shift did not really offer anything new (graphics-wise it came with a neat high-res texture pack, though), it offered the same cool atmosphere we loved Half Life for.
Blue Shift is a short but all the more entertaining ride! Highly recommended to all Half Life fans!

If you like Terraria, then yes this is a game to get.
True, it is in the early developmental stage and there are a plethora of bugs, incomplete items, and overall balancing issues that still need to be worked out.
For a game still well into its beta, i find it damn impressive that it wants me to keep playing as much as it does.
Gameplay is not as smooth as i would prefer, e.g. no invinicibility frames upon taking damage, enemies ridiculously hard to hit with guns, having a ceiling on the max amount of ammo you're allowed to have for everything besides phase weapons. In all honesty, I felt that Terraria handled the ammo situation for projectile weapons very well, where you could have as much as you wanted as long as you had inventory space. Reloading of course is something they didn't incorporate but the upper limit on ammo makes projectile weapons nearly obsolete. Haven't tried energy weapons yet, hope they are better, otherwise its sticking to phase weapons forever just because of ammo constraints.
Mining can be tedious, as i have not found any new ores or reasons to mine besides the fact i need resources to farm xp from the enemies flying around, and your upgraded picks dont seem to be digging that much faster.
Dungeons on here are very exciting to explore, i was amazed when i first discovered the headhunters dungeon, and again when i found maps to other dungeons as you went lower.
Transportation mounts, like the raptors, can't teleport with you to different command nodes, which i found to make them  not very useful since you get to them so much later in the game and need to move around between your main base and hub bases quickly.
random events that happen are interesting, they are usually pretty tough, although the rewards are severly lacking. Kill x/x monsters and you get a couple blocks of some ore thats not very rare? not worth it.
also can we get a map early on? exploring's a ♥♥♥♥♥ without one, even if we have to make it but make it available from a fairly early point please.
I am very excited to see this game get completed, hope that this review persuades others to invest in this game and help support the developers.

EN: After 20h of game (including the Big Alpha and Closed Beta), Evolve presents a similar gameplay to Left 4 Dead, but the cooperation is incredibly further. We don't have 4 survivors VS the Tank, but 4 hunters VS the Monster (or the Beast, whatever you prefer :p). TurtleRock  won the challenge : it's an incredible transition between an apocalyptic world (Left 4 Dead) and a hostile and futuristic universe (Evolve) ! If you have a crush for Left 4 Dead, then try Evolve ! You will not be disappointed (except if your PC hasn't sadly a powerful graphic stuff...). Otherwise, I find DLCs quite stupids for the prices !
FR : Après 20h de session de jeu (incluant la Big Alpha et la Bêta Fermée), Evolve présente style de jeu qui ressemble fortement à celui de Left 4 Dead, sauf qu'ici la coopération est incroyablement plus poussée. Firstly, to address the elephant in the room, the game is incredibly pretentious. There is no getting around that, there's no arguing it, it's just plain pretentious.
However, that's not necessarily a bad thing.
If you're familiar with other "walking simulator" games, you know what to expect gameplay-wise. It's just more of that. The game is also INCREDIBLY short at that. And while it really sounds like I shouldn't recommend this game, I will for a very specific audience.
I recommend this game for people who can not only tolerate the "gameplay" in these sorts of games, but people interested in a well-delivered, if a bit odd, meta-narrative about game design and creative instinct in general. The game's story is hard to explain without spoiling, but it's seemingly a commentary of creativity and self-worth. If that sounds interesting to you, you would probably enjoy The Beginner's Guide, but I recognize that this probably is not a game for most people, and that's just fine.
I got the game for a very low price (through a Humble Bundle) and am therefore happy with the purchase. That having been said, I probably would not pay more than $5 US for the experience.

Don't get me wrong, this game is great and has amazing potential, but I cannot say that I enjoyed myself while playing. Obviously in the nature of a 1v4 game, this is bound to be asymmetrical, but the monster is far too weak. Take a level 10 monster player and even just 4 level 5 human players, and the monster is bound to lose.
Not being able to attack the power relay while being shot at is ridiculous. I had about 1/4 health in one game and was about to destroy a relay when the hunters came. This is a serious issue. At least make it so you destroy it at a slower rate, but don't rob the monster of that ability.
In addition to the power relay, too many of the abilities of the hunters heavily outweigh the abilities of the monster. The monster can get passive abilities, sure, like extra damage or movement speed for a while, but never did I feel certain that I was strong enough to take on 4 hunters with really powerful abilities.
To sum up, my issue with the game isn't at all the concept or the gameplay, as both are pretty well developed. My issue is the weakness of a skilled monster against a skilled group of hunters. With the monster being so weak, few players offer to play as monster and thus matchmaking is  painfully slow. Until some sort of change is made to the balance issues this game has, I will not be playing and I am certain many others will not either.

It's enjoyable and deep, but also quite slow and painful. I enjoy the game but my main problem is that combat sucks. Some ship or creature rocks up and you either try to fight and either die or win a phyrric victory, or try to run and get pummled. I'm sure this would be less problematic once you get some better ships, but you have to range far and wide and repeatedly to earn much coin, a lot of which you have to spend on fuel, supplies, and repairs, and any ship worth spit is expensive. I nearly had enough money once, but then got ambushed by pirates and ran into more pirates while fleeing.
There's very little guidance in the game, which given the odd format will be offputting for a lot of people, although I kinda like cobbling together how the game works on my own. If you like clearly defined goals and a notion of the consequences of the choices presented to you then you'll want to look elsewhere.
It also feels rather unfinished. Choices you're given have details about what you require to be able to select that option. Many, many of these include phrases similar to "When time passing in X is:". Is what? Nobody knows, and not in the oooh, it's mysterious way.
I'd love to see some improvements to the information you're provided in-game, better options for evading combat or possibly scaling combat to your progress somewhat. I'd also love to see more trade opportunities,  as currently most simple buy and sell trades garner so little profit as to be worthless unless you just so happen to be going in the right direction anyway and happen to have spare cash and cargo space.
It sounds like I'm canning the game, but I stand by recommendation despite the stong caveats presented. It is very deep and engaging and I've been enjoying it depsite suffering some crippling setbacks.

I guess you can all agree that Audiosurf is the best storage-file-based rhythm game the internet provides. But why is this the case? Here's my list:
Pros:
+works with literally EVERY mp3 file up to 59,9 minutes of length, unless it's "silence" (that'd ve cheating)
+doesn't require high end pc or much memory
+ignores Copyright-Disclaimer
+different game modes, each with it's own difficulty and mechanic
+interesting visuals
+astonishing VFX (at least on highest settings)
+overall challenging
+especially fun on two player mode, in case I may call it like that
+bug-free
+pretty much replayable
Cons:
-no innovative gameplay
-sound-effects in game (decreases experience)
-may cause epilepsia
-in game leaderboards/friend-system
-not working stats
Conclusion:
Audiosurf is pretty much an interactive visualizer. Although it's nice to hear some music, you might get bored of the gameplay. Still, this game is the best the genre has to offer and as it's said to be annother "casual game" you will play this many times and for many hours. Some of the achievements might seem a little unfair, and in fact, they are, but I'd suggest you aren't an achievement hunter. Let's hope so, Audiosurf is pretty much a challenge over all, especially on higher levels. In case that's too easy you can try to control two ships on your own, which is possible on the "Dual" mode, which is also fantastic to have a friend playing it with. Just not to ignore some explaination, the gameplay is based on collecting color patterns of blocks, placed in 3 (or 4, when played on "Dual") lanes, based on your mp3s' beat. That one's the big skill of Audiosurf, you can use (almost) every MP3 you've stored anywhere on your computer and as long you're doing on private purpose you aren't even injurying the copyright of the conposer's respective owners, meaning that you can use songs you have ripped of or illegaly downloaded as well as CC (creative commons; general distribution to all non-commercial uses) soundtracks. I see that I am talking to much, to get back to the point I love this game for I need to admit that in "Dual" mode you're under control of two independently moving characters simultaneously, one controlled by mouse and the other one by "A" and "D" keys, but both locally on the same console. There are other gamemodrs than this one, as well and each one features unique abilities. While "Ninja"
is about avoiding grey blocks to score a lot of bonus points, "Pointman" let's you catch and store blocks, "Pusher" allows you to, well, push blocks besides and "Eraser" makes you even erase an entire type of blocks...
But you'll better look that up by yourself, Audiosurf is worth the purchase. (Not just said to end this long review, but because it's true!)
Final score:

There once was a time, a long long time ago, when simulation games on the PC meant something.  They were large productions and sold well, creating such stars as Sid Meier among others.  I bring that name up because, it seems to me, that that is the only franchise that has been able to survive to this day.  A true simulation about the creation of your civilization.  Your choices mattered and numbers behind the curtain were calculating the outcomes of various action or non actions.  It gave you so many paths to victory or loss.  Yes my friends, you could actually LOOSE a game back then.  I know...hard to believe!
Since the rise of the tablets and smart-phones, something strange started to happen.  I'd go to the video game store and I'd see a 'Tycoon' game here and there and everywhere.  I would read in my PC Gamer magazine just how horrible these particular 'simulations' were.  This was back when game names that had 'Tycoon' in the title actually meant you were going to be getting a detailed simulation.  Not just a simulation of how Baribie's new haircut worked at the fashion show.  Games like the Railroad Tycoon series (another Sid Meier brainchild), Transport Tycoon done by Chris Sawyer who had earlier blown our minds with the infinite possibilities of a truly infinite universe as seen in Eliete II and later taking over the reigns of the Railroad tycoon series where you have virtually all the control and choices an actual person running the show would have.  He later moved on with the successes of Rolercoaster Tycoon, that still survives in one form or another to this day.
Now I can go on my phone and go to 'simulation' games and they give the option of a simulation on baking cakes and pressing the pad at the right time, or stir on
WTF am I simulating here??!!!
There were always a few bastions of hope that popped up here and there, for example the GameBiz (Excellent game series, not on steam, very text heavy but quite complex)series but by that point the word 'simulation' was such a dirty word...a stupid I-pad game for kids.  One game that actually had a bit of traction as being a little more in step with the simulation games of old was Game Dev Tycoon.  It spent some time on tablets and cell phones, then made a crack at a Windows 8 Marketplace for purchase.  (CORRECTION:  Was only for sale on the Microsoft Market for Microsoft devices, as far as I know.  Thanks DOWNPHOENIX!)  Even more time passed then the unthinkable happened.  They ported it to Steam!  Hooray!  Simulations are coming back!  And it was good.  It was a good game for a I-phone, great in fact.  It was great for that demographic.  Us Simulation game players were put off by the arbitrariness of the whole thing.  But again....it was something.  We had a little bit of fun, for a little bit of time.  But it was not the game we sought!
Summer: 2014, almost out of nowhere a challenger entered the ring.  It kind of looked similar, was a bit rough around the edges but it was calling itself a simulation.  Heck, they even offered a free demo.  After the first3 minutes with this demo, I knew I was dealing with a different beast entirely!  I felt that the executive decisions actually had a direct impact on the 'thing' I was tring to create.  For the first time in years I felt the bonds that held me away go loose and let my imagination.  I needed to think like a business person, I needed to care and experiment and figure out what worked and what didn't.  I failed!  All the time!  And felt it was a victory to just make it to the end of the demo!  Every company I founded was like a child that you needed to nurture and guide, and a loss was tragic and heart breaking.
Needless to say I purchased it for the horribly high price of $10 <Please note the sarcasm> on launch day.  I couldn't wait to delve into the things the developer was offering that would take me far away from Candy Crush, and Sally's Stable or staring down the sights of an AR-15 as some 12 year old called my mother fat among other things.
I played....lost in the game's trappings eluding to older times where these things mattered.
As a matter of fact I'm still playing my first company.  Hard to believe, but I do hop on and check out what's going on at headquarters, just like a real boss would.  I think of inspiration for my next project as I walk to the corner store for milk and bread.
The fact that this game could draw in a hardened veteran of simulator games going back to the early 80's was astounding to me.  I found out that the game was mainly developed by one young man.  And he was excited!  The ideas of free patches and cheap DLC expansion packs...it all just kept coming!
At the end of this lengthy review, I must say this:  Potential
This independent game has so much potential from a young and fresh mind that KNOWS the difference between fluff and a true simulation, I can honestly say that if this game see's any success, the entire genre will flourish yet again, thanks to such efforts that come from developers willing to push each other forward.
GamersGoMakers is a seed, and I can't wait to see her blossom the way she deserves to...

If you're buying this game for the story mode, you're probably making the wrong decision. I won't spoil anything but i will say this, it's rather dull, repetitive, and lackluster.
The heart and soul of the game in my eyes has always been and will probably continue to be the sandbox, I'd say it's worth your money. Lemme give you some pros and cons of both.
Story mode
Pros:
- It's nice having some kind of tangible motivation for surviving rather than making up your own story for a change.
- For what it's worth, the two main character's voice acting is pretty decent.
- The story mode is pretty much a narrative laid over the sandbox experience, so you still get a lot of enjoyment out of it just from managing your basic survival needs and whatnot.
- Very lengthy, if nothing else the story mode is great way to kill time with 10-16 hours gametime plus endless hours of sandbox, It's worth the $35.00.
- The soundtrack is amazing, music in this game can bring a tear to your eye.
Cons:
- The story itself feels like a massive waste of potential, it's a wonderful example of a great idea that was poorly executed. In short, the storytelling is bad and the dialouge is very poorly written.
- Nearly every mission you get is a fetch quest. Which I wouldn't mind, y'know, if it was interesting. One of the missions you get (In episode two, mind you.) is to prove you know how to kill and skin an animal. At this point I already had several skins drying inside and a metric ton of wolf meat outside chilling in the cold. You can't skip this mission either.
- The entire first episode is tutorial pretty much, which I understand, new players need to learn the game. But the tutorial itself does a god awful job of teaching the game mechanics. example, "You're cold, you need to make a fire" "Okay, I get that, but what's the button?" "I dunno lol"
-The game is a bit buggy but i'll admit the devs are working very hard to fix these, there've been something like six patches since release. Hats off to Hinterland
Okay enough about the story mode, let's get down to the sandbox and why I think you should still buy this game.
Sandbox
Pros:
- VERY atmospheric, the music, sound effects, and overall gameplay do a great job of getting you immersed in the experience. You'll feel cold in August.
- VERY in depth, this is one of my favorite aspects of a survival game, one that adds to immersion as well. You can die in a wide variety of ways, from wold attacks, to intestinal parasites, to the cold, hunger, thirst, exhaustion, you name it and it can probably kill you. Inventory management is also a large part of this becuase each item has a weight and condition. i could go on if I wanted to. Very in depth. You may have to die a few times before you really get all of it down.
- Beautiful art style. Admittedly, this could come down to preference, but I think the look of this game is gorgeous.
- Replayability. Remember how I said this game gives you a hundred different ways to die? Becuase of this and the massive depth this game has to offer, every time you play it you'll feel like you're having a new adventure. I've sunk over 400 hours into it, just trying to get all the achievements nowadays.
- If you get tired of aimlessly wandering the world you can do the challenges available as well, it's like story mode but without the awful storytelling.
- Survival mechanics are (mostly) well balanced, feels realistic.
- Very large open world map to explore, lots to discover and roam around in and discover.
Cons:
- Some of the controls aren't great, the left mouse click is binded to three or four different actions for some godforsaken reason. An example of this is trying to loot a cupboard but accidently lighting a flare or throwing a rock.
- Wildlife AI could be a bit more in depth, they often seem to just be patrolling.
- Harder difficulties need tweaking, an example being that cabin fever sets in after one or two days inside when you play Interloper. That's sorta not ok..
- You will rage. Probably a lot. Especially on harder difficulties, It's gonna take a lot of trial and error to get good at the game.
- Can't jump. This is like unacceptable.. there are too many times where all i've had to do is hop over a little log to escape getting mauled by a bear and gotten stuck. Just make it use a bunch of stamina or something devs, c'mon.
Overall, go ahead and buy it. If you like survival games you'll love this.

Were it not for a few tedious obstacles towards the end of the game (a puzzle with an obtuse solution to the exclusion of a dozen valid alternatives immediately on hand, and the game's first and only instant-death pool outside of Opposing Force), I would call Blue Shift a head-and-shoulders improvement over the core game.
If I had to name three downsides to HL1, an otherwise excellent game and undeniable classic, it's that it drags on for far too  long; late-game weapons tend to get very gimmicky; and your personal motivation is never really more concrete than "move forward and don't get killed" until you reach Xen, where it becomes "find the final boss and kill it so you can stop playing already."
Blue Shift solves all these problems. It's a good deal shorter than the core game, especially highlighted by a scene at the very end that shows that the story wraps up long before Freeman finishes his side of things. Its weapon selection is much tighter, with nothing really left as a useless gimmick - like the core game's Alien Bee Launcher, which pretty much served solely as a last-ditch weapon when you were out of ammo in everything else - or basically anything that runs on what I've come to call "Science Ammo." And finally, without getting in your way the plot is much more directed, providing you with actual motive to move from Point A to Point B besides "because there's no other direction to move in."

What do you think of when you hear the word, Limbo?
Do you think of being stuck in limbo? Do you like playing that game where you bend low and avoid touching a rope or bar especially if you're a certain phantom fighter? Or, do you think of a boy lost in darkness fighting spiders with bear traps, pushing various crates, and traversing through hotel signs with gravity inverted?
When you're in LIMBO, you're playing a dark (both in the literal and figurative sense) and atmospheric puzzle platformer game. You're a young boy lost in some weird looking place with forests and buildings and camps galore. The game doesn't have much of a story to tell other than the boy. Where do you go? Well, through various dangers where you use the environment around you to get through, from bear traps to gravity switches. This game can be difficult to say the least, but shouldn't most puzzle games give a decent amount of diffuculty without it being too obnoxious or random? Isn't it why it's called Limbo, to get you lost and wonder how in the world are you gonna even solve it? Don't worry, it doesn't take too long to figure out how to traverse it, and in fact, the game can be cleared in a single sitting. If you're good at this game, you can try and clear it in just a few deaths and in a fast time. Though if you want a real challenge, try getting the game's achievements by doing very special feats which require heavy thinking.
The game's atmosphere is dark and eerie. Everything is black and white, almost as if this is a film from the early times before colour was invented in movies. In fact, the soundtrack is very minimalist and only plays at certain areas. Other than that, the atmosphere does a big job at making you feel lost and scared. In addition, the art is rich and magnificent.
So, are you still in limbo reading this review? Hopefully not, because well, you should get a good idea on what this game is. And in the end, this is a pretty interesting game in its merit. A spectacular entry in the indie platformer genre and should be worth some of your time, no matter what platform you come from.

Currently, you only play the game in "sandbox mode." This amounts to an open world survival experience, where you spawn at one of a variety of points on a predetermined map. A geomagnetic storm brings your small plane down in the Canadian wilderness. You are unprepared, and it's freezing cold. As if that weren't enough pressure to get you moving your worthless tennis shoes, you soon find you aren't the only creature slinking along using the hills to break the wind as you hunt for shelter before darkfall.
Though everyone is talking, and gaming, the demise of modern civilization, not everyone agrees on the possible scenarios. If you prefer an end like that described in the book The Road, by Cormac McCarthy, where you wander the beautiful countryside, quietly chronicling the passing of an era; you may choose the Pilgrim mode to sure starving and freezing.  If you subscribe to the idea of a countryside ravaged by wildlife gone mad in a frenzy for food, as in the book The China Pandemic by A.R. Shaw, then you would probably choose the Stalker mode. This is described as a punishingly challenging survival experience in the menu.
There is a good middle road for those like myself who want a challenge that is somewhere in the middle. The Voyageur mode is described as equal parts hunter and hunted. Wolves and bears stalk you as you try to scavenge for food. This is the only mode I have played, as the Stalker seems a bit over-challenging for me right now. When you go out to find food, you are stalked by the wolves and bears. You try to hibernate as much as possible, but this won’t last long. Blizzards arise at any given moment. You don’t know when you leave your base whether or not a storm will appear, so you have to choose carefully what you will take with you. If a wolf is stalking nearby when you plan to return, you may not be able to get back to your base. This is the middle choice. You have been warned if you choose the Stalker mode. For the purposes of this review I will describe my 100 hours experience in the Voyageur route.
There is no forgiveness in this game. You will go out to find food with tools and weapons that you find. The shotgun takes a learning curve. The knife and axe are trusty. You can harvest meat and hides from carcasses you find, or you can kill your own meat. But, the game does not allow saving. It saves automatically when you enter the door of a building, and when you sleep in a bed, or fall into the Long Dark sleep of death. It’s too late when you are staring into the fangs of a wolf to use the alt-tab function and return to the last place you entered a door or slept. That route must be chosen before the wolf grabs you.
Survival methods in this game mirror real-world survival methods. First, I load up for a trip. Then I go outside the door, and immediately back inside to initiate an autosave. While I was out there, I made a quick recon of the area to be sure no wolves or bears were nearby. Then, having good info, I make some final decisions about my trip, and I am ready to venture out into the unknown in search of sustenance and survival.
Unlike many other survival games, TLD uses a more realistic crafting system. You must lay your collected hides out on the floor to cure them for an amount of time, before beginning to craft clothing. Then, you complete the crafting in your spare hours over a number of days, just as you would really make your own clothes. You must repair all your clothing and tools frequently, as they degrade in a realistic manner in the arctic cold winds. You are able to choose and change your clothing by degrees of warmth provided and by weight. Your stats are adversely affected by heavier weights over time, and your character is worn out by carrying too much. You must choose carefully or die sooner. You will die. But, it is better to survive and die, than to have never survived at all.
The Story mode is not finished as the game is in early release. But, I believe from dev comments that it is almost finished. In the year I’ve had the game, they have made frequent updates. I am very excited to see the actual story, which is already “showing through the cracks” so to speak, in the sandbox. The achievements, as well, pull in stories of their own, and provide a sense of accomplishment that is unparalleled.
There are several new maps in the Sandbox mode, and each one features the most surreal and hauntingly lovely nature scenes, in an art style that is screaming for an artbook in the final release. I only hope they go all out with that idea, as the art is phenomenal! And, speaking of final release... the story mode is nearing completion. I've already spent months on end in Mystery Lake's map alone, so I can imagine the hours of game play the story mode will provide.
Graphics are done in a realistic art that looks hand-drawn. The view is splendid from anywhere in the game. The music is great for this genre, as it doesn’t get in the way of game play, and yet appears at points of high-drama, like just as you near starving to death.
I bought this at the same time I bought Stranded Deep, and a couple of other intensive survival games. The Long Dark far exceeds every other survival game I've played. Where you find a lack of resources to build anything substantive in SD, The Long Dark keeps you immersed in crafting weapons, curing animal hides to craft deerskin clothes, finding bunkers, exploring ever-changing scenery, and a realistic survival experience that promises to define a genre.
There are many survival games. But, there is only one Long Dark. Where games like the Wasteland series and Sheltered come across slightly cheesy, (not to mention often clunky mechanics) TLD is realistic in concept and execution. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is a good game, with a great story, but it has more sci-fi elements to it, where TLD lives within the realm or today and tomorrow. And, some of those are not presented in life size action like in TLD’s silent apocalypse.
Savage Lands is life size, and appreciable for its own unique crafting, and somewhat medieval look. Yet, I found it somewhat unbelievable that you would run-up to an unmoving deer and slay him on the spot. In TLD you must stalk your prey, as in the real world, because they will run when frightened. I think that sums up the effect: the wildlife AI is responsive to the player.
* Unmatched Survival Realism
* Dynamic Weather
* Hibernation Simulation
* Stats react to loads carried and the weather conditions
* You craft your own meds and heal yourself
* Ice Fishing, rabbit trapping, and hunting with bows that you craft
* You can recycle tools and weapons to repair or build new equipment
* Frequent Updates
*The cook stove or campfire interface is “locked in” and you can’t perform other tasks while cooking.
*The same locked-in interface stalls your view of the countryside while ice-fishing. I only hope they will improve this, but it doesn’t affect gameplay.
* ATM, there is no ability to map your area. But, there are links to maps in the community hub. These are possibly created by the fan-base, and differ in degrees of accuracy.
This is no simple game. Firing the shotgun takes a learning curve, and trial and error. But, once you learn to fire it, you find yourself bringing in multiple animals in one hunt. The more challenging achievements require you to survive without firing a gun, and live off the land. One simple mistake leaves you facing the fangs of a wolf, or freezing to death. This is definitely a game you won't want to miss.

You can find yourself in some pretty nasty situations in this game. On my first trip to Pleasant Valley, I arrived exhausted, over-loaded, and the sun was going down. The wind started picking up, but I ignored it. My character was too busy checking abandoned cars for candy bars and matches. Before I knew it, he was in the middle of a ferocious blizzard. He hopped into the nearest car and tried to wait it out.
The temperature dropped lower and lower as the storm persisted into nightfall. The wind howled all around, and my character began to freeze.
I realized. I'd helped him survive for over 100 days, and I was about to lose it all. He lit his storm lantern to try to stay warm. He curled up in his sleeping bag and took little naps. The night crawled on, and his condition grew worse and worse by the minute. By the time the storm finally abated, hypothermia was setting in. He crawled from the car and used one of his precious matches to light a small fire with some sticks he had collected.
He huddled beside that fire and fed it one stick at a time while the wind did its best to blow it out. When dawn came, he abandoned the fire and staggered along the road looking for better shelter - a shack, a house, a garage...anything.
It was hard to see with his blurry vision, but he found what appeared to be some kind of an abandoned farm house. He made his way inside and stumbled around the house. Upstairs he found a bed, and crawled gratefully beneath the blankets.
He slept on and off all that day and the next, and bit by bit, he recovered enough to leave the house and collect some kindling. It was a nice sunny day, and he was able to save the last of his matches by starting a fire with his magnifying glass. He melted snow and boiled enough water to stay hydrated for a few days, then decided he'd better do something about food.
Luck was with him, and he was able to lure a wolf away from a fresh kill. As he leaned over the dead deer and pulled his hunting knife from his belt, I thought,

Five minutes later, he was dead. Another blizzard rolled in while he was breaking down the deer, and I was fiddling with my cell phone. I looked up just in time to see him fading into the long dark, and that was that. I stared at the screen in horror. There's no save to revert to... no retry button... no Phoenix Down to tickle his nose with. GAME OVER.
That's The Long Dark in a nutshell. This isn't a game in which you frolic about the hills, or hit the save button just in case what you're about to do turns out to be as stupid as you think it is - but you want to try it anyway...
There are no safety nets. No second chances. You have to constantly be on the lookout for danger. You relax, or get distracted… you die. So you listen to the wind. You keep an eye on the sky. You check the temperature. You look out for fallen trees you might be able to clamber up just in case there’s a hungry wolf over the next ridge. You hear one howl in the distance, and you crouch and count your bullets, or ready a torch and hope it’s more scared of fire than it is hungry. In the easiest mode, the wolves and bears act like they would in nature. If you leave them alone, they'll leave you alone. In the normal and hard modes, a geomagnetic event has made them loopy and aggressive. In Interloper, the hardest mode, the game is out to kill you however it can. There are far fewer tools and resources. The weather hates you, and the wolves are absolutely deadly. In their eyes - you're just a sloppy joe in pants - if you still have pants by that point.
A few other points:
- The graphics are stylized but attractive.
- The community's pretty good. Most active players are helpful and friendly.
- The developers are communicative and active. They still monitor the board to weed out jerks.
- The original music scores are absolutely stunning. Sometimes I find myself sitting at the title screen for a few minutes just listening to the music.
- The ambient sound effects are amazing. You hear the wind blow, the trees creak, ice crack, the song of a variety of birds nearby, the distant sounds of wolves, the light rattle of a chain link fence in the wind, and so on...
- You can craft and cook items utilizing natural resources.
- It’s a lonely, melancholy game.
- After surviving for long periods, you can get stuck into routines. Fortunately there are seven different regions in survival mode at this point. You can travel to another region if you get tired of the one you’re in. Each one has its own personality and challenges. Also there's Story Mode, as well as several challenge modes that are engaging, too.
- You can race through Story Mode in maybe ten hours, or play it more naturally for nearly three times that amount.
- The voice actors are talented and well known - from Metal Gear Solid and the Mass Effect series.
- Each game is different. You may have found a hatchet in a dilapidated little hut on your first run, but on your second run – there’s nothing there… Sometimes the cabin you squatted in last game is just a pile of burnt cinders in the next.
- You rarely spawn in the same place twice. In Stalker, you may spawn twenty feet away from a wolf while it's still dark outside and the temperature is well below zero. Or maybe you get lucky and spawn in the Trapper's Homestead and find a rifle hanging from the gun rack. You never know.
