Why the negative review? The game is perfect, isn't it?
Yes and No.
I have beaten the game and gotten the vast majority of achievements so why would I do that if I didn't like the game?
There is a lot to love about Cuphead but I don't see anyone pointing out its faults. So that's what I'll do.
I'm just going to skip over the part where the game is visually and audibly stunning and get into the cons. I'm sure these cons have the potential to ruin the game for some people. That is the only reason why I'm doing this.
Con 1: The game is really a compilation of boss battles. Each boss battle is unique and cool. However a lot of the times bosses will have seemingly random moves that make no sense. Moves that you would only know about through trial and error. If you want to get the best score, you can't take damage at all which makes the game very grueling at times as you constantly open menu and restart because a random shark jumped behind you and took up half the screen instantly.
Con 2: The items in this game are not balanced. Some are useful 90% of the time while others are good on paper but awful in practice (this doesn't apply to gun types really. there are only two useless guns but they are fun to use anyway. )
This includes one passive that if removed from the game I'm sure it would be impossible. (the smoke grenade, which makes you invincible when you dash allowing you to just teleport past enemies)
There isn't a lot of variety in items to begin with, so this just makes it feel like you only have 2 - 3 choices ever.
Con 3 : I feel like the game would be funner for everyone if the first few levels were easier. I'm not saying they aren't relatively easy, but to a new player it can be a frustrating experience and if it were easier it would make the transition a lot smoother. Something we can all learn from Super Meat Boy is that if you make a game that relies on being challenging, then you need to start the player off slowly.
Con 4: Building on what I mentioned before, Cuphead relies on being challenging because the game itself is not very long. If you don't worry about stats or getting perfect score the game can be completed in no time. This means it is really only made for the type of player that always tries to beat their own score, which is not everyone.
Con 5: Hitboxes and determining what object will hurt you and what won't can be really confusing. Usually you can tell because the game consists of the background, platform, obstacles that don't hurt you, and everything else that does hurt you. This is similar to my first Con that this creates a sort of artificial difficulty and encourages trial and error. However this is more due to the nature of the game's art style and outlining, which is usually consistent and not a problem.
That's really it. The game is fantastic in every other way, however these problems need to be noticed. A score wouldn't do it justice.

Okay. This is coming from a big, big Tropico fan. I played Tropico 3, 4 and 5. Let's get into this review.
I was very excited about the game before release. Ever since Tropico 4 came out, I've been waiting and waiting for news about the newer one. But sadly, this game disappointed me. First, let me talk about the things I liked.
The textures and graphics are amazing. They have been improved alot. I played the old versions on my Xbox 360, and right when I changed to PC and tried this one out, I noticed the differences. The buildings look very nice, and when you zoom in, full in, you see all the details. The interiors of a shack, the faces on the people and sometimes just the trees. The developers went all out on this game and I say that the graphics are a plus.
The new online mode is awesome. You can play against three other people in an island, and race to finish quests or even try to invade the other person.
But those are really the only things I liked about this game.
In Tropico 5, you play alot of missions in the same island. You're basically switching islands and going back to them. I didn't like this move. Alot of times you feel like you're handed the island to you again. I know how this would have worked, but I don't really like it. In the old versions, every single mission is another challenge to you. You go on a different, all new island and building it out of nothing. Alot of times this game just feels repetitive.
I feel like the direction Kalypso is moving is not helping the game. The game relies on DLC after DLC to try to keep it fresh again. A game shouldn't fully rely on expansions to make it better. Those DLC's could instead be implemented to the actual game and when you play the old game and the new one, you feel like it's a big step.
There have already been four DLC's out that could have instead been in the original game, that would have made it better. I still don't know how there's no offline multiplayer yet. It would be awesome to have people controlling different part of the island.
And also, the soundtrack. I loved the older soundtracks, but when you compare Tropico 5's to the older ones, it's just not as good.
Tropico 3 and 4 both amazed me. I loved both of those games instantly. I expected the same to happen with Tropico 5, but sadly that was not the case. It feels like this whole series just relies on DLC's to make the game fresh again. I can't see many people buying DLC after DLC after DLC. It's just, not how it should go. I feel like Tropico can be one of the biggest strategy/city-building games out there if it just fills in all the gaps. After just a few hours of playing this game, I was already disappointed. I felt at times I was forcing myself to continue, and that it felt like a chore to keep playing.
If you've never played a Tropico game before, or you're just new at city-building games, I recommend you try this out. But if you are a hardcore gamer, or a just experienced at Tropico, chances are you won't like this game - at least not as much as the older ones.
And for this, I give the game a 5/10.

It may not be a perfect format for a review but I will just compare Banished with Cities:Skylines (C:S). If you already own C:S this comparison might help you with assessing Banished. If not, you might be interested in this other city builder.
Banished and C:S are practically polar opposites.
The currency in Banished are the inhabitants of your village. Its biggest challenge lies in the first few hours of starting a new town. It takes some effort to keep your villagers alive and generating a surplus of resources for having a healthy growth rate. After a few hours, you have a small settlement that practically requires no more management and which generates a surplus of every necessary resource. All fun is gone now since all you can do is just build more of the same buildings, further decreasing difficulty since generation increases and there is no negative feedback to your earlier establishment. There is also no fun in following your citizens, unless you find it funny to see a builder arriving at a building site where he works one second before he leaves it again so he can go 'looking for food'.
Cities: Skylines is boring the first hours where you create a first district just for generating some money so  you can expand into a real city. And that is where C:S shines. As your population increases, the challenge of managing traffic increases and the game provides you with an increasing number of facilities which keeps you wanting to grow. C:S keeps enthralling you with beautiful graphics as you ponder over the lay-out of every district you (re)build as your town grows from a small village to a large metropole.
So... if it's on sale, Banished is not bad to spend a few hours onto.
If you're choosing between Banished and C:S however, buy C:S... unless you have a wooden pc, then Banished will do.

First of all, Tropico 5 is way longer than I expected, which is great, as I do enjoy long games that frustrate you. I played on hard and was forced multiple times to restart missions or redo the entire playthrough due to mistakes I've made. Which is just great!
Now lets get down to it, is Tropico 5 just like Tropico 1-2-3-4? A short answer would be no. A long answer will be hell no.
Tropico 5 is built on what made the tropico series great. City building and controlling your island as El President is addictive. All that you loved from the older games you will find here as well. However Tropico 5 is bringing a lot of new things to the series.
In the older games, you could find a balance and then you would NEVER have any kind of problems again with money, well Tropico 5 skull ♥♥♥♥s that and makes you work for it. Just as you think, “Ah ! I finally figured out how to keep my money in plus”, you will go in huge minus due to one of the many random events.
The interface and gameplay in many ways will make you feel like home. But all the new things will toss you a curve ball all the time and keep you on your toes, I had to play the last mission 6 times in a row (Yea ! I'm not kidding, 6 freaking times) to even understand what I did wrong and to finally beat it. In the other Tropicos this would never have happened.
The graphics are brilliant as well as the humor. Lets not forget that there is MULTIPLAYER. That's right, 2 Presidents trying to either kill each other or work together for a greater goal.
Tropico 5 is everything I personally wanted from a new Tropico game and I can only strongly recommend it. There are tons of DLC's but be careful what you buy as not all of them are worth the money.
So to sum up, grab the game for sure and grab the DLC's when they are on sale!

It wants to look at the proposition from the stranger, see the hints of danger, and say "yes" anyway (and if you say "no", you'll probably miss something great and/or beneficial).

I bought GamersGoMakers based on reviews stating that it is a more complex Game Dev Tycoon.
In my experience, the only added complexity is in the reviewable detail like spreadsheets showing current trends and company history.
Everything else, however, feels less polished than Game Dev Tycoon (which I also found to be a far from ideal game).
First, the user interface is sometimes confusing. Does that green checkmark mean I need to click it to activate it? Or does that mean it
activated? Oh, okay, that means it *is* activated. On other dialogues and interfaces -- oops, wait, come back! I didn't mean to skip that question or step! You're also forced into full-screen. For casual simulation games like this, I'd prefer to use a small window while I do other things. With GamersGoMakers, you can have full-screen or windowed mode. Both will take up your entire screen (in my case, on a 2560x1600 screen). Yes, there is a lot of information in the interface, but there are far more complex data-driven presentation games out there that I can play at something other than full screen, if I wish.
Second, the game play itself is essentially the same as every other iteration of this genre. Research tech, train skills, name a game, select genre and focuses for game, click button and watch while the money rolls in (or doesn't). Repeat and rinse until you're bankrupt (no way to take bank or private loans or anything else - when you go negative for a year, you're toast) or until you have enough money to invest in a bigger building and more employees and advertising campaigns.
Third, and what kind of drove me nuts over everything else, are the incoherencies. The game starts in 1980 and can be started in the 80s, 90s, or 00s, if you prefer. In the beginning, the only graphical technology which exists is "text based". You'll see something like the current 1980 trend being "race simulators". So, you might create a race simulator using the currently available technology. The game will bomb -- probably because you didn't invest enough focus in graphics (as per the game reviews for your product). You know, those sexy
graphics that really drive racing simulators of 1980.
If you play through production of a few games (which feels like it is always based around entirely random generation of events and desires, no matter how senseless) you'll reach the point where an ESRB-style ratings board appears. Only, not so much like the ESRB, because while the ESRB has no legal authority and are a voluntary industry ratings system, the ratings service in the game apparently has the capability to legally
a game in America, for "excessive language".
That's right. A game developed in the US for a US market is banned in the US by a ratings service for its language. For those unfamiliar with the first amendment and repeated court decisions over the decades upholding it, let's put this into context: Only two games have
been "banned" in the US. Ever.  One was an adult title in 2005 which, due to an under age (17yrs) model being revealed, was taken off the market and the other was an
game which was "banned" due to defective peripheral parts which were potentially dangers and therefore recalled for safety issues. In other words, neither was technically "banned" and certainly no game has ever been banned due to language or violence or legal representations of sexual situations. While this may seem like a small thing, it's an annoyance and representative of countless incoherencies in a title which otherwise asserts itself to be an engaging simulation of an industry, sectioned into characteristic decades.
Over all, it is not a terrible game. I just can not suggest it over Game Dev Tycoon at a full $10. Frankly, I can't suggest Game Dev Tycoon at its full price, either. Both are very lack-luster games; GamersGoMakers more so. I would really like to see someone put in the work to produce a high quality game of this genre and subject, with the depth and complexity and coherence that it really deserves. As it is, every one of these that I've encountered are little more than a cheap mobile phone quality distraction.

Quite possibly one of the finest roguelike games ever.  The overall game idea is quite simple, make your way in life in a steampunk version of London, where your best chance of riches in on the low seas of the Unterzee.  Pick up passengers and cargo and take them round the map to earn money to upgrade stuff and possibly eventually retire.  Along the way if you die then its all for nothing, death is the end, your relatives get a token inheritence from your will and then must start everything again (same quests, slightly different map, rubbish weapons and tiny boat).  This game after the death of your second captain will introduce a new fully fledged family member into your life, one you will cherish and protect like its been produced from your own DNA.
The roguelike nature may mean things can become repetitive although you may make different choices as ypu move from gung-ho to overally cautious wimp where you can't face starting again.
Would highly recommend, although not one for big couch to TV distances if using a Steam Link. There is a lot of text so you will need a big tv and to be sat very near it to really play this effectively. Probably best to stick to using the actual pc, this has the benefit of no-one seeing you cry when you stupidly run out of fuel, eat all your crew and are forced to watch and weep as all your hardwork is undone following a stupid course deviation to avoid pirates.

A decent top-down non-linear exploration game with some rogue-like elements.
You start the game as a newly-minted ship captain, choosing a background and goal. Then you chug into the dark unknown, uncovering various locations and mysteries, until you achieve your goal. You acquire crew, money, and ship upgrades. You have to carefully manage fuel, supplies, and levels of Terror (which grows/lessens through various events). The map is semi-random and is different each time you start a game.
The world is fascinating. Good writing (one part Gaiman with one part Lovecraft), decent art style, and atmospheric soundtrack. Sometimes the music doesn't seem to play, which is certainly a downside. There doesn't seem to be a single overarching storyline - the game is more about discovery. The biggest problems most people will have with Sunless Sea are (1) slow pace which requires some grinding (2) combat is clunky and uninteresting. There don't seem to be any mods, but some people have made posts about save game editing, which can create different results.
Things you'll see in Sunless Sea include: A church of cannibals. A living iceberg. A city of mirrors. Dream serpents. A forbidden empire of apes. An island of clay men and living objects. A woman waiting for her eyes to hatch. Rat postmen sorting lost mail. The world is strange, but not in a trying-too-hard way. Everything somehow makes sense within this universe and weirdness is never out of place.
As an aside: I'd enjoy seeing a Warhammer 40K version of Sunless Sea. Something reminiscient of Dark Heresy and Rogue Trader. It's definitely achievable. Maybe that's sort of what Fail Better Games is doing with their upcoming project Sunless Skies.
Overall, I would recommend this, especially during a sale. It isn't something for everyone, but if you're interested in the premise (and Sunless Sea's weird world), you will likely find this entertaining.

The primary complaint I have seen with this game is its similarity in visual style to Game Dev Tycoon.  This sort of complaint really doesn't make any sense, as the content of these sorts of games is often more important than the presentation: so long as the presentation is relatively easy-to-navigate and allows for a good workflow, it's acceptable if it appears lifted from another game that has done it well before.  But does GGM add anything to the genre?
Not really.  On the surface, it appears to be much more complex, with much more player control, however: a bug-ridden experience, clumsy UI, and lots of window-dressing all contribute to an illusion.  The reality is that the game is, at its core, a clumsier version of GDT that does right what it's lifted from its predecessor, and does wrong what it's contributed to the genre.  Therefore, the following won't be about what it does well, because you can read a review of GDT for that - it will be about what the game does poorly.
The first major complaint, the one which will be most readily apparent to players, is the clumsiness of the UI.  Even before expanding to a new office, the player will have hurdles to overcome in unresponsiveness, incoherent navigation, and unnecessary obscuration.  The main office is cluttered with interactable props which serve no purpose but to give a secondary measure to accessing data which can be accessed by the player menu, except for one or two: even then, accessing data by the player menu is hit-and-miss, with mouse clicks sometimes not responding, and other times unreasonably delayed.
The UI clears up somewhat at the development options, at least before you hire other workers to help you in your enterprise: relatively easy-to-manipulate areas of focus for the games, sliders for 'Violence' 'Profanity' and 'Sexuality', story genre picker and story budget; these are all options which present little-to-no difficulty in manipulating (though the story budget can be slow in response, and defaults in increment.)  The marketing screen is also straightforward and simple, and surprisingly the buttons click rather easily: at this point, as well, the game sale price per unit can be set.
Once the player takes on extra workers, however, a further screen for work allocation is added.  This screen is a nightmare to manipulate: removing workers from a certain area of focus requires double-clicking on the worker's name, which shouldn't be a frustrating action, but is made so by a general lack of responsiveness as seen in other menus.  Allocating workers to specific areas of focus is even worse: you click, hold, and drag the worker's name to the area of focus, and need to hit the right spot (often not even where the box for the area of focus is) in order to allocate the worker.
Perhaps, though, this clumsiness in UI could be offset by a wide plethora of options, giving players an unprescedented level of control over the games they develop?  At first, it appears so: there are multiple areas of focus that you must balance your time between - starting off with only a few options (Gameplay, Engine, Graphics, Sound, Level Design, Content Design, Sound Design, and Writing), but quickly conflating with the additions of UI, Scripting, World Design, UI Design, and Networking.  With 13 areas of focus, it may seem that the development of each game will be a complex process of determining where sacrifices can be afforded, and where they must be avoided.
To some degree, it is: at the beginning, before you figure out the 'magic formula' for your genre of choice -- which changes as you add the further areas of focus, so that's something -- you will make mistakes and have to change your approach a couple of times.  After that, though, you'll find you're spending the majority of your focus on 1/3rd to 1/2 of the game development, which is hardly different from GDT.  Put simply, the thirteen areas of focus are unnecessary divisions for which there is little necessity, merely more content for the illusion of complexity.
Similarly, worker allocation appears, initially, to be more complex than GDT: there are a lot of different areas of focus, so management of human resources appears to be something which may change on a case-by-case basis.  The only problem with this is that your areas of focus, especially if you stick to a genre (which is adviseable, as genre-switching is largely punished in a passive manner by the game), will not really change, so neither will your worker allocation.  The only added flexibility which this provides is that each worker specializes in specific areas of game development, but this is also something which occured in GDT.  Through real estate, though, you can hire enough workers to have specialists in each category, but after the costs of these human resources is offset by profit, one no longer needs to truly manage their employees in a meaningful way -- there is no room for compromise and challenge in that system.
Surely, though, the greater flexibility in story, content, and pricing/marketing make up for this?  Not in the least.  The three sliders for violence, profanity, and sexuality seem like an interesting subdivision of 'E', 'T', and 'M', except that ratings largely have little to no effect on maximizing profit, and you will nearly always be pushed toward developing 'M' or 'Ao' games.  Further, once you translate, there's the potential for necessitating player creativity in balancing the desires of the puritanical, but ultraviolent English demographic, and the trigger-shy, but perverted German demographic.  This doesn't exist, as the content largely does not affect the sales to a huge degree, unless you go overboard.  You can leave half the demographic wanting 'more', and they'll still eat up a game over 75% like hot cakes.
Story budget and story topic are unnecessary divisions from the 'topic' selection and 'story' slider in GDT.  The story budget has little to no effect on how well the reviewers will receive the story -- that comes from focus on the written content, at the areas of focus screen.  The topic selection is simply in a different place, and even following a current light or strong trend only results in a small discrepancy between profits from not following a trend.
After story and budget, one can decide how the game is packaged: really, it's just a choice between what terrible set of 2000s flash-grade art you'll force on your customers, and the casing increases costs of distribution but has either little to no effect on sales -- this can't be confirmed, really, by the player, as there is no feedback given on what seems to be a largely aeshtetic choice without any necessity.
The only feature that has been added which truly impacts gameplay is the pricing per unit option: this influences the profit margin and how well the game will sell.  Even this is done rather poorly, as the player will always be able to sell under average list, make a decent enough profit from distribution, and never have any incentive to play the market above the list price with a superior product.
Finally, there are multiple bugs and poor design decisions in user interactivity.  Switching between rooms to access your employees is a chore at best, and breaks the UI for critical amounts of time at worst.  Employees will often bring up concerns or suggestions with the player: this would be fine, except that when two content windows pop up, the employee one is lost and relegated to the news sidebar, which is a pain to navigate.  Multiple offices impacts the UI lag even further, making the game a sluggish and unfun exercise.  There are several one-off training and upgrade options, but these have little impact on gameplay as a whole.
At its core GGM appears to be a new, complex addition to the game development genre: when fully analyzed, it's little more than a badly-implemented clone, which would feel more at home in Early Access.

Can I just say that I freaking LOVE this game? Now, i'm not too big into to the survival genre, but this one just hits the nail on the head for me. Maybe it's because i'm Canadian, and basically surviving in the winter is something I learned in school  (i'm not even joking), so I had a little bit of an idea of what to expect when I first played this game. But all that aside, this game is amazing, even for just being in it's early stages.
PROS:
-The graphical art of this game is mesmerizing. It's beautiful, and I could take a hundred in-game screen shots and no two would look the same.
-The game world is pretty large, with 5-6 regions, and each region spanning a large area, not to mention all the interior areas to discover.
-This game gets you thinking, and I like that. It's kinda like a puzzle game, but with more starvation, wolves, and hypothermia.
-There is always something to do. Exploring the vast world around you, finding food, supplies, trying to avoid wolves and bears, and lots more to do.
-No two play throughs will be the same. You'll spawn somewhere different, luxury items will be in a different spot in the map/world, stuff like that.
-This game is more than just survival. This game freaking scares me somtimes when i'm exploring dark caves or i'm stranded in the middle of a blizzard. Always be on your toes when playing this game and be prepared to be scared a time or two.
-The updates for this game are pretty consistant. Though they can be a pretty long amount of time between eachother, they always add lots of content to make up for it.
CONS:
-None. I love absolutley everything about this game. I guess if I had to say something could be worked on in this game, it would be that it feels like you become hungry, thirsty and tired a little too easily. I mean, I know this is a game, it's not 100% realistic, but maybe making it so I don't have to eat 1000 calories and drink 2L of water every half an hour would be nice. But other than that, this game is a 10/10 for me.
I can't wait to see what Hinterland Studio adds to this game in the future, and I can only give them the highest of praise for this amazing piece of art this game is. If you don't own this game, you're making a grave mistake, compadre.
EDIT: I just recently began playing the story mode and, so far, it's interesting. You obviously don't have the same amount as freedom as in the survival mode, but I feel The Long Dark deserved a story mode from the beginning. I've also been seeing alot of negative reviews for this game recently, and I don't understand why. One review roughly described TLD as not being 'fun', and I think that, in a good way, that might be somewhat true. This game is ment to challenge you, make you stop and think about what to do or where to go next. This is a hardcore survival game, not some fast paced, CoD-style game.

Been playing for a few hours now, and it's really awesome the sheer amount of content that has been packed into an alpha game. There's a huge amount of depth to this game already. Not everything is mapped out for you, and while this may not seem like a big deal, with so many branching options on how you want to progress in the game it can become overwelming fast. Some sort of talent tree system, or unified menu for research and it's current level would be a huge help. A wiki for this game is something that the community is more responsible for, but as it gains momentum this type of resource will come naturally.
Updates for this game are seriously quick and seems to flow constantly. Be ready for new content or fixes often, and tweaks to things you already know.
Yes, I highly recommend the game for those who like sandbox games, and especially those who have a friend to play it with. Just remember that starting out is tough, and the end rewards are worth it. This is no terraria or minecraft or any other crafting game you've played. This is Edge of Space

This is my first telltale game(I did play LiS though and it seemed very much like a telltale game) and it was a disappointing experience. (Sorry for a long review!)
First off, this game is just buggy AF! The frame rate just keeps fluctuating like crazy. I have a mid-end rig that gets me 40-50 fps consistently in games like Shadow of Mordor at 1080p. Plus I am seeing other reviews mentioning it too. So clearly it is the game's fault. I would understand if this fluctuaion happens when something is exploding or there is bright light but I am just walking and the framerate drops for no reason. I did try to change my settings, lower the resolutions and stuff but all in vain.
(SPOILER AHEAD.)
Second off, the Batman/Bruce Wayne created here is difficult for me to get behind. Now, maybe the devs wanted to create a new Batman universe and I am all in for expereinceing a new Batman. I really appreciate that intent to do something new. But they can't just expect the player to forget everything else that they have known so far about him. If they are going to create a weaker Batman who is prone to simple emotions and mental manipulations from an uninteresting criminal(unlike Joker or Bane) they need to setup the universe better! They are changing the mold of a character that has been here for decades. They should have done due dilignece and should have given us a new background story or something of that sort. Maybe Batman isn't a member of the league of shadows yet. But they need to let the player know that!
It was just hard to watch a weak Batman without any reason for why he is so. He is just fawning over every female character. He just remembers things about his parent's death out of the blue! He has dialog choices that he obviously wouldn't say! Somehow he has all this physical prowess and he is a great detective(as always) but he has memory loss of the very moment that made him Batman and isn't immune to simple emotional manipulations? That is not the Batman I know and enjoy but I would've been fine with it if the setup was done properly. It felt like they just weren't sincere enough to do that.
Finally, at many points in the game it felt like a Batman story doesn't fit in as a pure point and click expereince. You do quick time actions for everyone, both common thugs and the main bosses, and for everything, for both stealth and guns-blazing. This ended up feeling monotonous. Even though Batman is fighting a main boss it didn't make a difference to me as a player. Even though Batman was taking a stealthy approach it didn't feel like it to me because all of it is just quick-time actions. This is an interesting problem and further innovations are needed here I guess. I will commend the fact that telltale did make a good attempt here with the whole strategising with the drone but it definitely needs more work. It just felt pointless because no matter what you chose you did beat up all the thugs! Maybe if some strategies were more likely to work than others and depending on the strategy I take the dialog choices changed it would be more interesting? They should also probably revamp the way we fight bosses and give something other than just quick time actions.
So to summarise, it felt like Telltale had the right intentions here but were not successful in their execution both due to some insincerity of their own and some shortcomings of the point and click genre itself. Hopefully there will be a sequel/prequel to this game where Telltale make a better game and sculpt a better Batman. Until such time it might be a waste to buy this one. Sorry Telltale but THUMBS DOWN! :-(

Quite possibly one of the finest roguelike games ever.  The overall game idea is quite simple, make your way in life in a steampunk version of London, where your best chance of riches in on the low seas of the Unterzee.  Pick up passengers and cargo and take them round the map to earn money to upgrade stuff and possibly eventually retire.  Along the way if you die then its all for nothing, death is the end, your relatives get a token inheritence from your will and then must start everything again (same quests, slightly different map, rubbish weapons and tiny boat).  This game after the death of your second captain will introduce a new fully fledged family member into your life, one you will cherish and protect like its been produced from your own DNA.
The roguelike nature may mean things can become repetitive although you may make different choices as ypu move from gung-ho to overally cautious wimp where you can't face starting again.
Would highly recommend, although not one for big couch to TV distances if using a Steam Link. There is a lot of text so you will need a big tv and to be sat very near it to really play this effectively. Probably best to stick to using the actual pc, this has the benefit of no-one seeing you cry when you stupidly run out of fuel, eat all your crew and are forced to watch and weep as all your hardwork is undone following a stupid course deviation to avoid pirates.

A decent top-down non-linear exploration game with some rogue-like elements.
You start the game as a newly-minted ship captain, choosing a background and goal. Then you chug into the dark unknown, uncovering various locations and mysteries, until you achieve your goal. You acquire crew, money, and ship upgrades. You have to carefully manage fuel, supplies, and levels of Terror (which grows/lessens through various events). The map is semi-random and is different each time you start a game.
The world is fascinating. Good writing (one part Gaiman with one part Lovecraft), decent art style, and atmospheric soundtrack. Sometimes the music doesn't seem to play, which is certainly a downside. There doesn't seem to be a single overarching storyline - the game is more about discovery. The biggest problems most people will have with Sunless Sea are (1) slow pace which requires some grinding (2) combat is clunky and uninteresting. There don't seem to be any mods, but some people have made posts about save game editing, which can create different results.
Things you'll see in Sunless Sea include: A church of cannibals. A living iceberg. A city of mirrors. Dream serpents. A forbidden empire of apes. An island of clay men and living objects. A woman waiting for her eyes to hatch. Rat postmen sorting lost mail. The world is strange, but not in a trying-too-hard way. Everything somehow makes sense within this universe and weirdness is never out of place.
As an aside: I'd enjoy seeing a Warhammer 40K version of Sunless Sea. Something reminiscient of Dark Heresy and Rogue Trader. It's definitely achievable. Maybe that's sort of what Fail Better Games is doing with their upcoming project Sunless Skies.
Overall, I would recommend this, especially during a sale. It isn't something for everyone, but if you're interested in the premise (and Sunless Sea's weird world), you will likely find this entertaining.

Right, so I recently played this game for the first time on Windows 8.1 and on a decent gaming computer.
First: What kind of game is this? It's an FPS with solid RPG elements – selecting upgrades for your weapons and choosing between 'spells' (plasmids) has a significant impact on gameplay, and it is something you will be doing a lot of.
BioShock contains traces of horror, and some jumpscare every now and then (but not too much, I'd say).
The storyline is at the centre of this game, and it has some political and philosophical undertones, which is cool.
The atmosphere
is, perhaps, the weakest point of this game. Occasionally, it feels artificial. I guess a  higher texture resolution could have helped somewhat when playing on resolutions like 1920x1080 or higher. This in order to make the world outside the tubes you are walking through look more realistic and real. The chatter of the splicers (your enemies) also feels rather repetitive after a while (one of the male voices also sounds conspicuously like Homer Simpson..)
The variety of weapons and how they work is quite refreshing and makes strategy pay off: you'll defeat your enemies much quicker if you use the right weapons and/or in the right combination.
It took me 17.5 hours to complete the game, so it can take a while to complete it. I did, however, try to collect and explore everything possible, so it should be possible to complete it a lot faster than that.
All in all, I'd give the game, say, 7/10; and that's not cutting it any slack because it's old.

I’m simply going to talk about this game, instead of talking about how it’s a carbon copy another game called “Game Dev Tycoon”.  It’s not, but let’s concentrate on the game at hand.
GamersGoMakers (not a great name, I know) is made by a small indie development team, and graphically the game is simple and cartoonish, which is to be pretty expected.  The graphics do the job enough, though, because pretty graphics are not the most important thing about management sims, which is basically what this is.
You can start your game from several points through history, but I think you’ll get the most out of it by starting back in 1980.  You begin your career as game developer as a one-man/woman team.  Over time – with success and no small amount of luck – you’ll expand into larger premises which enable you to open specialist departments, such as a design office, a development office, a sound studio, etc.  You’ll have to hire staff to fill the positions, who help you to make your games.  Your staff – yourself included – have skill stats, which you can improve by doing training as well as through the act of making games.  The higher their stats, the higher their wage, but if you want to be churning out those big AAA games then you’re going to need the best you can find.  Don’t be afraid to fire people so you can hire better staff members as they become available.
You can choose from an increasingly wide range of game genres, such as action, adventure, strategy, etc, most of which also expand into other options, such as ‘action, shoot-em-up’.  You need to decide where to place your emphasis with the game, such as graphics, game play, AI, sound, etc.  For example, shoot-em-up actions don’t require a lot of emphasis on writing, but game play and graphics are very important.  At first, you’ll be making games with the wrong emphasis in the wrong areas, but as you gain experience and can hire a producer, you’ll have a better idea of what to do.
After you’ve finished your masterpiece, you release it to the world, where you’ll get your all-important review.  You’ll get rated out of 10 for your game play, graphics, writing, etc.  The higher the better, of course.  But you’ll also get a percentage score out of 100.  Anything over probably 70% you can consider you did okay; anything under is a swing and a miss.  Lastly, you’ll get some comments on the pro’s and con’s of your game.  A few dud games in a row early on in your career can send you bankrupt very quickly.  Consequently, the early years are the most difficult and precarious.
As of the current version – which I believe is version 1.1 – there are definitely bugs in the game.  But it’s not just bugs that are the problem.  It’s not very intuitive or informative in telling you what areas you need to be emphasising and what areas are unimportant, even after you’ve made games in that genre a few times.  For a comparison, “Game Dev Tycoon” reveals more and more information on a genre the more times you do it, until you have a very good idea indeed on what you need to do.  It not only tells you what’s important, but what’s not important.  GamersGoMakers doesn’t make that clear enough in my opinion.
The good thing, though, is that the developers have expressed a desire to release patches and even DLC’s so I’m hopeful that the worst of the problems will get ironed out.
If you’re like me and played “Game Dev Tycoon”, liked it a lot but also found it a little frustrating because of how limited it was, then you’ll like this.  If you’ve never played “Game Dev Tycoon” but are interested in the idea of becoming a game developer bigwig then you’ll like this game.  It’s not perfect but patches will certainly go some way towards this, and even as it is, I find it a lot of fun and rather addictive!

I didn't know what to write about in my review, so here's a recipe for pancakes instead:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 1/2 teaspoons baking powder
1 teaspoon salt
1 tablespoon white sugar
1 1/4 cups milk
1 egg

For a game which took roughly 2~3 hours to beat, not including an hour and a half being out of my house, I can safely say that LIMBO definetly was worth to get while it was free on June 21~22nd of 2016's summer.
While the story is nothing too big or tries to go for any twist, it's pretty much a somewhat non-story type of game where you just try to accomplish the goal of going right, and eventually reaching the end.
The game itself gives off an atmosphere of uncanny, but instead of just throwing around blood and gore, the mere darkness speaks for itself. Sure enough, there will be some gruesome deaths to your protagonist should you make a mistake, but sure enuogh the game is not on the level of horror as in "oh noes I gots jumpscared", but rather the horror levels of not knowing really what's happening.
Gameplay wise though it's a mix of puzzles and platformers. Being that there should be one or few parts where you'd need an almost precise timing, but for the puzzles at most it's either simply using whatever's grabbable by your character, a slight thinking outside the box or trial and error, by which I mean trial and deaths, because it's quite unlikely anyone would get through the first time without dying to something that you didn't expect, which is...kind of annoying, honestly.
Besides that though, I really enjoyed whatever little time I had playing this, and I can safely say that this game is a 7~9. Reason is that while the game was definetly fun and the puzzles felt fair enough to not need a walkthrough to figure them out, there was still alot of cases where you'd need either some almost crazy timing that normally wouldn't be deemed as the solution to the puzzle, thus leading to alot of death in the way. And I can't give it a perfect score either because the story in general, while not too terrible, is still kind of basic and almost forgettable.
But I'll give you that, the infamous creature of this game sure was the most interesting story I had throughout it.

. The variables I'll cover in the next section.
In slow motion, you can almost always tell when you are going to die, and from where. However, some levels contain randomly generated enemies which actually determine whether or not you're going to win. For example, level
is easily one of the hardest levels to beat simply because after you kill the wave of red guys, several red guys spawn with random guns, ranging from bare handed to shotgun, all in a tight little room. It's unfortunate to say this, but winning some levels like this,
during challenges and time trials, might only depend on if you're lucky enough to play when all the red guys spawn with only pistols.

SUPERHOT has a few bugs which can make the game a bit more challenging, to occasionally stopping you from winning a level.
Going back to the level
, there's a good example of a challenging bug. After you enter the first room from the balcony-catwalk-thing, your in the line of fire of a shotgunner and a machine gunner. Your options include running straight at them, or backing up around the corner. However, backing up is a problem because there's a small height difference between the ledge and the room, which prevents you from backing up. And as long as you hold the "S" key, the bullets move closer and closer. Jumping over this is out of the question, because as long as your in the air, time continues to move as gravity pulls on you. Little details like this become major problems in Challenge modes. And this isn't the only example of bad world geometry, as some levels have invisible barriers that prevent you from exiting the line of fire altogether.
Another good example is the broken Time Trial mode. In at least one level (there may be others, I don't know yet), the timer starts counting before you even finish loading in, resulting in you starting with roughly .97 seconds already passed. This sounds minor, but when the goal is set at 4 seconds, losing that time is almost a quarter of what you should have. On that level, which is
, the best possible time I've managed is 4.07, and that was after nearly 20 minutes of retries, on what is only the third level in the game.
SUPERHOT is very unique and memorable for it's mechanics. It could have been improved during development by adding more levels to the story, but that's only an issue if you don't want to pay full price for that much.

Currently, you only play the game in "sandbox mode." This amounts to an open world survival experience, where you spawn at one of a variety of points on a predetermined map. A geomagnetic storm brings your small plane down in the Canadian wilderness. You are unprepared, and it's freezing cold. As if that weren't enough pressure to get you moving your worthless tennis shoes, you soon find you aren't the only creature slinking along using the hills to break the wind as you hunt for shelter before darkfall.
Though everyone is talking, and gaming, the demise of modern civilization, not everyone agrees on the possible scenarios. If you prefer an end like that described in the book The Road, by Cormac McCarthy, where you wander the beautiful countryside, quietly chronicling the passing of an era; you may choose the Pilgrim mode to sure starving and freezing.  If you subscribe to the idea of a countryside ravaged by wildlife gone mad in a frenzy for food, as in the book The China Pandemic by A.R. Shaw, then you would probably choose the Stalker mode. This is described as a punishingly challenging survival experience in the menu.
There is a good middle road for those like myself who want a challenge that is somewhere in the middle. The Voyageur mode is described as equal parts hunter and hunted. Wolves and bears stalk you as you try to scavenge for food. This is the only mode I have played, as the Stalker seems a bit over-challenging for me right now. When you go out to find food, you are stalked by the wolves and bears. You try to hibernate as much as possible, but this won’t last long. Blizzards arise at any given moment. You don’t know when you leave your base whether or not a storm will appear, so you have to choose carefully what you will take with you. If a wolf is stalking nearby when you plan to return, you may not be able to get back to your base. This is the middle choice. You have been warned if you choose the Stalker mode. For the purposes of this review I will describe my 100 hours experience in the Voyageur route.
There is no forgiveness in this game. You will go out to find food with tools and weapons that you find. The shotgun takes a learning curve. The knife and axe are trusty. You can harvest meat and hides from carcasses you find, or you can kill your own meat. But, the game does not allow saving. It saves automatically when you enter the door of a building, and when you sleep in a bed, or fall into the Long Dark sleep of death. It’s too late when you are staring into the fangs of a wolf to use the alt-tab function and return to the last place you entered a door or slept. That route must be chosen before the wolf grabs you.
Survival methods in this game mirror real-world survival methods. First, I load up for a trip. Then I go outside the door, and immediately back inside to initiate an autosave. While I was out there, I made a quick recon of the area to be sure no wolves or bears were nearby. Then, having good info, I make some final decisions about my trip, and I am ready to venture out into the unknown in search of sustenance and survival.
Unlike many other survival games, TLD uses a more realistic crafting system. You must lay your collected hides out on the floor to cure them for an amount of time, before beginning to craft clothing. Then, you complete the crafting in your spare hours over a number of days, just as you would really make your own clothes. You must repair all your clothing and tools frequently, as they degrade in a realistic manner in the arctic cold winds. You are able to choose and change your clothing by degrees of warmth provided and by weight. Your stats are adversely affected by heavier weights over time, and your character is worn out by carrying too much. You must choose carefully or die sooner. You will die. But, it is better to survive and die, than to have never survived at all.
The Story mode is not finished as the game is in early release. But, I believe from dev comments that it is almost finished. In the year I’ve had the game, they have made frequent updates. I am very excited to see the actual story, which is already “showing through the cracks” so to speak, in the sandbox. The achievements, as well, pull in stories of their own, and provide a sense of accomplishment that is unparalleled.
There are several new maps in the Sandbox mode, and each one features the most surreal and hauntingly lovely nature scenes, in an art style that is screaming for an artbook in the final release. I only hope they go all out with that idea, as the art is phenomenal! And, speaking of final release... the story mode is nearing completion. I've already spent months on end in Mystery Lake's map alone, so I can imagine the hours of game play the story mode will provide.
Graphics are done in a realistic art that looks hand-drawn. The view is splendid from anywhere in the game. The music is great for this genre, as it doesn’t get in the way of game play, and yet appears at points of high-drama, like just as you near starving to death.
I bought this at the same time I bought Stranded Deep, and a couple of other intensive survival games. The Long Dark far exceeds every other survival game I've played. Where you find a lack of resources to build anything substantive in SD, The Long Dark keeps you immersed in crafting weapons, curing animal hides to craft deerskin clothes, finding bunkers, exploring ever-changing scenery, and a realistic survival experience that promises to define a genre.
There are many survival games. But, there is only one Long Dark. Where games like the Wasteland series and Sheltered come across slightly cheesy, (not to mention often clunky mechanics) TLD is realistic in concept and execution. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is a good game, with a great story, but it has more sci-fi elements to it, where TLD lives within the realm or today and tomorrow. And, some of those are not presented in life size action like in TLD’s silent apocalypse.
Savage Lands is life size, and appreciable for its own unique crafting, and somewhat medieval look. Yet, I found it somewhat unbelievable that you would run-up to an unmoving deer and slay him on the spot. In TLD you must stalk your prey, as in the real world, because they will run when frightened. I think that sums up the effect: the wildlife AI is responsive to the player.
* Unmatched Survival Realism
* Dynamic Weather
* Hibernation Simulation
* Stats react to loads carried and the weather conditions
* You craft your own meds and heal yourself
* Ice Fishing, rabbit trapping, and hunting with bows that you craft
* You can recycle tools and weapons to repair or build new equipment
* Frequent Updates
*The cook stove or campfire interface is “locked in” and you can’t perform other tasks while cooking.
*The same locked-in interface stalls your view of the countryside while ice-fishing. I only hope they will improve this, but it doesn’t affect gameplay.
* ATM, there is no ability to map your area. But, there are links to maps in the community hub. These are possibly created by the fan-base, and differ in degrees of accuracy.
This is no simple game. Firing the shotgun takes a learning curve, and trial and error. But, once you learn to fire it, you find yourself bringing in multiple animals in one hunt. The more challenging achievements require you to survive without firing a gun, and live off the land. One simple mistake leaves you facing the fangs of a wolf, or freezing to death. This is definitely a game you won't want to miss.

Blue Shift is a second and last expansion pack of Half-Life by Gearbox. This time it only has single-player campaign, there is no multiplayer component. If you want to play some Deathmatch, you should better head toward HL1. It also came with HD models bundled in Retail, and so in Steam version too.
Now, the single player campaign is quite short and doesn't include any kind of new features, whetever weapons or enemeis. And that may dissapoint you when compared to first expansion pack. The reason for it being this way - it wasn't made to be a full expansion pack. Instead, it's origin was to be a bonus content for Dreamcast version of HL1. Shame that it was cancelled when it was almost done. So, not to lose work that been done, Gearbox released it for PC serapately. Another thing you might notice is that it reuses Opposing Force (the first expansion pack) soundtrack
In this campaign you are Barney Calhoun, the random security guard, who owes Gordon a beer. And unlike every other security guards, he actually passed advanced movement training and can navigate doorways just fine. And stairs. And vents. And shoots many crabs. And he is no hero and his only wish is not to stop alien invasion, but just to get the hell out of here. Ok, he, like a proper hero, has to get the surviving personel out of facility into outside safety.  So, you are back into usual Half-Life busyness, shooting, solving "puzzles" and exlporing levels, with fair share of plot conversations with scienists. All while getting to use realistical only weapons (no Gauss Gun fun), with ammo somewhat limited for each one.There is no real climax final boss, the ending seem to be a bunch of strange teasers, so to say. Otherwise it should be pleasent and make sense. I could say, it's the least repetive experience compared to HL1 and OpForce, maybe it just ends before it gets stale.
But yes, it would have made nice bonus content for Dreamcast, but lacking expansion pack. At least it came packing with HD models and Opposing Force on retail in some regions. Some even say that it contains leftover Dreamcast version codes inside cue some dissapearing corpses. Though, HL1 and OpposingForce on Steam had them as well, strange. Another strange thing is that none the soldiers here ever threw normal grenades at me, they would just place down grenade and run when heavily wounded. And most curiously, it uses soundtrack of Opposing Force... Which doesn't feel right. Cheerful military drumbs beat when the security guard falls to his demise due to two zombies? As looking at the footage of Dreamcast version (it leaked to Internet, yes) it's supposed to use Half-Life soundtrack instead.

You can find yourself in some pretty nasty situations in this game. On my first trip to Pleasant Valley, I arrived exhausted, over-loaded, and the sun was going down. The wind started picking up, but I ignored it. My character was too busy checking abandoned cars for candy bars and matches. Before I knew it, he was in the middle of a ferocious blizzard. He hopped into the nearest car and tried to wait it out.
The temperature dropped lower and lower as the storm persisted into nightfall. The wind howled all around, and my character began to freeze.
I realized. I'd helped him survive for over 100 days, and I was about to lose it all. He lit his storm lantern to try to stay warm. He curled up in his sleeping bag and took little naps. The night crawled on, and his condition grew worse and worse by the minute. By the time the storm finally abated, hypothermia was setting in. He crawled from the car and used one of his precious matches to light a small fire with some sticks he had collected.
He huddled beside that fire and fed it one stick at a time while the wind did its best to blow it out. When dawn came, he abandoned the fire and staggered along the road looking for better shelter - a shack, a house, a garage...anything.
It was hard to see with his blurry vision, but he found what appeared to be some kind of an abandoned farm house. He made his way inside and stumbled around the house. Upstairs he found a bed, and crawled gratefully beneath the blankets.
He slept on and off all that day and the next, and bit by bit, he recovered enough to leave the house and collect some kindling. It was a nice sunny day, and he was able to save the last of his matches by starting a fire with his magnifying glass. He melted snow and boiled enough water to stay hydrated for a few days, then decided he'd better do something about food.
Luck was with him, and he was able to lure a wolf away from a fresh kill. As he leaned over the dead deer and pulled his hunting knife from his belt, I thought,

Five minutes later, he was dead. Another blizzard rolled in while he was breaking down the deer, and I was fiddling with my cell phone. I looked up just in time to see him fading into the long dark, and that was that. I stared at the screen in horror. There's no save to revert to... no retry button... no Phoenix Down to tickle his nose with. GAME OVER.
That's The Long Dark in a nutshell. This isn't a game in which you frolic about the hills, or hit the save button just in case what you're about to do turns out to be as stupid as you think it is - but you want to try it anyway...
There are no safety nets. No second chances. You have to constantly be on the lookout for danger. You relax, or get distracted… you die. So you listen to the wind. You keep an eye on the sky. You check the temperature. You look out for fallen trees you might be able to clamber up just in case there’s a hungry wolf over the next ridge. You hear one howl in the distance, and you crouch and count your bullets, or ready a torch and hope it’s more scared of fire than it is hungry. In the easiest mode, the wolves and bears act like they would in nature. If you leave them alone, they'll leave you alone. In the normal and hard modes, a geomagnetic event has made them loopy and aggressive. In Interloper, the hardest mode, the game is out to kill you however it can. There are far fewer tools and resources. The weather hates you, and the wolves are absolutely deadly. In their eyes - you're just a sloppy joe in pants - if you still have pants by that point.
A few other points:
- The graphics are stylized but attractive.
- The community's pretty good. Most active players are helpful and friendly.
- The developers are communicative and active. They still monitor the board to weed out jerks.
- The original music scores are absolutely stunning. Sometimes I find myself sitting at the title screen for a few minutes just listening to the music.
- The ambient sound effects are amazing. You hear the wind blow, the trees creak, ice crack, the song of a variety of birds nearby, the distant sounds of wolves, the light rattle of a chain link fence in the wind, and so on...
- You can craft and cook items utilizing natural resources.
- It’s a lonely, melancholy game.
- After surviving for long periods, you can get stuck into routines. Fortunately there are seven different regions in survival mode at this point. You can travel to another region if you get tired of the one you’re in. Each one has its own personality and challenges. Also there's Story Mode, as well as several challenge modes that are engaging, too.
- You can race through Story Mode in maybe ten hours, or play it more naturally for nearly three times that amount.
- The voice actors are talented and well known - from Metal Gear Solid and the Mass Effect series.
- Each game is different. You may have found a hatchet in a dilapidated little hut on your first run, but on your second run – there’s nothing there… Sometimes the cabin you squatted in last game is just a pile of burnt cinders in the next.
- You rarely spawn in the same place twice. In Stalker, you may spawn twenty feet away from a wolf while it's still dark outside and the temperature is well below zero. Or maybe you get lucky and spawn in the Trapper's Homestead and find a rifle hanging from the gun rack. You never know.

The graphics are a little different, but they are not bad. I actually appreciate that the game has its own appearance and doesnt attempt to be the next "most real" looking game. Music and sound effects are pretty good, too.
I like the animal AI, and animations. I do hope that more animals are added since there are really only 4 animals which you can hunt/eat/interact with (other than fish and crows, which dont actively react to the player).
Overall, this game has a really good feel. Although it seems still somewhat early in development (hopefully much more to come), what exists already is very well put together. You get sucked into the whole atmosphere of the game pretty easily.
Can't wait to see what the story mode will be like!

There is art here, despite what many would say isn't possible with games, from Roger Ebert to game designers like Hideo Kojima. But it's in BioShock--it's in the gorgeously realized, watery halls of Rapture. It's in a Little Sister's expression of thanks when you choose to save her, or the utter silence if you harvest instead. It's in the way the characters develop, in the testimonials of the recording boxes you pick up along the way. It's in the way the narrative is structured, and the way it blends so seamlessly with the action. Irrational had a clear vision with this game, something pulled off with remarkable precision in every department. They didn't just deliver something that's fun to play, a criterion so often cited as the benchmark of what makes a game worthwhile. BioShock stands as a monolithic example of the convergence of entertaining gameplay and an irresistibly sinister, engrossing storyline that encompasses a host of multifaceted characters. This is an essential gaming experience.

While not a terrible game, it lacks in focus and polish. I received this game from a friend who wanted me to "figure out" how to play it and tell him. - menu's don't remember your place. I scroll all they way down to a menu selection, enter that submenu and when I come back to the previous menu I have to scroll down again to locate the next item in the list.

- icons are often similar and hard to differentiate between at a glance nor is it clear if the net result will be positive or negative (are you spending or receiving) without hovering over and reading the, sometimes lengthy and/or confusing, descriptions.

There was one quest where my clothes are taken and I get up to embarrassment lvl 55 or something before it ends but there seems to be no effect on the game outcome that I could tell. It seemed the designers were trying to convey some level of absurdity through numbers. The English language ( or any other for that matter) is full of better ways of descibing something than numbers. - Journal entries, especially quests, sometimes lack important details

I really like the core mechanic of
, where "the townspeople... are your primary resource," and nothing can be done without individual citizens doing it. It's sort of a hybrid of the RTS genre with the traditional city sim, and as both of those are genres I enjoy, I really thought I would like this game. And I do, kind of, but a lack of polish, tedious pacing, and a frustrating sense of unfairness leave me unable to recommend it.
First, UI is really bad. All of the action buttons are docked in the bottom right corner of the screen in a sort of visual menu, which means it takes two clicks to access common functions like increasing or decreasing the simulation speed. And rather than having sensible, easy-to-memorize hotkeys (like "B" to build and then "H" for house), actions are hotkeyed according to their order on the dock. For instance, F1 selects the first menu, and then 1 selects the first item in that menu. This scheme works, but it's a lot harder to memorize than it has to be. It's a weird design choice given that so many other games in this genre do it so much better.
Moreover, the UI only presents the most basic information about your economy, which exacerbates the balance issues I'll discuss later. For instance, there's no information about how your resource production vs consumption is trending, so you have to guess based on what you used and produced over the last year compared to how your population has grown or shrunken. If you get it wrong, you'll have a resource shortfall which will lead to a cascade of citizen deaths.
There are only a small number of buildings to construct, and there is no tech tree to upgrade, which quickly leaves the player with the feeling of not having much to do in the game. Of course, the ultimate goal is to build the biggest town possible, but with no ability to invest in upgrades to spur growth, it feels as though the player's ability to actually influence the rate of growth is limited. You'll always need new citizens to gather more resources so that you can support your growing population, but if you try to expand
fast (e.g. by building a large number of houses, which can lead to a baby boom), you'll end up consuming more food than you produce and half your population will starve to death.
It seems to be better to let the population grow slowly and organically, but this means that you'll spend a lot of time with the speed on 10x (the maximum), just sitting around waiting for things to happen. Often, the most interactive part of the game will be micromanaging villagers' jobs to try to find the right resource production balance. It takes
of real time to get beyond a population of 100. As I was writing this, I thought "maybe I just suck at the game," but then I went on YouTube and searched for videos on how to grow your population quickly, and found... nothing.
This lack of control is even worse in the event that you make a mistake or get unlucky. Maybe you build too many houses, maybe a particularly harsh winter befalls your town and ruins your crops, or maybe an important citizen dies in a workplace accident when you don't have the capacity to replace him or her. Whatever the case, once you're in a resource shortfall, you'll usually find that it results in a death spiral where your economy becomes inefficient, and each death leads to yet more deaths as you're unable to produce the needed resources. When this happens, it tends to be difficult to recover from, and if you don't save frequently you may be set back several hours worth of population growth. Worse, the game doesn't do a good job of making it clear
the disaster happened, so you kind of have to figure it out on your own.
had the potential to be an excellent game, and it gets enough right that it held my interest for many hours despite these complaints. But the more I play it, the more I find myself wondering why I'm not just playing
instead, and if I had to choose between the two,
is definitely the game I'd choose.

I was drawn to Morphopolis for the wonderfully unique art-style and the promise of relaxing music and gameplay. Morphopolis delivers on style and audio, but the gameplay swings between calm, maybe even boring, and on the other end of the scale it can be infuriating. If you like hidden object games I'd definitely recommend this, but to most people I would say give it a miss. I'm personally not keen on hidden object games, but I thought I'd give this one a go anyway for a change of pace. Some some of the puzzles in Morphopolis left me without any clue how to interact with them, and I had to resort to Googling to know how to even grasp some basic controls. The most important thing I could have known going into the game is that clicking/tapping on your own bug is something you can (and should) do, which simply didn't occur to me until I read an introduction on how to play the game after becoming stuck, which kind of seems like the sort of thing the game should be guiding you into doing. The most positive thing about this game was that I was able to draw my wife into playing it with me. It works great on a touch screen so we were both able to tap away at the screen together working on puzzles and looking for hidden bugs and junk. It's not a long game, but at the end of it we were glad it was over.
4 out of 10, would not dig around for bugs again. Purdy though.

One issue the game suffers from is that it has double has multiples of the same decisions for instance you have to chose between what you should focus on for instance A.I., engine, graphics, but has both sound and sound design to choose from (surely they are the same thing), this section is in my opinion to challenging I have managed to get 2.3 rating for parts that 50% focused on that feature (could do a beter job of showing how to create good games)

Archaica is an indie puzzle game developed by Two Mammoths. All throughout the game you try to match lasers with crystals of the same colour, which even though this game is a  casual relaxing game, makes you think hard about the placement of you mirrors and also makes you plan how you can match colour with colour.
The puzzle element of Archaica is very well done using an intuitive style. It was challenging having to manoeuvre the lasers around the map using mirrors splitters and other objects. The sole aim is to match the lasers with a crystal that is the same colour, sometimes having to mix colours given like mixing blue and red lasers to get purple, and then sometimes having to also split one of the colours away to get that main colour for example having to connect to a red, blue and purple crystal. All this mixing and matching is controlled with mirrors, what I call ‘splitters’ and amplifiers. You use the mirrors to move the direction of laser around corners at either a 90 degree angle or with an angled mirror at a 45 degree angle. As well as mirrors you can use splitters to split the beam into 2 allowing you to take it to 2 or more crystals or allowing you to mix the colours. The final one is the amplifier this boosts the laser so it can reach further. All these elements must be placed on different squares on the level making you think about the placement so you can move the lasers correctly to the crystal. This is an element Archaica has nailed bringing me thoughtful and enjoyable times.
Throughout the levels there are also collectables like crystals, stone keys and stone slates that contain hieroglyphs. These collectables can be distracting from the game even though they do serve a purpose, these are still a bit tedious and I would rather just have the actual puzzle part of the game.
Achaica’s story is interesting, giving a back story to the barren deserts and thehistory of this world, but sadly I feel it has been poorly implemented. The story was more a side thing only being shown through a few cutscenes and through the different collectables . Personally I didn’t take much note of the story and mainly just focused on the core puzzles. The backstory of this game designed but and it would have been way more interesting if they implemented the story better, like adding more cutscenes and not having lots of it found in collectables that aren’t really a main part of the game. Otherwise I found the Archaica backstory to be interesting and would have loved it. Though this is just an issue in my opinion and it didn’t take away from the game or the story itself, it just made it harder to learn more about the world.
Archaica looks beautiful, it looks realistic but also cartoony making it look great. It uses lighting and colours to give it its graphical style. The looks of this game are defiantly a plus and when I launched it, it was something I quite enjoyed.
The sound in this game is also well done, the sound effects and the music are placed nicely throughout the game. The music gives you the mood of the game and is enjoyable to listen to. The sound effects are also well made.

-  Puzzles well made
-  Great Graphics
-  Well designed sound
-  Poorly implemented story
-  Annoying collectables

The first thing that strikes you when you start up the game is the gob-smacking beauty of it. It's like a UE4 game which is totally unexpected in the puzzle genre, for me at least. It's all in 3D and you're introduced to the main menu by a camera panning cutscene that glides you to the exquisitely-lit stone monument where you can select your levels. Here there is also a Totem that records your achievements by activating each stone block that lights up with a blue glow.
You click Play and the next uncompleted level is loaded. Every level starts with an appetizer of an easy hidden object game. There are 2 or 3 white crystals to find and usually (not always) Cryptoglyphs (half-buried glowing tablets). The crystals activate the hints; the Cryptoglyphs show you a short cutscene and a poetic verse of some ancient lore involving battles, pseudo-historic events and so forth. Once in a while it will refer to the mechanics of the level you're about to attempt. This part of the level is always very easy, you drag the scene around to find the objects, and the area is not very large so it rarely takes more than a minute or so. Then it's on to the main course with the lasers.
If you've ever played Lara Croft GO, you'll find the level layout very familiar. The puzzle is totally different, of course, but you drag the scene around in the same way; hidden object aspect is the same, the board grid is the same and even the environments could be swapped between the two. I had to double-check to see if it was the same developer, but no. Anyway, I'm not complaining, it's all very pleasant.
So you're presented with a grid containing a number of mirrors (there are 90 and 45 degree types) and various types of tools such as power boosters, colour-change crystals, beam splitters... there are at least a dozen different types, and more are introduced as you progress. The goal is to position and rotate these items on the board in order to guide the laser beams to light up the exit crystals with the correct colours. Blending and splitting the coloured beams to get the right colour is often necessary, so the obvious route is rarely the solution. For example, in the early stages I would position my mirrors in the spots where I expected them to be, switch them around and try various arrangements, then finally succumb to the hints... which would reveal the positions to be in weird places on the board that I never would have expected. It's fiendish!
As you light up each target, a portion of the 'solution circle' lights up. When you've successfully lit up all targets and the solution circle is fully lit, you click it to trigger a cutscene and sometimes an animation of the stonework of the level moving around and taking you to the next level. All very slick indeed.
There are five main themed Areas: Desert City, Eternal Islands, Crystal Mines, Jungle, Temples and each is more beautiful than the last. It's not exactly flashy and the levels have a limited area, but the use of lovely glowing colours, swaying plants, glittering water and so forth makes it feel so stylish and upmarket. The background music, if you can call it that, it also nicely understated so as not to interfere with your concentration. A gentle drumbeat, occasional chime or bird call to break the silence, no more than that. Every level has an imaginative and wistful name, there is no numbering here at all.
This is the type of puzzler I love where you can decide for yourself how hardcore you want to play it. If you're a purist you'll complete the levels without using the hints. I think I managed to beat most, if not all of the first area without hints. By the second area I started to struggle and was tempted more and more by the hints. By the third area my pride was well and truly in the bin, and I was routinely taking all hints immediately. After the initial 2 or 3 hints it forces you to wait for a while before allowing any further hints, giving you a chance to maintain at least some dignity. The thing is, even after you've mashed the hints circle to reveal the whole board you only have a set of positions. You still don't know which item goes where, and in what rotation, so it's still hard even with hints!
Some levels have bonus difficulty where you have to light up Stone Keys to reveal hidden levels. These are extra tough, and thankfully they're optional so you can leave them for later. There's an achievement for these, of course.
There are NO TIMERS WHATSOEVER within the game. A big plus for me! A puzzle should be a relaxing, thoughtful affair in my opinion - not an artificial race against time.
It has the lot - Trading Cards, Cloud Saves and Achievements - which are represented very nicely in-game as well as via Steam. There are no plans for Linux, unfortunately, which is a bit of a disappointment for me in an otherwise perfect game.
I know what you're thinking. This is just a lasers puzzler, it's going to get repetitive. I can honestly say that the game is packed with variety and no two puzzles are remotely similar. Amazing to think how much has been done with a seemingly limited mechanic. There are 62 puzzles (in 42 levels) + secret levels and additional puzzles needed to unlock them. By the time you get past the first couple of areas, you're talking about a good hour or so to beat a level, especially without hints, so I'd say this is well worth full price.
There's one word for this: classy. Every aspect of it has been expertly crafted and the result is a lavish feast of puzzling, fit for a king... or pharaoh or whatever they're called in this lore.
A top contender for my puzzle game of the year.
