When I say
I mean that. However, before you purchase the game, I should warn you about the numerous problems that the game has. You
get SUPERHOT, but let me give you a few warnings first.
SUPERHOT's defining feature is that time only moves when you do. This isn't entirely true, as
This isn't exactly a problem, because if you're taking that long to think which way to dodge a bullet, chances are you deserve to get hit anyway.
The game's campaign is very interesting and spooky, but can be beaten inbetween 2-3 hours depending on how well you do, and some
. The variables I'll cover in the next section.
In slow motion, you can almost always tell when you are going to die, and from where. However, some levels contain randomly generated enemies which actually determine whether or not you're going to win. For example, level
is easily one of the hardest levels to beat simply because after you kill the wave of red guys, several red guys spawn with random guns, ranging from bare handed to shotgun, all in a tight little room. It's unfortunate to say this, but winning some levels like this,
during challenges and time trials, might only depend on if you're lucky enough to play when all the red guys spawn with only pistols.
The other variable is shotgun fire. Those guns are impossible to predict.
SUPERHOT has a few bugs which can make the game a bit more challenging, to occasionally stopping you from winning a level.
Going back to the level
, there's a good example of a challenging bug. After you enter the first room from the balcony-catwalk-thing, your in the line of fire of a shotgunner and a machine gunner. Your options include running straight at them, or backing up around the corner. However, backing up is a problem because there's a small height difference between the ledge and the room, which prevents you from backing up. And as long as you hold the "S" key, the bullets move closer and closer. Jumping over this is out of the question, because as long as your in the air, time continues to move as gravity pulls on you. Little details like this become major problems in Challenge modes. And this isn't the only example of bad world geometry, as some levels have invisible barriers that prevent you from exiting the line of fire altogether.
Another good example is the broken Time Trial mode. In at least one level (there may be others, I don't know yet), the timer starts counting before you even finish loading in, resulting in you starting with roughly .97 seconds already passed. This sounds minor, but when the goal is set at 4 seconds, losing that time is almost a quarter of what you should have. On that level, which is
, the best possible time I've managed is 4.07, and that was after nearly 20 minutes of retries, on what is only the third level in the game.
SUPERHOT is very unique and memorable for it's mechanics. It could have been improved during development by adding more levels to the story, but that's only an issue if you don't want to pay full price for that much.
The only thing that keeps SUPERHOT from being "super cool" is the obvious missed steps taken in testing the game, but development is still semi-active so the game might be fixed in the future.
I only hope that the developers are listening to bug reports, and are willing to fix the small stuff. After the game isn't broken enough that I stop raging at trying to complete it 100%, I'll give it my thumbs up.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a game that has admittedly become something of an horror game icon and is generally revered as one of the scariest games ever by todays gaming media. And while it does indeed put the wind up you a bit with it's jumpscares, that's basically it.
All of the horror comes from jumpscares which are more or less a punishment for failing to keep a track of the game's animatronics. While this might be exciting and heartpounding the first few times, most people will likely get used to it after a while and then it just becomes am extreme game of 'Red Light, Green Light' and once the fear has been taken out of the equation, the whole game just seems boring.
It is entirely possible for a game to be simple, yet fun, but for me Five Night's at Freddy's loses it's main draw fairly quickly. It's challenging, sure, but if you're not having fun then what's the point? There is some satisfaction to be had in beating Fazbear and pals at their own game, but again, just like the jumpscares, it's likely going to fade after a while.
What I do like is the lore that exists within the game and the implied storyline, as it's rather well handled and at least somewhat interesting.
The graphics too, while nothing special, have a unique flavour to them, to the point that I personally rather like them. They remind me of the pre-rendered graphics of the PS1 era and, well, i'm not sure if that was the intention but it pleases me nontheless.
So would I reccomend this game? Probably not. If you're looking for something that can provide you with a few adrenaline pumping jumpscares before slowly petering out, then this game will likely be alright for you.
However if you're planning to buy this game based on what you've heard from other people then enter at your own risk, as the hype train has severly overblown this one. It is not one of the best horror games ever. It isn't even a great horror game. It's probably just 'good'.

I really like the core mechanic of
, where "the townspeople... are your primary resource," and nothing can be done without individual citizens doing it. It's sort of a hybrid of the RTS genre with the traditional city sim, and as both of those are genres I enjoy, I really thought I would like this game. And I do, kind of, but a lack of polish, tedious pacing, and a frustrating sense of unfairness leave me unable to recommend it.
First, UI is really bad. All of the action buttons are docked in the bottom right corner of the screen in a sort of visual menu, which means it takes two clicks to access common functions like increasing or decreasing the simulation speed. And rather than having sensible, easy-to-memorize hotkeys (like "B" to build and then "H" for house), actions are hotkeyed according to their order on the dock. For instance, F1 selects the first menu, and then 1 selects the first item in that menu. This scheme works, but it's a lot harder to memorize than it has to be. It's a weird design choice given that so many other games in this genre do it so much better.
Moreover, the UI only presents the most basic information about your economy, which exacerbates the balance issues I'll discuss later. For instance, there's no information about how your resource production vs consumption is trending, so you have to guess based on what you used and produced over the last year compared to how your population has grown or shrunken. If you get it wrong, you'll have a resource shortfall which will lead to a cascade of citizen deaths.
There are only a small number of buildings to construct, and there is no tech tree to upgrade, which quickly leaves the player with the feeling of not having much to do in the game. Of course, the ultimate goal is to build the biggest town possible, but with no ability to invest in upgrades to spur growth, it feels as though the player's ability to actually influence the rate of growth is limited. You'll always need new citizens to gather more resources so that you can support your growing population, but if you try to expand
fast (e.g. by building a large number of houses, which can lead to a baby boom), you'll end up consuming more food than you produce and half your population will starve to death.
It seems to be better to let the population grow slowly and organically, but this means that you'll spend a lot of time with the speed on 10x (the maximum), just sitting around waiting for things to happen. Often, the most interactive part of the game will be micromanaging villagers' jobs to try to find the right resource production balance. It takes
of real time to get beyond a population of 100. As I was writing this, I thought "maybe I just suck at the game," but then I went on YouTube and searched for videos on how to grow your population quickly, and found... nothing.
This lack of control is even worse in the event that you make a mistake or get unlucky. Maybe you build too many houses, maybe a particularly harsh winter befalls your town and ruins your crops, or maybe an important citizen dies in a workplace accident when you don't have the capacity to replace him or her. Whatever the case, once you're in a resource shortfall, you'll usually find that it results in a death spiral where your economy becomes inefficient, and each death leads to yet more deaths as you're unable to produce the needed resources. When this happens, it tends to be difficult to recover from, and if you don't save frequently you may be set back several hours worth of population growth. Worse, the game doesn't do a good job of making it clear
the disaster happened, so you kind of have to figure it out on your own.
had the potential to be an excellent game, and it gets enough right that it held my interest for many hours despite these complaints. But the more I play it, the more I find myself wondering why I'm not just playing
instead, and if I had to choose between the two,
is definitely the game I'd choose.

First off, I really appreciate what this studio has done in terms of graphics and music.  A+ on that.
I also appreciate the difficulty.
The mechanics are great.  Bosses usually telegraph moves well enough that you don't have to learn by trial and error.  Some mechanics give the player choice in how the battle unfolds (do you want more difficulty with more opportunities to parry?)
However, I think there could have been a few game design tweaks that would have made the game more enjoyable while maintaining a high level of difficulty.
1) hitboxes are a little stingy.  With tiny bullets and only 8 directions of fire, it can be very difficult to hit enemies while you are trying to juggle the rest of the action.
2) jump control.  The highest jump and lowest jump you can do only differ by about half of cuphead's height (probably a little more).  The ability to hop would help give the user more options instead of forcing a jump that results in a mid-air collision (basically a no-win situation sometimes).
3) parry only works at the jump apex.  Split second timing, tiny range, AND only works at the top of the jump?  Any two of these would be fine, but all three seems a bit much.
5 stars.

In memory of Adam West.
The best Batman story to date. TellTale have outdone themselves at bringing a modern spin to the Batman mythos. Character interactions and dialogue feel natural, the story is not overly dark like previous adaptations, and a great mystery filled with many fresh twists and turns. The game features a newcomer to Batman’s rogues gallery, Lady Arkham, who, thankfully, is a much more interesting (and less wasted) than the Arkham Knight. We even get a special appearance from everybody’s favorite, John Doe! Who I really liked as less insane.
In this Batverse, Bruce Wayne has been the masked vigilante Batman for about a year now; he is good friends with with local District Attorney Harvey Dent (hell, he’s his only friend), and is an apparent ally of Police Lieutenant James Gordon. Bruce is funding Harvey’s campaign for Mayor of Gotham City, but when a party promoting the campaign is crashed by local mob boss, Carmine Falcone, Bruce begins to discover that his parents may have been involved with him. Not only that, but a old friend from Bruce’s past, Oswald Cobblepot, has come back out of nowhere speaking of “revolution”. As Bruce digs deeper to find the truth, he discovers some things he wished he never knew or just weren’t true…
If you read my first review on Tales from the Borderlands, you’d know I don’t have the best computer I should have. Though keep in mind that this game did suffer from some technical issues when it first released, so that could just be it. What I’m speaking of is that I had a few bugs while playing, nothing game breaking that made me have to reset or be killed in-game, but sometimes when the scene would transition to the next shot the game would freeze for a moment. Just moment, that was the only technical I suffered.
I meant to write this review sooner, so that the game could still be more in my memory, but I didn’t and I can’t recall anything that really disappointed or annoy me. If there was it’s likely it wasn’t anything that majorly impacts the game. If you’re fan of Batman in anyway, play this game. It’s a whole new spin on the Batman mythos that I think almost everyone will enjoy.

I have enjoyed playing both Tropico 3 and 4, not because of the unbelievably easy AI as seen in 5, but because of the ability to control my city and fix its problems. Tropico 5 not only shields you from changing your laws in less than 28 months, but linearly guides you on what to build next. In previous titles, missions were an optional thing that you could participate in, depending on the mission. But, in Tropico 5, say the communists want you to build them a row of 15 houses; you now have to option to cancel the mission, causing the communists to hate you literally for the entire game, OR, you can go into national debt by building the houses, and have a nice little +1 boost to happiness.
This prevents players from building the island nation of their dreams, and instead they get a moshpit of infighting communists, capitalists, and acoholic religious zealots. But, don't worry, you can fix the opinions of EVERYBODY for the new DLC called Waterborne, at the low cost of $40! You get off-shore oil derricks for the capitalists, more coastal homes for the commies, and the religious--well, you can get alongside a future character creator expansion for only $15.
Seriously, though; every month it seems that features that should have been in the game already are released as DLC bundles. If you look closely, you can see that, in the time of the game's original release, it was coded so that future DLCs would plug right in; before the off-shore oil derricks, we had off-shore oil deopsits visible. Why? Because monehs.
The game with every DLC is a good game, but until Kalypso stops dicing off features and putting on a price tag for all of them, do NOT buy this. My final verdict is a petty 3/10.
5/24/2015 Edit:
I finally came back to the game to see if they had added anything in new patches; all I got was four new DLC's. Expect Tropico 6 to be even sketchier; maybe we will have a one-time 10 population boost for the price of a $5 gem pack.
Everybody, go home, back to Tropico 4; this was a bust.
6/4/2015 Edit:
I laughed this morning when I opened Steam to find Kalypso gave me the Green DLC for free.
I now completely change my mind about this game and the developers, they are so generous by giving me their cheapest DLC for free. 11/10 would be bribed again

TLDR - the game needs speeding up and interface polish
While not a terrible game, it lacks in focus and polish. I received this game from a friend who wanted me to "figure out" how to play it and tell him. I think that sums up the why this game doesn't get a thumbs up. It is not always clear on what you are doing. That being said, my main gripe is that crossing the oceans is a tedious affair meaning there are long slow periods between actual interaction. I don't feel like it is a good investment of time to fun. Things need to be speeded up. My second complaint is that this game lacks clarity of action. At first I would say this game is too wordy but it's more nuanced than that. Now I don't want to complain about story and backdrop, they are part of the games charm. You should read it in order to get the most out of the game. But there needs to be clearer distrinction between game effects and color story. There is too much reading required to ensure you are not glossing over something important.
A list of minor grievances
- menu's don't remember your place. I scroll all they way down to a menu selection, enter that submenu and when I come back to the previous menu I have to scroll down again to locate the next item in the list.
- the tabs in the popup menu act as buttons rather than tabs. There is no visual association with the current tab and the content.
- icons are often similar and hard to differentiate between at a glance nor is it clear if the net result will be positive or negative (are you spending or receiving) without hovering over and reading the, sometimes lengthy and/or confusing, descriptions.
- too many numbers used in quest flags that don't give you any sense of their meaning. "something something level 3". There was one quest where my clothes are taken and I get up to embarrassment lvl 55 or something before it ends but there seems to be no effect on the game outcome that I could tell. It seemed the designers were trying to convey some level of absurdity through numbers. The English language ( or any other for that matter) is full of better ways of descibing something than numbers. "The other day someone stole my parking spot and I was shock 20 and angry 59." The numbers I realize are for triggers, but It feels too exposed to the player.
- Journal entries, especially quests, sometimes lack important details

If you are into city planning games, this is one of the best there is. The thing that makes this game so addicting is that its difficult. I find myself constantly pausing just to make sure I dont make a mistake. One little thing and the whole mojo of your city is thrown off balance.
It can be very addicting; once you have found balance, you will want to keep expanding and expanding. I found this game to be worth the price and time. There are a lot of mods and amazing user-created content for this game as well.
Some cons of this game is that it can be a little frustrating at times; I can put in a lot of time and effort only to have my entire civilization collapse in one day. The mechanisms can also be a little complicated at first, and there were a lot of things I had to google. The graphics are particularily beautiful, but that really didn't matter. Also this game has no set quests or endgame, so I find if I dont space out my playing times I get really bored after awhile.
I feel the pros outweigh the cons.
I would give this 7 out of 10 stars.

There are also differences in the way leveling up characters work. Instead of training a certain treat, you level up generally and distribute skillpoints afterwards.
With that said, we come to the question: Is it worth it? Yes, it is, but there are some restrictions from my side:

This game is fantastic! I have been watching for many months to see the progress and here are my impressions.
It's similar in graphics to Game Dev Tycoon but it is NOT Game Dev Tycoon! While I was a big fan of Game Dev, there were a lot of things about that game that I kept on thinking would be great to have in this type of game. Well GamersGoMakers delivers in a big way!! It's got a wonderful "feel" to it. You start out small, and sell your first copies of your first game and you might be lucky enough to crack 1000 copies sold! Up to 10k copies, it keeps track of exact numbers and then rounds them off which doesn't bother me at all. After that, you can start to do a little bit of research and open up a few new options as you go. Your second game might be a hit, or it might totally tank! I made a game in the same genre and people had high expectations because I was doing the same genre again, and I totally failed. The game got higher scores but I made a lot of people upset because of my previous experience earned in the genre, it should have been better!
My 3rd game ended up being a hit! 10K copies sold and I entered a new genre and it put me on the map and some money in the bank so now I was able to purchase training and researtch options! This was all in just the demo! I made a few more games and I found the pacing was excellent, you weren't rushed to get things done asap, you can take your time. Only want to make 1 giant game each year? Go ahead! Want to make 3 or 4 games quickly your first year and each of your first few years to get on the map? Go ahead! It's really up to you. You have so many options to choose from, even the country you want to start in each with it's own perks and bonuses.
I did enjoy in Game Dev being able to make your own engine and while it's nice, it's not totally necessary. You have many skills which level up and I actually think the leveling up system in GGM is much better. You don't have skills level up very quickly, it takes a long time. I made 6 games and only a few skills had gone up by 1 level which is awesome. It makes you really focus on what you want to do as a company. Do you want to be a specialist in game design and sound? Go ahead! Prefer graphics, game engine and gameplay? Go ahead? Want to be well rounded? Keep it focused on spreading out points evenly!
After 6 games I had marketing options and extra genres/sub genres open up. You don't choose the ones you want, they just open up over time which I actually quite like too because it's exciting to see which topic comes along next. I love the way you get to "write" your game story and you get to choose what the actual game will be about.
You also get to design your game cases before you release and choose your selling price! There are lots of helpful indicators of how much games in your genre are worth at the current time, which ones are trending right now, you can choose to release in many languages if you want, you can risk a higher price if your game is trendy right now and it even tells you how many similar games to yours are on the market currently!! I can't even begin to describe all the content in this game but it's amazing and there's so much depth to it!
Yes there will always be things people aren't happy with and there's always room to improve in everything in life but this game has really captured an amazing feel and I will be ranking it very highly! I love sim games and this to me has delivered on everything that I was hoping for!! VERY impressed with the game and the people that made it! I am giving it a 9.5/10 Simply amazing game!

Things like this are a crying shame.  This is nothing more than an extended tutorial.
This game has an interesting mechanic, and that's pretty much all there is to it.  It is absurdly short, where I played it through to completion in under two hours, and beat a bunch of other challenges under an hour thereafter.  Not all of them, mind you, but enough to say that I've played most of what this game has to offer, and it's not much.
If you watched the videos of this game, you've probably seen a full quarter of the gameplay available.  The levels are very short and confined.  Despite this, some levels are actually very fun - one where you start off surrounded by three people in an elevator and you have to figure out how to best all of them without one of the others shooting you first, or the elevator doors opening and revealing two more dudes shooting at you.
There's also a pretty, ahem, bad*** moment early on where you start a level with a demand "Come with us".  Then a few seconds later, the screen flashed, "HOW.  ABOUT.  NO!", and you start the level with a gun pointed at your head and you have to fight your way through a bunch of dudes.  It's a moment that made me grin and fistpump in the air, but that was the only such moment this entire game provided.
I think a more experienced development team could have hashed out a much, much longer campaign, and perhaps gave more nuance to the game, more mechanics, and so forth.  About halfway through the game you get a body-switching power, and it's almost entirely optional to use.  It's useful, yes, but a creative dev team could have dreamed up a level where you had to body switch with a guy on a balcony to keep fighting, because there was no other way to get up there (for example).  But really, the mechanics in this game are never fully realized.
I said in the beginning that this game is an extended tutorial.  A cool mechanic like this is akin to things in other, more developed games, where they grant you a new power and some easy time to mess around with it, before flinging you back into the main game to use it in a dozen different ways.  This game never gets past the tutorial phase with it.  Too short, too easy, too simplistic, a waste of an awesome pair of concepts (bullet-time as a norm, and body-switching), and a waste of money.
If you get a chance to get the game for free, it's definitely worth playing then.  But that's the problem here - this game is a neat and quick diversion but nothing worth paying for.

Other reviews of this game have stated that Morphopolis is better as a work of art than a game, but I have to disagree because having bought primarily for the aesthetic of it I found out very quickly that this fails as both a game and as an art project.
First, throughout the game there are huge lags in frame rate, which I initially thought was just part of the trippy look of the whole thing, then I thought it was a problem with my computer. But nope, I can run Skyrim with no drop in frame rate on my laptop but this simplistic thing jarrs just by having your insect change direction or if there are too much stuff going on in a particular level.
The art work that made me buy the game in the first place quickly became irritating the more I played, the style is not well integrated into the gameplay at all, the title screen made the animation look fluid but when playing the game you often just have your legs animated while they drag your whole immovable body through the levels, the same type of animation cheats they use on most of the non-playable insects and environments, making the whole experience look clumpy and ugly.
The controls are equally awkward, you don't use wasd keys because I guess that would not be “arty” enough for the developers, you have to hold the left mouse button in the direction you want to go and there's a 50% chance you might actually get there if you don't have to find something to click on to solve a tiresome puzzle. Most of my playthrough was spent just trying to get my bug in the right direction so that I could crawl on a narrow route through invisible walls just to collect foliage to open the next level. Only to find I had to backtrack to collect a different set of items to actually move on, if they had individual puzzles open every time I had to do this that might have been barely tolerable, many times it's just busy work to pad the game.
I spent on average more than 20 minutes doing this alone nearly every level, this is already a short game and most of playing it is navigating nonsensical pre-determined pathways that made me want to kick my laptop into the ocean, if it wasn't through my stubbornness and the promise of achievements and trading cards I would have given up much earlier.
The hidden object portion of Morphopolis is really difficult, and not in a challenging or clever way, just in a frustrating eye-squinting way. This is where the art work really works against game, the objects you need often blend too well into the background or are so small you really have to get close to the screen to truly see them, or you have to access them by clicking the bug you control at a specific time, I only found this out through randomly clicking everything in sight and looking at let's plays, the game does not give you any of this information.
Most of the levels are a homogeneous mass of art, which would be fine if it was just a very detailed background for a different kind of game, as something you have to slog through in order to complete the game it's a sickening and confusing mess that I tired of very quickly.
Which brings me to the puzzles, you don't get much help in this game, that's not necessarily a bad thing, but it is if finding the hidden objects you need often comes down to clicking everywhere and hoping you get what you need, looking through a walkthrough (where many of the let's players seemed just as lost as I was), or hitting the hint button which straight up tells you where objects are but only when it's charged up and when you're in the right area. Can't find how to access the area you need to be in through the invisible walls? Hint button not fully charged until the next minute? Well tough, you have to wait for the hint button to charge and if no hints are available just wonder about hoping that you can reach where you need to be by clicking on anything, maybe the game will help you find how to complete the level, maybe it won't, maybe you'll figure it out through trial and error, you probably won't, there is no merciful god here.
And while we're on the subject, “immersion” does not mean slow and ponderous, being “arty” doesn't mean just plodding through weird surroundings with a weird non-story, you can't layer your game with arty visuals and call it immersive without any further effort on story, character or playability. While I'm sure many defenders of this game found it beautiful and meaningful, I and many others were praying for a skip button or any kind of save feature where we didn't have to go at a snails pace through the same level over and over again because we had the audacity to want to do stuff we enjoyed or look up a guide. Even an option to get out of some of puzzle modes so you can come back to it later or save so you don't have to repeat everything up until that point would have been a logical thing for this game to have, but I guess functionality doesn't win you illustrator awards so that isn't a feature. If the game wasn't so short it would be completely unplayable because of this, as it is it just makes the game annoying.
This game even fails to do a jigsaw puzzle properly, the art style while pretty (depending on taste) made what should have been a straightforward jigsaw puzzle into a frustrating rage game. Some of the pieces simply did not look like they were supposed to fit, lumps and bumps that were on pieces slotted perfectly into smoother areas, if it wasn't through a process of elimination I doubt I could have solved the puzzle. If this was unintentional then the developers cannot even develop the simplest puzzle with their art style properly, if it was intentional all it did was baffle me and frustrate me further, either way it made what should have been a beautiful game into an ugly experience. This isn't “challenging”, some of the puzzles fundamentally don't follow reasonable rules, there is no skill involved in these, only guesswork and irritation.
I simply did not care what was going on by level 4, there was no incentive to fully complete level 5 for me, Morphopolis gave me no investment in the gameplay, the story (what little it has) and what few characters we see (if you can call them that since we know nothing about these insects and we can't know anything about them because “art”). I wasn't relaxed or charmed, I was bored and angry, even if the game's conclusion was so mind-blowing that it completely made all the flaws I found in it meaningful I simply cannot muster any energy to give a damn about it at this point.
As a further insult, the achievements feel hollow because they are awarded for just the level and puzzle completions, no easter eggs or prizes for additional effort seem to be on offer, and the trading card drops for me were only available towards the end of the game and are worth squat on the market.
This isn't what a puzzle game should be, this isn't what a hidden object game should be, and it is not what an art game should be. It failed to be good at any of these things, and even though I spent less than 50p on it at the time I still feel ripped off, the developers should feel incredibly lucky to have gotten a positive rating for this.

A truly great, meditative and mesmerizing puzzle game with a touch of HOG. It feels like a top-tier indie, very polished, aside from a couple of technical cons (see below). While the first puzzles are pretty easy, the rest are really tricky and most likely will crack your brain up, especially the secret ones. Yes, aside from the main levels, there are also secret levels which you unlock. The game has its own world and lore, which is presented in an interesting and atmospheric way.
Overall the game is quite an achievement, considering it's a debut project from the 2-man studio.
Some techinical cons so far:
1) Achievements will pop up only after you quit the game (improper implementation of Steam SDK)
2) In-game options redirect you to the launcher, not sure why they are there at all then
3) You need to change your desktop resolution to the preferable game resolution before starting (i.e. if you desktop is 960p and the game is set to 1080p in the launcher, then you won't even the see main menu GUI)
No crashes, no freezes whatsoever, optimized perfectly as well.
NEEDS COMMUNITY MARKET but otherwise is a great game to pick up in a sale because its a bit pricey

Since I first started playing EOS I have noticed a ton of improvement.  The game gets regular updates and the devs are very involved with the community here on Steam.  One thing I really enjoy about EOS is the multi-leveled crafting.  Each resource is needed from the start to the end, so I don't feel as though I'm waisting my time gathering dirt, mud and rock on the way to the more valuable resourses.  You unlock new crafting opportunities by earning XP.  With this XP  you can "buy" data.  The data (once you get enough) gives access to better equipment.  I really like this system, I'm hoping that this is the one the devs settle on.
There are a few frustrating things about the game, such as the amount of time required to gather resourses for the equipment you need to progress.  Also, much like Terraria, the player is super vulnerable at the start of the game (this can lead to much frustration for players not accustomed to this type of game). The issue I struggle with the most is the lack of direction in the game.  The crafting is so much fun, but I have no idea what certain resourses are for or how some of the better equipment is crafted.  If you get too lopsided with buying data from one or two catergories you will be totally lost.  Make sure you unlock the data evenly to avoid any problems.
In conclusion, I totally recomend EOS.  I remember being frustrated as hell when playing Terraria after it first came out, but as time went along and I slowly learned new things the game became really fun.  I am 100% convinced that EOS is offering the same type of experience, who knows, maybee it will be even better than Terraria when all is said and done.

Can I just say that I freaking LOVE this game? Now, i'm not too big into to the survival genre, but this one just hits the nail on the head for me. Maybe it's because i'm Canadian, and basically surviving in the winter is something I learned in school  (i'm not even joking), so I had a little bit of an idea of what to expect when I first played this game. But all that aside, this game is amazing, even for just being in it's early stages.
PROS:
-The graphical art of this game is mesmerizing. It's beautiful, and I could take a hundred in-game screen shots and no two would look the same.
-The game world is pretty large, with 5-6 regions, and each region spanning a large area, not to mention all the interior areas to discover.
-This game gets you thinking, and I like that. It's kinda like a puzzle game, but with more starvation, wolves, and hypothermia.
-There is always something to do. Exploring the vast world around you, finding food, supplies, trying to avoid wolves and bears, and lots more to do.
-No two play throughs will be the same. You'll spawn somewhere different, luxury items will be in a different spot in the map/world, stuff like that.
-This game is more than just survival. This game freaking scares me somtimes when i'm exploring dark caves or i'm stranded in the middle of a blizzard. Always be on your toes when playing this game and be prepared to be scared a time or two.
-The updates for this game are pretty consistant. Though they can be a pretty long amount of time between eachother, they always add lots of content to make up for it.
CONS:
-None. I love absolutley everything about this game. I guess if I had to say something could be worked on in this game, it would be that it feels like you become hungry, thirsty and tired a little too easily. I mean, I know this is a game, it's not 100% realistic, but maybe making it so I don't have to eat 1000 calories and drink 2L of water every half an hour would be nice. But other than that, this game is a 10/10 for me.
I can't wait to see what Hinterland Studio adds to this game in the future, and I can only give them the highest of praise for this amazing piece of art this game is. If you don't own this game, you're making a grave mistake, compadre.
EDIT: I just recently began playing the story mode and, so far, it's interesting. You obviously don't have the same amount as freedom as in the survival mode, but I feel The Long Dark deserved a story mode from the beginning. I've also been seeing alot of negative reviews for this game recently, and I don't understand why. One review roughly described TLD as not being 'fun', and I think that, in a good way, that might be somewhat true. This game is ment to challenge you, make you stop and think about what to do or where to go next. This is a hardcore survival game, not some fast paced, CoD-style game.

Great puzzle game. As a kid, I was enchanted by one of these old light reflect games, in the early days of PC games when people ran MS-DOS. Archaica is like an evolved, modern version of that. The visuals are beautiful, the sound creates a nice ambiance and a magical feel to your actions. There are plenty of different puzzle pieces to influence light in many ways, from reflection and splitting to teleporting and refracting.
There are two things that I find less good. The first is the story. It doesn't matter much, but if you're going to put a story in your game, make it fitting. This particular type of story is not one I would put in a puzzle game. It seems at odds with the atmosphere of the gameplay.
Second: the difficulty. Maybe it's because I don't play puzzle games often, but this game is hard. I often find 4 or 5 near-solutions, where I could solve the puzzle if I could turn one mirror into another, or have one more tile of space. Sometimes after a long time of staring at variations of what I already made, I find the "real" solution, but sometimes I don't.
There is a hint system, but it doesn't help with this. Knowing the location of a piece but not knowing which piece is supposed to go there barely reduces the difficulty at all. The only thing that worked for me is using the hint system to get all locations, but then it's suddenly very easy and just a matter of swapping stuff until it works. So instead, I've been using the solutions post on the Steam discussion forums when I really couldn't figure one out. Usually it's one small thing that I missed. For example, "a color changing lens can be used to change the color of 2 orthogonal beams". I had one puzzle all figured out except for that one fact. The hint system does nothing in that case, except funnel you into the right direction until by pure coincidence you stumble upon the solution.
I think this game could benefit from a difficulty setting, where the current, single-solution game could be the highest difficulty, and one lower (medium) could give you a few extra tiles of space or an extra mirror here and there, to allow for secondary solutions for the non-hardcore puzzlers.
Great game, as good as puzzle games get, as long as you don't care too much for story and don't mind a high difficulty.

This game is amazing for the most horrifying reasons.
It's tense as hell, even when you know what you're doing, and that's because the limited visibility and mobility cause such strong, primitive fears within players.
The atmosphere of the environment heightens this. Dark, somewhat-decrepit hallways with barely functioning lights, and all this while bloodthirsty, malfunctioning animatronics are after you.
Limited power makes thinking quickly and strategically very important, as (for some inexplicable reason) the doors that can be used to ward off animatronics chew up power, meaning the player has to rely more on observation than brute force defence. And once the power goes out, you can only hope your shift ends before Freddy Fazbear himself tears you a new one.
That being said, the game itself is surprisingly simple, and once you know the patterns, warding off the animatronics is not as hard as you'd expect, or at least you can easily prepare yourself for the jumpscares. But that's half the challenge of the game, getting good enough to survive the 5 nights.
Oh, and there's an extra two nights, but I bet you knew that already.
All in all, a very well-built, and utterly terrifying, game. I strongly recommend it to people with strong willpower (and a lack of heart- or bowel-based medical conditions).
Just don't complain to me if you get spooped.

The creators of cuphead are determined to make you suffer as much playing the game as they did creating it.
....or at least make you work as hard!
Hand crafted, eyecatching 1930s cartoon visuals and character designs sets cuphead apart from the pack. Enough so to merit a play through alone! However the simple to learn hard to master difficulty will halt a lot of players right off the bat. Even with the somewhat popular resurgence in brutal game difficulties. Im not ashamed to admit (as a rusty/inexperienced platformer player) even the first stage kicked my butt back to the 30s!
The game it's self isn't litered with stages as you'll spend more time on a handful at once. learning to master enemy telegraphs, move sets and multiple phases. The game length is defenitly derived from the harsh difficulty that doesnt spike but sets the bar at a firm neck height from the word go, or as phrased "you're up".  without it would be a few hours at most for the average gamer content wise. The difficulty drawing ample time in substitution to where more time consuming work on extra stages would take. This isn't to far of feild though as the games it draws inspiration from, (contra, metal slug) are also known for legendary old school difficulty. Keeping the games retro charms not just to sound and visuals but gameplay wise as well.
While the controls are simple they handle well and feel responsive to player input making player death often feel justified.  Comparison to the dark souls franchise is fitting for these reasons as you'll also be collecting multiple boss souls to beat the game. A major difference here being there is no option to grind your way out of a hard situation. Only persistance reflex and learning the various attack patterns will ensure your survival. This all being paired with little wiggle room for error courtesy of the old skool 3 live system. Even with this said not every death feels entierly fair and may result in uncontrolable profanity. My biggest gripe with these bosses being so difficult is the total lack of any enemy healthbar that leaves you wondering how much longer you'll be plugging away at the boss and if your attacks are having much of an impact at all. This does keep the play feild open but limits damage feedback and makes hte combat its self a lot less satisfying. An option to show one or not would be greatly appreciated.
The overarching hubworld conects the levels well enough and the ability to roam from one boss fight to another at will removes the frustration of completing a stage before every boss attempt. This sadly also works as a doubble edged sword as it gives little breathing room to players after fights to enjoy the acomplishment and progress for victory as another lies imediately around the corner. subsiquently this diminishes player satisfaction with only world progress payouts from fights. New powers are not given as rewards for the boss fights themselves you will not get a chance to enjoy new found strength after each fight. It's hard to feel the entire journey of cuphead in this regaurd, and time in an expanded if somewhat inconcievable cuphead verse would set it leagues apart, with more room for the game to breath and curve in difficulty.
What Cuphead sets out to achive it hits the mark in all the right places. The emulation of classic animation and sound design are top notch and exceptional detail has been taken to ensure some highly creative boss designs. High praise from the eye of a fellow cartoonist! (a somewhat amature one by comparison!)
Im glad to be alive in a time where games with unique and intersting approaches are breaking through to poular culture and the fact something this cool even exsits at all! Even when the difficulty is overshading the artwork cuphead is really quite a landmark. Inovation to push the boundary further and draw interest to the experimental side of games is a healthy by product to be left in its wake.
Even if i never beat the game cuphead has sprung new life into an often overlooked asthetic approach that is still as timless as it was in the age of classic cartoons

There are few fans more engrossed in the Tropico series than me.  I have every one of them from the Franchise, I have in many cases, both hard copies (and digital copies...).  I have made a Tropico Mod for Mount & Blade.  I have re-created the Tropico world on my multiplayer sim-city's (with other fans), even in my World of Tanks game, I created a clan to represent the Army of Tropico (complete with rank system and Tropico flag).  I have bought copies of Tropico for friends and family.
I have said ALL this to qualify my review of Tropico 5.
PRO's:
-Amazing graphics
-Beautiful integration of theme music (a classic strength for the series)
-Great voice-overs (a classic strength for the series, but perhaps not quite as good as its predacessors)
-New strong balanced integration of the war/combat mechanics, as requested by many players
-Multiplayer !/?
-Expansive content!  Seriously expansive
-Stronger road system than the original Tropico games
-New El Prez family role-playing dynasty features
-More El Prez role-assuming immersion than Tropico 1-3.
-DLC adds to gameplay, but is not NEEDED to win or enjoy the game.
CON's:
-Less El Prez role-assuming immersion than Tropico 4 (ie: No custom speeches or assemblies)
-Less voice-acting immersion, than previous titles.
-Signifigantly less world/map customization and options than ALL previous Tropico titles.
-Multiplayer, takes away from the series' successful "Island Nation" atmosphere. TWO Presidente's?
-DLC (Latest DLC cost the price of an entire game) pricey with mixed content.
-Weak Dynasty RPG and Character Attribute customization options.
Overall Summary. Tropico 5 is an amazing game, its visuals and expanded content are sure to please ALL players of the genre.  Its new hands-on use of the military is well-balanced and integrated.  Newcomers to Tropico will find a game that  is poilished, with few bugs or inconsistencies in gameplay - a well polished fun game!  Veteran Tropico players may find themselves returning to the older games, for better immersion in the role of Tropico governing, humor, and better customization and scenario design, without sacrificing meaningful fun content.  I like Tropico 5... but don't discount the previous installments, for the immersion lost in this newest addition.

As an avid Batman fan, I had initially disliked this game for a number of reasons. My initial distaste was due to the writers' adulteration of some of the characters. I felt that, generally, certain core characteristics of the characters should not be modified. I was frustrated, for example, by Bruce Wayne no longer being a stereotype suave billionaire, but appeared to be more of a soft-spoken pushover.
As the story progressed, I came to appreciate it and its characters as being something of a one-off, isolated universe. While at first it seemed the writers were wholly unfamiliar with the Batman mythos (while I still believe this), I now see that they used the audience's expectations to their advantage. The modified characters of this story worked well for it.
My only lasting gripe with this game was its poor performance. Frequent lagging or stuttering, low frame-rates, and cursor issues. The cursor would occassionally drift across the screen while my mouse was still. There was also a painfully slow delay between my mouse movement and the cursor's movement. It made playing at a high resoultion impossible, as I could not move the cursor across the screen quickly enough to play. Another problem at high resolution was that the cursor could not reach the bottom of the screen. I found playing at 720p eased these mouse troubles.
Aside from the performance problems (which tended to effectively break immersion) the game was overall enjoyable. However, if future Telltales games have similar performance problems, I think I'll refrain from purchasing them.

Tropico is one of the better strategy/city builder franchises around. It's similar to Civilization, but it's real time and not turn based. There is a military factor, but this is only a small portion of the game. You have the ability to pause and even speed up gameplay so this isn't a difficult transition. Tropico 4 is very similar to Tropico 5 with some minor changes in the administration of the game. If you liked 4, then you will like 5 as well. If you've never played Tropico and want to try it out I suggest buying one of the earlier versions of the game first.
- They didn't add enough variation in the buildings and there are only 4 total islands in the storyline. There still are not nearly enough buildings as has been a constant issue with the Tropico series. Tropico has always needed a lot more options in buildings as every single game is going to look exactly the same, which is boring.
- There's not nearly enough new content to warrant a new release of the game.
- The initial price (if you don't buy it when it's on sale) is too high. It took me less than 40 hours of play to beat it and I was more concerned with building the islands than actually following the storyline. There are not enough islands and the gameplay is too linear. If I were to play straight through only going for what's needed to beat it, it would take less than 20 hours.
- The DLC is insanely expensive and the worst part is that most of the DLC was already on the disc when the game was released and blocked off while fully functional (search google for more on this). All of this simply so the developer could make more money later. Most of the DLC only gives you one new building, one mission and one costume that you'll likely never use. They want $2-5 for each of these.
- The trade feature was poorly implemented and very rarely allows you to export. Almost all trades are imports and you can produce most everything you need much cheaper yourself. No reason to import anything unless you've exhausted a resource you need for production (which only happens if you're just playing and ignoring the storyline) or if you can't produce enough food to feed your people.
+ There are plenty of variation in islands if you want to do a sandbox game and you can even generate a random island.
+ Multiplayer is a new feature. Unfortunately I've yet to use it and cannot comment on it.
+The new mechanics on your dynasty and swiss bank account are great, but barely affect gameplay at all and is more cosmetic and gives you something to do with your swiss bank account than anything else.
+ Cosmetically the game is better and it's more difficult. If you're not keeping up with what the citizens want then they will become rebels and will relentlessly attack you. This was the best change in the game as it greatly increased the difficulty.

This would be a short review, but I'll try to be explicit to whom the game will appeal to (and, consequently, not).
One line about writing.
It is. that. good.
Seriously, writing quality is way above anything a game should have. I keep reading small masterpieces again and again, each time they appears.
Lovecraftian Pirates
--------------------
Not a typo :) - the game mechanics are much alike Sid Maiers Pirates - you have a ship which could be upgraded or replaced later, have a crew, fuel and food to keep an eye on. And you sail the Unterzee, doing... something.
That 'something' are mini-quests, or larger pieces of story, that you can chose to take or not.
The atmosphere is truly remarkable, play in the dark and see! Not being based on actual Mythos, it is Lovecraftian in core, with the unstable protagonist (you/me/us) doing questionable actions and progressing into terror and madness.
Who must have it?
--------------------
I do.
Apart from me, players which love horror-themed games and a perfect story.
Pen & paper - it is wise do write down events and requirements - some names are not quite intuitative and some parts of the quest are easy to forgot. Write it down - after all, you're zee-captain - shoulda 'ave log, anyway.
Go to youtube or wherever and see the gameplay - what you'll see there, you'll get (gameplay-wise - irritating voice-overs completely ruin the atmosphere, so might as well turn the volume down).
Who'd been disappointed?
----------------------------
Players that expect action from combat, rich reward from doing quest and firm and progressing storyline.
/this is not an action game; rewards from quests are... extremely well written stories, or new story arcs, but not the super-ultra-canon; storyline is open and without visible goal/
Players who hate writing anything down.
/as said, it is wise to/
Players dissatisfied with what they seen on youtube (or wherever).
What else?
-----------
Well, a difficulty warning - despite what everyone says, zee-captains don't drop dead all the time - I am playing my 2nd captain (will restart probably because of Zubmariner addon) and there are few nasty places where bad rolls (or very unwise decisions) can kill you - well, I save the game there and that's it. Uncommon sense (game doesn't support 'common').
A 2nd captain?
----------------
There are things I've seen and done, that I regret bitterly. I cut off some ties and made unneeded mistakes. There will be a 3rd captain.
This is meant for endgame / replayability info. While endgame could be better, replayability is there - one can play a game at least couple of times, doing things differently.
Zubmariner?
-------------
An add-on, that adds more of the same. And more of the similar. I like it. Try the game first and if you like it, buy Zubmariner also. If you don't like core game, there's little chance that add-on will change it...

Archaica: The Path of Light uses a fairly well known puzzle method - reflecting light off mirrors to reach a target. This has been used as a mini-game mechanic in adventure games (as well as an education tool) many times, but Archaica takes the concept to the next level and bundles it up in an extremely attractive package.
There are a set amount of mirrors on a level and you can move and rotate them. By deciding where to place them and in which direction they point, different shaped mirrors refract the light in different directions. Some amplify the strength of the beam whilst some split it into two directions. The aim is to activate pillars to complete the level - some of which require two different colours to blend into a new one. There are also other puzzle elements, like activating keystones to unlock secret levels, filling orbs to trigger map changes and other mechanics that I'll let you explore.
The gameplay concept alone wouldn't have hooked me although it certainly is good; what really drew me in was the visuals. The maps are stunningly detailed. Through beams of light we explore ruins and unlock ancient magics. If you really stop and study a map you can see the time and effort that went into the artwork. It's not just the maps, it's the menus, the achievement screen, the cutscenes/animations (of which there are plenty, simple but very effective). I've never looked at an achievement screen before and said "wow", but as you unlock achievements you light up and activate an ancient totem, making progression feel very satisfying.
This is an entire world to unlock, not just a simple light puzzler. On each level there are lore items to unlock - optional environmental collectibles that provide an interesting narrative and add a hunt and seek element of gameplay. By finding cells you can also power up hints, so if you need a little nudge you can get it. The lore of this ancient abandoned world and the Light Bearers who used to control it is surprisingly deep and interesting. It's rare to find a puzzle game that puts this much work into the back story and universe.
Archaica has been polished until it's sparkling. It's a full package that I rarely see from a small indie development studio. It has a genuine atmosphere that you often don't find in puzzle games. On the surface, this is a very simple puzzle concept - but everything about it just feels satisfying. It's on a custom engine and founded by two Polish brothers who spent three years of their life perfecting it. All I can say is what a talented family! I've not been this excited about discovering a new indie studio in a long time - I can't wait for their next project.

I rarely review games. Only if a game really excels in what it sets out to do I feel I have to give my 2 cents. Archaica is without a doubt such a game because it does everything it wants to achieve in a mesmerising way.
Archaica is a light redirection puzzle game. It contains 87 separate puzzles that split into 6 chapters with a total of
The player is gradually made familiar with the basic puzzle mechanics in the first chapter and more intricate mechanics are introduced in the following chapters. Generally speaking you have to direct light beams of different colors through crystals of the same color by using mirrors, splitters, filters, etc. As to the difficulty curve, I'd say that starting from chapter 3 puzzles are getting pretty hard to solve even though some may be less difficult.
Each puzzle of Archaica is very well designed. Your goal is clearly defined and most of the time I had a pretty good understanding of how the light has to be directed in general. Puzzleing therefore mostly consisted of trying to make this general solution work with the limited resources available. It follows that in many cases, finding the actual solution resulted in a very rewarding experience.
I never had to resort to fundamental trial and error which is also due to a hint system that perfectly fits my needs. Almost all puzzles have so-called cells hidden in them. Each cell you find allows for a hint to the puzzle. And for a hint you have to select a couple of neighboring squares in the puzzle area and the game will show you in which of these fields you have to place one of your puzzle items ... not which item though. So hints only very gently nudge you into the right direction.
Further things to look for in the puzzles are so-called cryptoglyphs. Most puzzles have between two and four of these items hidden around the puzzle area. If you find all of them, you will get some explanations as to the background and the items of Archaica. Which brings me to the 'story' of the game: generally, when you solve a puzzle you will get background information about the history of Archaica or about the Path of Light that you, the player, are wandering on. In my opinion, those text bits add to the feel of the game but I can appreciate that some might find them superfluous, after all they are quite generic.
Finally, and
, the game has beautiful visuals that perfectly support the feeling of intrigue when solving the puzzles. There are deserts, caves, fiery pits, jungles, and more.
Having said all that, Archaica stands out amongst all light redirection puzzles I've played and I have played quite a lot. So my advice to any lover of puzzle games is to get it right away, it is well worth it's price! If you think 15€ is too much get it in the next sale.

Updated review from my last one.
In my previous review I stated how bad this game was and how it seemed to be going nowhere. It felt amateurish and pointless. The tutorial was vague and taught very little.
That was at the beginning of the year and I recently reinstalled the game to see what was new and if things have improved. I'd like to talk about these changes after some brief gameplay:
The first impression that I got was that the tutorial is way better. They aren't always necessary for this kind of game, but before I was baffled on how to build things, now I know. Immediately you are given a gun, fairly weak, but it does the trick, whereas before there seemed no way to kill enemies other than using the mining laser on them or the plasma saw or whatever it was.
So what do I think now? Alot better, my hat is off to you guys for improving upon a royal mess. Not perfect, but still not released. At this rate of improvement I am confident, however, that things will get ironed out.
Some minor problems:
For some reason the install for a game of this type and look is enormous. 1.5 gb download and 3gb disc space. Where it all goes, I'm unsure, but as the art seems to be bitmap and bitmap has large file sizes, I'm inclined to think that it is that.
Screen tearing is quite bad.
Bloody snails pushing me around. Probably by design but annoying.
The worlds seem extremely small. Could perhaps do with you being able to go to other planets or at least make the worlds alot bigger.
Overall, my opinion has swayed. I see potential in this game and I am impressed with the improvements. Keep up the good work.

Dear readers,
I highly recommend this game, for a range of reasons. Perhaps most importantly, it is actually fun to play. I was initially dubious, since I am new to this genre of game, but, at the behest of a friend, I decided to give it a chance. I am very glad that I did, because flying (even for short distances) with a jet pack is all that I hoped it would be. I am still waiting for my real-life jet pack, universe!
As I have never played this type of game before, it took me longer than the average person (I assume) to get through the tutorial. This was not, however, because the tutorial was not well-structured. In fact, it taught me all the basics I needed to know for this game without much superfluous fluff. I just had trouble with, for instance, remembering that I could jump down platforms.
In addition, it is clear from the regular patches and updates that the developers are highly invested in making the game-play experience as bug-free and enjoyable as possible. This is the first early access game that I've purchased, and thanks to my positive experience with Edge of Space, I will be taking my chances on other early access games in the future.
Best,

It has everything I love from Half-Life. the difficult puzzles, simple yet eloquent combat, come to think of it that might be the problem. It's too similar, nothing new really at all. If you want a continuation on Half-Life, which is why I purchased this, you won't be exactly disappointed, but not really impressed either. I did like the addition of getting armor from literal armor and the reticule reacting to being over the enemy, but all-in-all it never made me stop and say "Wow, they put a whole lot of effort into designing these new mechanics!". If, like me, you just wanted another run through of Black Mesa, feel free to purchase this, but if you are given the choice, go with Opposing Force.

Audiosurf is a rhythm and puzzle-solving game that transforms your music library into a track of colored blocks you have to match to get points for.
Gamplay is split between several modes, including dodge the grey blocks, hit the colored ones, co-op, collecting multiple colors, etc. The game can read in your entire iTunes library, which is very convenient and does well in generating a good course.
Visually, there's not that much going on, outside of colored blocks and lines, but when the music picks up, there are more colors and the course speeds up.
Overall, Audiosurf is a basic rhythm/puzzle game that can read in your music library. It's got both easy and hard levels, so there's a lot of variety in addition to the different game modes. Very enjoyable and relaxing.

This would be a short review, but I'll try to be explicit to whom the game will appeal to (and, consequently, not).
One line about writing.
It is. that. good.
Seriously, writing quality is way above anything a game should have. I keep reading small masterpieces again and again, each time they appears.
Lovecraftian Pirates
--------------------
Not a typo :) - the game mechanics are much alike Sid Maiers Pirates - you have a ship which could be upgraded or replaced later, have a crew, fuel and food to keep an eye on. And you sail the Unterzee, doing... something.
That 'something' are mini-quests, or larger pieces of story, that you can chose to take or not.
The atmosphere is truly remarkable, play in the dark and see! Not being based on actual Mythos, it is Lovecraftian in core, with the unstable protagonist (you/me/us) doing questionable actions and progressing into terror and madness.
Who must have it?
--------------------
I do.
Apart from me, players which love horror-themed games and a perfect story.
Pen & paper - it is wise do write down events and requirements - some names are not quite intuitative and some parts of the quest are easy to forgot. Write it down - after all, you're zee-captain - shoulda 'ave log, anyway.
Go to youtube or wherever and see the gameplay - what you'll see there, you'll get (gameplay-wise - irritating voice-overs completely ruin the atmosphere, so might as well turn the volume down).
Who'd been disappointed?
----------------------------
Players that expect action from combat, rich reward from doing quest and firm and progressing storyline.
/this is not an action game; rewards from quests are... extremely well written stories, or new story arcs, but not the super-ultra-canon; storyline is open and without visible goal/
Players who hate writing anything down.
/as said, it is wise to/
Players dissatisfied with what they seen on youtube (or wherever).
What else?
-----------
Well, a difficulty warning - despite what everyone says, zee-captains don't drop dead all the time - I am playing my 2nd captain (will restart probably because of Zubmariner addon) and there are few nasty places where bad rolls (or very unwise decisions) can kill you - well, I save the game there and that's it. Uncommon sense (game doesn't support 'common').
A 2nd captain?
----------------
There are things I've seen and done, that I regret bitterly. I cut off some ties and made unneeded mistakes. There will be a 3rd captain.
This is meant for endgame / replayability info. While endgame could be better, replayability is there - one can play a game at least couple of times, doing things differently.
Zubmariner?
-------------
An add-on, that adds more of the same. And more of the similar. I like it. Try the game first and if you like it, buy Zubmariner also. If you don't like core game, there's little chance that add-on will change it...

Whereas previous Tropico games had the best game soundtracks I've ever heard, filled to the brim with authentic Latin tracks by great artists, Tropico 5 has mediocre music farmed out to a game composer. The only thing I can think of that's better is the graphics. And they're not that much of an improvement from Tropico 3/4.

This latest installment of the Triopico franchise has its plusses and minuses.
In the minus category:
Keeping your factions happy has become much more difficult with the removal of the faction advisors, building bonsuses (e.g., childhood museum and school settings), and advice on the political impact of your constitutional choices. Furthermore, when viewing the thoughts/approval of unhappy citizens there's no indicaiton of what you can do to make them happy -- or, more problematically, if the only thing you can do to make them happy is change your politics, you're often prevented from doing so in a timely manner because of restrictions to constitutional changes (I'm a goddamn dictator, I should be able to change my constitution any damn time I please).
Roads are still deeply problematic and the "fog of war" that shrouds your entire island at the beginning of the game in the colonial era makes proper city/road planning that much more difficult. Speaking of the "fog of war", I'm seriously annoyed that it costs me $1000 per exploration, especially when what I want to explore is a tiny little patch of undiscovered territory that keeps me from placing a mine on an entirely visibile deposit. And what's up with the lack of overlays? I'm no longer able to see fish or oil deposits at a glance and I have no idea how many mineral deposits are located on any given island -- which is deeply distressing when you have an island with only one bauxite deposite and a mission task requires that you mine that depoist.
Finally, my biggest greivance is the fact that one of the best features (IMHO) of Tropico 4 is no longer present -- the ability to go back and choose to replay certain campaign misisons. Given the structure of the campagin, where each mission builds on every successive mission, having screwed yourself by expoliting too many resources in an earlier mission means that subsequent missions become that much more difficult. If you're not into saving games on a regular basis, this means that if you want to try a different strategy on one particular mission you have to go back and restart the whole damn campaign all over again.
On the plus side, I feel like most of the same features that I love about the Tropico franchise (the economic aspects, the micro-managing city planning/building) are still here and I do love the way the campagin has you build upon existing island structure. For all of its problems, I'm stlil pleased that I purchased this game...but not as happy as I was Tropico 4.

Who is this Game For?
==================
For people who don’t mind the long tireless grind that many rogue like games offer. I think this is where my first major criticism with Sunless Sea lies; there’s an inevitable inertia to failure. While it’s nice to have some kind of lifeline when you run out of fuel, often you’re left paying such a high cost that you’d be better off restarting. Indeed, with little real chance of recovery when things go wrong, I found myself quitting out of games long before my fate was sealed.
Is it good?
=================
I don’t want to give the impression that Sunless Sea is a thrill-less ride. Indeed, the gentle chugging of your boat and the drip dripping of the underground sea and the languorous sailing is really thrilling. It’s the excitement of discovery combined with your knowledge of just how dangerous the world is that makes each new voyage a joy to set off on. The “tat tat” you hear each time you find a new location is incredibly satisfying as it rewards you each time with some pages towards your next “secret”, while the soundtrack is dynamic and never, ever stop’s being great. In truth the chug-chug of my ship combined with the atmospheric soundtrack were the main factors in making me boot up Sunless Sea over and over again even when the actual gameplay began to grate.
Does it have any problems?
========================
As things start to go wrong, your problems tend to multiply with little chance of recovery. For example, when you run out of food you start to lose crew. When you lose crew your ship slows down. You are left limping around the sea at minimum speed, hoping desperately that you can find an as-yet undiscovered port to buy supplies. Similarly, if you take damage in combat then you need to use supplies to repair your ship – the same supplies you use to feed the crew. I think about 60% of the time I played Sunless Sea, I was already “dead” – skulking around with a damaged ship and a crew that was starving, hoping beyond hope for the respite of a well stocked port.
And while there’s a certain stark, bleak beauty to courageous journeys that end in tragedy, too much of this hopelessness can drain the game of any fun. In particular, the cruelty of making it all the way back to (perceived) safety in London only to realise that you’re doomed anyway because you don’t have enough money for fuel or food was always enough to push me over the edge. I went very quickly from “bring it on!” to “♥♥♥♥ right off!”.
Couldn’t returning to London reward you with some complimentary fuel and food? Or am I just really bad at the game and I’m missing something? Either way, Sunless Sea taught me that persevering in the face of adversity was a waste of time and I was always better to cut my losses and start over again. And that approach seems antithetical to the spirit of epic adventurers who defied the odds. I’m sure the developers didn’t intend for Sunless Sea to so handsomely reward the cautious and lucky and brutally castigate the courageous and intrepid.
And seeing as the game is so text centric, it’s frustrating to be looking at a tiny journal most of the time. I would love to have seen large images of the ports and places I visited instead of thumbnail sketches, while most of the interface remains useless and unused. Scrolling around is a pain when there’s potential screen space that’s unused. Sunless Sea’s interface does a poor job of prioritising the information that’s important to you.
Final Thoughts!
====================
I don’t want to sound too down on Sunless Sea. Sadly though, it’s one of those games that I respect and appreciate more than I enjoy and one that I find it easier to recommend than to actually play. There were moments that I really liked, but every time the music and atmosphere and writing engaged me, some aspect of the gameplay would conspire to ruin my fun. I’m really glad that it exists, and I can’t argue too strongly with the people who love it. There’s a lot to love! For me though, it’s a half-sketched outline for a better game. It’s more intriguing than it is enjoyable.

The only real issue I have with this game, is that it often creates copies of your ruling family. After playing half the campaign mode, and 1 game in sandbox mode, I had 5 copies of my single ruling family. Not 2: 5. I like the idea of having your family bridge multiple games, but I'll have to throw away 50% of the time spent playing this game if I want to use my family in its most advanced state. It's unfortunate this feature wasn't implimented better.
The music and atmosphere of this game is great. It's relaxing to play, and makes you feel stress-free: like being on a tropical island. At the same time, you have a lot of choices to make, and really feel like your decisions are critical for your island's well-being, although quite possibly your citizenry would be well off if you took a ten year nap.
. . there are a few annoyances regarding how the game ships resources: effectively all resources are always sent to the docks: if another building on the island requests them, then those resources won't ship off the island--right away--but as your island gets larger, and more demanding, it can be months before resources get picked up. and they end up getting sold instead of transported forward. The addition of a checkbox you could tick to not sell an item if it's stored at a dock, would solve this, but instead the solution is to import much more of a resource than you need and hope some of it's still there when someone arrives to transport it. And don't get all uppity at me and be all "oh, just build more resource moving dudes:" the rate of resource movement is fine when there's a surplus of resources. The issue is that, when your power plant needs iron, and then a ship comes in and all your iron gets sold, and now the task "transport iron to the power plant" gets lost. . . Then another ship imports iron, and the task "transport iron the power plant" is added again, but to the bottom of the queue. Then, before it reaches the top of the queue, another ship arrives and all the iron is sold again. Do you see how this is a problem? Yes, there are some things you can do to outplay the system and get to your own iron before it gets sold, but just having a option to not sell the iron you critically need for your island, would be a much more realistic, simplier solution, which does not exist. Why not?!!
I've given you two issues, and these are really the most serious issues I have with the game. Most everything else is clear, and fun to play with. Oh! It does suck that you can't build new buildings during an attack: the time my island got invaded just as a two large military facilities were about to complete, and so I lost: that sucked. The island was in a state of war for a year and half: you're telling me the new barracks couldn't finish training their troops in a year and a half and come to finish off the one enemy unit that survived and slowly plinked away at my manor until it was destroyed?! Okay, so those three things suck, but a lot about this game is really enjoyable
I hope that, being more aware of the issues with this game, will help you enjoy it more, because they are issues you can prepare for, and this is really a relaxing, fun, game to play :)

This game reminds me of APB: Reloaded because it's like GTA on steroids; LOTS of destruction and the game is very challenging. The open-world atmosphere is amazing. You can cling on to and operate just about everything in the game that you find. Very fun game! Extremely fun if you like chaos and destruction.
