People who have watched it being played could not contain their laughter, neither can I most of the time even after years of playing it off and on. Since the game can be saved anywhere you can have all of the fun it provides whenever you like and continue where you left off or start a new game that doesn't effect your other saves. Well worth the cost if you like this type of game. Way more destructive capabilities than what I've seen in any GTA game or APB although it is very comparable to those titles, just more fun and in my personal opinion a better story line. I have not tried the multiplayer mod and probably won't, because I am just not in to running around destroying things with no plot or goal to acheive in a game other than destroying things, in my opinion it's a ton more fun destroying things when the things you're destroying are actually a goal/achievement in the game's plot/story, this game has that. Highly recommended if you like single player games with great explosions and a goal to reach.
And the goals are not easy to achieve. Most of it is taking over territories by destroying targets that are protected by a lot more enemies than just you. You either have to go all out and destroy absolutely everything in sight which is hectic, or try and be as silent and strategic as you can.
The remote C4 bombs are my favorite because you can be silent and strategic and destroy all targets for the goal at once by the press of a button with very little injury to yourself and a lot of death and loss to your opponents achieving the goal . This is the most difficult tactic but in my opinion it's the most fun. It takes a lot of whoopsies and deaths to figure out how exactly to take over each territory completely without being seen, shot at, or worse.
Some of the humerous parts is random AI that's constantly roaming around. Not all of them are enemies and they will sometimes argue amoungst each other which breaks out into a gun or RPG fight between multiple people. Hilarious!
And it also creates a diversion for you when you're trying to take over villages.

This game is brilliant.
The game spawns you into a random location on a map, and then the clock starts ticking as you try to survive as long as possible. The catch is not only are you trying to find the important aspects of survival like food and drink, but you are also being hunted.
The game spawns wolves who are just as hungry as you. The wolves will hunt in packs to try to find their next meal, which may be you. This keeps you on your toes constantly as you never know what may lurk behind you or around the corner. It is very unnerving and really gives the game a creepy atmosphere.
The fight for finding food, water, and shelter, as well as trying to fend for your life give the game the desperate struggle for survival it was trying to achieve. The maps are big with plenty of places of interest, and the gameplay will keep you coming back for more!
Oh, and don't die. The game has permadeath, and I mean PERMADEATH. It will delete your save the second you die automatically. Every second is a fight for survival, as well as for preserving all your hard work up to that point. I go back and forth if I like this feature or not, but the stressful and desperate atmosphere it creates is definitely worth it. Pick this game up now! I can't wait to see what the future holds for it already has enough to keep me occupied for months to come :)

Evolve is a gorgeous game with an appreciably thick and interesting atmosphere.  The characters, with no defining backgrounds, are well developed, well balanced, and compliment one another both physically and psychologically.  The hunt for the monster feels new, exciting, and interesting every time you jump from the dropship.
The only problem that I have with the game is in the monster itself.  Throughout a hunt there are a number of ways to track the thing--local fauna and creatures react to it as it passes through an area, and it leaves tracks that are easy to follow, and if you're ever just completely lost, the tracker's hound, Daisy, usually runs in the right direction, but the mechanics are easy to abuse as well.  Knowing what areas of a map don't have reactive creatures and simply backtracking over your own tracks mean that once you're separated from the hunters, there's a decent chance you can stay hidden for long enough periods of time to create much greater separation that you would by just running away.
And running away seems to be the best way to play the monster until you reach the last stage--and yeah, that's the point, but it also feels a little easy.  Even trapped in an arena, if the monster doesn't engage the hunters directly, there's little chance they do enough damage to make a difference before the arena powers down and the monster takes off again.  It doesn't benefit in any way by engaging you early, and if it chooses not to, there's no way to make any appreciable progress against it.  Once it reaches stage three, in my limited experience, at more than half health there's very little that can be done to stop it.
It's fun.  I've enjoyed it.  My friends have enjoyed it.  It's probably worth the price.

Let me start off buy saying, you might die the first few time you play. It all depends,  there are random start point,  and random items depending on level of difficulty.  You might have a gun early on,  but just as easily,  you're undefended .  You might find a hatchet,  then again,  maybe not,  making it all the more difficult to find and harvest firewood.  How about a hunting knife.  One of those would be handy early on, but there's no guarantee you find one of those either,  cause it might be on a dead frozen corpse in the snow,  but you have to stumble on it,  to get it.  There's no map for you.  There's no compass for you.  You're just dropped into the middle of nowhere in a frozen wasteland,  under dressed for the condition,  trying desperately to find shelter to stay alive.  The Odds are not in your favor.  To top it off there are packs of wolves searching for food too.  They'll take down one of the deer that are foraging around,  but they'll target you if they see you.  And thats a scary prospect.
This game satisfies the single player gamer in me,  and the real life outdoorsy camper who has spent a bit of time out in the wilderness.  The game feels right.  There is an intellectual payoff to an accurate portrayal of trying to survive in a brutally harsh environment.  The game acts as you would expect and there are payoffs when you make the correct decisions  and consequence when you don't.   You can't run and gun your way through this.  You have to think.
And the most important part in the thinking process is the managing of scarce resources.  You never have enough stuff.  If you're playing on Voyager difficulty or above,  you never have enough wood to burn, or enough calories to consume or enough bullets to protect yourself.  You might just have enough strength to fight off a wolf attack with just a torch in had,  but you'll have to deal with the injuries that result.  There is a level of challenge in the game that makes hitting the DAYS SURVIVED achievements meaningful.   And that makes the game all the more compelling.
The various maps and environments tie together nicely and each has its own unique visual characteristics.  Discovery of the various areas make you want to explore further as you hunt for those scarce resources and shelter.  The sandbox is wide open of a good storytelling adventure game.
Now we have to remember this is an Early access game  and plenty of elements will probably be tweaked,  but a couple things that are worth mentioning in the grand design of making a better game which is pretty awesome already and can be even more accurate ;  If you have a hatchet of breaking down firewood,  it should in someway be available as a melee weapon in a wolf attack.  It may cost it being destroyed in the process,  but if its in your inventory it should be a weapon too.    If you heat up an enclosed space using a wood stove that has been burning for a couple hours,  the entire space would acquire ambient temperature that should not dissipate instantly after the fire goes out.  The gradual drop in temperature should happen over atleast 1 hour.
If you've been looking to pick up this game,  do it.  It's well worth it,  even at the early access stage.   There's enough here to keep you involved for hours.   But be warned,  just cause you manage to escape a pack of wolves chasing you outside on some traintracks,  into an abandoned dam,  don't think you're safe just cause you're inside,  because there's just as likely to be another wolf in there as well, which you'll have to deal with,   before you can pillage the place for resource.  You've been warned!  Enjoy.
PS:  I like the back story on this too;   Canadian Game made in Canada and set in the Canadian Wilderness.  6500+ backers on kickstarter,  some money from the Canadian Media Fund,  the Unity game engine,  a team of game makers and designers with various levels of industry experience.  An Indie game success story.  And now a half million downloads on Steam.  Again.  What's not to like.

Overall the game is pretty good. The graphics are nice, the gameplay is varied, and the progression insures that noobs still have a chance against veterans when it comes to weapons.
One thing to note when first playing is this is not counter strike, Call of Duty, or battlefield. This is much slower and methodical.
You have extreme bullet drop, and you must constantly gauge distances or else be killed.
The game doesn't tell you whats a friendly or not, you must decide. Friendly fire is always on.
The game will not help you spot enemies, meaning sneaky tactics are very powerful not only for you but for everyone else. Camoflauge has an actual effect here.
Pros:
Good graphics.
In depth Gameplay and mechanics.
Ballistics that rely on bullet drop over distances. No hit scan weapons with no bullet time or drop.
CONS:
Small, incredibly dedicated community that will wipe the floor with you when you first start out due to a difference in experience. These guys know the maps and distances for bullet drop by heart, but you don't. Once you familiarize yourself with the maps and the bullet drop, this will cease to be a problem.
In game custom map downloads tends to be slow, and the community tends to avoid them for that fact which limits map variety.
The way the game loads means those with an SSD or good internet get first pick on classes before anyone else even loads.

Obludia is an old-school arcade-arena-action game. If you look at some screenshots, it might look like a rogue-lite game like The Binding of Isaac, but it is not.
You have to defeat waves of monsters through 50 levels in 5 different worlds (one boss every ten levels) using both weapons and magic. You have access to only 3 spells (you will need to buy them first, then use mana to cast them) and to a lot of weapons. Sadly, only a few of them are effective, I recommend the classic crossbow plus the machine-gun, and maybe the dynamite. The melee weapons are too dangerous because you would have to be very close to the ennemies to damage them.
There are some RPG elements, like shops (you can buy a dog that is going to fetch gold, potions are available as well as ammos, ...) and a kind of level-up : after defeating a boss, you can increase your attack, your life, your mana or your speed. You can also get some boosts or special items that will help you killing the ennemies.
Both graphics and music are nice. Regarding the difficulty of the game, I would say that it is easy on "normal" and challenging on the other one (tips : upgrade speed after the first boss because ennemies are too fast for you + use machine-gun as soon as you can, buying ammos at shops).
Once you have completed the game on both difficulties, there is almost nothing to do. You can try to get a better score to appear in the leader board, or you can try the mutli-player mode. Nevertheless, developers are listening to people and updating the game according to feedbacks, which is a good thing, and we might get more content in the future. Fun and enjoyable game, especially with a pad :)

There are some games that I play to have fun, to really immerse myself into the game. Then there are some games which I play with the sole purpose of getting 100% in the game relatively quickly. This game falls squarely into the latter category.
Obludia is a game from Slovakian developers FobTi Interactive. Apparently it's a
. The game was programmed in
- not an entirely bad effort, but nothing special either.
A game inspired by Robotron and Smash-TV, you basically descend the levels of...whatever it is you're descending...killing enemies, gaining gold that can be used to buy items from shops that appear along the way, and doing it for 50 levels total.
The main problem with this game is the amount of comparisons it gets to
, when in reality the two games can't be more different. For instance: TBOI features randomly generated dungeons while Obludia uses the same level layouts over and over again. The only "rogue-like" aspect of Obludia is the permadeath, but even permadeath can be cheated with the possibility of save slots that can be bought from shopkeepers. With the game interface also looking similar (...okay, to be honest they look rather different, but the main elements are there in their spots!) it is hard not to be reminded of TBOI, especially if you, like me, are a veteran of the latter.
With that out of the way, here's what I found that I didn't quite like about this game:
That being said, I did like the music overall. It helped to lighten the mood, considering what I was going through.
Boredom.

It really pains me to rate this down, since I desperately wanted to like it as a BOI replacement, but...there you go.

I wasn't able to tell why I didn't like playing this game until I tried it on hard. Then I realized it's the pacing that's more glaringly wrong for my tastes on the normal difficulty.

Banished is a little gem among city/town/colony building simulation games. The game definitely isn't easy but once you get the basic knowledge of how things work then you shouldn't be having any difficulties with this game anymore. The game has a thorough tutorial which will help you learn the basics of the game. The graphics aren't top notch but the gameplay quality is superb. This is basically a survival simulation where you will be given some colonists to help you get started and then you have to slowly ensure their survival which leads to the growth of your colony. You will fail many times. But that is the point of this game. By failing, you actually learn from what you did wrong in your previous game. The best thing about this game is the achievements. If you are an achievement hunter, this game will keep you busy. If you are not into achievements, then the game has a vast active workshop where you will find so many fun and essential mods. By the way, using mods disables achievements so be careful. You can experiment with the survival aspects of this game to find out what suits your playstyle.
Pros:
- Casual and relaxing gameplay.
- Calming soundtracks.
- Weather, disasters and seasons. They affect the gameplay.
- Decent graphics.
- Good tutorial which covers the necessary basic and advanced features of this game.
- Achievements.
- Mods.
Cons:
- High price.
- Random performance issues like edge scrolling causing the game to stutter a bit, sudden crash, auttomatically change of DirectX11 to DirectX9 setting of the game which then causes massive fps drops until you change it back to it's original setting etc. These happens very rarely though and can be fixed or it gets automatically fixed. These issues might almost never appear but when it does, it becomes really annoying.
- Turning off the v-synce heats up the GPU really high, like 70-75 degree but turning it back on cools down the gpu to 45-55 degree. Not sure why it happens with a game like this. If this happens to you, just keep the v-sync on.
- After you finally make a huge settlement with all the needs of the colonists fulfilled, the game becomes repetitive and there won't be nothing much to do.
- You can become addicted to game. Not really a con though.
If you are into city-building, management, simulation games then Banished is perfect for you. But not at full price.

Banished is the kind of game that can really, REALLY click for people who found just what they are looking for, and be quite boring and shallow for others looking for more depth. Thus, it is important that you know what type of game you are looking for, and what you will find in this game.
The gameplay in Banished has much to do with resource management. The basic gameplay loop is - sustain population, then build more to expand population, and the cycle repeats. You need food for the people. You need to assign people to mine, find food, chop wood into burning material to keep the houses warm during winter, and so on. You need rocks and wood to build more houses for your population to expand, so that you will have more people to gather more resources to build and expand more, all while avoiding starvation.
When you first learn to play, you may struggle and can end up with food crisis, lack of materials for tools, or other shortages that can cripple, if not outright exterminate your entire population. After a few tries however, it shouldn't be hard to grasp the way this game works, and you'll find your next few playthroughs quite easy and devoid of challenge.
Some people like myself enjoy this, as I can then build a village to try out different layouts, aesthetics and mods, or simply wanting to see how fast I can expand on certain terrain settings. For others, this may be a letdown, due to the lack of challenge and depth as was stated earlier.  In its vanilla form, this game lacks research trees and technological advancement other than the use of slightly better tools by your villagers. The access to new tools or buildings are gated by resources rather than research progress.
The impact of food and happiness are also simplistic. You unlock new crops, fruits, vegetables and livestock via trade with an AI boat that comes and goes, and the food variety do not do much other than give better health rating due to a varied diet. Your villagers have a simple happiness meter that may decrease due to death of villagers without graveyards, or working in poor conditions such as in mines, and will increase from the influence of churches and pubs.
This game has a modding community, and there are sizeable mods that can add more flavour to the game via additional building tiers, more building designs, more types of resources and livestock, and upgradeable mining shafts. However, the core gameplay is almost always the same - you manage your villagers' roles, resources, and development. If the core gameplay is not appealing to you, the mods may not be a convincing factor in purchasing the game.
Apart from less-than-occasional crashes (thankfully I save quite often, and the game has autosaves), I have not experienced any glaring or gamebreaking bugs as of late 2014. The developer patched the issue faced before in which villagers travel too far to complete far-away buildings, causing them to starve/freeze to death during their journey. That has since been patched, and currently I see little to no problem while playing the game.
Because of its simplicity, I really liked playing Banished as a chill-around relaxing game (after I learned not to starve my entire village). Banished does not have much depth in terrain management, or traffic (villagers won't be slowed down by large crowds using the same path), nor does it have much in aspects of crime, societal culture or waste management. There is no combat in the game either.
If you are looking for a more simplistic city- (or medievalish village-) building game that you can play in a relaxed manner without having to worry about combat or conflict, or some of the deeper aspects that exist in other city builders, Banished might just be a game you're looking for.

Positively surprised at first glance, I found that the dynasty system is in fact boring and useless. Throughout the game I prefered to stick to my first El Prez, than give power to the other dynasty members. This could be made much more entertaining by making the characters age, or even die over time, forcing the player to change El Presidente.
As pointed out by other players, the game does not feature any building variety (apart from gardens). The player can build an entire city with exactly the same buildings; for example, the tenement from 1930 (World Wars Era) will look the same as the one built in the next Era. Take heed: if you prefer your nights peaceful, you might want to think twice about purchasing this game. THE ZEE WILL HAUNT YOU. You might lose sleep from the vivid images of terror the stories of the zee will bring--of walls of knives and ungodly feasts and the vicarious fear of both the total absence and a too-easy excess of light--but what will stick with you most as you try to fall asleep is the question: have I done the right thing?
This is a game of immersion and perspective. You will know what it means to feel helpless in your power over another's fate. You will question your loyalties. You will sell your soul--or somebody else's--for a faster engine. You will have to find... something to eat... after your rations run out and you're nowhere near any port that sells food. You will consider genocide. You will witness terrible rituals of death and find yourself saying, "That kind of makes sense."
And then after you close the game, after the pretty art and music and the even prettier words are gone, you will ask yourself: how much of the Captain was really me? And you will lay the Unterzee right next to the real world, look at them both and wonder: how much different, really, are their moral shades of grey from each other?
Some more practical things to think about before playing this game: the stories are great, but you will have to do a ton of reading, and if that isn't your thing, you will get very bored. There are no real tutorials, and you will have a hard time understanding how to go about in the beginning. The choices can also get confusing as some are permanent, while others may be revisited. A tip: if the Gazeteer tabs are greyed out while you are being presented with choices, then the "Go" button will require you to make a more or less permanent decision.
While this is not exactly an action game, you will need to be very careful as you steer your ship, and it will require 100% of your attention and quick reflexes. It's a good counterbalance to what some might consider the "walls of text" aspect of the game.
The music is beautiful and really drives up the tension: hearty and upbeat, sinister and eerie, exotic or trippy. It complements the Lovecraftian artstyle perfectly, and both create an atmosphere that will keep you in the Unterzee for hours (that's another thing: this is a game where you will have to invest long stretches of time at a time to be enjoyable).
One thing that I feel might be lacking is a way to keep notes in-game. There are a lot of stories to keep track of at any given time, and the Journal is a lot of times not sufficient in helping you remember story and area details.
So... will you wither from the weight of your questions or, like one from Whither, delight in them?

"The Zee," the man says, smelling of salt. "There is no place in all the earth as terrible as the Zee. More men have died by the zee then I can count, and yet more throw themselves to it's mercy," he laughs, "and it has little of that, I assure you." As he speaks, you begin to notice things; a stub where a finger should be, a massive scar across his shoulder, a tattoo, faded with time. Yet all of these seem secondary to the glint in his eye, a crazed wanderlust that sings of distant shores in dulcet tones. "I have seen things, out on the Zee. I have witnessed zaylors, stolen from the deck of a ship by tentacles so large that they dwarf the bazaar, I have seen the place where the drownies sing in their underwater catherdrals, I have even seen the place of dreams, Irem, where men deal in secrets and stories." He is smiling now, reveling in any audience willing to listen to his old zee-stories. "Why I could tell of you my runs as a merchant from Mt. Palmerston to Khan's Shadow, selling devil-bone dice to those old barbarians for a profit you wouldn't see here in Lodon. Why I've even seen..." He's paused, and his smile begins to fade. "I've...I've seen..." He shivers, and he turns his old eyes on you. "Don't go to zee. You will not escape. You can't escape. It promises wealth, but it will only swallow you whole. The zee has eaten my father, his father, and his father before him. It almost ate me." He shivers once more, before looking east, towards the great, black Unterzee, and its strange and shifting isles. "And somehow, it still calls me." He shakes his head. "It will eat me yet, mark my words. It will eat me yet..."

Does that make any sense? Anyway, that is how the story of your adventures as an Unterzee captain begins in Sunless Sea. First there was Tropico.
Then there was another one of it.
Then there was a 3D one of it.
Then there was another one of that.
This is another one of the 3D one.
Now I would imagine that most people who have rad this far will know that Tropico is amoderately amusing city builder / dictatorship simulator with a distinctly caribean flavour. And most of them will have at least tried one of the prequels, and yes to use a rather obvious cop out, if you liked them, then you will like this. If you didn't, the you won't.
The question really becomes, is there enough new material to jutify shelling out for, what is really, the same bloody game all over gain. Are Kalypso simply doing a FIFA and gouging their fanbase?
Well the single player campaign is a not unlikeable mix of pop culture and zeitgeist meme pastiches which holds together more effectively than the sort of rubbish that strategy games typically breach trading standard regulations by calling a "story". There is a not so subtle difference from previous games where instead of being installed on a new island for each "level", you select between two different islands and every decision you make will carry over throughout the story.
Its an interesting dynamic, making you consider carefully each and every decision, though it can make subsequent levels really easy, or really hard, depending on how you performed throughout the story. Liberally dot guard towers around the island, and the "Island Invasion" level (erm spoiler?!?) becomes a cakewalk,tank your ecconomy in the first level and you maywell be struggling for the rest of the game, or at least until the next island section is unlocked.
However the "campaign" is short. A lot shorter than previous games, with a literal handful of islands to play on and a run time of maybe 15 hours. This sort of playtime is pretty much a given now for a FPS campaign, but strategy gamers tend to expect a bit more.
That said, there is still the sandbox mode, which will generate an infinite number of islands to continue your thirst for megalomania upon.
The main substance of the game, the actual building, has been much improved in a variety of ways. Farms now show exactly how much space they will actually farm, and whilst you can still build on their land, this will have a subsequent impact on their production levels. It does make it much easier to judge exactly how close to the sugar plantation you can build the bunkhouse for its workers.
You can also assign managers from the general population to buff most buildings, increasing productivity, or happiness or even the standard of localhousing for example. Buildings can also be upgraded as time progresses increasing the customisation options available to you. And indeed time does now march on, with options only being unlocked once a certain timeframe has been reached.
Trade is also greatly improved, no longer reliant on simply shipping goods off the island, you can build a fleet of trade ships to export specific goods at inflated prices, or turn your island into a modern day Japan, importing cheap raw resources and processing them into more lucrative luxery goods for export.
The big draw that Kalypso has made a big thing of is the "dynasty" system, which I cannot help but think of as an attempt to tap into the cult status of Crusader Kings. Unfortunately its the weakest new adition and really a bit of an abject failure. The characters in your dynasty simply exist to give you an alternative character to play as.
They don't age, or die, they don't enact their own plans to overthrow your rule, or assasinate their older siblings in order to inherit the presidency (eh? Presidency is inherited, just ask the Bush's!).
Its a bit like Nick Clegg.
They don't really do anything, they are just there.
Still, you are free to completely ignore them.
So thats alright then.
Tropico 5 is certainly a good game, I'd go so far as to say one of the best city builders currently available, and certainly the best entry in the franchise. If you haven't played the franchise since the second game, then its an easy recommend (provided you liked it. NATCH).
BUT
Even with the new additions, it really is just tinkering around the edges. It looks the same and plays the same as 4, and with the reuse of many building models and music remaining unchanged since the third game, a convincing argument could be made that you already paid for the game.
Twice.
It also seems to have been released with fewer building choices than either three or four, and theories of a DLC gouging plan cannot really be dismissed out of hand as the paranoid ramblings of deranged conspiracy theorists.
Now if you will excuse me, whilst my body may well be freezing its extremities off, at least my mind can be whisked away to, well if not a tropical paradise, a close approximation of. After all, I'm running it!

I'm a pretty big fan of games of this kind. I grew up playing the different versions of Sim City.
I'm also a big fan of Tropico 3 and 4, and bought this game on sale. Even on sale, I can't really recommend it and here's why:
They haven't fixed the most important problem.
If you've played Tropico extensively, like I have, you've run into the problem with road congestion. It has not been fixed. You must plan out very meticulously your road network from the VERY beginning of the game. Each subsequent story mission builds upon the progress you've made in previous missions. You use the same Island and city as before (there's 2 different islands, and thus two different cities). If you're not very careful, you'll end up like I did, 6 or 7 missions in without the means to really go in and rework everything, and it's not until that far in that the problem becomes very large and difficult to solve.
If you have a diverse economy, which is actually very easy to achieve in Tropico 5, it's not difficult to make quite a lot of money that can be invested into infrastructure, but the problem for me doesn't lie in having to rework infrastructure, it's that I'm working to circumvent poor coding (the road system I mentioned earlier) that has been in every Tropico game I've ever played.
Road management is a part of the game, I'm fully aware, but there is no management options. Tropicans will take the shortest route available. There are no one way street, or high volume highway like options. I can't do anything but build a singular type of road which nearly every building needs to be attached to. The only way to be completely efficient is to have EXTREMELY ugly circle roads that never connect to each other except by adjacent garages. Someone actually developed a circumvention system for Tropico 3 (which has persisted into 4 and 5 out of necessity). If you google "road congestion tropico", I'm sure you can find more information (if interested).
This Tropico is a little bit more challenging than the last ones in terms of Rebels and their threats. They attack much more often, and your army cannot be controlled beyond telling them which buildings you value the most. Rebels will attack from multiple points and your army sallies out of wherever you built your buildings. Since all you have is men on foot and eventually very slow tanks, the rebels will usually destroy several buildings before your army can even respond.
Rebels are also able to target your army squads while you are unable to control and choose targets for your own. What this means is that your army will be running to defend a certain building, and the rebels will follow along and continually fire at them while your army DOES NOT RETURN FIRE, and simply dies. It's EXTREMELY frustrating.
There's also a huge problem that persists with housing.
As you might remember, people get old and retire and their income falls. There are children, unemployed and students as well. In Tropico 5, Houses now have budgets like employment buildings do. It is essentially the rent charge.
NO MATTER WHAT JOB PEOPLE HAVE, most of them will not live in a house because it is too expensive. Even if you've maximized the budget (and thus their pay) at their place of employment. You must lower the rent to a single point (out of a maximum of 5) in order to allow people to live there. YOU MUST turn on social security. Otherwise you will CONSTANTLY be attacked by rebels. YOU MUST do this for every housing building.
People will also not live in a building that is too far from where they work. Couples make a decision based upon both their work locations. If not satisfied with how close they live to work, they toss up a shack!
It is not uncommon to see shacks right beside housing units that are completely empty.
For some ungodly reason, Tenements lose housing value over time. There is no option to remedy this. This only way to circumvent is to completely destroy the building and replace it. It would have taken a few lines of code to add a renovate option, but no, they didn't do that. I wouldn't be surprised if it was in a DLC.
The graphics are improved, a lot of the mechanics of the game have been streamlined, but not fixed. There are improvements here, although the dynasty system is tacked on, stupid, and useless.
It feels like it's still Tropico. I don't know what it is that provides that feeling, the enjoyment of the game, and the music (I've always really enjoyed it) or the same bloody bugs that have persisted forever without attention.

First off, unless you get this game for free or extremely cheap, I would strongly recommend you look to other alternatives - if you need to whet your appetite for rogue-likes, you need to focus on the endless amount of much better choices.
If you like rogue-
, comical art styles, and broken achievements, then you might enjoy this game. You probably won't.
The aesthetics are mediocre - the art style is very reminiscent of the old-school Robotron. After playing over 45 hours of Binding of Isaac, it is a bit difficult not to think of this as a very cheap, very bland clone attempt. The music and sounds are decent, but get annoying fairly quickly. The level design doesn't really change, and the only random element seems to be the item drops from containers - which are very basic, like score multipliers, temporary attack power-ups, etc. Initially, I decided to keep this game instead of trading for it (got it in a bundle) because it looked like Binding of Isaac, however, be warned that the doorways on each side are merely spawn points for enemies. The game is linear, which is why I refer to it as a rogue-
. You can also buy a save point when you reach the store (occurs every few levels).
The controls are basic, keyboard to move and mouse to aim/fire. You can use the number keys or mouse wheel to cycle through your weapons, however, one thing that irritated me is the one-way direction of item cycling when you use the mouse wheel - if you happen to overshoot the weapon you want, you'll have to cycle all the way back to it. The E, R, and T keys are used to activate spells (so long as you have one unlocked and enough mana), but they feel awkward when you try to press them. I recommend using a controller if you have the option. There is no tutorial, and the learning curve is minimal to moderate, depending on your experience with rogue-likes and bullet/enemy dodging in particular.
Overall, the gameplay falls short and feels very bland - you start off with a sword and crossbow, and certain levels have more weapons like a pistol, shotgun, minigun, etc. These are miss-able, and a few appear in the bonus levels where you must kill chickens for a higher score and some gold drops. After a set number of cleared stages, you will be brought to the store, which has the same items for sale, including: a save point, ammo for the different weapons, 3 spells, mana/health refills, and even a dog that automatically picks up gold for you. After defeating a boss, you will be given the option to upgrade your mana, health, damage, or speed by one point. I strongly suggest starting with speed, as it will allow you to move and dodge more effectively. The bosses rush you, so maxing out only strength will cause them to hug you to death.
For the achievement hunters, note that a few of the achievements seem to be broken, so obtaining 100% completion may be tricky - the discussion board has a few topics concerning this.
Again, if you have other alternatives, avoid this game in favor of those. The game is a weak time-filler at best, and I sincerely believe you have better uses of your time.
Do not recommend.
Cheers,
DJSF

Overall the game is pretty good. The graphics are nice, the gameplay is varied, and the progression insures that noobs still have a chance against veterans when it comes to weapons.
One thing to note when first playing is this is not counter strike, Call of Duty, or battlefield. This is much slower and methodical.
You have extreme bullet drop, and you must constantly gauge distances or else be killed.
The game doesn't tell you whats a friendly or not, you must decide. Friendly fire is always on.
The game will not help you spot enemies, meaning sneaky tactics are very powerful not only for you but for everyone else. Camoflauge has an actual effect here.
Pros:
Good graphics.
In depth Gameplay and mechanics.
Ballistics that rely on bullet drop over distances. No hit scan weapons with no bullet time or drop.
CONS:
Small, incredibly dedicated community that will wipe the floor with you when you first start out due to a difference in experience. These guys know the maps and distances for bullet drop by heart, but you don't. Once you familiarize yourself with the maps and the bullet drop, this will cease to be a problem.
In game custom map downloads tends to be slow, and the community tends to avoid them for that fact which limits map variety.
The way the game loads means those with an SSD or good internet get first pick on classes before anyone else even loads.

Obludia is a fitting name for the game that it describes. Much like arcade classics such as Zaxxon, Sinistar, and Galaga, it’s a striking one word title that also belongs to an eventual end boss named Lord Obludia who can only be conquered by players who spend hours mastering the game’s controls. It’s the kind of title that makes me glad we don’t live in an age of quarter munching cabinets, as practice really makes perfect in this fantasy themed Smash TV-esque twin stick action game. Of course, the more recent release also means that the game trades in a retro art style for more Flash based graphics and chiptune music for a downright hokey soundscape. Still, what it lacks in presentation it makes up for gameplay, and Obludia should be on your radar if you ever spent an hour in a dimly lit room waggling a joystick.

This game is brilliant.
The game spawns you into a random location on a map, and then the clock starts ticking as you try to survive as long as possible. The catch is not only are you trying to find the important aspects of survival like food and drink, but you are also being hunted.
The game spawns wolves who are just as hungry as you. The wolves will hunt in packs to try to find their next meal, which may be you. This keeps you on your toes constantly as you never know what may lurk behind you or around the corner. It is very unnerving and really gives the game a creepy atmosphere.
The fight for finding food, water, and shelter, as well as trying to fend for your life give the game the desperate struggle for survival it was trying to achieve. The maps are big with plenty of places of interest, and the gameplay will keep you coming back for more!
Oh, and don't die. The game has permadeath, and I mean PERMADEATH. It will delete your save the second you die automatically. Every second is a fight for survival, as well as for preserving all your hard work up to that point. I go back and forth if I like this feature or not, but the stressful and desperate atmosphere it creates is definitely worth it. Pick this game up now! I can't wait to see what the future holds for it already has enough to keep me occupied for months to come :)

If you like the original Half Life, you'll also like Blue Shift.  It's a very similar game, with the same type of action and puzzles (and even the same weapons).  Many of the same enemies return as well, both from Xen and Marines.  If you haven't played the original Half Life, I'd recommend starting there instead.  Both have excellent gameplay, but you get more of the story in the original.
I'd recommend Opposing Force over Blue Shift, however.  Both are the same price, but Opposing Force is about twice as long, and is also a much more innovative expansion, with interesting new weapons and levels that differ more from the original than Blue Shift's.  Blue Shift itsn't bad by any means, it just doesn't add new content to the series in the way Opposing Force does.

This game is completely awesome. Starbound was great for a while, but it will never have the "chase the dragon" addiction this game offers with it's leveling system. If you played Ultima Online, compare it to that with more control. You spend your mined resources on data for certain skills which allow you to build nicer items in that particular field. It seems very class oriented. There's like 13 skills right now as well as 6 stats. 3 armor skills and 3 weapon skills, giving you a fair amount of customization. Your skills allow you to do things like build different vehicles, different accessory buffs, an interesting spin on animal taming where you clone different animals that each have their own separate function, specialize in gathering+passive buffs, similar to UO Alchemy an entire skill dedicated to consumables, and even a cosmetic skill to make your forts look nicer. If these developers know what's good for them, they will continue to add more skills without changing the actual skill system.

An excellent game I was given the priviledge to play in its Alpha stage, despite its HORRENDOUS crashing frequency and horrifying lag that I can only say fits perfectly with the fact it's Halloween, quite possibly the scariest thing I've seen this week.
The idea is awesome, 4 different classed players working together to take down the 1 player as the huge monster, whom to begin with hides, feed's, grows in strength and can then either fight the hunters or destroy the Power Array should you be able to reach the top level 3 of 'Evolving'. I definitely had the most fun as the monster as the sheer thrill of running, hiding from the other 4 players, quitely gaining strength and then pouncing on them was epic! With the idea of unlocking different characters in each class, including different monsters, greatly extends the life of the game and gives it a slightly different twist with different perks and weapons, aswell as the multiple maps to hunt in.
The controls are easy to use and simple, with only a handful of buttons to remember, you could probably fit all the key bindings on a gaming mouse. The landscape and terrain design is excellent, from roaming fauna, to other dangerous monsters roaming around, the maps are excellent, despite perhaps their size, I think the overall size of each map should be increased as I did find a lack of places to run to as the monster but I do understand they can't make it too big as otherwise the monsters would be too hard to find.
Overall an awesome gaming experience I look forward to playing again when it's released, however in the servers current state, I wouldn't even say it's fit for alpha.

I will do my very best to avoid any spoilers... I just finished the game as of writing this so I am very raw emotionally. This is a game that has brought many reviewers to their respective knees. Jim Sterling for instance instead of directly reviewing this game instead spoke at length about his father and his past... and my review will simply be this:
Games are quite able to provoke emotion, much like traditional art. While the vast majority of games do this via death and dismemberment of a cast of characters before your eyes, sometimes all it takes is a skilled story teller to weave something for you that forever changes your views on the world around you. Your views on who people are, what their hopes and dreams... who you are as well, all of that may be affected by this game. It took me around 80 minutes to complete, and honestly it's something I plan on sharing with those around me. It's a game where your interpretation may be quite different than the person next to you, but know that when the screen fades to black for the last time, you won't be the same person you were when you started the game up for the first time.
Do yourself a favor. Play this game, experience the story it presents, and realize that video games can be amazing art. If you give it a chance that is.

Fallen, fallen is Babylon." Scrawled across the wall above a board covered with photographs, these words greet you in the waterlogged, decaying opulence of Adonis Spa after you awaken. Ten years have passed since the surprising events of BioShock 2's opening cinematic, and you're a man with a mission: to find your Little Sister. As Subject Delta, one of the original Big Daddy protectors first introduced in BioShock, you were pair-bonded with a Little Sister named Eleanor Lamb through a love that could literally kill you. Your mutual desire is to be reunited, but Eleanor is now being held captive by her mother, Sofia Lamb, the new master of Rapture. As an altruist and collectivist, Lamb is the diametric opposite of Andrew Ryan, the wealthy industrialist who founded Rapture as a place where mankind could be unfettered by petty morals, the hand of government, or the word of God. As an antagonist, she lacks Ryan's charisma and larger-than-life presence, but her personal philosophy and particular brand of madness nonetheless provides an interesting, if heavy-handed, alternative to his.
Though it is essentially a first-person shooter, the key component of BioShock 2 is its story, and while it features a powerful and compelling narrative with a satisfying conclusion, it is not without its issues. Whereas much of the first game focused on the city of Rapture and the mystery of how it fell from grace, BioShock 2 barely touches on these aspects, and as a result, prior knowledge is required to fully understand what is happening. There is supplemental reading on the big details buried within the menus for those who need it, but unfortunately, this isn't effectively brought to your attention. Furthermore, there are a number of inconsistencies present that are never satisfactorily explained. These range from small, nagging issues with the way certain story-based gameplay elements or characters from BioShock were grandfathered in, to larger problems with your very existence as a Big Daddy. It never becomes clear why you alone among the Big Daddies can use plasmids, for example. And while your pair-bond with Eleanor lightly manifests throughout the game, there is never any emotional connection there to latch hold of--the only reason you have to pursue her is that you're explicitly told you need to find her.
Standing between you and your Little Sister is The Family, Lamb's semireligious cult of splicers, or former citizens of Rapture whose years of abusing a genetically enhancing drug called ADAM has granted them superhuman powers at the cost of their sanity. The years have not been kind to the splicers, who are far more warped and disfigured than ever before. They're also more dangerous now, having spent the last ten years honing and refining their predatory skills and abilities. Most of the splicers you encounter, such as creepy wall-climbing spiders and teleporting houdinis, are recognizable from the first game, but they’re now joined by brutes, who can ruin your day with a charging tackle or a thrown piece of concrete. To keep up with these dangerous freaks, you have no choice but to splice up yourself to increase your potential and unlock new abilities. This means you need ADAM of your own, which is where things get interesting.

Obludia caught my eye as I have a deep love for topdown action shooters, especially with RPG elements and perma-death. However, I definitely by no means loved this game, I don't hate it either, it's just a bit bland at the moment.
(I haven't played the most recent build, but I've included edits at the end to state improvements since the first build, so take the do not recommend with consideration.)
Main factors as to why I currently discourage buying this vidyagame:
-Both the character and most enemies are sluggish movers, but you can always effortlessly dodge them (EDIT: dev has since increased the speed of certain enemies and their projectiles)
-Most enemies just run towards you and occasionally shoot a slow moving projectile at you when in a certain proximity (may not be the case any more, dev is also adding in new enemies)
-Bosses easily killed by spamming dynamite, which is absurdly cheap from the store. Even without it you can safely kite them with almost no risk
-Somewhat short and easy, I beat the game on my first attempt in about half an hour without coming close to death at any point (EDIT: dev has balanced the difficulty as well as added in a hard mode and a bonus area)
-Traps are banal and pose no threat as you can just stand in a safe spot and kill anything before it gets to you anyway (EDIT: recent updates have introduced more challenging traps)
-Level up system and spell unlocking seems pointless as there's no NG+ or difficulty increase and stats reset after the game ends
It's worth noting that the developer(s) appears quite dilligent with their updates and responds well to feedback, updating with tweaks, fixes, etc. within a few days of release, and has continued to provide constructive and well-executed updates.
I do look forward to them being able to make this game far more enjoyable, as it definitely has potential once they add in a mode/feature that provides extra replay value.

Batman TTS is yet another entry to the never changing formula of TellTale "games", where we are still stuck with this archaic engine with mostly ugly visuals, clunky animations and newly added graphical glitches and occasional stuttering during some of the action sequences (and all "previously on" flashbacks). So why do I recommend this game? Because it's pretty much the best Batman story I've seen so far. I really like the new twist on old Batman characters and smaller and bigger changes to Batman lore. It was really refreshing to see those characters in a different light, appearing on unexpected places, looking completely different than what we are used to (Christopher Nolan style), and having this really unexpected story twist with one of the characters halfway through the game.
So, basically, if you are still not fed up with the TellTale Games QTE "gameplay" and want more Batman in your life, I'm sure you will not be disappointed.

If you are after a true survival, not preparing yourself for a zombie attack, a true need to survive from starvation, dehydration, and the harsh bite of the coldest winter, then this is the game for you.
Don't let the early access fool you, this is a fantastic game as it is now, and certainly the best survival on the market. The game has very few bugs, regular updates, and the dev's DO listen to any comments and suggestions from the players.
The game has 3 levels of difficulty; with the easiest option allowing you to play without the worry of any animal attacks, (ideal for fraidy cats like me) so you can concentrate on staying alive rather than looking over your shoulder constantly.
You start off in a randomly spawned location, on an area of your choosing with a few bits to get you going and light clothing. To progress through the game you need to stay warm, find food and water, and if you're brave enough to not stay on easy, a weapon to protect yourself from the wildlife.
You can choose to try to survive outside or look for shelter, to hunt and fish or look for what ever food you can find.
The game gets highly addictive, and I can't wait for them to activate the storyline.
Do I recommend this game? Without a doubt.
As I mentioned before, don't be put off by the fact it's still in Early Access, I have not once regretted buying this game, I've seen a lot of new content added that were suggestions from players and every new update gets me just as excited as the last.
If you are still unsure after this then keep it on your wishlist, keep an eye on the developments, wait until it goes on sale, or just give it a try, but please don't let such a good game get away.

I was excited to receive this game because I love Sherlock Holmes and I really like mysteries.  However, this really isn't a mystery game, and it certainly isn't a Sherlock Holmes thriller.  This is a simple puzzle game, where you are presented with simple challenges and have to overcome them, if you want.  You can skip the puzzles, so there isn't even an incentive to solve them in order to continue the plot.
The game is divided into bare-bones LA Noire-style investigation sections, puzzles (of which exactly one was challenging, and only if you aren't into math puzzles), and boring, awkward sneaking sections.  The story has an interesting premise, but it is ruined by how wildly everyone breaks character making this a game that suffers from having the Sherlock Holmes name attached to it.  The game
, and the ending should anger any true Holmesian.
In short, if you can pretend this is a Hercule Poirot game, you might enjoy it a bit more, since the direction the plot takes works better for the more aloof friendship between Poirot and Hastings than it does for the tight-knit camaraderie of Holmes and Watson, but that one change won't negate all of the bad this game has to offer.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the second single player expansion of Valve's Half-Life and is arguably weaker than the first expansion pack, Opposing Force.
The campaign puts players in the role of Barney Calhoun, one of the security guards at the Black Mesa Research Facility. Soon after Calhoun starts a typical shift, aliens begin invading the research base and chaos ensues.
Gameplay is identical to the original Half-Life with no tweaks or changes that were seen in Opposing Force. The campaign is also much shorter and can be completed in one short playthrough.
Fans of the series will no doubt enjoy another trip to Black Mesa but for the uninitiated they may find Blue Shift a disappointingly short experience.

This is a cute game where you control various bugs which go around solving puzzles and collecting hidden objects. It looks vaguely like one of those adult colouring in books and has a calming (if somewhat repetitive) Zen-ish soundtrack to go along with it.
The main problem is that the puzzles vary wildly in their difficulty. Some are really easy, like the Memory puzzle with beetles with different numbers of spots on their back or the glowworm pattern repeating puzzle. Others are harder and really difficult to do without a walkthrough, like the petal Draughts and the last Beetle Lock (never doing that again). There are also a few weird bugs (!!) here and there, like when my aphid (part 3 I think?) refused to dissolve the little red balls surrounding the squiggles I had to collect (I prefer to call them squiggles to imagining they're gross maggots or whatever). Like, he would spray his green goop and make his little sucking motion, but he just wouldn't suck up the red balls. Resetting the game entirely and redoing everything he did it fine, but that was really weird and I suspect would have put off someone who does not like wasting their time as much as I do.
It would also be really nice to include colourblind options in this game. A lot of the puzzles really need it (like the beetle lock puzzle) and, besides, it's the year of our luigi 2015 - you should be including colourblind options just by default.
I would tentatively recommend this game, because it's cheap and very pretty. I wouldn't recommend paying more than a dollar or two for it, though.

Having played the main story for the Half-Life series years ago, I wanted to play the lesser known Half-Life: Blue Shift.  After finishing it, I didn't find it as fun as I thought it would be but that's mostly because of bugs.  Now the bugs may actually be from the original Blue Shift, it may have came along with the steam port, or I'm simply too used to Valve's more recent games, but either way here are my complaints.
- Pressing the use key "E" stops the player from moving, and pressing it repeatedly makes your character stutter.  If you miss grabbing an object and try to grab it again, you will stutter.
- Pressing the use key on an object and pressing left or right launches the object at a high speed, sometimes dragging you along with it.
- Whenever loading a saved game, attack is almost always on auto, so if you have a crowbard you'll keep swinging until you press attack again.  If you saved with your gun as your weapon, you'll autmatically be shooting when loaded.
- Loading spots can sometimes be near an enemy, so if you're moving back and forth to shoot the enemy, you'll keep on loading and lagging.
- Not necessarily a bug but there are some things that look like you can crouch jump onto but actually can't.
When there are obstacles that involve moving objects around, it becomes kind of frustrating.  I guess the only directions you should use is just forwards and backwards when grabbing things.
If you can get past over these it's not a bad game, but not that interesting either.  I would recommend if you're interseted in another perspective on the Black Mesa incident.

For my opinion on Half-Life as a whole and it's expansions, go and read my Half-Life or even my Opposing Force review so that I don't have to repeat it here. It was Game of the Year back then for a reason and to me it will ALWAYS be one of the all-time greats in gaming.
I don't feel that there is a bad extension to Half-Life, the vast multiplayer extensions and Opposing Force, and yes, even Blue Shift are worth their weight in gold.
Blue Shift has received quite a bit of flack from the gaming community and the Half-Life fan base, and I can understand why it's not as popular as Half-Life itself or Opposing Force, but it really isn't deserving of a lot of the criticism it receives. The only real fault with the game is that it is incredibly short, so I don't feel it's worth it's full retail price, best to pick it up for cheap during a sale, but I still think it's a must-have for any Half-Life fan. This small expansion requires you to think before you make an action and to use your ammunition/armour wisely.
It is questionable as to whether this game is canon to the entire series, some say yes and some say no, but that doesn't really matter, the point is that it is another way to experience Half-Life through a different perspective, that of a Black Mesa Security Guard - Barny Calhoun.
As already mentioned, the game is short, VERY short, so you won't be playing for long, but it is still fun. There are no new weapons or enemies, I'm afraid, but if you have ever played Decay, this is a great storyline to experience as it goes along with that story extremely well (again, Valve proves their story-telling genius).
I don't really have much else to say, so to sum it up in a few words: This game is, in my opinion, worth getting despite the flack it has received, but not at it's full retail price (unless you're loaded). You can not have Half-Life without Opposing Force and Blue Shift. Just remember - It's short and you won't be in-game for long, so don't be disappointed when you reach the end much sooner than you may think.

Now I've owned a copy of this game since before it was on steam and it is interesting to say the least.
While the game is certainly lacking as of right now, it is to be expected since this is after all an early access game. That does not however mean that it doesn't have the potential to become an extremely popular game. I will admit that I haven't really explored many of the features of the game that are avalible because when you run around for awhile just gathering supplies to set up camp, it can get rather boring. But now that the multiplayer has finally been introduced the game will run at a better pace and won't be slow. As I have yet to explore the multiplayer features of the game (somebody should help me with this, because none of my friends own the game, btw) I cannot go in depth on that subject but I'd assume with a large group of players you could create a safe haven for the human population to survive. Or even split into groups and fight for supplies and stuff like that.
The main focus on the game is that eventually you will die. Until that day, you will survive for as long as you can, looking for food, establishing a safe house, avoiding boredem, diseases and mass hordes of the undead. As you progress on and survive for months upon months the power, gas, and water shut off, leaving you to fend for yourself. One of the game mechanics is sound. If you run zombies in a certain radius can hear and find you, smashing windows attracts attention, accidently setting fire to your safehouse while cooking up a can of soup.. the list goes on. It is handled really well. The graphics too, have been vastly upgraded since the very early versions of the game.
With that said this game is a definite must watch. I wouldn't say to buy it as of yet, but if you're interested it would definitely be worth the $15 it's currently listed as. If you're not too sure I'd wait until it's out of beta and has more to offer. If I had to give it a rating out of ten? 6 or 7.

I keep reading that to find it fun, treat it like an exploration game, but nevertheless I run out of fuel, my ship's terror (which limits your time at sea) gets too high, and I feel like I'm scraping for pennies for hours and hours.
The stories and settings are fascinating, but if I'm supposed to explore, why is it so hard?  If I'm not supposed to trade, why am I allowed - heck, even encouraged - by the game's mechanics to trade?  There is a lot of good stuff here, but getting it is too damn hard. I've put about 13 hours into it at this point, and I'd say that it's definitely worth it at the current sale price.  It's obviously a work in progress so there are things that are in flux and there are tweak issues (finding particular types of elements), and what feels like a memory leak (not confirmed yet...the last hour was getting laggy and warping, but the twelve previous hours ran perfectly).
I admit I was slightly cautious about picking the game up for months because the art seemed a bit "fuzzy" (not as crisp as some of the other similar games), but didn't seem that way when playing...maybe it was an impression I got from early gameplay videos.
Gameplay is close enough to Terraria that you won't be totally lost; though there are a lot more items to craft and there's more of everything.  The variety of weapons and the distinction of the armor, etc, are a plus.
The world is alien and more broken up than Terraria...morea bunch of floating islands, some of which are quite large.  I haven't played it enough to distinguish layers and there is some environmental damage mechanic which resulted in the odd death when going to far down but is still a bit mysterious in its workings.
Monsters and combat are more complex and interesting.  One thing I find interesting is that somethings are neutral under certain conditions and then hostile in others (sleep mode?).  You will often be in a situation where you have to decide how you will engage because indiscriminate shooting may aggro otherwise neutral beasts or plants that will jump in your combat and make your day really bad.
There is a bit of silliness, but so far the majority of the game plays pretty straight...just had the occasional polar bear with jet boots thing but otherwise seems staple scifi.
So yes, I would recommend if you like this type of sandbox game and are willing to do your own research rather than have everything spoonfed in one guide.
<Note:  Reservations below are describing the current gameplay experience I am having.  They are just things to note and may be addressed tommorow for all I know.  On the whole, I am enjoying the game and look forward to seeing it get the polish that will really make it shine.>
My main reservation is that, especially in such a "complex" type game with many concepts and crafting being such a main component, that documentation is sparse.  Of course documentation is one of the last things put in a game but even the community is really light in consolidated guides (at least in English...there are other language guides that may be more fleshed out).  This isn't a reason to not pick up the game but it will get a lot easier to play when you don't need to troll forums for basic game info (ie: what are dungeons, what do you need to go there) or how do you upgrade weapons.
Other more minor reservations include "Hmmm, I build this item and put it in my base...just what does it do again?  Perhaps pop up tooltips for placed crafting stations or maybe an intergrated icon to jog the memory.
Ladders, or other ways to go UP besides jump packs.
Some sort of ablative heat shield/air bag for when you jump into an abyss that is many screens deep.
In the crafting menu, have another grouping "misc" for all items that don't fit under weapons or base items or any of the other crafting subgroupings, so that when you want to craft something you don't need to scroll through the "all" category to find it.
An interface to show you what items you can make in list form all on the screen at once (and the ability to hide items that are outdated).  Sort of a tech tree at a glance.
The ability to choose how long info stays on screen before disappearing, and the ability to configure what is displayed.  IE:  I don't need to know xp as it accrues, but I would like to know when I ding a level in crafting what new recipies I had without looking through the browser.
I assume XP bar fills and you get no more?  If so, maybe some sort of on-screen alert so you know to burn that XP instead of wasting time doing things with a full bar.

A fantastic zombie apocalypse simulator, helmed by one of the nicest and most determined developers I've ever seen in the industry.
The game starts by spawning you at a random location in a massive world map filled with flesh-craving zombies (Which you can fully customize... want a shambler? Runner? No problem, the game allows you to change almost every aspect of your undead foes.) after which, you must then search for supplies and an adequate safehouse for survival. The game is very hardcore, with permadeath as well as essentially an insta-kill system, if you get attacked by a zombie, you either get bitten or scratched, being scratched has a small chance of you becoming infected, while being bitten is pretty much always going to infect you (95% chance I believe). Infection leads to a slow, unavoidable death.
The game also has multiplayer, however it lags a good deal for me to the point where it just isn't fun, but I do have extremely poor internet, so it probably will be a lot of fun for those with proper internet.
The developers are also currently working on an amazing NPC system that could very much rocket this game into one of my favorites of all time, it's supposed to be able to generate events that are similar to situations from the walking dead, but randomly!
Of course... being early access does mean that the game has bugs, it is however fairly stable from what I've played so far. But it does have a fair share of annoying bugs and issues, particularly with the UI.
Overall... I can't recommend this game enough, it's just amazing so far, and they're planning on adding a huge amount of stuff that'll make the game even more worth the purchase! If you like zombie games, and extremely nice and helpful development teams and communites centered around your games, then you should get this game.

The game starts you off in the wilderness wearing some basic light armour, a jetpack, and a rifle in-hand. This is one of the better old weapon mechanics games out there. Granted, the Graphics are not highend, however, it's quite tolerateable, even in 2015.
Some of the quick recaps of the game that is worth buying it for;
Weapons "level" the more you use them (thus getting better), and you unlock more whilst playing classes.
Maps are rather large and for a new player, one can easily get lost the first few times, untill the map is memorized.
Diversity of playmodes, meaning there are some for almost anyone who enjoys online warfare.
Servers are running at all times, in case of missing players, it fills them with Bots (Might I add, some modes of Bots are insane, worse than actually playing against humans), which is a good thing when you play on a 32-64 player server. There is always activity this way, and you are never running around on a big map, looking for those 3 other players.
If you enjoy tactical play, this game is suited best with a few friends (or a bunch), so you can actually do some tactics. Most of the FFA servers out there are just "kill this person, ignore objectives" mainly.
A few of the negative ofc would be;
Insaaaaanly slow at starting up, like 1-2 minutes even on a decent computer that runs most games at this date on ultra.
Bots are ofc bots... That means some maps you can just sit and wait on them to line up in a pile. Not a huge disadvantage, more a small annoyance, but again, that's bots.
Graphics doesn't allow you to look that far in the distance, it's awesome that weapons can shoot up to 1000m, but when you can't see past 200m on most maps, what was the point :P
Bushes tends to "grow" the more you zoom in from a distance. So someone you see running behind a small bush, zoom and totally hidden by a fully grown bush all of a sort. Easier to shoot from unzoomed at that point.
If I had to rate the game I would properly throw it around 8/10. It's not a bad game at all, and it does have alot of fun in it, esp. if you got a friend or two to team up with (or play against).

This is not your Justice Legue Batman.  Batman here is a symbol; an expression of the desire to protect Gotham by the true focus of the game, Bruce Wayne.  I was tepid at the idea that Bruce Wayne was the focus, as generally in the comics and cartoons, Bruce Wayne is boring.  Not here.  In fact, based on how I made my choices, I had much more respect for Bruce Wayne as a hero than I ever did for Batman.
The story is fun and comic booky.  The dilemma's for Bruce Wayne are not agonizing life and death choices, but the choices of temptation and the push to give in to our baser desires that every man makes.  As such, Batman has never been more relatable and human as he is here.  Don't get me wrong, when he puts on the cowl, its all business.  But when we're Bruce Wayne, we see a man like us.
I think the full season took me around 8 hours, and I enjoyed it the entire time.  If you would pay 20$ for a good movie, you're money will be well spent on this game.

You play as Bruce Wayne, playboy billionaire and Batman! The story picks up at the the Harvey Dent fundraiser for Mayor. Can you help Batman clean up the city of Gotham or will you fall victim to Falconie, Penguin, Joker and more?
I have mixed feeling about this one; I mean it's Batman and TellTale so of course you are going to enjoy it but it really fell short of my expectations. First, there were a few discrepancies that I noticed from this game to the movies and TV series that just seemed like an oversight or a rush-job.
Furthermore, this was 10-11 hours at best which is about the second shortest game behind 'A Wolf Among Us", but that was a really rich and amazing story. It does feel like this game was spit out of the cookie cutter press much more than the other games.
Next, I purchased this game when it came out and the optimization, bugs and overall polish of the game needed attention. This is pretty rare for a TellTale game! The optimization has been fixed and things have been cleaned up however this is easily one of the worst optimized games of their lot.
Overall, definitely worth playing and buying at the right price. If you haven't played any TellTale I would try another title first to get a great impression. At only 10 hours play accordingly; full price is too much for me on this one.

I was originally drawn in by Morphopolis's vibrant, hand-drawn art. It's color palettes are rich, the environments are complex, and its cast of flora is so lush it almost borders on surreal. It is, without a doubt, one of the most visually stunning hidden object games that I've played  to date.
Unfortunately, those stunning visuals make for unclear level layouts and hidden objects that are almost indecipherable from the scenery. The game's graphic elements encourage rampant clicking and inspire frustration in the player when they suddenly discover there's a whole new area they would have known they could explore if they had just climbed up one particular branch (that is, of course, identical to all the other branches that you can't climb). Many of the levels were aesthetically pleasing, but irritatingly busy.
The biggest flaw in Morphopolis, however, is the movement speed of your character. Your bug crawls at an agonizingly slow pace and is often confused by the clicks of your mouse, causing them to "dance" back and forth wildly. On top of that, despite being able to spot many hidden objects as you advance through the screens of the level, you can't collect them until you've received a task from another bug. The game forces you to walk back and forth several more times than necessary to collect items you already knew were there.
If you can get it for cheap and are a fan of hidden object games I would pick it up just for the art, but otherwise there are more polished hidden object games to spend your time and money on in the Steam store that are guaranteed to give you more fun than the slow, trudging pace of Morphopolis.

I happened upon this game during the summer sale, and since I am a huge Sherlock fan, I had to buy this.  FINALLY!!  We have an adventure/puzzle game that is very involved and quite lengthy.  Kudos to the team for putting the famous bullet-hole initials VR!  It is such an iconic part of 221B Baker Street, and I am so glad that it was not left out.  First off, the voice acting is wonderful!  Sherlock Holmes is not an easy character to portray as he is quite complex by nature.  Kerry Shale played this role brilliantly.  David Riley was on point with Watson.  If Watson gets on my nerves, then I know that the portrayal is spot on, and he definitely got on my nerves.
Gameplay wise, mostly smooth.  There were three different types of views one could use while playing.  I typically do not like 1st person, but unfortunately that is the view I had to use for most of the game.  Switching to 3rd person, a lot of times got Holmes and Watson on a continual walk, and nothing you could do save for smashing a lot of keys, would get them to stop.  In 1st person, there is no issue with sticking or just walking no matter what your commands are.  I loved the idea of actually playing as Toby the dog during one of the chapters, but he also had the same sticking issues, and with him being so low to the ground, it was easier to blow past things that you really needed to see, which caused a lot of doubling back for me through the warehouse.
All in all, this was a beautfiul game.  While there were a couple technical issues, they could be forgiven with this roller coaster of a mystery that you are presented with.  Just when you think you have it figured out, Holmes finds something out of the blue and it completely changes everything.  Definitely a must have if you like mystery games.

The first time I played, I misjudged the resources I would need and ran out of food in the middle of nowhere. I died.
The second time I played, I ran out of fuel while looking for an island that had moved since my last game. I died.
The third time I played, I was attacked by a sentient lump of rock and didn't stand a chance. I died.
Many, many games followed a similar path. I started playing, I made a mistake, I died. I stopped playing for a while.
Then Zubmariner came out and I thought "one more chance". It clicked, and things finally started to make sense to me.
Sunless Sea is utterly brutal, unforgiving and in an unholy alliance with the RNG Gods to make sure it screws you whenever it can. It won't be quick to learn, it won't be easy, but it will be worth it.
It's a slow-paced game which can be very grindy at times, and when stuff does happen you'll spend a lot of time reading. There will be several stories progressing at once and they can be difficult to follow, but carefully plotting a route around the map to tick off as many objectives as possible and make a bit of cash on your next trip before you make it back to London with only a few drops of fuel left and a crew so terrified of the beasts that have been chasing them that they're about to mutiny is so immensely satisfying.
It doesn't have big-budget graphical bells and whistles, it doesn't have 100mph gameplay, it doesn't have the most intuitive UI. It does have atmosphere, it does have (several) wonderful stories, it does have a level of strategy more subtle than "blow up building A with tank B". It has sentient icebergs. It has an officer who can improve your skills by blowing up bits of your ship. It has the option to eat your crew.
I tried that once. I died.
