The game suffers from the path-finding issues and it's hard to control the units because their are no formations available and you have to click on each unit and send it where you want it to go in order for them not to all lump on each other in narrow passages for example. When units bump with each other they might need too long to entangle themselves. This is by far the single most pressing issue I have with the game. Another thing is controlling the battle stances of your foot soldiers, I haven't really come around to learning the hotkeys for them which speed up your commands by not having to click on the unit, then on the stance order button and finally on the type of the stance you want - too much micromanagement.
Gameplay wise don't expect a simulation - it's only very largely abstracted but gives good enough feel to not be considered too arcady. Mind you that it is quite hard on normal difficulty (I'm playing the German campaign).
All in all I give it a thumbs up.

Dear Davey and Everything Unlimited Ltd Staff,
I am writing this review in the hopes that you would find it in the sea of likewise steam reviews of your game (however unlikely that may be). I, like many others, saw your game come out and though "That is a neat idea, but it is a bit expensive for only an hour or two", and then I moved on. Then one day I saw a playthrough pop up on youtube and I watched the entire thing though. It was a journey of both the game designer in me and the person that I am. And at the end I was moved by your game, it changed who I was as a person.
And I did this all for free.
All because I told myself "the game is short" and "it was only $10". But then I started thinking, "does time equal value" and "Would it have been a better game if it was longer". Then, of course EC put out their video on short games (which I would recommend along with all of their videos). And then I bought your game. Now it is sitting in my library and I doubt I'll actually play it longer than I needed to make this review. I did it because I realised that just because a game is short or doesn't use conventional mechanics to deliver their narrative, doesn’t mean that I could just enjoy their game and not give them the money. So while I am writing this to you, and other game developers like you, I am also writing this to my fellow gamers, because I loved your game and its impact on my life. Not only did I want to do my part to help you, but I also wanted to make my stance on the importance of short games.  I hope my contribution will help you make more games in the future, and I hope that more games in the future will have the same dedication that yours did.
Best of wishes,
The Data Doug

A lot of my friends and colleagues recommended Bioshock to me since I liked action horror games (like Resident Evil 4) and RPG FPS (like Borderlands). The critics of this game are overwhelmingly good, with a Metascore of 96.
But I don't like Bioshock.
The story seems interesting at first (under the sea, steam punk style, mad inhabitants of a once flourishing city of progress and freedom) and the sound and graphics quality is quite good. More than once I got a racing heart when an enemy lurked around the corner.
The voice quality (English and German synchro) is quite good, if not a little too polished and "clean". The options you have for customizing are pretty good, also the different ammunitions of your weapons add to the rock-paper-scissors gameplay of enemy strengths and weaknesses.
After a while, the game gets boring, though. The story – albeit twisted and unique – gets predictable, the "escape and save the world" tunnel view gives you a feel of limitation. Sure, you can't really expect an open world masterpiece from a game so old, but there were a lot of games with more linear levels which were still more interesting to play.
The enemy types repeat themselves over and over again. After the thirty-third Rosie and the sixhundredth small guy who you have to kill because he respawned and you can't just run past them, you just don't want to kill anything anymore. Which is bad for a first person shooter.
I always play on the hardest difficulty for a challenge, since most of the games nowadays are too easy. Bioshock however isn't _hard_ on the "hard" setting, it's just unfair. I never had the impression I could've killed all the enemies of one floor without dying; sometimes you just run into a horde of enemies or a mean trap and die in less than two seconds. Even Dark Souls made that better, there you always have the feeling you could have beaten this enemy if you were just better at blocking or similar.
I might continue this review when I have played the game through. This could take a while, since I don't enjoy this game a few hours in.

I absolutely love this game. Absolutely. Love. This. Game.  It has wonderfully simple and beautiful quality aesthetics, a vibrant thriving modding community, micromanagment heaven and pleanty of tough achievements to keep you busy when you get into late game.  You will forget to sleep. Timesink warnning.
Start a village in the beautiful landscape and help them hoard for winter, survive disease, and natural disasters, lay out lovely fishing/etc villages, stock up for trade opportunities, look after their happyness, try to reach a stable population rate. Try to fill the map or find out how large your population can get before all hell breaks loose! Rinse and repeat
The vannila game is a wonderful base game with lots of charm, it throws players right in with little guidance and is at its most difficult for new players at the start and new players first disaster event encounters. Once you find yourself a working stratergy and know whats possible and/or give into looking online for tips its easy breezy from then out, aside from difficult to manage population numbers which would be easier to maintain and plan for with adequate UI.
UI is something that could have been improved on its not bad but its not perfect, and a deeper level of stats available for the seasoned players would have been nice too.
Theres a level of complexity to the game hidden with little explanation, some call those things bugs or bad AI, but i read about them online as actual depth to the behaviour of the citizens and part of the stratergy game. The lack of explanation for these traits can cause unexpected problems for players who dont know to plan for them or understand them. Again the game could benefit from explaining things to players who dont want to discover everything for themselves after 50 hours of play.
Sadly its playtime really depends on the modding community heavily, it lacks little direction other than survival and once youve mastered that in the vanilla game and have tired in started new villages in different maps for the sake of eyecandy  towns you find yourself looking around for "more". The modding community has done a fantastic job creating different scenario setups, themes and decorative packs, and interesting trade and commerce opportunities that really breaths new life into the game. Sadly and not unexptecedly adding mods disables the achievements so i recomend giving the achievement hunting a go before you let yourself loose interest and delve into the world of mods, because its unappealing to turn them off once your used to them.
I do agree with other commenters that the game feels unfinished in hindsight of playing it modded. But in no way let that affect the enjoyment of the vanilla game, perhaps buy at sale price.
TL;DR
Its setting is stunning raural beauty, early settler civilisation style, simple objectives, simple gameplay, lacks difficulty once you undertstand the game, could do with better begginer tips, vanilla game doesnt have long gameplay life but really enjoyable, Modding community have essentialy 'finished' the game and keep it alive long into the 300 hours.  Lots of seasonal based micromanagement :D
Perhaps get just under 100 hours AT BEST out of base unmodded game from even an avid player.

Moreover, every time someone is chasing you the music changes. And as soon as the monster stops looking for you the music gets back to spooky ambient. This way you always know that something is up and you should run or hide.
Anyway, everything else in the game is just great. The visuals are gory and disturbing, the story is intriguing, the characters are believable, and the voice overs are finely done. And the fact that you have to use your camera as night vision goggles adds to the atmosphere.
Overall I've found the game quite enjoyable, albeit to me it's more like F.E.A.R. without shooting than Amnesia or another horror. I.e. Outlast is atmospheric, but not really scary.

Blue Shift takes the perspective of security guard Barney Calhoun during the Black Mesa Incident. Barney would go on to become a major character in Half-Life 2 and its episodes, and playing as such an awesome character brings a lot of fun to Blue Shift. There are no new weapons or enemies, but Blue Shift manages to dish out more amazing action while giving a fittingly different feel from Half-Life and OP4. Playing as Barney makes the player feel ill-equipped and often lowly, due to the limited arsenal and wonderfully condescending dialogue from scientists who give you crap for no reason whatsoever. It may be short, but Blue Shift hasn't a single dull moment and remains a triumph of expansion packs with its intuitive puzzle design, interesting story, and pulse pounding action sequences.

Stalingrad is a typical "Blitzkrieg" type of RTS - you are getting limited amount of troops with that you have to fulfill certain objectives put into missions of a campaign. You do not have the ability to build a base and produce units, however the units you receive mostly get multiple tasks or actions they can perform.
The missions have mostly different touch, but sadly are really repetetive in itself - take a point & hold a point.
The story in Stalingrad is told over course of multiple missions stringed into campaigns. The missions dont depend on each other besides the fact, that you need to finish first to start second. Besides that, there is no real connection between the missions (like which units get transfered to next missions / map; or actions having influence on following missions; etc.). The videos shown in the game are not really connected to the story or your progress of the missions and are just trying to help you immerse into the battles of Stalingrad. The missions have mostly different touch, but sadly are really repetetive in itself - take a point & hold a point.
The combat in Stalingrad is simple and in most campaign missions no serious tactic is needed. The armored units go first if the enemy has soldiers and heavy MGs and soldiers should go first if enemy has anti-tank weapons waiting. Basically this is enough to progress in this game on hard more. Fire fights do mostly take some time, but luckily there is a speed up (and slow down) function that you activate by pressing + or - respectively. Due to the fact, that immersion is rated higher because of sound, the combat feels more impactful and fun.
The game was released more than 10 years ago, so the graphics are quite dated. The landscapes do look fitting, but are mostly repetetive. The units are not that distinguishable as one would wish them to be - the soldiers are mostly with squads while the tanks and armored vehicles dont have any details. The interface is old and clunky, offering not many choices. Menu sometimes offers duplicate settings, ingame you have small icons that you have to read first to be able to know which order performs which action. Sadly with a higher resolution the text gets small, so its not making the interface look any better. The interface has been improved somewhat compared to some older Blitzkrieg games (like "World War I").
The progress is simple and linear - finish one objective, you will be given the next one. Finish all objectives on a mission, you will be given then next one. If it is compared to more modern strategy games that do actually leave you choice how to finish a mission or give you multiple optional objectives to change the course of the battles, Stalingrad definetely lacks in terms of progress. Few points are given for the "rank" progression that you receive after completing missions. Depending on how good you performed, you will receive points. Since there are no mini-games or other activities in Stalingrad besides missions, this rating sub-point is not taken into consideration.
The videos do help the immersion a bit at the start of the game, but already the first mission does not show the city being destroyed of fought for like it was shown in the intro video, so you feel like the game slows down a lot after feeding you some candy. The sound however is nice in this game, the heavy metal music do underline the battles you take and based on the sound the units can be distinguished.
If you do enjoy Blitzkrieg or older C&C games, if you like seperated missions with clear tasks and limited amount of units to perform your tasks, this old strategy game might be for you.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

Disclaimer - This review was based on the Alpha Weekend and Closed Beta builds of the game. I have not had a chance to play the new game modes or the new characters included in the final version. My "Not Recommended" rating was meant to dissuade people from pre-purchasing what I consider to be a 'wait-and-see' quality game, and as such the review is less applicable now. If I ever purchase the game, I will update with my final thoughts. I will leave it up for now becaue 1) the comments are hella amusing and 2) I think some of my criticism still applies to the final product, if the professional reviews coming out are any indication. Thanks for reading!
ORIGINAL REVIEW(S) -
A QUICK CLOSED BETA UPDATE:
(Also, note that my hours in closed beta aren't reflected in the 4.8 above)
Played some more in the closed beta. I realized that a lot of the people saying "you're playing the game wrong" in the comments are nicely outlining one of my issues with the game. There's a specific, pre-defined way you're 'supposed' to play, and the challenge is in sticking to that script. In multiplayer games, the human element allows incredible breadth of strategy and personal style - but Evolve is constantly trying to get you to play it on its terms. By so rigidly structuring each match, Evolve is severely limiting its own replayability. This is reflected in the current pricing situation: it seems to me like they are trying to set themselves up to make most of their profits in pre-orders by bundling content in different ways, because interest in this title isn't going to last very long.
I hate being so negative, because I really wanted this game to succeed. I hope Turtle Rock rediscovers the spark that brought us Left 4 Dead with their next title.
ALPHA WEEKEND REVIEW:
This game ticks all of my boxes: it's a unique, asymmetrical, jetpack-fueled FPS that relies heavily on teamwork (or being a sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, in the case of the monster). Sounds great, right? Game of the year material, yeah?
Not
.
It's in alpha, so you have to take the following complaints with a grain of salt. I do feel, however, that my issues with the game are deeply rooted in the current design and won't be fixed with more content or polish. I would be very surprised if any major changes are made this far along in development, and I think it would take some major changes to fix the issues with Evolve.
First off: GRAPHICS. It's very pretty. It's running off of Crytek, so this is to be expected. Great textures, models, and monster animations. But the visual design is terrible. Everything is a muddy grey color, and they've got the 'dark and moody' dial cranked up to 11. It gives all the levels a very samey feeling. And it doesn't help that the  -
LEVEL DESIGN is homogenous. The maps are all fairly small, mostly open, with a fantastic amount of verticality. There are places to hide as the monster, and good chokepoints for the hunters. The levels are decent, but at this point too similar (hopefully the new maps will spice things up a little). The issue is the size of the monster prevents the level design from influencing the mechanics of the game in any meaningful way. Whenever you encounter the monster (outside of the final defense), the battle will play out similarly no matter where you threw down the 'mobile arena,' with little influence from your environment. And it doesn't help that the -
HUNTERS have few meaningful decisions in combat and otherwise. Your class defines pretty strictly what you will be doing in combat. Use lightning gun until its cooldown kicks in, switch to assault rifle until cooldown is up, switch back, place mines, repeat. The classes DO interact in interesting ways, with the support providing temporary invincibility to one player, the medic healing, and the REALLY interesting ability to tag spots on the monster with a sniper rifle to create vulnerabilities. The problem is that these abilities are so specialized, and you have such a small repertoire, that sometimes it feels like the battles are playing themselves. It only takes a few encounters with the monster before things start to feel repetitive. This wouldn't be an issue if the gunplay itself was interesting, but aside from the jetpacks, it's some of the most uninspired, unsatisfying, console-esque 'hold button while reticle is in vicinity of enemy'. It probably feels great for console owners, but for PC shooter fans, this is some mediocre combat.
The hunting itself is lackluster. For the most part, you bumble around, sort of following the monster's path, sort of just hoping you'll run into him. I suppose this could be better with a more skilled group, or a group of friends who communicate well - but relying on friends for fun is really lazy design. The idea of 'hunting' is so central to this title that it really needs to FEEL like you're tracking down a monster, which it rarely does. It mostly just feels like you're chasing something much faster than you. That's not a super gratifying experience. There are environmental hazards that insta-kill you if you teammates don't rescue you quickly enough, which is frustrating. I guess they're there to spice up the combat, but I've never seen them act as more than a nuisance. Luckily, it's much better as the -
MONSTER: the best times I've had playing Evolve were as the monster. Knowing when to engage, the constant feel of being hunted, the tense moments of vulnerability as you evolve into the next stage, the terror as you're surrounded by a dome of light and can no longer run away... It's good stuff. I can see myself putting a lot of hours into this game in the hopes that I can play as the monster.
CONCLUSION: This feels like the developers plucked an interesting boss fight from a larger game, and then tried to duct tape a bunch of stuff on in order to justify selling it as a standalone experience. If there are major changes made in the next few months, they might make that duct-taped mess interesting enough for this game to have staying power. But I'm not holding my breath.
EDIT: I've thought a bit more about Evolve, and I've come to the conclusion that another reason (and perhaps the main reason) it fell flat for me is the pacing. Every form of entertainment has an ebb and flow of action that keeps the audience engaged, and I feel Evolve was sorely lacking in this department. Even when you're hot on the heels of the monster, hunting has little tension as the hunters, but as soon as the mobile arena comes down tension is immediately ratcheted sky-high. There's no natural ebb and flow, there's just periods of mild disinterest with the occasional intense battle. I sort of feel like the 'mobile arena' is too contrived of a concept, and that there should be objectives during the match to force confrontation. This would allow the designers to control the interest curve and keep people engaged at the same level for the length of the match.

I love the Tropico series *very* much, but I just can't get excited for this one. It feels much more like a run of the mill city builder game, they changed a lot of the voice actors for the main characters, they brought back the annoying radio host idea, and a whole smattering of other poor design choices. The jokes fall flat for the most part, and a lot of control has been taken from the player, and a lot of the smaller details that used to make the series great are missing. Where that's been removed, however, needless complexity has been added. Now you need a library to research technology- yep, a tech tree. Military affairs are much more integral and like many, many other terrible city sim games, it too is bland.  You are supposed to appoint managers to your buildings- but why should I waste my time flipping through all the potential managers to try to find the one that actually fits, only to get a 10 point effectiveness boost?  And if you have a plantation colony, say, you always end up with a bunch of managers for things like tourism or landscaping or speed-cubing or whatever else. I played for a few hours and lost interest. Your island is consistent across missions, which is cool, but you'd best hope your crystal ball is accurate. One mission starts with you being invaded, so I certainly hope you thought to build multiple forts and towers. Overall, it just feels like a shadow of the 4th game in the series. The 4th game, with the modern times expansion, offers a much more entertaining, satisfying game, and you can probably grab it for a small fraction of the price.

Dear Davey and Everything Unlimited Ltd Staff,
I am writing this review in the hopes that you would find it in the sea of likewise steam reviews of your game (however unlikely that may be). I, like many others, saw your game come out and though "That is a neat idea, but it is a bit expensive for only an hour or two", and then I moved on. Then one day I saw a playthrough pop up on youtube and I watched the entire thing though. It was a journey of both the game designer in me and the person that I am. And at the end I was moved by your game, it changed who I was as a person.
And I did this all for free.
All because I told myself "the game is short" and "it was only $10". But then I started thinking, "does time equal value" and "Would it have been a better game if it was longer". Then, of course EC put out their video on short games (which I would recommend along with all of their videos). And then I bought your game. Now it is sitting in my library and I doubt I'll actually play it longer than I needed to make this review. I did it because I realised that just because a game is short or doesn't use conventional mechanics to deliver their narrative, doesn’t mean that I could just enjoy their game and not give them the money. So while I am writing this to you, and other game developers like you, I am also writing this to my fellow gamers, because I loved your game and its impact on my life. Not only did I want to do my part to help you, but I also wanted to make my stance on the importance of short games.  I hope my contribution will help you make more games in the future, and I hope that more games in the future will have the same dedication that yours did.
Best of wishes,
The Data Doug

Probably the definitive WWII RTS. It's hard, but it's oh so satisfying when your plans work out, (or you snatch victory from the jaws of defeat). It's not about brute force. Well, it kinda is. Schwerpunkt. You concentrate forces on a narrow point in the line to achieve breakthrough. Stack armor columns in waves and maintain critical pressure on the main point of attack to achieve advantage by disrupting the enemy's rear. As Guderian said "Klotzen, nicht kleckern!" ("Kick, don't spatter them!")

The Testament of Sherlock Holmes is a game developed by Frogwares and published by Focus Home Interactive
The Testament of Sherlock Holmes is a very pleasantly surprising puzzle game, with a high standard of quality and a humorous undertone. Any fans of the puzzler-adventure genre should easily find this game enjoyable. Once you start playing you will likely find yourself engrossed by the experience
It has a much thicker, richer story aspect than many other puzzler-adventure games out there. I was truly entertained by the narrative throughout my entire playthrough. The interesting plot goes a long way to elevate this game above the standard. Furthermore, I thought the graphics were nice and the voice acting was solid, which reinforces the high quality of the writing. The end result is a very enjoyable game with an excellent presentation
This inherent quality in the writing, atmosphere, and overall presentation results in a game which feels much more true to the Sherlock Holmes brand than the other couple of games I have played that were franchised the intellectual property. The others feel like standard adventure games with the words "Sherlock Holmes" on the title. This game, to me, really felt like what I believe a Sherlock Holmes game should feel like
The puzzles were very challenging and quite fun; though to be honest I lost patience and had to seek assistance once or twice because of how tricky some of them were. Some of the puzzles are doubly complicated because the objective of the puzzle isn’t always made clear. So first you have to figure out what you are trying to do, and then you have to actually do it. This does add an extra layer of challenge, but it also can be a bit jarring
And lastly, something I thought was a pretty cool feature is the fact that you can choose to move around in 1st or 3rd person, or play in classic point-and-click adventure style. Having this freedom sounds trivial, but it is really nice to be able to tailor the style on a whim as you play through the campaign
In summary, The Testament of Sherlock Holmes is a pretty sweet ride. It should appeal to both fans of the game genre and fans of the Sherlock Holmes novels or films (like me!). Give it some consideration if it sounds up your alley

On the other hand, one wonders if this was a game that needed to be made at all, especially as there isn't much mystery left by mid-game and a cursory google search will lead you to video lecture confirming your suspicions: there is no higher meaning to this game besides: "Sudden fame is hard to handle, especially in an internet-driven age of instant, mindless communication".
This is not an especially powerful message, and its convoluted delivery hit doens't hit you like "Dear Esther" does.

NO SPOILER
Story - Very simple, don't expect anything super complicated or surprising. Don't buy it for the story but for the points listed below.

Positives:
-The music is very relaxing.
-The art is pretty.
-Some of the puzzles are pretty fun, and you feel pretty smart for having solved them.
-Nice if you like "find the hidden object"-type games.
Negatives:
-The controls for moving are crap.  Half the time you won't even realize you can go somewhere until you accidentally hold the mouse in the wrong area.  Other times, your bug keeps moving back and forth in the same spot as you try to find the place that'll make it go not just right, but right and downwards.  Sometimes you'll try clicking an object and end up moving your bug back over to the other screen for no apparent reason, even though you weren't clicking in that direction.
-On a similar note, you are SLOW.  Slow, slow, slow, slow, SLOW.  Which wouldn't be SO bad, but since you're constantly moving back and forth between screens (using the same crummy controls) to find stuff you missed, it's just unbearable.  I feel like the game would have been at least a half an hour shorter if I could change screens faster.
-So much random clicking to figure out what's important.  See, you don't actually find out what you need to collect until you click on something, like another bug, or a plant.  Sorta like they're giving you a quest.  Usually it's easy enough to figure out what needs clicking, but other times, you have no freaking idea how you're supposed to progress without taking a hint.
-By level three, you'll start to recognize that the weird orange orbs are gonna need collecting before you can burrow into your next target's brain.  But no, you can't grab anything you know you're gonna need until after the 'quest' is given to you, forcing you to slowly, SLOWLY backtrack through all of the screens to grab them.  I don't mean to sound impatient, but God.  Crawl across the screen a little faster, bug.  Come on!  Hustle, hustle!
-No idea where the "pathways" to the next screen are.  Have fun crawling (SLOWLY) across the screen, only to realize it's a dead end.  Then crawl (SLOWLY) back, not sure whether there's another screen, or if you're just bad at finding items.
-Did I mention that you're slow?  Because you're slow.  SO FREAKING SLOW.
-A couple puzzles are really annoying for the wrong reasons.  For example, the flower puzzle gives you no indication of the controls.  I spent ages clicking around and hoping something would happen, but nope!  It's actually a Chinese Checkers-style puzzle where you have to try and get all but one of the seed thingies to disappear, but without a walkthrough, I never would have figured out the rules and controls.  Figuring out what the freaking puzzle is isn't a puzzle.
-No mid-level saves.  Levels aren't usually that long, but if you get stuck on something and call it quits for the night, have fun slowly, slowly, SLOWLY crawling across the screen several more times to complete the initial collection quests again.  SLOWLY.
-I don't know if I just accidentally skipped it, or what (in which case it shouldn't be so easy to accidentally skip, because I'm not gonna freaking replay that last puzzle just to see it) but I went into the place I was supposed to go, and... That was it.  The game just ended.  I got an achievement, and then I was back at the menu.  Ghosts 'n' Goblins had a better ending than that!
Summary:
If you can get it on sale and really, REALLY like hidden object games, it might be worth it, but there are plenty of free games on the internet that aren't so, well, SLOW.  Seriously, I'm not kidding, it's really gonna get on your nerves.  Don't even think about paying the full five dollars for this.  I mean, I appreciate the effort the developers put into it, and everything, but this isn't worth two dollars and fifty cents per hour.

I feel like I've put off rating this game for a while because I was hoping that my opinion on it would change. Like some new groundbreaking patch would come out and rewrite the gameplay experience and what it was trying to be. Sadly, that hasn't been the case. Banished is a game that really struggles to find its identity in a sea of other city and civilization simulators, and can't seem to come up with any measurable way to differentiate itself and shine among those. If you want city management, you have Cities Skylines, if you want a start-with-nothing builder, you have Rimworld. Gees, if you want a city-starter with a pre-modern theme you have Black and White 2, for heavens sake, that can outclass this game.
Banished has two fundamental issues that limit its potential and keeps as a low priority on my playlist. The first is that it simply doesn't have enough content. You can start the game with your basic warehouse and come to build homes, blacksmiths, tailor shops, town buildings, churches, etc. And these are all great for basic building blocks to throw a town together. Wonderful. However, at this point, the content just stops dead. Nothing. It doesn't teeter off or wind down, after you get through what I would consider just the fundamental basics of a settlement, absolutely nothing follows it to give it character, memorable, or unique identity from playthrough to playthrough. All of these structures can be built in the course of about an hour and after that, the only thing there is to do is to simply grow your population.
The second issue is that it's simply uncompelling for the reasons mentioned above. Certainly, you can keep going and grow your population to 100, 200, 300, but the entire point behind doing that seems to be seeing if you are able to balance your food storage with your increasingly monumental demand through the winter, while slowly filling up the world with mining structures that you are unable to remove after they have been built and depleted. Eventually, something will slip up and you will run out of food and your people will starve or freeze to death and the town will be destroyed. But there's absolutely no reason to feel bad about it because there's nothing in particular to customise or advance or pursue after five or six hours of playing. The aspect of permanence and growing personality and character are so essential to city sim/building games, it gives you something to come back to and something to be interested in trying to add to tomorrow, but that's completely missing here. So there's really no reason to come back to it.
There's really no reason to have started at all.

I really enjoy this game so far. It's extraordinarily fun , if not a bit repetitive. Currently there is no tutorial other than a small video. Gives you the basic idea of how the class/monster rolls. That said, I actually enjoy that aspect. It seems to me that many people hate it, but, for me at least, I thought it forced me to actually pay attention early on. Sure I got curb stomped my first time as a monster, but after a game or two I learned enough to hold my own. I had the same happen for me when it came to the hunters. At first I was lost. I took a second and figured out how my♥♥♥♥♥♥worked, and then after that I was fine.
The Monster -
First off I cannot stress enough how important it is to get to at least level 2 as the monster. Any engagement before that is pretty difficult. Especially if the hunters have any form of teamwork.
Currently there are 2 monsters; the goliath and the Kraken. The Goliath is all about up in your face, ♥♥♥♥ you up with his fist, and just an all-around♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at close combat. The Kraken is a long range ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who only wants to shock your♥♥♥♥♥to death for thinking of living. Both play fairly fluid, and the combat feels well put together.
Hunters -
Alright here we have four classes; Medic, Tracker, Support, and Assault.
The medic for healing, Tracker for Tracking. Support for negating damage. Assault for ♥♥♥♥ you monster damage.
I have most of my hunter time spent as a support, but have played a few games in all classes. Currently the tracker feels the weakest.
Balancing. When I first played a hunter I felt the monster was too strong, and when I first played a monster I feel the hunter was to strong. Then I realized that it came down to how I was playing. In truth the game feels a fairly well balanced. The monster is easy to take down early on, even with no teamwork, but the longer you let the monster go on the harder it got. This also meant that the higher the monster level the more teamwork you need to take it down. The game punishes you as a monster for instigating the fight to quick , but also punishes the hunter for not forcing a fight early on. I found that as a hunter the best tactic was to, at the very least, get the monster down a in health early on. As long as he was low it was a much easier fight, because the shield he has is easily peeled away by the Assault class.
This game is about team work. I want to say that one more time. THIS GAME IS ABOUT TEAMWORK. There seems to be a lot of complaining about the difficulty, but in the games I played it all came down to how well the hunters were working together. WORK THE ♥♥♥♥ TOGETHER.
Performance.
This is something a lot of reviews have touched on. Truth be told even maxed out I wasn't having that much of a performance drop. Yes, at max settings I did notice an FPS drop, but not enough for it to completely hinter my enjoyment. That said, I did drop the game down to high, and ran it just fine. Yes it is demanding, but I have a feeling that many other people were exaggerating the problem.
HOLY♥♥♥♥♥HEREARESOMANY♥♥♥♥INGLOADINGSCREENS. I found myself completely zooning out between matches because of how many times the game had to load. In all I think I usually had about a 3-5 minute wait between matches. I might have gotten lucky, because it seems everyone else was getting crazy wait times.
Pros:
- Very fun

Cons:

Well a Batman fanboy who plays telltale games playing Batman - a match made in heaven.  Well, nearly.
This game has a good story line though it appears to rift off the 'cout of the owls' storyline with a few new twists.  There are some familiar names here and the interesting part is more playing as 'Bruce Wayne' rather than 'Batman'.  This is good because you don't get to play as Batman often.
If you're a fan of Batman, the story wont surprise you and you'll see lots of usual tropes and situations that you'll find in most Batman stories.  I was interested at the way that the game records your decisions and you can see what kind of Batman you would be at the end of the game (100% merciful - I am Batman). «Stalingrad» is best  strategy game, based upon one of
the pitched battles of World War II, a Battle of Stalingrad .
The game takes place during the period of July, 1942 - January 1943
and tells a story about one of the most dramatic episodes of World War
II. Featuring two detailed campaigns, «Stalingrad» lets player take
command over Axis army and lead German forces into the city, then
take command of Red Army forces and liberate soviet stronghold from
fascist soldiers and eliminate the 6th Army of Wehrmacht.
In contrast to many other RTS games out there, each mission of
«Stalingrad» is created with historical authenticity in mind and with
reference to the actual place and time to real events that took place
during the war. Besides, missions are created in such a way that
campaigns show authentic picture of events at the theatre of war
operations.
Although a player is able to start the game as a Red Army commander,
we strongly recommend beginning with Wehrmacht campaign. First,
this will give a proper picture of actual events at the front, and second,
the game’s difficulty is leveled up gradually as the campaign develops.
Opening missions for Wehrmacht are easiest to play, while final
missions for Red Army are naturally the toughest.

You are a boy searching for his missing sister. You wander through gloomy forests, explore forbidding caves and try to escape a industrial complex of whirring machines and smoke stacks – all painted in silhouette against the smoky greys of an old flickering film. It's amazing that such a simple approach can create such a nightmarish atmosphere.
'Simple' is an excellent word to sum up this indie platform game. From its monochrome presentation to its single sentence storyline, it creates a spare, deadly, lonely world, devoid of colour and distraction. You brave yawning landscapes with nothing but the rustling of your feet to keep you company. Large sections of the game are silent but for the occasional drip of water, or a cavernous echo, sometimes punctuated by fractured, urgent music, or footsteps racing into the distance. The only humans you come up against are hostile, chasing you away with spears and darts.
Everything in Limbo is out to harm you. From the moment the scenery come to life when that first giant spider-leg unfurls, a hundred times more menacing than it has any right to be, you're in world that doesn't want you there.
It's a meat grinder, coldly snapping beartraps around your fragile little frame, crumbling the boy into a pile of body parts. It stresses you into making mistakes: you know exactly what horrible thing is about to happen to your little ward when presented with a pressure plate and a crushing device.
Limbo's obstructions are grossly imaginative, requiring morbid solutions: one puzzle's resolution comes when you drag a corpse into a pool so you can use it as a bloated, floppy stepping stone to the other side. When not being chased by implacable spiders with a penchant for skewering bodies, you'll be feverishly searching for floating crates to ride as water rises above your ankles, or plucking the remaining leg off a maimed spider and rolling its body to block spikes and clamber to a ledge.
Limbo's initial morbid world of beartraps, corpses and ravenous arachnids eventually leads you into industrial levels, full of more conventional puzzles, such as gravity switches, elevators and even machinegun turrets. It's around this mark that the puzzles become far more frustrating, requiring precision timing to progress. You'll occasionally be reduced to a weeping mess of tears and tantrums, defeated by a straightforward but deadly puzzle that can only be overcome by getting everything just so.
I spent a lip-gnashing, keyboard smashing 20 minutes trying to run across a length of railway track before a descending minecart hit a switch to electrify the rails. Twenty damn minutes watching my boy judder as his tiny legs failed to make the last jump.
Your most horrific foes are the brain slugs, which drop from above and burrow into your skull. Once nestled in your cranium, they force you to stagger in one direction – normally straight into a pit of spikes.
Make no mistake: you're going to die. A lot. It's impossible to pass five minutes without succumbing to Limbo's sick snags. But finally realising the infuriatingly simple solutions and achieving that bloody jump will reward you with Portalsized feelings of smugness and relief.
It's a little disappointing to have waited a year for this game to get ported to PC only to find keyboard control is locked to the cursor keys, but in spite of that – and Limbo's short playtime (around three to five hours) – you simply cannot miss out on this darkly evocative experience. It has its frustrations, but it's a beautiful argument for games as art.
Limbo is a beautifully designed masterpiece of a platform game, that will chill, challenge and charm in equal measure. 8.5/10

The Testament of Sherlock Holmes is a hard game to nail down as to whether it is good or bad. So I'll give it the patented "Zacryl: Meh+".
There are many moments, particularly in the first 2 acts of the game, where the opportunities to explore a (for a 2012 Indie title) incredibly beautifully-rendered Victorian London are a real treat. And trapsing around 221B Baker Street and looking at all the fun nods to the original stories is a pleasure... for a few minutes. Then the clunky mechanics and occasionally asenine puzzle-solving makes it feel less like a game about Sherlock Holmes, and more like having Sherlock Holmes' name slapped onto a rather dull point-and-click adventure.
The voice acting is pretty good, though Watson (whom you hear more of in this game than anyone) was a bit too whiny and nasaly to want to listen to for 10 hours.
In all, if you're a big Sherlock Holmes fan like myself, it's definitely worth buying when it goes on sale. The game is wonderful when it pays homage to the original stories and keeps to the established canon. But when things start going off the rails story-wise toward the end, or when the puzzles start just being puzzles for puzzles' sake rather than real mysteries to be solved, it becomes a bit of a chore to muscle through.
TL;DR? 6.5/10, Good graphics, decent voices, good fanservice, but clunky and story gets dumb at the end.

Disclaimer/Summary: As of writing this review, I have played Cuphead for around ten hours, beaten the last boss, completed all six of the run & gun levels and have beaten all of the first area's bosses on expert difficulty. I have enjoyed my time with Cuphead overall, and I would recommend the game to anyone who enjoys trial-and-error focused platforming games. As for me however; I do not feel motivated to play any more of Cuphead at the moment. It is a good game that would serve as an effective introduction to old-school run & guns due to its forgiving nature, but it fails to reach the greatness of the games it takes inspiration from in a few key areas.
Cuphead is the newest entry in a line of games that has attracted considerable attention from game journalists and average gamers alike due to its demanding approach to difficulty. Coupled with a striking visual style and soundtrack that alludes to the "rubber-hose" animation and swing music of the 1930's, Cuphead has managed to leave quite an impression on the indie gaming scene in its first week on the market.
The core gameplay of Cuphead is based around traversing a small but dense overworld to fight a variety of bosses, which play out either in the form of a platforming-heavy run & gun sequence or a horizontally-scrolling shoot-em-up boss encounter. Since the player has unlimited ammo, the focus of gameplay is tightly-centered around dodging projectiles and other physical attacks from the bosses. There are also a few run & gun sections in which the objective is to progress to the end of the level whilst managing infinitely-respawning enemies and stage hazards. These sections are optional, but the coins that you can find in them serve as a good reward, as you can use these to purchase other weapons and abilities that can be effective against certain bosses. Once you have beaten all of the bosses in an area you can progress onto the next area and rinse and repeat.
The formula is as a result pretty simple, almost too simple to some degree, but the constantly charming visuals and variety of bosses keeps it feeling engaging from the beginning until the very end. Each boss feels completely unique to the others in terms of its attack patterns and appearance, and although not every boss idea struck gold, there is more than enough here to satisfy anyone looking for a firm but fair challenge. Each boss has multiple forms each with their quirks and surprises. The presence of a ranking system and patterns that can play differently on each attempt of the boss means that there is more replay value than you would first expect from a short game with such simplistic mechanics.
The game's unique mechanical flair is the parry move. Although parry moves are not unique by themselves, Cuphead has an interesting variation on the move by allowing you to only parry in midair, and you can only parry pink objects. Parrying is incentivised by the scoring system and the fact that successful parries will charge your super meter, which could help you beat bosses more quickly. These mechanics coupled with the aesthetic flair of the game makes Cuphead an overall engaging experience that is worth more than the sum of its parts, with a difficulty progression that feels just right for the most part.
However; the design of the game reflects heavily on my biggest issue with Cuphead. Although Cuphead is clearly designed after the high-intensity arcade games and run & guns of the 80/90's such as Gunstar Heroes and Contra, even featuring boss fights with similar gimmicks to the ones found in these games, Cuphead is more of a simple exercise in trial-and-error such as IWBTG or Super Meat Boy than a true arcade game. Although I would say that Cuphead is better designed than its peers, the gameplay is focused on dying to short, extremely-demanding segments with no room for error ad nauseum until you finally beat it by brute force, only to find yourself having to do another short, demanding segment and start the process all over again.
Of course, arcade run & guns have their fair share of trial and error, but even in their hardest areas they would leave some room for error, and the challenge was based around attaining consistency throughout the whole game as opposed to bashing your head against repeating series of brick walls until the game gives up and hands you the ending. Cuphead may have a similar level of difficulty to the games it takes inspiration from, but it is not nearly as punishing by design. You will probably die a lot to the bosses, but dying just sends you back to the start of the boss, and almost all the bosses can be beaten within 2-3 minutes. This means that Cuphead lacks the stakes that a level progression and lives system can provide. The best arcade games understood that running out of lives and being sent to the start of the game isn't necessarily a bad thing - replaying earlier stages can give the player a better sense and appreciation of the pacing and level design, and secret paths and alternating routes can mean that subsequent playthroughs still feel fresh. This approach to design also means that the game is testing the player's consistency throughout the whole game, not just their trial and error in regards to a single boss fight. Cuphead, with its boss selection overworld and infinite retries, offers none of this, making the experience feel ultimately shallow as a run & gun.
There are other issues more specific to the design of the bosses and the mechanics of the game, that sometimes feel indicative of a lack of polish to the gameplay: During the shmup-style boss fights, there is a slight amount of movement inertia on the player ship, and oftentimes foreground objects can pop out and obscure the view of the action. Although these issues never make the shmup sections unplayable, it has to be understood that arcade action games, especially in shmup sections, are based around precise dodging, and this inertia and foreground obfuscation is counter-intuitive to that objective.
Secondly; there is a striking lack of visual feedback on damaging bosses. Outside of their scripted knockout and phase-transition animations, bosses will show no reaction to getting shot besides a short flash of white. Not only does this make the shooting feel dull at times, it makes it hard if not impossible to gauge exactly how far you are through a boss fight until you die, which again feels counter-intuitive to run & gun action sequeces.
Although I wrote earlier that the parry mechanic feels unique, it feels as though the game doesn't use the mechanic to its fullest potential. Only late-game boss fights incorporate the parrying directly into their attack patterns, and in a couple of these the usage feels overly gimmicky. Parrying should have more of a presence in the game other than just as a means to attain a higher rank.
Finally; there is a large degree of randomness in several of the boss fights and attack patterns in this game. Sometimes this can be something as simple as bosses changing up the order of the attacks in their cycle, which is fine, but the degree of randomness can be much greater in other bosses, to the point where the positions of platforms the player has to stand on is randomised. Although the randomness never makes any part of the game impossible, it does mean that certain patterns will sometimes be arbitrarily easier or arbitrarily much harder than usual for no good reason. 100% static boss design can be boring, but in a game genre about testing the consistency of a player's skill, a large degree of RNG is antithetical to the goals and purpose of the game.
Cuphead is not a game to be missed, but its design bears the mark of missed potential. Many mechanics are not as well realised as they could be, and the forgiving, "retry-spam" format of the game is playing it safe in an indie market saturated with games sporting this exact format.

I feel like I've put off rating this game for a while because I was hoping that my opinion on it would change. Like some new groundbreaking patch would come out and rewrite the gameplay experience and what it was trying to be. Sadly, that hasn't been the case. Banished is a game that really struggles to find its identity in a sea of other city and civilization simulators, and can't seem to come up with any measurable way to differentiate itself and shine among those. If you want city management, you have Cities Skylines, if you want a start-with-nothing builder, you have Rimworld. Gees, if you want a city-starter with a pre-modern theme you have Black and White 2, for heavens sake, that can outclass this game.
Banished has two fundamental issues that limit its potential and keeps as a low priority on my playlist. The first is that it simply doesn't have enough content. You can start the game with your basic warehouse and come to build homes, blacksmiths, tailor shops, town buildings, churches, etc. And these are all great for basic building blocks to throw a town together. Wonderful. However, at this point, the content just stops dead. Nothing. It doesn't teeter off or wind down, after you get through what I would consider just the fundamental basics of a settlement, absolutely nothing follows it to give it character, memorable, or unique identity from playthrough to playthrough. All of these structures can be built in the course of about an hour and after that, the only thing there is to do is to simply grow your population.
The second issue is that it's simply uncompelling for the reasons mentioned above. Certainly, you can keep going and grow your population to 100, 200, 300, but the entire point behind doing that seems to be seeing if you are able to balance your food storage with your increasingly monumental demand through the winter, while slowly filling up the world with mining structures that you are unable to remove after they have been built and depleted. Eventually, something will slip up and you will run out of food and your people will starve or freeze to death and the town will be destroyed. But there's absolutely no reason to feel bad about it because there's nothing in particular to customise or advance or pursue after five or six hours of playing. The aspect of permanence and growing personality and character are so essential to city sim/building games, it gives you something to come back to and something to be interested in trying to add to tomorrow, but that's completely missing here. So there's really no reason to come back to it.
There's really no reason to have started at all.

From my earliest introduction to classic black-and-white animation as a wee lad, the seminal "Popeye The Sailor with Betty Boop" (1933), even my prepubescent brain could easily grasp the thematic importance of Popeye using a lovingly blackface-rendered Person of Color as target practice at the fun fair. It's not a real 30s cartoon if you don't get to rock and sock a few Africans or Native Americans and I am frankly flabbergasted that, for all of their high-level understanding of the medium and history of animation, Studio Moldenhauer could make such a flagrant slip-up.

Clearly some effort and skill went into creating this title. The weather/season effects are cool. The whole thing runs fairly smoothly and I only encountered one obvious bug (tutorial got stuck first time through). The premise seems cool; I love survival / city-building type games like RimWorld and The Sims. If the title were Early Access, we could hope for cool new features in the future such as achievements, objectives, lifeform personalities or events.
Sadly, in its existing state, this isn't really a *game*. There is no *fun*. It is more like a limited interactive simulator of low-intelligence lifeforms that have a small handful of activities they can perform that might prolong colony survival. You don't directly control these lifeforms, and they may die performing an irrelevant task as they walk right past a task that would have saved their lives.
In my first simulation, with modifiers at maximum harshness, all lifeforms died. Even though there were four homes. Those who journeyed too far from home, froze. The remainder starved. Starved even though there was a fishing dock. Apparently tools are required for efficient fishing. Starved even though there was plenty of wildlife everywhere. A hunter's cabin and tools are required to hunt. Can't make tools, need a blacksmith shop. Can't harvest resources quickly enough to build a shop or cabin, need tools to harvest resources quickly. Can't build the shop or cabin once enough resources are in place, no adult lifeforms have survived. Once every single lifeform had perished, the simulation was quite happy to continue on forever, from season to season, no interactions possible, until I finally shut it down (*quit*). I could even save and restore the simulation in that "dead" state. In other words, even if everyone dies and you can no longer do anything, you still don't *lose*. Make notes in your sciency journal and start another experiment when ready if desired. Note to self: need homes, firewood, blacksmith shop, fishing dock, hunting cabin, lots of resources - no fun yet.
After a few simulations on maximum harshness, I figured out the right sciency/magic balance needed to help the lifeforms "flourish". They built houses and mines and hunter cabins, etc., and... I suppose they could keep building forever, but after a few hours of status quo, I still didn't see any fun on the horizon. Who cares if they build a well and a town center and the colony grows larger and larger? I suppose some people might enjoy just watching the simulation - hours and hours of tree planting/chopping, fishing, building, hunting, foraging, changing seasons - just wonderful for the right person.  For myself, after running a simulation on maximum harshness where the colony survives indefinitely (there is no *win*), I don't see any point to running additional simulations.
As is, the title feels like an abandoned early access project. I suspect the developers realized that not only was it not fun to run the simulator, it was no longer fun to work on it either. Here's hoping their next project goes better.
TLDR: It's a basic simulator, not a game; not fun - not even for free.

I really enjoy this game so far. It's extraordinarily fun , if not a bit repetitive. Currently there is no tutorial other than a small video. Gives you the basic idea of how the class/monster rolls. That said, I actually enjoy that aspect. It seems to me that many people hate it, but, for me at least, I thought it forced me to actually pay attention early on. Sure I got curb stomped my first time as a monster, but after a game or two I learned enough to hold my own. I had the same happen for me when it came to the hunters. At first I was lost. I took a second and figured out how my♥♥♥♥♥♥worked, and then after that I was fine.
The Monster -
First off I cannot stress enough how important it is to get to at least level 2 as the monster. Any engagement before that is pretty difficult. Especially if the hunters have any form of teamwork.
Currently there are 2 monsters; the goliath and the Kraken. The Goliath is all about up in your face, ♥♥♥♥ you up with his fist, and just an all-around♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at close combat. The Kraken is a long range ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who only wants to shock your♥♥♥♥♥to death for thinking of living. Both play fairly fluid, and the combat feels well put together.
Hunters -
Alright here we have four classes; Medic, Tracker, Support, and Assault.
The medic for healing, Tracker for Tracking. Support for negating damage. Assault for ♥♥♥♥ you monster damage.
I have most of my hunter time spent as a support, but have played a few games in all classes. Currently the tracker feels the weakest.
Balancing. When I first played a hunter I felt the monster was too strong, and when I first played a monster I feel the hunter was to strong. Then I realized that it came down to how I was playing. In truth the game feels a fairly well balanced. The monster is easy to take down early on, even with no teamwork, but the longer you let the monster go on the harder it got. This also meant that the higher the monster level the more teamwork you need to take it down. The game punishes you as a monster for instigating the fight to quick , but also punishes the hunter for not forcing a fight early on. I found that as a hunter the best tactic was to, at the very least, get the monster down a in health early on. As long as he was low it was a much easier fight, because the shield he has is easily peeled away by the Assault class.
This game is about team work. I want to say that one more time. THIS GAME IS ABOUT TEAMWORK. There seems to be a lot of complaining about the difficulty, but in the games I played it all came down to how well the hunters were working together. WORK THE ♥♥♥♥ TOGETHER.
Performance.
This is something a lot of reviews have touched on. Truth be told even maxed out I wasn't having that much of a performance drop. Yes, at max settings I did notice an FPS drop, but not enough for it to completely hinter my enjoyment. That said, I did drop the game down to high, and ran it just fine. Yes it is demanding, but I have a feeling that many other people were exaggerating the problem.
HOLY♥♥♥♥♥HEREARESOMANY♥♥♥♥INGLOADINGSCREENS. I found myself completely zooning out between matches because of how many times the game had to load. In all I think I usually had about a 3-5 minute wait between matches. I might have gotten lucky, because it seems everyone else was getting crazy wait times.
Pros:
- Very fun
- Harsh penalty for no team work
- Balanced (Mostly)
- 8 different hunters  ( between 4 classes)
- Quick games
- Nice Graphics
Cons:
- Load Screens
- Boring Maps
- Repetitive
- High asking price
- Not enough people using mics or typing
- Demanding on most rigs

Adventure game with lots of QTEs, where players' choices actually affect the gameplay- sounds like every Telltale game, right? But this one has Batman- my favourite superhero, so it gets some extra points at start. Points, that will pretty quickly be taken back, I have to say. But more about the flaws later on.
The story is set in the beginning of Bats' career. None of his famous enemies have assumed their evil identities, though one or two already acts outside the law. What I like the most about the plot is the heavier than usual emphasis put on the Bruce Wayne side of things- family matters, business, etc. Obviously these aspects are not completely seprate from what's going on in the Batman world, but this is a refreshing take.

When it comes to gameplay, I really enjoyed the planning part of combat. In some cases when we have to face several bad guys, the game allows us to choose how to deal with each of them, and then string these individual actions into an effective combo. Too bad, that the QTEs that are activated then (and all the others, too) are way too easy- I
died only once during the whole season, and it was only because I looked away from the screen when my phone rang. Similarly, the puzzles are also not challenging at all, which makes B-tTS a bit boring. The last flaw is strictly technical- the games has the poorest animation I've seen not only in Telltale games, but also in most of the contemporary releases.
Still, the Batman lore alongside with interesting main plot, and me being partial to the Telltale productions in general, made it a quite pleasurable 8 hours (single pass, without exploring alternative choices). However, if you don't care that much about the Caped Crusader and are easily annoyed by the lack of challenge in games, this one's not for you.

Its a good game, but it is not the best in the series. You can either equip your plasmid or your gun, which means combat can be clunky/frustrating since you will be accidentally switching from one to the other from time to time. The game also has an unusual difficulty curve as the game is at its most difficult through the first couple levels. Once you get the research camera to add damage bonuses, it gets much easier. I've not played on Hard so I can't comment on what the difficulty is like there. The section where you get the big daddy suit is the most annoying part as it is part escort mission-part forced perspective through a tight helmet (Bioshock 2 got the look through the helmet much better). In this section FOV is nonexistent. Nevertheless, its satisfying to shock an enemy and run up on them with the wrench and knock their brains out, or incinerate a houdini splicer and watch them reappear elsewhere only to still be aflame. Or uprgading a shotgun to shoot faster and blowing down a Big Daddy before he can even damage you--seriously a good feeling. My favorite part about this game is how deliberately you must play, but this only lasts through the early and middle game. Late game is too easy and can essentially be walked through. Early on though, actions must be planned, resources scavenged, secrets found. The story is interesting though the ending feels too short. The game could've been a few hours shorter and actually been a better game because of it, as some of the missions feel overly long. Still the various plasmids in conjunction w/ the tonics provide for some variety in playstyle and the ambiance will suck you in.

This is an outstanding little game. Sort of a cross between COH/Faces of War and Theatre of War/Combat Mission. It's heavy on historical fact and covers the Stalingrad campaign from the summer of 1942 and the drive on the city by Army Group South, right through to the battle for the city itself. You can fight campaigns for both sides too.
There is no skirmish mode and ovbiously the graphics aren't state of ther art any more. Having said that it's graphically rewarding compared to some of the more serious games where you only move units on a bland map.
Just about every vehicle from both sides is represented along with all types of infantry squads. You move from battle to battle in a type of operations mode, each battle faithfully reproduced and historically correct. Expect to fight for fortified villages and river crossings early on, and later fighting in the ruins of Stalingrad of course.
You even get to use resupply halftracks and trucks, to re-arm and re-provision your tanks. A first for me. If one of your tanks is immobilised then it just has to sit there until you can repair it, often under fire.
Highly recomended, especially for wargamers who prefer historical type games.

I played this game for 70 hours so far, 110 days of pure survival... and yet there is so much to be explored! the Game has huge potential, but now it is crucial to see toward which direction it will go.
I have two different approaches to this game:
1) Pure Survival Experience: in this aspect, the game is wonderful, no objective, no ultimate explanation of what happened, no ending. It's just you, alone, in the wilderness.
Walking quietly in the snow, you look for animal tracks, collecting herbs and mushrooms, you hear, you see, you feel the environment.
and while playing you start thinking: "it's getting late, better turn back and my way home, a shelter, a cave, anything to protect you from wind and snow...and you light a campfire, the night is dark and cold, wolves are howling, minutes, hours passing, pure relaxation.
2) Survival with a scope: after some days of survival and exploration, you start feeling there is something wrong in there, too many corpses, all human activity ceased, what happened here? Surviving isn't enough, you start feeling the urge to explore and understand, you have a scope, there is an end to the game (apart from dying of course).
In the end, what can I say, I love Sandbox mode, no clue, no objective, just you and nature. Very mature and relaxing.
On the other side, what will be the Story mode? will it be another among countless catastrophic survival game that ends to be meaningless and lose their appeal after few game hours?
I hope the developers keep improving the first aspect of the game, Nature, its mechanics, the environment, everything that is moving around you. Story maybe an intriguing part of the game, but definitely, this game is great for the atmosphere and the amazing details of the environment, wind, tracks, sounds, calories, cold, dehydration...
I hope the game will improve more and more on this side

I have very mixed feelings about this game. On the one hand, it's very pretty, and the puzzles and scavenger hunts are mostly fun and clever, which is usually all I ask for in a game like this. The setting is gorgeously done and sucks you in right away. When I first started playing, I was thrilled with this game; my only complaint for the first three levels would have been that the puzzles were too easy, and that's highly forgivable in a game meant to attract players of all ranges in age and skill. On the other, the inability to either back out of a puzzle once it was initiated (short of forcing the game to minimize/quit) or save midlevel meant every new puzzle involved a level of commitment and occasional stress I really wasn't looking for in a casual point-and-click. Since the only two puzzles I had real trouble with were at the end of their levels, I had to redo those entire levels just to get at the puzzles again, which was kind of aggravating since this is the kind of game that's only fun when you don't already know the answers.
Despite the extreme minimalism in terms of storytelling, I was also intrigued by the narrative, and disappointed when there was no real closure to the story. The last level ended about like any other. Did my weird glowy bug spirit make it to where they were going? What was the ultimate point of this strange and arduous journey? I'm not saying I want concrete answers, but some kind of closure would have been nice. It's similar to the problem I had with Lilly Looking Through, which played like the demo to a game I'd love to play in full.
I wish Steam reviews didn't require you to say whether you recommend or don't recommend a game, because there's enough good in here that I'd like to recommend it but enough bad that I'd have heavy caveats. I picked Morphopolis up for ten cents during a Steam sale. For ten cents, if you like puzzles and scavenger hunts, it's pretty good. For the current price, I'm going to not recommend it. Maybe keep an eye on the folks who made Morphopolis to see what they do next, instead of getting too excited about Morphopolis itself.

Day 1:
Plane crashed south of ... somewhere. Came to in a blizzard. Found a rocky outcrop that kept out much of the wind and got into my sleeping bag. Disaster. No, not so much. Wolf left dear alone. Attacked me. Tin opener did no good. Died of blood loss.
Day 1:
Plane crashed east of .... somewhere. Came to in a place I didn't recognise. Walked a short distance. Found a logger's trailer park. Didn't find many supplies, but thought it might be a nice place to make camp. Sadly,my food and basics began to run out even before I'd been to bed. Ventured outside to see if I could find somewhere with more equipment. Froze to death without succeeding.
Day 1:
Plane crashed west of ... somewhere. Came to on a hill, surrounded by trees. Very scared of wolves. Walked until I found a cabin. Seemed remote, but it had some good stuff in it. Decided this time I wasn't going to die after one day, so learned some basic things like melting snow for water and boiling it to make it safe. Still have no idea where I'm going to get something eat, and it's getting dark outside ....
You know what? I absolutely love this game :)
In all seriousness, I must have died 100 times since I started to play it, in weird and wonderful ways and in terrible and beautiful places. I've frozen to death climbing to the top of the Forestry Lookout and in an ice fishing hut on the lake. I've died of thirst, hunger, infection, wolf attack, blood loss and food poisoning after eating raw animal carcasses.
I've seen a wolf bring down a deer. I've stumbled across an old power station which probably contains a lot of goodies but was too dark to explore without a lantern or a flare. I've woke up in remote cabins, in the dead of night, and heard wolves howling and even thought I'd heard one growl at the door. I've thought, many times, that I'd reached a place and point of saftey before it all came crashing down.
My record thus far is four days. I once survived four whole days, which made me very proud.
One of the finest features of this game is called permadeath. I will never get those four days back because when you die your save game is erased with you. That would infuriate me in other games ... in this one it raises the stakes and makes you work hard to stay in the land of the living.
It won't be enough. It's never enough.

I had actually never played this before, so this one was all-new to me. This is the other spin-off game that Gearbox made from the original Half-Life. This time, you play as one of the security guards at Black Mesa: specifically Barney Calhoun, whom you meet and shoot people with in Half-Life 2. So here's his story about how he managed to get out of there alive.
The only real new thing is that since Barney wears "body armor" and not "power armor", you get your armor upgrades via scraps on the ground rather than the energy charger cells or those charger stations on the walls. Beyond that, there's little to nothing new here. The number of weapons is the smallest of any Half-Life game, and there are none that are new. You are pretty much exclusively using "conventional" weapons like pistols, shotguns, and grenades.
This is also even shorter than Opposing Force. Took me 2.5 hours without ever having played this before. That's... rather sad.
Anyway, this one gets a no vote from me. It has even less stuff than the game it's based off of, and doesn't have any cool new elements like Opposing Force did. I guess play it if you are *really* interested in finding out how Barney got out of Black Mesa, but beyond that... this isn't really worth it.

Banished: send (someone) away from a country or place as an official punishment. forbid, abolish, or get rid of (something unwanted).
What is this game? It is a town building game. You view the game's world from a top-down perspective and interact with it like a god reaching down from the heavens. Why is the game called "Banished"? The premise of the story is that a group of people were banished from their home town. However, that has nothing to do with the actual game.
When you start a new game, you start with a group of people. These people are dumb. They have no personalities and almost no free will. They just do whatever you tell them to do, provided the game's AI doesn't bug out. In that regard, they are excellent workers. There is no apparent reason why these people were banished from wherever they came from, and there is no element in the game that ties in to their previous home town.
At first, the game was fun and challenging. Figuring out what to do first, when to build certain structures, deciding if school was worth it, saving up enough food, etc.. But after 16 hours, I had cracked the winning strategy, and I felt like I was just going through the motions. I quit playing the game and I haven't felt the urge to ever go back. The problem with Banished is  a problem that I see with other building type games - the strategy part of the game plateaus after a while, and then the game turns into window dressing ("look at my neat patterns", "look at this beautiful landscape", etc.). I don't care about window dressing, I only care about the strategy. For reference, I quit playing Cities: Skylines after 24 hours for the same exact reason. The only building type games that I've played for a long time are Prison Architect and Factorio. My final conclusion for the game is not to recommend it. There are better building games out there, and the developer has ceased updating this one.

Its a great game if you are the fan of a zombie survival genre. It has a steep learning curve which will get you killed in your early lives playing it. You ever wanted to setup a base at a Gas Station - now you can. You can establish a base anywhere from a self built hut in the forest to a diner off the freeway, some buildings of course are more practical for survival (houses,motels etc). Just remember you need a place with multiple exits and thats has the basic survival aspects. The game itself looks exremely good it doesn't need good graphics I personally feel that it would ruin the atmosphere. But the lighting and the vision effect is a nice touch to deepen the atmosphere.

They were loaded with supplies - I just got lucky but Multiplayer doesn't summarise the game up in hole as its mostly a single player game and regardless on which mode you play on you'll always find it tense!
Survival is key as you can make a character very skilled only to die from something as silly as eating off meat. So try to establish a base and get non perishable food at first, eat all the perishables early on. Try to get a farm setup and a water source, as you'll need it once the Water + Electricity runs out which is random (unless your in sandbox).

An amazing shooter. No need for them to go with faced-paced-MLG-360 no scope grenade throw
This is a fun and amazingly polished game.
PLays slower than most war games, but it is not the BAD SLOW
You have to be patient, and more strategic. This game is very punishing.
In the realistic mode (which is what most of the players will choose) you can kill in one-two shots, but remember, the enemy can.  So it literally gives that grim, dark, nervous and anxiety of what can happen in a firefight.
But play patiently and think out before running in and gunning, you will be rewarded well.
Guns feel like guns. The sound loud and intimidating.  The animations for reloads are basically what you would actually do when reloading a gun, no need to have these flashy flips, throws, or tricks with anything. Just reload as fast as you can to shoot back.
The graphics are not super super ground breaking, but it is very atmoshperic. The light shafts/godrays coming through boarded windows of crevaces make the rather simple graphics look amazing.
And the sounds are amazing. Echoes in the correct places, explosions rumble and really come out the speakers.  Gun fire can be heard through out the maps.
and the screams, groans and yells of the soldiers really give you a cringy, almost saddening feeling.  The voice acting is done really well in this game.  When your soldier is in pain or is feeling confident of attacking the enemies, they will scream or snicker when it is appropriate.
Music is very amazing as well. Orchetrated amazingly (lol get it Red Orchestra and the music is Orchestra HA!).  And it is mastered and mixed very well.
Overall, the pros:
Gameplay done correctly, the time-to-kill is well balanced with the pacing, the balance comes down to skill of the player, graphics and visuals are very atmospheric, sound design is clean, music is very entertaining
cons:
THE FREAKING BOTS ARE ANNOYING AND THE STG-44 OP
but other than that, this game: 9.5 rating out of 10
