Evolve has some truly wonderful mechanics and characters - the way that all the myriad strategy's unfold themselves to players as they become more familiar with the game is unique and well managed on the part of TRS's production. While each match plays on a small variety of well crafted maps, and against similar players, the depth of the game reveals itself continuiously even at high level play given the variety of play styles and characters at work.
It's also important to note that many of the bugs and balance issues that plagued the games initial release are now mostly fixed (as of July, 2015) and generally the game plays wonderfully.
As my original review stated, which was very lukewarm, after a (very) lengthy amount of time playing the game, match making, is still a bit hit or miss sometimes, and can be slow. A lobby system, which I believe is potentially in the pipeline, would serve to radically address this though.
Furthermore, the communication from TRS and 2K has been particularly poor, as was there launch marketing strategy, as has been said countless times. It does sound like they've taken on some of the criticism, though the T2 launch, while exciting, has again had very poor communication as to its actual release window and content. It's clear that they're trying to take steps to address this and are engaging the community.
Don't let these minor gripes turn you off - I recommend this game for good reason - though I would suggest holding off until it's a bit cheaper (currently $60USD), or is packaged with the 2 Season passes.
-  -  -  -  -  -
Note: I've changed this review a couple of times, relative to stages of the game / updates; generally the gist of the review has always been the same though; fantastic game, a few niggling issues, definitely worth picking up when on sale.

Its a good game, but it is not the best in the series. You can either equip your plasmid or your gun, which means combat can be clunky/frustrating since you will be accidentally switching from one to the other from time to time. The game also has an unusual difficulty curve as the game is at its most difficult through the first couple levels. Once you get the research camera to add damage bonuses, it gets much easier. I've not played on Hard so I can't comment on what the difficulty is like there. The section where you get the big daddy suit is the most annoying part as it is part escort mission-part forced perspective through a tight helmet (Bioshock 2 got the look through the helmet much better). In this section FOV is nonexistent. Nevertheless, its satisfying to shock an enemy and run up on them with the wrench and knock their brains out, or incinerate a houdini splicer and watch them reappear elsewhere only to still be aflame. Or uprgading a shotgun to shoot faster and blowing down a Big Daddy before he can even damage you--seriously a good feeling. My favorite part about this game is how deliberately you must play, but this only lasts through the early and middle game. Late game is too easy and can essentially be walked through. Early on though, actions must be planned, resources scavenged, secrets found. The story is interesting though the ending feels too short. The game could've been a few hours shorter and actually been a better game because of it, as some of the missions feel overly long. Still the various plasmids in conjunction w/ the tonics provide for some variety in playstyle and the ambiance will suck you in.
This gane combines 20 of my tastes into one package; may noy be for some but ♥♥♥♥ing amazing by me.

There are some frustrations, due to it being so early in the process. Atrocious load times, Inconsistent hit detection.

Bioshock is a must have game for you steam library, and is an amazing first person shooter with a lot more story than most shooters today.  With plot twists left and right, decisions on what to do with the little sisters you find left and right, and amazing plasmids to decimate your enemies, this game has it all. The controls feel a bit weird and different than other first person shooters today, but it does the job and does it well. The enemies are interesting and a bit unique, even though they all seem to look alike with small deviations, and it’s very satisfying to obliterate them with your plasmids and many weapons you get throughout your journey. But besides mechanics and weapons, the underwater city of Rapture is an amazing site, beautiful and elegant, but with a sinister post-apocalyptic feel about it. And the story is amazing. The ending might not be the best in the world, probably far from it, is still amazing and intricate, with plot twists and characters you really connect to. I defiantly recommend this game, and is worth every penny.

The Long Dark - RECOMMENDED
This one is a breath of fresh air for survival / scavenging games.  Where the popular genre is with zombies or lots of weapons, the beauty of this one is its simpliscity:  You versus Nature.
You are left with a sense of fear for well being.  The unease felt as repercussions begining to roll in on prior decisions made.
Why did I roam the forest...at night...in a blizzard...with poor clothing...and no food supplies...when any single one of these  in isolation can mean "the long dark" for you.
Of particular note are the sunsets.  Yes...  In honesty, its like an oil painting each evening on Mystery Lake :)
19 hours in....have survived 50 days, not thinking it would be possible.  Enjoyed every minute, and still going.  Had to google how to save game...when you sleep, it creates a save game where you can then logoff after waking.  And then resume game next time you login.

If you're a veteran of Blitzkreig you'll know what to expect out of this game.  However, Stalingrad improves in areas where Blitzkreig fell short. For example, infantry is much more useful. They don't die so easily and can hold their own in gunfights.
Also, your units can't shoot through solid objects like in Blitzkreig.
For those that haven't touched Blitzkreig, Staligrad works like this: In every mission, you're given goals to accomplish with a selected amount of units at your disposal. It's your job to use these forces in such a way that inflicts heavy damage on your enemy's forces while you're miminalizing damage to yours. All while completing your goals.
Sounds simple, right? But there's a catch. Units aren't replaceable when killed and ammo is scarce. That's right, you are left at the mercy of whatever reinforcements the game decides to give you and what supplies are available.   More accurate realism as opposed to having supplies at the ready constantly in Blitzkreig.
So you best take your plan of attack/defence very seriously if you expect to last long.
In terms of Story/theme, Stalingrad is a WWII RTS based on historical facts on the invasion of Stalingrad during WWII. You can play as the Nazi's or the Red Army in two lengthy campaigns.
It's a good game that strives to improve upon  where Blitzkrieg fell short and certainly will scratch that hardcore strategy gaming itch.
There is only one complaint I have with this game. The music. It sucks and doesn't fit at all. I can understand maybe if they were trying to make this game stand out. But the gameplay already does that for Stalingrad. We don't need some really low-quality rock music blaring in our ear drums to appreciate good strategy gameplay. You'll want to mute it and play some good old Blitzkreig music or WWII themed music instead.

Where's my Sunday?
Well, I started out in the woods. Luckily found a cabin real soon, gathered its supplies and tried to figure out the mechanics. Sprinted through the woods again, taking too long and halfway freezing to death. Then, I finally spot a cabin heavenly towering on a small hill. A hunter's cabin? I find some rifle ammo, a rifle repair kit and...an empty rifle rack. No rifle hidden elsewhere. I find one in the snow later though, and shoot a wolf even while shaking hard. I go on, finding rail tracks, being attacked by a wolf and noticing that I've been sprinting too much again. Seems to tire me a lot faster, I should walk instead. Due to the comparably warm weather, I decide to sleep real quick.
...Then I died. :|
The long run I just finished consisted of filling a garage with everything I could find in all the cottages along the shore of a huge lake. Sleeping multiple days in a row and indulging myself in feasts while waiting for the gathered leather to dry, I slowly started running out of supplies. I decided to go on a last journey. I filled my pack with 5 litres of water, tons of food, newly sharpened tools and matches. I took the other way of the road, where I haven't come upon a dead end yet, and found myself in a new area. This one I passed real quick since it seemed to be quite desolate, and I soon found a passage through a mine.
I didn't bring a lantern.
I somehow navigated myself through the corridors with matches, while being intimidated by random sounds and the creaking of beams, urging me to leave this place as fast as possible. I found a piece of coal on the way and abandoned miner's tools. Finally I saw light, it was the exit! Oddly, this place was just as desolate. After running away from wolves, I finally found my resting place.
A stone church.
I found a likewise lonely, but frozen, soul sitting on a bench, whom I'd join soon, too. I found some ammo, but no use without a rifle, took apart the planks lying around and started a fire inside a conveniently placed barrel inside the church walls. I ate, drank, collected more firewood from outside the walls when it wasn't too cold, repelled wolves with my mightly barrel of fire, and just enjoyed those last few peaceful days. Four days passed, I still had two litres of water, enough food to go another two days, but no immediate firewood sources except the scraps worth another four hours.
And one match left.
I looked outside, slept for another few hours at uncomfortable temperatures, and the night was about to set in. I started the fire, made it as bright as possible, threw that lump of coal I found in the mines in, and ate a warm meal. Slept for another three hours. Cooked up another warm, final meal with the remnants of the fire, and went to sleep again. Then I woke up, freezing. I ate and drank until satisfied.
...And then went to sleep again.
Then I took 30 minutes trying to throw myself at a bear and walking too long on thin ice. Results were as expected.
Not a significant enough improvement over Tropico 4 to warrant an additional purchase.

I am going to continue talking about the game, but highly recommend you just dive in without reading too much into it.
This game is a set of games made by a single developer, none of which were released. A narrator walks you through small projects, and attempts to explain the creation of them. This is how the story unfolds, by changing emotions portrayed through the atmosphere of the various games you play.
The narration through this is really quite incredible. In fact, everything ties itself together very well into a cohesive story, even though you are in drastically different games throughout your playthrough.
There is also a very good representation of timelines, as the games improve in quality over time. Overall, everything was just really well done, and very well polished.
I can't remember how much I paid for this game, perhaps I paid full price, perhaps it was through some bundle somewhere. Regardless, it was definitely worth it.

Lately I've been holding off on reviewing many things, due to the nature of many games being worked on continuously and things changing very fluidly.
Today I write a big thumbs up for the Tropico 5 team for pulling through on two things that many in the community thought they had ripped us off on.
The first, prisons. Why these weren't there at launch is beyond me, considering they were in Tropico 3 & 4, the community thought perhaps we would get nickled and dimed for a prison DLC. The dev team to the surprise of many, at patch 1.08, have hadded the prison and the ability to arrest citizens for FREE.
In addition to this, the second large complaint was the 2000 population limit. Tropico 5 offers various huge Islands for the players to build on, much of which would stay empty due to the low population limit. Not to mention the horrible side effect of this limit and multiplayer - in which the total cap was divided among all players. New with patch 1.08 is the ability to change the max population anywhere between the original 2000, and the new high limit of 10,000.
I have to say I am very happy to see the devs change their stance on the population cap after community feedback, and would highly recommend this game to anyone. It's done a lot for the series, and is very unique in its approach compared to T3 & T4. Not to mention the devs, while a little slow on the action point here, nontheless pulled through for the community.
With my restored faith I may just buy the large upcomming DLC at full price :)

Banished: send (someone) away from a country or place as an official punishment. forbid, abolish, or get rid of (something unwanted).
What is this game? It is a town building game. You view the game's world from a top-down perspective and interact with it like a god reaching down from the heavens. Why is the game called "Banished"? The premise of the story is that a group of people were banished from their home town. However, that has nothing to do with the actual game.
When you start a new game, you start with a group of people. These people are dumb. They have no personalities and almost no free will. They just do whatever you tell them to do, provided the game's AI doesn't bug out. In that regard, they are excellent workers. There is no apparent reason why these people were banished from wherever they came from, and there is no element in the game that ties in to their previous home town.
At first, the game was fun and challenging. Figuring out what to do first, when to build certain structures, deciding if school was worth it, saving up enough food, etc.. But after 16 hours, I had cracked the winning strategy, and I felt like I was just going through the motions. I quit playing the game and I haven't felt the urge to ever go back. The problem with Banished is  a problem that I see with other building type games - the strategy part of the game plateaus after a while, and then the game turns into window dressing ("look at my neat patterns", "look at this beautiful landscape", etc.). I don't care about window dressing, I only care about the strategy. For reference, I quit playing Cities: Skylines after 24 hours for the same exact reason. The only building type games that I've played for a long time are Prison Architect and Factorio. My final conclusion for the game is not to recommend it. There are better building games out there, and the developer has ceased updating this one.

I'll start by saying that this game very much follows the standard Telltale formula.  If you like Telltale games, you'll probably enjoy it.
That said, following the standard Telltale formula makes this fail as a Batman game.  There are several reasons for this.  One is the practice of putting the main character constantly in situations that couldn't have been anticipated.  This normally works fine, but for Batman it doesn't make very much sense.  Part of what makes Batman/Bruce Wayne so formidable is his strategic mind and overall intellect.  Here, he's blindsided so frequently that it's just hard to believe this version of Batman.  On top of that, Batman's overall behavior while wearing the cowl doesn't fit the character.  He'll charge headlong into a group of three or four armed guys and beat them up with QTEs, where he should be sneaking around and taking them down one or two at a time.
Also in the narrative department, Telltale have taken several creative liberties with established characters.  This is partly done to mess with people who know the Batman ethos very well, tempting them to trust characters who are well established as good people, while in this game they may be much more sinister than their comic book counterparts.  Some of this works, but I find it disloyal to the source content, and it would've been better if Telltale could've created more original characters to flesh out their plot rather than shoehorning established characters into places they don't fit.
There are also a few technical issues here that detract from the experience.  I played almost a year after the release, and throughout one playthrough I experienced four or five crashes.  There's also some frame hitching here and there, and sometimes characters' lips don't move when they speak.  Finally, the entire game is played in weird letterboxed aspect ratio.  For people on 16:9 monitors, this means the entire game is letterboxed.  For people on 21:9 monitors, this means that the entire game is letterboxed AND pillarboxed, instead of just taking up more of the screen.  It's a small issue, but it's really damn annoying especially on 21:9 monitors where it seems like half your screen is black.

I wanted to completely 100% the game before I made a review. Before I get into anything, I want to thank the developers for extending the game past the original length of the game, thus giving it more substance.
Now into the review!
I will go into detail on three things: quality, quantity, and replayability.
QUALITY:
It is obvious that the animation is smooth, but the gameplay is smooth as well. I have only encountered a handfull of minor bugs and exploits throughout the game. Other than that, every death felt like I deserved it. Even at times when the game had thoroughly tossed my salad, the playful and fun animation kept me from getting genuinely frustrated. It is obvious that they made every effort to replicate a 1930's feel. I actually found myself thinking that the game came out in 1930 so I'd say they nailed that on the head. The filter on the screen to make things glow and color bleed like an old timey cartoon certainly made the 1930's-feel more authentic. It takes more than just the drawing style to have that genuine old-timey look. As for the variety, every boss and enemy have unique character qualities, death animations, behavior, and attack patterns. Each boss is so memerable I could probably name them all off the top of my head. And since the game is relatively short, it's easy to remember the whole game and enjoy it in its entirety.
The major bosses in this game really want you dead. To call this game a bullet hell is not entirely accurate, as the projectiiles, rather scattered clumsily, are methodically placed so that you will dodge out of the way of one thing into another. You cannot stand still anywhere, as you must keep moving and dodging in order not to get hit. Every boss plays slightly differently each time you die and restart, so memorising a certain attack pattern wont entirely help you. At this point you just hope that the boss uses the easier of the attacks so you can deal more damage in that time.
The plotline to Cuphead strays from the usual cliche of hero saves the day/damsel in distress. In Cuphead, the two protagonists are actually gamblers and manage to lose to the devil. From that point they are simply doing everything in their power not to die. This is a very subtly done yet relatable story that is easy to follow. Every boss because of this felt like Cuphead actually walked into a bar and picked a fight with the meanest person there. There is an understood three dimentional backstory to every character on screen and it makes it feel like the world is truly alive.
MINOR SPOILERS: as for the ending, albeit brief and abrupt, cuphead and mugman are shown to not be half bad, after seemingly killing all residents of Inkwell Isle. This innocence wraps the game up very cleanly with no loose ends.
GAMEPLAY SUGGESTION: Perhaps it would have been useful to be given the choice to play as Cuphead or Mugman during single player mode, because throughout the game you are reffered to as "you two" even though it is only Cuphead that can be seen.
QUANTITY: Cuphead has three worlds and a final-boss-eque area. There are only 6 run and gun levels, 18 bosses, and quite a few minibosses. This might not seem like much but the difficulty and quality of each boss certainly drags out the game time. It is mostly beneficial, however, that the game is brief, because otherwise the game would feel way too lengthy for its difficulty. Personally I think you should get at least as many hours as the amount of dollars you spent on the game. I was pretty decent at the game right off the bat, so I could have easily invested another 7 hours perfecting it.
Outside of the levels, there are many different power ups and short side missions on the world map that will have you looking up tutorials on how to complete them. MINOR SPOILERS: There are many secret modes such as 2-strip color mode, black and white mode, and classic audio mode. All of which are unlocked by completing certain tasks the NPC's hint at but never directly give you an objective.
REPLAYABILITY: This game is amazingly fun and I could imagine myself playing this game again and repeating certain bosses just for fun or to watch my friends react to its creativity and difficulty. But once you beat it, the game will have really worn you out and the organic animation and traditional style becomes normal in your mind and at that point it just feels like another colorful sidescrolling boss rush. The ending wraps up everything so neatly, the game doesn't leave much for you to think about. But this isn't really the kind of game to have you "think deeply" about it, as that isn't what 1930's cartoons are known for. I think that the feel of the game was maintained at every level and I respect the developers for so creatively limiting themselves on that front. MINOR SPOILERS: Once you beat the game, an expert mode is unlocked for each boss, allowing you to play a much harder, and faster version of the regular versions of the boss. This gives a little extra to the sadists and completionists who thought this game wasn't hard enough.
I give Cuphead an astounding definite buy. If the 1930's era is your taste, this game will 100% satiate your appetite. You don't need to be into boss rush or side scrolling shooters to enjoy this game, as you will find yourself enjoying it no matter what you're doing. I wouldn't recommend waiting for a sale because buying this game at full price is definitely worth it. With only a few scratches, this game perfectly fits in with the classic animation of the 1930's.

The game continues to refine the formula familiar from the previous Frogwares Sherlock Holmes titles. Despite everyone's inexplicable fondness for weird puzzle locks, it also stands out in the puzzles by and large being sensible -- in contrast for example to Nemesis, where most of them seemed very forced and out of place. The game doesn't fear to get grisly, either, bringing back the unforgivingly realistic graphics of The Awakened in murder investigations, in contrast to the cartoonish diagrams of Sherlock Holmes vs. Jack the Ripper. The deduction board is back and has been further refined, so that it's very rarely one has to resort to guessing, but
Many of the weaknesses from the previous games are also present: Budget constraints are evident in every aspect of the game, and it's far from being as polished as the AAA titles of the day. The controls are still suite clunky, the voice-acting leaves MUCH to be desired, and the game crashed on me a few times. All in all, however, it's likely the best game in the series so far, so if you liked the others, you'll like this one, too. Having played the previous games is also recommended, as the stories thereof are heavily referenced, and you may have some difficulty following the narrative otherwise.

This is possibly one of the easiest games to either recommend or not recommend - it is more Half-Life. If you enjoyed Half-Life, you should get this game. If you did not enjoy Half-Life, you should not. If you have not played Half-Life, you should get and play that game first.
Simple as that.
As for the game itself, it's a competent, if rather short, side story to the original Half-Life, following the story of Barney (who returns in Half-Life 2), one of the security guards from the Black Mesa facility. When everything goes to hell...err....Xen, he tries to help the scientists and escape from the facility himself. It's a fun little romp back through Black Mesa, but it is no different mechanically from the original game - it does not add anything, and is missing some of the features of the original game. It's worth a budget price purchase, but is the lesser of the two Half-Life expansions.

You wake up in your house, alone, and confused. You walk to the next room, timidly peeking to see if anyone is home. Where have they all gone? You hear a thumping at your door, so you decide that must be one of your friends. You go to the door, and they seem so impatient with the constant thumping. You open the door, and there is your best friend, bloodied and hobbling into the house. His eyes are glazed over, so clearly he can't have just any wound. He takes a swing at you, ripping some flesh from your arm, and you scream in pain and stumble backward into the kitchen, then you open a drawer and pull out a knife. You turn and he's right behind you, raising his arms to take another swing. You get in close, and just before he hits you, you stab him right between the eyes. The thing goes limp, and collapses in a gory bloody heap. You see something else throught the doorway and in a panic, you run for the door to shut it just in time. You pant and sigh, tired and exhausted from the whole ordeal, as well as noticeably shaken up from killing your deranged friend. Your arm is still bleeding, and you've lost a lot of blood. You get up and go back to the bedroom to find some clothes to bandage yourself up. Just as you're tearing bandages, one of the things sees you through the window, and shambles over, but luckily the window is shut. You patch yourself up and decided to look for something to eat, so you go through the cabinets and you only find a can of beans. You look in the drawers for a can opener, but there doesn't seem to be one, so you put the can in your pocket for later. You walk to the bathroom to see if there are any painkillers, and as you round the corner you see another one of those things, but it's facing the other way. You calmly walk up, and shove it down. It makes a dull thump as it hits the floor, and gurgles in protest. You jump on top of it, and stab it through the eye, killing it. Again, tired, you work to catch your breath. You stand up and look in the medicine cabinet, only to find your anxiety medication but you grab it just in case. You look down again at the dead thing and realize it was your friend Susan, and you suddenly grasp what is happening. You just killed her, and what if she wasn't one of those dead things? What if she wasn't like the mindless zombie that clawed your arm? You sit down and quietly sob, wondering if this is a dream, or if you went insane. You hear glass break, and as you look through the bathroom window, you see one of the rotting... things, come through the broken window. It practically sprints toward you, then it's dead. You don't even remember getting up to kill it. Has it already become second nature to you? You decide you HAVE to make a decision on survival. If you survived in your sleep, then someone else has to be alive too. You realize that these things can't open doors, so you make a rule for yourself; always shut doors behind you. You move to shut the door, and the room is flooded with the dead that had heard the glass break. You panic, shut the door, and sprint to the closet. The only thing here are sheets and bleach. You take the sheets and start covering windows, in a desperate attempt to stay hidden. You double and triple check your doors, and realize you are finally safe. Exhausted, and emotionally distraught you decide to sleep, hoping to improve your mood. You settle in the remaining bedroom, shutting the door. You have horrible nightmares of bombs going off, people screaming and clawing at you, calling you monster. The bombs continue to sound, maintaining a fierce rythm when they suddenly stop. You sit bolt upright in the bed, in a cold sweat. You see a zombie shambling twoard you and you push him back. As he falls his teeth reip into your other arm, and you cry out in frustration and agony. With him on the ground, you stomp him until he makes no more noise or movement. He apparently busted the door off of it's hinges, and crashed through. You decide to use the broken wood to barricade your front door. You round up some nails, and a hammer, and finish the front door. You feel exeptionally warm, so you take your shirt off. You glance at your arm, and notice the wound isn't as bad as it feels, so you don't bandage it. You go into the kitchen and get a drink from the faucet, and feeling much better, continue on to barricading the back door. As you're hammering, you hit your thumb just perfectly. You started to yell, but quickly realize it didn't hurt. Puzzled, you continue to barricade. You can't seem to hit the last nail on the head so you give up. You sson start to feel your arm itch, and hurt a little more, so just to be safe you bandage it up. You hear more thumping outside, so you try to check the windows to see where the monster must have come in. You find yet another room infested, and so you quietly shut the door. The thumps and thuds get more and more intense, driving you mad. You start to feel nauseous, and so you drink some more water. You open the curtains and glance out the window to see a zombie vomit a bloody mess of bones and skin. You soon feel even worse, and running to the bathroom, puke up whatever you had to eat before this whole mess. Feeling hotter and more fatigued you stumble to the kitchen before you realize what is happening to you. You must be changing into one of those things.... You calmly go to the closet, take the whole bottle of anti-anxiety meds washing it all down with bleach, and in a drunken, stoned haze pry the boards from the door. You wander toward the street, slowly stumbling over yourself, and then you yell, "Hey, over here!" out of the haze you see dead figures ambling toward you, so you try to take a swing, but it grabs your hand and bites you. You see the blood, and hear the ripping flesh, but you don't feel it. Getting more and more dizzy you watch as more take you over, chewing you and ripping you apart, before you finally collapse to the ground. You start to black out, then you think to yourself "Well, at least I got three..."

I came to Edge of Space expecting a lot, having heard so much about it in relation to Terraria and Starbound.  I suppose that was a mistake on my part, and I'll admit as much.
As such, I tried my best to look beyond the horrifically clunky and unhelpful user interface, the occasionally slightly janky graphics and the various spelling mistakes, grammatical errors and so forth...  And, for a while, I did.
Unfortunately, what lay underneath wasn't all that great.  Yes, being able to "fudge" resources and use one thing in place of another is nice, but you can't combine two different types and the drop-down list bugs out if you have too many candidates.
But then we get to the matter of the actual tech tree and what you're building with all this space junk...   The game praises its "unique, Borderlands-style procedurally generated weapons", but all this means is that rock gun 1 may have +2 minimum damage and +1 clip size, while rock gun 2 has considerably less of either but 15 more accuracy (note, I have yet to discover what, if any, effect "accuracy" actually has on anything.  It certainly doesn't do anything with the projectile spread) and a different abstract "quaility" [sic] rating.  And between the three first tiers of weapons, with a really vast difference in required resources, there was only a tiny upgrade in regards to damage and clip size.  All other stats were pretty much the same, and they all looked like so much jumbled bulk.
There's no smooth progression, as all tech is unlocked by picking up and consuming data bricks that get dropped randomly by enemies.  Yup, you're gonna have to shoot a LOT of electric jellyfish before you can build that kitchen counter you always wanted.  You'll also need to do a spitload of grinding to get all the metals you need for anything beyond just dirt guns and mud armor, because ore veins are very rare and often stupefyingly dangerous to go near.
Speaking of danger, this game incorporates a life system.  It's not game over once you reach 0, but if you die after that all the items in your tragically small inventory will get expunged onto the surrounding terrain.
This game is early access, VERY early.  It's fully possible it will shape up in time, but right now it's clunky, incredibly grindy and half the items in the tech tree are obscenely expensive and serve no purpose.  In closing, I figured out how to infinitely duplicate any resource in the game before I managed to work out how to split a stack in two.  Wouldn't recommend in its current state.

Let me start off with this, which contradicts what many negative reviews say: This game is 100% possible to complete in it's current state.
You're thrown into the life of a hacker, who, starting from humble beginnings, ends up taking on huge corporations. There are a few paths/at least two endings you can get. The missions probably aren't 100% realistic, but they're still fairly so and pretty cool to go through. You have several "hacking" applications to use, depending on what type of hack you're performing. The tutorial/instruction is a little lacking, but the construction is high quality overall.
I was able to complete the game, as well as get all achievements, in a little over and hour. It was very enjoyable, lowkey, and right up my alley of interests. I did use a forum guide to get past a few missions, so my time may be lower than what it would be figuring it out 100% myself. However, without the forum guide it would be quite difficult to pass the levels described in many other reviews as "impossible due to a website being down".
I definitely would recommend this, but $3.99 may be a little high of a price. I got it in a bundle so I'm perfectly happy, but I think $3 would be a little more fair for a base cost.

Evolve has some truly wonderful mechanics and characters - the way that all the myriad strategy's unfold themselves to players as they become more familiar with the game is unique and well managed on the part of TRS's production. While each match plays on a small variety of well crafted maps, and against similar players, the depth of the game reveals itself continuiously even at high level play given the variety of play styles and characters at work.
It's also important to note that many of the bugs and balance issues that plagued the games initial release are now mostly fixed (as of July, 2015) and generally the game plays wonderfully.
As my original review stated, which was very lukewarm, after a (very) lengthy amount of time playing the game, match making, is still a bit hit or miss sometimes, and can be slow. A lobby system, which I believe is potentially in the pipeline, would serve to radically address this though.
Furthermore, the communication from TRS and 2K has been particularly poor, as was there launch marketing strategy, as has been said countless times. It does sound like they've taken on some of the criticism, though the T2 launch, while exciting, has again had very poor communication as to its actual release window and content. It's clear that they're trying to take steps to address this and are engaging the community.
Don't let these minor gripes turn you off - I recommend this game for good reason - though I would suggest holding off until it's a bit cheaper (currently $60USD), or is packaged with the 2 Season passes.
-  -  -  -  -  -
Note: I've changed this review a couple of times, relative to stages of the game / updates; generally the gist of the review has always been the same though; fantastic game, a few niggling issues, definitely worth picking up when on sale.

Day 1:
Plane crashed west of ... somewhere. Came to on a hill, surrounded by trees. Very scared of wolves. Walked until I found a cabin. Seemed remote, but it had some good stuff in it. Decided this time I wasn't going to die after one day, so learned some basic things like melting snow for water and boiling it to make it safe. Still have no idea where I'm going to get something eat, and it's getting dark outside ....
You know what? I absolutely love this game :)
In all seriousness, I must have died 100 times since I started to play it, in weird and wonderful ways and in terrible and beautiful places. I've frozen to death climbing to the top of the Forestry Lookout and in an ice fishing hut on the lake. I've died of thirst, hunger, infection, wolf attack, blood loss and food poisoning after eating raw animal carcasses.
I've seen a wolf bring down a deer. I've stumbled across an old power station which probably contains a lot of goodies but was too dark to explore without a lantern or a flare. I've woke up in remote cabins, in the dead of night, and heard wolves howling and even thought I'd heard one growl at the door. I've thought, many times, that I'd reached a place and point of saftey before it all came crashing down.
My record thus far is four days. I once survived four whole days, which made me very proud.
One of the finest features of this game is called permadeath. I will never get those four days back because when you die your save game is erased with you. That would infuriate me in other games ... in this one it raises the stakes and makes you work hard to stay in the land of the living.
It won't be enough. It's never enough.

Lately I've been holding off on reviewing many things, due to the nature of many games being worked on continuously and things changing very fluidly.
Today I write a big thumbs up for the Tropico 5 team for pulling through on two things that many in the community thought they had ripped us off on.
The first, prisons. Why these weren't there at launch is beyond me, considering they were in Tropico 3 & 4, the community thought perhaps we would get nickled and dimed for a prison DLC. The dev team to the surprise of many, at patch 1.08, have hadded the prison and the ability to arrest citizens for FREE.
In addition to this, the second large complaint was the 2000 population limit. Tropico 5 offers various huge Islands for the players to build on, much of which would stay empty due to the low population limit. Not to mention the horrible side effect of this limit and multiplayer - in which the total cap was divided among all players. New with patch 1.08 is the ability to change the max population anywhere between the original 2000, and the new high limit of 10,000.
I have to say I am very happy to see the devs change their stance on the population cap after community feedback, and would highly recommend this game to anyone. It's done a lot for the series, and is very unique in its approach compared to T3 & T4. Not to mention the devs, while a little slow on the action point here, nontheless pulled through for the community.
With my restored faith I may just buy the large upcomming DLC at full price :)

Here is a list of things that Limbo did a pretty good job at:
Aesthetic of the world/environment.
An errie/creepy feel to the game.
Now, here is a list of things that Limbo did not do very well at:
Literally everything else.
Limbo is a part platformer, part puzzle game, part story-driven game, and it doesn't deliver on any of these very well. From what I can see, there is hardly a story at all, and I haven't even seen the main character's sister even hinted at. There are no parts where any real platforming skills are required or developed, it's only a means of travel and presentation. There are no real puzzles, for it it's not one of the few puzzles that isn't trial-and-error, then it practically solves itself, since every puzzle is completely linear, requiring little more than getting Object A to Point B. For the majority of the levels (there are exceptions to this, and these are pretty fun, however...) the game requires the player to enter blindly, and to solve many puzzles in a trial-and-error format. This problem is caused by objects not being identifyable due to the aesthetic (bear traps in trees, boulders completely merged into a hill), spilt second reactions to things that appear from off-screen (pendulums, boulders, more bear traps (Puzzles requiring a quick reaction from the player would be alright, except the controls and player movement are designed for the complete opposite purpose, negating any chance of pulling it off your first try)), and the game making "puzzles" out of giving the player a rule of the game, and then immediately breaking it (ground switches, pendulums, physics). Whenever a game creates a clear rule for itself, and then breaks it in front of your face, it completely ruins any immersion that you would have had with the game, and is pretty much one of the golden rules of game design (DON'T BREAK YOUR OWN RULES). Any time this happens, it just makes you feel cheated on, and normally in a bad way. Another issue that this game has a lot of is the COMPLETE lack of things to do between the puzzles. The only thing you are able to do during these periods of time is look at the trees, and that's it, and there is a lot of time spent looking at trees in this game (they do look good, though).
I've only played halfway through the game, so this may change later in the game, but the description of the game tells more story than the game itself. Any sign of story telling would have been through subtle environment clues, which just didn't work very well here, and I see no sign of a clear way of telling what's going on, or why you're there in the first place. The almost complete lack of music in place of ambient sounds is an interesting choice, and this could just differ depending on your opinion, but I believe that it was a missed opprotunity that didn't pay off. The controls also are a little iffy in how responsive they are, but this is a pretty minor issue.
Now that I've talked about just about everything else in the game, now would be the part where I give the game some credit for the main thing it delivered on. Right? Nope.
The aesthetic, as you can probably tell, is supposed to be more of a darker, errie feeling. This is done pretty well, for the most part (music could have added to it), but then the game, at a point, becomes ridiculously violent. You can hear your own character's bones and flesh be crushed, snapped, shredded, and completely mutilated. Everytime you die too, except for when you drown. You can literally hear (and see the shilouetes of) more bones and flesh being desotryed than when Doom Guy is killed in DooM 4. No joke. That sort of complete brutality towards the character doesn't feel like it should belong anywhere near a platforming, atmosperic puzzle game, focused on telling a story. The game also has this interesting suicide theme going about it? Along with machinery, giant monsters, and spear-hunting villagers, objects and motifs in this game are completely scattered across the map, with nothing seeming to connect them together, and no real reason for them to be in the same game. I'm pretty sure that the constant children hanging in nooses from trees and dead bodies floating in water, being used as platforms, and as bait for monsters, is trying to progress something about the story or anything that's going on, but I'm not really seeing it. Maybe the real story of this game is how explorers that came over from Europe and killed off millions of Native Americans from disease and war can be compared to Hitler and the Holocaust. Who really knows?
TL;DR: Limbo failed in every regard of gameplay and design to try to be an atmosperic 2D art game, and failed at that as well. If it's ever free again, sure, go ahead and try it out. Other than that, spend your money on a better game that delivers on some of the same points, like Braid (for the gameplay) or Read Only Memories (for the story, and they totally deserve your money).

I have to say, I really, really enjoyed playing through this game. I wish it was longer- but, that being said, it is of such quality and contains such great amounts of content, I found it hard to believe it only lasted about 90 minutes.
I am going to continue talking about the game, but highly recommend you just dive in without reading too much into it.
This game is a set of games made by a single developer, none of which were released. A narrator walks you through small projects, and attempts to explain the creation of them. This is how the story unfolds, by changing emotions portrayed through the atmosphere of the various games you play.
The narration through this is really quite incredible. In fact, everything ties itself together very well into a cohesive story, even though you are in drastically different games throughout your playthrough.
There is also a very good representation of timelines, as the games improve in quality over time. Overall, everything was just really well done, and very well polished.
I can't remember how much I paid for this game, perhaps I paid full price, perhaps it was through some bundle somewhere. Regardless, it was definitely worth it.

Unlike the Stanley Parable, which was about exploring the possibility of abandoning the narrative of a game and going off to seek your own story, the Beginner's Guide is a more rigid journey. You explore a world of simple indie games strung together into a story by the narrator, Davey. Nevertheless, the story quickly becomes strongly compelling and has a building sense of dread I remember feeling when playing Gone Home. I enjoyed this game differently than I did the Stanley Parable, because the Beginner's Guide tells a complete tale with a beginning and end, letting me put the game down with more of a sense of completion.
Davey Wreden has amazing skill and talent at using the game format to tell a story in such a way that could only be explored in a game. Even if there's no choices for you to make or problems to solve, it still needs to be you pushing the buttons that move the story onwards. The result is an experience that has neither the length nor the replayability of a more interactive game, but a very powerful experience condensed into a shorter time frame. I really enjoyed my time.

Why do bad things happen to good people? Or why does good art happen to bad games, for that matter? After playing this, I'm even more confused about it than ever.
Morphopolis feels like a blend of a small scale, 2D, point and click adventure, mixed with the weaker elements of an offbeat hidden object game. You'll control an insect as it gathers objects for an array of bugs or plants and occasionally assemble the body parts of other, larger dead bugs so you can occupy its carcass to progress to the next stage. No, really. I didn't make that last part up. I never knew that's how evolution worked, I'm learning things already from this game, which is an unusual exception, given how unwilling it is to teach you anything else at any point.
Aside from a not very helpful cursor appearing at the start to prompt you how to move, there's no other attempt to guide the player in any way. I don't expect a game to hold my hand the whole way through, but surely page one of chapter one of the game design manual should tell you the first thing you do is teach a player the mechanics of your game and how to navigate and interact with it. When you struggle to move from your starting position in a game then you know you're in trouble. And that's a problem that persists the whole way through.
To move you have to point to your desired destination then hold down the left mouse button. The first problem here is understanding where you can even go at any point. You can click on your insect to momentarily summon a trail of green dust around your immediate area and show potential paths, but even this felt surprisingly unhelpful. But even when you do understand where to go, getting there is a task in itself. Movement seems temperamental at best and my bug would frequently appear to get stuck, waggling back and forth while rooted to the spot, or else fail to move at all, requiring repeated attempts before it would eventually go where I wanted it to... slowly. Very, very, slowly. Because, y'know... insects are notorious for being some of the most slow-moving and cumbersome creatures in the animal kingdom. Really, something so fundamental as basic movement and navigation should not be an infuriating obstacle the player should have to constantly wrestle with as part of the game's challenge.
There are a small handful of puzzles added to the mix, but these aren't especially satisfying to complete, and like the rest of the game, no attempt is made to explain them to the player in any way. At one point you control a bee with the ability to hop. It doesn't seem like something important when you discover it, more like a cute little idiosyncrasy, but later in the stage it proves vital for completing a section. I found this purely by accident rather than having it hinted at in any way, and were it not for being in the right place at the right time, I likely would have needed to resort to a guide to complete the game. That kind of methodology to progression just stinks of bad design to me.
It's not a game entirely without its charms, as the sound, look and short play time are its greatest virtues, but when a game's world is more fun to look at and listen to than to actually interact with or inhabit, then you have to ask yourself "what's the point?". I'd sooner recommend looking up images or videos of the game and experiencing its finer points that way. Otherwise, I'd strongly advice passing over on playing this one yourself.

I picked up this game after it got the Game of the Year from the New Yorker (a magazine I didn't even know covered video games). I love the quirkiness, the world building, the flavor text (to be honest, this game is nothing but flavor text), and the artwork. It's immersive and compelling, and despite the small map, I still felt like there was more for me to discover and unlock.
That being said, it is a brutally punishing game. I finally gave up after trying to play on the auto-save only mode and dying for the six or seventh time with my story quest only marginally completed. It would not be so bad if you could transfer more between captains (ships, for instance), or if the quests continued instead of resetting, but starting over from square one and grinding through the same quests in your very slow boat starts to feel less like fun exploration and more like a chore. The captains legacy feature is really cool, and I wish they would do more with it, keeping the progress you've made on quests that change the worl (the establishmen of the rat/cavy colony, for instance) and expanding on it. Overall, it's a great game, but it definitly would benifit from some updates to the gameplay that make it less punishing and build on the incredibly well-written world to make it more immersive.

Half-Life: Blue Shift.  I wish there was such a thing as a Blue Shift in the real world of work, seeing as a Blue Shift at Black Mesa only lasts 3 hours.  Now Half-Life and Half-Life: Opposing Force are not known for their lengthly storylines but one would come to expect a little more from an expansion to one of the greatest games of all time.
Blue Shift places the player in the shoes of Black Mesa security officer Barney as he attempts to escape the Black Mesa science facility during the events of the original Half-Life; which run in parallel with the Blue Shift storyline.  Unfortunately the very limited script and lack of anything that could be considered an expansion of the original Half-Life experience means you will feel rather unsatisfied by the rather lacklustre ending to what feels like no more than a fan made mod.
The only reason I can recommend for playing Blue Shift is to that you are granted an additional 3 hours of Half-Life gameplay, which can only be a good thing.

Red Orchestra does so many things right. It was the right atmosphere, then right balance of teams and classes, and the right  challenge. If this game's goal was to make the player immersed in the second world war, it beats any other game on the market. The emphisis is on realism; It's gritty, harsh, and unforgiving, and likewise RO2 is NOT an easy game. RO2 wants you to know that you are but a single lowly footsoldier in a much larger conflict. You'll be lucky to have a sidearm, you MUST travel in numbers, and sometimes there is nothing you can do to avoid death. Artillery falls, tanks fire, and people shoot without hesitation. You will die. A LOT.
If you like to be the bloke getting all the kills in the server like a badass, I cannot reccoment this game. Prepare for 3 kills a life, if that. Headshots are difficult to make, but even a sigle shot to the chest is enough to kill. If you get hit at all, you have most likely been killed. Don't prepare to read off your kill/death ratio, becasue RO2 is about teamwork. Imagine teamfortress 2, exept much more serious, much larger in scale, and more of a challenge.
The servers have 64 players max, and the maps are fitting for that huge number. There is plenty of diversity in the diffent maps, so don't fear repitition. With the large number of classes, there are many ways to play. Be warned, upgrades for weapons and classes are limited. Each weapon can be progressed up to level 50. You get the base weapon, one upgrade at level 25, and then SOME weapons have another at level 50. The Mosin Nagant rifle, for example, is the basic weapon used by the soviet forces. At level 25 you get a bayonet. That's it. Leveling this gone to 50 gets you nothing. I like this feature because it keeps things both balanced and realistic. If you want a scope, you need to choose the sniper class, but you better be quick! Each class has a limited number of slots to keep things balanced and interesting so theres usually only 2 snipers and 4 LMG guys on a team of 64. I do wish the graphics where a little better, as the player models do seem a bit basic, however overall the presentation is great, focusing on the large scale of war. It actually makes you feel pretty small and insignificant!
My only real complaint about the game is actually the DLC. There isnt any DLC required to have fun and progress, which I love. You don't need Rising storm to enjoy yourself, but I guess that's the problem. It is awesome to see the other side of the conflict and to have a whole new  way to play, but the fact is the Rising Storm DLC is just so overshadowed by Red Orchestra 2. If you are really curious or if you are a die-hard fan of the base RO2, then yeah, go for Rising Storm! If you havent played Red Orchestra much, I would wait until you see if you enjoy it before purchasing Rising Storm. Another small factor i dislike is the AI, which makes the singleplayer a little dull, but is a good way to learn to play as the bots present little challenge
Finally, I want to recommend the Heros of the West mod for RO2. It's a free mod here in the steam workshop. It's the western front of the second world war, pitting the yanks against the germans. It's unpolished, but it's fun, and just as important, it's free.
Overall, Red Orchestra 2 is one of the funnest games I have played, and it's probably the game I play most, seeing as the replay value is so high. There is no such thing as the perfect game, So I'm going to have to rate RO2 9.7 / 10

I will say in advance that I’m generally very grumpy and extremely strict when I review stuff, (I gave GTA V a bleeding 7 for crying out loud!) so it may surprise you when I say I gave this 10/10
Basically:
This is one of the best games I have played all year! It does everything I could want for a fun but still amazingly realistic ww2 strategy, it takes all the fun bits of games like blitzkrieg but makes them far more fun and far less tedious, if anyone is wondering this actually runs on the exact same engine that the first blitzkriegs ran off of
So if you ever missed blitzkrieg I think you’ll find this right up your street!  If you have never played one of these games you will be in for one hell of a treat! Especially if you love hard core ww2 strategies (but don’t worry it’s still pretty laid back for those of you who want a more relaxed rts)
What do you do? How does it play?
In Stalingrad you’ll get the choice of either leading the Russian or German forces to victory (with the odd bit of help from their Romanian and Bulgarian allies). Instead of most ww2 strategies you’ll play Stalingrad will give you a reasonable sized force, and your marching orders, it’s then your problem to make what they have given you  complete the mission, your troop are not replaced once lost, SO BE CARFUL however you are given supply trucks and repair vehicles so you can resupply your troops with ammo and fix up your damaged vehicles this means most of the time its far better to carry out small organised skirmishes and fall back before the enemy gets wise as opposed to enormous spams  or bum rushes. Your also often given allot of air support in the forms of fighters, bomber, fighter-bombers, and recon planes.
My personal opinion
Over the years I have seen countless games made on this engine spanning from the scorching deserts of north Africa to the bug ridden jungles of the Philippines even the bloody trenches of the first world war one, and now finally the frozen wastes of Stalingrad so it’s very easy for me to say this is one of the best uses of the engine it’s probably my favourite to be honest (maybe World War One is A BIT better) although the previous games allowed you to replenish you troops from supply trucks, this game works far better with that slight struggle,  and shortage on men you experience in the later missions  (especially since this was a major issue for Germany during the war) besides, the game usually gives you more than enough equipment to achieve your goals, most of the time. Which more than counters this short coming.
In a nutshell this easily makes my top 30 games ever and possibly 20, which says something since I have over 260 games on steam and over 50 PlayStation 2 and Xbox 360 games

Evolve has some truly wonderful mechanics and characters - the way that all the myriad strategy's unfold themselves to players as they become more familiar with the game is unique and well managed on the part of TRS's production. While each match plays on a small variety of well crafted maps, and against similar players, the depth of the game reveals itself continuiously even at high level play given the variety of play styles and characters at work.
It's also important to note that many of the bugs and balance issues that plagued the games initial release are now mostly fixed (as of July, 2015) and generally the game plays wonderfully.
As my original review stated, which was very lukewarm, after a (very) lengthy amount of time playing the game, match making, is still a bit hit or miss sometimes, and can be slow. A lobby system, which I believe is potentially in the pipeline, would serve to radically address this though.
Furthermore, the communication from TRS and 2K has been particularly poor, as was there launch marketing strategy, as has been said countless times. It does sound like they've taken on some of the criticism, though the T2 launch, while exciting, has again had very poor communication as to its actual release window and content. It's clear that they're trying to take steps to address this and are engaging the community.
Don't let these minor gripes turn you off - I recommend this game for good reason - though I would suggest holding off until it's a bit cheaper (currently $60USD), or is packaged with the 2 Season passes.

Limbo is something different, not your usual platformer. It adds a unique approach and a distinctive style to the platformer genre and it uses a dark atmosphere to create an unsettling environment. The gameplay is simple and the progression is continuous not level oriented, one puzzle leading to the other. The checkpoint system is great and the game is very forgiving when you fail something and die, be it a jump, a timed event or something else. You are respawned very close to the spot you failed at.
Did I like it? Yes. Do I recommend it? Yes. Should you try it? Probably.
It's something different and the overall experience is nice.
One thing I found interesting is that it has no story nor any spoken, written or interactive description of any sort. Basically you are thrown into the game and you must figure out what your next step is, what is your objective and what are your available options. The game doesn't hold your hand at all and everything you do, you do on your own. The puzzles are not difficult although their difficulty level slightly increases towards the end.
You can beat the game in under 4 hours first time around without knowing anything about it.

Morphopolis knows what it wants to do.  Provide a game that runs off the player's curiosity, and provide a few simple puzzles for the player to figure out on their own.  I
how it had no dialogue, leaving me to try and figure out what the heck I was doing for most of the time.  Though it's controls are restricted to the mouse, the game still feels like the antithesis of a lot of modern games, and feels like it pays tribute to an era lost in gaming where hand holding wasn't mandatory.
Very pleasing asthetic.  From what I understand, it was hand-drawn, and looked very good.  A lot of life from a soft palette, and I didn't feel like any problematic circumstances were due to the visuals.
Again, I had a lot of freedom (even though the gameplay was technically on rails) to explore and tackle the puzzles as they came.  You don't see that often nowadays.
The music was a bit of a wash.  My experience only lasted about an hour and a half, but most of the music is just some percussion and a xylophone - which wasn't as immersive when it hasn't noticibly changed 80% through the game.  I think there were other types of music at the start of the levels, but they inevitably sounded the same.
I think anyone who is considering buying this should understand what it was made for - a brief session of immersive puzzle solving in a visualy pleasing art style.  I personally, enjoyed my experience with it (where others clearly have not).  It's short, sweet, and - though I don't think of it as a particularly memorable experience - believe it was worth my time.

This is one of the latest chapters of Frogware's Sherlock Franchise and if I have to describe it briefly with a word or a concept that would be "Experience". Experience doesn't mean perfection but seeing how they started (the mistery of the mummy) and all the other titles they went through you can see how all the titles evolved, improved and changed chapter by chapter with good news and new mistakes. Even though The testament of Sherlock Holmes isn't perfect I really consider it a great improvement, a big leap into a new generation of the Sherlock Franchise.
The Testament of Sherlock Holmes is a point and click adventure with third person view. Gameplay uses pretty much the usual mechanics, you can observe, use or pickup items according to the icon it displays when you get on it with your cursor, and besides the usual combination of items there are riddles and puzzles and some of the are tough and random. when you're done with the clues of the current section you will be prompted to complete a deduction scheme, where you will link concepts and clues together with deductions (which YOU must choose between a choice of three possibilities). From this point of view this chapter doesn't represent anything particularily new, but it's mostly a very refined and polished verion of what has been already done in the previous chapter, Sherlock Vs The Ripper. The real innovation and leap forward to a new level is represented by three factors, Story, graphics and soundtrack.
The story begins with a small section used to explain the gameplay in which Sherlock will quickly solve a case of a stolen necklace. Later they will learn from newspapers that Sherlock is being accused of returning a false necklace. And from here the story is a succession of facts and situations that will lead to a dangerous degeneration of his good name. And I won't say no more because this is a great story with plot twists which represent its best parts.
Graphics is a great improvement considering the previous chapters and their remasters. It doesn't surprise much the fact that they employed the Unreal Engine 3 and even though you can't say the result is a true miracle of beauty you can undoubtely see that the results are great and various locations filled with many contour details and even though some animations can be a bit rigid, some situations can be a little buggy and few areas here and there are simply clipped to prevent exploring useless zones, now you see a new type of approach for the narration as it has been paid more attention to camera settings with focus and effects, new expressive animations (even though they're the same ones often repeating they're still new).
This chapter's soundtrack is completely new and it's a magnificent set of orchestral pieces that will pleasently accompany you during all your investigations and will also set a more pressing atmosphere when there will be some tense situations. First of all, I just want to thank Frogwares for making this game. I for one am I Sherlock Holmes fan, and have played most of Frogware's titles. The thing about their previous games within my experience are, they tend to glitch out at the point where I'm not able to proceed and finish the game. The Silver Earrings. I got stuck in the master's office. The Awakened. Watson wasn't able to follow up in order for the cutscene. Jack the Ripper. It didn't allow me to interact with clues without pulling me into the inspection of A. Chapman. This is the 2nd title I've finish from Frogwares. The 1st being Sherlock Holmes vs. Nemesis (Arsen Lupin). What I'd like to point out about Frogwares is that within their storylines, they tend to blow things out of proportion and pulling straws out of the blue in order to progress. In this game, they've managed to do the same thing with very nice and touching plot twists.
The gameplay portion of it surely improved a lot from the previous games. The interface is beautiful, along with the enhanced graphics and such. From its predecessors, it was from an omniscience point of view. First-person was then added in the series, finally third-person. It gave their gamers a versatile choice. Allowing to use mouse only, keyboard only, and mouse and keyboard. It's an improved feature, but some of the time you'll have to switch between the views in order to interact with some of the clues. I did enjoy the 360 angle inspection feature, truely great idea. All in all, they certainly evolved this series from a point-and-click adventure to something similar to L.A. Noire, another great title. The only thing you really need a guide for are the puzzles, anything else is self-explained and you just need to explore and interact more.
Moving along with the storyline. Now with this game's story, it's not neccesary for playing some of the older games; however, it'll be somewhat helpful to understand just a bit. The story just slowly let's the gamers view that Sherlock does some questionable things. Slowly tarnishing his name and reputation, also making some of the gamers not liking him. The authors surely did a great job doing so, in order for some plot twists. Then there's the whole taking things out of proportion. First scene shows of three toddlers, and how they're connected to Sherlock and John. Moving on with the story it appears to be that they're grand children of Sherlock and John. How Sherlock, one of the greatest minds can also become the greatest criminal, ruined his reputation by handling the rich with a fake heirloom, rigging a bomb to murder a judge, and murdering an inspector. Here comes the first great plot twist as it was Moriarty whom set to frame Sherlock. Graspped from the straws, because in the previous games (The Awakned) Moriarty has lost his mind and was in an asylum. Though it did eliminated the possibility of him being behind all of it. Then it was grasping straws by pulling in the Prince by teaming him with Moriarity. Second great plot tiwst was that Moriarty has been hiding a child of his own all this time. After his last breathe, he told only Sherlock is worthy of teaching her. Sherlock moved by it raised the child from child to adult. From a beautiful young woman, to a married woman. The girl then birthed a child, a young girl. The girl from the first scene. This was a great scene, as it showed Sherlock didn't turn away from one of his most ignored subject. Love.

Ah, Red Orchestra. Where do I even begin?
If I run from cover to cover, I get shredded by machinegun fire. If I peek my head to get a clear field of view, a sniper somewhere hears angels chanting and pierces my brains, splattering the wall behind me.
This game is hard, nerve-wracking, and not for the faint of heart or anyone who is used to 1337 720ºNoscopesnipah kills.
This game encourages camping.
This game is like a severe parent punishing your every mistake.
This game is
. Get it if you can. Play it if you have the time. I know I only clocked around 20 hours on it, but I would play the hell out of it if I could.
So, let us get serious.
Hardcore shooter with cover mechanics. Somewhat glitchy, too, but I don't find it unplayable by any means. Servers are typically 32 vs 32, with bots usually filling any slots left (which gives both teams an impressive amount of cannon fodder), so you know the battles are going to be big.
Weapons lack variety, which is to be expected considering it aims to be a realistic, historically-accurate game. And, bear with me here,
. Remember COD 2? A semi-auto rifle will never, or hardly ever, one-hit kill, which is understandable for gameplay reasons. Cue Red Orchestra's Elite Rifleman class, armed with a semi-auto rifle: it has the same power as the humble breech-loading basic rifles, but is semi-auto and holds more ammo. Then again, it's limited to, say, 3 per team. Same happens with the LMG, with astonishing firepower, or the SMGs, which can make mincemeat of anything at close to medium ranges.
However, this not only means that there are, naturally, players better equipped. Those same players have responsibilities: take a marksman rifle and go lone wolf scoring random kills? Wrong. Use it to clear the way for a capture point, to find the machine gunner who is tearing your team apart. Squad leader? Stay alive to allow respawning on you, make judicious use of your smoke grenades. So on and so on. Teamplay is king. Armies win wars.
The cover system works well. You can sprint crouched. Grenades can be gently dropped instead of having to throw them at the ceiling hoping they stay in the damned room. Gunplay is smooth, graphics are really good, sound and effects immersive as it gets. What more is there to ask for?
Ah, yes. Satisfaction. The satisfaction of out-aiming an enemy 120 metres away. Looking at the top right corner, those seconds lying in wait, thinking "
". Then you see it. You hit him spot on, you got the kill. You may get pistol-whipped to death a second after, but getting a kill in Red Orchestra is as satisfying as it gets in a shooter.
Of course, there are shortcomings. Optimization is poor. Some glitches can get a bit annoying. As I said, weapon variety is low and you may get relegated to basic Rifleman for rounds on end. You will get frustrated. The game is punishingly hard. But in the end, this is a top-notch shooter. Go get it. Go get 'em.

Yes, I would definitely recommend the game.  "Out of the Box," it wasn't working on Windows 7 64-bit.  I had no audio in the demo and then, after getting the full game, changing my resolution made the game crash.  I found an easy fix for both issues in the discussions, though the resolution thing was a bit more of a pill to fix. (all I had to do to fix the audio is run the game in Copatibilitly Mode for XP) Since getting that all sorted thanks to some help from the community, it's been smooth sailing.
Bioshock is a game that came out in 2007, though I mostly ignored it at the time due to not having a good system on which to play it.  Fortunately, it popped up in my Steam recommendations yesterday, so I tried the demo and then had to get it.  The environment is fantastic.  It's a Dystopian underwater city that's all done up in beautiful but gritty and grimy Art Deco styling.  Though the environment is closed off for obvious reasons, there are plenty of windows you can look out to see other parts of the city, ocean and ocean life, which give the environment a massive feel.  The story is pretty gripping so far, but I'm probably nowhere near being done with it.  I don't rush through games, so at about 6 hours in, I've probably got a long way to go.  The combat in this game is very exciting, I don't know why some people criticize it.  No, your enemies don't wince in pain when you shoot them but, as they are genetically altered, bullets may not have the same effect on them.  Though, a shot to the head is always effective.  There's no auto aim in this game, you have to be able to keep your reticle on your target, and accuracy matters.  Some games are forgiving and will hit the target if you're close, not this one.  I've been slightly off and seen a bullet whiz by the target's head.  The choice of weapons and Plasmoids makes the combat even more enjoyable.  So far, my favorite Plasmoid is the shock ability and my favorite weapon is the revolver.  Yes, I have more advanced weapons like a Tommygun, shotgun and grenade launcher, but I just like shocking them and then putting a bullet through their dome.  It's effective.  Aside from the combat, game play is very typical of older shooters, you have to find stuff.  Yes, I know, some people hate this, but I like it.  There's minimal "hand holding," you often have to explore your enviroment to find your objectives.  So far, I can't really think of any negatives, it's just a good game.  It's challenging (I'm playing on "medium" skill level) and there are a few light puzzles, but nothing too hard so far.
So, bottom line, I think this game is fun and fantastic.  It's definitley a credit to the genre.  It's hard to say how good the replay value is going to be.  This may be one that I finish and don't touch again, or I may let it sit for a while and then go back at it on the highest skill level.  But, even for a one time run through, it's a good buy if you love this genre and style of game.

Red Orchestra 2 (at least from my experience playing it) is a rather interesting game. A rifleman is the most common class used, but what really makes a team is the command structure (Squad Leaders and a Team Leader) and how well they can carry out their objectives. For example, a TL's job is not only to call in recon planes and drop mortars, but to also give distinct and precise orders for the squad leaders, so that the squad leaders then give orders to their squads to complete the orders given out from their Team Leader. Each squad has something special about them, whether it has a machine gunner, engineer, assault class or simply an entire squad of rifles, all of them play a specific roll.
In the end, the outcome of a battle in RO2 is not from who gets the most kills or who gets a so called "360 degree noscope on a camping n00b", but from tactical decisions, strategic planning and making sure that each member of the team does their part, commander and all.
