"Edge of Space" is a construction/adventure game in the vein of Terraria, only in space!  It's a very simple premise, but somehow, as of this writing, the game doesn't quite deliver on either its potential or the intellectual legacy of Terraria, which great effort is put into establishing.
The first thing to realize about this game is that there are some really cool ideas!  You've got a laser drill, and you start with projectile weapons!.  The graphics are a miss for me (I'll get into why later), but are certainly more detailed than Terraria's, and may not be as offensive to another gamer's eye.
(The following edited as of 21 May 2015...)
The game has vastly improved since my playthrough last year!  The general user experience is far less irritating than it was, and actually warrants my giving this game a chance now.
The game's crafting system is awesome.  Pretty much, the game is already similar to the "Terraria Leveled" mod in some ways mechanically, but the research lines are well-defined, and the experience amounts required to unlock a tier feel correct.  What's more the amount of things you can craft without a crafting station is great for upgrading your field arsenal (from what I've seen so far.)
They fixed the guns to always hit.  This was
dealbreaker for me before.  Thank you.  Note to other game developers: in an action game, RNG-based miss mechanics are
.  What's more the base tier of stuff after completing the tutorial is
, which is nice!
Speaking of the tutorial, it appears simplified from the version I played earlier, and is effective at basically teaching the game.  Less was indeed more!
You can rebind keys.  This helps to mitigate some of the confusing keybindings in this game, and let you play Your Way™.
First, you still spawn on a sky island instead of the planet's surface.  I think this is a mistake, even with jetpacks being available immediately, because jumping into a void beneath your little sky island is too much of an early risk, that I don't think a new player wants to take - at this point, we're still getting a feel for the game and the world.
Second - re-evaluate your default key bindings.  V for crafting and C for character are really counterintuitive to me.  While providing rebindable keys is nice, nailing a good preset will help this game immensely.  It was irritating to have to click the menu button every time I wanted to craft something, until I found the hotkey.
Speaking of crafting, the way you spend XP feels
clunky, and the increment/decrement textfield used to implement it clashes with everything else.  Since the upgrades are straight lines, not trees, why not just allow me to click an upgrade or a button on the upgrade in order to "buy" it with the XP?
The visual style to me is hit or miss, but this gets into personal preference; if Terraria is a Saturday-morning cartoon, then this is
on Adult Swim, which is what I think they're going for.  This point may or may not be a sticking point for you; this "Doesn't Work" bit is purely subjective.  Some sprite mods or the ability to create sprite/tile image mods might be a good idea, though.
Once, I did not recommend this game; it wasn't ready for the public.  Luckily a few patches seem to have come and gone to help resolve that situation.  The developers need to study up on good User Experience (UX) quite a bit more, and take it as a lesson learned going forward - UX seems to be one of their weaknesses that they have to fight against.  However, the interesting ideas in this game seem significantly closer to fruition.
I recommend watching this title more closely...

***I will retain the original review here, but I will add and mark new points. If  you want my most up-to-date review, scroll down.***
I'm going to be completely honest; there's a lot of potential here and I hope it reaches it, but so far I'm just not seeing it. I'm trying not to be too harsh, I respect the dev team and their game, but here are my impressions...
The first thing that comes to mind with this game is; There's alpha games, and then there's ALPHA games. While I play a lot of games in alpha and beta stages, I usually enjoy the experience because they often bring something new and innovative to the table to make them interesting. Sadly, I'm just not seeing it with the alpha of this game. There's little that I would consider standout, innovate, or unique. The mining lazer is cool, but not groundbreaking, and mindnumbingly slow without any upgrades in sight. At the very least, it should have the option to heat the targeted rock and at least one sqaure of the rocks around it at a slower rate. This would speed up the process while still allowing precision. Jetpacks are cool, but the limited energy and energy regen followed by blind jumps makes them more frustrating than anything. If nothing else, the early jetpacks could use a massive buff until more is added and that situation is sorted out strictly for exploration purposes. Beyond those two features, the game doesn't have much to offer.
My next gripe is the actual game's goal and layout. The game gives you the goal of terraforming, and that's about it. I really didn't like that goal. I don't feel like it's a goal at all. Terraforming is just something you DO in this kind of game from start to finish. I don't feel like something I'm going to be doing anyways -and can do at any point- should be my final goal. It gives little to work towards other than "look I mined out this rock lol." If my goal is to terraform, than I want to be given a final idea of what I'm terraforming towards, rather than just changing the landscape slowly. Which brings me to my other argument; the real "goal" players give themselves is simply going downwards. I feel like the only way to progress is to mine resources and then continue falling downwards in hopes of new discoveries. There's also multiple levels as you fall downwards, resulting in higher risk areas. This is great and all but then why terraform anything on the top levels if the better resources and more interesting stuff is downwards? Why even set your roots and your house at the top just to work your way back down and farther again? I'm not trying to be harsh, I just think some good thought has to be put into these concepts before the game moves forward and falls flat on its face.
I'm hoping that my investment, and the investments of everyone else gets put to good use here. I think somewhere in this alpha is a great game, but right now it's barely in a playable stage. It's just very unsinspiring when compared to the games everyone, myself included, will immediately pin it to- being Terraria and Starbound. Both of those games have unique and recognizeable art, music, gameplay, and attitude. Even the art in Edge of Space feels cluttered and weird and just like it needs to have its own personality to it. I will say that I love the music at the opening menu though.
Closing thoughts; I don't regret supporting this game and I hope it continues getting support so that it can become a full-fledged competitor with other similar games, and hold a meaningful spot in a steam library. That said, until the game brings proof that it's serious and has something to prove to the gaming world, I wouldn't recommend putting coin into it to have it gather dust in your steam library.
*** As of Jan. 30th, a few months after original review
Well I'm not entirely sure I can list everything they did, but the devs are pulling through on this one. With some UI overhauls, and massive variable tweaks, even the initial few minutes feel much more active and fluid than before. The progress curve is much more obvious right now and you have to work towards your progress points individually. Exploration is a bit easier now as jetpacks have recieved decent buffs, nulling my earlier complaint about them. Also mining has been considerably buffed, with an early "overcharged" mining lazer now available that damages at least 2 layers of blocks at a time. So my mining complaint is decently nulled. There's a bunch of other tweaks/buffs that improve fluidity of gameplay including changes to weapons, monster health, so on so on.
My initial impression before was that the game was an unplayable wreck and I was a bit disappointed in it. Right now my impression is that I can really start to get into this game. Although I feel it's a bit lacking in overall content right now, yaddayadda it's an alpha, we've been here before. It could just use a bit more... Variation? Maybe just several different sprites for the wildlife or something. The sights get a bit repetitive at the start. I haven't moved too far in yet as there is quite a lot of grinding involved now.
All-in-all I'm refraining from saying I recommend this game just yet. While it has shown significant improvement and I feel like the devs have listened to complaints and worked to better the game, I'm still not ready to recommend this game. I'm going to see if the devs are still dedicated to improving the game and adding content, and if they seem committed and the game starts to come together I will change it to recommended in a heartbeat.

Five Nights at Freddy's is one of the few horror games I have played in my life. And I believe this was the best one in all of them (Played Slender and Amnesia back then). I bought this game last Halloween on Daily Deal as I had a few bucks on me after the Halloween Sale that time. Was going to play it for the first time to celebrate Halloween. I have beaten this game this week and believe now is a good time to make this review...
When you begin this game for the first time, it's important that you know what you're doing. I never saw any information on how to play once I started. I died twice in Night 1 and this night was supposed to be very easy and serves as an introductary night. But later on I've developed a strategy to make it through the later nights. I came up with a strategy which really helped me through Night 4, 5, and even the bonus Night 6. I've beaten Night 6 on my first try with this strategy. So whenever you're playing this game, it's best to come up with one or else you'll panic trying to save yourself from a jumpscare.
This game was quite a thrill for me, one of the best indie games I've played of 2014. It has really good innovation for a horror game, how you check cameras in a Chuck E Cheese-esque facility with cartoon animatronics wanting to kill you. And the sounds and ambience during gameplay makes you paranoid and makes the jumpscares more intense. But with this strategy I came up with, and plenty of experience playing the game, this game has became less scary for me. You too will feel this game is less scary once you're used to it.
Now that I've played this game long enough. I will start Five Nights at Freddy's 2 soon. 2 is waaay harder than 1. I recommend playing 1 first for a while before playing 2 so that you get a general idea of what to expect.

This was a fun little hidden object game with a fresh new style in terms of the genre.
I love the HOG genre of games and anyone else that does has bound to have noticed by now that most of them are pretty standard in terms of story and style. Whether it be an Indiana Jones style treasure hunter, an antiques trader, a supernatural entity or just the classic crime detective, Morphopolis puts an interesting new twist on HOGs.
“Lose yourself in the mesmerizing, fantastical world of Morphopolis, a game about transformation and discovery.”
It reminds me a little bit like The Tiny Bang Story, which was another small but unique HOG, in the way the HOG elements are laid out. It’s more interactive and visual then your standard HOG game. Instead of just being given a list to things to find, you play as a bug, traversing its way across a lucid insect world. You click and drag your mouse to move and although the direction isn’t entirely clear I think it’s easy enough to explore and figure things out. You can interact with things around you and figure out what you need to be finding from that.
The gameplay for me was fine. I read a few reviews before I bought the game that suggested the controls and direction of the game was annoying to some seeing as it may have been a port over from touch screen devices. In all honesty, I found it completely fine to control and didn’t feel that directions were ever necessary. Although on gameplay alone I would say that if you took away the stunning visuals, there wouldn’t be much too it.
The art in this game is beautiful, especially on a bigger screen. The many different colours and details will keep you interested in what’s going on. Which is great given the games quite laid back pacing. The visuals in the game definitely make up for the lack of actual gameplay as mentioned above.
With that said, every now and then you get puzzles of which I thought were pretty good. There were a few that I did have to actually think about to solve. The last one especially being the hardest to do.
Overall the game took me just under 2 hours to complete. It’s a fairly short game but I felt that it was neither too short nor too long, which is always good. It’s a nice little game to kill a few hours with and also get another 100%ed game.
As far as I am aware, the achievements are purely for completely the game’s milestones and its puzzles without using hints. So it’s an easy one to do.
All in all I really liked this game, it was short but sweet and generally a nice little indie game.
TL:DR : An interesting HOG game with a unique new style for the genre. Basic gameplay but beautiful art, which more than makes up for it. Good puzzles, short and easy to 100%. Definitely give it a try.

Recreating the feel of lonely dread in the best of the "slow zombie" genre, Project Zomboid's retro graphics do not detract from it being nail-bitingly good.  No plan, no, base, no resources, just you and your wits against a seeming unending tide of walkers who want your flesh, and not in a nice way.
If you want hand-holding, this game is NOT the one.  Scratched by a zombie?  You have a chance to survive, but not the best of odds.  Bit by the undead?  PACK IT UP, BUTTERCUP.  The game becomes a revealing exploration of how you choose to meet your end.  Melee? Chug a gallon of bleach? Quietly lay in bed while the sickness takes you?  Your choice.

TL;DR: A casual, nice but pretty short hidden object adventure with a bug theme.
The first thing you notice with Morphopolis is that it is extremely colourful. The screen is full of mesmerizing plants, leaves, branches and bugs. A relaxing string-music is playing on the background. Because of all the colours it is initially difficult to focus: what am I looking at exactly?
It turns out you are a caterpillar. Crawling around (using mouse) feels slow and wonky, but you'll get used to it. A cursor appears and instructs you to crawl and click on objects. Surprise, it's a hidden object game, the casual version of adventure genre! Every one of the five levels has several different things to find, some of which only trigger if you go near them and use your bug magic (by clicking the bug).
Some stuff is difficult to make out of the background while others are very easy to spot. Finding stuff gives you power to influence other bugs or plants. This way you'll open paths to other areas. Your ultimate purpose is to morph into a greater
bug.
Occasionally, once a level or so, a puzzle is triggered. Simple puzzles require arranging seeds in the right order, deducing perfect shapes or rebuilding scenes. Most of them are relaxing and simple enough though a couple of them were even pretty challenging.
Finding stuff can be a pain because of the bright-coloured scenery. Never fear, as mercifully there's an in-game hint system that shows you where the elusive stuff is hiding. True to the casual theme, there's no punishment whatsoever for using it - you just have to wait a bit for it to cool-down to use it again.
Two and half hours later I had completed the game. It was perhaps a little short and scarce on content for the price. Nevertheless, it was a pleasant experience and also a relaxing write, idling in-game waiting for the last couple of card drops and listening to the music. Get Morphopolis if you don't shy away from puzzles but also wish to relax for a single evening.

is a very pleasantly surprising puzzle game, with a high standard of quality and a humorous undertone.  Any fans of the puzzler-adventure genre should easily find this game enjoyable. Once you start playing you will likely find yourself engrossed by the experience.
It has a much thicker, richer story aspect than many other puzzler-adventure games out there. I was truly entertained by the narrative throughout my entire playthrough. The interesting plot goes a long way to elevate this game above the standard. Furthermore, I thought the graphics were nice and the voice acting was solid, which reinforces the high quality of the writing. The end result is a very enjoyable game with an excellent presentation.
This inherent quality in the writing, atmosphere, and overall presentation results in a game which feels much more true to the
brand than the other couple of games I have played that were franchised the intellectual property.  The others feel like standard adventure games with the words "Sherlock Holmes" on the title. This game, to me, really felt like what I believe a
game should feel like.
The puzzles were very challenging and quite fun; though to be honest I lost patience and had to seek assistance once or twice because of how tricky some of them were. Some of the puzzles are doubly complicated because the objective of the puzzle isn’t always made clear. So first you have to figure out what you are trying to do, and then you have to actually do it. This does add an extra layer of challenge, but it also can be a bit jarring.
And lastly, something I thought was a pretty cool feature is the fact that you can choose to move around in 1st or 3rd person, or play in classic point-and-click adventure style. Having this freedom sounds trivial, but it is really nice to be able to tailor the style on a whim as you play through the campaign.
In summary,
is a pretty sweet ride. It should appeal to both fans of the game genre and fans of the
IP. Give it some consideration if it sounds up your alley.

Not one of Telltale's best works, but definetley not one of it's worst.
The episodes vary in length, some being two-three hours while others are only an hour and half. Maybe that's just me getting through the game quickly, but even so, they do vary. The story is defintely very unique for something made in the batman universe. Telltale uses the lore very well, and even expands on it in some cases. The main villian (and villian group) in the game was made specifically for the game, like Batman: Arkham Knight, so expect some suprises. I won't go much else into the game's story here because I don't want to spoil it, but it's worth the play. That being said, this is also probably one of the least interactive telltale games I've ever played. There will be long scenes of dialouge or expostition that will have you sitting there doing nothing except pressing a button every once in awhile, and NOT for dialouge options. I didn't mind it that much, but it doesn't help the case that Telltale doesn't make games, rather interactive movies. To combat this, though, there were plenty of action scenes. Not as many as I remember Tales of the Borderlands having, but almost as much. These sometimes brief (and sometimes long) engagements are choreographed very well, some even letting you plan out your course of attack before you jump into the fray. Your not doing much other than quick-time events, but they're usually done very fast, and having one or two mistakes usually means your dead, so you have to stay on your toes during these sequences. The puzzle parts of this game are done very well, most of them making Batman have to prove that he's the world's greatest detective again and again. While these puzzles are very simple, they complement the story well.
Now graphics and audio-wise, there were many bugs. Some parts didn't have audio where there was supposed to be audio and sometimes the lip-sync was off. While very small mistakes when it comes to the whole game, it's those little things that will constantly break your immersion, and constantly make you sigh.
All in all, like I said, not the worst but not the best. If there ever is a season two, I hope they know what to work on. Bottom line, yea you should play it. If your a fan of Telltale like me, you'll still love it.

Military power is straightforward and easy to handle, although I wished for more options.

Concerning transportation, I expected multiple road systems, such as: bridges, tunnels, ext.
Tourism in the game is really exciting, but most of its buildings are expensive, which can halt construction for a period of time.
DLC? meh, don't even bother.
In conclusion, Tropico 5 runs smoothly and is fun to play. It brings this simultaneous feeling of simulation and pleasure.
Go buy it if you liked Tropico 4.

This was my first time officially playing a Telltale game. As far as I am concerned, this studio offers an exciting and unique experience in a manner quite divergent from other video games.  Be warned, for minor spoilers follow.
As an overall storytelling experience, I was surprised and impressed by Telltale's liberal use of the Batman canon. To name one, the take on Penguin as a younger, stronger and more intelligent villian was refreshing, to say the least.  As far as the response-choice system goes, I appreciate the attention to detail in showing how in-game characters genuinely react to your words and actions. As I work my way through again, I look forward to seeing how the subplots change from my original playthrough.
Another surprising, but slightly irritating fact was that I found myself spending less time in the kevlar boots of Batman and more in the Italian-made shoes of Bruce Wayne. As a result, when given the option to play through a sequence as Bruce Wayne or his alter ego, I pretty much always picked the latter.
In spite of this, I finished this tale satisfied and hungry for more. Four stars!

In Outlast, you are investigative journalist Miles Upshur. You've decided to act on an anonymous tip, and so you set off to explore Mount Massive Asylum, an old and decrepit building that has recently been re-opened by the Murkoff Corporation. The nightmares and horrors that lie in wait are beyond anything that you can imagine, and your only possible way out is through hordes of deranged mental patients who've fallen victim to hellish experiments and medical torture. Armed with only a camcorder that has night vision capabilities, you must survive.
Set in a first-person point of view, Outlast is very much like a playable "found footage" horror movie; most of your time will be spent looking through your trusty camcorder, which will help you navigate immensely dark areas. Crazed lunatics and mental patients litter the tight corridors and open expanses of the game, most of which have some sort of deformity; be it mutilated flesh, or stumps where a limb should be. Many are harmless, and will chatter nonsensically, while others are out for blood... your blood. There are a small handful of primary bad guys that you will repeatedly encounter, all of whom are utterly gruesome and terrifying in their own way. You're no fighter, so you must run, hide, and outsmart your foes in order to navigate beyond them.
Much of the interaction between you and the enemies in the game consists of a mixture of chase and stealth sequences. An enemy will burst in out of nowhere, and it's up to you to find the nearest place to duck into; a locker, under a bed, behind a shelf. Sometimes the only thing that you can do is keep running. While these intense moments will make your heart palpitate, and the hair on the back of your neck stand up, near the end of the game it really gets both redundant and expected. Found a key? Well, I guess I'll go hide in this conveniently placed locker because Mr. Huge Pecks is going to come stomping down the hallway any second now! This is really the only downfall of Outlast, and honestly with the deep atmosphere and immersive graphic quality of the game itself, it hardly takes away from the scare factor that the title has. Not to mention, each of these foes has a lavish background to indulge in if you take care to read the collectible documents and notes.
While exploring the gore-soaked, entrail-laden rooms, hallways, and basements of Mount Massive Asylum, you will come across various documents and camcorder notes (if you have your camcorder on during certain events) that will give a large insight into the storyline of Outlast. It seems that the facility that you're exploring has been used for religious surgeries and scientific experiments that have turned many patients into unholy abominations. Many of the ill have been subjected to deranged forms of hypnosis, which has caused their mental state to deteriorate rapidly. Even the doctors have gone rabidly insane. It would be a travesty to suggest that this title relies on jump scares, but the ones that are placed sparsely throughout the gameplay are completely unexpected and scream inducing.
The biggest majority of Outlast centers around navigating from one area to the next, although the game never feels like a walking or key-finding simulator. There are a few puzzles to solve, which usually involve turning a couple of things on or grabbing a couple of items to help you progress; typically while avoiding an enemy that's filled with bloodlust. While this may sound tried, true, and typical for so many horror games, Outlast just does it the way it should be done. This title really brings out all of the stops with AAA quality graphics, detailed atmospheric lighting, memorable characters, constant environment and AI interaction, an extraordinarily suspenseful soundtrack, excellent enemy AI, and some of the most dense atmosphere of any horror game that I've ever experienced; and trust me, I've played nearly every horror game that there is.
Beyond a shadow of a doubt, Outlast is one of the greatest survival horror games since Silent Hill 2 and Resident Evil 4. I would go as far to say that as of this moment in time, it is the best modern horror survival title. No, you don't fight. No, you don't have a gun. You're a regular journalist, and you must use your wits to survive truly insane, deadly enemies. If you're like me, and you love games that are dripping from every corner with blood and gore, boast noteworthy bad guys, have a captivating storyline, and pull you in with an impenetrable atmosphere, then Outlast is the horror game for you. Also consider picking up the Whistleblower DLC, which is a phenomenal prequel addition to the main game.

You've just crashed on a planet. All you've got is some utilities from your ship you were able to grab. You can mine, you can build, and you can craft. What will you do to survive?
If you're a fan of Terraria, but want something a little more bizarre, and more focused on space, this is definitely your game. Don't see it as Terraria or Minecraft knock-off, though. This game is one of the most unique games of this type that I've seen. Most notably, the crafting system. The way this game's crafting system works is just fantastic. Rather than picking around for specific blocks, you are able to craft things by finding blocks to fit the requirements for density, permiability, and other criteria for creating an object. There is more to this, but I'd rather let you find that out for yourself, as there are many machines in this game that would take a while to fully explain.
As you can see the graphics in the screenshots, and audio in the trailers, I'm not really going to dive that deep into them. The only thing I'd like to note is character creation. There is at least a moderate amount of customization for your character off the bat, and even more when you consider vanity and armor further in the game, so if that's the type of thing you're into, consider it another plus.
This game isn't completely great though, and I won't be able to stress enough that this game is EARLY ACCESS, and that's what you're paying for. A lot of it isn't done. There are bugs and glitches (though not really anything that will ruin the experience).
+ Crafting system
+ Plenty of other machines to play around with
+ Block variety (there are vending machines, TVs, etc that you can craft)
+ Customization
+ Boss fights
+ Misc. world events (worm holes and such will crop up here and there)
+ Concept (the idea is cool)
+ Playtime (lots of playtime in this, even at this stage)
- Graphics (while the graphics aren't bad, you could get sick from watching the world backdrop)
- Not finished (bugs - bugs everywhere)
- Emphasis on not finished (not that much content)

Not one of Telltale's best works, but definetley not one of it's worst.
The episodes vary in length, some being two-three hours while others are only an hour and half. Maybe that's just me getting through the game quickly, but even so, they do vary. The story is defintely very unique for something made in the batman universe. Telltale uses the lore very well, and even expands on it in some cases. The main villian (and villian group) in the game was made specifically for the game, like Batman: Arkham Knight, so expect some suprises. I won't go much else into the game's story here because I don't want to spoil it, but it's worth the play. That being said, this is also probably one of the least interactive telltale games I've ever played. There will be long scenes of dialouge or expostition that will have you sitting there doing nothing except pressing a button every once in awhile, and NOT for dialouge options. I didn't mind it that much, but it doesn't help the case that Telltale doesn't make games, rather interactive movies. To combat this, though, there were plenty of action scenes. Not as many as I remember Tales of the Borderlands having, but almost as much. These sometimes brief (and sometimes long) engagements are choreographed very well, some even letting you plan out your course of attack before you jump into the fray. Your not doing much other than quick-time events, but they're usually done very fast, and having one or two mistakes usually means your dead, so you have to stay on your toes during these sequences. The puzzle parts of this game are done very well, most of them making Batman have to prove that he's the world's greatest detective again and again. While these puzzles are very simple, they complement the story well.
Now graphics and audio-wise, there were many bugs. Some parts didn't have audio where there was supposed to be audio and sometimes the lip-sync was off. While very small mistakes when it comes to the whole game, it's those little things that will constantly break your immersion, and constantly make you sigh.
All in all, like I said, not the worst but not the best. If there ever is a season two, I hope they know what to work on. Bottom line, yea you should play it. If your a fan of Telltale like me, you'll still love it.

In spite of this, I finished this tale satisfied and hungry for more. Four stars!

Outlast was written and developed by people whom I would describe as competent idiots. Mechanically speaking, their game is well done. It suffers from no obvious technical errors, and while the environments are generic, they are still well designed. The gameplay isn't even remotely scary and I struggle to see how someone could be scared of this, but we don't really play these games for the sake of playing them; we play them for their story, and the story here makes no damn sense whatsoever.

The game plays like an isometric, less graphics intensive dayz, and feels kind of simulator-y. I really enjoy this game and have easily lost track of time playing it on more than one occasion, the gameplay is not always fast paced, but it is always spent trying to keep your character alive. This game is at it's best when there are multiple players, all surviving as a group, it makes carrying things like wood and heavy objects less of a chore (mostly because your character has the carrying strength of a sickly child) , and allows you to rely on them to keep you alive as well. The game however, is not without it's faults, and has many areas that need a lot of work. After a while of playing you begin to realize that some of the "moodles" your character has like being in pain, being sick, or having an injury, don't always work as intended, sometimes you'll take painkillers only to have the pain get worse, other times you'll work hard to recover from an illness only to have it reappear 5 minutes later for no reason (in the online at least). The zombies are great in this game, in the beginning, but it feels like their numbers start to wane too easily, after a large shootout at the pile-o-crepe I found myself having a hard time running into big mobs of zombies in the city, if the survival experience is to stay scary there needs to be some form of  respawning zombies or zombies that have a difficulty increase in order to keep the threat real.. The game has it's highs and lows but it's great fun with a friend or two, requires very little to run it smoothly, and is currently only 15 dollars.

Still trying to get through the game, but while it has it's moments, it is so mundane and tedious. The story would be passable, if it had some element of gameplay, But there is ABSOLUTELY no game involved. You don't have choices to make, you can't leave one room to get to another until you uncover all the clues, in the correct order, and there is no possible way to get them wrong. Some of the puzzles are boarder line impossible, well, not really, but they take a long time to figure out. But again, you can't fail, and you can just skip them. For the story, there is no way to die, no way to get caught, no way to fail, no way to move on to a different objective until the one your on is done. There are no choices to make, no deviation from a very linear story. Even in the conversations where it looks like you have options, you don't, it just rotates through the options until you get to the correct one.
There is one fairly funny point, where as watson, you're talking to this landlady, and the conversation goes
"I'm a medical doctor and I'm here to see a patient who is losing his teeth, it's highly contagious"
she replies "leave, or you'll be one losing your teeth"
so he says "I'm with the department of health to inspect the neighborhood for (something, I forget)"
and she says "something something, get out of here"
so he says "I'm a painter, here to paint your portrait"
So far, three times I've been wandering around trying to figure out why I can't move forward in the story, and looked in my inventory to see I have three peices of rope, but haven't combined all 3 to make a longer rope, or I have a bottle of water and a dry cloth, but the quest needs a damp cloth... or that you have the wrong item highlighted in the corner of the screen, so while you need to cut something, it's not the knife, it's the clippers, or that you need to pick up the pipe to hit the glass, but you inspected the pipe before inspecting the note, so you didn't pick it up, and after reading the note, you have to go back and inspect the pipe again, this time picking it up, even though nothing in the note had anything to do with the pipe, it just wasn't in the required, pre-determined order.
Luckily, half way into the game, after about 3 hours of mindlessly clicking on every blue (luckily they turn green after you've finished the sequence in the correct order, but also turn from blue to green and back to blue if done out of order when you unlock the sequence you should have done them in, which gets frustrating) and an hour or two of puzzles (there's really only about 6 in total, one of them, the roman numeral box, can be done correctly, but not the "correct" correct way, which was also frustrating) they have about a 20 minute cutscene to recap what actually happened in the story up to that point. Which is pretty much necessary, because you're so mindbent on mindless clicking and backtracking (if that's possible never leaving the same place, more just walking in circles to the same objects over and over) that you have no idea how all the broken fragments of the story are supposed to fit together. I completely forgot who the guy I was following was in the third act of the first scene.
Even in what I assume to be the final act, which is a stealth mission, sort of, you can't get caught. You can run into view of the guard, and you just get turned around to look for the blue icon you haven't finished. By this point, they've even given up explaining why you're looking for them or how they work, you just run along the edges of the room until you see a blue icon, then rotate through the 3-4 things in your inventory until one of them works.
The achievements in this game even get annoying. Since you can't do anything outside of the pre-determined linear story mode, you finish the last blue icon, and you get the achievement for that area... but there is still no way to not get the achievement.
Anyways, the game is good enough for a time waster, and has some good puzzles, but just realize there is absolutely ZERO game in this game. The story is fine, it's pretty bland, but for a sherlock holmes story, it goes exactly how you would imagine. Sadly, you have absolutely no contribution to this story, no matter what you do, how hard you try to succeed or intentionally fail, you just can't. You either do things exactly how they were programmed and go on to the next chapter, or you stand there, and wait, until you do things how they are programmed and move on to the next chapter.

Then there's this new thing called corruption, which takes a % of your revenues and makes off with them into the ether.  I have no idea how it works, and amending the constitution ( the only hint the game gives ) has little to no effect.  I'm mother♥♥♥♥ing presidente ♥♥♥♥♥, let me start executing people who's hands have been caught in the cookie jar!  Alas, instead, tropico 5 continues on the trend of previous tropico's in that your control over the island is less and less with each iteration.
Do I recommend it? No, just go pick up any of the first 4 which are better...

Disclaimer/Summary: As of writing this review, I have played Cuphead for around ten hours, beaten the last boss, completed all six of the run & gun levels and have beaten all of the first area's bosses on expert difficulty. I have enjoyed my time with Cuphead overall, and I would recommend the game to anyone who enjoys trial-and-error focused platforming games. As for me however; I do not feel motivated to play any more of Cuphead at the moment. It is a good game that would serve as an effective introduction to old-school run & guns due to its forgiving nature, but it fails to reach the greatness of the games it takes inspiration from in a few key areas.
Cuphead is the newest entry in a line of games that has attracted considerable attention from game journalists and average gamers alike due to its demanding approach to difficulty. Coupled with a striking visual style and soundtrack that alludes to the "rubber-hose" animation and swing music of the 1930's, Cuphead has managed to leave quite an impression on the indie gaming scene in its first week on the market.
The core gameplay of Cuphead is based around traversing a small but dense overworld to fight a variety of bosses, which play out either in the form of a platforming-heavy run & gun sequence or a horizontally-scrolling shoot-em-up boss encounter. Since the player has unlimited ammo, the focus of gameplay is tightly-centered around dodging projectiles and other physical attacks from the bosses. There are also a few run & gun sections in which the objective is to progress to the end of the level whilst managing infinitely-respawning enemies and stage hazards. These sections are optional, but the coins that you can find in them serve as a good reward, as you can use these to purchase other weapons and abilities that can be effective against certain bosses. Once you have beaten all of the bosses in an area you can progress onto the next area and rinse and repeat.
The formula is as a result pretty simple, almost too simple to some degree, but the constantly charming visuals and variety of bosses keeps it feeling engaging from the beginning until the very end. Each boss feels completely unique to the others in terms of its attack patterns and appearance, and although not every boss idea struck gold, there is more than enough here to satisfy anyone looking for a firm but fair challenge. Each boss has multiple forms each with their quirks and surprises. The presence of a ranking system and patterns that can play differently on each attempt of the boss means that there is more replay value than you would first expect from a short game with such simplistic mechanics.
The game's unique mechanical flair is the parry move. Although parry moves are not unique by themselves, Cuphead has an interesting variation on the move by allowing you to only parry in midair, and you can only parry pink objects. Parrying is incentivised by the scoring system and the fact that successful parries will charge your super meter, which could help you beat bosses more quickly. These mechanics coupled with the aesthetic flair of the game makes Cuphead an overall engaging experience that is worth more than the sum of its parts, with a difficulty progression that feels just right for the most part.
However; the design of the game reflects heavily on my biggest issue with Cuphead. Although Cuphead is clearly designed after the high-intensity arcade games and run & guns of the 80/90's such as Gunstar Heroes and Contra, even featuring boss fights with similar gimmicks to the ones found in these games, Cuphead is more of a simple exercise in trial-and-error such as IWBTG or Super Meat Boy than a true arcade game. Although I would say that Cuphead is better designed than its peers, the gameplay is focused on dying to short, extremely-demanding segments with no room for error ad nauseum until you finally beat it by brute force, only to find yourself having to do another short, demanding segment and start the process all over again.
Of course, arcade run & guns have their fair share of trial and error, but even in their hardest areas they would leave some room for error, and the challenge was based around attaining consistency throughout the whole game as opposed to bashing your head against repeating series of brick walls until the game gives up and hands you the ending. Cuphead may have a similar level of difficulty to the games it takes inspiration from, but it is not nearly as punishing by design. You will probably die a lot to the bosses, but dying just sends you back to the start of the boss, and almost all the bosses can be beaten within 2-3 minutes. This means that Cuphead lacks the stakes that a level progression and lives system can provide. The best arcade games understood that running out of lives and being sent to the start of the game isn't necessarily a bad thing - replaying earlier stages can give the player a better sense and appreciation of the pacing and level design, and secret paths and alternating routes can mean that subsequent playthroughs still feel fresh. This approach to design also means that the game is testing the player's consistency throughout the whole game, not just their trial and error in regards to a single boss fight. Cuphead, with its boss selection overworld and infinite retries, offers none of this, making the experience feel ultimately shallow as a run & gun.
There are other issues more specific to the design of the bosses and the mechanics of the game, that sometimes feel indicative of a lack of polish to the gameplay: During the shmup-style boss fights, there is a slight amount of movement inertia on the player ship, and oftentimes foreground objects can pop out and obscure the view of the action. Although these issues never make the shmup sections unplayable, it has to be understood that arcade action games, especially in shmup sections, are based around precise dodging, and this inertia and foreground obfuscation is counter-intuitive to that objective.
Secondly; there is a striking lack of visual feedback on damaging bosses. Outside of their scripted knockout and phase-transition animations, bosses will show no reaction to getting shot besides a short flash of white. Not only does this make the shooting feel dull at times, it makes it hard if not impossible to gauge exactly how far you are through a boss fight until you die, which again feels counter-intuitive to run & gun action sequeces.
Although I wrote earlier that the parry mechanic feels unique, it feels as though the game doesn't use the mechanic to its fullest potential. Only late-game boss fights incorporate the parrying directly into their attack patterns, and in a couple of these the usage feels overly gimmicky. Parrying should have more of a presence in the game other than just as a means to attain a higher rank.
Finally; there is a large degree of randomness in several of the boss fights and attack patterns in this game. Sometimes this can be something as simple as bosses changing up the order of the attacks in their cycle, which is fine, but the degree of randomness can be much greater in other bosses, to the point where the positions of platforms the player has to stand on is randomised. Although the randomness never makes any part of the game impossible, it does mean that certain patterns will sometimes be arbitrarily easier or arbitrarily much harder than usual for no good reason. 100% static boss design can be boring, but in a game genre about testing the consistency of a player's skill, a large degree of RNG is antithetical to the goals and purpose of the game.
Cuphead is not a game to be missed, but its design bears the mark of missed potential. Many mechanics are not as well realised as they could be, and the forgiving, "retry-spam" format of the game is playing it safe in an indie market saturated with games sporting this exact format.

So... This was a thing. I'm a Tropico fan.  Only played the 4th one though. So make of that what you will. I WILL say that it was-In my opinion- better then this one. This game made alot of changes to the game, and where some of them are good, the rest ruin the game for me.
This game had 4 changes that made this game nerve-wracking.
-COMBAT
Starting with this one as it's might be the most annoying. In Tropico 4, the combat was very simple. You and the enemy each had your own forces, and each combatant had his or her own "EXP" bar. The side that had the most soldiers with the highest "EXP" won. If you won, you would have thinned the numbers of rebels, or stopped a uprising. If the other side won, you'd lose a building, or the game if it was your palace. (I won't go in to the process of blowing up the buildings used by the rebels, but I'll just say i like it more than 5.) Your army was expensive, but nothing too high. A armory got you 3 generals, and each general got you the ability to build a guard post, which had 3 soldiers in it.(There was also a army base, but that was just to make life easier for your soldiers.) Simple(ish) but fun.
In Tropico 5 they changed it. I was actually hoping they'd make it harder, since if I could find one flaw in 4's combat it would be that they made it too easy. They did. And I don't care for it. Instead of soldiers, you have "Squads" now, each with their own "Health" and "Combat Strength". Numbers are still a big factor though. And that's where the problem lies. How much did a guard post- 3 "Squads"- cost in Tropico 4? Around $1000. How much does one low level squad that can't even beat pirates cost in this game? $7000! I don't have that kind of dough! This is the sole reason I can't get past mission 3. You need a very strong army there. And everything costs so much. I wouldn't mind the increased price, if it wasn't for the next change...
-ECONOMY
In the 4th game-I compare this game to that one alot, I know- The Economy worked pretty much like this. You'd find one or two products to export, and build your economy around that. Meanwhile, your treasury would slowly go down,down,down... Until the freighter came and you sold your goods, giving you cash to farther build and mantain your island. In this way, the game gave you a sort of "Allowance", which I thought was a good way of letting me know what I could and could not afford. (And it had graphs just in case you were spending too much on something.) Trade was automatic too
In this game however, There is no "Allowance". Your revenue and expenses are constantly at war with each other. I never have any idea how much money I really have, nor how much I can spend. So I'm forced to build extremely slowly, which would just be annoying and not game breaking, if it wasn't for number 4 on our list... In my opinion the worst flaw of them all, the one that, combined with the other 3, suck all the fun out of this game... Silly me, I forgot number 3! We'll get back to number 4 in a bit. For now...
- THE FLIPPING CONSTITUTION
There are 4 era's in this game, Colonial, World Wars, Cold War (Where Tropico 4 was based,) and Modern Times. To get out of the first era, you need to write a Constitution. I don't have any problem with these in real life, but in this game... Screw the Constitution. Why? Simple. IN THE FOURTH GAME(sowwy for yelling) all special things you could do with the island were mostly defined by edicts. Need a bigger army? Conscription's got you covered. Want money in your swiss ban account?( your "score" pretty much) Building Permits' are there. Need to wipe out the smart guy faction? (PS. You never do.) BOOK BBQ! In order to use 5/6 of the edicts, you needed a ministry. It wasn't that hard to build it, and I liked the ministers themselves.
In Tropico 5, You unlock these edicts automaticly as you move into new era's, So don't think you can provoke the rebels till the Cold War. But even then, Some of them are missing! Where'd they go? I don't see- oh. Ooooohhhhh.... There're in the Constitution... That sucks. "But why does this suck? you ask. Two reasons. Reason 1, You can't change the Constitution on a whim. You have to wait like 5 in-game years, which is a really long time in even in Tropico standards, especially since they took out the 3rd zoom button. So I hope you don't need to change anything, cause you wont' be able too for a long, long time Reason 2, No matter what you write in that piece of paper, Everyone on your island will be mad at something. Which ties us in to the 4th one... I hope you didn't forget all that build up back in the Economy section, cause i didn't. This is it. The main reason I don't like this game. And it is...
-PUBLIC APPROVAL
Back in my day, the days of Tropico 4, There was no "approval". There were two thing: Happiness, and Respect. Happiness was determined by how well you satisfied the needs of the people. Each person on your island had "Preferred needs" that effected their happiness more than others. One citizen would like liberty more than housing, for example. However, it was in your best interest to try and canter to everyones needs. Respect, on the other hand, was how likely a citizen was to take action against you,(I think) be it voting against you, rebeling, or just protesting. I think Happiness had a hand in determining how much someone respected you. They were separate however. Respect was also determined by fear, so a large army would also increase resprect, among other things. You island could be the worst place in the carribbean, but as long as you were careful, you wouldn't be overwhelmed. In Tropico 5...... They were combined into "approval". I don't even think I need to explain the problem here, but I'm going to anyways. In this game, 50% approval is the magic number. It's INSANLY hard to keep it at 50 or above, but you have too. Why? In the first era, Colonial, You need to get too 50% approval as fast as possible. Your just a govener at this point see, and will get replaced by a new one unless you hurry. Most of the people on the island don't want a free Tropico, so they don't have any "Respect" for you. And because Respect and Happiness are the same thing in this game, everyone is SUPER unhappy. The entire first era is a race against time, Fending off the deadline while hoping enough people get on you island that want a free Tropico. Assuming you make it in time. You get to World Wars. And then you pull out your hair and curse. You kinda have to hold elections. You technincly don't have too. but the game mechanics basiclly assure that you do. And Respect and Happiness are the same thing. So unless your island is happy, which you don't have the money to make happy, you are going to lose the election. You could cheat the election, or just not have it, but then everyone will be FURIOUS! And because there is no Respect or Happiness, only Approval, they will rebel. And you can't fight the rebellion because you don't have a good enough army. And you don't have that because you don't have money. And you can't use conscription because you didn't put it in the constitution. And you didn't do that because everyone would be mad. Which they are still. Because you can't make everyone happy till late in the game. Not that you will make it that far, because unhappy people in this game feel no fear, nor patience. They assume that everything is constant, so if they are unhappy, they assume it will always be so. Tropico 5 is a dictator game where you live in fear of your subjects. Case in point.
In summary, Tropico 5 has problems. I could go in to the other problems I havn't talked about. Or I could talk about the good things Tropico 5 does. But I don't see the point. Normally I could overlook the problems presant here. But this is a direct sequel to Tropico 4, which means I expect it to be better, or at least on the same scale. My advice? Buy Tropico 4.
Final Vertict

The style of this game is very like the later game Crimes and Punishment, but this game only has one story and the cases are all related. Unlike C&P this game's deduction board only allows you to progress if you find the right conclusion, and it's not always obvious. (You can always click absolutely every option in every combination and the board will 'click' open instantly if you get the right one).
If you're the type of person to click everything and solve everything without help from the game there is only one missable achievement and that's for choosing a specific dialogue option in 3 different conversation throughout the game and you may need a quick guide for that; or do it on a 2nd playthrough. The game saves for you in different slots in addition to allowing you to save whenever you want, which is very nice.
The game also has many neat mechanics, as in some parts of the game switching between Sherlock and Watson, and you get to control
, who may be even smarter than Sherlock himself.
The game only has one ending and one story, but you get to do little changes for choosing different dialogue option; mostly if you pick the nice one the other person will find things for you as if you pick a 'bad' one you have to do that yourself.
Afaik the voice actors are the same as in C&P and are done well, as is the sound and music in the game. The puozzles are decent and not so hard that they would need a guide, though the explanation of the puzzles can be a litttle too minimalistic so much that I had to internet one just because I didn't get exactly what I was supposed to do.
The game lets you choose between third person view, first person view or classic point&click; I personally preferred third person with first person used as a zoom-in in some areas. In general; if you're stuck and can't find an item: Look up. The game mentions other cases, especially if you click everything and some are "souvernirs" from other cases (and therefore games), but you don't need to have played any to understand the story, but it helps to know the basics of Sherlock.
Overall a very enjoyable game, my game time is one playthrough plus a speedrun through some parts to get that last pesky achievement, so there is plenty of playtime, story and content.

Here's my 2nd review of the 'best FPS's of all time', as promised.
(Bragging note: dont mind my Playtime of the game on Steam, i played and did 100% on all 3 Bioshock games on the PS3)
Bioshock is the most stylish game of all time.
While HL2 is the traditional FPS, great in every department, but following previously established archetypes, Bioshock revolutionizes most of those formulas. So i'll also try my best to 'stylize' my 'review formula':
Rapture.
Truly, this amazing underwater city defines everything this game does well. From the very start, you feel like Alice, going into the rabbit hole, into Wonderland... Except you're late for this one, it's already in ruins.
The art style is absolutely amazing, the 20's Art Déco combined with the sci fi / mechanical aspects results in a sense of confusion, not knowing if you're in the past or future, which adds to the mysterious tone of the ruined city.
The combat system is also very refreshing, instead of just relying on weapons, they added plasmids, which can be mixed with the guns for fun gameplay, with an added layer of depth. The exploration and scavenging were a nice surprise for me (as an obsessive explorer in gaming), presenting both some RPG elements and the backstory of the city, before it collapsed (metaphorically), through the eyes of its previous inhabitants.
Another unique, iconic element of the game is it's enemies, more specifically the almighty Big Daddy, who provides an amazing dynamic to the combat (i was gonna describe it, but i decided it's best to let the players found out for themselves).
Finally we reach the Story, praised as one of the best in videogames, proving that FPS's dont have to be mindless with virtually no story (you guys know what games im talking about!), by presenting complex philosophical, moral and political ideas, as an amazing social commentary that should probably be studied and debated by the experts of those departments. All of this, with a limited amount of characters, that you can count witth the fingers in your hands. But even though few, each counts as a hundred, with powerful personalities crashing, which results in the infamous plot twists that catapulted this game into stardom.
Now, would you kindly do yourself a favor, and go play this game immediately, if you havent yet (or even if you have!)

Don't get me wrong the game is solid already,  but even at this point early access,  the base game just doesn't feel very involving.  You start out in a game with a spawn point and are given lots of blueprints to activate then craft.  Where I get pretty annoyed and usually give up is the whole downward scrolling aspect of the game.  To reach the first 'layer' of a surface, you need to drop down,  which requires building stairs back up to the initial block of dirt you spawn in to presumably build your starting base.
Getting back to the whole verticle scrolling aspect of the game.  Going up and and down all the time requires building lots of stairs and frequent use of your jetpack.  The problem is, it recharges extremely slowly,  resulting in a lot of time just waiting to use it.   Lighting is also trickier than in other survival games:  there's a few flareguns and torches to be placed,  but they all require using the crafting menu,  which is tedious. For example, to craft an item you need to select the materials you want to use first,  sometimes there's a huge list of materials you need and if you are missing one, you'll have to re-select all of them again if you want to try and craft again.   A lot of the time you'll find yourself in the dark trying to climb out of a pit of some sort, and hope you don't accidently fall further downwards to certain doom.
Speaking of tedious,  everything just feels tedious to me about the game.  Mining is about as exciting as watching blocks smoke from heat before turning into collectable ores.  Crafting requires dragging a blueprint to your inventory slots, selecting the slot,  holding left click to activate the blueprint,  then right clicking the inventory slot to remove the blueprint.  This is just a typical example of how something is done in this game and honestly I don't feel like any of it is as intuitive as it should be.
Combat is also pretty sleepy.  You shoot enemies,  and they die.  There's no real weight to the combat and it's just not very gratifying.
Overall tho, the game does feel solid as I say.  Personally I just fall asleep trying to figure something out,  but that's just me.  Many will find the game appealing because there is much to do and there's a lot of content,  so if the aforementioned things don't bug you, feel free to dive in.

This game is actually really interesting. It’s a beautiful piece of art with high details and bright colors. No, I am not talking about a painting; I’m talking about the game although the game is like a painting in a way. It has a very calming feel that helps you relax as you try to work out the puzzles and find the items in which you’re looking for. It’s a very short game, only about an hour or two depending on how good you are at puzzles and hidden object games. Behind the puzzles and artwork, we have an interesting sort of story that is abstract enough for you to take what you want from it. It is one of those games that might have a deeper meaning if you really want to look for it.
They don’t really explain a story line for the game much, you are thrust straight into the game as a little larva or caterpillar wiggling around. It keeps you in that insect world as you go from a small larva to a grasshopper to a bee and so on. There aren’t any times that you actually fly or jump which is kind of strange but you walk around gathering items and the end of the stage is crawling into what looks like a carcass of the bug you will be next. I know the game is called morphopolis and is supposed to be about metamorphosis but this feels more like you taking over the dead bug instead.
The game play is… at times its pretty good when you get into the puzzles but the movement of the character walking around is a little hard to deal with. Times when I am clicking to find the objects, the little character that I was playing would move and go into a different scene when I am not ready for it. That’s the problem with clicking the screen being both for finding items and moving your character. There are times when my character also had trouble finding the pathways I wanted him to go on.  I think it would have been a bit easier if they had the arrow keys to move the character as I could hit the down button or up to go on those paths. The character moves very slowly which can make that part of the game boring when you have to go back and forward to collect items. There is a lot of back tracking in this and it would have been nice to be able to have the character speed up. There is one other problem that I do have with the puzzles. The puzzles don’t tell you how to do them, you sort of just have to try different things to figure it out. There was one puzzle I got stuck on because nothing I did was actually working that I had to look up what the puzzle was supposed to be so I could play it.
The artwork is so amazing. It’s very high detail and is almost like a surreal painting with how playful the colors and designs are. The problem with this though is that there are times you can’t find the path you need to go on most of the time. The paths just blend in with the background or are really hard to figure out. They luckily have it so that when you click your character, a couple green sparkles will resonate from him and travel a little way along the path though sometimes its hard to see depending on how high detailed the area is around them. On the other hand, the high detail does make finding the objects your looking for all the more rewarding as it is hard to see them.
The music is so calming and a little mysterious. There is one track through the whole thing and yet I never got bored of it. It’s a piano solo that almost put me to sleep a couple of times during the long walk parts. That is all I can really say on it as its just calming.
Overall, it was a nice little game to play. Is it worth the money that it is on steam right now? Maybe not. I got the game on a steam sale and It was worth the amount I paid for but I’m not sure if it’s the full $4.99 worth. My recommendation is to get it on sale because it is a good game, and it is beautiful. If you get it for the normal price, then you’re mostly paying for the artwork.

At first glance, this game is a very cool pacific rim/transformers type mech game where you can transform back and forth between a jet plane and a mech with guns. However, in later levels you end up barely using the mech at all because it's just too slow and you get ganged up on by all the enemies, meaning you have to spend more time in jet mode taking out all the enemies just to land as mech and not do as much damage
Pros:
+fun game, challenging collection of levels that have a wide variety of missions
+2003 style, able to run on lower power pcs with still decent graphics
+cheap
+wide variety of weapons that do have a slight impact on gameplay, taking a op weapon for one mission wont help in the next one, etc
+xbox controller compatability, very fun way to play
cons:
-game is glitchy, i had to restart a couple times after one level's radar died and then my hud vanished
-you never use mech in later levels unless im just bad and dont know how to
-mech mode has an autotargeting system that doesnt pick up enemies, your crosshairs don't follow your joystick
-a lot of weapons are useless
-flying controls are rough at times, if you get too close to something and accidentally knock into it you sometimes get flung out of your direction and pointed towards the sky or ground
-the game uses "terrain destruction" as one of their draws but it plays a very miniscule part and you can only blow up like trees and buildings, and the buildings are usually yours
It's a good satisfying jet fighter game, sort of a reverse transformers style. The mech mode is usually stronger for them than the dump truck they drive as, but in this game the jet is clearly superior. If you really like playing jet fighter games id say it's worth the $10, otherwise wait for the sale and you can gave a couple afternoons of slightly frustrating fun

The game "Morphopolis" is a pretty little, short puzzle/hidden objects game that builds on a relaxing atmosphere in a natural, colourful environment (to be more exact: the world of insects).
In five levels you take control of an insect trying to get to the end of the level but a row of obstacles get in your way. To get rid of them you need to solve a few puzzles or find a certain amount of objects (which is more challenging than it sounds considering the detailed backgrounds you have to look at to find the objects).
What's nice is that the game is quite relaxing which is because of the soothing easy-listening soundtrack and the design which make you feel you're in some sort of jungle right now.
You won't get any help in the game on what a puzzle is about but most of the time it's easy to find out. Only the very last puzzle in level 5 is very tricky.
Aside from the lack of game help in the game, it can get very annoying when the screen moves and you have to way until the next screen slowly appears (because your insect moves slowly, too).
So if you like a short puzzle/hidden objects game for about 1-2 hours and if you don't dislike insects, feel free to entertain yourself. But because it's so short, better keep your eyes open for a discount offer instead of paying full 4,99 € for this game.

In Morphopolis, you play a sort of microscopic parisitic intelligence that seeks progressively larger corpses to inhabit and animate, which is a very cool concept.  You accomplish this by painstakingly crawling your zombie bug of the moment around a few few screens of a fantastical insect realm, all drawn in a psychedelic art style, clicking on a lot of not-particularly-hidden objects and playing a couple of minigames.
You may at first find that the game is very, horribly slow, but understand that this is your fault, gamer.  Just because Morphopolis was described as a "game," you thought that it would be something you could "play," while having "fun" and worst of all, maybe even "win" it.  Those are your preconceptions and they are wrong, wrong, wrong!  Morphopolis is not a game to play, it is a game to
!  See the fantastical setting?  You didn't see it enough!  An artist went to a lot of work to draw those environments, and you will look at them properly!  Your avatar will keep crossing back into previous screens, where you didn't intend to go, just to ensure that you have properly appreciated the art!  The object-collecting quests will send you creeping back and forth again and again, so you
spend sufficient time staring at the art to demonstrate proper respect.
Hear the beautiful, trippy soundtrack?  No!  You weren't paying sufficient attention, what with your gameplayer attitude of rushing through looking for enemies to kill and goals to accomplish!  The developers will helpfully correct you by slowing everything down to the pace of a slug crawling through wet cement, to ensure that you have the time to correctly appreciate the music!
There are also no instructions, other than some pictograms, which sometimes makes the nature of the game a bit unclear -- that was to make the experience more immersive, and not in any way a cheap trick for saving money on localization.
So don't play Morphopolis,
it.  It has beautiful art and sound.  If you were expecting to have
, well, that's your selfish attitude.  Shame on you.

I loved Tropico 4, rule your own country, make your economy rise, satisfy your people, execute those in your way,♥♥♥♥♥♥off foreign countries and wave your nuke around to prevent them from invading. These are just some of the things you can do in the previous game and are still present in 5.
But Tropico 5 changed in different ways, military became much more critical, forces are stronger thus stronger defense is required. Trade routes can be chosen and relations with foreign countries' relations affect these. You progress through time and things change even more than Modern Times DLC in 4. Housing is more interconnected with job salary and sometimes you experience problems but don't know the details until you see a detail that changes your prespective. The game provides a bigger mirror to the perspective of a dictator, things need to be watched more often and closely, you must be prepared and at the same time be able to adapt to the situations you must be watchful of such as civil unrest and the end of WWII.
Everything got more difficult, more complex, in some cases worse than 4, I miss the old Penultimo, I missing allowing no rent to all residentials, I miss the diverse set of characters and more. But 5 had some things I really liked, the campaign was something I didn't expect and loved, the fact that you make your island grow and don't abandon it at the end of the episode makes you see how difficult it gets to run a country the longer it stays alive. You have multiplayer (which sucked earlier on until some updates) where you cooperate or kill each other with armies and resources. Military played a bigger role, both a good thing and a bad thing because I didn't give a damn about it til 5.
Bottomline, Tropico 5 is like a more difficult version of 4, things need to be watched more often as the threat level of everything got more critical such as rebels, civil unrest and pirates and the campaign requires you to realize that you are NOT going to abandon your country and ALL problems you experience now WILL happen into the future unless YOU fix it while you can. Tropico 5 is a great game and I value it as I value 4 but in different ways.
If you've played Tropico 4 and loved it as it is and don't want things to change, then stick with it. If you value a bigger challenge, a more complex way of playing it, a chance to compete with other dictators (heads up, few people go online anymore so find a friend) and to realize how difficult it is to manage your own lil island then go buy this, hell it's Steam anyway. Price too high? Steam Sale!

Note: This review is only for the game as of 8/2/2014
The big drawback for this game is the user interface (which is so bad that I gave up after less than an hour, hence the lack of play time). At its current condition, the UI is far too complex and spread out to be used effectively. There's something like 5-10 different 'windows' that you can bring up, each with their own UI's and submenus, all of which the player must navigate in order to effectively play the game. Did I mention that the windows can only be brought up by hotkey, and have no onscreen hint as to which hotkey brings up what?
Compare this to similiar games such as Starbound,  Terraria and Minecraft, which are far more streamlined in terms of UI. Starbound is the most complex out of the three, but even that has only a couple of "main" user windows - the inventory/equipping/status menu, and the crafting menu. Minecraft has a similar setup, with a combined inventory/equipping window and a crafting window, plus some other assorted windows depending on gameplay style. Terraria has only one "window", which is the inventory/crafting/equipping/status overlay that is accessed via the escape key.
The graphics are ok, and the gameplay is nice, but unless the user interface gets a rework, I wouldn't recommend playing this game - you'll be stuck navigating windows, menus, and submenus half the time.

A game without characters, without faces; with but a single, relentless voice that tells its own story, endlessly and painfully and without closure.

Experiment? Well, maybe. There is a lot of play, a lot of joshing, a lot of wondering what you will do next.
Narrative? Difficult to say when everything is so blurred. And so much of what you learn is from reading between the lines.
Catharsis, then. And in that respect it hit me hard and left me breathless.
Sometimes a story tells you more about yourself than the characters it's portraying. And perhaps that's the lesson of the Beginner's Guide.

While The Beginner's Guide delivers a unique flavoured story as well, it just pales in comparison to it's predecessor; the gameplay is much more linear, the idea is much bland and straight forward, and it's not nearly as thought provoking as the first game. When I saw the trailer, I thought the game was literally about going through a collection of short games in any order we want and discovering the person through our own merit, not getting spoon fed a series of game in a linear fashion.
To sum it up, The Beginner's Guide is by no means a bad games, but if you played Stanley Parable and were expecting the same quality experience you're gonna be disappointed. As for pricing, imho, 10.99CDN is probably only a smidge too much, only a smidge. Decided right away to play on the hardest difficulty.
Make my way through a frozen Canadian forest.
Find some kind of worn down barn and an axe inside.
Continue exploring.
Find rail tracks.
Go to my right a bit, found a few train carts and a collapsed tunnel. Dead end, no loot.
Walk along the tracks the other way and encounter a wolf who was hidden by a fallen tree.
He attacks.
I run away from him towards the hut in the distance.
I make it!
I shut the door and explore the hut.
Find a frozen body of some poor chap.
Nothing on him.
Investigate the hut some more and find some wood, food and fuel.
Lit a fire, melted and boiled some water for myself to drink.
Eat dinner, make some hot coffee, spend the night in the hut.
In the morning I decide to explore the fishing huts around the lake behind the hut I spent the night in.
I avoid about three wolves in the process of exploring the lake.
A deer runs by and one of the wolfs takes off chasing it. Thank you, deer, your death wasn't in vain!
This distraction opens a clear way towards another set of huts.
A blizzard starts. Still no warm clothes to be found.
Nearly freeze to death while exploring the lake, but make it back to the hut with enogh fuel to recover.
Light a fire and warm up.
Still around five hours left until night. I can explore some more.
I go outside into the forest.
Explore a lot, but lose my way.
A blizzard starts again.
Poor visibility,
Freezing.
Wander around with no hope to find a way back.
In the end I find some kind of abandoned hydro power plant.
I go inside, 40% health left.
Can't find a way to make fire inside and outside is a raging blizzard.
I take out my sleeping bag and try to sleep a bit to get warm.
Was that barking?
A wolf cames out of nowhere and jumps on me.
I stab it with a knife a few times and it runs off.
But the damage to me is done.
1 hour until night, everything dark.
10% health left, I am bleeding and freezing.
No bandages.
Vision blurry.
Is this the end?
I wander further inside the powerplant and find a first aid box.
Open it — yes, bandages!
Treat my wounds.
5% health left, still cold, the wolf is still somewhere inside the dark building, waiting for me to lower my guard.
I crawl into a corner fall into sleep praying to surive the night.
Morning comes.
50% health — I miraculously recover.
Drink some water and eat a can of cold tomato soup for breakfast.
Grab a lantern and wander throgh the dark and narrow halls of the power plant.
Find a body of the wolf — he seems to have bled to death after my successful act of defensive stabbing.
Explore some more.
I find a body of some man, some clothes and a lot of equipment.
This is taking forever but I find so many rare items needed for survival!
Finally I make my way outside.
Walk out of the powerplant like a boss with loads of stuff on me.
I find an entrance to another area.
Decide to explore a bit.
I see a cliff with railcarts hanging off it.
Try to make my way down.
Accidently fall off the cliff and die of internal bleeding.
