This is a difficult game to review because, without giving too much away, at its core it is about critiques and meta and the story behind games.
I will say, without a doubt, people who say it's not a game are wrong. It's a different kind of game. You have little influence and choice, it's more a story you're along for the ride for. The idea is probably a little ironic if you've played The Stanley Parable. In the truest sense, it is the narrator saying "this is my story and this is how it goes and we've got to get to the end I prepared and it will be so good". I don't mean that as a critique! It's just that, in a way, the games are an antithesis to each other, and if you think about the end a bit, maybe they're meant to be.
The game does share a meta look at gaming, so if that's your thing you'll find it in bunches and I wholly recommend you try it.
It's going to be a hit or miss with people depending on how they feel about the end. If people feel the journey was worth it, or if they didn't. That's vague to say, but really, what determines if the game was worth the money to you is the emotional resonance you feel with the end.
I personally found the journey fulfilling. As a final note, I'll say I think it's probably not the best game to play when you're down in a depressive spiral. If the emotional resonance of the game hits you, it packs a punch, so be prepared.

This game doesn't change
from previous games, but certainly brings new concepts to the table and then punches "Holmes and the Mystery of Silver Earring" right in the teeth.
"Holmes: Testament" is probably one of the more story-based games compared to the majority of its predecessors, in that
.

The plot-twist after the middle of the game was also commendable for making me question the deeper intentions of Holmes' action throughout the game, but it was slightly expected (I watched the BBC "Sherlock" series long before playing this, and a similar plot-twist was utilised there).
And the ending is certainly an unexpected one, but I feel as though
was thrown in at the last minute, just to give the game a villain to defeat. I mean, it felt like his character lacked depth in his particular style and his motives were a little too generic (i.e. "I want ot rule the world by force"), compared to say, Lupin from "Holmes: Nemesis", Jack the Ripper from "Holmes vs. Ripper" or even that insane guy who jumped off the lighthouse in "Holmes: Awakened".
The puzzles vary greatly in terms of activity, from looking into photographs for details to picking locks, so there is a wide range of challenges and tasks for all skill levels. Having said that, there will be different puzzles that appear rage-inducing and near impossible for you, because everyone's good at different things.
For example, during my first lock-picking puzzle, I thought I had to connect the wire to a certain mark on the board. I try doing that for a good half hour, and it turned out that the mark was purely aesthetic and all I had to do was recreate the shape on the top half of the screen (which I hadn't paid much attention to, since I was so focussed on the wire itself).
Like "Holmes vs. Ripper", the deduction board feature is back, but it's not as extensive (but still a bit of a challenge). The worst part is the fact that
; it's either all right or all wrong. Still, I suppose that makes the game all the more challenging, and all the more satisfying when you've got it all correct.
"Holmes: Testament" brings new mechanics to the game, which in turn, open more opportunities for engaging (and slightly frustrating) puzzles.
The most notable example of this that I can recall immediately is that you get to play as Toby, a sniffer-dog employed  by Holmes to find a man in the docks. In other words, YOU GET TO PLAY AS A DOG! TOTALLY DOG-TASTIC! And while playing as Toby, you have to solve environmental puzzles to give Holmes access to certain areas.
Of course, the ol' "Holmes Vision" (i.e. pressing spacebar to see all the interactable elements on the screen)  is back, but a bit more dulled than in previous games. Here, you can only detect
, and you have to be a lot closer to things before you can detect them.
Also, it's worth making a comment on the achievements in this game. The majority of achievements can be obained simply by working your way through the storyline. Some will require a little more work, like "The Holmesian" and "Pea-Souper".
And then there's "Blackmailer", the one achievement that relies on
. It's achievements this that make me want to strangle the game.
But otherwise, they're alright... I suppose.
Graphics haven't changed too much from "Holmes vs. Ripper", and the facial flexes are still fairly basic, in that a character can be yelling but still exhibit a mostly regular talking animation.
I still like the inclusion of Watson walking animations, since it makes the game MUCH less creepy than it was in "Holmes: Awakened", where he'd be spawning behind doors and around corners.
The cutscenes have also improved a bit from previous games.
And lastly: technical issues. Although they don't constitute as part of the game itself, it still affected my enjoyability of the game. I remember when I first installed this, I couldn't actually run the game. Even though a simple machine restart solved this issue, I don't think I've ever had that problem with other Holmes games.
Saving was also a weird problem, as sometimes the game would crash
, and so I'd lose the autosave AND have to redo parts of the game where the save failed.
Also, the game synchronisation times with Steam are abhorrent. So, I'd finish playing "Holmes: Testament" for the night, and then wait a good 5 minutes for the game to synchronise with Steam. This is strangely inconsistent with other games I  play, like Team Fortress 2, which also synchronise with Steam with much less required time.
In summary, "Holmes: Testament" is a slight improvement to previous Holmes games, so I think this deserves... an 8/10? The game has a decent quality, but could brush up in a few areas.

Is it scary? Yes. Is it fun to play? Sadly, no, not at all. The core mechanics are a poorly executed version of those from Alien: Isolation, and the game handles so sluggishly and communicates so poorly that the frequent deaths felt unavoidable rather than the fault of me as a player and my lack of mastery. Specifically, expect to repeatedly die because an enemy was right around the corner you just turned, or able to see the locker you were hiding in, and you had no way of knowing this or preparing for the event before progressing towards certain failure. In Isolation, as a contrast, the fairly audiable opponents, working looking-out-of-lockers mechanic, less sluggish looking around corners, and availability of the motion tracker solve this, making for a much better experience. In short, save your money for Alien: Isolation, or one of the two similarly excellent Amnesia games, instead.

Mediocre adventure game with very little actual sleuthing. After 4 hours of disjointed logic, pixel hunting, and excruciating mini-puzzle games, I gave up on it.
I was hoping for a stimulating, Holmes-style mystery to solve. Instead, it was just me hunting down clues and the game character connecting the dots. I didn't feel like Sherlock at all. I felt like his errand boy.
Holmes would frequently explain how he figured something out *after* we reached the conclusion. Meanwhile, I was confused as hell as to why I was doing any of it. I had little to do with solving the mysteries.
The dialogue was mostly in cutscenes. There is occasionally a "dialogue wheel" that tries to act like you have control of the character's conversation, but there are no actual choices to make. It was kind of obsurd. The only real brainwork is in the mini-puzzles, which seem like they're designed more for tedium than to flex your mind, and have absolutely nothing to do with the story or theme.
It just wasn't worth my time. There isn't enough meat to sink your teeth into. It's more like a cash machine aimed at casual gamers than a serious adventure game.

Ok folks, here's the deal. If its on sale, go for it. If you pay $30, you are going to be disappointed. Most of the bad reviews I've read seem to be from a position of overpriced instead of not being fun. I love it.
First of all, time never stands still (except in one challenge mode.) Time always churns at a snail pace and the more character movement you have, the more time speeds up to normal. So when you move your mouse around, you are moving and time does speed up. Some people call this a super annoying flaw. We call those people ♥♥♥♥♥ gamers. But before I digress...
There are no graphics to speak of. The lackluster screenshots do it accurate justice. It is not a beautiful game by any stretch. For what the game is, however, they work. The stark contrasts and geometric simplicity are kind of refreshing when many games over-saturate backgrounds. It started as a design constraint and turned into a legitamate style.
The gameplay is hectic. And loads of fun. I will say there exist ways to exploit the AI, which I have used to my advantage more than once. You hide behind a corner and run into the wall until someone comes. Then you clober them.
There really isnt a story to the game. Something about a hacker game that sucks people into the computer and turns them into hitmen or something. I dunno. You really don't need it though. The main 'campaign' doesn't take exceptionally long to beat, but it does unlock endless mode. And at heart this is an arcade style game.
Once I stopped trying to "win," I began to have massive amounts of fun just trying to pull off ridiculous feats and failing over and over and over (there are no load times btw.) Its when you pull off a brutal combo thats fluid and technically magnificent, you can get a lot of satisfaction seeing it replayed at regular time.
Pros
-Insanely fun
-No load times
-Lots of replayability
-You can cut bullets with a sword
Cons
-If you pay more than $15 you are overpaying.
-No modability in a platform that begs for it.
-"Graphics suck" if thats your position on things. (Trying to be unbiased here)
Bottom Line: 6/10
If the regular price were $15 bucks I would bump it up to a seven. Its loads of fun, but I would like to see more done with it before it deserves a higher score.

The ethos of sequels back in the day used to be that they were bigger, better, and with more content. Unfortunatley the modern mindset seems to be that you can push out a minimal product at full price, and charge for "DLC" that should have been in the main game.
Every step taken by kalypso seems to be a step backwards. There are less buildings, less avenues for economy, less player agency. In tropico 4 you could entirely eschew certain areas of economy and still make it work. Want a industrial complex that sucks the minerals from the land for massive profit? No problem. Want to protect mother earth, build your economy by becoming a tourist trap, or an island vegas? Go for it! Do you want to create an atheist state, a complete theocracy, a communist regime, or a capitalist paradise? All do-able!
Not so with tropico 5. Make a single move that the people dont like, and you're done. in some cases there is no way to correct this (sign the wrong thing into your constitution, watch your approval tank. just watch, you can do nothing about it now.) its game over. You -must- build a church if you want to have any hope of making out of colonial era. You -must- build a mine if you want to have any economy at all.  While in tropico 4 you had to keep citizen happiness in mind, now it is the single driving factor of the entire game, and you will have to play it their way, not yours. Now that buildings are tied to eras, the game is completely homogonized. Every game is "A" leads to "B" leads to "C". you -must- start with farming, which -must- lead to industrialization, with no options for tourism or even entertainment until the right era.
And the DLC that is planned for this game is beyond insulting. there are so many features from tropico 4 that were taken out so that they could be resold in bits and pieces. Remove jails and make the game activley punish you for trying to deal with criminals. Oh but dont worry, there is a prison DLC coming out that you can buy. It reminds me of a mobile free to play game, only i unfortunatley payed money for it.
Tropico 4 was one of my favotire city building games, with many interesting mechanics and conecpts that couldn't be found elsewhere. Tropico 5 is an incredible disappointment, i cant recomend anyone buy this game. To echo many other sentiments, buy tropico 4 if you are interested in it.

This Half-Life addition sees you playing as a Black Mesa facility security guard, Barney Calhoun, as you experience his trials and tribulations to escape the perils of "the incident" which occurred in Half-Life.  Blue Shift scraps many superfluous weapons from the first game, settling on a modest but satisfactory arsenal. Its storyline, the events that occur and the spectacular sights, along with some quite satisfying puzzles, will keep you entertained the whole way through; that said, it's not very long, as the duration of the game only spans a somewhat 'measly' 6 chapters, so it barely even has enough time to wear out its welcome. However, several high plot points and subtle (or not) details that serve to further intertwine its story's timeline with that of Gordon Freeman himself make the game wonderfully memorable and worth playing, especially if you've played Half-Life first.  Simplified, short, and pretty dang fun, Half-Life: Blue Shift isn't quite that full of a game in its own right, but it seems "just right", with a reasonable arsenal, and a far more manageable length than the first.  Considering it's more of a sister story to the first game, I might even say it serves this function--and then some.  A short but sweet and enjoyable ride.  A memorable experience, it's worth checking out Half-Life: Blue Shift.

Part RPG adventure, part sandbox, and part survival game, Sunless Sea is both challenging to get into and fun to play.
:
* The ability to create my own character. I consider this a must for any game wishing to be taken seriously as an RPG.
* There is plenty of excellent ambiance created by a combination of wonderful music, appropriately dark visuals, and intelligent writing.
* The game does not pull its punches. If I don't manage your resources with a mind toward how I will make it back home, I usually won't make it back home. Not without a lot of luck, anyway.
* The game makes me think. It asks me to make some fairly uncomfortable choices, and it makes me care about those choices.
* There is definitely quite a bit of replayability here. Which is good, because if you play anything like the way I do, you'll be dying a lot in the beginning while you figure things out.
:
* I was disappointed with the grind involved in leaving any meaningful legacy to my next of kin.
* Said grinding encourages the use of metagaming via abuse of certain of the game's mechanisms. I don't have to do this, but the conventional wisdom out on the 'net certainly recommends it. Seems to me this would be a game design flaw.
* There are so many things in the game which are so poorly explained that consulting the wiki at times is almost a necessity for those of us wish to complete the game. Many journal entries could and should be improved to provide clearer and more consistent information. I love a good mystery as much as anyone else, but being obtuse simply for the sake of being obtuse is not clever. It's annoying.
* Combat is sometimes also annoying. I have despised cooldowns on every RPG I've seen using them so far. This one is no exception.
I recommend buying the game if you enjoy exploring, experimenting, reading, and discovering things at your own pace. If you want a game that is combat/action oriented, you're likely to be disappointed with this one and should consider buying it only on sale.
Whatever you decide, I wish you happy gaming!

Sunless Sea is a very peculiar title in the modern game scene. In a land where survival games flourish, low-budget games pass Greenlight by a landslide and succeed by thousands of sales, and where a 2D game about humans and monsters can touch the hearts of hundreds, a slow-paced walking simulator-esque game about chugging along in an underground ocean doesn't seem like the kind of game that fits the modern market.
In its gameplay, Sunless Sea lacks true substance. It's very simple, with most of the time investment coming from laborious grinding. You play as the captain of a steamboat on the subterranean Unterzee, which is where London now resides after it lost a war to Hell in years past. I'm confused, too, don't worry. You can cruise around and do anything you'd like - run trade routes, kill monsters for loot, or just explore.
Sunless Sea's design, however, really prevents you from doing much of this. For one, your starting boat is slow, weak, inefficient, and weaker than paper mache against any zee-monster worth its weight. Running trade routes is hard because your hold can't really do its job because your engines are inefficient and need a lot of fuel. Killing monsters is completely out of the question because you'll get ground to a pulp beneath the weakest auroral megalops, and exploration is difficult for both of these reasons, plus a mechanic called Terror that causes you to go slowly insane away from land and in the dark.
"A grindy game with slow pace where it takes a long time to get anything done," I can hear you saying. "Why would anyone want to play this?" The real meat and gristle of the game comes in the form of its writing. I can already see you rolling your eyes, but hear me out. The writing in Sunless Sea is phenomenal. It's not just the story and themes - which, as a fan of the eldritch, I adore - but also the writing itself. Take the following passage that you read when visiting Mount Palmerston, an underground volcano that serves as the entrance to Hell:
"Sullen lights glow green at the jetty's edge. Behind the port buildings, the island is is knee-deep in ash. There are ruins here and there, of houses destroyed by fire. Far above, the mountain's top flickers red: just for an instant."
There are few games with writing as well as this one, and it lays out its mysteries and stories in a way that tantalizes you and dispels the chore of grinding. At one island, after becoming trusted with the locals, I searched around one of the offices and found a door. After I went through, a cavernous, spiraling staircase descended into darkness. I could either attempt a skill challenge (which I had very little chance of succeeding in), use some candles and flares to descend further (which I didn't have), or come back later. I chose to return all the way to Fallen London halfway across the map, buy the supplies, and go all the way back to explore what was down there.
And that was made possible because of how Sunless Sea lays out its stories. It leaves a breadcrumb trail for you to follow, and you'll quickly find that you're desperately getting to each subsequent crumb as fast as you can for just a tiny little bit more development and information. And the game rewards you for this. See, in the Unterzee, secrets work strangely; once you tell them, you lose them, and secrets deep enough can shape reality itself. By completing a long storyline, you might get a searing enigma, the most powerful form of secret and priceless among the high and mighty.
But I'm rambling, so I'll wrap this up. Sunless Sea is a game about stories. The gameplay it lacks is repaid by the interesting locations, strange people, and darkly beautiful Unterzee that it presents to you. If you're the kind of person who loves story and can accept lacking gameplay, definitely pick this up.

Just Cause 2 is a large, open world game set in the fictional nation of Panau where you play Rico Rodriguez, a member of The Agency, who is tasked with bringing an end to a dictator called Baby Panau. Is the game perfect? No. But is it fun? Oh, yes.
I'm not mincing words when I say that the story in Just Cause 2 is a hot load of garbage. Your character is brought to the Panauan conflict to usurp a dictator and find a member of your organization who is gone rogue. In order to find said rogue agent, you seek out 3 faction leaders. They agree to help you find this member of yours in return for favors of their own. Only... Rico finds this rogue agent in the second or third story mission in the game and learns that the agent is only giving the appearance of going rogue. Which brings us to the question - why does Rico then continue to do favours for 3 reprehensible, odious characters? Like I said, the game's story is a hot load of garbage. If you come into this game expecting a grand story, you'll be sorely disappointed. But that's not what this game is about - Just Cause 2 gives you a large world to do fun shenanigans and with just the tiniest semblance of a plot to tick a box called 'Story'. Nothing more, nothing less.
Just Cause 2 is a straight up Third Person Shooter. You can have upto a maximum of 3 main weapons, in addition to 2 types of explosives in your arsenal to kill baddies and cause all sorts of 'Chaos' - the points you earn to unlock new types of missions, weapons and vehicles. Returning from the first game, Rico has his trusty grappling hook that you will use to zip to and from places, objects and occasionally, use it in melee to bash an enemy to death.
Mission variety is limited to killing people, taking over strongholds, blowing stuff up, dropping off people and objects, races - stuff we've seen before. There are only 7 story missions and 49 faction missions. You can't just play through the story missions - you will have to unlock additional story missions by raising Chaos. You also gain Chaos by finding a huge number of collectible items like weapon parts, vehicle parts, armour parts and faction specific items like drug drops and skulls. There are lots of racing missions, 50 colonels to assassinate, towns and settlements to 100% individually, and they are littered all around the map, which is huge - around 400 sq. miles. You will get stumped as travelling around is difficult in the beginning. But once you get a hang of the various cars, bikes, planes, jets, helicopters and boats, you'll be able to travel around quickly. The game also allows you to use your grappling hook in conjuction with your parachute to travel - this is a boon especially when traversing tricky terrain like mountains and hills as you can save a lot of time.
Pro Tip : When piloting planes and jets, press and hold Left or Right key to make sharp turns. Tap lightly to make small corrections and fly in a precise manner.
After a couple of story and faction missions, you will unlock the option to Fast Travel by calling in a helicopter from which you can also buy equipment, upgrages and vehicles. One annoying thing I've observed is that if you fly over a new location and you are too high, that location will not be registered in your map. You have to lower your flight down till the location is registered. Obviously, you cannot Fast Travel during missions but you can call in equipment or vehicle drops.
The game has checkpoints during missions in case you fail though some missions will force you to repeat all the way from the beginning. The game wasn't too hard on the default normal difficulty in my 26 hours playing this game.
Enemy AI is not the smartest as occasionally you'll see enemies stand around doing nothing while you pick them off. The game does throw a lot of enemies at your way. As long as you've been upgrading your arsenal properly (focus on the Assault Rifle first as it is your most reliable weapon), you'll have no difficulties. This game has a threat meter that steadily starts increasing as you cause wanton chaos so expect reinforcements in the form of attack helicopters.
Rico can hijack vehicles whether they are on land, air or sea, provided they are within the reach of his grappling hook. You'll have to do a QTE to gain control of the enemy vehicle. There are also QTEs when you have access certain consoles, laptops and terminals - though these appear to be benign enough.
The game has a free 44 MB Multiplayer Mod that you can download from Steam. I have not played Multiplayer as I'm more of a single player kinda guy.
Visually, the game looks decent. Animation is a little stiff, lip synching is not that great, and expect a lot of bug eyed characters. One thing I recommend every gamer to do is to use the command /filmgrain=0 in the Launch options to disable the film grain; it ruins the game's presentation. There is no in-game setting to turn the grain filter off.
The game runs well, even on budget laptops.
Just Cause 2 does look beautiful at times, especially when you see the massive world open up in front of you. Expect to see anything from packed cities, lush forests, arid deserts and snowy areas.
Voice acting is campy but does the job. I didn't find the music to be memorable and I can't think of one track that stood out. Sound effects are okay. The audio front is one area that Just Cause 2 could have done a little more better.
I'd rate this game a solid 7. It drops you in this huge world and gives you the toys you need to go cause rampant chaos. What flaws it has are forgiveable when it's stupid, silly fun and well worth a playthrough or two. If you want your game to be serious, then this game is not for you. If you like fun games, then you should play this game. Just check videos of Just Cause 2 on YouTube to see the funny kind of stuff you can pull off in this game.
The game was a 4.8 GB download on Steam.
Just Cause 2 works on Windows 10 and for a game of this size, it is VERY stable. I didn't have a single crash when I played this game.
Just Cause 2 does not have Steam Trading Cards.
I've managed to get 31/50 achievements playing this game in my 29 hour playthrough. This game will take some time to 100%. Fortunately, you don't have to find every single item or resource in the game. Just Cause 2 is pretty generous in what it requires you to actually collect in order to gain certain achievements.
The Multiplayer Mod for Just Cause 2 has achievements of its own.

This game hits a difficult spot for me, because I absolutely adore the style, the music, the graphics, the stages, all of it.
And if you can take a look at the negative reviews, it's just a bunch of people whining about the difficulty. Git gud or get out. It's not an easy game, but the ease of restarting a fight and learning boss patterns, level designs, types of enemies, etc. are all fine tuned and polished to a level I haven't seen since Overwatch.
HOWEVER,
From what I can see, both from playing and from the average time spent by players that review this game, it's not long by any sort of definition. I cleared the first world in under 2 hours, and although I can see a difficulty spike and plenty of more boss fights ahead, it doesn't seem like it's replayable. I hate likening it to Binding of Isaac, but that game had a million different ways to play it, whereas this has only several. The boss battles are great, but the problem is while THEY are very dynamic and malleable to change with each different stage — defeating one stage of a fight only to have to switch up your strategy completely is an absolute joy for a player imo — the PLAYSTYLE itself is so much of the same. I get it, it's a platformer, and to the developer's credit, they put in plenty of weapon modifications to try and switch it up, as well as not giving you a ton of money so you have to choose what you really want or need for an upcoming fight.
It's a great game, and the developers have put in inordinate amounts of effort with the bosses, scenery, style, music, everything. They 100% deserve this upvote and have earned my approval easily. I feel like the game, however, struggles in terms of playstyle and replayability. So much of what the player does is the same, and there's not a ton of variation here, even with weapon modifiers. Additionally, I don't feel like the bosses are that hard after I've memorized their patterns, and for me that kind of kills it. In Dark Souls, for example, I could always do another run through with a new weapon, build, gameplay (i.e. SL1 or no armor), and it would always be at least a little different. I don't see a ton of that here, and that's why I'm most likely going to refund it. Not because I don't like it, but because, for $20, I want to be getting more than 13 hours of gameplay, and that's the absolute max I saw on reviews.
TL;DR Music, bosses, level design, style, all fantastic. Low variability and replayabilty, and short game relative to the cost of $20.

Giant mechs have always been a staple of gaming, from BattleTech all the way to Titanfall. The greatest entries in this armored pantheon usually had a talent for making you feel the weight and power of your mech as you stomped on tanks and lobbed mortars into other less fortunate mechs. The less great entries treated their subject more like a regular shooter that just happened to be huge, taking a more arcadey approach to enormous metallic combat. That’s where you’ll find Gun Metal, a dated offering in the mech genre that doesn’t offer much beyond the most basic stomping, flying, and shooting you’d expect from anything involving giant robots.
I know there’s a story in here somewhere, but unless you’re super stoked about sitting through early 2000’s budget CGI you’re probably going to skip it. I’m pretty sure you’re on another planet, judging by the space dinosaur farms, and you’ve got some colonies that bad guys want to explode. Fortunately your side has pulled ahead in the giant robot arms race with the Havok Suit, a Macross-style transforming robot fighter jet that packs more firepower than everyone else on the planet combined. With plenty of guns and mobility at your command, it’s up to you to save a bunch of presumably good guys from the presumably bad guys.
Every one of the game’s 14 missions drops you into an open map of fields, hills, valleys, and mountains to navigate in your transforming suit. Objectives can range from search and destroy to defense to the dreaded escort, but no matter what the briefing tells you your job is to destroy every enemy you see. Your suit is equipped with machine guns and homing missiles, and as you progress you’ll unlock additional weapons like flak cannons and lumbering torpedoes to help with heavier enemies. Robot form is ground-bound and slow but has shields, while jet form is faster through the air but takes more damage and can’t stop moving. Make no mistake, you’ll need both forms to take down the scattered targets in each mission.
At first blush there’s a certain retro charm to crashing about and blowing up chunky sci-fi enemies. There’s not a lot of detail to them or the landscapes but you can stomp through farmland and coastal regions and river valleys as you blast foes. Aside from some super annoying lens flare when facing the sun the graphics are fine and the sound design does its job, but real fast you’re going to realize that what you’ve seen in the first ten minutes is about all there is. Like I said, objectives may change but you’ll always be blasting the same enemies, just in different locations with different levels of urgency.
It’s the retro design that ultimately drags this one down, despite the retro action being up to par. Some objectives are braindead easy and obvious, while others in the same mission might be borderline impossible unless you anticipate them coming up. The fourth mission has you defend a base until it powers up its weapons, which is incredibly simple using the jet to strafe waves before they get anywhere near the target. After 5-10 minutes of that you have to thwart a surprise attack on another base by four extremely heavy enemies. I saw this coming and started on it before I was instructed to and still failed, forcing me to restart the entire 15-minute mission.
And that wasn’t even the escort mission. Other aggravations are sure to crop up, like how it’s impossible to tell what condition your mission-critical targets are or how there are no throttle controls for jet form or how you can’t really free aim in robot form. There’s very little feedback on hits or damage as well, so enemies can go from harmlessly plinking away to suddenly destroying you. The controls themselves will need to be remapped if you use a controller since this game predates most modern ones, and even then it’s kind of a pain to switch between your weapons or use your mobility to the fullest. It works, it’s just not great and can be a little annoying. And that’s Gun Metal in a nutshell, really, a competent shooter without much compelling about it, and with enough little annoyances to really limit its appeal.

It's not a bad "game". I'm only downvoting because I don't think it's worth the asking price. Maybe 2-3 bucks at the most (should be free). But for the limited content, very short story (you'll complete in about an hour), lack of replayability  and constriction of the player, 9.99 is a bit too much.
The Beginner's Guide is about as close to a walking simulator as you can get. You tour chapters (aka games of the dev's friend coda) while the narrator explains the backstory (between him and his "friend" coda at the point of that game's development) and his own take on what it means...presuming any meaning was intended. You actually do encounter a puzzle at one point but once solved it's repeated again so the challenge is gone. And you can "die" in one part but no serious obstalcles that hinder your storied trek.
Some things (in partiuclar the abstract, artsy portions of his games) are typical "open for interpretation", but the story is never too vague. As you progress towards the end, there will be a message apparent depending on how you rationalize/interepret the events and dynamics between Davey and "coda" (as well as "himself"). Not spoiling anything, but it get's depressing towards the end. Depressed because I actually was emotionally invested to a degree (mostly "coda") and if any story of any medium manages that, it has value.
You're playing a story. Not playing a game. So if you are looking for a game, look elsewhere. But if you want an experience with unconventional storytelling methods, you might dig this.  I think it closely resembles art because its interpretative nature allows us to look at the story from different angle and thus experience different emotions. Whatever the designer's intended point doesn't have to be yours.
I'm glad I experienced it but I still didn't think it was worth the asking price. Get it on discount.

I only paid $15 for this game and I still feel cheated. On top of being short, the content that's there is so bare bones and at times frustrating (in partiuclar the nearly endless waves in the final level).
The narrative is cryptic and insulting, prompting me to alt tab out of the game for spite alone. They cleverly saved a bunch of money and effort by not coloring in any textures and not putting in any music aside from the credits. Mooks are equipped with one of three guns, though the strategy for effectively dealing with them all is the same regardless. Just hide behind a corner and pick them off as they come into view.
The absolute worst♥♥♥♥♥♥is when an enemy spawns through a portal and shoots you dead before he's finished rendering. Instant death from the other side of the mook spawner, bullets from a gun that aren't even visible. Sure it glows pink to warn you in general that someone's gonna spawn, but you need more precision in a game focused around one hit kills. It's impossible to be fully aware of your surroundings, so enjoy getting shot from behind. Turning around eats up time too, so when you look behind yourself enjoy being shot from what was just a second ago in front of you.
This game got hyped beyond the stars when it came out. Probably related to the prenatal shill campaign embedded right before the credits. That's right, this game shamelessly goads the player into shilling for it on social media and to their friends, all under the flimsy pretense of it being tangentally related to the plot.
I should have steered clear of this game, but my morbid curiosity got the better of me. Despite what the game would have the playerbase say, an fps that runs entirely in ZED time doesn't make for the most innovative shooter in years, nor do FPS games benefit from being innovative so much as being visceral and loaded with action. Bulletstorm. Doom. Binary Domain. Bioshock 2. Mass Effect 2. All more innovative, and all certainly more fun.

Overall, I liked The Testament of Sherlock Holmes. It has some technical flaws, which make it not the greatest game, but I'm glad I played it.
Pros:

+ Good story. Nice twists an turns.
+ Good mixture of point and click, puzzle, and deduction elements. The deduction puzzles make it feel very Sherlocky.
Cons:
- A little too much pixel-hunting in the point and click. A couple of times I had to consult a walkthrough because I missed picking up some tiny item in a large level. A couple of the point and click puzzles are annoying.
- The story (while good overall) is framed with a really stupid meta-narration that kills the mood from time to time. Also I did not like the ending at all.
- Game starts to drag a little towards the end, where there is an extended and annoying last level. I was ready for it to be over.

Unfortunately I just can't recommend this game as much as I would have loved to.
When I first played it, it was a nice refresh and continuation of Tropico 4. As I played it more, I found more and more problems with the game. The fighting, the buildings, the overlays (pre building placement and post placement), rebels, population cap, to name a few. I'll summarise these quickly:
The fighting: Essentially, its build a huge military or be wiped out. Once rebels appear, if they break through your military (which they will as they are OP most of the time), they head straight to the palace and game over. Your military doesn't respawn, you cannot rebuild military buildings either. Even if your barracks refill with 8 troopers, they won't go and fight the rebels attacking the palace. Totally ridiculous and to me, its a game breaker.
The buildings: Only apartments have 'variations' and even then they look pretty much the same. Throughout the eras, the building all look the same, modern housing in colonial periods. Really? There needs to be much more variation in models. As it stands now, its bland. There are buildings missing too that should really be in there. Since when did a police station act as a fire station? Seems lazy. Modern tanks appearing in the cold war era too.
Overlays: When you place buildings that say 'Affects nearby plantations' or 'Generates funds off nearby housing', there is nothing to say how far this radius is. You have no idea what it will affect until its placed and built. These buildings often cost alot to make and many times where you place can be a total waste of resources. For a modern 2014 game, this is not acceptable to me. Kalypso merely say its meant to be this way and is fine, and then point about overlays in the Almanac which are irrelivent to the point raised to them. There is nothing to say what the radius is of any building. This is a poor effort.
Rebels - too common, too OP. Doesn't give the feeling of a dictatorship game at all. Even on high happiness (some people have rebel attacks at 100 happiness). There are no real reasons for rebels alot of the time, and to many, its unknown why they are attacking since everyone is happy. The only real way to counter rebels is to have a huge military, which generates more rebels in itself. Lose lose situation ultimately.
2000 people population cap. You have often use 1/4 of the island and reach this pop cap. Very poor. Dev excuses for this are poor and obsurd. As of patch 1.08 a population slider has finally been implemented. Only took them 9 months.
Last point i'll make is the DLC for this. £3 for most DLC, gives 1 building,  an outfit you never see, 1 short mission and a music track. Most of the DLC was already included in the base game and can be unlocked via mods and working correctly. Your paying to play with what should have been there in the first place really. Considering the base price of the game is £29.99, its really not worth it.
Could only recommend the game if game price drops below £15 and all DLC included.

Just Cause 2 is a large, open world game set in the fictional nation of Panau where you play Rico Rodriguez, a member of The Agency, who is tasked with bringing an end to a dictator called Baby Panau. Is the game perfect? No. But is it fun? Oh, yes.
I'm not mincing words when I say that the story in Just Cause 2 is a hot load of garbage. Your character is brought to the Panauan conflict to usurp a dictator and find a member of your organization who is gone rogue. In order to find said rogue agent, you seek out 3 faction leaders. They agree to help you find this member of yours in return for favors of their own. Only... Rico finds this rogue agent in the second or third story mission in the game and learns that the agent is only giving the appearance of going rogue. Which brings us to the question - why does Rico then continue to do favours for 3 reprehensible, odious characters? Like I said, the game's story is a hot load of garbage. If you come into this game expecting a grand story, you'll be sorely disappointed. But that's not what this game is about - Just Cause 2 gives you a large world to do fun shenanigans and with just the tiniest semblance of a plot to tick a box called 'Story'. Nothing more, nothing less.
Just Cause 2 is a straight up Third Person Shooter. You can have upto a maximum of 3 main weapons, in addition to 2 types of explosives in your arsenal to kill baddies and cause all sorts of 'Chaos' - the points you earn to unlock new types of missions, weapons and vehicles. Returning from the first game, Rico has his trusty grappling hook that you will use to zip to and from places, objects and occasionally, use it in melee to bash an enemy to death.
Mission variety is limited to killing people, taking over strongholds, blowing stuff up, dropping off people and objects, races - stuff we've seen before. There are only 7 story missions and 49 faction missions. You can't just play through the story missions - you will have to unlock additional story missions by raising Chaos. You also gain Chaos by finding a huge number of collectible items like weapon parts, vehicle parts, armour parts and faction specific items like drug drops and skulls. There are lots of racing missions, 50 colonels to assassinate, towns and settlements to 100% individually, and they are littered all around the map, which is huge - around 400 sq. miles. You will get stumped as travelling around is difficult in the beginning. But once you get a hang of the various cars, bikes, planes, jets, helicopters and boats, you'll be able to travel around quickly. The game also allows you to use your grappling hook in conjuction with your parachute to travel - this is a boon especially when traversing tricky terrain like mountains and hills as you can save a lot of time.
Pro Tip : When piloting planes and jets, press and hold Left or Right key to make sharp turns. Tap lightly to make small corrections and fly in a precise manner.
After a couple of story and faction missions, you will unlock the option to Fast Travel by calling in a helicopter from which you can also buy equipment, upgrages and vehicles. One annoying thing I've observed is that if you fly over a new location and you are too high, that location will not be registered in your map. You have to lower your flight down till the location is registered. Obviously, you cannot Fast Travel during missions but you can call in equipment or vehicle drops.
The game has checkpoints during missions in case you fail though some missions will force you to repeat all the way from the beginning. The game wasn't too hard on the default normal difficulty in my 26 hours playing this game.
Enemy AI is not the smartest as occasionally you'll see enemies stand around doing nothing while you pick them off. The game does throw a lot of enemies at your way. As long as you've been upgrading your arsenal properly (focus on the Assault Rifle first as it is your most reliable weapon), you'll have no difficulties. This game has a threat meter that steadily starts increasing as you cause wanton chaos so expect reinforcements in the form of attack helicopters.
Rico can hijack vehicles whether they are on land, air or sea, provided they are within the reach of his grappling hook. You'll have to do a QTE to gain control of the enemy vehicle. There are also QTEs when you have access certain consoles, laptops and terminals - though these appear to be benign enough.
The game has a free 44 MB Multiplayer Mod that you can download from Steam. I have not played Multiplayer as I'm more of a single player kinda guy.
Visually, the game looks decent. Animation is a little stiff, lip synching is not that great, and expect a lot of bug eyed characters. One thing I recommend every gamer to do is to use the command /filmgrain=0 in the Launch options to disable the film grain; it ruins the game's presentation. There is no in-game setting to turn the grain filter off.
The game runs well, even on budget laptops.
Just Cause 2 does look beautiful at times, especially when you see the massive world open up in front of you. Expect to see anything from packed cities, lush forests, arid deserts and snowy areas.
Voice acting is campy but does the job. I didn't find the music to be memorable and I can't think of one track that stood out. Sound effects are okay. The audio front is one area that Just Cause 2 could have done a little more better.
I'd rate this game a solid 7. It drops you in this huge world and gives you the toys you need to go cause rampant chaos. What flaws it has are forgiveable when it's stupid, silly fun and well worth a playthrough or two. If you want your game to be serious, then this game is not for you. If you like fun games, then you should play this game. Just check videos of Just Cause 2 on YouTube to see the funny kind of stuff you can pull off in this game.
The game was a 4.8 GB download on Steam.
Just Cause 2 works on Windows 10 and for a game of this size, it is VERY stable. I didn't have a single crash when I played this game.
Just Cause 2 does not have Steam Trading Cards.
I've managed to get 31/50 achievements playing this game in my 29 hour playthrough. This game will take some time to 100%. Fortunately, you don't have to find every single item or resource in the game. Just Cause 2 is pretty generous in what it requires you to actually collect in order to gain certain achievements.
The Multiplayer Mod for Just Cause 2 has achievements of its own.

Basically, you help a group of scientists fix the teleporter and teleport out of the Black Mesa facility. The only cameo is at the start of the game when you see Gordon riding the train.
Gameplay wise, it's basically the same as the original game, except there are no "Class 4" Type weapons (gravity guns and such). The game also has a few puzzles here and there.
In the end though, i like the first expansion (Opposing Force) much more. It had it's own identity i would say.
This expansion is short, pretty much all assets are reused from the original Half Life, and thematically it just does not do a good job, unlike its predecessor - Opposing Force.

Oh well. After Playing through Blue Shift on Hard difficulty I have to say that I can understand the criticism this game got. But after all it was a really good ... little campaign. I think the points of criticism (no new Weapons, no Endboss, no new Enemies etc.) are valid considering the original Half Life and its quality. But surprisingly enough these points seemed very fitting to me. I mean after all we aren't the Hero of the story. We are nothing special at all. We are just a security officer that tries to get the hell out of the catastrophy he got into. Why should he use some super powered Weapons ? He uses what he can find. Why should he beat a giant Alien or Endboss ? He is simply trying to get away, not trying to save the world (like Rosenberg pointed out during the Elevator Scene). Other than that I have to say that I found the atmosphere to be really amazing. I felt like a confused lonely surviver trying to stay alive running for his life. All these dark coridors and the environment crumbling away. Electricity shooting out of walls and stuff like that. The biggest personal point of criticism for me is that it only took me 4 hours to complete the campaign on the hardest difficulty. Ultimately, if you enjoy the Half Life Universe I can recommend you to play it. Its short, its atmospheric, its intense.

Simple and Fun. More fast paced than the original game, and obviously require less skill than the 3-dimension world.
But still a little improvements to expect:
- Though there's no "headshot" in 2D, players should still be encouraged to shoot towards the center of the body in order to deal maximazed damage.
- Since there's one less dimension than actual CS, guns with faster fire rate is way more powerful (yes, M249) even if recoil is turned on, and sniper guns are way less useful in this case.
- Should add more recoil to guns, and reduce accuracy when walking.
- Should lift the camera when the mouse is close the edge of screen (with a slightly offset center), such that you can see further at that direction, which will also make sniper scope useful.
- Should add a jump/roll mechanic that could give player the ability to temporarily dodge the bullet, or move between platforms. It's boring to just move by WASD.
- Map lacks a dimension in height, so there are some spots that turn out to be too good especially when the map is actually derived from the original CS.
- Just don't turn on friendlyfire. It's way too easy to shoot your teammates accidentally, and the punishment is not welcome in this situation.
Overall, It's worth trying as a free to play game on steam, so I would recommend this game. But as I mentioned above, such improvements could still be beneficial here.

When I installed Bioshock it suggested the difficulty to play based on your FPS experience.  However I would be hesitant in calling it a FPS with such bad and arbitrary shooting mechanics.  All the characters are the worst bullet sponges I've ever seen in a game.  It’s like they all have body armour.  While it’s difficult to kill them even when blasting them at close range while they are standing still they have no problem being deadly accurate shooting back while in full gallop.  To kill any character I found that there is no one shot kill you literally have to empty your weapon into them.  And that shotgun, I’ve never seen such a slow reload as in this game.  If you snuck up on someone and blasted them in the back of the head with the shotgun, (which of course doesn't even phase them, it just makes them aware of your presence so they do a quick as lightning about face and start blasting you), by the time your character pumped out the empty and reloaded you were already hit multiple times.

Alpha testing review:
The game is way over hyped. Sure it's a fun game to play with friends and even strangers (so long as they have a mic). But that fun slowly turns into tediousness after several hours simply because it all feels very repetitive, and the constant loading screens don't help either. You spend more time waiting for delay timers, different sections of the game to load, and then the generic cutscenes than actually playing the game. So it's like 10 minutes of waiting to 5 minutes of actual gameplay. The map feels very small as a monster because you constantly run into the edges of the map and too big as a hunter because it's so difficult to find / catch up to a skilled monster. The graphics are nice and very smooth, no lags at all while on default high graphics settings (haven't tried ultra settings yet), using GTX 660 S2 3GB graphics card. I'm not sure what the FPS is like though as I can't get RivaTuner to work with it yet. Run / walk switching and aim switching is a toggle rather than hold the button which is very annoying, they have auto run option which basically makes you permanently running to bypass that stupidity. Monster at first level stands no chance against the hunters, but monster at level 3 is way too OP, we stand almost no chance at killing it. So when a skilled person plays a monster and they reach level 3... there's no way for the hunters to kill it. It's only if the monster is new to the game and just so happens to be lucky enough to reach level 3, that's when the hunters might stand a chance at killing it. Overall, this game really doesn't add anything unique in which we haven't seen before. It basically just feels like a Left 4 Dead multiplayer vs mode, but instead of a group of special zombies, there's just 1 "tank" with a crap load of health which can level up to have even more health.
As a hunter, then the goal is simply to locate, trap and kill the monster as quickly as possible while sticking together as a group... the strategy is extremely predictable and constant. As a monster, the goal is to run away like a ♥♥♥♥♥ and maintain a minimum distance away from the hunters for as long as possible, never engaging them until at least stage 2, but preferably stage 3 if you can manage it. The monster feeds on the animals around the map to reach those stages. Once at stage 3, it's decimating time.
All that hype over this game, yet look at all the mixed reviews for this game so far. Clearly they over hyped it to the point where a lot of ppl are disapointed now. If they had kept the news about it more honest, I would imagine the reviews for this game would have been a lot better.
Would I pay $70 for this game... hell no... are you kidding me? Would I pay $20 for this game... probably not, my friends would really need to do some convincing. Would I pay $10 for it... sure.
It's not a bad game by any means, it's just way over hyped. It doesn't have nearly as much content as we expected. And I know we'll get a bit more content when the game is released (more maps, more hunters to select from, 1 more monster), but what about weapons and equipment variety? What about monster skill variety? It's not even mentioned as a future plan... so in other words, it will feel exactly the same even with the new hunters, new monster and maps. The only thing that might save this game are the other game modes... that is, if they're any good. Somehow I really doubt the single player mode will save it since it's unlikely to have a story mode or any reason to wanting to play alone other than to practice or get away from bad ppl if that ends up happening in this game.
Oh, and I can already tell that there will be some DLCs for this game based on the unavailable stuff that is greyed out in the game, and not mentioned for release date. Nothing like spending $70 now and then even more money later just to keep the game up to date with everyone else right?

I'm a big fan of the series and tycoon games in general.  Unfortunately, a low population cap makes Tropico 5 unplayable by its second half.
The player will find his citizens emigrating en masse starting around the beginning of the Cold War, which will cause his economy to collapse.  Factories go unmanned, exports are never transported to the docks, expensive buildings are rendered useless by rolling blackouts as power plants run short on staff and fuel. Pulling people from entertainment and welfare buildings causes Happiness to plummet.  Hiring even illiterate foreign workers quickly becomes prohibitively expensive, and pointless, as they're likely to leave on the next transport.
As the population cap is invisible to the player, he may spend many frustrating hours trying to placate his citizens before he realizes it's nothing he's doing wrong.
In order to play successfully, one has to very consciously limit expansion from the start of the campaign onwards. (Unlike in previous installments, scenarios don't start with a blank slate; everything you've built in earlier eras is still there, although the money in your treasury, mysteriously, is not.)
In short, this game is essentially broken without mods.  I appreciate the detail, beauty and realism that Haemimont have added, but they are in no way worth the losses in gameplay.

Although some may commend it for its beautiful art style; the gameplay is infuriating, unrewarding, and far too slow for me to really appreciate all Morphopolis has to offer. There also isn't a menu where I can tinker with the sounds, which means I have to listen to that annoying bug chirp in the background for the entirety of the game.
The controls are maddening. You click and drag your cursor in the direction that you want the bug to move, but unfortunately the controls don't always work. You'll find yourself dragging, only to watch your bug go back and forth. In certain points, you'll have to wait for an animation to finish until you can move your bug again - which can be upsetting if the controls are screwing up constantly.
There is also tons of backtracking, which makes every level feel tedious. Since every level that you play seems to end with you collecting a serious of orange balls, I know that I am going to have to do that at the end, but I can't collect them all before I receive the quest. Subsequently, I'm forced to backtrack through every single level to collect all of the orange balls in order to go to the next level that will ask me to do the same thing.
Backtracking wouldn't be that much of an issue if your character didn't trek along at the speed of molasses. The two hours that you'll spend completing this game could be cut down to about an hour and half if the bug would move just a tad bit quicker. Unfortunately, that never happens and you're forced to watch your bug move uncomfortably slow through every area - which can be upsetting if you're someone that enjoys gameplay that actually moves at an appropriate pace.
Also, the last puzzle is a treat. By that, I mean, you'll be shouting at your computer screen and wondering why the hell anyone would develop a puzzle as ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as the one you're playing. In the end, Morphopolis is slow, boring, and unrewarding - the gameplay is too little movement, too much grinding and that's just no fun. I cannot recommend this game.

Is it scary? Yes. Is it fun to play? Sadly, no, not at all. The core mechanics are a poorly executed version of those from Alien: Isolation, and the game handles so sluggishly and communicates so poorly that the frequent deaths felt unavoidable rather than the fault of me as a player and my lack of mastery. Specifically, expect to repeatedly die because an enemy was right around the corner you just turned, or able to see the locker you were hiding in, and you had no way of knowing this or preparing for the event before progressing towards certain failure. In Isolation, as a contrast, the fairly audiable opponents, working looking-out-of-lockers mechanic, less sluggish looking around corners, and availability of the motion tracker solve this, making for a much better experience. This is amongst my favorites WWII games made for PC. If you liked Saving Private Ryan, Enemy at The Gates, and Fury this is the game for you. The game features the typical features of an FPS especially if you're a BF/COD kind of person but with an altered state of realism with intense graphics, story and extremely fun and engaging multiplayer I would give this game 9.5/10 with it's only flaw is start up issues on low end computers. Anyone who owns a laptop or desktop that uses a Celeron card or intel low end cards this game will not run at all. It will blackout on you and crash. For laptop users if your laptop has Celeron or anything near that or if your laptop is a simple laptop a notebook with beats audio etc. any of that stuff that's just nice for simple tasks will  not be able to play the game or even access the menus having played this game on multiple desktops and laptops this game runs best for at least average builds or awesome ones. The options aren't very optimal for the users is part of why I don't give this game a 10/10. Anyways I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys great stories and MP gameplay with great visuals, sound effects, and FPS games. COD players should enjoy this game but this can be enjoyed by anyone who just wants to play a game. Novice players can play anyone. Enjoy.

Overall, it means that there is a lot of micromanagement in this game. I still enjoyed it though.

Sunless Sea is a game that requires patience, and planning. Making a mistake grants swift punishment, but if you think ahead, and stay careful you'll find yourself strong enough later to do just about anything you want. To get to that point can require quite a bit of a grind, and if you make the wrong choices you might lose a lot of chances, but even then this game can be quite entertaining. I was going to leave my old review below to compare, but Steam has a character limit so I didn't. Consider this first paragraph a big ♥♥♥♥-you to whoever implemented a character limit ON REVIEWS.
Now, the actual thing.
First I want to acknowledge issues I had previously that have been fixed, the foremost of which is the ability to craft better weaponry. The devs clearly listened to their player community on this one, replacing the old system with a way of generating research data and using THAT progress to create better guns (and better everything else as well!)
The ridiculous placeholder drops on the second biome flora have been replaced with the real deal, and though I suspect it took me about as long to get there as the last time (seeing as I have neither x,y coordinates nor a map nor my old world to reference for comparison) I found the trip less crappy for having a weapon that can KILL THINGS. This is a major improvement over the last attempt.
Some of the new tools available include better saws and picks. THANK YOU, DEVS. THANK YOU SO MUCH! Being able to mine -quickly- makes generating both resources and science xp (used for science) much, much faster and more reasonable to accomplish. I am also fairly certain that either the costs of chests (in terms of aluminum) have gone down or the availability of aluminum has increased: either way, THANK YOU AGAIN. Early game resource management sucked the last time, much less so now.
Combat got more fun. This is partly due to the fact that I CAN KILL THINGS NOW because my gun NO LONGER HAS TRAINING WHEELS. Seriously, I cannot say enough how this particular change makes the game better (and I also cannot say enough how confused I am that the old loot % system was used AT ALL before, eminently terrible as it is: good change is good). The enemies feel overall a bit less the same, and I genuinely live in terror of those little blue bugs in the second biome. Guh.
Now for the less cool stuff.
Screen shake. Cool effect, but this (like controller rumble) should always have an off switch. Making it non-optional is excessively lame to your players.
Weaponry NEEDS a key that reloads it that is NOT shared with another function. Maybe the R button? Just a thought.
Disabling jetpacks in headhunter temples. This is kind of awful, honestly. I have the entire rest of the game to get used to using my jetpack to maneuver, only to have to change my reflexes in the more challenging parts? Where I would dodge basically without thinking before, here I am forced to remember a change in play that IS NEVER PREFACED while in the middle of genuinely tougher combat. Let the player use the tools you've given them in game. Let them think laterally. Don't feel like you need to take away one of the most fun parts of your game to add "challenge": execution challenge isn't satisfying. Depth challenge is satisfying. At the very least give some warning about the change beforehand.
Weapon customization needs to happen. When reload times are long, a mod to make them shorter is muy bueno. When ammo counts are small, a mod to make them bigger is muy bueno. Not having this sort of thing to replace the old random weapon stats system? No bueno.
Tl;dr, The changes I've seen are massive, and merit me changing from a not recommended to a recommended. Way to go, game devs! You guys genuinely fixed things that were broken, and what I'm seeing now is much, much more enjoyable than when I bought it. High hopes, guys.

An atmospheric Sherlock Holmes game with a good story.
The 3D characters look nice but are somewhat robotic, including the protagonists. The voice acting is generally good, although Holmes and Watson's exchanges can be weird; Watson especially brings to mind an alien trying to figure out the correct reply, at times.
The puzzles are hit and miss, but all the coffee break style minigames can be skipped if wanted. The larger problem is that there's a fair amount of item hunting, in areas where it's unclear what you're even trying to achieve.
There's a deduction board which you must fill with clues and then use the power of deduction to make the right conclusions. This was one of the best parts of the previous Frogwares titles, and it's nice to see it's still present.
From a technical standpoint the game is fairly solid. The graphics and sound are both very good and the game runs well. The control scheme is simple and doesn't get in the way.
I do wish Frogwares learned to program proper mouse controls, though - the 1st person mouse control is even worse than in their previous 3D Sherlock titles. There's an annoying dead zone in the vertical axis in addition to the general floatiness, which is not caused by vertical sync or low frame rate. At least the vertical axis can be reversed.
The Testament should also get a prize for the weirdest intro video in a long time, in which a trio of really weird looking children find a book in an attic. It's a complete mess. One of the kids looks like a ventriloquist's doll and they all behave like they're from a fever dream.
Still, it's a very good game and definitely worth playing.

Oh boy, this is a tough thing to review. First, it's not a game in any real sense, but an exploration of themes about rejection, in the context of viewing some "unreleased" games by a vague developer named Coda. The experience lasts about an hour and a half. It's not unfair to call this a walking simulator, as that comes close to capturing what's happening here. There's a fair amount of pretentiousness, which is a staple of walking simulators. Sometimes I like that, sometimes not.
With that said, this didn't do it for me. The baseline conceit - that this is game is an "apology" to Coda for releasing his games, completely fails for me. If you take that as true, it's super-skeevy as I paid $10 to also peek at Coda's stuff, and I gathered from the walkthrough that he was all about the art, not the money. But I don't actually believe the story is based in reality so we'll put that concern aside.
So if you take the Coda thing as a bit of colorful fiction, I can more easily accept what is being offered. Even so, I didn't find it terribly compelling. Which is to say: the concepts and narrative are fine, but I didn't feel like paying $10 for the privilege of experiencing this story, told in 1.5 hours, was worthwhile.
I'd rate this as 2/5. It didn't click for me. Maybe it will for you.

There's no reason to try and express hpw awesome this game is, instead I'll give some tips to those, who think that the game has major flaws
The parry is a crucial part of the game, expecially on some bosses. First of all it charges your ex ability or whatever its called, which is quite a lifesaver if used right. 2nd - it lets you jump higher and further. 3 - it can block some attacks. If that's not enough for you, I don't know what is.
The character is rather slow only until you start truly utilizing your dash, which boosts you drastically. It is very easy to overlook the dash at the start, but the further you go - the more crucial its mastery becomes.
The game IS difficult and the ability to practise bosses on an easier difficulty is nice, since it lets you prepare to some boss forms that would catch you off guard on a successful run. And don't forget - the game is a boss fighter. The run'n'gun levels are simply there to open a new path and give you a few coins for upgrades. And yes, completing easy versions of bosses lets you advance through the map as well.
The upgrade system is neat and allows for quite some combinations. It is by no means a key feature of the game, which is boss fights. They could've dismissed upgrades alltogether and it'd still be a ton of fun.
And yes, did I mention that the game is very difficult? There are often scenarios where you might think that you can't escape the damage, but that can only mean one of 3 things. 1) You've trapped yourself, 2) You didn't master some mechanics enough, 3) You forgot about some mechanic.
And you can't just use your abilities whenever you feel like it, after all, there's a separated invulnerability ultimate for a purpose of defense. All others must be used with caution.
P.S. While bosses usually have some degree of random, if you plan your movements accordingly - you can always evade.

Been playing platformers since Apogee era games in the early 90's and have to say that this is among one of my favourite games out of the entire genre. Cuphead isn't just a masterpiece in terms of its artistic, audio and visual work, the games design and gameplay shines just as much as those do.
The games art style is a tribute to 1930's cartoons and the gameplay mechanics are a mish-mash of 90's shoot-em-up side scrollers such as Contra, Metal Slug and Gunstar Heros (more so the latter) and though there are a few 'Run and Gun' levels which involve platforming, collecting coins, shooting/avoiding enemies until you reach the end of the level, the games main focus is on boss fights, each being very unique from the last.
The game itself is not easy either although I wouldn't say it's as hard as a lot of people make it out to be, it is very forgiving seeing as you're able to retry bosses/levels at your own leisure rather than getting slapped with a gameover screen after your continues are depleted. The fights are completely fair too, although punishing should you lose concentration and mistime a dodge or not memorize the way certain attacks work and repeat the same mistakes over and over again until even the announcer begins to sound bored of announcing the start of battles.
The audio/soundtrack is incredibly well done, all original music composed for this game sound in place for a 30's cartoon as do the sound effects.
Meticulous effort went into every aspect of this games design, it was hard to wipe a smile off my face while playing it, although a few bosses came close to achieving that. Beyond having a great time with this game, what's even more great is that something like this exists in this era of gaming aswell being a critical and commercial success, it gives me hope for the future of this industry. For newcomers, don't be intimidated by people complaining that it's too hard, it really isn't, each fight is fair and although admittedly some bosses for me almost took the same amount of time to defeat that others took to complete the entire game, the joy of overcoming a challenge was monumentally satisfying.
Highly recommended game and deserves every bit of the praise it has recieved. Looking forward to seeing what this developer delivers in the future as there was no lack of effort put into the creation of this game.

A wolf cames out of nowhere and jumps on me.
I stab it with a knife a few times and it runs off.
But the damage to me is done.
1 hour until night, everything dark.
10% health left, I am bleeding and freezing.
No bandages.
Vision blurry.
Is this the end?
I wander further inside the powerplant and find a first aid box.
Open it — yes, bandages!
Treat my wounds.
5% health left, still cold, the wolf is still somewhere inside the dark building, waiting for me to lower my guard.
I crawl into a corner fall into sleep praying to surive the night.
Morning comes.
50% health — I miraculously recover.
Drink some water and eat a can of cold tomato soup for breakfast.
Grab a lantern and wander throgh the dark and narrow halls of the power plant.
Find a body of the wolf — he seems to have bled to death after my successful act of defensive stabbing.
Explore some more.
I find a body of some man, some clothes and a lot of equipment.
This is taking forever but I find so many rare items needed for survival!
Finally I make my way outside.
Walk out of the powerplant like a boss with loads of stuff on me.
I find an entrance to another area.
Decide to explore a bit.
I see a cliff with railcarts hanging off it.
Try to make my way down.
Accidently fall off the cliff and die of internal bleeding.
10/10 intense survival simulator!

Set in the distance future of 2002, Gun Metal came out during this weird time when Xbox games were surprisingly experimental.
You play as a pilot of the Havoc suit, a mech that can change between a humanoid form and a jet form, and totally isn't like the Valkyrie from Macross. The game has an actual story, but I had to dig up a wikipedia article on the game to actually get it outside of mission to mission stuff.
Humanity has sent out ships to colonize a new world, but these ships were tailed by an enemy alien fleet hellbent on destroying the new colony. So it's up to you piloting the Havoc suit to protect the colonists and defeat a tireless enemy that fires red lasers while you fire blue lasers.
Transforming the havoc suit is as easy as pressing a button, with both forms having their own set of weapons. While it's implied that ground form is used to fight land units while flight form is used to fight air units, there's a surprising amount of options given to you.
You unlock more weapon to choose from as the game progresses with both forms having four or five weapons each. It's just as easy to carpet bomb an area of enemy tanks as it is to transform mid air, land on an enemy ship, and just aim down and fire.
Which I do, all the time. Because it's radical.
Aiming and shooting takes a few moments to get accustomed to. And much like my violent alcaholism, you just need need to get used to it. Your crosshairs move around the screen, and the mech doesn't turn until the crosshairs reach the edge of the screen. It's kind of reminiscent  of other games from the same genre, but just how wonky is feels at first could throw you off.
Luckily, it doesn't take long to get use to and you even kind of appreciate it being there. It means you can keep your eye on all of your targeted enemies instead of having to look away and hoping your missile still meets its mark. Like eating a sandwich in front of a pack of hungry racoons, you just know the second you take your eyes off them they'll attack.
Gun Metal actually reminds me of another game that came out around the same time, a game kind of lost to time known as "Battle Engine Aquila." or something along those lines.
Looking deeper into Gun Metal and the time it was released I was actually surprised to find out that some graphics cards at the time actually released packed with Gun Metal and BEA together.
Now isn't that neato burrito.
It's a neat little gem, thats to be sure. It crashed on me a total of one time and then never again. The bloom from the sun on this game is absolutely brutal though, so you may want to turn it off. I didn't because I'm a big strong man.
The maps are actually fairly impressive, even though they reuse them a bunch. It reminds me of other games like Giants: Citizen Kabuto by just how big they are. Luckily, the Havoc suit is fast and nimble and it doesn't take long to get anywhere.
If you want a solid, classic mecha shooter, then I don't see how you can do wrong with Gun Metal, especially since it usually goes on sale for about a dollar every now and then. I'd also suggest Battle Engine Aquila if you can find it.

Batman - The Telltale Series is an episodic adventure game, developed and published by Telltale Games, the same people behind other such great adventure games as The Wolf Among Us and Game of Thrones. The game is based on DC Comics' comic book series of the same name
Although the game does not follow the same exact storyline as the comic book series, it follows the same universe as the comic book follows only seeing it in a different point of view
The game is split up into five episodes. The game works as a normal television series. Each length of an episode is roughly two to three hours or more long
The gameplay is very simple, you move around, selecting stuff and talking to people and using button prompts when told to. The main bulk of gameplay is through the dialogue options. What you say and what you do will effect the game in the long run
The game's graphics are nice for the most part however there are some ugly texture work here and there. The sound and music options also vary in quality. Sometimes the sound quality is really good and sometimes the sound quality is bad. I have encountered numerous amounts of glitches which seems as if Telltale Games never got round to fixing them, too many to mention in this review
Batman - The Telltale Series is a new take for Telltale Games and I personally enjoyed every single episode of this series and cannot wait for a continuation into the story of Batman and his mission to protecting Gotham!

One of the crtiticisms levelled at Tropico 4 was that it was purely an extension of Tropico 3; not so much a new game as an expansion pack.
In a way, the same can be said for this new offering albeit with a different engine and management focus.
Running through the campaign means juggling between two islands; once you complete a scenario, you either continue on your current island or switch to the second. They have the same buildings and workforce, just the scenario parameters change.  This can be quite annoying if you've spent so long playing on one island as switching means remembering where you were up to, particularly with the new management system.
Gone is the focus control of El Presidente, running him around the map to help with building times and increasing productivity; instead we get an increasing number of managers with different abilities who you have to allocate to buildings.  This can be very micro-managing, especially with your `family` who you have to send abroad on tasks and then re-allocate to a building.
The scenario tasks remain pretty standard compared to previous Tropicos.  Exports/imports, tourism and rebels are still present as are the natural disasters.  A nice design touch is being able to rebuild all your destroyed building post disaster rather than finding individual ruins.
Overall, there are some nice improvements and the graphics engine is certainly an improvement.  This is still a Tropico game though, and not wholly different to its predecessors.  Recommended to previous El Presidente's but if you're new to the series, you would be better off starting with Tropico 4 and the Modern Times expansion.
