This is the first modern Sherlock Holmes game that I've played; my last outing was an old point-and-click on my family's old 386 when I was about 13.  Being that I hadn't played any of the new games yet, I wasn't sure what to expect.  I'm a fan of Holmes from the books and later the new series, and I wasn't sure how the game would capture the right atmosphere.
I'm pleased to say that, in my opinion at least, they knocked it out of the park.  Settings were extremely evocative of the time period.  I thought especially that the slums of Whitechapel were very well done graphically and atmospherically.  If a game can make me say "oh my god why can't I help these poor people" and actually make me distressed about it, I call it a win.  Good immersion, I'd say.
Fans of the books will appreciate some easter egg references to past adventures, plus the fun of taking Toby for a spin once again (with some added skills he didn't have in the book; I think he was smarter than Watson in this one...)
The puzzles had that perfect balance of challenging without making me tear clumps of my hair out.  The very few times I consulted a walkthrough was in situations where I knew I'd forgotten to pick something up earlier and didn't want to have backtrack too far for it.  It was unnecessary for the puzzles themselves, which took me a lot of thinking but no random rage-quits over it. :D
I will mention there is some "digital" gore due to a couple of rather grisly murder scenes, in case that matters to you.  I cringed a little bit at doing a post-mortem exam, but the sequence was mercifully short.  I'm naturally squeamish and it really wasn't enough to bother me much.  Just wanting to throw that out there for anyone who wants to know!
Overall, an excellent experience and one that was so entertaining I'll probably go back and play it again at a later date, which isn't a treatment I give to too many games.  I'd pay the full $19.99 cost without flinching, knowing how much I enjoyed myself, but if the cost is bothersome, wait for a sale.  Either way, pick it up and give it a play when you can!

This is more of a Batman-themed visual novel with QTEs than anything else - if you're expecting gameplay or dilemmas in the vein of previous Telltale games such as The Walking Dead then you won't find it here.  I rarely found myself pausing to consider a choice being offered at critical plot junctions, or wishing I'd gone about things differently.
However, I rarely found myself
either.  The QTEs (and there is at least one setpiece QTE per episode) move at a fair clip without being too punishing, and combined with the conversions (of which there are many) mean you rarely have a moment to pause and catch your breath.  Puzzles appear perhaps once an episode, taking the form of reconstructing a crime and/or planning out an upcoming fight; these sequences in particular I really enjoyed.  I ended up whipping through the whole thing in a few evenings and don't really feel the need to revisit it to see how I might change parts of the outcome.
Overall I would recommend this if you are already a fan of previous Telltale titles, or want to see a slightly new spin on familiar Batman characters.

The Testament of Sherlock Holmes stands as a leap forwards for the Sherlock Holmes games. The voice-acting of Holmes himself has greatly improved, though many of the other voices in the game still sound weird most of the time. Nonetheless, the voice acting of Holmes is wonderful and really fits the character. The mysteries that Holmes and Watson have to face this time aren't all too complicated to solve, but the puzzles in this game are different. They range from incredibly easy to ridiculously hard in some cases, though this experience may be very different for other players. Luckily, there is always the option of skipping a puzzle if one cannot solve it after trying for some time.
The Testament's storyline, while slow and a bit frustrating at some times, has its captivating and even moving moments. The friendship between Holmes and Watson shows strongly throughout the story, as the bonds between them are tested by the mysterious events that seem to point out that the great detective himself may have become a criminal. The conclusion of the game is a moving and fitting end to this story which, as a whole, I highly recommend to fans of the world's greatest detective and those who enjoy a challenging adventure.

I have mixed feelings here: With Tropico 4, it shares the graphics and the great humor. Not much changed here. But the economics/simulation part has changed a lot: You now have different ages you have to master (colonial era, age of world wars, cold war, modern times), and you have certain technologies to discover in each time period. You need to finish specific tasks to come from one age to another (yes you have to hurry sometimes), and the danger of invasions on your island is much higher now.
Some informations are not that good organized as it was in Tropico 4. I had to look for some things, and it seems other parts of the game are not really well thought out. The trading part with contracts with other nations needs to be revised, there is some tweak to be done. Another thing is that you have to explore the whole technology tree in every age, you cannot set priorities (well at least roughly in the order of invention). But maybe that's just me.
But there are some more weak spots: You can't control El Presidente anymore, and you can't control your army. There are fewer options to make your city more beautiful (no statues, no palms and trees, only two types of parks are left), and there are less buildings left to build. I think they have been put much more into DLCs than before.
So, the game is in some parts more complex, in other parts it is simpler than Tropico4, but it has some new aspects, but with well known elements.
In total, for me, there is a lack of long-time motivation to play this game. The city-builder-part is great, but you have to deal with fewer buildings you can build. The ages-part is great as well, but too simplistic to hold the fun in the long run. I think they cut too much out if it, and added not enough new stuff to motivate me for a longer period of time. However, if you liked Tropico4 and this game is on sale, you might consider to buy it. Other than that, I can't recommend it.

Klang is a difficult rhythm platformer developed by Tinimations and published by Snow Cannon Games. It is currently exclusive to PC. I am not the biggest fan of 2D platformers, but I do love rhythm games so I decided to accept the challenge and play through the game.
Klang has an interesting visual style. Most things in the game glow with bright neon lights while the character models have some bizarre designs. I am not especially fond of this style, but I would say the visuals are all in line with the aesthetic the developers were going for, so I certainly would not complain about them.
During gameplay, there are a few issues with the visuals. Things that you need to keep track of often overlap which can lead to frustration as you fail to avoid things that you can barely see. Of course, this could be considered part of the game’s challenge.
All of the music in Klang fits into the electronica genre. There are quite a few songs that I like featuring some good, complex melodies over a steady beat. The other songs also feature a strong beat which makes them work well for a rhythm game, even if I do not enjoy them much. The hardest difficulty uses alternate tracks which makes the complete list of songs impressive. The game does not feature any dialogue or text narration.
Klang’s gameplay feels somewhat unusual. At its most complex, the game requires players to press buttons in time with the music while also moving to avoid hazards. Keeping track of environmental dangers while also hitting buttons on cue is often pretty difficult. There are also sections in which the player only needs to navigate the level while areas periodically turn hostile. Furthermore, there are times when the game only requires the player to hit buttons in time with the music.
On normal difficulty, the rhythm gameplay seems pretty easy. The timing is pretty loose and as long as you attempt to hit a note, you will probably avoid taking damage. However, different difficulty levels send different amounts of attacks your way and also change the speed. Once you complete the main game, you unlock “nightcore” difficulty which can be brutally difficult due to all the fast moving notes.
The platforming tends to be where the difficulty lies. The levels can be unforgiving with their jumps over pits of certain death and temporary platforms. There are also sentries that will destroy the protagonist in one hit if he enters their field of vision or even stands on the edge of it for too long. Thankfully, it does not take long for the character to reappear and checkpoints pop up very frequently. The game also features some hidden paths that lead to bonus levels. I managed to find them all on my initial run, so they are not hidden too well, but getting to some of them was still tricky. Completing these bonus levels reward the player with access to the in-game music player and additional post-game levels.
I tried playing with multiple controllers for the sake of a thorough examination. The keyboard works perfectly well with the game and sometimes feels like the best option. On controller, jump and slide are bound to the should buttons which may seem odd at first, but it works surprisingly well and frees up your right thumb for hitting incoming attack prompts. The game includes diagonal attacks which do not work well with controller buttons. For these, the game recommends using the right stick. My Xbox One controller had a habit of misreading my inputs, but my PS4 controller did not have that issue. Of course, operator error is likely the cause of this and your experience may vary.
Klang is a unique game. The aesthetic definitely stands out and the unusual gameplay offers a decent challenge. The main game is pretty short overall but the nightcore difficulty and post-game levels add some longevity. For a game developed by one person, it certainly is not bad at all. I would easily recommend the game to anyone looking for a trippy, challenging rhythm platformer. However, anyone who is not interested in those adjectives will probably not care much for the game.

Is the idea of the game fantastic?  Absolutely!
Can I recommend this exact game?  No.
The execution needs a lot of work (mainly heavy stuttering, which is #1 on the list of things that should NEVER happen under ANY circumstance for a rhythm game).  In addition, lining up more than just the immediate next action NEEDS TO BE THERE and it's not (unless you know what to look for).  E.g. in Rockband you see every single note coming at you down the track.  In Klang you only see a timer for the immediate next action.  Is the next action only an 8th beat away so you have less than a beat to respond because you didn't see the teeny-tiny marker coming at you?  TOUGH LUCK.
That being said, most of the game is good.  The mechanics are solid, the graphics (when they're not stuttering) look amazing, the soundtrack is of course amazing.  It's just a few execution issues that just completely kill it for me.

First off: I have played Tropico 4 and 5 only for a few hours each, so as far as gameplay and comparison goes, you'd better stick to the other reviews. So far it's pretty enjoyable in both campaign and multiplayer mode.
For all you Linux people out there, I just wanted to point out that the Linux version works flawlessly. No crashes, limitations or apparent bugs, smooth framerate, no dropouts in multiplayer. It's always nice to see a native port of a AAA title done this well.
(Tested on different machines, all running Ubuntu and proprietary Nvidia drivers.)

.Story.
There’s not much of a story to speak of here. From what I’ve gathered from the flashy cut scenes is that the monkey protagonist is being bullied in a sort of God of War 3-esque manner by other neon-drenched beings of animal and human origin—much like Kratos was by the gods in Olympus.
.Gameplay.
Rhythm is everything.
Klang controls better with a gamepad (though not a Steam controller because of the whole track pad-instead-of-a-second- analog-stick thing). You use the left joystick to move about, the right trigger button to jump, and the second stick OR the face keys in order to do a violent little swinging motion that will be used for the majority of the game to parry attacks. The former is the most comfortable option.
Your mission, if you choose to accept it, is to make your way from the beginning of a stage to its end as quickly as possible while taking as little damage as possible.
Klang’s controls are very smooth, which means doing just that is a  satisfying feeling—after you’ve died a few dozen times trying to figure out how best to proceed. Everything from wall jumping to the timing of platforms to the enemies’ roaming line of sight to the dynamic backgrounds—just everything—sways to the beat and you will have to join them in their deadly dance in order to progress.You’ll be given on-screen cues to parry, jump, slide, and a special ground pound ability during combat. For the most part, it’s up to you to figure out how best to proceed.
Every stage is built into little segments which serve as checkpoints (an amazingly fair system, if I do say so) that you’ll respawn at should you fail to time a jump or get caught in an enemy’s line of sight.Failure means bursting into a million pixels and is results in a cacophony of sound. It also means you won’t be getting the best score because death slows you down.
At the end of each segment, you’ll be given a score calculated based on how quickly you cleared it based on combo (that is: how many times you deflected enemy attacks without faltering), life lost, accuracy, and time elapsed. Scores range from D-S with S being the best possible. Once you’ve completed all of the segments that make up a stage, you’re given a final grade for the area. Then, you’re taken to the world map where you’ll be able to continue to the next stage or try your hand at a better score.
Even if you aren’t up to the task of getting the best possible marks, there’s no score requirement in order to progress.
Within stages you’ll find portals that give you access to a bonus challenge. Completing one nets you a key, which is used in the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which is the game’s cleverly named jukebox.
.Atmosphere.
Fair warning to those with any sort of photosensitivity or epileptic tendencies: this game is not for you. Klang runs through a spectrum of neon colours and starkly contrasting negatives upon receiving damage or dying. The way the protagonist kind of moshes in place when idle is great and the cut scenes, though eerie and sometimes incomprehensible, are gorgeously animated.
Klang has one of the best soundtracks I’ve heard in an indie game. My opinion is, of course, biased by the fact that I love this rave-y, EDM sort of music. Turn up the bass.
.Pros.
•	Fantastic music. An audiophile’s wet dream.
•	The music is so good.
•	Did I mention the music?
•	Gorgeous, Tron-esque neon aesthetic.
•	Dexterous mix of precision platforming and rhythm game.
•	The check point system makes the game’s difficulty bearable.
•	Scores give you something to strive for without hindering your progress.
•	Fast, fluid gameplay.
•	Everything from wall jumping to enemy movement/attack patterns to how the stage and its platforms moves hinge on the music’s beat. Very cool.
.Cons.
•	The difficulty may be a turn-off to some. I’ll admit I had my rage quit moments.
•	The game can be controlled with keyboard, but the gamepad is FAR superior.
•	Sometimes it’s unclear what needs to be done to proceed. A lot of trial and error is required for some puzzles/fights.
•	Heavy reliance on the beat makes this title inaccessible to those without rhythm.

.Bottom Line.
A beautiful marriage of platformer and rhythm game, Klang will test your dexterity. A must buy for rhythm game lovers and a solid recommendation to those who enjoy platformers as well.

Perhaps I need to complete more of the game (on the third island now), and for the sake of seeing the art I would love to, but there's not much driving me to do so other than some sort bragging rights I care nothing about.
There is so much about this game that is absolutely stunning. Unforutnately, the gameplay is not one of them. The original art and art style, the original music and musical style are all incredible. There is a cohesive unified artistic vision and it's well executed. The gameplay, however, is unimaginative to say the least.
It's really dissapointing that the parry mechanic seems to only be used for getting better scores and supers. The timing with the parry button also feels just slightly off. Some of the boss designs seem very poorly thought out. There are randomized elements that can combine for literally inescapable damage. It's also a huge bummer to launch a super attack only to see your inevitable fate of inescapable damage awaiting for you after it finishes.
I get it. It's hard. It's difficulty, however, merely feels like a novelty. A gimmick. Games on the NES were hard too, and this game feels like it was reaching for the same level of arbitrary difficulty.  Cuphead feels hard for the sake of being hard. Which is unfortunate when there's so much of the game I WANT to see. You can play the bosses on simple mode and still progress through the map, which is a nice concilliatory prize, but not worth the price of admission.
The game is much more fun to watch than to play. So if the artstyle and music interest you, but you don't want to do the exact same thing over and over and over until you finally memorize the patterns (only to have them nulified by RNG), do yourself a favor and watch someone else play it.

For an early access game it certainly shows some potential, but there are a few things that really bring it down for me.
Pros:
- I like the art style, characters/enemies/backgrounds all look nice.
- Some character customization is nice.
- Space age laser pick axe type thing with rifles to defend yourself is always promising.
- Has a decent tutorial that I would have probably been 100% lost without.
- I liked the quest/task system in place that was used for the tutorial. I would love to see this used a good bit in later builds of the game. Random quests/tasks/challenges while exploring the world would add a good bit of excitement for me.
Cons + personal opinions/feedback:
- The UI. Oh man the UI. This is the one thing that, if not updated significantly, will stop me from playing this game again. Every time I'd look for something I felt myself straining my eyes trying to discern exactly what I was looking at. Similar looking icons in inventory, small text in several places, and a very clunky and unrefined crafting menu (in a crafting game) made it so that every time I'd stop blasting things with my laser saw to go look at my loot or craft something I would grumble to myself a little bit about how I had to go back into the menus. I hope updates are coming for some of UI/menus, especially the crafting menu and/or system. Please oh please.
- Also didn't care for the health/jetpack meters being on such a noisy panel up in the corner like they are. It was a hassle to try and read while running/fighting anything. I would rather just have a couple of bars or numbers above my character or some such thing so that I can see a gauge while I am looking at my character and moving about.
- The [lack of] transition from day to night was so abrupt that I thought it was a bug or my game was crashing or textures had stopped drawing. Day/night is great to have, but needs to be a transition, not instant.
- It seems like the way to unlock new things to craft is by collecting these little book things that give +25 or so to various crafting skills. I don't much care for that as a gating mechanic, maybe it would be better if more was available initially or if there was a better indication of how using different materials to craft the same item would make a better one. Additionally, I really didn't enjoy that I would find these little books, then have to go into my inventory, select them, equip them on my action bar, and then pull them out and use them in order to gain experience from them. Unless they are to be used for something else I am unaware of, I don't understand why they are inventory items instead of just experience type pickups that occur automatically and scroll a nice little "+25 Furniture!" or something over your head.
I should stop rambling. There's my 2 cents.
I hope some of this has been helpful if anyone's read this far. I know people compare this game to Terraria, which I have not played. It may very well be that much of what I don't like is based around Terraria's success and these elements I don't like just aren't to my tastes. If that's the case then I guess it just isn't for me - ignore all that junk above. :)
My conclusion - As it exists now, several different issues come together to make a disappointing experience. I hope that is just due to it being in an early stage, and that we'll see much more polish/improvement in the next few months. I think that when/if the right things are made better the whole game could come together quite nicely.

This game is an interesting one. Despite the plethora of first person survival games on Steam, and everywhere else to be honest, this game changes the formula. While most games might have a focus on crafting and an overall threat of zombies and alike, this game takes the divergent path. The crafting system is somewhat muted and can be played entirely without, and the only real threat is the elements. While there are prowling bears and stalking wolves among the vast frozen wastelands, they are easily scared off with a flare or a torch, or even a gun. The real enemy is nature itself, as the player is made to survive the cold, harsh winds, freak blizzards and minimal shelter. The gameplay essentially breaks down to traversing the areas looking for shelter, food, water, and other essentials in order to keep death away for another day. The tricky part about this is that in each area the food and water are minmal enough to make it so players feel the need to move on in order to survive.
While one can subsist on melted snow and the animals of the area, eventually either boredom or lack of rescources will cause the player to move on. This is where I find the one real problem I have with the game. Because of the need for exploration, I found myself often moving through areas quickly in order to find more useful materials. This is good for the first few hours because I was always seeing something new. Then I died, and respawned. The problem now was I had to traverse the same landscape I had. This wasn't a major problem because the game is well varied in each area. There was certainly never a moment where I could become complacent, because the game doesn't let you. The moment you think you have the game down, it decides to rain the all singing all dancing♥♥♥♥♥♥show of this games brutality upon you.
Allow me to demonstrate: I was backed into a corner with a flare in front of me and a rifle in my hand, two bullets to my name. There were, conveniently, two wolves ahead of me. The ultimate gaming challenge of "but I might need it later" was on my mind so I hadn't fired. Then my flare died, and the wolves began inching towards me. As I fired my first shot, the other wolf broke into a sprint. I fired again and missed. Now I was fighting off a wolf with my knife and barely got it off me in time to survive. I then walked back to my cabin with a scrap of clothing still intact and blurred vision, staggering through the snow. About half a mile later I collapsed, and faded into "the long dark". This game is wonderful. The graphic style hides the low budget well and the sandbox nature meant I never felt I was retreading the same path. The surprising depth of this game kept me pushing forward, and so I would give this game a 9/10.

Being a fan of the TV show 'Sherlock', I had to play this game. This is my first Sherlock Holmes game and I was pleasantly surprised. The Testament of Sherlock Holmes is a point-and-click adventure game where you play as Sherlock (and Watson) trying to resolve the murder of a Reverend in his own church. I won't say more about the story since the main reason of playing this game is to discover that.
The gameplay is faily simple. Where you can interact, there is either a magnifying glass to look at some items or a hand to show that you can take the item or that you can interact with it. That's it. Most of the time, you'll have to look through everything to be sure that you didn't miss any important clue. The rooms are small enough so it's really easy to find everything.
Also, as a detective, there is a deduction board. You'll have to discover every clues to see statements about them. With these facts, it's up to you to choose between 3 answers which one is the right one about what happened in this case. There are multiple questions to be answered and you won't know if you're right until you have all the right answers. It can be hard but if you pay attention to the story, it will be fairly easy. There is also a lot of puzzles in this game. Some are logic and really easy once you understand how they work but some of the puzzles that does NOT involve any deduction/logic can be really hard and frustrating for some people. There is a skip buttons after some minutes so don't worry !
One of the problem in this game is that it's too linear for a detective game. There is no real choice to be made and even if you choose to go to a location instead of another, you'll end up going to both places without any change.
The story is really interesting and there are a lot of twists (I found it similar to the TV show and it's a good thing). The problem (because it's a videogame !) is that Sherock is not as funny as Cumberbatch's Sherlock (but it's understandable since there is no actor involved).
In conclusion, if you like point-and-click games, you'll like this one. It will definitely entertain you for hours ! (I finished the game in about 7-8 hours)

What is Klang?
In a nutshell, it's a rhythm based platformer, that will have you wielding two tuning fork swords as you run, jump, slide, and slash your way through a hectic, unrelenting, EDM world.
Early on, the game starts off rather simple, letting you get a hang of the controls. Soon however, you will be doing everything at once, as Klang does not waste time getting going. The first major boss battle is a decent step up in difficulty, but it is the second boss where Klang gets going and does not let up. This game gets quite hard, and I found myself dying quite a bit. Fortunately, the game has a fast respawn and good checkpoint system, allowing you to get right back into the action without a lot of down time. For the short runtime of the campaign, this game runs hard and fast. Once you complete the basic campaign, though, there are plenty of addtional challenges for you to take on.
That is not to say the game is without flaws. Some inputs in the game do not line up exactly with the beat, causing you to miss hits seemingly at random in places. In addition, the flashing colors and constant motion can get distracting. This especially true when you miss a note, as every change in multiplier includes a change in color scheme, which can cause you to lose track of what is coming next and create a series of missed notes. And of course, the actual campaign for the game is quite short, so if you cannot get involved in extra content or challenge modes, you may feel cheated.
Overall, I can highly recommend this game and am looking forward to seeing what issues that do exist be fixed to create a stellar game.

Klang is not much of a story based game but I'll try to summarize it:
"Klang is a game about a person who is seeking great power from the all seeing eye. Solus however stopped Klang and threw him to the bottom of the world, forcing Klang to go and fight for what he seeks."
When I played the demo at EGX 2016 (and even the prologue in the full game), it was quite a challenge for me playing this for the first time. This game is clearly for gamers who are good at multi-tasking. You use WASD for movement and the arrow keys for attacking (however you can use a controller instead). But later on, you will face new gameplay styles and you will die many times. All of the gameplay styles you will encounter throughout your game session will collaberate into one hard trial that you will need strong fingers to play with. Trust me. I have died 100+ times, mostly on the dissapearing platforms section at Angel City.
Now visually I like the style of a futuristic setting along with some musical elements. I like the choice of genre, even the choice of the artist bLiNd. The beats really help keeping you focus on attacking.
I have finished the game in over 2 hours, but I can see some replayability with it. After you finish Hardcore Mode, you will unlock Nightcore Mode. I haven't went on Nightcore Mode yet but I will look forward to it.
I know people would complain that the game is "too hard to play" but that's a stupid excuse. It was meant to test your multi-tasking and skill in both rhythm and platforming.
I don't have anything bad to say about the game other than a few bugs I have encountered that could be fixed through an update. I'd highly recommend this game to any gamers who likes rhythm games, platformers, speedrunning, or even a hardcore challenge.

There is so much to say about Evolve! I have become instantly hooked and I must say that Valve and 2k games have taken the right approach by releasing what is practically an open-alpha. I mean it's brilliant. It works for the player and the developer. You want us to buy your game? Sure, let's just see what you got so far. Okay I like it! Only in alpha but it builds up hype for the real deal. Which you best believe I'll be doing. This game will be worth the money for sure. It is the perfect game for a cold, rainy night.
You start off with a cutscene. You and your team are in a ship and you're about to get launched to the ground to go hunt the Goliath. Each player has their own special abilities. For instance, one player can track the monster, while the other provides a shield for other players, or the reconnisaince-type hunter can shoot the Goliath with a dart that slows the Goliath down. A simple game of chasing the monster turns into a large scale hunt as each map is massive in its own right. From tall mountains to deep valleys, you can go anywhere, which makes the chase exhillerating!
Despite being in alpha, the only problems I've received so far has been severe lagg/frame drops. I can't be worried about that though, it's only alpha for pete's sake! This game can only get better. It can't get worse so far. If this was activision or DICE, I'd say otherwise. But 2K and Turtle Rock Studios know what they're doing and I have faith in them. So much faith that I plan to buy this game instead of drugs. Crazy right?
All in all, this game is what I need. It's a wonderful, open-world, suspenseful quest to kill a monster, another player! It's unheard of! 2k,Valve, and TRS, I will give you my money! Please do not dissapoint. I reccomend you buy this game when it is available. I look forward to hunting with you!

Morphopolis is a very casual game. I got it on sale a while back. I will tell you why I did not think it was worth even that price.

In the second mystery you're presented to the "Deduction Board" in which your findings are noted and you are supposed to figure how all things connect by yourself. This part is more rewarding. But you're also presented to a puzzle in which you have to move a chess piece though a chessboard
. Though it's easily solved by trial and error and taking notes not to try the same solution multiple times, it's tedious.

So, if you're into solving puzzles and finding clickable spots, this game is for you!
If you're into mystery solving you're better off reading a book. Since I now despise everything related to Holmes, I'd recommend Agatha Christie's novels.

This is an origin story of sorts and I'd recommend it to anyone who loves Telltale and/or if they're interested in Bruce's story, newbies and veterans alike. It has a lot of noir fiction elements that everybody loves about the Batman series. The narrative is well-paced; it goes from calm one moment to suspenseful action the next—something Telltale always does well. The game introduces a beefy roster of villains whose stories mesh together nicely. I love the choices you get for the kind of Batman/Bruce Wayne characterization you want. If you'd prefer to have a more compassionate Bruce-Bat, the options do not disappoint and remind me of what Gotham's (the show) Bruce Wayne might be like as an adult. However, if you'd prefer a more violent approach, the dialogue and actions are canon to writers who opted for a more ruthless Batman. Regardless of what you choose, Telltale did a great job illustrating the way Bat-Bruce wrestles with how he wants to be portrayed by his beloved city and who he's becoming. They coupled this well with the amount of twists and some subtle imagery/symbolism (others, not so subtle). Another thing I really appreciated was the large role Lucius Fox played in the game. I wanted him to show up more because he's just as important to Bruce as Alfred is. There is no Batman without Fox. So I kind of wish that relationship was shown a bit more outside of their work relationship.
The voice acting is some of the best I'd heard in a while. Telltale hired performers whose voices are immediately distinguishable upon hearing them. I also enjoyed the linking mechanic added for Bruce's detective work. It gave more varied combat options rather than just throwing the player right into  the thick of things. I appreciate that Telltale is trying new things to try to improve upon their storytelling. It does need to be fixed a bit. For instance, I'd hover over a link, click, and it would disappear; a very minor inconvenience. One last mechanic that I appreciate is no more Q and E-mashing! The combat has improved so much! The quick-time events actually made me feel a sense of urgency and I appreciate not having to abuse the crap out of my Q and E keys.
Onto the issues. I'd get random FPS lag, especially in the last chapter of the last episode. There were a few times when it would lag so badly that the subtitles would show dialogue but no audio. Other audio glitches include a character talking and stopping mid-sentence or there would be audio coming out the left side of my headset but nothing out the right. There were a few times when the visual glitches were hilarious. Other times, I didn't find it so fun. Every time there was a computer monitor or a television screen that was supposed to be playing footage of something going on, it would be blank or display something that's not supposed to be there. I don't know about you but seeing Bruce analyzing an "Elect Harvey Dent" poster so meticulously as he talks about saving an innocent civilian isn't exactly immersive gameplay. Lastly, I don't understand the decision to remove important Telltale features like chapter rewinding. Hopefully it just slipped their mind because it's so important to be able to undo decisions made by misclicks.
Overall, I hope we get to see more of the caped crusader in Telltale's roster of future projects. The final ending certainly left a perfect beginning to a new installment which I will sit and wait in anticipation for. Make it happen, Telltale/DC!

I could go on & on like this as lack of care and effort is everywhere to be found in this game, if you can pick this up for £5 then do so, but its not worth a penny more.

My Game Rating: 9/10
I recently picked this up as part of the BioShock bundle and I was immediately immersed in the storyline.  BioShock has one of the best in game stories (in my opinion) and the story progression was well paced from start to finish with enough twists and turns to keep me always wanting to play a bit longer.
The gameplay was a lot of fun with the variety of weapons, upgrades, and special abilities providing some interesting customization and combination options.  My only complaints (and minor nitpicking ones at that) were in regards to the constantly respawing enemies which made a few of the later sections feel a bit dragged out when the story moved you back and forth across the same large sections.  I felt like the initial challenge provided by the big enemies ("Big Daddies") was significant, but their challenge decreased dramatically as the game progressed removing some of the challenge so the only major concern was being overwhelmed by many enemies.
Again, regardless of these very minor issues, the story was fantastic and the various upgrades and abilities provided enough variety that I was always trying to play with something new along the ride.

I never expected to like this game.
I actually thought the art style would wane and the gameplay was overly simple to really catch my attention, but after a friend's recommendation and a such a generous price, I cannot speak more highly of a $20 experience.
It is the type of game that'll force its players to become better gamers as a whole with an emphasis on in-game awareness, rhythm and strategic positioning, all while maintaining a very simplistic gameplay experience; akin to Mega Man or Super Metroid. It's the game that can be picked up by all, but if you're not willing to work, learn or improve, you will not find any enjoyment as bosses eat you over and over.
The art style is actually rather endearing. Coupled with the jazz music that reminds me of cartoons like Tom & Jerry, I'm having dumb fun whilst on a nostalgia trip. This might not be for everyone and I understand that, however I was originally a little standoffish to the art when I saw the trailers and showcases for this game and grew to love it. You can tell that the people who designed this game really put in the effort into giving you an authentic, 1940's cartoon that doubles up as a game.
If there was anything this game has left me wanting, it would be more platforming elements. The boss battles are difficult enough to keep you preoccupied, but I only wish there were more platforming segments to act as the filler between bosses, rather than traversing the map. The platforming elements that are there, are nice, simple (as is the rest of the game) but just as punishing as the rest of the game and I could only really just wish for more.
Overall, this game is wonderful in its contrast of simplistic gameplay, difficult bosses and 40's cartoony design.

The creators of this game, Failbetter Games, have run a web browser game for a while slowly building up a world, filling it with endearing characters, bizarre locations and fascinating situations; all in words and pictures. And at the center of it all was you "the delicious friend" the perilous knife fighter, the inconspicuous "law abiding" citizen, the... et cetera. However, this was really a game as much as it was a pick your own adventure book with no permanent endings(as far as I know). From this Sunless Sea was conceived.
A great first attempt at video game design, with a few kinks to be worked out. The gameplay its self is as intended by the devs. slow, methodical and mostly permanent. Your management decisions will dictate your chances of survival, your swift actions will decide the course of battle and your "stat" distribution will unfold more of a story as a reward...or punishment.
Sunless Sea puts you in the shoes of a soon to be zee farer "mysterious and indistinct" gender and past in the docks of Fallen London. Your task is what you choose to make it, become a high risk trader, arm a drednaught in search of a challenge, be renowned throught all the ports. But your goal will always be to explore this hostile and curious environment.
What you need to know about Fallen London:
The zee is dark, the atmosphere is grim, and your ship is just not as fast as you wish it were; all in order to put you in the shoes of your cap'n. All fine and dandy, untill you have to do it all over again after being defeated by your own greed, mismanagement or plain stupidity. Nothing wrong with punishment for lack of foresight, but a fastforeward button would really help cutting some of the less exciting aspects of the game. Atmosphere and immersion are fantastic but your time is tickin' and once you have explored every Nook and cranny in the zee the only thing to stave monotony of is a good hunt whether that is a not-so-helpless pray or you is a 50/50.
With all that said, if you don't like reading, you don't like the setting and you can't stand slow pacing chances are this may not be the game for you. But if you like the cut of it's jib then: Welcome aboard

For an alpha this game is good. It still does have its flaws and some of them major. I will start with the bad. While it does have little bugs that aren't huge or game breaking they are there none the less. Now for one of the giant flaws. FPS. If you have your game at anything higher than medium graphics settings and the default AA this games fps will go slower than a dead rock. It doesn't matter how powerful your rig is. You’re screwed. Once put at medium the game flows well for the most part. Also this game does have some other graphic related issues. The render distance is not very far and colors can pop in and out/turn black for no reason. The graphics in this game are also not fantastic. They do the job but it's not the next gen game that makes your eyeballs melt and your brain explode like we have all been wanting it to. The graphics look even worse with the setting being forced to be turned down. The game also lacks content. So far we have been given 3 maps and by the looks of it they all look and play the same. There is also no tutorial.
Now that was a lot of bad but don't worry there is a light at the end of a tunnel and don't worry it's not a train. This game is good. The gameplay is fun and works well. Everything is generally balanced and there is no class (including the monster) that is overpowered or that beats out the rest. All the weapons in this game are fun and interesting to use because each class has a purpose and when used together can make a killer team. All the classes are fun and interesting. The class choosing system is also cool. You put in priority what class you want to play. 1-5 the game then tries to find a match based off of what class you want to play. This system almost always works (about 95% of the time) and is fun to use. This game being made by some of the developers of l4d has some similar features. Most notably is the take a break system. This system was introduced in l4d1 and lets the player take a break to do whatever and the npc take control of the player so the team doesn't suffer.
For an alpha even with the many bugs, glitches, and lacking content, is very funny but not worth the $60 unless some major added content comes to the game. For an alpha 8/10 thumbs up. If this wasn't an alpha 4/10 thumbs down

Great game for those of us who wonder how long we would survive in the zombie apocalypse.  What most of us don't realize is that its usually not the zombies that get you, it's yourself.
Fought, sneaked, and sprinted my way through the vast forest that surrounds the in-game town to the distant farm. Why? Smaller groups of the infected, and a well full of water. Soon realized that I didn't have the supplies i'd need to barricade and defend my new home. Didn't have the supplies i'd need to start growing my own food. My regular, small-town hero had already survived for 2 months in the harsh worled. Defending that farm had improved my characters combat skills to that of a zombie slaying legend. I knew he would easily survive another trip back. After a full day of following the road Into town I found myself a few miles out from the nearest neighboorhood. So I decided to take refuge in a small cabin that I knew to be located nearby.  My character now so sleep deprived that he could barely stand, drenched from the rain, and only able to see a foot or two in the darkness of the night.  Clearing the undead that lingered near my temporary shelter I opened the nearest window and crawled inside. I'd made it another night! Soon i'd have the saw and trowel i would need to start my farm and build my def--! Lost in thought; I turned to the right just in time to see a lone zombie grabbing at me. Ending its pathetic life, i stood triumphant once more. Wait, whats that moodle to the right. Pain. I quickly open the health tab and see that my characters wrist has been scratched. The feeling that follows in the pit of my stomach is something that reminds me of the scene from the walking dead game that a certain character is bitten. with fingers crossed I bandage myself up and choose to get some sleep. I awake the next morning to a fever. Maybe its from the rain? I struggle to find a few scraps of food in the cabinets of the cabin as my conidition worsens. Within a few hours my hero falls to the ground and succumbs to the virus. ''This is how you died'' I stare at the screen for a moment, feeling as if I had just watched an epic film of one mans struggle to survive the end of the world. Theres no going back with the games perma-death system. With a smile I re-open the game and create a new average hometown hero.
Dealing with real circumstances, heat, cold, fear, hunger, thirst, sleep deprivation, boredom, sadness with an average character whos positive traits are weighed evenly by his/her negative ones. Want a brave, strong construction worker? Be prepared to choose equal things such as overweight, hearty appetite, and claustrophobic. You've got yourself a real person who feels... believeable.
10/10 Would play again.

SUPERHOT, is an amazing game and certainly lives up to the hype it got when it first came out, but is it worth the price? The short answer is that it depends on what you are buying it for. If you are buying this game just to play the story mode and learn why so many people enjoy it then you should wait for a steam sale because its current price is a little too steep given the short story mode. The story mode took me about 3-4 hours to complete which is rather short for a 25$ game, but I also spent time in other places that made up for it. The endless modes offer a great time of just shooting red guys and perfecting your slowmotion dodging skills. The challenges offer a unique twist to the normal story with restrictions like only being able to fight using fists, or having time stop completely when you do. There are a bunch of other little details hidden throughout the game that are quite enjoyavle like the minigames in the menu, and various other features. in terms of the graphics, this game is beautiful the contrast that the red guys offer to the blank white environments coupled with the sparse black objects sprawled around the map make for a very eye appealing experience. The game runs very smoothly, and the gameplay is just as smooth allowing you to slow down time and plan out your next move to determine what will kill you and what wont. All of these combined make SUPERHOT one of the most innovative shooters I have played in years, and well worth the recommendation.

I have been following Project Zomboid for some time now, since some of its earliest releases, and it has only gotten better with age.
The crafting system has been refined, the character animations have improved and so has the use of weapons.
The best thing about it all though is the freedom to live (as long as you can) in your own zombie survival story. You can spend days perfecting a character, building or fortifing a home for yourself and collecting weapons and food, but then there will be that one day you go out on a supply run and you forget something stupid like closing a door, or you trip an alarm, and what goes from a well practiced science turns into a scramble for saftey or a last stand.
I would recommend this game to any fan of zombie lore, it is one of the few games to really capture the essence of the genre.
There are other games, like State of Decay, that do a similar job, but none so far have made me feel like I am playing my own character and my own story. And eventually, my own death.

Whereas Opposing Force was Half-Life if Gordon never went to Xen, Blue Shift is just a rerun of the first few levels of HL1. There's no new weapons (even less than HL1 for that matter), very few, if any, memorable set pieces, a handful of easy puzzles, lazy enemy encounters, and the whole experience in general just feels like it's going through the motions.
It feels as if it was incomplete, not just because it's incredibly short either, but also because there's no real climax throughout the entire campaign! While Opposing Force was shorter than Half-Life, the tension was constantly rising until it was noticeably more difficult than HL1 ever became. Furthermore, OF introduced many new weapons and (somewhat finnicky) mechanics! You'd think if Blue Shift had nothing new to offer, they'd at least grab everything that made the original so great and go out with a bang, but sadly instead it goes out with a whimper.
Shame really, the High Definition patch (circa 2000 standards) is nifty, but I can't say I would recommend going back and playing this one.

Blue Shift an expansion to the Half-Life franchise but as with any expansion to Half-Life it feels a little underwhelming when held up against the multitude of magnificent mods available for free.
Blue Shift casts you as the security guard Barney, letting Gorden Freeman have some quiet time until Half-Life 2 is released and sends you on your marry way through alien monstrosities and overzealous government soldiers. It plays much the same as the original, the weapons and enemies remain unchanged and the maps will feel eerily familiar as you battle through the corridors of Black Mesa.
The game just doesn't do anything new, it's feels almost like a recycled game, like you did all this before only it was fun the first time around. Thankfully the game is extremely short so your pain won't last long and you can safely uninstall this and go back the playing the various superior mods for Half-Life, both single- and multi-player.
Perhaps the only redeeming quality is the high definition models pack that comes bundled with Blue Shift that gives the game a little a extra. However it should be noted that Half-Life can look much prettier than even that, you just have to play maps and mods that weren't made by Valve.

Let me start out by saying that I am not a fan of Horror-Survival games.  This review is posted for those of like mind.  I don't play video games to act as I would in real life...I play to do amazing things.  I play Total War because in real life, I'll never command a massive army and build an empire.  I play Fallout and Metro because I'll never actually live in a post apocolyptic world where amassing weapons and slaughtering bandits is the means to my survival.  And I don't usually play Horror-Survival, because in real life...I'd run away and hide from these threats.  So I don't want to do that in my gaming.
Having said that...many die-hard fans of the genre may disagree with my review, and that's ok...I would not dare to challenge the assessment of more experienced players in this space.  Personally, I didn't think the game was "scary",  but that's a pretty subjective term.  What one person finds frightening, another may laugh at.  So I'll just say that I found the game to be an awesome excersize in stealth.
Regardless of what anyone may think about the 'horror' aspects of the game, it boils down to the ability to effectively sneak past adversaries, gather intel or items, and get out without being detected.  And the tension and anxiety that accompanies those efforts is delightfully intense.
Bottom line, I enjoyed the game start to finish.  Die-harders may take issue with my comments, and as I said, I won't take exception to the opinions of more experienced horror-survival players.  But for those of you who are NOT fans of the genre, I would suggest you pick this one up.  If nothing else, it's a good way to expand your horizons.
P.S.  Just finished the dlc, Whistleblower, and it contains the most disturbing scenario I've seen in 20+ years of gaming.

some other noteworthy things:  i suspect the individual citizen simulations are simplified now.  i suspect that citizens no longer are exactly 100% individually simulated, as i have noticed many strange things, like that "needs" would fill without visiting the required building, and goods would "instant" deliver to locations.  i could be wrong, but something definitely is "different" here, and i noticed it pretty quickly, and noticed i didn't like it.
overall i give it a positive recommendation,a s it's a mother♥♥♥♥jing tropico game, and a decent one.  it's just not the version i will be playing over a hundred hours on and raving to my my steam friends about.

This game.
THIS FREAKING GAME.
This review gets a bit long, so TL;DR at the bottom
I adore this game. Honestly, even though it's in an alpha state it is currently my game of the year. Where do I even begin? You play as either one of 4 hunters or a big beastie monster (Working Title). Your goal (As the hunters) is to kill the big beastie monster. If you happen to be said big beastie monster, you have to kill the hunters (Or evolve and destroy a big power thing or whatever).
I can't even put into words how great this game is. It takes FPS's (Which are traditionally mindless point and shooters) and refines it, transforms it, and twists it. It has really great shooting, but relies more on tactics and strategy. Those guns aren't gonna do much against the big beastie monster, so you better make sure you can hit it a lot. Trap it! Limit its mobility! Drop an orbital bombardment on its head!
If you want to play this as a "Traditional" FPS cause you love Call of Duty and Battlefield, prepare to be disappointed. If you're looking for something smarter, meaner, tenser, play this game. Play this goddamn game and love every minute of it. They rush of being hunted or hunting is undescribable. The adrenaline as you think you've escaped the hunters, but only barely? Heart pounding. I had to take a break after playing as the big beastie monster, simply becasue my heart was beating way too hard. Simply great. And it'll only get better!
TL;DR : This game is great if you enjoy strategy over blind run and gun. And Holy Hell is it fun.
BUY IT.
BUY IT NOW.
THE END

Banished presents itself as your typical city-building game where you gather then allocate resources appropriately. You, therefore, are an omnipotent and extremely incompetent god that drew the shortest straw and are forced to keep your collection of ever-breeding ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ alive to the best of your ability. Slowly grow attached to your villagers as you see them grow and settle, see children rise to adulthood, and see the fruits of your labor come to life. And then watch everything fall apart as your mentally handicapped villagers suddenly get too lazy to walk the extra 20 meters to gather food, and instead starve on the journey to their place of employ.
Banished is an exercise in nihlism and futility, where no matter how hard you try, and no matter how grand your creations may become; it is all in vain. Soon decadence will overcome your villagers, and they will be slaves of their own retardation - leaving you in confused dissapointment. Nothing you do matters.
10/10 would experience again.

Five Nights at Freddy's is the horror game thats so popular right now you cant go to youtube without hearing about it but will you want to jump on the band wagon ? In Five Nights at Freddy's our goal is simple. We are the security guard at Freddy Fazbears pizza and the goal is to watch over 4 animatronics while trying to stay alive until 6 AM before the animatronics kill you. So how is this game ? This is actually a really fun game and its quite challenging too. The game is a very simple game you sit a room and watch over cameras to see if the animatronics arent near you. If they do get close you have a set of doors to close until they go away but theres a catch. The place is a run down dump and has very limited funds. So to save money the place runs on limited power. The power runs out when you use the cameras the lights and the doors. If you run out of power and youre near 6 AM you can win because it gives you time to get to 6 AM. The game is also really nerve racking and its quite intense because the nights do get harder and the animatronics move way faster so youre reflexes need to be on par to win this game. There are a couple negatives. The game can get boring fast because nothing reallly changes up as nights go on. The game is also pretty difficult. So be ready to repeat nights over and over again. Overall Five Nights at Freddy's is a very fun horror game and is definetly worth the asking price. I give Five Nights at Freddy's a 8/10

Conveys the Sherlock Holmes I know and love from the books and short stories, in a way most other visual media won't do.  The puzzles are brilliant. Without a shadow of a doubt one of the greater shooters to ever exist, this game is brilliant - where else can you still play on the battlefields of Stalingrad with old school iron-sighted bolt-action Kar98's and Mosins? Besides bolt-actions this game does so many things every other game in the genre should strive for - you actually need to work as a team (squad leader has smoke, forward spawn, and artillery marking but needs his team to cover him), you have to take cover behind sandbags or windows or trenches if you value your team or life, melee charges are legitimately effective as Imperial Japanese forces, people only take more than a few bullets to kill if you use the garbage PPS-42, and tools such as recon, smoke, mortar fire, tanks, snipers, and machine gunners all require at least some degree of skill to time and place effectively.
Above all else, in this game one must not get too caught up in one's self - of all the games I have played, none have actually *encouraged* taking one for the team and sacrificing yourself for the better of your comrades rather than simply "stay alive as long as you can" - an exceptional and revolutionary design mechanic where you have to put your team above yourself as did so many soldiers in the real Great Patriotic and Pacific Wars. This is the largest feature that proves that there is so much more to this game than simply firing a gun and reloading, which others cannot say as easily.
I've played other shooters - in fact, I've played more hours of Battlefield 3 than this game - for sure, but of all of them this one simply does it right. In addition, this game has the greatest atmosphere out of all; where else can you be part of a horde of fervent Soviet troops screaming in an auditory rally for the Motherland in their native tongue just before battle? I hate to sound like some kind of arrogant "fanboy" who thinks his favorite game is better than everyone else's, but of all my forays into shooter games this has been the most extended and by far the most enjoyable, and as a strategy gamer at heart I don't see this changing in a long time.

When it comes to combat it's how you'd imagine a tell-tale game to play, with a little a twist on it, it can get pretty intense and you have to be constantly aware of where your fingers are to be able to press two keys simultaneously which can lead into a satisfying rhythm and I liked the use of the mouse for the grapple, the only beef I have is I wish there where more game overs for when you f up, that would've made the fighting just that much more engaging.
The story is very well orchestrated, at first I thought everything was a bit too simple and I didn't feel like the decisions I made really matter (which honestly they really don't, because thats telltales secret ingredient, the illusion of choice) but the further on in the game I went the more I said to myself 'damn maybe i should've done this or said that?' and wanted to play it over again, see what might happen if I chose a different path and to me that makes this game a success of TT's formula.
Sure some of its campy, and the characters and there relationships with one another aren't exactly 100% canon, but its telltales game at the end of the day, it has its own continuity, but still keeps with the spirit of batman and gotham that I love, so I'm going to happily await the next season to see how things turn out for my save ;)

Telltale Games have a formula. You're going to have multiple choice dialog. You're going to do a little puzzle solving. You're going to have some quicktime action sequences. Knowing this, going into any particular Telltale game, the question becomes "can they use this formula to tell a compelling story?" For Batman - The Telltale Series (BTTS), that answer is yes.
BTTS discards and rearranges a lot of Batman mythology, and that's okay. It's difficult to tell a surprising or original story involving those characters that hasn't already been told in comics. Rather than retell one of those stories, they've given us something original but deeply in the vein of the character. Even better, the choices you make as Batman and Bruce Wayne allow you to play the character as you see him. Is Batman a shining light of justice or a terrifying monster of vengeance, or some balance between those two? Is Bruce Wayne a billionaire playboy caught in the political machine, or a cog driving that machine within Gotham? It's all up to you.
What I found interesting about this game is that it could be seen as an evolution of a previous Telltale game, A Wolf Among Us, based on the Fables comic book. Both games involve an outside-the-law enforcer trying to solve a mystery. The way they balance the dialog, investigation, and action is basically identical, and it could be assumed that A Wolf Among Us was a prototype for BTTS.
However, what BTTS is kind of missing is the tension of being a monster. Bigby Wolf was a literal monster among monsters. Sometimes, he had to be a bigger monster than the rest simply to get things done, but doing so would reduce his standing in his community. When Bigby killed someone, he was playing into a stereotype he was trying to fight against. On the other hand, Bruce Wayne can largely separate himself from Batman. Batman can be a monster, but Bruce Wayne won't suffer the consequences of his actions. When I played Batman as a good guy trying to get things done that a corrupt government would not, the people I wanted on my side were largely there for me. When I played Bigby the same way, I was still treated as dangerous and a liability. BTTS doesn't really capture that feeling as well as A Wolf Among Us did.
My other gripe with the game are the technical difficulties. These cause this game to lose points because they've been a part of Telltale games for far too long. For being a fairly uncomplicated adventure game with good-not-great look, it hitches on framerate far too often. Combined with a save game problem that caused me to have to replay episode 1 because it ate my save, these problems are difficult to overlook. They're not showstoppers, but they're frustrating to deal with.
For Telltale and Batman fans, it's easy to recommend BTTS. You'll know what you're getting into here, and you'll get a largely original Batman story with some creative twists on well known characters. However, if you're not familiar with Telltale games, or you don't care for Batman, A Wolf Among Us is essentially the same type of game with a better sense of character progression.

I see that Tropico 5 share the curse of all the good series, the curse of predecessor. If you already have a very succesful game in your hands, developers are facing somehow a dilemma: if they try to keep the old mechanics and game design, fans will accuse them of copying the old game. And if they try to implement new mechanics, then fans will complain about how the new game spoiled what it was good.  The curse of homm3 over its succesors is the best example of that.
In case you had great fun playing tropico 3 or 4, this game probably won't give more to you only because it's developed few years later.  In this perspective, i find most of fan's critics are right. Yet, for those who didn't play a tropico game before and for those who seek an enjoyable simulation, i strongly recommend Tropico 5. Particularly the campaign is well designed, and most of all game is fun.

Sunless Sea is simultaneously, one of the most frustrating and fascinatingly engaging games I've ever played.  While ultimately, I do recommend it, I can't guarantee it's the right game for you.
I love the characters, the story, the world, the quests and the game's expansive backstory and lore.  The mysteries and secrets of the game are presented very well, being expertly hinted at, slowly revealed and mostly ending with interesting and creative conclusions.  The mix of melancholy, bizzare, funny and horrific themes come together to form a satisfying and entirely unique whole.  This only feels marred by key lore points not being in Sunless Sea itself, only being found in "Fallen London," it's obnoxiously freemium predecessor.
The music is evocative and ties in wonderfully with Sunless Sea's locations and themes.  I only wish the Zubmariner expansion had added more tracks, instead of just putting an underwater-sounding effect over the exsisting music.  If you find yourself hooked by the game, you'll wish tracks were longer or more numerous as you find yourself hearing key tracks repeatedly.  Ambient sound is adequate, but could be much better with a little work.  Improved ambient sailing and cave noises would aid greatly in increasing player immersion.
The game world is lovingly presented in 2D.  The overworld is fantastic.  City and island images are evocative and imaginative.  Character portraits are... servicably OK.  Enemy and ship variety and design are a little lacking.
Gameplay is punishing.  I understand thematically why it has been designed to be, but that doesn't stop it from feeling annoying.  Your ship starts slow, and if you want to go faster, you're punished with a less favorable fuel consumption rate.  Want to upgrade to a bigger ship with more cargo space or more hull points?  Well, you're traveling slower then.  Trading initially is very frustrating due to the razor thin margins you'll be making.  Again, I understand why it's been designed this way, in this case, to push the player towards exploring and completing quests, but I just can't help but feel like the developers only want players to enjoy the game their way, "the right way."  Sunless Sea has a steep learning curve, not so much from any difficulty, but simply the player comming to terms with it's own philosophies and way of thinking.
As a last note, Failbetter games commit a sin with Sunless Sea that I, personally, find inexcusable; Kickstarter supporters having access to significant, exclusive content.  Sunless Sea has been out for a long time now.  Offer this content as reasonably priced DLC.  We want to support you, Failbetter.  Don't punish newer players for not having been aware of a crowd-funding campaign.

Right off the bat let it be known I am a MASSIVE fan girl of this game, 10/10 honestly, so I'll just be mentioning all the things I love about it and blindly ignore the flaws (ignorance is bliss).
Story
Perfect for your cult-like reader of Lovecraftian tales; eerie and confusing but enticing. If you can deal with incredibly cryptic hints and long blocks of texts then you'll enjoy this. At times wacky but it stills makes sense in the universe, never quite knee-slappingly hilarious but pretty amusing. At first you might be annoyed like a city slicker visiting a small fishing village but soon enough you'll be speaking like one of your fellow zailors and getting immersed into the lore of the zea.
Gameplay
Think like a survival/hardcore FTL on an ocean, except way harder. You will NOT win this game on the first playthrough without incredible knowledge of every single island and quest (and insane luck); even on the 8th playthrough you'll be dying in the middle of the ocean having no clue what went wrong but having to start a new life anyway.
Graphics
Incredibly simple, nothing breathtaking. That being said if you can get immersed enough you will go slack-jawed at the sight of the ice castles of the north, fear of the creatures of the deep, and pure joy at the lights of Fallen London.

Without a shadow of a doubt one of the greater shooters to ever exist, this game is brilliant - where else can you still play on the battlefields of Stalingrad with old school iron-sighted bolt-action Kar98's and Mosins? Besides bolt-actions this game does so many things every other game in the genre should strive for - you actually need to work as a team (squad leader has smoke, forward spawn, and artillery marking but needs his team to cover him), you have to take cover behind sandbags or windows or trenches if you value your team or life, melee charges are legitimately effective as Imperial Japanese forces, people only take more than a few bullets to kill if you use the garbage PPS-42, and tools such as recon, smoke, mortar fire, tanks, snipers, and machine gunners all require at least some degree of skill to time and place effectively.
Above all else, in this game one must not get too caught up in one's self - of all the games I have played, none have actually *encouraged* taking one for the team and sacrificing yourself for the better of your comrades rather than simply "stay alive as long as you can" - an exceptional and revolutionary design mechanic where you have to put your team above yourself as did so many soldiers in the real Great Patriotic and Pacific Wars. This is the largest feature that proves that there is so much more to this game than simply firing a gun and reloading, which others cannot say as easily.
I've played other shooters - in fact, I've played more hours of Battlefield 3 than this game - for sure, but of all of them this one simply does it right. In addition, this game has the greatest atmosphere out of all; where else can you be part of a horde of fervent Soviet troops screaming in an auditory rally for the Motherland in their native tongue just before battle? I hate to sound like some kind of arrogant "fanboy" who thinks his favorite game is better than everyone else's, but of all my forays into shooter games this has been the most extended and by far the most enjoyable, and as a strategy gamer at heart I don't see this changing in a long time.

Also known as Game Journalist Sim 2017, Cuphead is a platformer-action boss-rush game with bullet-hell shoot-em-up segments, and can probably contend with the Indie Game of Year. Based on the old "rubber hose" style of 1930's American Animation (Such examples can be seen with Fleishcer Studios, who created Betty Boop and Popeye the Sailor). No two levels are the same, each having a gimick and a pattern, all with a swinging soundtrack, it's a blast to the past in the modern era.
Cuphead goes with a "episode" format, with each episode being either a side-scrolling level or a boss fight, and in boss fights, you'll be fighting them in Contra Run-And-Gun style, or in a airplane similar to horizontal shoot-em-ups. Theses episodes each have a unique challenge to them, as you buy power-ups throughout the game to change your strategy to adapt to the current levels demands. Level and Boss knowledge is also a must in order to survive difficult attacks, shooting and parrying pink objects to fight through the multiple phases of each boss.
All this creates an interesting, dynamic expereince. If you are a Wings of Vi veteran, this game would be a great fit, along with fans of other hardcore platformers and bullet hells. Each boss puts just enough stress that beating them creates an adrenaline rush for you to face extreme relief. This game is definintly not for the faint of heart or the easily frustrated.
Really worth the 20 bucks, give it a shot.

I thought I'd talk a little about one of my favourite games, Sunless Sea, and one tiny smidgen of why it's so interesting. Sunless Sea (and its antecedent Fallen London) occur in the Neath. Neath is short for Beneath—where most everything in the game is, since the devils of the Echo Bazaar sank London underground, closer to Hell. That's all fascinating, of course, but what I want to talk about is money.
The economy of the Neath is information (particularly, stories), the more secret the more valuable. The most basic unit of value is the echo. That's not a kind of coin or bill. It's a piece of information, an Echo, like a rumour. Secrets are common but are valued at about 999 Echoes. Fragments are are earned as you explore the map, as you encounter wild happenings, share confidences with other figures in the Neath, overhear curious mutterings, and dissect abominable creatures of the sea. 300 or so Fragments combine to forge Secrets (the better your Pages stat the few Fragments you need to unveil a Secret, think of Pages as a kind of Lore-gathering-and-facilitating stat). You can also combine Fragments with Memories Of Distant Shores or with Zee-Stories to discover Secrets as well.
Secrets are fascinating because they operate as either currency or XP, depending on your need. You can trade Secrets with officers to increase your stats, making them essential for grooming your captain to be respected and feared. Alternatively, you can trade Secrets for Echoes, if you must. Alternatively again, there are plenty of instances in which a situation will call for a good Secret or five if you hope to get out of a scrape or convince a person to aid you (or not report you to the authorities) or hope to build some fell device or other.
Tales Of Terror and Zee-Stories and Memories Of Distant Shores can all be traded for goods at various ports. Everyone is hungry for knowledge, whether it turns out to be true or not. Even Recent News is valuable and some ports will only let you on shore if you have it. Visions Of The Surface and information about Moves In The Great Game (espionage!) and Strategic Information and Vital Intelligence and Extraordinary Implications are each valuable (or maybe invaluable) in their own ways.
In one case, in one of the most drawnout storylines of the game, you are asked to "witness the death of something that is the oldest of its kind, and return," at which point you tell the tale and are rewarded handsomely, first with information in the form of stats increases and then later with the location of one of the biggest secrets of the game.
Searing Enigmas are nearly the most valuable thing in the game and are quite rare. The game describes them thus: "Mysteries are fire. Truth burns." These are secrets so rare and so important that men will die to learn them or keep them safe.
And still more valuable than that: the Dread Surmise, described as "the awful daring of a moment's supposition which an age of ignorance can never deny." This is incredibly high-level information or secret. Something essential that no one knows. It would be on the order of ironclad evidence that God exists that anyone, having seen it, would be forever changed.
The game, for all its weirdnesses and intrigues, does a great job of the idea of trading on one's terror of the unknown for comfort in the unknown.

Yep, it's another Tropico game...
There really isn't much more to say other than that.  It just feels lazy.  All your old favourite buildings return,  very few new ones.  DLC is silly expensive, customization is meh.  Save your money and go play one of the other tropicos.  Either 1,  or if you like roads,  3.
To elaborate.
Building Variety - Tropico has never been big on this, but it's 2014.  Would it kill to have 2 models for a Bunhouse/house/etc?
Eras - These are esentially mini-goals.  If you fail to achieve them within the time limit,  you lose.  That's about it.  All they do is lock buildings from you,  making it harder to layout a good city -from the start-
Ships -  You get to own ships,  that sounds cool, and I really thought it was going to be like Tropico 2 managing pirate fleets.  But it's not.  You couldn't have any less interaction with them, No naming,  no colouring, and with each era, the ship just poofs into the next eras ship and keeps doing what it does.    Huge let down.
Mines - Ugly eyesores that just look silly when you upgrade them.   A mini Bagger 288 just sits there, and it's grosly undersized.
Tanks - Yep, I'm gonna say this too.  The introduction of Tropico tanks.   They are T-34.  That's it. Every nation be it america,  soviets,  modern armour,, oh and of course Tropico,  all use the same model T-34.
Bring Back TNT radio - I mean the Tropico 3 one, (but 4 is even better than this schlock).
Some of these sound nitpicky,  but this is why the game just feels lazy.  Would it of killed them to make a few differnt tank models?  Woud it of been that much of an effort to make another bunk house?
Sure, these are just visuals,  but this game is very difficult to mod.  And there are virtually no new gameplay from say Tropico 3,  or 4.      So if the game play is the same, then the visuals better be amazing......but they aren't.  Hence  a lazy, forgetable, "next tropico game".

Sunless Sea is a sort-of-but-not-quite roguelike game set on the Unterzea. You depart from the City of Fallen London aboard your tramp steamer to find a journey of discovery, wealth, horror, and almost certain death. The meat of the gameplay experience is zailing through the procedurally generated Zea to strange new lands, trying not to starve, be eaten by monsters are go mad with fear until you reach an island where you can pick up supplies and playthrough a story, and it's in the stories that the game truly shines. The writing in Sunless Sea is excellent, more than making up for the lacklustre combat and generally slow pace of exploration. They tend towards the creepy and the bizzare, and the top notch visuals and sound design complement the mood of the text brilliantly.
The zailing makes up most of the game though, and while I certainly enjoy it, it's far from perfect. Exploring into uncharted parts of the zea, with no idea how long until you find land, watching your fuel and supplies slowly run out and your crew become more and more frightened is compellng stuff for the first few playthroughs, but play the game long enough and you'll be able to figure out where you should go and how much supplies you should bring even at the start of the game with a whole new unuxplored map. This is because the island positions change, but for gameplay balance can't change to dramatically; certain islands will always be near each other, others will always be close to london, some always in the southern part of the map, etc. This means that no game is generated where success is impossible, but since the content of the islands tends to stay the same you eventually become so familiar with it that the sense of exploration is dulled considerably.
Of course, as of writing I have 121 hours in Sunless Sea, so I obviously think the good outweighs the bad.
