I played the free flash version of Superhot before it was a real game. Just that small taste seared the extreme amounts of potential into my head, and the mind-blowing opprotunities of the mechanics.
And the full game delivers. The few glitches from the free version have been polished out, and the white with bright red astetic gives the game a clean and professional look. The brilliant mechanic, in which time slows down and speeds up relative to the players movement speed, is used to the fullest, and combined with the 1 shot 1 kill, the game makes gun battles tense and exciting, while offering a playstyle geared towards planning and thoughtful placement. The sound design is very well done, and the levels are quite varied, giving a health amount of variety in terrain.
As good as this game was, I still have a few quarrels with it. The campaign is very short, and took me around 3 hours, knocking it out in an afternoon. I also feel that ammo counters on the weapons would have been a good idea. You also get an ability later on which allows you to possess an enemy, and a recharge meter or bar would have been very useful. While the level are varied, the enemies are not. Yes, they will ocassionally use different weapons, but they are all red, crystaline mannequins at the end of it all. I hoped for enemies with say, different body types, or sepcial weaknesses, or specialized abilities. The same goes for the weapons. You have a pistol, a shotgun, and a burst fire assault rifle. You also have some melee weapons, and a katana. The throwables are all basically reskins of one object, and I feel that more variety would have helped. Possibly a sniper rifle, or a minigun of some sort, or just more types of weapons. The player character feels quite bulky at times, as bullets you were sure missed still manage to hit you, making the player feel like they're wearing a cardboard box. When you finish a level,
The plot is quite interesting, being about virtual reality and the like, but I felt that they designed the game, then bashed the plot about with a hammer until it fit together, which I feel is the wrong way to do things. I feel that the plot should be written, then events connected with levels and fights.
When a level is completed, a video plays of you doing the level in real time, which would have been great, but the video is obscured by the phrase, "Super...Hot!" flashing infront of the clip.
After the campaign is finished, endless modes and challenge levels, which is the campaign with a certain twist added, or removed, are added.
I must say that I quite recocmend Superhot, it's great bloody fun, and it really breaks up the monatany of the twatting about in modern war shooters. It's wonderful, has a few issues, but it's very worth it, and is still great.

I received this game as a gift from a good friend.
At its heart, Morphopolis plays like a hidden object game with several simple, yet fun puzzles thrown in.
The artwork is quite charming, bright and colorful. It would be at home in classic illustrated children's book.
If I had one gripe about gameplay is that there is a point and click element to the movement (or more correctly, hold a direction and click) which is quite slow and sometimes it's not obvious what areas of the screen transition to a new area. That said you can at least click on your little bug several times to send out little 'feeler' particles that branch off in the different directions you can move to, although you may have to be much closer than you'd think for this to show you a path you've been missing.

Father’s Island is an exploitation video game and you better keep that in mind while you’re playing it. In recent years, more and more Steam games have tried to exaggerate certain features found in our society and thus, the exploitation genre has its well deserved niche in gaming, as it does in the film industry. The indie scene makes good use of over-the-top “B-movie” style topics and the game I’m reviewing today was created by Homegrown Games, whose previous projects were Painkiller: Ressurection and  Into the Dark: Ultimate Trash Edition. What I found particularly interesting, was the hands-on approach of Homegrown’s CEO and founder, who is taking an active role in his creations, like a video gaming’s equivalent of Ed Wood.
Back to our game now. Father’s Island starts off in an ambiguous manner yet we are introduced to our vocal protagonist, John Richards. A high school teacher who wants to prove his innocence despite mounting evidence of a robbery commited by him. He travels to an unnamed island that is apparently the last known location of his father and brothers. The place looks deserted, with only a few rabbits and some sheep grazing while being oblivious to our hero's presence. You must explore a fairly vast territory, look for clues about your family’s whereabouts and try to find some peace of mind at last.
It won’t be as easy as it might seem at first glance and once again, this being somewhat abstract as well, I feel compelled to warn you that Father’s Island may not contain the amount of action or adventure you’re used to. It is first and foremost, a walking simulator which uses the relatively lengthy journey across the island from one place of interest to another, as the story’s exposition. The intrigue and conclusion will surely upset some players who will be left wanting for more. Keep that in mind, before purchasing this title.
For a game that’s been made entirely with GameGuru assets, Father’s Island doesn’t look too shabby. Sure, it can’t be compared to more complex game engines, but if I didn’t look close enough, I might have mistaken the assets for an early Unity Engine build. Still, it has plenty of custom objects and textures that weren't just copy-pasted from GameGuru's standard package. My biggest gripe is not with the loading times (about 3 minutes of waiting even on  a high-end PC) or the textures (which feature a mix of low and high res elements), but with the unstable frame rate. It would fluctuate from 60 to 25 on 4K resolution (it runs in your monitor’s native one, so can’t even lower it through settings) and I find that unacceptable. So I understand where the mixed ratings and reviews are coming from, but the game has redeeming points as well.
The soundtrack and voice acting is one such positive note, which tips the scales in favor for Father’s Island. I’ll start with the OST. You can listen to anything from relaxing music that reminded me of Buddha Bar, piano tracks and even a military march. And the voice acting? None other than John J. D1ck (thanks for the censorship, Valve) of Serious Sam fame, among other titles. His deep voice impersonation is just as funny in Father’s Island as in his previous projects. The icing on the cake comes in the form of live action cutscenes featuring the game’s developer himself. Intentionally awkward cinematics which reminded me of Ed Wood starring in his own exploitation movies.
As for the gameplay, you’ll spend a lot of time going back and forth from one island location to another. No map has been implemented in the final version of the game, so you better keep a close eye on your surroundings and memorize certain landmarks in order to navigate smoothly through this creepy place. Luckly, the annoying loading screen when you’re starting a new game or going back to a previous save file, is the only time you’re gonna encounter it while you’re playing. The relatively large map has no other sections that need separate loading screens, so you’re free to roam in a seemless manner.
You will hunt for both clues and keys to access new buildings. The backtracking involved in this title may deter the players lacking sufficient patience. Fortunately for me, years of gameplay grinding in some games have allowed me to view backtracking as a necessary evil, in order to extend an otherwise short trip from point A to B. Nobody likes predictable outcomes though. They shouldn’t, even if they do. Plenty of notes to read and you can always pause and admire the nearly apocalyptic vistas offered by the island’s permanent state of dawn/dusk. Red skies always have a hidden beauty of their own and if the game’s also Cold War-themed, then the scenery could remind players of a sky after a nuclear test.
One thing that I really appreciated in Father’s Island, is the inclusion of propaganda material in a tasteful way that offered some much needed insight into the convoluted storyline. Propaganda posters, predominantly from the Cold War era, but also a few from Nazi Germany as well, thrown in for “good measure”. It all screamed of Operation Paperclip. Formerly registered members of the National Socialist German Workers' Party which became “upstanding American citizens” after WW2 since their skills were needed in the upcoming Space & Arms races against the USSR. Yeah, I’m a history buff and proud of it. I go crazy for high-res posters of printed brainwashing, since I shall always find the darker side of advertising (as if the rest is any better) to be fascinating. Sadly, this kind of carefully packaged bulls**t was actually convincing people into hating and killing each other, against all logic or common sense. But that’s the definition of “war” in a nutshell, for you.
It’s a polarizing game to say the least. At the same time, you need to understand that it’s intentionally ambiguous, so it was never intended to be a conventional adventure or walking simulator. It’s affordable, has Trading Cards and you can enjoy it for over three hours. Why so many negative reviews? Sometimes Steam users are a bigger mystery to me than some of the games I get to write about. Nobody’s forcing you to buy this at its full retail price or even during a Sale, but random hate is always free, right? I strongly recommend Father’s Island for fans of the exploitation genre and its many colorful subgenres.
+ Pleasant graphics.

- No game map or clearly explained set of objectives.
- No Steam Achievements.

I've had this game long enough, I might as well write a review. Its a great game if you have the patience to learn it. RO2 has  a steep learning curve when compared to most fps. If you can see your enemy, he can see you, if you can't see him, he can still see you, if you're behind cover, he can see you, if you just spawned, he can see you, if you're behind him, he can see you. And he will kill you. He will kill you a lot. You will be spawn killed when  spawning off your squad leader. You will see a sniper rifle on the ground, and you will spam the pick up key. The pick up key will only work 1/3 of the time. A grenade will land near you and you will spam the prone key. This key will work 3/4 of the time. You will wrestle with the controls as much as you fight your enemy. You will be team killed by free weekenders and people who bought this game on sale. When playing as the americans in RS, you will die 2/3 of the time by aimbotting heatseeking knee mortar nukes, and have your character do an automatic 180 spin to expose his back during a banzi charge. When playing as the russians you will be destroyed by the german's superior machineguns. As the Japanese you will be dominated by the M1 Garand and the flamethrower. As the Germans the russian smg's will cut through you like swiss cheese and their inferior MGs will still give you a run for your money. When you try to join a match with ~3 open player slots, the map will load and only after the map has loaded will you be kicked back to the server browser with the server full message. this happens 1/2 the time. If you are however willing to learn the game and put up with a lot of the stupid stuff that happens way too frequently, this game is EXTREMELY fun. Very tense, very satisfying to do well in. It captures war in a way that few games can, and has lots of small details that add so much to the game. One notable one is the game's unique bolt action mechanic, where, if you choose to turn it on, you have to manually cycle the bolt of the rifle. There are lots of times where you can have awesome Alamo style last stands, as well as adrenaline fueled assaults. Put time into this game. learn from veterans. keep your head down. You'll enjoy it.

Yep, it's another Tropico game...
There really isn't much more to say other than that.  It just feels lazy.  All your old favourite buildings return,  very few new ones.  DLC is silly expensive, customization is meh.  Save your money and go play one of the other tropicos.  Either 1,  or if you like roads,  3.
To elaborate.
Building Variety - Tropico has never been big on this, but it's 2014.  Would it kill to have 2 models for a Bunhouse/house/etc?
Eras - These are esentially mini-goals.  If you fail to achieve them within the time limit,  you lose.  That's about it.  All they do is lock buildings from you,  making it harder to layout a good city -from the start-
Ships -  You get to own ships,  that sounds cool, and I really thought it was going to be like Tropico 2 managing pirate fleets.  But it's not.  You couldn't have any less interaction with them, No naming,  no colouring, and with each era, the ship just poofs into the next eras ship and keeps doing what it does.    Huge let down.
Mines - Ugly eyesores that just look silly when you upgrade them.   A mini Bagger 288 just sits there, and it's grosly undersized.
Tanks - Yep, I'm gonna say this too.  The introduction of Tropico tanks.   They are T-34.  That's it. Every nation be it america,  soviets,  modern armour,, oh and of course Tropico,  all use the same model T-34.
Bring Back TNT radio - I mean the Tropico 3 one, (but 4 is even better than this schlock).
Some of these sound nitpicky,  but this is why the game just feels lazy.  Would it of killed them to make a few differnt tank models?  Woud it of been that much of an effort to make another bunk house?
Sure, these are just visuals,  but this game is very difficult to mod.  And there are virtually no new gameplay from say Tropico 3,  or 4.      So if the game play is the same, then the visuals better be amazing......but they aren't.  Hence  a lazy, forgetable, "next tropico game".

This could have been a very nice game, except that in its current version it is plagued by far too many bugs, making it impossible to enjoy it. It still feels like a beta, not quite ready for prime-time yet.
Here are some of the problems I came across:
- Loading the game takes a long time, even on my PC (Skylake, GTX980Ti, SSDs, etc.) This wouldn’t necessarily be a problem if it only happened when you start up the game. But if you want to reload a save, or if you accidentally die and you have to reload a save, it reloads the whole damn thing all over again, and you just have to wait, and wait... every time.
- Default music volume was too loud and the soundtrack would start at the wrong time, overlapping some voice-overs and causing you to miss some important information. Solution: reload a save, and wait, and wait...
- Occasional crash on save. Restart; and wait, and wait...
- Occasional crash on load. Restart; and wait, and wait...
- Green screen after load. Restart; and wait, and wait...
- Ground textures disappearing when looking out through an open door, from inside a building. They usually reappear as soon as you step aside, but one time they did not, so I had to restart, and wait, and wait...
- Some textures are misplaced and some vegetation appears to float in mid-air.
- When pressing "E" once, doors and gates would fling open and immediately close again. Pressing "E" a second time will cause them to open normally.
- Once opened, I had to "space bar" + "W" in order to pass through most doors and gates.
With all these problems, I almost feel like I did more waiting than gaming, and these interruptions served to completely break the mood of the game and to make the entire experience more annoying rather than enjoyable. And that’s a pity too, because otherwise I liked the story. It could be a really nice mystery game, if they could fix these issues.

A walking simulator which stimulates thoughtful reflection on various topics.
Those are the two core components of The Beginner's Guide. Walking and reflecting. Unfortunately, the strength of the latter is insufficient to carry the weakness of the former- well, not for me at least. I found the mechanics of playing the game to be incredibly boring. There were no meaningful choices, challenges, or failure states. You're told exactly what to do at nearly every turn. You don't play this game insomuch as you experience it. And that experience for the most part is pretty somber.
People who place more value in the narrative and the thoughts it provokes may understandably rate this game very highly. But for me, it simply wasn't fun.

I went into Edge of Space, hoping for something of a cross between Terraria and Starbound. Unfortunately, it did not deliver.
Firstly, there are several menus. too many menus, assigned to keys that you could possibly change, but why? why are there so many?
Navigating story text is also a pain, and the tutorial is horrible. it conveys the controls, but the way it does it is more of a chore it has to do, ticking off parts of the game on a checklist. You don't feel like you've learned anything.
Then there is death. this is perhaps my biggest axe to grind. it turns death into some complex process involving crafting a chamber, and using rods, and I just give up at that point.
I spawned in, tried to slowly edge down from the top of a goddamn asteroid field it dump-ed me into really? couldn't have started with rolling hills? something normal??) and died. I had no idea what to do or how to do it.
Edge of Space is a game full of potential. however, it is far, far too complicated. it has a LOT of work to do to get the gameplay user-friendly, and the death mechanic needs some serious reworking.
It feels like this game is trying to be terraria 2.0, while also trying to be starbound, but not grasping what makes starbound fun. It takes the sci-fi all right, but it takes the grungy abandoned-spaceship theme. Not the adventuring and simplistic controls.

Ok, I really wanted to like this game, and I'm guessing that most of the reviews here are made by shemps close to the developer and I can't believe so many people would reccomend this game, but here are some general issues I have with it -
- Buggy. Not a surprise for an ameturely made game, but being able to pick up objects through walls? Overlapping dialog? Textures that pop in and out? The game dropping to about 2 fps just because you dared to put your face near green glass?
- Terrible writing. It's just...bad. Cheesy. Poorly written. Non-sensical.
- Bad acting. So the short video clips that are triggered are poorly acted, but they're actually pretty awesome. As somebody who loved 90s adventure games, which heavily used FMV to propell the narrative, I'm definitely a fan of that part. However, the voiceovers are just awful. I think it may have been the same guy in the FMV videos doing all the voice work, just employing an accent for one and "I just ate glass" for the other.
- Awful graphics. I mean, they aren't horrible, but the constant red on brown...the whole game looks like a scab. Trying to find brown keys on brown objects - all the while being blasted with red everything else...I mostly found objects just by happening to get near them and seeing the text about picking it up.
- The worst sin of all - it's boring. The story is actually somewhat interesting, but...not a lot happens in the game. You wait forever at the intro loading screen, which wouldn't be much of an issue if...you know...it actually loaded things for you to do. All it does, though, is load a wipe open expanse of nothing. There's no reason to explore. There's nothing to do. I found a key in the game, which opened up a building, and except for a brief voiceover explaining that the building smelled like♥♥♥♥♥♥ there was nothing else to do in there. What was the point of making me find a key to a building that housed absolutely nothing?!
Like I said, I really, really wanted to like this game. It gave me somewhat of a FPS version of Harvester vibe and I dug that, but there's just a lot going wrong here that I can't recommend it.
Full disclosure, I didn't actually finish the game. I think I got near the end where you have to find your fathers house, but I died in the worlds smallest pond (yes, water = instant death) and didn't want to wait for that initial loading screen just to pick up where I left off.
There's something good here. There is a right idea somewhere in this game. It just needs more development, more playtesting and a rewrite. As it is now, take that $2.50 and buy a box of pop tarts. You'll get more enjoyment out of them.

This game is... probably not worth ten dollars. For most people that is. But for those seeking something deeper, something that treats its audience maturely and intelligently, then this Guide is for you; and, in that case, it is certainly worth more than ten dollars.

I have been a longtime fan of the Tropico series. Honestly though I feel like the series peaked at Tropico 3, I enjoyed 4 and I enjoy 5 but they are both lacking some of the freedom and zaniness of 3. Tropico 5 has its good points, I am very greatful for Linux support and there was obvious effort put into switching things up from the normal model. However to me Tropico was a multiplayer game and the addition of that feature changed the dynamics of the gameplay a bit too much. I am not a fan of the Dynasty feature either, I prefered having my El Presidente having ultimate power and I miss some of the touches of the charicter creation system (no longer can you have the charming but flatulant El Presedente) instead you only assign a point to a charicter (+1 foriegn relations etc). Which builds when you have a dynasty, but it removes a little of the soul of the game. I am not a fan of the new Radio announcer either, I miss Penultimo. Finally I wish there were more diversity in the islands, while it's interesting to return to an island and continue building on it I miss the diversity. Overall it's a fun game, and if you like Tropico 1-4 you'll like it, but overall it feels like the weakest entry so far.

Only recommended if you like hardcore gameplay and storytelling.
This is a fairly small game but very lore deep.
Don't expect hand holding with this one.
You start with a lowly captain, on search for wealth and/or fame.
You can start with preset bonuses and goal, or with none.
You will die atleast the first 2 journeys, whatever you do.
The point of this game is to become familiar with his story, handle the resources you get taken from and throwed at.
Aside from the 'realistic' gameplay, its lore is very immersive.
If you used to simulations or tycoon, but want something with some more action, this is what you are looking for.
You'll take resources from point A, to sell them at point B, take some passengers from point C and deliver them at D (or sell them at E, your choice).
While you're travelling, you come across enemies (other boats or monsters), see your crew has enough food and sanity, and checking how much fuel you still have.
Don't expect to do a quickrun on this, this game is hard but doable in a couple of sittings.
It also gets slightly easier every time your captain was further in the lore / resources, since your successor will get some of those resources / knowledge transferred to him / her.
Again, very recommended but only to those old school gamers.

I have been playing this game for years now, feels great for it to be on Steam and be reinvigorated, as playerbase dwindled over the years and it was always only about word of mouth for people to find out about it in the first place. When I heard about it in 2013, I thought it was a meme.
This game is just good, no matter what type of entertainment you seek.
If you are more into serious stuff, you can find standart Bomb and Hostage games with round death and economy and stuff, with a twist that top-down view gives (firing blindly, fog of war, etc.)
If you want some twists, it can be a completely different game, just with visuals of CS. Construction modification of a gamemode, where everyone has a wrench and can build and upgrade several types of buildings, often resulting in hour long CTF matches. CTF matches by themselves, Zombies, Free for all and Team Deathmatches. Unique equipment like mines, RPG's, Lasers, Portal guns etc.
On top of that, in-game eidot and Lua scripting provides more stuff by the community, minecraft maps, deathruns, PROP HUNTS (really fit in this game) roleplay and other stuff.
Game looks good for indie, has gorgeous particles, can run on a potato.
This is not a serious game to spend a lot of time in for sure. Even Standart servers are free to leave whenever. But if you know there is a spare half-hour - hour in your schedule, or even just some 15 min breaks that you need to fill in with some genuine fun, get this game, it's fast to install and it's free. It takes a bit to get used to, to learn new modes, but it certainly provides that fast and easy fun factor of "pocket games". Some less-mainstream modes have faded out, but it's up to you, call some friends and fill the servers again.
Oh right, no lootboxes.

Tropico 5 is a welcome sequel to a great series. Many fans were underwhelmed by Tropico 4. While the game was solid it did little to innovate on Tropico 3 and its expansions. Tropico 5 took notes, and now offers a very different gameplay experience.
The biggest changes are the multitude of little tweaks, such as how farms work, a new research system, new specialist system, the dynasty mechanics and a dozen other little things that overhaul the game hugely. Each is well implemented with the level of detail and balance we've come to expect from the series.
The new time based campaigns are also something that Tropico players have talked about for a long term- persistent islands. Traditionally each level in Tropico is its own map, but no longer. You have only two islands in this game, and you develop them through the campaign. This requires much more foresight and planning and led to me needing to restart the campaign twice because I didn't think far enough ahead. I thoroughly enjoyed overcoming this great new challenge.
If you've never played Tropico I'd suggest starting with 3 or 4. 5 is a very different game but it maintains the tone, feel and gameplay shape of its predecessors. As such you can spend a little less seeing if you like the style before you commit to spending more on the recent title.
If you know Tropico and love it, then you'll love Tropico 5. Faithful, but not afraid to break new ground. And they break it with extreme competence and authority.

This game is rather brilliant. For those who are interested in the Zombie Apocalypse from a realistic standpoint and aren't looking for another action packed chainsaw adventure.
This is a very straight forward survival simulation. You must eat, drink, sleep, watch your body temp and conditional, treat your wounds and otherwise try to survive.
Pry windows open, or smash them to save time but compromise your security and draw the attention of nearby zombies? Switch on the lights to search a dense room, or try to manage in the dark? Highly recommended. I can't wait to see all the content realized for this game.

"Morphopolis", or "A Bug's Life", is a short hidden object game with slight point-and-click elements, mainly in directing your character, which is a bug, by pointing and clicking. The bug grows from larvae to bigger buggy forms, while collecting hidden items and solving occasional puzzles.
The game features 5 stages, a soothing soundtrack, beautiful artwork, sluggish and unresponsive controls, and a frustrating last puzzle which may take you minutes or hours to complete, based on your luck. I was lucky and finished it in about 10 minutes, completely by accident.
Since I got it for €0.19 on sale, I consider it money well spent. At its full price of €4.99, eh, not so much. Beautiful audio-visuals aside, the core gameplay is really boring and at times frustrating because,
(a) the bug moves really slowly, and
(b) the boundaries of the playable area and paths to take are often not clearly visible.
All in all, expect some 1.5 - 3 hrs of playtime, with no replay value. Overall, OK, but "Would not morph into a cricket again," to use the lame review trope.

A real solid survival game that unfortunately ends up falling a bit short due to the huge and arguably broken random factor. Surviving your first couple of days is easy since food is borderline abundant in every house along with water being a common commodity at every tap, toilet and bathtub. Eventually, however, these resources will dwindle, not only by the human consumption but due to the basic services shutting down.
Electricity and the Waterworks will abruptly be cut off after some time, leaving any fridge-dependant foods to be almost instantly spoiled, leaving you very dependant on rare canned foods, chips and other conserverd commodities which will run out real fast depending on your character. "Just create a farm!" you say? Fantastic Idea! Just one flaw: You need to find a shovel/trowel and plant seeds. While seeds are rather common, trowel/shovels are not. I have spent countless of hours, killing hundreds of zombies to clear out a big piece of farm-land just to spend even more time searching dumbly for seemingly common tools In order to have any kind of chance to survive. And even then, surviving for any seriously long amount of time won't be possible because your sources of water will run dry faster than you can say "Kebab" as any and all plantations require gigantic sources of water that will need to be hauled back and forth by you, consuming very large amounts of time for little to no actual food seeing how the watering of plants doesn't last for more than half a day or so.
But that Isn't even your biggest issue. The method of getting these supplies of water will be unavailable eventually as the city's water works off will turn off. "Just go to a lake!" you say? Nope. No lakes, no rivers and no oceans. Only the very rare 1-2 wells per map which are waaaay outside the actual playing zone/spawn and the only real other way to create a sustainable, although random way of water income is to create rain collection barrels. You'll need Nails, a hammer, a garbage plastic bag and some planks for that.
Doesn't sound too bad, right? Wrong. To create planks, you need wooden logs. To create wooden logs, you need to chop down trees... Which you essentially need an Axe for. An even moreso rare item than Trowels and nowhere does this get more annoying than when you search through countless workshops in hope for an axe and Instead get a Saw! "Cut down trees with that"! You say? Nope. Can't do that. You NEED an axe to produce any significant quantities, which comedically enough, has an ingame model of a fireaxe out of all things. No common house-hold hatchets, no making your own improvised axe, no machete or other blunt cutting weapons. You need. An Axe. To produce ANY significant amount of logs. Sure, you can get a good laugh and chop down trees by using a fork If you want to humiliate the already embarassingly stupid sense of logic programmed by the devs but that will take over 200 swings (literally and figuratively slapping a wet blanket up against a tree) but If you're playing said survival game with the promise of It being realistic, it better damn iron out the assigning of item usages and a more realistic loot palette, preferrably designed by someone who doesn't live on an deserted island in the pacific.
And as I also described earlier, In one of my playthroughs, I cleared out a huge farmland that had a gigantic harvest of Wheat/Corn in the middle of it, which I couldn't pick. No big deal there, would have been overpowered. Now what I did get frustrated on was another smaller piece of farm land, with fences around it and the ground already being dug up neatly. I cleared the remaining zombies before i eagerly grabbed my seeds and the dozens of water-filled Gardening Spray Cans I found earlier in Workshops/storages and ran out in the dug-up mounds of dirt, standing there like an idiot for minutes on end, trying to figure out just how the game wanted me to put my seeds into the ground before trying all possible combinations, visiting the game wiki and getting a big "F*ck you" finger up in my face on how you NEED a TROWEL/SHOVEL to drop seeds from your hands and into the loose dirt.
Adding on a 25+ digit of the previously 40+ houses I searched before reaching the farm, I still ended up with not finding an axe. Not finding a trowel. Not finding a shovel. Nothing. Just more nails, some glue, duct tape and a saw, endlessly taunting me In the face on just what I could have done at my small farmstead in the forest at this point Instead of running around like a complete and utter jackass, struggling to find a specific bent piece of metal so I can put down some seeds on an already processed piece of soil Instead of using my hands, other tools such as hammers that have plowing capacities with the tail, a shoe, an empty soup can, a spoon or my hands. But no, that wouldn't be according to the game logic of this "Simulator". Simply put, If you run to a nearby Workshop and don't get a Shovel/Trowel, a Fireaxe and a Saw, your playthrough already has been signed It's death warrant by none other than the developers.
And as I said, Project Zomboid is by all means, a solid game that I also happen to enjoy much personally. but If you look at the on-going 3-4+ years of development time and the current state It is in, one is fair to call it a pile of f*cking rubbish as mods made by lone people in their spare time develop features into this game so much faster than a team of 6 (discluding dozens of associates) fully paid professionals, It's downright frikking embarassing, especially considering the game Is not even 3d, so as of right now, I will unfortunately recommend everyone to avoid this title right now until the developers take the energy they do on advertising updates or explaining why they screwed up on delivering these updates in time and put that effort into making said, promised updates.
I would however, recommend to buy It on a sale.

There's also Cuphead's optimistic outlook, which is deftly woven into his characterisation - his ability to stay optimistic when literally having his soul on the line, for instance. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of these characters, to realize that they're not just fun- they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who dislike Cuphead truly ARE idiots- of course they wouldn't appreciate, for instance, the humour in the Announcer's catchphrase "This match is about to get red hot!" which itself is a cryptic reference to 1930s wrestling/boxing announcers. I'm smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Evan Skolink's genius unfolds itself on their computer monitors. What fools... how I pity them. 😂 And yes by the way, I DO have a Cuphead tattoo. And no, you cannot see it. It's for the ladies' eyes only- And even they have to demonstrate that they're within 5 IQ points of my own (preferably lower) beforehand.

Father's Island is a comedic horror game brought to us by Homegrown Games, the same developer responsible for Into the Dark: Ultimate Trash Edition and Painkiller: Resurrection; don't let the latter fool you due to the franchise name. Before you go any further, be aware that this game is made in GameGuru, and the company's prior two titles are a mangled mess of problems.
You play as a man named John Richards, who was framed for armed robbery and assault at a convenience store on Christmas Eve of 2009. He was imprisoned for 5 years after refusing to plead guilty to a crime he didn't commit, despite his face appearing on an evidence tape and his DNA being found all over the crime scene. Right before his release, a priest directed him toward an island off the coast of New England, and said that he'd find all his answers there.
To start things off, let me relay that I love B-Grade horror films; the cheesier the script and the more low budget the better, I say. While Father's Island has that corny B-Grade quality and style to it, its attrocious optimization and performance problems are its biggest hindrance. As of writing, the most recent "optimization update" was on September 27, 2016, but the game still runs between 30-45 FPS at best on a GTX 1080 and i7 6700k combo; for non-techies, that's extremely top-o-the-line gear. Also with 16GB of DDR4-3000 RAM and a decent SSD, the title still takes forever to load. These problems could be avoided entirely if the game didn't load its complete, rather large, map all at once in full detail.
On top of sub-par performance, I could not get a save file to load properly for me at all. Every time I attempted to load one, I'd wait the 2-3 minutes for the ENTIRE GAME to load again, only to be met with a green screen and subsequently a crash. The music within the title is also jarring, as it splices in and out of different tracks depending on where you're positioned. As well, the overall look of the game has a very dark, high contrast level that just makes it harder to see... and not in a pleasant, scary way.
Many of the mechanics can simply be bypassed by climbing hills or skirting around awkwardly placed fences and trees, and generally you'll just be set out to find keys anyway. Weirdly enough it seems that one key fits all in this game, so you'll spend most of your time exploring a rather bland landscape and being taken aback by sudden cutscenes that feature a "live" video of a guy laid over a scene from the game. The voice acting is pretty good in a B-Grade kinda way, and it's reminiscent of POSTAL.
I did manage to make it to one ending (out of four) within the half-hour that I spent with Father's Island, but upon loading my save for the third time only to be met with another green screen of doom, I gave up. I thought about revisiting it to try to make it through the story, but quite honestly the performance and technical issues are a complete put-off. No matter how compelling that the story may end up becoming, in good conscience I cannot recommend this game based off of its functionality... or lack thereof. I sincerely doubt we will see it fixed, given the state of Homegrown's prior two titles.

Batman - The Telltale Series is a fun ride for fans of action and storytelling, and a strong new entry in Telltale's library. Those familiar with their work will likely feel right at home, and know pretty much what they're getting into. To newcomers, as long as you aren't put off by the action and fighting in the game being based essentially around pressing specific buttons when told, you'll be treated to a solid, interactive Batman story with a good variety of characters and nice voice acting.
Graphically, I enjoy the game's style, looking like many Telltale games seem to, although more up to date, and with some appropriate thought put into the comic book aspects. Batman looks better here than in many of the movies. There's a stylized quality and a bulky realism to his suit, a human element and some coolness factor, some quintessential bat tech, and a nice combination of fluidity and strength to his movements. The scenery, while not jaw-dropping, is generally engaging and immersive, the lighting and mood making the repeated locations feel appropriately different on subsequent visits. Characters emote well and are familiar at a glance, hallmarks of good design in a game like this.
The voice acting is top notch, as is often the case with Batman, evoking everything from Catwoman's smooth yet complex nature to Gordon's gruff and overburdened sense of burgeoning command. I wouldn't say Bruce Wayne steals the show, but he carries the narrative well and I wasn't upset about the lack of Kevin Conroy. Instead of ridiculous, played-up fake gravel in his voice, as we've seen in some versions of Batman in the not too distant past, the character uses a voice modifier in his suit. The pitch on this is just right to make sense in universe and also sound appropriate to the player.
The writing, as mentioned earlier, is good. The plot progresses in an engaging way, dragging the player into a variety of messes while giving them a sense of control and moments to collect their thoughts, deviating to different subplots that all tie nicely into the big picture when their time comes. I didn't expect one of the main twists, and although it's not world-shattering, I appreciated being taken by surprise in an otherwise familiar-feeling story. The game isn't an outright origin rehash that you come to expect with franchises like this, but it does pick up early in Batman's crime-fighting career, with some villains still being introduced and established. This is done well with the pace of the game, without long expositions or flashbacks; the characters live out their vices and vendettas in real time, and you watch them degenerate or reveal their true colors. The choices you get to make, as seems to be the case in Telltale, vary in how much impact they have. Most of the same major plot points will happen either way, but after you beat the game, it may be worth either a replay or a peek via Google at some of the variations that can happen based on your choices.
The gameplay feels slightly different than the Walking Dead games I've played, overall an improvement, although there are some quirks and rough areas. Occasionally, when given a dialog choice, you might wish you had a little more time to answer, but compared to the other games, I think this one has about as good of a balance as I could reasonably expect.
When you explore an area and look for clues, there's a cool mechanic to tie multiple pieces of evidence together and look for a link. Doing this correctly allows Batman to formulate a play-by-play of what happened in a crime scene. I might have enjoyed a few more of these, and ultimately you can get by with trial and error, but it was a welcome nod to Batman's deductive prowess. Less delightful was some of the camerawork in these scenes, which, combined with the shuffling walking speed, made poking around in these areas a bit awkward. The camera seems to fight you, and its constraints and responsiveness maybe aren't the best fit for the general size and shape of the areas it's used in. This doesn't come up too often, and doesn't render the game unplayable or anything, but in a game that creates smooth immersion so well, it manages to stick out.
The combat is done slightly differently than TWD, while using the same overall system. Some changes seem to just be tweaks to Telltale's formula, others reflections of Batman's combat style. Fights incorporate a mix of WASD directions, a few targeted mouse clicks, use of the E and Q keys, and occasionally the Shift key as well. For the most part, the timing and difficulty is generous to the player. I'm not entirely sure I'm sold on the mouse use sometimes, but it wasn't so bad. There were some times something was highlighted for me to click on it, but my cursor didn't appear to be visible - I had to flail around while my time was running out until it appeared I had, by chance, hovered over the target. Generally, for whatever reason this wasn't a problem.
Sometimes, the key to be pressed is stylistically overlaid, like the E key looking like it's part of your grapple gun. While cool, this went too far a few times - I saw pauses in the fighting where I felt like I should press something, but had no options - only to then have a character's face, or something like that, move better into view, and there's a big E plastered on it. How long was that E there?? You guys know I could barely see it until the last second, right? I think I missed a handful of inputs like that, but it's hard to be too bitter. In a system like this, it's hard to balance challenge with accessibility.
Anyone who's played FPS games is probably comfortable with the Q and E keys, but unfamiliar players may find their use a bit awkward at first. Thankfully for them, instead of incorporating deaths upon failure like in TWD, this game has a sort of health meter. Pressing the prompts quickly keeps it full or even adds to it I believe, while pressing them too late will deplete it - Batman will still perform the move (which created some feedback confusion for me the first few times) but eventually, if the meter bottoms out, you'll lose. I suppose at the end of the day, the game is fairly easy, as I never died, but I do prefer this to a cheap death.
Speaking of cheap deaths, I'm espectially happy that the "Tap key rapidly" sequences are nowhere to be found this time around. I suppose they do make a little more sense in TWD, where desperate strength would be required when grabbed by a zombie, but I've always hated when this mechanic gets shoehorned into games. I hope this is a change we continue to see in future Telltale games, but that's partly just my own taste.
Lastly, I feel I should mention a couple of performance issues. The game has options when you launch it for running in Windows 7 or in 8+, so users of older systems should hopefully be accomodated there. My own experience wasn't perfect. Occasionally the game exhibited a bit of what seemed like loading lag - not when loading a new area, but when switching to a new camera angle within an area. It wasn't constant, and over time it tended to be more minimal and tolerable, but I'm confident my specs are good enough to play this game, so it raised my eyebrow several times. Also, I had two mysterious crashes while playing this game - one a mere few seconds into the first chapter, and the other during the final fight of the last chapter. Ironic, and slightly frustrating timing, but not unforgivable. Buyer beware that you may notice a few things like this, but in my case I was still able to thoroughly enjoy the game without much real setback.
All in all, I would definitely recommend the game to big Batman or Telltale fans. To anyone else, it's worth keeping an eye on. Give it a try if you want something engaging and story-heavy, and won't feel cheated by the low dollar-to-hour ratio. I suppose there is some replay value for some people, but most, myself included, are probably good with the one-and-done.

I realize the game is a little dated, being from 2011 and all. It has been rotting in my library since then, but today I finally had time to play it.
This game is alright. It's a short story about a boy wandering through a forest and being victim of all kinds of bad stuff.
He also solves puzzles along the way, which never become much more interesting than pushing a block onto a switch. So it's basically the first test chamber of Portal 1, drawn out over multiple hours of gameplay.
The game looks pretty nice, with the dynamic lighting and all. It stands out in its own way. The enemies and surroundings are subtly animated, but that's about it. It's mostly a black and white flickering experience.
The puzzle gameplay is okay-ish. There are a lot of non-intuitive puzzles, which means that you will die on your first try. This trial-and-error gameplay is just game length padding. Were these puzzles designed in a better way, then the game would be twice as short and twice as exciting.
The rest of the game is platforming. This is also okay, not great. The character feels sluggish, but none of the platforming segments require good timing or mechanics anyway. It's hard to say whether this is on purpose to hide the poor controls, but it occasionally looks that way.
What bothers me greatly is how incompetent the character is. You can literally pull a minecart towards you on a flat road and die that way. You can't fall very far, which is a very strange mechanic for a platformer. If they were going for realism, then...they just didn't do a good job.
In terms of art and uniqueness and whatever, yeah, there are some elements of that in here as well. It feels too forced to me, but I'm sure some people like this sort of approach.
In conclusion, I wish there was a meh option instead of a Yes/No recommendation. Sure, I'll recommend this for when it's 75% off during a sale, but please don't buy it at full price. For the less than 3 hours of puzzle platformer gameplay, you can spend your 10 bucks in infinitely better ways.

Comunication, teamwork and SNIPER RIFLES! ok, i'll leave out the last one if I can be a useful supporter...

Ya know, Im was sitting here with an extra dollar on my account, and I wanted to blow it on some random indie game. So I am looking at reviews for all these other games and most of them are the usual stuff. Okay, but many bugs here. Doesn't crash but no real plot. I struggled to see the point of spending my single dollar on these games, and then I saw it. Blood and Bacon. The name caught my eye from the start. I clicked on it and was immediately shocked to see an 'Overwhelmingly Positive' score from steam. I read some of these previous reviews and figured that this game truly was what I should spend my single dollar on. I purchased the game and quickly installed it. I started the game totally unknowing the most plot-filled, graphically-intense, jaw-dropping game had come into my steam library since Half-Life 2. I hastily jumped into a single player game to really understand the reviews I had read minutes earlier. I picked up my first pistol and went outside this PC master-race level barn. Pigs spawned and I mowed them all down like the pigs they were. I felt good. I went on and grabbed my AK47 and mowed down more. Some pigs exploded. I started crying tears of joy as my dreams of a plot-filled, $1 indie game were fufilled. I played and played. My mother stopped bringing me food in hopes that I would come upstairs and see the daylight for once. But no. I must replay this endlessly fufilling storyline to its fullest. I grew tired of my other games. Only Blood and Bacon would suffice for my gaming needs. Day after day, night after night I slaughtered pigs like my farming friend told me, but my mom had had enough. She took my steam account and changed the password to a string of text so large nobody could remember it. She told steam support that she was sure someone was going to get into my account, so they wouldn't beleive me when I tried to get it back. I am forced to write this review on my other, less used account. 10/10 would probably play again.

It is challenging to write a recommendation for 'The Beginner's Guide' without spoiling the experience. What initially appears as an unassuming guided tour of another person's work turns out to be a clever short story which explores the relationship between an artist and their audience. While this is indeed a short and linear game, lasting about 90 minutes, it has to be experienced as such. I do not recommend watching a Let's Play of it—as tempting as it is—as the very experience of playing the game is meaningful. By following in the narrator's footsteps and thinking about both his and your own experiences in the context of the game itself, you will truly appreciate what Davey Wreden is getting at here. Like Marshall McLuhan said, "the Medium is the Message".

This was the first game I played in the series of The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, by Frogwares and Focus. I was skeptical at first, because I originally bought it in a $5 bin at a game store (and this was just after it had been released). I can only guess as to why this is, but after playing the game, it would be a very educated guess. Since then, I have voraciously consumed the series, and any games developed by Frogwares. I had falsely believed that a Russian developer could not do the character justice, and I apologize to them for this prejudgement. My review is not all blind praise, however. Some of the puzzles are very difficult, which is normally preferred in a puzzle game, but many of the puzzles do not even state the objective. I found myself spending nearly 45 minutes trying to figure out what was being asked of me as I placed blocks on a lockbox in a childrens classroom. Mostly, these puzzles give an overwhelming sense of satisfaction once you've mastered the objective. The story left nothing to be desired, true to form for the great detective, and although the visuals are less than Next-Generation, I found myself enraptured by the characters and deduction involved. I sincerely felt as Dr. John Watson feels: compelled to follow and trust Holmes, and severely angered when it seems he betrays my trust. Ever since I first played Maniac Mansion, I have been a fan of Point-and-Click adventures, but this series turned me into a full fledged fanatic. If you crave good storylines, enjoy Sherlock Holmes (who doesn't?), or just Love puzzle games, you can't go wrong with The Testament of Sherlock Holmes. Enjoy!

Well, I've played through it now, and overall i'm pleased with my purchase.
It's not perfect, but then again what game ever is perfect?
Are there things I don't like about it?
Sure, the lighting isn't what I would choose, it's far too "orangey" and makes many of the entities look grainy to me. It's a little too "open" in parts, there's quite a few areas where you can bye-pass mechanics completely, "oh I need a key do I?" .. "nah i'll climb this hill here instead" .. etc. To me in a story driven game your character needs to be directed by the story and the map a little more, sometimes it's not clear where to go and you can end up going around in circles. The voice acting is a little over acted for my liking, and the Chroma key work just doesn't blend with the game, a video of a real person just seems out of place with the art style of the game in my opinion. My biggest bug-bear is the keys, keys, keys scenario, I see it a lot with indie games, the developers get it stuck in their head that every door needs a key that you have to find, many of the keys could be replaced with a variety of simple puzzles, the "key" here is variation, nobody likes doing the same thing over and over and to be honest I found myself saying "oh don't tell me, I need another key!".
But none of that detracts from the fact that it is a good game, and when you factor in the software used to make it, a very good game indeed. You can tell that Ertlov has put his heart into the work behind the scenes, the story is very creative, the placement of objects and terrain is very well done, and it's obvious a lot of care and attention to detail has been made here.
So, in short: While I feel that the lighting downgrades the look a little, and it could do with a few invisible walls and such to guide the players around, as well as more variation to the puzzles (ie less keys), I still find it a very pleasant, and to be frank impressive game, it's a thumbs up from me!

A very disappointing follow-up to the Stanley Parable. The description warns you that this has "no traditional mechanics, goals or objectives" but TBG is so utterly without meaningful interactivity that even that warning isn't strong enough. The only thing differentiating this experience from a film is that you can look around, but there's nothing to see. All you get is a dull capital-A Art presentation of a message about how you shouldn't attempt to see meaning put into art - which is an interesting self-negating premise, in principle. Unfortunately, as a player forced to hold the forward key and nothing else for 90 minutes, the message feels more like an extended middle finger directed at it's audience than anything profound.

In terms of the options available to build your city, Tropico 5 fares worse than the previous versions. First, there is that fact that you have to alternate between two islands that keep the previous developments (i.e. you keep the same two islands for the duration of different stages in the campaign). Second, the various industries follow a timeline (e.g. the tourism industry is not unlocked until you reach Cold War era, if I'm not mistaken). These two factors basically force your island to develop on a specific path. Natural resources (logging and mining) to light industry to heavy industry or tourism then advanced stages of the industry and toursim. This makes logical sense in the real world but this is a video game. It doesn't have to make sense. It would have been better to letter the player develop the island anyway they wanted from the beginning.
I still recommend just because I am a fan of the previous Tropicos 3 & 4.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

Firstly, the combat is annoying and clunky, especially when all the enemies are darting around erratically making it infuriating to try and hit them; and when you do eventually land a shot, the enemy (in the first zone, less than 20 minutes in) is totally immune to your weapon, and firing back homing explosives which are very had to evade or shoot down. Secondly, the crafting is on a tech tree, requiring spelunking with useless tier-1 equipment to try to unlock tier-2 and so on, sadly, the depth you can reach is restricted, and a player will often never find anything before death forces them to their respawn point. The crafting is clunky and difficult, the UI is a battle to navigate with almost no quick access to the comically named "hotbar", and the tutorial is laughably incomplete. I bought this game believing I was buying into alpha software, and it felt like that, in mid-beta. The gameplay feels confused, torn between rogue-lite and Terraria-esque sidescrolling sandbox.
Enemy variety is good, and the art style is unique and appealing, but the gameplay needs severe work. Avoid buying this title for full price, if you must buy it at all.

Well, that game was strange.
Graphics: Probably the best thing about this game. It's very pretty to look at, the colors are quite vibrant and interesting. The problem is that everything is so colorful that it's hard to tell what's part of the background and what you can walk/click on, which unfortunately is the main game mechanic.
Story: Uhh...basically you're a bug trying to bring all the other bugs back to life or save their buddies. Yeah it's a little weird.
Gameplay: REALLY BORING AND SLOW...I guess you could use this game to relax before you go to sleep? It certainly made me tired. You play as a bug that moves ridiculously slowly across branches that are terribly hard to distinguish from the rest of the background. This is basically a point and click game in which you click on various objects that you see labeled on the left side of your screen until you've gotten all of them. Each level has one or two puzzles that are usually knockoffs of pretty popular puzzles (matching games, checkers, and finally a rubix cube type puzzle which I couldn't complete in 30 minutes so I gave up). That final puzzle is absolutely ridiculous, so unfortunately I couldn't beat the game because I got sick of pressing buttons to no avail.
Other than that, the music is kinda nice. It's very ambient, and gets annoying after you've heard it for a while, which is usually what happens given how slow the bug moves. I got this game for 20 cents and I'd say it's worth about that. I could see this being a free online flash game. There are only 5 levels, I (almost) beat it in a little over an hour. Get it if you like lots of bugs and looking at pretty pictures and moving really slowly. 3/10

A great game for anyone who loves classic 2D animation, especially fans of early 1920s/1930s animation. With some heavy inspirations from Fleischer Betty Boop, Superman, and Popeye, Ub Iwerks Flip the Frog and Oswald the Lucky rabbit, and early Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies like the Cookie Carnival, Flowers and Trees, the Skeleton Dance, and of course Mickey Mouse, along with countless other nods and references to that era and style, which is captured PERFECTLY with smooth hand drawn animation (actual pencil and paper!!) for each and every character and boss encounter.
The gameplay is pretty much Contra/Metal Slug/Mega Man, there are a handful of fun sidescrolling platform levels, but the game is mostly boss battles that have multiple stages with creative patterns and forms. Some of them platforming, others shoot-em-up air battles, both work well enough once you get the hang of the controls and mechanics. It's not just repetetive shooting either, bosses and objects will have you using parry attacks and dash dodges that keep you on your toes. It's fun, but it is tough! With some great bullethell moments too, dodging a myriad of projectiles bouncing all over the screen. The difficulty is fair though, every boss attack gives you fair warning and an opportunity to react, it's just very demanding of the player, and you'll have to have proper execution to defeat each and every creative foe you come across. It can get frustrating though, and some bosses you'll have to replay nearly a dozen times before you get the hang of them, that is if you don't exhaust yourself... And I can't recommend that type of game for everyone, it's very demanding. Though if you like old school Arcade/NES run and gun games (like Ghosts and Goblins, but much less cruel!), you'll love this game.
But, it's nothing revolutionary, not gameplay-wise at least. It's competent, it's fun, but it doesn't change the game, it just does something comfortable and familiar, and does it well. It's somewhat analogous to Donkey Kong Country, a game that didn't play all that different than prior platformers, but the aesthetics and art created such a living and vivid world that it was well worth the price of admission. Cuphead is similar, it doesn't rely on the brilliant charming art style alone, it has a good gameplay structure holding it up, but let's get real here, if you're getting this game, you're getting it for the animation, it's a loveletter, and it's the star attraction, just like CGI was the star attraction for Donkey Kong Country back in 1994. It's worth it, a solid game, and a beautiful looking one too.

I have mixed feelings about this title...
was it bad? no, definitely not...
was it good? ... hmm...
ok, I liked the story, although a bit too far fetched and somehow clumsy in places, it definitely had the right ingredients and a few well placed plot twists to keep me interested throughout the game... I also liked the puzzles - none of them were impossible to pass and at least some were actually pretty amusing :) ... though in particular, I found the recurring "lockpick" puzzle unnecessary - as simple as it was, I found it more of a nuisance than a pleasant deviation from the storytelling... I couldn't help comparing that to an excellently designed lockpick puzzle from "Still Life" and even the purely manual lockpicking from the new "Fallout" games was more believable than that in TTOSH... I didn't like the "chemistry" puzzles too much either...
what I liked most, I think, apart, of course, from the more sophisticated locking mechanisms on various containers as mentioned above, were the deduction puzzles. even though you could theoretically solve them by randomly ticking options, they still actually made you think about how to connect all pieces together...
the graphics was pleasant, nothing too fancy but nothing particularly bad either - still looking pretty good though maybe not very sophisticated given its 2012 release date... I liked it...
what I didn't like then .... the linearity... yeah, I know, it's neither the first not the last point-and-click that does that but there were a few moments where being very artificially bound to the one location you're in at the moment was particularly jarring...
the whole "story read by the creepily-modelled kids in the attic" arc - what purpose did that serve?...
the glitches (the game crashed on me more than a couple of times in just less than 20 hours of gameplay and, in one place, almost blocking me from playing further), the simplistic inventory-based puzzles, the place where you played _a_ _dog_ ...
all in all, yeah, as I said, I did enjoy this game, it did have a few nice moments and amusing puzzles... but would I recommend it? no, not really .... I don't know... maybe I set my expectations too high but I just simply don't feel it's up to the hopes other recommendations here suggested... and given its price, and provided you haven't already played it, I really think another sleuth-themed title - the "LA Noire" is a much better bargain ... (of course, that's a pretty different kind of beast)

Excuse the quotation marks in this review. They're necessary as my choice of words is often not precise enough to be fair.
This is a short experience that can be completed in about an hour and a half or less. It's not quite a "game", nor is it really an "interactive story". It's merely a "story" that unfolds from your perspective, at your own pace. To summarize the story would eliminate the point of it. Unlike some other "story" games, this one is narrated by the game's creator, as himself, and you play as yourself, being guided through it by the creator.
It suffices to say that it plays with your expectations a bit. You may think you've pinned down the particular subversion that it's approaching, but it'll very likely surprise you. Also, I should say that it's very hard to tell if this is entirely sincere and "true", entirely an artistic piece, or somewhere in the middle.
In any case, this is worthwhile. It's pretty powerful. I think the standard price (at the time of writing) of $10 is a bit pricey for what you come to expect of Steam's price/content ratio, but it's probably worth it. It's defnitely worth a sale price. (I got it for $5.99.)

The good well it has all the good bits you would come to expect from a Telltale title. The artstyle still has the same good old comic look. The bad well first off it feels rushed from the episode intro text all the way down to the god awful animation bugs. Almost everything feels scripted here, it's kinda hard to explain... it's as if none of the choices have that Telltale charm to it, even though they are sometimes pretty good choices. I can say though not once did I have an emotional connection to anyone or anything. Some episodes felt super rushed, it felt as if they got half way in and said what the ♥♥♥♥ are we doing repeating the same story everyone has seen a million times with tiny differences. While the performance has improved since launch, stuttering still exists and oh my god the bugs... the amount of bugs. Faces turning 360 like satan himself took over Bruce Wayne, voices not sycing up to lips, choices made don't alter certain things... just alot of bugs I wouldn't say game breaking bugs but immersion breaking for sure.
This game has a solid template and clearly they set out to do something different with the Batman IP but they ruined it. I wouldn't say it wasn't enjoyable but this is definitely the last game in the Telltales series I would recommend to anyone and that's coming from a DC Comics fan.

After speaking with LadyAijou extensively regarding Edge of Space. I would like to update my review with some further information.
The reason advancement isn't working is right before the steam summer sale most of the NPC code was gutted out for revamping, very similar to what Rust is doing. The team at Handyman Studios was not expecting to get featured in the flash sale and ended up receiving more orders during that eight hour period than they had gotten in their previous best week during the 2-1 sale.
The development team consists of two people, one of which had a system failure right after the change to the NPC code was implemented, which meant that what should have been fixed either right before or right after the flash sale was unable to be fixed. The chests dropping from nests is related to this issue because the nest/event has to spawn the appropriate creatures and then track that they have been killed, which with the changes to the NPC code is not working properly, so you're "failing" every nest/event you start.
This means that yes, at this particular moment it is not possible to progress past the first biome. With full aluminum armor you can make it pretty much to the end of the first biome, but beyond that is not possible. I will be leaving my review as "not recommended" for the time being due to the non-available features, but will hold my final opinion in reserve until such time as the current mess is cleaned up.

Unfortunately, once the sheen of this massive world begins to wear thin, you're left with an empty husk of a game. The story, missions, and characters are generic 80s Action Nonsense -- lots of spectacle, but lacking the razor sharp writing and subversive wit that makes GTA tick. I quickly dropped the campaign, and didn't miss it for a moment.
Speaking of GTA -- because island dressing aside, this game's DNA is obvious -- Avalanche could learn a thing or two about worldbuilding from Rockstar. There are no minigames to discover, no cool NPC behavior to observe, no insane radio hosts to listen to, no far flung jungle isles teeming with tropical fauna. As beautiful as this world is, it just feels dead.
So...why do I recommend it? Because this game is capable of some incredible moments you just won't find elsewhere, courtesy of its vast scale:
At one point I decided to set out across the entire game map -- heading up from the shore over the mountains and back down to the other side. About 20 minutes(!) and multiple vechiles later I found myself climbing a snowy peak on a winding road to who-knows-where, as the sun sunk low and dusk approached. And then, in a moment of distraction, I sent my jeep careening over a hairpin turn down into the snowy abyss. Boom.
At this point I had little choice but to walk (okay, hookshot/para-glide) towards the nearest highway to 'borrow' a new ride.
Except...I couldn't. I suddenly found myself miles -- many miles -- from anywhere.
A few minutes later I'd grappled up to the tallest peak in sight. From there I could look down at the island chain I'd started my journey from. See familiar islets, and the shimmering city lights in the night air. It dawned on me that walking back there would literally take hours. So many games focus on making the player feel larger than life, but suddenly I felt small.
Turning away, I looked towards the far side of the island. An unfamiliar landscape beckoned. The glow of unknown cities and towns, impossibly distant, blinked up at me...and one set of lights not so impossibly distant.
This was no town, not in this wilderness -- a military base perhaps? I wasn't particularly well armed at the moment...but what choice did I have?
With a running leap, I parachuted into the abyss. Towards the lights.
I hope they have a jeep.
(7/10 -- if you like campaigns, subtract 2 -- if you love sandbox exploration, increase by 1)

Review: Play the hardest mode on your first run (just what I did) to get an idea of how brutal this game is. I survived for under 3 minutes and then got mauled by a wolf. This game is also the most realistic survival game out there that I could find believe it or not. No base building, no no no, you gotta make-do with the crap that's already there. It is an amazing experience too.
My story/experience with the game: On the hardest difficulty, I got to a point where i was missing two things. Food and heat. I needed tinder, but going outside to retrieve some was suicide. I'd get frostbite and die, probably not even returning with proper tinder, as it wasn't too common where i was sheltered at. I also needed food, but i had to go outside for that too. I was too cold to risk finding another settlement in an attempt to find nourishment there (which may not even be there anyways). I finally got to the point where I couldn't wait any longer, and ventured outside. About a minute after attempting to gather tinder (and failing) I saw a deer get murdered by a wolf. I slowly crawled up the slope it had been slain on and the wolf was gnawing on the carcass. I waited around ten minutes for the thing to mosey off, but it didn't. So i lit my only flare and tossed it at the beast. It ran and I went to grab some meat off the carcass, which would've taken around an hour. I tried to light a fire, but alas, still missing the materials to do such. So I simply took the risk and began harvesting meat. I stopped in the middle of it because I had just realized if I kept going I would freeze to death. I don't know how long I was going at it, but when I stood up I swear I couldn't even feel my legs. I saw my shelter and began to stumble down the hill towards it. It was about 75 feet away, but it felt like a kilometer having to drag myself to it. I kept stumbling backwards, left and right and falling over uncontrollably. By the time I made it to the door I couldn't feel anything, yet I knew it was all over. I knew my time was coming very soon. I got up to open the door, but stumbled backwards, fell over to my right, and struggled to even grip the knob correctly before getting in, taking another minute away from my shortened time left. I finally got in, pulled out my lantern, and set it up on a bench in hopes that it would warm the room enough to help me recover. I struggled to reach the fireplace, and opened it. I was going to attempt to start a fire, but then i remembered I had no tinder. I scrambled around for one last option, and finally thought to make a torch. I struggled to piece it together, but once I did, I squatted in a corner and hoped that the lord would help me or a miracle would happen, because I didn't think much else could save me now. I still kept getting colder and colder, and at that moment I thought "No, this can't be the end, I can't die in the middle of nowhere in some cabin! I need to find help and I need to get back home! What about my family?? I've got to do something!!!" and something I did. I threw myself around the tiny shack furiously, in a fit of rage and in hopes of generating some warmth. I thrashed around inside the building for like fifteen (realtime) minutes, before the world began to start fading in and out of darkness. I finally calmed down, got back into my corner, and looked around the room. I didn't think much. The only thing I could do at that point was reflect on my life. I shed a tear (an actual tear) as I thought about all of the things I could of done better. I regretted so much. I wished I would've paid more attention to my children, wished I would've respected them more, and most of all, wished I would've been able to give a final "goodbye"...
The light of the room slowly faded into darkness, and the only thing I could see for a solid thirty seconds was the fire emitting from my torch. Everything became calm, and I started to feel peace flushing through my veins. I stared at the fire...It was...pretty...the light guided me....and I couldn't look away....
"You faded into the long dark..."

My Husband actually recommended this game to me, he saw that it was about Canada, and created by a Canadian and rightly thought - my Canadian wife might like this game!  I've put in about 10 hours so far, and I've enjoyed them all.  So far I've only played on the newbie level, I was just trying to get a good feel for the game and what I'd be in for.
Some quick things that stood out for me are:
* The attention to sounds; The crunch of the snow, the soft woosh sound of nylon clothing rubbing when you walk, the sound of the wind when it picks up (sounds so cold..), and the moment when the fire takes and picks up intensity (I can almost imagine the smell of the wood burning).  It makes the game way more real for me, maybe it's because these are things I recall from living in Canada during the winter months - dunno, but I love it and hope they continue to add more.
* It's not too intense; so many games right now are all about scarying you out of  your chair, or zombies.  This game is just quiet, and alone.. it's a nice change.  It reminds me of being a kid outside in the snow and that feeling of alone - and that building fear of being really alone - and wondering what might happen. I dunno, again - this might just be me - but it's a great change from all the running and constant death and fighting.
I hope this game continues to develop, I can't wait to see more new stuff and explore further.  Highly recommend, one of the best games I've purchased in 2015! :)

Evolve is a extremely nice looking asymmetrical game where four hunters tangle with an apex predator.
You have your average DPS, a medic/sniper class, a support class who can call down artillery and turn teammates invulnerable or invisible, and a class dedicated to trapping the monster in a dome arena so both teams can engage in battle.
As of the Big Alpha, it only has 1 gamemode and a kind of grindy progression system, but as long as the devs keep working hard, this game will have a heap of new content.
It's currently very fun for a decent amount of time, but it has a pretty hefty price tag. Grab this during a sale, unless your pockets are full of money.
