I picked this game up while it was originally in Early Access and since then I've found myself coming back to it time and time again. The atmospheric music and enthralling narrative stories I feel are what make this rouge-like game quite amazing. Of course, like many other Rouge-Like games it can be quite honestly one of the most frustrating experiences at the same time as you die again and again trying to learn the mechanics or a series of unfortunate events ruin what would've been an otherwise perfect playthrough.  The game is quite hard, and as far as I've seen it makes an effort to tell you so, and even gives some small tidbits of advice here and there to help the player out.
Of course, this can be offset by using the manual save option, that while does lock you out from getting one particular achievement, gives you the security of being able to learn from your mistakes and eventually understand the way the system works.
Another downside side is that a lot of the narrative stories lose some of their impact after you work through them once, but there are a great number of them and with the Zubmarnier Expansion pack, a whole new region of stories and environments open up to explore to slightly lessen the impact of repeating the ame stories.
I should note that the game's universe is also connected to another game, Fallen London, which is a browser based game with the same tyle of narrative stories, but different playstyle entirely. As a bonus you can connect your accounts between the two games for some small bonuses and extra stories in Sunless Sea.
Ultimately, I would say that Sunless Sea is a great game for those that love atmospheric worlds and deeply interesting stories, but if you find yourself easily bored with repeating stories to advance or you find yourself easily frustrated with unforgiving difficulty and certain elements of random chance then I'd recommend getting it on a sale price or letting this one go past your radar.

I've played city building games since the original Sim City and I'm a big fan of survival/sandbox/crafting games, so this seemed like it'd be the kind of game I'd love.
Sadly, Banished has the bare bones feel of an early access game that has been abandoned. In most games of this type, I usually feel like I've barely scratched the surface of what's on offer after 20 hours or so. In Banished, I felt I'd experienced everything after an hour and the novelty was already wearing off. I had already constructed every building type possible. There is no building progression apart from upgrading wooden houses to stone ones. All that was left was to unlock different crops and animals at the randomised trader who visits once per year, which didn't seem compelling enough to keep me going.
I am OK with simplicity as long as a game remains fun, but beyond the initial colony construction there's just too little of interest to do in Banished. There is no possibility of cultural or technological advance, no politics, no contact or conflict with other groups, nothing to aim for besides building more of the same stuff and increasing your population. If this was an early access game I'd say the scope for development was huge, but it's not and as things stand it's shallow compared to the competition. You can pick up an older classic like Anno 1404 - with rich diplomacy, upgrades, trade, seafaring etc - for almost nothing these days.
My biggest issue given the relatively intimate scale of the game was that I felt no emotional investment. It seems like a wasted opportunity, given how fascinating the intrigue of interpersonal relationships in a new community like this could be. Play Rimworld to experience a masterclass in this. In Banished, I felt no connection to or compassion for my colonists. They're crude identikit stick figures with no personality and little to set them apart or make you care. They all switch jobs constantly depending on who lives closest, with only a basic 'education' stat affecting their efficiency at anything from teaching to stonecutting - good in terms of optimal pathing I suppose, but totally immersion breaking. The colonist AI is woeful, by the way.
I have recently had a blast with games like the aforementioned Rimworld and This War Of Mine, in which characters are full of personality and incredible and varied interpersonal stories constantly unfold that really draw you in and made you care. Losing one of my people in either of those games elicited a genuine emotional response. By comparison, Banished felt incredibly hollow. Yet another stonecutter has been crushed by a rock? No worries, another interchangeable faceless drone has automatically taken their place in the pit!
The graphics are what I'd expect from a small indie developer. Sadly, Banished has a very clunky modular UI that deviates needlessly from established genre conventions. For example, speeding up and slowing the passage of time - which are easy to locate, always visible and quickly altered with single keystrokes in similar games - are in submenus here, requiring extra clicks or 2 hotkeys to get to. I could live with this if the game was perfect otherwise, but it's symptomatic of deeper issues.
Other reviews complain that starvation is too hard to counter, but I found I had no problem as it was easy to feed the colony through the winter by assigning plenty of colonists to fishing.
I can see how some people could get into a relaxed, zenlike state whilst playing this and might appreciate its simplicity and lack of progression. However, I feel like I already have plenty of other better games in my library which accomplish that. I'd say if you love building games and want any kind of depth or incentive to persevere, look elsewhere. Or do what I do and try it on sale - it's only a 300Mb download, so it's quick to give it a shot.

Cuphead is a great game, simply put. That being said, I think it does have its drawbacks and problems.
For one, the game is relatively short. Depending on how much time you have on your hands and how "good" you are at games like this, it shouldn't take more than a week to beat it. This is remedied by the fact that its difficulty and replayability pads out the game's length. Plus, its cost of $19.99 USD is pretty fair.

Secondly, despite its positive effect on padding out game length, I have had issues with the game's difficulty. Most times it was completely fair, but there have been times where you question how you were supposed to dodge a projectile or attack. It is a difficult game and you WILL have a hard time beating it. So, keep that in mind as you play it.
Besides that, the game is a beautiful experience with art, music and aesthetics that are pleasing on so many levels. The customization option is also great in giving players a choice that suits their play styles. Ultimately, I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes a challenge and enjoys the appeal of the 1930's style of cartoons.

If you wanna play a Batman game, either go buy Batman:Arkham City or Arkham Knight. While I can't vouch for the latter as much as I can for the former, I can say that you will enjoy those two far more than the Telltale take on the Caped Crusader.
If you wanna play a Telltale game and you are either A)A fan of their work or B) A newcomer coming to see what the fuss is about, I would recommend passing this one over and moving on to one of their other works and if you're a newcomer, I would recommend checking out Walking Dead Season 1 and the Wolf Among Us over this one.
While I can applaud Telltale for doing something new with the Batman formula and tweaking characters to better flow within their narrative. That however is one of the few pros I can think of for this story, while the list of cons seems to grow larger as I dwell on it.
Dull choices, poor voice acting on several characters, the janky animation on some of the models can be jarring, most action sequences are bland and over in a handful of prompts, the big twist coming much sooner than it needed to and a very unmemorable chapter 4 and 2 are some of the bigger problems I had diffuclty swallowing. The largest gripe I had with it had to deal with Telltale's strange desire to keep me playing as Bruce Wayne. Despite being called "Batman-The Telltale Series",  the majority of your playtime will be spent as Bruce and that amount of time will be spent in some of the most boring and unfun parts of the narrative, in fact most of the most boring and one-sided choices in the game will be made as Bruce. While I admire Telltale's attempt at making Bruce more than a typical facade for the cape crusader, the way they handle it fumbles the experience and just made me dread the segments were I had to play as him.
Just pass over this one guys. Its not worth your 8 hours of playtime and you can get your batman fix at a cheaper price and a better quality with Arkham series.

Picture a hybrid of Far Cry and Grand Theft Auto, but on a vastly larger scale. Then add on one of the greatest weapons/tools ever -- JC2's inimitable hookshot. And away we go!
Unfortunately, once the sheen of this massive world begins to wear thin, you're left with an empty husk of a game. The story, missions, and characters are generic 80s Action Nonsense -- lots of spectacle, but lacking the razor sharp writing and subversive wit that makes GTA tick. I quickly dropped the campaign, and didn't miss it for a moment.
Speaking of GTA -- because island dressing aside, this game's DNA is obvious -- Avalanche could learn a thing or two about worldbuilding from Rockstar. There are no minigames to discover, no cool NPC behavior to observe, no insane radio hosts to listen to, no far flung jungle isles teeming with tropical fauna. As beautiful as this world is, it just feels dead.
So...why do I recommend it? Because this game is capable of some incredible moments you just won't find elsewhere, courtesy of its vast scale:
At one point I decided to set out across the entire game map -- heading up from the shore over the mountains and back down to the other side. About 20 minutes(!) and multiple vechiles later I found myself climbing a snowy peak on a winding road to who-knows-where, as the sun sunk low and dusk approached. And then, in a moment of distraction, I sent my jeep careening over a hairpin turn down into the snowy abyss. Boom.
At this point I had little choice but to walk (okay, hookshot/para-glide) towards the nearest highway to 'borrow' a new ride.
Except...I couldn't. I suddenly found myself miles -- many miles -- from anywhere.
A few minutes later I'd grappled up to the tallest peak in sight. From there I could look down at the island chain I'd started my journey from. See familiar islets, and the shimmering city lights in the night air. It dawned on me that walking back there would literally take hours. So many games focus on making the player feel larger than life, but suddenly I felt small.
Turning away, I looked towards the far side of the island. An unfamiliar landscape beckoned. The glow of unknown cities and towns, impossibly distant, blinked up at me...and one set of lights not so impossibly distant.
This was no town, not in this wilderness -- a military base perhaps? I wasn't particularly well armed at the moment...but what choice did I have?
With a running leap, I parachuted into the abyss. Towards the lights.
I hope they have a jeep.
(7/10 -- if you like campaigns, subtract 2 -- if you love sandbox exploration, increase by 1)

A nice update from the previous titles in the series, this one new graphics and mechanics to make the experience new again. The campaign itself is very enjoyable as it takes place over several ages where you begin in the colonial time and progress to new periods as the campaign progresses.
Some of the new mechanics involve the economy, as you can now select specific commodities to import and export, granting you the ability to buy low and sell high, while also allowing you to target industries you'd normally lack resources to develop. Other changes also include military buildings also producing different kings of military units (e.g., Army Bases result in 3 tanks per base), which makes military expansion more strategic compared to the previous interations.
Also with this version is the inclusion of Online Multiplayer, which unfortunately, I have not been able to participate in.
Should you buy?
-----------------------------
Very much so. This is a fun macro-oriented city builder that provides an enjoyable experience. If you are a person who is compelled to buy DLC, then I suggest waiting for sales or special editions that bundle all the DLC together.

Evolve is a perfect example of a game with a few great ideas that's ultimately bogged down by the difficulty of realizing them. That is to say, 99 games out of 100, it will not even be a contest. In the rare case when a four-man coordinated team is as good as the monster, the game shines really well. The problem is that it is so often a one-sided game, and there is no significant gameplay changes for each phase; run away until you're level 2 fully armored or level 3, then attack at the Power Grid until one side is dead.
I say all of this while acknowledging that the game has a significant avenue of potential change. The core concepts, however, will not.  Evolve, much like Titanfall, has a lot of cool concepts about it, but will inevitably turn into a grinding-stone of hide-and-seek. The metagame will make everything ten times worse.
All in all, public play is doomed. Nobody will ever be coordinated with random strangers enough to be competitive with even a mediocre monster player. Private/competitive play might hold some promise, but that's a pretty slim, masochistic range of viability for a full-price title.

Morphopolis is a game of transforming into a higher being. An art game at its core Morphopolis tells the tale of a caterpillar who transforms into the insect god. Since this is an art game the meaning of it can differ from person to person. I interpreted it as the rags to riches tale of a business, as you go further up the food chain the puzzles get longer and larger which can relate to financial problems from being a start up to being a corporation.
As you ascend the food chain you are greeted by a very smooth and calming song which complements the artistic coloring of the scenery. While the animations and controls were a bit funky at times I found them to be only slightly detracting from the overall experience.
With the colorful scenery and the swell music playing I found it hard to figure out what I was doing and why I was doing it. All I knew was that there were puzzles to be solved and levels to progress. Thankfully while searching for everything I needed to get to the next step, whenever I would not know what to do, the help button saved me from going into a frustration based rage.
Like many puzzle games before it, the Help button only shows one thing hidden in the scene or one thing you have to click on to get the mission from. Unlike many other games you cannot abuse the help button. If you need help the game will show you one thing in the scene that is needed to continue and then it goes on cooldown for the next 30 seconds.
While the help button is present while on the scavenger hunt portion of the game, the puzzle part does not include a help button. For two of the puzzles I had to read the walkthrough to simply understand what I needed to do. Once I figured out what to do the puzzles still possessed a challenge. Though some puzzles are drop dead easy and others are fairly hard, I got through each of them in under five minutes.
Overall, enjoyed playing through Morphopolis and I recommend it to any gamer who likes to play puzzle games, scavenger hunt games, and art games. While I know this game isn't for everybody I recommend giving it a try for the overall gametime is only about an hour.
My price tag for this game is a solid $7.00, the music and the scenery were enough to carry the game through the occasional slow part and it was not very difficult overall making this game a pleasurable game to play when you have an hour to kill. While this game does not possess a lot of replay value, it is worth it for the single play through.
Score: 68/100

I've played city building games since the original Sim City and I'm a big fan of survival/sandbox/crafting games, so this seemed like it'd be the kind of game I'd love.
Sadly, Banished has the bare bones feel of an early access game that has been abandoned. In most games of this type, I usually feel like I've barely scratched the surface of what's on offer after 20 hours or so. In Banished, I felt I'd experienced everything after an hour and the novelty was already wearing off. I had already constructed every building type possible. There is no building progression apart from upgrading wooden houses to stone ones. All that was left was to unlock different crops and animals at the randomised trader who visits once per year, which didn't seem compelling enough to keep me going.
I am OK with simplicity as long as a game remains fun, but beyond the initial colony construction there's just too little of interest to do in Banished. There is no possibility of cultural or technological advance, no politics, no contact or conflict with other groups, nothing to aim for besides building more of the same stuff and increasing your population. If this was an early access game I'd say the scope for development was huge, but it's not and as things stand it's shallow compared to the competition. You can pick up an older classic like Anno 1404 - with rich diplomacy, upgrades, trade, seafaring etc - for almost nothing these days.
My biggest issue given the relatively intimate scale of the game was that I felt no emotional investment. It seems like a wasted opportunity, given how fascinating the intrigue of interpersonal relationships in a new community like this could be. Play Rimworld to experience a masterclass in this. In Banished, I felt no connection to or compassion for my colonists. They're crude identikit stick figures with no personality and little to set them apart or make you care. They all switch jobs constantly depending on who lives closest, with only a basic 'education' stat affecting their efficiency at anything from teaching to stonecutting - good in terms of optimal pathing I suppose, but totally immersion breaking. The colonist AI is woeful, by the way.
I have recently had a blast with games like the aforementioned Rimworld and This War Of Mine, in which characters are full of personality and incredible and varied interpersonal stories constantly unfold that really draw you in and made you care. Losing one of my people in either of those games elicited a genuine emotional response. By comparison, Banished felt incredibly hollow. Yet another stonecutter has been crushed by a rock? No worries, another interchangeable faceless drone has automatically taken their place in the pit!
The graphics are what I'd expect from a small indie developer. Sadly, Banished has a very clunky modular UI that deviates needlessly from established genre conventions. For example, speeding up and slowing the passage of time - which are easy to locate, always visible and quickly altered with single keystrokes in similar games - are in submenus here, requiring extra clicks or 2 hotkeys to get to. I could live with this if the game was perfect otherwise, but it's symptomatic of deeper issues.
Other reviews complain that starvation is too hard to counter, but I found I had no problem as it was easy to feed the colony through the winter by assigning plenty of colonists to fishing.
I can see how some people could get into a relaxed, zenlike state whilst playing this and might appreciate its simplicity and lack of progression. However, I feel like I already have plenty of other better games in my library which accomplish that. I'd say if you love building games and want any kind of depth or incentive to persevere, look elsewhere. Or do what I do and try it on sale - it's only a 300Mb download, so it's quick to give it a shot.

If you haven't played Half Life or Half Life Opposing Force (which is an expansion to Half Life), then here's the gist.  You play as Barney the Security Officer.  He makes a few cameos in the first game (and in Half Life 2 is a major role).  Opposing Force has you playing a soldier from the US military doing missions during the play of the Half Life game.  Blue Shift is the same.  In Half Life, Opposing Force, and Blue Shift you are all playing in the same time period, just different roles.
Now for the game itself.  It is short.  It isn't crap, though.  It is quite well done, and shows a bit of the inner workings of the Black Mesa compound.  If you haven't played Half Life 1 then you might be confused on what exactly is going on, but if you're just looking to play a short singleplayer FPS, then this is something to hold you over.
I bought it back when it was around 10-20 bucks.  I don't know the price of it now, but I wouldn't pay more than 5 dollars.  If it's not 5, then wait for a sale.  It really isn't worth more.  The only reason it isn't worth more is that you can complete it in 2-3 hours, maybe even less.  But the gameplay is still fun and interesting and has the original Half Life touch to it.

Another strong linear storytelling experience from the Telltale crew. It's up to you whether you make decisions from a pre-determined perspective (such as going all out to be the most brutal Dark Knight possible), or whether you go with your gut. One of the things I really love about the Telltale series is how, if you do play from the heart, the protagonist becomes a reflection of you - and how you react to the character that emerges can be quite revealing about the way you feel about yourself. Deep.
A couple of quibbles about this title: there's no option to have multiple save slots, so if you want to replay and explore different choices, you'll lose all your data (including choices and overall moral compass breakdown) from the first playthrough. This won't be an issue for some, but for those who feel a sense of attachment to their personally-crafted Bat, this may be annoying at the least, especially if Telltale bring out a second season in the future and you can't get back your original choices.
There is also an (ahem) action sequence where the - how do I phrase this without spoilers? - movement and mapping of characters' mouths just isn't up to the activity at hand, and it's visually clunky to the point where it disrupts the experience. Telltale have always done a brilliant job with choreographing naturalistic body language and nuanced facial expression, including in this title, so it's really jarring that a crucial story element involving physical interaction between two characters doesn't seem to have had the care and attention paid to its execution that it deserves.
Finally, *what* is with Penguin's accent? Part East End London,with a significant detour to outback Australia and finished with a light sprinkling of Mancunian, it's definitely up there with Bert from Mary Poppins in the annals of terrible "British" accents.
These are the three things I didn't like about this game, and in the grand scheme of things, they're fairly minor. Telltale have delivered another immersive and gripping storytelling experience where, very often, the best you can hope for is that the choice you go with is the one with the least devastating consequence, and you care about the outcomes of your actions. Action-oriented gamers might find the mostly passive gameplay frustrating or dull, but I really enjoyed the six or so hours I spent wearing the Batman's cape (figuratively speaking), and found myself thinking about the choices I'd made, and the potentially different experience I could have had, long after I'd finished.
A solid addition to the Telltale portfolio that carries a strong insinuation that a second season is to follow...

This game is my #2 game of the last generation (behind Red Dead) and #3 of all time (both being behind Yoshi's Island). That's not to seem pretentious and give you my particular opinion of games in general, but I'm just saying that after several years and lots of replays (especially on console), I've put a lot of time into thinking about BioShock. And I think it's just one of those games that will be remembered years down the line for doing something actually important for the structural evolution of games, along with Metal Gear Solid 2, KOTOR and Fallout 3 (to name a few).
BioShock is a game about an underwater city. It's a shooter. You shoot a lot of things. It's actually the one thing in the game that I think is equally as bad as it is good. Lots of the killing things gets tedious. If you don't know where certain things are, or know much about ammo conservation with the particular guns, you're done. Also, because of the shooting the last four hours or so of gameplay are pretty weak. Shooting electricity out of your fingers is cool, though, and always will be.
The main thing that you might have heard about the game is its heavy critique of Ayn Rand's concept of objectivism that is steeped deeply into what is art, what culture means and what is actually the point of mankind. In the first few minutes, you hear Andrew Ryan (the general antagonist of the game, and the original founder of this city of Rapture) explain what other governments think is the point of mankind. It's an iconic speech, and it does a great job setting the mood.
If you're not interested in philosophy and social affairs, the game is still worth playing because of the aforementioned mood. The game's ambiance and believability for this fantastical concept is astounding. Rapture is the coolest place I've ever been to in a video game. Crazy stuff is happening. Mothers have pistols in their cradles because they can't deal with the loss of their children. Splicers are jacking themselves with powers the same way real life parallels would do with heroin. The blood of this run-down city stains the beautiful art-deco architecture and all memory of the incredible personalities that used to populate it.
It's a good game. It was a big deal at the time, and it seems to have lessened since, much to our collective disadvantage.
Additional notes:
Bobby McFerrin's Beyond the Sea is worth the price of admission.

Ok I only recommend this game for anyone who has _never_ played Tropico before. Otherwise I'm on the same side as everyone else who says Tropico 5 doesn't bring anything to the table that Tropico 4 didn't already have except multiplayer if you are into that sort of thing.
I find Tropico 5 to be sort of a handicap actually, in that the information the game gives you is a lot less than previous versions. Namely that is what you have, what your selling, how much profit you make making off it in the Almanac view. So micromanagement of these things is more intense and makes the financial management duties of the game a bit harder. The trade window isn't that intuitive either. Al these things take time and money lost to figure out. I'm still figuring it out actually.
On a side note, a pet peeve of mine remains as in previous versions and that is the awkward way in which you connect buildings to roads. It is an annoyance actually. Sure the game is built on a "new engine' but I don't see any improvements except in some graphics.
I do think the change up in buildings is a plus. Some were merged,  and some new ones took their place.The new campaign method of jumping between two islands you have alreayd developed and the multiplayer mode certainly add in refreshing mix to the game.
That said, it could be my last tropico. With all that is new, I still find it to be the same game with slightly different rules and a new paint job. I've played since verison 1 and I had a wonderful time. The only thing I really look forward to in this version is the new multiplayer mode.
TLDR: If you are new the series, you will enjoy Tropico 5, but I do not recommend it over Tropico 4.

Evolve is a perfect example of a game with a few great ideas that's ultimately bogged down by the difficulty of realizing them. That is to say, 99 games out of 100, it will not even be a contest. In the rare case when a four-man coordinated team is as good as the monster, the game shines really well. The problem is that it is so often a one-sided game, and there is no significant gameplay changes for each phase; run away until you're level 2 fully armored or level 3, then attack at the Power Grid until one side is dead.
I say all of this while acknowledging that the game has a significant avenue of potential change. The core concepts, however, will not.  Evolve, much like Titanfall, has a lot of cool concepts about it, but will inevitably turn into a grinding-stone of hide-and-seek. The metagame will make everything ten times worse.
All in all, public play is doomed. Nobody will ever be coordinated with random strangers enough to be competitive with even a mediocre monster player. Private/competitive play might hold some promise, but that's a pretty slim, masochistic range of viability for a full-price title.

This review comes with the understanding that the game is far from polished and lacks a lot of the content expected in forthcoming updates. I didn't let that affect my enjoyment of the game, though I understand if there are people who would expect something more from a game this far along in development.
That being said, Project Zomboid is just about perfect in it's execution of a zombie survival game.
It's level of detail is so immersing that I'm often stricken with anxiety in the first few seconds of playing. There's chaos all around you, and with your death assured, there's no telling if you'll make it through the night. If you do, and you find yourself in a presumably safe place, then paranoia starts to set in. You ask yourself, "Should I just take a peek out of the curtains to see if there's any out there?", "Maybe I should take a run for it, my house could be next". No matter how prepared, or how safe you think you are, you're never safe. No matter your fate, though, you will end the game with a story.
If your looking for a game to vicariously project your zombie survival plan/fantasy, this game is worth the look.

BUYER BEWARE!
I am fully recommending this game but beware... it is frustratingly difficult. If you plan on playing this with a controller like the Xbox One of Xbox 360 controller do yourself a large favour and remap both the Dash and Secondary/Super buttons. I can't tell you how many times I Dashed into a boss or enemy simply because I gently rubbed the Y button while reaching for the B button.
Although this game is a gem it isn't without it's issues.
First of which is the obvious artificial difficulty. Graphics in the foreground frequently hide enemies and obscure you from seeing animation patterns. This will cause you to get hit by attacks that would otherwise be easily anticipated had the animations not been hidden. Certains levels will have other issues such as the terrain being angled vertically while your main attack shoots straight.
Secondly, the default controls are passable yet as already mentioned can cause problems in a fast paced game like this. Accidentally pressing the wrong button while reaching the right one can mean absolute failure. Remap the Dash button to be as far away from the other buttons as possible. I recommend a trigger or a bumper.
Thirdly, there will be many times when there is just too many things happening to keep up. Frequently you will find yourself pinned and unable to avoid taking damage. Avoiding 1 thing will sometimes mean taking damage from 1 of 4 other things that have you pinned in a corner. This can be extremely frustrating given that certain bosses have a tight camera  and a small playable area to move Cuphead around.
Now let me talk about all of the things I love about this game.
This game is a nostalgia trip. As a child I had hundreds of old cartoons of this style on VHS. The genre damn near defined my entire childhood between the ages of 3 and 10. Cuphead makes me want to dust off the old VCR and dig out my old VHS tapes and just binge for hours. There is something to be said for any modern work of art that brings back such fond childhood memories precisely how they are remembered.
The game is very skill intensive. You will die... a lot, until you have the patterns of enemies down pat and can play around them. There is a large focus on boss battles in this game. There are side scrolling run and gun levels however they are mostly there to collect coins needed for skill upgrades.
Once you get the hang of it you will find Cuphead is an extremely challenging yet equally rewarding experience. If, like me, you grew up on old cartoons like Betty Boop and the works of Max Fleischer, your childhood is not only being respected by everything this game is, it is being celebrated and cherished.

There are perhaps more flaws to this game than it can get away with. However, the areas in which it excels are the most important aspects of a puzzle game such as this, so I'm inclined to give this a thumbs up overall. Bear in mind though, that this game is probably not everyone's cup of tea, depending on how sensitive you are to annoying details and minor flaws.
Pros:
- The plot is surprising and genuinely intriguing, and keeps you wanting to find out where your next clue leads you.
- The puzzles are sufficiently varied and well-made, and not too easy to solve.
- The atmosphere fits the game and the story perfectly, including some very good voice-work.
Cons:
- While the plot is great, it also contains quite a few loose ends and logical shortcomings. Some of the deductions of Mr. Holmes are so far-fetched you've got to wonder if he's high.
- Some of the puzzles are overly difficult, and most of them has only rudimentary instructions which are of very little help as to what you're actually supposed to do.
- The gameplay is as linear as it gets, and consequently the game has absolutely zero replay-value.

Having structures blow over would also be a nice twist, to wake up in the middle of a blizzard to find your log cabin falling on all around you !

- Great depictions of Batman, Bruce Wayne, and the surrounding characters

The game [story] really hooked me. I love Batman's position as a 'super'hero and Bruce Wayne's complex, at times powerful, interactions with Gotham. I also really liked that the game gave you the option to be Bruce or Batman in certain situations, and broke up the conversation-focused gameplay with action sequences and some of the cool technology of Wayne Enterprises.
- A few brief, minor visual/performance bugs
- They did well with the action, but there's some missed potential there
- 'Choices Matter' but their effects don't
With that last point, it's really bothered me quite a bit actually. This game pulls on my chest cords a bit.. it's so darn close to being a game I'll forever come back to (like the Mass Effect series or FNV) because it gives the player a ton of freedom in-game and thus really immersed me (along with the fact that I <3 da BatMan). BUT, the big ol' BUTT is that there's just no major effects on the game by your player choices.
I'm hoping, with all the hope in my blood, that this is because it's all in preparation for a follow-up series, where your first season's decisions will really come to fruition.. maybe this was Telltale's test to see how much they're willing to invest in this aspect for a pending follow-up. If not, I'll be forever bothered with not being able to feel the results of my in-game choices. We shall see, for now, I'll say I loved this game, I enjoyed my first experience of Telltale, I'm not yet on their dev team's bandwagon.. but I would buy follow-up series of Batman - The Telltale Series in a heatbeat.

1) If you like Batman & story-telling games: you will like this game; if you resent Batman or story-telling games: you won't like this game...
2) If you buy it, you may feel like you were fed a really delicious appetizer, or some fancy, gorgeous small-plate at a 5-star restuarant; and be left thinking: "it tastes lovely and I'm not really that hungry, but now I'm mildly desperate for more."
3) If you do buy it, consider writing Telltale to tell them how badly you want another series that follows up on this story. If you don't buy it, be a pal and do it anyways.

This game is my #2 game of the last generation (behind Red Dead) and #3 of all time (both being behind Yoshi's Island). That's not to seem pretentious and give you my particular opinion of games in general, but I'm just saying that after several years and lots of replays (especially on console), I've put a lot of time into thinking about BioShock. And I think it's just one of those games that will be remembered years down the line for doing something actually important for the structural evolution of games, along with Metal Gear Solid 2, KOTOR and Fallout 3 (to name a few).
BioShock is a game about an underwater city. It's a shooter. You shoot a lot of things. It's actually the one thing in the game that I think is equally as bad as it is good. Lots of the killing things gets tedious. If you don't know where certain things are, or know much about ammo conservation with the particular guns, you're done. Also, because of the shooting the last four hours or so of gameplay are pretty weak. Shooting electricity out of your fingers is cool, though, and always will be.
The main thing that you might have heard about the game is its heavy critique of Ayn Rand's concept of objectivism that is steeped deeply into what is art, what culture means and what is actually the point of mankind. In the first few minutes, you hear Andrew Ryan (the general antagonist of the game, and the original founder of this city of Rapture) explain what other governments think is the point of mankind. It's an iconic speech, and it does a great job setting the mood.
If you're not interested in philosophy and social affairs, the game is still worth playing because of the aforementioned mood. The game's ambiance and believability for this fantastical concept is astounding. Rapture is the coolest place I've ever been to in a video game. Crazy stuff is happening. Mothers have pistols in their cradles because they can't deal with the loss of their children. Splicers are jacking themselves with powers the same way real life parallels would do with heroin. The blood of this run-down city stains the beautiful art-deco architecture and all memory of the incredible personalities that used to populate it.
It's a good game. It was a big deal at the time, and it seems to have lessened since, much to our collective disadvantage.

Bobby McFerrin's Beyond the Sea is worth the price of admission.

The worst thing about this game is trying to explain to friends how a black & white, side scrolling platformer can be so atmospheric and so bloody good!  After all, most modern games are all whizz-bang, cinematic affairs, so how can something so simple be so much more involving?  Simple:
*Atmosphere - The depth of the screen goes far beyond the protagonist you play and the use of every shade of black, grey & white makes up for the lack of colour.  The low hum of the 'music' also adds to the overall immersion.
*Puzzles - From basic "move this block" and "switch this switch" to mind-bending, screen flipping, "get the timing right" puzzles, the variety and complexity (in some cases) really get you scratching your head.
*One more go & Satisfaction - Yes you will die (a LOT), and often you need to die to work out how to beat a puzzle, but it rarely gets so frustrating that you won't dust down the little guy and crack on beating the thing that just caused his demise.
*Saves - once you've completed a puzzle you've done it.  No re-doing sections or boring bits to get right again and again.  The loads are super quick too!
*Awww my poor guy - You get to see the character die in many gruesome ways, from spiders to guns and from mad falls to drowning.  You'll also see him dismembered and crushed by unfeeling machinery, along with having his mind taken over by....*Spoiler stop!
Only negatives are:
1. Some of the later puzzles are extremely reliant on timing and leaps of faith.  But it rarely gets frustrating and it's often your own lack of button-pressing skills that are at fault, rather than the game.
2. The ending is..... well, do yourself a favour and find out for yourself.  Buy this game!

I felt compelled to check out this game when it was on sale for $.19, because how could such a beautiful looking puzzler be only $.19? I'm so glad I did. This is a very small, quirky game, but it's a beautiful little gem well worth your time.
The music and hand-drawn insect and nature art create a very peaceful, otherworldly atmosphere to explore. There are no words or text instructions, but the game has a hint button which will highlight your next step if you can't figure out what to do next. Gameplay is basically hidden item-gathering exploration, interspersed with a puzzle in each chapter. The game progresses in a way that feels natural to understand. The puzzles can be tricky, but not impossible, and everything about the game is satisfying when you figure things out on your own. That said, if you get totally stuck on a puzzle and need a nudge in the right direction, check out the excellent Steam guides people have written.
Some caveats: There are five chapters, and if you close the game in the middle of a chapter, you'll have to start from the beginning of that chapter again. I can't find this as a flaw since the chapters take so little time to complete (you can finish the game with all achievements in 2-3 hours), but it's something to know before you play.
You also can't close the game during a puzzle, but again, most of them don't take very long to solve. One reviewer complained that puzzles have no reset button if you mess them up, but none of them can be messed up except the chapter 4 puzzle, which does have a reset button (the yellow spot on the right of the puzzle).
This is a very small, lovely little world to spend a couple of hours in, and I recommend it.

A very different setup from Tropico 4, but maintains very similar gameplay with improvements and new features, like multiplayer. I personally suggest this as the Tropico to get because of the multiplayer. It's fun to play with friends (even though we fail quite frequently).
The singleplayer is also different in what I'd say is a very good way. Instead of being thrown onto an island and having to basically start from scratch with the intention of building up a specific industry like you had to do in Tropico 4, you now have two islands to build up over the course of the campaign. You switch between the two islands for each level, and must build upon what you've already established to meet the new criteria. This let's you actually spend time building up two different islands to be as close to the way you want them as possible. The downside is that this means if you create a very shaky infrastructure early on, you might be caught in a sticky situation down the road. On the other hand, once I learned the ropes and restarted the campaign after meeting some hardships on later levels, I was able to create a booming nation and handle most any challenge thrown at me.

Evolve is a 4v1 game where you can either play as a hunter or as a Monster. Monster needs to kill all hunters or destroy Power Relay in order to win the game. Hunter's need to kill the monster in order to win the game. Gameplay might seem familiar to some people who have played "Nosgoth" or "Primal Carnage" which also have similar concept.
Hunter's have four classes, each class has multiple characters with different playstyles:
Heals teammates, Slows and marks the Monster. Hitting the marked points using assault weapon results in huge damage.
Main damage dealer. Has weapons like rifle, flamethrower etc. with utility abilities like grenades and mines and a self shield.
Traps the monster within a certain radius and helps tracking the monster using pet, sound trackers etc. Also has an ability to pin the monster in place for a short time.
Negats the damage done to allies, Stealths allies and has the ability to Air Strike the monster dealing huge damage.
There are currently three monsters in  the game Goliath, Wraith and Kraken both having different playstyles.
General gameplay of the monster:
- Relies on stealth early because of weaker early game.
- Requires feeding on neutral monsters in order to get stronger to face the Hunters in an upfront battle.
- Once reaches level 3 can steamroll the hunters 1v4 or destroy the power relay to win the game.
Melee  monster who destroys hunters 1v4 once level 3. Fun to play once you learn to use the stealth and feeding to level up. Weak at level 1, Too hard to take down once it hits level 3 so patience and stealth is the key early game. Never won a game against a level 3 Goliath or lost a game as a level 3 Goliath.
Ranged monster with sniping abilities and can destroy hunter level 1. (Needs balancing) Fun to play with skillshot abilities and brings in a totally different playstyle. Needs to be nerfed and should have lower health/armor compared to Goliath.
Wraith is the stealthy assassin. She’s a space alien Monster who warps around the battlefield, ripping into her enemies with her blade-claws. She can hit – then run – before you even see her coming.
The Wraith has considerably less health and armour than other monsters but makes up for it in agility and surprise element, favoring a stealthy gameplay style.
- Hunter classes are fun to play and evolves as you gain experience with different characters unlocking with each class.
- Fun to play as the monster and destroy faces 1v4 after levelling up.
- Nicely designed map.
- Amazing monster design.
- Good sense of progression as you put in hours.
- Competitive gameplay since co-ordination is required at a very high level.
- Some hunters are totally useless against certain monsters. For example: Maggie's traps are useless against Kraken.
-Pay to win inclined model since you must have certain hunters in order to deal with a particular monster and new Hunters are shipped as purchasable DLCs.
- Balancing issues. (cant complain due to Alpha)
- Monsters are hard to play compared to Hunters in terms of overall effort required.
- Sometimes you have nothing to do as a hunter if Monster is playing super stealth mode, need more activities for Hunters.
-New Game modes.
-Kraken got nerfed but still pretty strong mainly because you need certain Hunters to counter his a ss.
-Improved Performance.
-New Hunters and a new monster. (Only available to pre-purchasers right now)

This game is something else. You're a Zea Captain, exploring the world of the Underzea ('z' instead of 's', get it?), battling other captain, killing monster, finding new locations, officiers, riches and trophy.
The gameplay is similar to those space exploration / mining / destroying space pirate / trading kind of game, but with some main differences:
1) You chose at the beginning of the game what are you winning goals (riches, be a legend, finding your father's bone, etc.)
2) The commerce and mining part is more or less absent (which is ok, since I've never really liked the way those games approched this, i.e. grinding).
3) A terror system which works pretty well
4) The storylets (THIS IS AWESOME); you see, the writers of this game know what they're doing. Every places have got small weird interactions which will affect you and your crew. These interactions are well written and they go deep into the lore of the Underzea. This creates reason to return multiple times to different place to progress "quest". I use quotes since I never got the feeling that I HAD to do these, more that I WANTED to do them.
5) Dying is not a problem. When you die (and you will die), parts of your character legacy is given to your new Captain. There's way to have your heir replace you, have a will so more money/resources are transferred, and some rare artifacts will also be transferred.
5) Finally, the soundtrack, while subtle, will stuck with you.

There is so much about this game that is absolutely stunning. Unforutnately, the gameplay is not one of them. The original art and art style, the original music and musical style are all incredible. There is a cohesive unified artistic vision and it's well executed. The gameplay, however, is unimaginative to say the least.
It's really dissapointing that the parry mechanic seems to only be used for getting better scores and supers. The timing with the parry button also feels just slightly off. Some of the boss designs seem very poorly thought out. There are randomized elements that can combine for literally inescapable damage. It's also a huge bummer to launch a super attack only to see your inevitable fate of inescapable damage awaiting for you after it finishes.
I get it. It's hard. It's difficulty, however, merely feels like a novelty. A gimmick. Games on the NES were hard too, and this game feels like it was reaching for the same level of arbitrary difficulty.  Cuphead feels hard for the sake of being hard. Which is unfortunate when there's so much of the game I WANT to see. You can play the bosses on simple mode and still progress through the map, which is a nice concilliatory prize, but not worth the price of admission.
The game is much more fun to watch than to play. So if the artstyle and music interest you, but you don't want to do the exact same thing over and over and over until you finally memorize the patterns (only to have them nulified by RNG), do yourself a favor and watch someone else play it.

I bought some AAA games in the Winter Steam sale, but this is the one I can't stop playing...and can't stop thinking about. When I try to explain it to people, it sounds depressing: you scrouge for every scrap that you can and try not to starve to death, but it's just as likely that you'll be killed by cold or wild animals.
But, when I'm playing, I'm thinking about how the game makes me realize how precious life really is. Things I overlook in my everyday life make me overjoyed when I find them, like a granola bar. And, I've never had a more intense experience than when I was deep inside an abandoned mine with no light source and a single flare to light the way. Will it last long enough for me to find the way out?
I finally found a gun, but I only have one bullet. I decided to let the rabbits go that could have given me some food and instead save it in case I ran into a predator. But, when the moment came, I was so shaken by the charging wolf that I didn't aim straight when it charged. I died in the encounter, which ended my longest run in the game. I should have been sad or mad that I had a full pack of provisions. Instead, I'm planning to play again. I can't recommend this game highly enough, even without Story Mode enabled.

If enjoy city-builder games, you'll likely enjoy this one.
It's sandbox city-builder with a twist- you have to keep the town alive as long as possible (I'm pretty sure some players have found ways to run a self-sustaining town that keeps itself going- I managed to get mine killed in a couple of "years"- which was pretty funny actually).
Unlike other city-sims, it nails the essentials of survival, and thinks of clever ways to make players more thoughtful in how they acquire the resources to survive, along with replanting forests. It takes a few new mechanics that allow a bit more customization by the player including setting variable worker limits, allocating patches of farmland for different crops, and actual time delays for orchard trees to grow, adding some extra tactics. Also trading is more of a "Lucky dip"- the river merchants have all kinds of materials or seeds to sell, and have somewhat specific products they'd like.
The interface can be a little bit pedantic sometimes- you have to manually assign staff to every structure you make (rather than the structure getting auto-assigned the minimum-required workers to function). I do see why the developers did this (part of the "more customisation" idea).
So consider whether the payoff suits your play style. That said I think it's worth checking out.

i've now played this game for over a hundred god damn hours so i should probably review it.
sunless sea fills a niche in the horror genre that i haven't really found elsewhere, which is to say moody, silent horror that flickers into view and entices you to search for it. it's a game about secrets, and it's absolutely full of mysteries of every size (that you can make all sorts of horrific sacrifices to find out the truth about), monsters of every size (that you can try to barely inch past and pray do not notice you), and all kinds of gorgeous, terrible islands and seaports that make you feel sort of like a moth to a flame. for as long as i've played, i've yet to figure out all the secrets in this game.
the process of playing the game itself is slow, deliberate and perilous. if the stuff i mentioned above seems less rewarding to you than it does to me, then there's a chance you'll find the game sluggish and frustrating. it doesn't help that the starting curve of difficulty can be pretty harsh until you're familiar with the places you can travel.
basically if you are okay with a game demanding your patience but rewarding it with a lot of fantastic secrets and stories and sights, sunless sea is for you. get out there and sink into the watery abyss.

I love Sherlock Holmes. I have read the stories over and over since I was a kid. I've watched the old Basil Rathbone films, and the British Sherlock and American Elementary. Enjoyed all of these adaptations, as each has something unique to offer. So of course I was super excited to play a game based on the famous detective.
Then I read the reviews. And got less excited. Waited for it to go on sale, thought I'd try it out despite the criticisms. But I should have listened.
Full disclosure: I haven't finished the game yet. Not sure if I ever will, because I'm already sick of it.
The Bad:
Oh my god the dialogue animations. It's so awful, it completely distracts you from what the character is saying. The opening cutscene with the little kids is the worst; it's almost a joke. It doesn't help that the children look like terrifying soul-less ventriloquist dummies.
Looking for clues doesn't really feel like looking for clues. It feels like wandering around until your cursor turns into a magnifying glass. Which is exactly what it is. No brain activity required.
Sherlock doesn't really feel like Sherlock. I think this was deliberate on the part of the game creators; this is supposed to be a darker, less heroic version of the detective. I see what they were trying to do, but it just felt so... wrong.
The environments are very closed, and you can only travel along a very linear path, even though it looks like you should be able to walk everywhere. It really takes you out of the game.
The Good:
Puzzles are sometimes fun.
The deduction board is a good idea. These were the only moments during the game when I actually felt like I was solving a mystery. But there are no consequences if you get it wrong; just keep clicking until you get it right.
Environments are kind of pretty. Not mind-blowing, but ok.

Cuphead is an astounding indie game.
The most notable aspect of this game is its art style, inspired by 1930's cartoons. Everything is hand-drawn which makes the game feel genuine and as if the people at Studio MDHR put their hearts and souls into it.
The music is classified as classical jazz, a fitting genre for the era that only further contributes to the classical tone of the game.
Gameplay consists of run-and-gun action inside of mostly boss-only stages but also several platforming levels. The bosses typically have three or four phases each with completely original attack patterns for each. Platforming levels are not too long and not too short, you should probably finish them just before you're tired of playing it.
But if you read the game description, you already knew most of these things.
What you might not know is that this game is absolutely rigorous. If you aren't on your A-game, bosses will bring you to your knees; and if you are, you still won't beat everything on your first try (and if someone did, I would personally deposit $150 into their PayPal account if they could prove that they did it all on their very first try). Trial-and-error is a large component in gameplay and you may find yourself attempting to beat a boss with anywhere from 20 tries to 200 tries before winning. I would say it's 50% about memorization and 50% about reaction. The platforming levels are similar in difficulty, but I personally think those rely on your reactions more than they do your memory.
With all that said, this is exactly why I love Cuphead. I know a game is doing something right when I can get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me dozens of times by the same boss and still enjoy the game very much. I played it on single player and I'm sure it's even more fun with a friend. The game keeps you enticed with creatively designed bosses, unique attack patterns, great complementary music and art, and the thrill of a challenge. If you do not like to be challenged, this game might not be for you, even on easy mode. You don't need to be an amazingly competitive player to play this though. You just need to, at the very least, be willing to invest some time into boss fights.
Is there some RNG involved in battles? Sure. Maybe the projectile comes from the left side of the stage instead of the right; maybe the attacks the boss uses aren't always in the same order. But this is what I was saying earlier: it's half memorization and half reaction. You already know which attacks are coming, so there's your memory, but you still have to react to identify which one it is at that very moment. It's challenging, but not at all unfair. In my opinion, RNG is NEVER the sole factor that determines if you win or lose in Cuphead. You might make the argument that it can make the boss harder sometimes; and that is a subjective but fair thing to say. But if RNG is really the thing getting you, then you probably aren't very good at the fundamentals of the fight anyway.
I will say this though: the game has bugs. I only had two in my run that came towards the end of the game:
1. One time when I started up the game, I was right by the final boss stage yet I had no abilities or coins and I freaked out for a second. SImply reloading the game fixed this; but it was not a comfortable ten seconds of panic.
2. During the final boss, there's a glitch where an invisible entity damages the player. This is documented in the community bug report in the forums but I just wanted to mention it anyway.
Honestly, these bugs are easily overlooked in the grand scheme of things. It would be nice if they were fixed, but by no means are they game-ruiners.
TL;DR: Cuphead is a treasure of a game that we may not get to see again for a long while. The art style is in a unique class of its own, the music complements everything, the bosses are designed creatively and carefully, and the gameplay is very fun yet very challenging. 10/10. Buy it!

The Long Dark - Hell of a fun game right from the start...graphics are different that what most of us are used to...but I like them; they seem to work with the feel of the game very well. This game is much bigger than I first thought after playing for a few days. There are several zones... there is a wiki about them somewhere...ought to have a look... plus maps online.
The concept is excellent and it delivers and you learn that more and more as the game continues...with weight of objects playing a real role, temperature playing a real role, item durability playing a real role, needing to eat and drink cooked and fresh food and water very important. I could go on and on about the good things they have done in this game. The modes are great...just want to explore and not get attacked by wildlife? There is a mode for that.
You also need to be careful how you travel you can sprain your ankle, wrist, break something or just flat out die if you don't travel right. Lucky for players there are bandages, antibiotocs, and antiseptics.....bad enough injury...you will also need to sleep...very cool.
A ton of detail to player experience...very impressive. My one ♥♥♥♥♥? You can't save games incase you screw up....I've never been a fan of that...you die...you lose it all and start over. Took me two days to come back because I was so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ off when I found out. I hate that mechanic and think even a 'noob' mode ought to be made with saves or maybe if you fall and break a leg you always walk slower, maybe if you get too cold you wake up with a lung problem that causes you to get winded faster...etc... until you essentially can't play anymore because your character can't do much... I don't know I think that would be more fun than....start over after a ton of hours of collecting only to fall 10 feet to your death....in the snow...anyway..
Yeah, it's a great game besides the perma death thing being crammed down your throat...in every game I've played like that I've never played again after my first death...except this one. That says something about this game. It is an exceptional game imo at this point...and with the detail to which the devs have paid attention to the game I only expect it to get better.

Frogwares has been doing Sherlock Holmes games for more than ten years. You'd think they'd gotten pretty good at it, but judging by The Testament of Sherlock Holmes, they've just gotten sloppy. The engine is getting visibly long in the tooth, and the mystery you're solving this time does some very un-Holmesian leaps of logic and plausibilty towards the end.
The production values are just plain mediocre all around. While some of the puzzles are fun, there is an alaming number of inventory puzzles requiring you to combine various ropes and ladders into longer ropes and ladders. At its worst, the gameplay just devolves into a hotspot hunt, a variation of the dreaded pixel hunt. Not recommended unless you're either a hardcore Holmes fan, or a hardcore adventure game fan.

The game is absolutely gorgeous, the artistic style lends itself beautifully to the environment. This coupled with the great environmental audio (howling winds, snow crunching underfoot, etc.) really has a great immersive effect.
Honestly there have been times walking through mountains in Pleasant Valley that I've stopped to look out over the beautiful scenery even though I was freezing my♥♥♥♥♥off and the sun was setting and it might kill me. Or the desperation when you're trapped at night in a blizzard dying of cold with just your storm lantern and 10 ft of visibility just praying you find shelter soon because if you stop to try to harvest wood for a fire it might kill you. All the while the wind is howling in your ears, snow is crunching under your feet and you're breathing ragged and shaking from the cold. Oh and you walk/run slower into the wind. Those types of details are the best.
It looks like once story mode is released (Spring 2016 is the latest word) the price will be bumped so get this game now. The sandbox mode alone is worth it, I honestly can't wait for the narrative they're planning to bring. The episodic nature should also be really interesting.
And a final note: Don't ♥♥♥♥ with bears. Bears will ruin your day.

I never played this game on the original console so my opinions are about the PC port alone and I've never played it before until recently.
The game has a very straightforward concept where you pilot a giant robot that can also transform into a jet. While the concept is simplistic the execution is good enough to make the game entertaining and quite unique. In all missions you are introduced right into the action (After a quick mission briefing) and you’ll have to destroy enemy buildings as well as their vehicles using a variety of weapons you’ll unlock as you play. If you’re satisfied by this simple concept, you won’t be disappointed. The game doesn’t have much of a plot other than having you defend your base and destroying the enemy, and sadly the game isn’t very long being a 4-6 hour experience, but it allows you to replay the missions as you unlock them, most of the missions being quite open to different alternatives to go through them due the transforming mechanic, the weapon variety and the size of the maps.
The controls might be very clunky on the start (Especially the mouse controls) and I won’t judge the people saying it felt unplayable, it takes some time and effort getting used to it but it’s worth it and doesn’t take long to get used to the controls on both the giant robot and the jet, both which control differently and have their ups and downs on their gameplay. Customizing the controls is not hard either, and it didn’t took me long to find the most comfortable settings to play the game with, and I used a keyboard all this time. Give it some time and you’ll blast enemies with accuracy soon enough.
There’s no difficulty setting in this game, but the game’s only difficulty felt fair, challenging but not frustrating. The enemies are a bit bullet spongy, but as you unlock better weapons it becomes easier to get rid of them as well destroying everything around you. Some weapons felt a bit lame, but it also counts with many satisfying weapons that makes you feel like you’re in a Michael Bay film because of all the explosions and destruction you’ll be causing around you, and this game has plenty of destructible environments.
It’s a solid experience for those fans of action games and giant robots but it’s not flawless. Some weird experiences I had with it is that the mouse doesn’t work during the steam overlay, and any key you press during the overlay that triggers an action in the game will still work, so you can still play with the overlay open which can be annoying if you need to send a message.
All in all, I’d recommend buying it during a sale considering its limited length and some of its simplicity, but it was a great throwback to simpler times and I am extremely satisfied with the game.

A very different setup from Tropico 4, but maintains very similar gameplay with improvements and new features, like multiplayer. I personally suggest this as the Tropico to get because of the multiplayer. It's fun to play with friends (even though we fail quite frequently).
The singleplayer is also different in what I'd say is a very good way. Instead of being thrown onto an island and having to basically start from scratch with the intention of building up a specific industry like you had to do in Tropico 4, you now have two islands to build up over the course of the campaign. You switch between the two islands for each level, and must build upon what you've already established to meet the new criteria. This let's you actually spend time building up two different islands to be as close to the way you want them as possible. The downside is that this means if you create a very shaky infrastructure early on, you might be caught in a sticky situation down the road. On the other hand, once I learned the ropes and restarted the campaign after meeting some hardships on later levels, I was able to create a booming nation and handle most any challenge thrown at me.

What will add some life to the game is that no two matches play the same, being that everyone in human controled.

Evolve is a 4v1 game where you can either play as a hunter or as a Monster. Monster needs to kill all hunters or destroy Power Relay in order to win the game. Hunter's need to kill the monster in order to win the game. Gameplay might seem familiar to some people who have played "Nosgoth" or "Primal Carnage" which also have similar concept.
Hunter's have four classes, each class has multiple characters with different playstyles:
Heals teammates, Slows and marks the Monster. Hitting the marked points using assault weapon results in huge damage.
Main damage dealer. Has weapons like rifle, flamethrower etc. with utility abilities like grenades and mines and a self shield.
Traps the monster within a certain radius and helps tracking the monster using pet, sound trackers etc. Also has an ability to pin the monster in place for a short time.
Negats the damage done to allies, Stealths allies and has the ability to Air Strike the monster dealing huge damage.
There are currently three monsters in  the game Goliath, Wraith and Kraken both having different playstyles.
General gameplay of the monster:
- Relies on stealth early because of weaker early game.
- Requires feeding on neutral monsters in order to get stronger to face the Hunters in an upfront battle.
- Once reaches level 3 can steamroll the hunters 1v4 or destroy the power relay to win the game.
Melee  monster who destroys hunters 1v4 once level 3. Fun to play once you learn to use the stealth and feeding to level up. Weak at level 1, Too hard to take down once it hits level 3 so patience and stealth is the key early game. Never won a game against a level 3 Goliath or lost a game as a level 3 Goliath.
Ranged monster with sniping abilities and can destroy hunter level 1. (Needs balancing) Fun to play with skillshot abilities and brings in a totally different playstyle. Needs to be nerfed and should have lower health/armor compared to Goliath.
Wraith is the stealthy assassin. She’s a space alien Monster who warps around the battlefield, ripping into her enemies with her blade-claws. She can hit – then run – before you even see her coming.
The Wraith has considerably less health and armour than other monsters but makes up for it in agility and surprise element, favoring a stealthy gameplay style.
- Hunter classes are fun to play and evolves as you gain experience with different characters unlocking with each class.
- Fun to play as the monster and destroy faces 1v4 after levelling up.
- Nicely designed map.
- Amazing monster design.
- Good sense of progression as you put in hours.
- Competitive gameplay since co-ordination is required at a very high level.
- Some hunters are totally useless against certain monsters. For example: Maggie's traps are useless against Kraken.
-Pay to win inclined model since you must have certain hunters in order to deal with a particular monster and new Hunters are shipped as purchasable DLCs.
- Balancing issues. (cant complain due to Alpha)
- Monsters are hard to play compared to Hunters in terms of overall effort required.
- Sometimes you have nothing to do as a hunter if Monster is playing super stealth mode, need more activities for Hunters.
-New Game modes.
-Kraken got nerfed but still pretty strong mainly because you need certain Hunters to counter his a ss.
-Improved Performance.
-New Hunters and a new monster. (Only available to pre-purchasers right now)

This game is slow. It's pacing. It's methodical. It's maddening.
Maddening, like sailing into the pitch black sea with no land in sight and with nothing to go on more than someone told you there was land "to the east." But you've been out at sea so long you've forgotten where you started from and where you were supposed to go and all you know is you need to keep going east.
Then you see the problem. You're low on fuel. You're low on food. You're low on sanity. And you are far, far from home. You scramble to try to get home, trying to draw a balancing act, since if you run out of fuel you'll be stranded, but you can burn some of your food and use it as fuel, but what's the point of making it back to London if you're all starved to death and all that reaches home is a boat filled with corpses?
But in the end, you make it. You burned your last ration, you may have sacrificed one of your crew members to some nameless god in exchange for fuel, but (most of) you made it. A harrowing experience that drove you to the brink of madness in which you saw horrible things that would drive most people to claw their own eyes out.
And then, after you rest for a day or two, you head out to sea again.
Sunless Sea is a game about commanding a crew of sailors (or 'zailors', if you've taken up the local accent) through the nightmare of the Unterzee, a massive ocean entirely inside a massive cave system. Populated by madmen and nightmarish creatures, you strike out, seeking fame, fortune, an empire, or perhaps your father's corpse. Whatever your desire is, you will run into strange places and stranger people. An island of LARPers where everyone is expected to play a role and wear a mask. A place with a civil war going on between two bands of sentient rodents. The underwater descendants of Ghengis Khan. A hidden cave with a sentient force asking to play a game of chess against you. No place is quite like the one you just left.
There is no voice acting in this game. This is important for many people. There are thousands upon thousands of carefully handpicked words for you to read. The stories are beautifully and enigmatically written. Everyone has a story, and everyone has their secrets. What will yours be, Captain?

I really wanted to like this game.  I think that they started with a really good concept, and just failed to properly develop it.  I can see how the developers would look at this game as something that should be really fun, because it's basically about exploring this world that they've created and obviously put a lot of effort into.  Unfortunately, the pace of the game is just horrendous and that kills the excitement of exploration.
For me, the game turned into a series of quests that I had to undertake in order to get the resources I needed in order to explore.  The quests are interesting and fun the first time you do them, but the way the game is set up you'll continually die and start over.  By the fifth time you're accepting or completing a quest it's no longer fun.  It's tedious.  The same happened with the ports I was discovering.  The first time I got to a port I really enjoyed the stories I found there.  But then I'd die and start over and rediscover the same port.  You have to go through the motions of rediscovering the ports because that's how you get the resources you need to survive.  So, you revisit the same 20 ports you discovered in your last life and go through the same exact story at each.  It's tedious, and after a while I stopped paying attention to the stories at new ports because I knew that I'd be seeing them all 100 times over.  It just became a habit to click through without paying attention.  And that's how the one thing I really liked about this game disappeared and the game became a chore and I quit playing it.
I think with some refinement this could have been a really great game.  As it sits now, I wouldn't recommend it.  I really hope that the developers keep working though, as I appreciate their attention to detail and would like to see them mature as game designers.

Pros:
-Good programming, especially in contrast to other similiar Sims and City builder games like Stonehearth, which has serious memory leak issues. Also villagers WILL obey your order to do their jobs and they do not get stucked fetching resources.
-Good balance. Every building/infrastructure is useful, and player must expands and plans his village with reasonable consideration.
-Low graphic and hardware requirement
-Supports steam workshop for mods. Given the solid foundation of game engine and programming, this makes the game a good platform for all sorts of mods.
Con:
-Lacks endgame contents: Once the player managed to survive for about 3~5 years and setup his own blacksmith and tailor, it becomes quiet boring and spreadsheet like. Not much else to do but to expand and farm for more resources.  The endgame is not very eventful either, with nothing else but disasters to look forward to.
-Short expected playing time: took around 6hrs to figure everything out, then it becomes too simple and sort of boring. One must resort to mods to extend the game's life.
-Lacks variety in Farm/Orchard crops, despite a large number of different selections: What you grow in your lands doesn't really matter except the time they require to get ready for harvest, and some of them are raw material for alcohol. Other than that, everything has same score as food resources.
Do recommend it, 6.5/10 or so; at least it does not have any serious issue and is totally playable.

Probably one of the first "artsy" games I picked up and played back in 2012, but didn't get around to completing most of it until recently. It's a brutal Mario esque platformer with a stark aesthetic that works wonderfully with the vaguely dystopian, stygian atmosphere. The music is subtle and nuanced with appropriate variations for different areas - lots o ambient sounds, many of which are cued to hazards you need to avoid, and the platforming itself is quite solid although it has it's share of annoying features.
The game itself can be completed in an hour or two but the difficulty is such that unless you're familiar with platformers you will die a LOT to various traps, hazards, and the rare enemy. The puzzles in the game are frequent, but light, and mostly involve teaching the player something about the world, showing it in use, and then solving a platforming puzzle to continue forward.
The story is strong in its absence, leaving the player wondering what is going on, and for me personally, it comes off very very well purely because the oppressing atmosphere - from backgrounds to empty fields - tell a story to me. LIMBO is a classic indie game by the people known as Playdead Games. LIMBO is a puzzle platformer and thankfully it isn't a very hard puzzle platformer but it certainly ain't easy
LIMBO is known for its monochrome art sytle and I have to say it makes the game really pretty even though it's all black and white apart from some butterflies and the sun rays
The music and sound effects make this game the most atmospheric and believable game I've played in a while, it fits so perfectly with what the game is trying to place in front of you. There are many disturbing and unsettling things such as dismemberment, flies and bugs, numerous amount of traps and... spiders. I hate that spider
There is a sort of story but isn't told to you through cutscenes or anything just you wandering through a deep dense forest then making your way into industrial buildings. You play a boy... that's it a boy and you have to venture through the game without trying to get yourself killed
As mentioned previously, the game isn't completely hard but it ain't easy either, you will die a fair amount. But LIMBO is more like a trail and error game, you do it once, you die. No problem! Try it again but this time with a different approach. The game also has a very incredibly fair checkpoint system
LIMBO sits with other such great indie classics such as Braid and Super Meat Boy, and it rightfully deserves that place!
