So FNAF it's a game about the Nigth guard of the Freddy's Fazbear Pizzaria, he's is contracted to work from 00:00 PM to 06:00 AM, looks like normal stuff but just on his first day, he is warned that the animatronic characters can walk during the nigth and if they ever manage to see him, they will think that he is an Endoskeleton without a suit, so as this is "against the rules" on the Pizzaria, they will try to stuff you inside of a suit, this suit being filled with robotic parts and wires, so it's very probably that this action will result in the guard's death.
The story was simply enough and for me, at least the first time i played, was a very silly one, but amusing. But the developer, Scott Cawthon, added some easter eggs on the game, that revealed the real story behind the events of Freddy's Fazbear Pizza.
I'm not going to stretch myself too much, if you're reading this you probably know the plot, but if you don't i suggest you to read the game's wiki before reading the rest of the analysis.
So i'm going to start from what really got me, the story.
The setting of the game was so original and creative, at some point it got me wondering "why did nobody did this before?". And the fact that it leaves much space for theories and mistery it's just perfect to me.
But i still finding some problems on the plot, the story of the game can get really confusing because too many things are presented to you at the same time. In one call the phone guy talks about the Bite of '87, and then Golden Freddy appears, and then the poster's change in the hall, and then "IT'S ME" it's everywhere!
It's really hard to concentrate when there's so much things happening at the same time!
But if you're not looking for all the theories and stuff, the story by it's own it's good enough.
Talking about graphics, i can't say too much. The ambient it's well made, the 3D models looks pretty good. But something that i really liked was the animatronics designs, they are all very unique and distinct. They make me remember old cartoon characters. But even they're appearance being charmy at one point of view, in another they can look very menacing, like in the Teaser for FNAF 2,the image with Freddy, or when all 3 animatronics appear on the trailer for FNAF 3. So, they have a balance betwen charming and creepy, that makes a perfect combination.
So the Story is great, the character are awesome, but a game is meant to be played! So, how is the Gameplay?
I sadly need to say that when it comes to gameplay the game really lacks...
The game brings an very unique idea of being locked in one position and monitor cameras to make yourself safe from the monsters. This idea was great, as much people pointed out it resembles Nigth Trap for the Sega CD, but in this game you're supposed to trap the monsters, and on FNAF it's the opposite. So the gameplay can be fun, for a while, until it becomes kind of repetitive after the 3º nigth were freddy starts coming after you, and once you beat the game, you'll probably left it rotting or unistall it.
But still, beating this gaming for me was really satisfying, it felt very good give Freddy the middle finger after i beated it!
Also i have to mention that the game can get pretty unfair sometimes, there will be times where Bonnie will not move his♥♥♥♥♥from the door, draining all your power, and for for completly♥♥♥♥♥♥you off they can disable the doors,this means your dead, the door don't come back to work, and if you pull up the monitor they get you. I really hate this because it happens by random, and after that you only have two choices: Hope that Foxy don't come for you and don't look at the monitor, or simply suicide and start over, but it's can be very annoying if this happens at 05:00 am nigth 5!
And now, finally, the ultimate question...
Is the game really that scary?
Well, i can totally say, the game is really scary, but maybe less than what the youtubers led us to think that was...
The scary factor of the game comes from the pressure of being " jump-scared", you really don't want this to happen, but happens so fast, that at the end it wasn't so bad has it sounded. It's like holding an Ballon that is close to burst, the pressure of seeing the ballon getting bigger and bigger make it look that the explosion will be much stronger, but when it explodes it happens so fast, that even if you got scared, you just need a time to catch your breath, it's not something that won't allow you to sleep at nigth.
The setting of the game is very creepy, the pizzaria looks seems morbid and gloomy, the sound effects also do a very good job, it really adds to the atmosphere.
The game it's really really scary when you first play it, mostly by the fact that you don't really know what to expect and what to do. But after some time it get repetitive and predictable.
I give this game 7 out of 10.

I picked up this game because it was on sale and wanted to try it because I really didn't know much about Sherlock Holmes. Unfortunately, I didn't like the game very much because of three reasons:
1. The Characters: I went into this game not knowing much about Sherlock Holmes (I never read any of the stories and only knew him as a famous detective). He, in my opinion, is nothing but an arrogant a**hole who talks down to everyone while making himself out to be hot sh*t. He goes around constantly breaking the law in the name of his investigations and then expects everyone to accept his deductions. A perfect example of this is in the beginning of the game (minor spoiler) when he lockpicks a bishop's office all by himself and expects everyone to believe in what he's found. Dr. Waston isn't much better because he, in my opinion, is a yes man who serves as Holmes' bottom b*itch; he is constantly manipulated by Holmes and the game does have him question some of Holmes' decisions, but in the end, he still blindly follow Holmes because of reasons. Also, you switch control between these two sometimes, but there is absolutely no point because they control EXACTLY the same.
2. The Story: I must admit, I was first intrigued by the beginning (A high ranking bishop was tortured and killed), but as it progressed, it got convoluted to the point of being stupid. Spoiler warning: The overall story is that Moriarty was hired by someone (We never know by who) to overthrow the Queen and replace her with the Prince through magic poison (No, I'm not kidding) and bombs. Plot points are thrown at you with no explanation (Or that Holmes won't tell you until the end) and when he finally tells you everything in an exposition dump,  it doesn't make much sense and he tell you in a very smug tone to imply that he is the only one who can stop them.
3. The Puzzles: The exploring parts were ok (Think of the Walking Dead movement scheme). The sixth sense button was a nice idea, but it worked when it wanted to (Sometimes, I clicked it and no buttons came up until I was right next to the object I was supposed to look at). The actual puzzles were hit or miss with mostly misses because most of the puzzles came with no explanations on the actual mechanics of them (Meaning that the puzzle would be "figure out the mysterious substance in the test tube" and it didn't explain how to actually do that. I found myself randomly clicking around in most puzzles, stumped on what to do until the skip puzzle button appeared.
All in all, I would rate this game a 3 out of 10 and would highly suggest you buy this game for $5.00 and not for the $19.99 full price.

Now that I have finished my first playthrough of Batman - The Telltale Series, I thought I'd share my two cents. First off, let me say that I am a huge Batman fan and I thoroughly enjoy the Telltale series style of story telling. I also bought the game at 50% off and I feel like I got my money's worth.
OVERVIEW: What a rush!
If you're anything like me, i.e. a Batman and telltale fan you will probably enjoy this game very much. It was quite a roller coaster ride. Choosing your actions and forging your own path as the Batman isn't something the Arkham games really touched on, and it was quite the experience. This game gave me highs and lows like few others have. I enjoyed every second of it and the only regret I have is that I can't forget all about it and play it again. (Amnesia tips anyone?) If you are considering buying this game, I can comfortably say that you will not regret your decision - provided that you know what it is you are buying. This is basically an interactive movie. Not an openworld RPG.
The Pros: Everything.
I loved this game. The story was captivating, the voice acting sublime, the animation, though it does get buggy at certain points, is artistic.
Replayability:
As I said earlier this is a review after my first playthrough. I intent to update this review as I go through the game a few more times and try different story arches to see how they play out. (Something I am really looking forward to doing). After that I will best be able to say whether this game has any replayability or not. At the time of writing, I feel like this game is well worth two or three playthroughs, depending on what degree the story will actually vary.
The Cons: Few and Far Between.
My first gripe is that this is not the most optimized game in the world. My computer specs are well above the recommended ones but the performance still tanked at some points and I had to set the graphics for balanced performance instead of quality as I would have liked. Thankfully I didn't have to face any gamebreaking bugs, nor did it ever lag too much at any point. However I don't think that there should really be any performance issues given that this is hardly more than an interactive movie. But above all I wish they had a difficulty mode of sorts, and a stronger system to punish players for missing button clicks. In the end it became a little easy. I just wish there was some way to make the input system more challenging, if only by decreasing the time allowed to successfully press a button. That would have made the final boss fight a tad more intense.
The Story:
This was something of a point of contention for many Batman fans. Some said it was a good twist while others cried fowl because it deviates from the standard Batman storylines. This is not a conventional Batman story. It really has some shocking twists and breathtaking bends. Is it different? Very. Is it absurdly predictable? No. Did I enjoy it? Extremely.
Verdict:
I give this game a solid 8/10, which would have been a 9 if not for the optimization issues. Would I recommend buying this game? Yes indeed, especially if you can get it 50% off like I did. If not, it is still worth the full price. I am really hoping for a sequal in the not too distant future, but until then I am definitely going to give this a thumbs up and a few more playthroughs. :)

I just finished the game last night and I have to say I was only slightly disappointed, which is actually a pleasant surprise. Let me explain.
With the way Telltale ♥♥♥♥ed up The Walking Dead Season 3 and the way that their games are essentially just an interactive movie where your choices change some dialogue here and there, but otherwise have no significant consequences, except for maybe the main one, I was expecting them to drop the ball on this one.
PRO's
+ Telltale
+ Genuinely got me on the plot twist, I was not expecting that.
+ The characters are nice re-invisionings of classic characters. They aren't so differnet that they're unrecognizable, but they're more realistic, making the story as a whole a bit more believable.
+ The quicktime events were actually enjoyable, and you felt a bit like Batman during the coolest parts.
+ The voice acting was superior in quality.
CON's
- Sometimes it's hard to peg the dialogue summary choices. What I mean is that you don't find great options in the list, or you just pick one you think is the best, only to have Bruce Wayne or Batman say something that does not sound at all like them. There were a few times I had to go to the menu, even if it meant doing the whole chapter over again, just because they didn't say what I expected.
- Sometimes the crime scene events are a little queer. Sometimes the clues are too obvious and you feel silly for essentially reconstructing the obvious. Other times there's a clue that's so hard to find or out-of-the-way that you spend forever watching the World's Greatest Detective blindly walking in circles looking for something that was missed the first time because your mouse wasn't in the right position.
- I found that saying nothing was a lot more like Batman and or Wayne than saying anything, which is a plus, but sometimes the dialogue doesn't smoothly follow along with this option; like sometimes you could tell the characters' response to saying nothing was really the same as another option, because that was the expected response or something.
- They were obviously setting the ending up for another season which is okay, but it really took away from the ending, it made you feel that everything you had just done was empty and just a precursor, a prelude. Normally that would be okay, but I played this game expecting for the plot to be resolved one way or another. Idk, it just didn't feel exectued perfectly.
Overall, I really enjoyed playing this game, and I was fully aware of the listed flaws before I went in. Will I play it again? Probably not. Maybe if they make a sequel, just so I can refresh myself, but otherwise nah. I got the game 50% off, though, so I'd say that's well worth it.
T.L.D.R.: The game is $5.00 an episode, and I'd say that's fair, especially if you like Telltale, and ESPECIALLY if you like Batman.
8/10

Normally I would give this game a bit of slack. I've played bullet hells worse than this one and sucked it up because "hey, it's free, it's made by inspired fans and as a frequently inspired fan, I wouldn't want a wet blanket coming in and telling me it sucked."
But this time... I have spent weeks wondering if I should write about it publically or send a message directly to the creator, and finally decided that this message could stand being seen by more people. Especially since I have seen a few people reuploading music used in this game as part of the OST when, well...
I'm going to get the music out of the way first because that makes up the bulk of my complaints. Do note that all of this is coming from a big chiptune fan, who's also tried writing a few things in the format herself.
Right before the title screen appears, the viewer gets to see a list of musicians whose works had been used in the game. The problem here is:
. In fact, if you go into the game files and try to drag the public audio files into audacity, it crashes... but you WILL be able to drag them into a video converter of your choice - and you'll notice that nearly every song has a different album art embedded in it. I've also noticed that some of the albums that had their audio stolen are MUCH older than the game - for example, "Lost! (in the valley of shadows, can you see the light??)" and Fails at Life first appeared on the albums Rad Like Whoa and Splchipts recently, which were both published all the way back in
, when the game is from 2016.
What's worse, the choice of music is outright awful at times, and more often than not give some very bad first impressions of the artists' works. The strongest example of this just happens to be Laika as well. I came to Laika's bandcamp with the goal of reporting that his stuff had been used without permission because I felt a moral obligation to even if I didn't like said music; I came out having listened to his latest album while I was at it, with my opinion on his works dramatically improved. In fact, that might be the reason this usage of music pisses me off so much in the first place! If the creator of the game had tried to make covers of the songs being used and those didn't turn out so well, I could have patted him on the head metaphorically and gone "keep trying! It might work out!" - but since he's just taking other people's songs unedited regardless of quality, he's just making them look bad, and I can't stand it in the slightest.
With all that off of my chest, it's time to move on to the other criticism.
One of the game's strong points is letting you play as various characters with their own routes - six player characters and more bosses is quite a lot for a bullet hell, especially among touhou inspired ones! - and I do enjoy that character profiles were added in the game itself explaining a little bit more of them. The problem is that most of them don't fit together setting-wise. Tenshi, that woman accompanied by animals who she fights in the first stage, and the astral/dream traveller look like they would fit together, but then we have the cat girl with short jean shorts and the mute alien girl who both look like they stumbled out of a completely different show or series - or two series, rather. Why are some people dressed contemporarily but others in a fantasy-esque manner? Where do all these fairy-like people you fight during the stages come from? Unfortunately I haven't played enough of the game to figure out if they're all part of an overaching plot, but the interactions I did see between them were very, VERY shallow, as well. Apart from possibly the fourth boss but I honestly have no idea what was going on during the entire stage??
Finally, the gameplay. It's... Actually, the gameplay's fine. From time to time I have experienced a tiny bit of lag in my inputs, but in general the game as far as I played it was responsive enough that I could survive until the fourth boss, no problem. The patterns themselves were alright, albeit not breaking the mold.
tl;dr: as a player, the game itself is shallow, but decent if you're starving for bullet hells. But as a musician I can't recommend it with a clear conscience.

Morphopolis is an incredibly short hidden object puzzle game and art showcase, where you control a bug in a series of astonishing, hand-drawn scenes.
Morphopolis is a simple hidden object game, where the goal is to gather a series of similar items. These items unlock a minigame, another item, or a new screen you can explore.
There is no real story: you control a bug which ends up in a larger body in each chapter, and that’s about it.
Therefore, the game sells itself with a unique (slightly Moebius-like) art style. This somewhat alien landscape is a marvel to look at, but doesn’t overstay its welcome: most chapters are barely ten minute long– even though your movement is incredibly slow. Naturally this means the whole game lasts barely an hour, but if you like this distinct visual style, Morphopolis is an excellent pick.

Pros:
-Good programming, especially in contrast to other similiar Sims and City builder games like Stonehearth, which has serious memory leak issues. Also villagers WILL obey your order to do their jobs and they do not get stucked fetching resources.
-Good balance. Every building/infrastructure is useful, and player must expands and plans his village with reasonable consideration.
-Low graphic and hardware requirement
-Supports steam workshop for mods. Given the solid foundation of game engine and programming, this makes the game a good platform for all sorts of mods.
Con:
-Lacks endgame contents: Once the player managed to survive for about 3~5 years and setup his own blacksmith and tailor, it becomes quiet boring and spreadsheet like. Not much else to do but to expand and farm for more resources.  The endgame is not very eventful either, with nothing else but disasters to look forward to.
-Short expected playing time: took around 6hrs to figure everything out, then it becomes too simple and sort of boring. One must resort to mods to extend the game's life.
-Lacks variety in Farm/Orchard crops, despite a large number of different selections: What you grow in your lands doesn't really matter except the time they require to get ready for harvest, and some of them are raw material for alcohol. Other than that, everything has same score as food resources.
Do recommend it, 6.5/10 or so; at least it does not have any serious issue and is totally playable.

It's been some time since I initially got involved into Sunless Sea, and after the Zubmariner DLC I thought I'd give it another go. Since now my knowledge is rock solid about the game's strengths and weaknesses, I can begin a fair review of it.
I can best describe the game as being a 2D top down roguelike naval RPG, with high emphasis on survival and resource management. Information like stories and knowledge in general are represented as resources, commodities which are traded with the various ports the players encounter while discovering the map. One of the biggest impediments to new players getting a know-how of the game and enjoying it is delivered by the cryptic nature of the game's lore, as well as the unusual mechanics. It does not play like any other naval sim/RPG (Patrician, Pirates!). Trade is not a viable option, at least not at first. Combat is not a viable option, not until much later. The main focus of the game seems to be to steer the player into going on risky discovery adventures, grab as much intel as possible and then return to cash in. Combat and trade mechanics are very simplistic anyway, and the whole discovery mechanic is just a medium to deliver the story.
The story is unfolded in text, so get ready to read. The lore itself is very witty, although alembicated and cryptic, and has the quality of holding vast amounts of internal consistency. As described by numerous other reviewers, it is the highlight of the game. However, the roguelike nature of the game forces the player to replay story snippets over and over, and coupled with the game's difficulty, can expend the user's patience.
The gameplay content is spartan. It is there to hold the game together and to project the feeling of difficulty, and it delivers. However, it does not excel in any aspect and thus combat and trade quickly become dull, repetitive while enemy AI is simple and easy to overcome with the right knowledge and resources. The pacing of the game is quite slow and this can be either a minus or plus depending on personal taste.
The art and music of the game deliver greatly on the atmosphere. They represent a high point in game design.
Modding tools are insufficient and bugged. Basically, there's not much that the devs have given so this game can be further improved. Such a shame.
TL;DR:
5/7
++ Great story
+ Good art and music
+ Pushes games medium forward through innovative concept
- Roguelike elements do not sit well with story delivery
- Bad modding platform
- Wasted potential for a groundbreaking game due to lack of gameplay resources
- Lacks better tutorial mechanisms to hook new players in
For >1€ per hour played, it was a well-priced experience for me.

Half-Life was one of the first FPS to propose a complex story, with graphics still angular but with the best 3D for 1998. You were Gordon Freeman, a scientist turned hero for the Black Mesa staff, in a place where an alien invasion was happening, where Marines and Black Ops were the "cleaners". G-Man, mysterious man with a case, was monitoring you.
The game was a real success and an add-on was released in 1999. Opposing Force was shorter than HL (normal for an add-on) but with the return of the G-Man, with new weapons, new enemies. One big difference: you weren't Gordon. No, you were Adrian Shepard, corporal in the HECU, belonging to the famous Marines who were adversaries in HL. You were a Marine now but fortunately, you changed your mind: no more scientists or guards killings, as you can suppose that they'll be an useful help.
HL, HLOF and Blueshift are the three main games of what we can call, now that that Half-Life 2 and Co. are released, the Black Mesa Era. So what is about Blueshift?
The Black Mesa Era is special because of the multiple points of view you can play. Gordon was the scientist side, Adrian the military one, so, it was missing the guard one.
Many can argue that we could have played a Black Ops, a Xenian (the mod Point of View is taking the matter in its hand), the woman that was pushing the crystal (the exclusive mission on PS2, Decay, is taking the matter in its hand, as the mod Decay, a port for PC of this mission) or anything else (a janitor - well, a mod is existing, an external person - the mod Half-Life Visitors is... oh well, you know what I mean). But Gearbox choose what was called Barney, the guards of Black Mesa, taking that name for making an hero. It could have been Otis, it would have been really funny to be healed by donuts.
So, you're returning into Black Mesa Hell. You're Barney Calhoun, a guard, beginning your adventure before the incident triggered by Gordon. Then, eventually, you will have to fight your way in a chaotic facily, trying to escape, finding a certain Rosenberg and... well, it's not a spoiler, Barney did escape Black Mesa, like Gordon and Adrian, apart from the fact that he was still free.
I need to say something: it's a stand-alone, where a lot of gamers tended to call it an add-on.
Story is basic, hell, it's just another day in Black Mesa, so don't expect something different. See the community mod for it. But Gearbox did a crime, an offense in the Half-Life Mythology.
G-Man is appearing once. What? Half-Life 2 Episode One did the same? Hey, the story was about saving Gordon from him. But G-Man did come back in the next chapter, still following Gordon.
G-Man was interested in Gordon and Adrian. But not in Barney Calhoun, who is in the Combine Era one of the most famous Resistance leader. G-Man was involved with Eli and Alyx Vance's story. Why not with Barney, who is one of the few that were really struggling. Where is my fun to spot G-Man?
Gameplay hadn't change a bit and I don't complain about that: it's Half-Life, I mean, you have to climb ladders, find a way to kill enemies when your weapons aren't sufficient, you have to be careful when nearing toxic areas and when you're jumping on Xen...
The game had a big bug, meaning that you're obliged to download a patch: Flashlight wasn't working. Other negative point is that you can't use the HEV device for protection... in total contradiction with Adrian Shepard, not belonging to Black Mesa, who can use it! Also, BlueShift didn't solve the problems of these dangerous ladders when it comes to climb down.
Graphics are still the same if you don't install the High Definition Pack. If you do so, the HDP is making the characters less angular, your environment is less sterile and a new skin is given to your weapons. Anyway, Blue Shift's graphics are good if you're not allergic to "old" engines.
With an established universe like Half-Life, Blue Shift couldn't forget to make some references to the two previous games: you see Gordon in his tramway when you're trying to enter to your department for work (a scene present in the original Half-Life) or just before he's entering in it. You're seeing him in the Sector C, walking to his destiny, you're seeing the famous crystal that will triggered the portals being carried to its final destination and last but not least, the professor you're rescuing is thinking that Gordon will not solve things, that it's a foolish idea to believe in him. Oh, have I mentioned that the last you'll be seeing Gordon is when he's captured by the Marines? Next time, it would be years later, in City 17 train station. Well, Blue Shift is taking place at the same time of the first part of Gordon's story, so, it's normal to have a lot of references to Half-Life. For Opposing Force, the only mention of Adrian Shepard is made by a Marine when throwing Otis, the fat guard, in a pit you're climbing.
Blueshift is really lacking of novelties. It isn't bringing something new besides the story. Barney only uses Half-Life's weapons (no Opposing Force did make it) and worst of it, he has less than Gordon. No more experimental weapon, no more crossbow. Then, the enemies are reduced to what Gordon encountered (less the giant boss like Gargantua), so, no Race X from Opposing Force. And last but not the least (for me), soundtrack is good but isn't renewed like in Opposing Force. No new tunes, no new sounds, well, it's kind of frustrating for me who loves soundtrack, particularly when a game set in an universe has a different music than the others.
Finally, Blue Shift, for a stand-alone, is shorter than the add-on Opposing Force... who was shorter than Half-Life. Five hours of playing (and more if your flashing is buggy) isn't enough for Half-Life. Well, the episodic games set in HL2 universe are as short as Blue Shift but the content is more extended than Blue Shift's. Here, we're in 2001, players were waiting for HL2 and well, they're in the right to expect much more for HL. It was like the game was rushed for giving something to impatient fans.

Five Nights At Freddy's is a fantastic game! I myself am quite a fan and I love the unique take it has on the survival horror experience. While the horror quality can degrade after playing it for so long, like I have, the tension is always there to complete every night alive.
The most dramatic parts for me are when I am at 5am and my power runs out. I sit still, trying to delay Freddy's attack, hoping and praying to hear the familiar children's cheers as the night ends. Overall, a great game experience, but not for the faint of heart, atleast on the first few attempts. Being immersed in the world of Rapture is like spending time in a really nice fishtank. Its very enviromentally encompassing and I loved being able to really feel like I was there, but seeing the same stuff over and over get kinda boring. From water dripping everywhere and wet surfaces to underwater volcanos, the city of Rapture is an immersive scuba dive to a lost world.
The storyline was pretty good as well, certainly somewhat of a mindfk along the lines of the original S.T.A.L.K.E.R. in that questions are raised as to who you are and where you came really came from. The gameplay was smooth as silk--spot on and tons of fun to go up against hordes of drug addicted underwater folk and big daddies.
The only major drawbacks to this game are its length and the capacity for items and ammo. I wish it was longer and playing through it on easy difficulty really did not take that long even though I think I explored almost every inch of Rapture. The small inventory size made so that once the ammo for one weapon ran out you had to rely on others until you filled up again, which forced you to utilize a variety of spells and guns. However, searching boxes and bodies for ammo for lenthy periods of time, and then going from full to empty in a matter of seconds, isnt really the most convenient thing in the world. And realistically, is it that hard to be able to carry say 100 or 200 pistol bullets instead of 48? I mean this guy can lug around a crossbow, grenade launcher, shotgun, machine gun, flame thrower, and a wench in his pants. How much harder would it be to put 100 pistol rounds in his pocket? He also must have a damn small wallet since he can only carry 500$. I guess Rapture money only comes in silver dollars.

Something different for Batman, more of the same for Telltale.
Telltale has some great writers, and they do story very well. It's nice to see them given the freedom to do something different with the Batman series. While it doesn't reinvent the character, it plays fast and loose with some of its canon, and offers some unique takes on some old characters, which adds up to an engaging story that manages to distinguish itself from the many variations of the Batman story that have come before.
Of particular note is the emphasis placed on Batman's dual identities. Bruce Wayne is given at least as much face-time as his masked alter-ego, and he's equally pivotal to the story. Some key moments even offer you the choice to go as Batman or as Bruce Wayne. The duality between Bruce, a man encumbered by his personal history and family legacy, and Batman, a wholly invented persona  is at the core of the narrative. Its villains likewise get a lot of time with their masks off, outside of their villanous personas.
It's a great story, well told, but not much of a game. There are very light puzzle and exploration bits, but for the most part, your interactions are limited to tapping QTEs through the action sequences, and choosing dialog during the story bits. The choices you make here can have interesting consequences, but only for a scene or two. The majore beats of the story are wholly linear, even if it gives you some wiggle room to role-play. None of these decision moments are interesting enough to compel multiple plays-through. The thin gameplay is forgiveable, though, because the storytelling is strong enough to carry the experience. If this was a non-interactive animated mini-series, it would still be enjoyable.
Unsurprisingly, the game is also a bit glitchy. During my play through, it crashed twice, had moments of weird animation, diagonal cel-shading lines across the screen, or bad lip sync. I didn't experience any performance issues, but wouldn't expect to on my system, which is well above recommended spec.
If you've played other Telltale games from recent years, like Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us, or Game of Thrones, you know what to expect from the gameplay, graphics, and performance. This is one of Telltale's stronger efforts, with an interesting, original story, which is not easy to do with a subject as well-worn as Batman.

Coming late into this franchise, I picked this up on sale along with Bioshock 2 and Infinite in a triple pack for a measley $10. This game may be a bit dated, but in my opinion it doesn't show it. The game still looks beautiful in maxed out settings. Textures, especially water looks great along with other environmental effects. The story is fresh and exciting for an FPS game and the environment is truly unique playing in the underwater city of Rapture. The games dark and creepy undertones however, are quickly over looked due to the fast paced combat. However, a sense of survival is ever present, forcing you to conserve ammo and EVE Hypo, which allows you to use superhuman abilities called Plasmids.
The game took me almost 11 hours to complete and it was well worth all the time. In order to truly understand the story you have to listen to what people say, find every audio log, and pay attention to small details, as they may come up later. In conclusion, Bioshock still lives up to its name as a faced paced, fresh FPS, which rewards satanic tactics with gruesome yet satisfying results. If you're tired of all the basic shooters out there and over looked Bioshock like I did when it came out, I highly recomend you play it to expierence this truly amazing series that is still being made.

Bioshock is a game dating all the way back to 2006, that's 8 freakin years this game has been out and it still holds up amazingly well! The game takes place in the destroyed undersea dystopia known as Rapture, whose remenants remain in disrepair after a brutal civil war destroyed the place. The story for this game I won't spoil, as it is just too good to do so. Most of the story is very subtle, coming mostly in small clips of audio that you find all over the place; these give the world a depth and complexity that really does serve as a way to completely immerse me. The horror elements, of which there are quite a few, work very well with the violent and broken world that you find yourself placed into. The story is filled with twists and turns that you cannot forget, and the characters are all very memorable and charming. The atmosphere in this game is probably better than any other game I have played before or since, partly due to the engenious writing, and partly due to the stunning visuals. The game, as it takes place underwater, was an incredible feat at the time for its realistic simulation of water which couldn't be as quickly and automatically rendered as it is able to be today. The water effects are definitely a result of many dedicated hours of care and refinement because they still look absolutely stunning! That's not all, however, as the rest of the game, especially the lighting desgin, helps to contribute to the astonishing atmosphere of rapture. Harsh shadows make the place seem cramped and mysterious, but at the same time natural. The design of the splicers are just as nice, with the hiding of their "hideous deformities" through masks and such making them both dangerous seeming and at the same time sympathetic, what with their drug destroyed figures lying about the place.
The gameplay also holds up surprisingly well, giving a good balance between the use of plasmids and regular weapons, and the opportunity to use both effectively in synchronization if you're a skilled player (sadly, I am not one of those players). The plasmid system is utilized to its fullest potential, providing good challenge, flair, and usefulness with most of them. There are some faults in the game, however. Many sections of the game can feel excruciatingly long, with arbitrary fetch quests dragging out the areas to obnoxious lengths, which is espeically annoying if you are running low on supplies but need to kill a big daddy to save (or slaughter) the little sisters. The game's difficulty is also a bit odd, with some parts being laughably easy and some being unreasonably annoying, but not in a linear "getting harder as you go" kind of way. All in all, though, the game really does provide an unforgettable experience, from the atmosphere to the characters to the visuals and the all around charm of it, I can whole-heartedly recommend this game to anyone who is willing to give it a chance.

This game is the most overrated FPS in the past decade.
Every objective in this game is a fetch quest. "Gather these items," Bioshock says, "and I will give you a small snippet of plot in return." Screw you, Bioshock, integrate the plot into the gameplay! Don't make me go backtrack twenty times to explore your set piece, MAKE MORE SET PIECES.
Here is why Bioshock sucks: after 6 fetch quests in a row, with INCREDIBLY mediocre boss fights interspersed (i.e. standard enemy bigger health bar), they show you a super cool narrative twist. And you're like "Oh! Nice! Finally, this game is going to go somewhere!"
Wrong. Fetch quest, fetch quest, and then a fetch quest to enable an escort mission. Mustache-twirling bad guy, Arkham Asylum end-boss fight, ending that only has something to do with a sideplot in the game. The End.
The world-building is pretty nice. It's interesting to see a fictional treatment of a Randian society. It would have been more interesting to see it functioning and then watch its inevitable implosion, rather than just sifting through the rubble to find some garbage the game wants you to find.

---Alpha Review---
*Take this review with a grain of salt* since things will change when beta/release happens
Reviewing after 3hours of play. roughly 2hours Monster, 1 hour as Trapper only.
Okay so this is Evolve as other people have mentioned it is a 4v1 Player vs Monster(Player) action game.
the Monster is supposed to evolve and evade the hunters till level 3 and then either KILL all the hunters or Destroy the Power Generator (As Monster i won Twice Killing all humans, and 3 times destroying power relay).
humans are supposed to track, hunter, and kill the monster before level 3 if possible if not they have to defend the power relay which at that point the monster usually is really hard to kill unless u got a good group of humans.
Now Reviewing the 2 Chars ive used Monster, and trapper.
Monsters get 3 points every level to spend into abilitys and these are mentioned below
Goliath Abilities: Rock Throw, Charge, Leap Slam, Firebreath. (After watching other monsters use firebreath i feel it is not needed and wasted points)
I focused on the main aspect the Monster should be doing. SNEAKING And hunting.
so i invested 2 into leap slam for extra distance, and 1 into charge. then 2 into charge 1 leap.
At Max evolution i just throw 3 points into rock throw.
Until ur level 3 hunting the Hunters is really not a smart idea. At level 2 the Monster can deal signifigant damage and possibly kill off 1-2 hunters before retreating if hes bold enough (or when you get traped it will happen).
I really enjoyed the movement of the Monster and it felt very fluid and everything about it is nice.
Crouching to move sliently and not leave footsteps. was my favorite aspect.
Overall the Hunters have the advantage 2/3rds of the game. It takes a smart monster to evade them. usually a good team of hunters will always be on your back. leaving you only a small time to eat and then evolve after like 5mins. level 3 evolution usually takes me 15mins since game start.
I hope more people try to get good at the monster. currently im 6-0 with the monster. (im pretty good at hiding, sneaking, and when traped knowing when to attack and when to move, evading most of the damage till the trap ends.)
I feel a good monster atm will overpower any good human team after level 1. (Level 2 Monsters become bulletproof taking signifitantly less damage, doubles the Hp of the monster, and has better armor and deals Really nice damage enabling some earily kills if your more offensive).
Now with the Trapper:
The Trapper is unique as its the unit that can keep the monster in a closed area and can track it with the pet Daisy. Daisy is pretty good overall but i think she needs track a bit better. its easy to lose the scent from the monster if they know what to do.
I feel the harpoons are good but some be buffed a bit. (little bit longer range). its really easy to break them as the monster. (leapslam or charge can get you out pretty easily) or climing up a cliff to disable it.)
But its fun setting traps against an unsuspecting monster and while your team starts fighting u rotate to where hes gonna run to. then ARENA TRAP.
trapping you all in and you can deal some sigfigant damage.
I have not tried the other classes yet but i think if i were to play one it would be the assault as i find his abilities the best suited for me outside trapper.
Overall for First Impressions i am surprised how smooth it ran with my Graphics card. but i do get Weird Frame drops from time to time. cant wait for the full optimized game/drivers for it. It ran beautifully with an alpha and i didnt find any Real major bugs or grips about it.
i also like that it has like 3 playable maps. which are all pretty balanced and nice. (one seems to favor the monster, one the humans and one is even.)
Cant wait to play more of it.
My only Real Con atm is that its gonna be a full priced 60$ Game :P
From what ive experianced i would rate this as a 30-40$ Game. The Music is nice, the gameplay is nice. But it needs fine tuning (its an alpha i know so not a con in my book).
Overall would like to see at least 6-9 Playable maps and some other things.
Since this is only a multiplayer alpha i can see that they really didnt scrimp.
hopefully in the beta phase we'll see the single player aspect that will also POP.
But overall i hope they keep the quaility going for the multiplayer.
TLDR:  I really enjoyed it, Good Overall, Worth 30-40$ ATM in my eyes, Would recommend other people to try it.

TL;DR Unless you're looking for about 40 hours of gameplay, don't bother.
I've played since the game entered early access. The reason I played is because I enjoy games with a sense of progress, usually through acquiring loot and levels, that can be played quickly and without a large time commitment per play session. Up until the new expansion, progress meant maxing out gear in chaos 7 trials and acquiring ascension levels. They put a cap on how many ascension points you could spend per skill tree node, but that was fine with me. It didn't impact play much, and it meant I could focus on one hero per class, rather than having a hero for each and every tower I use.
Before the expansion, you would play through the campaign, fight your way up through the trials and spend the remainder of your playtime mostly in chaos 7. The climb was painful, but in the end, you become overpowered for the content and waiting for new chaos trials (or incursions, though I don't much care for those). I could set up and complete a chaos 7 map in roughly 8 minutes. I could gain 25-30 ascension levels in a good day of play (8+ hours). The progress wasn't much, since ascension level spending was capped, but it was nice to feel overpowered for a bit while waiting for new content.
I don't know that adding new chaos trials would've been better than what Trendy came up with, but I do know I'd still want to play the game. Progression in the new expansion means going through the new Onslaught challenge and using the Prestige system. You can choose to avoid the Prestige system, which many do, but then you're not really progressing. You can only go so far in the infuriating and frustrating game mode that is Onslaught right now.
So progress is no longer about acquiring gear or ascension levels. It's all about resetting. It's all about doing it over. And over. And over again. It's all suffering, from start to reset. At least until you've reset 50 times, which is the cap. The top players will manage this in roughly 1,250 hours (being generous), while the average player can look forward to considerably more. I doubt they'd come close to 50 resets before quitting in frustration though.
The rewards for resetting are too small, imo, and mostly inconsequential. The biggest reward, raising the ascension spending caps, won't matter until you're done with the Prestige system and are back to grinding out ascension levels. You'll be able to feel overpowered again once you reach ascension level 3000, I suppose. Who will honestly make it that far? That's thousand of hours in a frustrating system.
What makes it frustrating? Aside from all the bugs and disconnects, the bulk of Onslaught floors require you to beat multiple maps to move on to the next floor. It takes a lot of time, patience and scrutiny to set up a map now (15-20 mins), and a single mistake means failure. There are no do-overs. Sorry, no mulligans. If you fail once, you're back to the beginning of the floor. It doesn't matter if it took you over an hour to get to the third map of a floor, and a bugged hex thrower blew up your core. Sorry, start over.
"Sorry, start over." is the running theme of this expansion.
That's fun, right?

tl;dr Was on the way to being a good game, but ran out of fuel before it got there.
When I first played this game it had serious potential; there were unique and interesting gameplay ideas, regular updates, and most importantly devs who respond on the forum. I spent a fair amount of time playing the game, eagerly anticipating updates, until I felt I had got this jist of what the game was and where it was going, so decided to wait a couple of months before playing again. When I booted it up again half a year later the only obvious changes were some haloween gimmiks, as far as I could tell updates had ground to a standstill. A year (and a bit) later and no further changes, until I saw a post saying that the devs hadn't abandoned the game, however they could tell us why they weren't working on it at the moment (which was what promted me change my review). For comparison I've left my original review below, showing how excited I was for this game.
ORIGINAL REVIEW
This is a really promising game, with dedicated developers who are eager to share their creation with the community.
It is not a finished game at the moment, but is what a beta game should be. Updates are designed to test specific features so that they can be polished, submitting tickets is on the main menu and the developers actually respond to posts in the forums. Although it sound like these are obvious aspects for any beta game there are too many early access games that care too much about people playing them, instead of testing them to make a better game in the long run.
The gameplay itself will be familiar to anybody who has played terraria, starbound etc, but with enough unique features to make it interesting. One of the best features is the crafting system that classifies materials (eg ice is a chemical, which is a raw material => raw/chemical/ice), therefore some recipes will require any chemical or any raw material etc.
Overall, if you are looking for a good beta that will turn into a great game, I would recommend buying it now. If you don't want to be actively involved in improving the game, then wait until it is fully released so that you aren't disappointed and forget about it.

Banished is a well-polished game that is both challenging and relaxing. While most city builders encourage rapid expansion and constant growth, Banished encourages the player to expand slowly and focus on sustainability, as one disaster, mistake or bad crop can end everything.
Despite its simple forest setting, Banished looks beautiful and it' nice to see the seasons change (despite famine). The modelling has been done perfectly and everything fits the theme. Human-made things feel as though they could realistically be built by pioneers and be built using the materials found in that environment. The music is simple and relaxing, which fits perfectly with the slow gameplay. However, I've found it more enjoyable to play the game without music.
The one man team behind Banished has done something exceptional, and that is release a full game. No early access nonsense and no DLC. Just patches to fix things. It's tragic how this is something deserving of praise but it really is.
It's not saying much but Banished is the best Indie Game of 2014.

SUMMARY: A slow-moving, well-detailed "roguelike seafarer" with great depth (pun not intended) for those willing to take the time.  Take control of a freelance vessel in a subetrranean London that's Monty Python by way of HP Lovecraft, explore a world of terror and wonder while trying to survive  - and if you don't, you can leave a legacy behind.  Great purchase for fans of well-written games who like trading/adventure games, and probably one of the most well-written games you'll play.
Sunless Sea is set in the world of Fallen London, a well-detailed universe made famous in a browser game which you should be playing anyway.  Unlike it's text-based predecessor where you play an adventurous individual, you're a captain of a ship on the underground "Zee," out to make your fortune in the vast underground world of fallen cities, religious cults, frost castles, devils, and of course, Rubbery Lumps.
The basic gameplay is one of voyaging from place to place running errands and perhaps trade - this is made complicated by the challenges of the Zee - no light except for beetle-bouys and habitations, monsters, and a map that shifts each new character.  You've got to manage fuel to avoid being stranded, food to avoid . . . unpleasant meal choices . . . and terror to keep your crew from going bonkers.  You're one tiny ship in a gloriously macabre world that doesn't care if you live or die.
However the travelling is only part of the game - the journey between locations is important, but the locations matter.  Each port has its own quirks, stories, opportunities, and horrors.  You will get choices you can't go back on, and amazing opportunities.  Ports change in time, having their own tales.  Missions will send you to wonders and terrible places. The stories and choices in this game really bring it to life.  I found myself feeling affection towards some of the characters with their generically descriptive names, like the Dark-Spectacled Admiral.
On your ship, you'll recruit assorted crewmembers with their own tales and options and traits.  Many will help you, some have their own ambitions, and some might end up becoming your lover.  Life's complicated on the Zee, and everyone has stories.
As for your ship, get ready for a dizzying array of options that may take awhile to afford - guns, extras, equipment, and more.  Plenty of choices await you.
Finally, back home in London, you'll have options for how to live your life and maybe even retire.  Buy a house, get married, create a personal museum, live your lifelong ambition, raise a child.
Oh, and if you die?  You get to leave a legacy behind, making the next game easier.  Choose wisely on this, by the way - I made a few unwise choices that kept me stagnating for hours.
Finally, read EVERYTHING.  The game is witty, well-written, and packed with humor both dark and sparkling.
So who's this game for?
* If you like a challenging sim-type game and like stories it's a good call.  It awards careful thought.
* If you like trade/resourcing games you'll probably do well.  There's plenty of challenges that, at the same time, aren't overly complicated once you figure them out - but the difficult story choices will spice it up.
* If you want something with a truly different world and are ready for a challenge.
A fair warning to those intrigued by the storytelling aspect of the game - the game is brilliant, but hard.  It rewards attention and planning.  The storytelling is great, but the game can be brutal, so be ready for that.

Disclaimer: This particular review is based on Rising Storm and not Red Orchestra 2.
This game is a very interesting shooter which tries to be realistic, rather than downright fun. It has it's merits, but for the most part I do not suggest this game to a normal shooter person.
Good things:
- The health/healing system. This game has a unique healing system which is better than almost every other game out there. As far as I can tell, there is no insta-kills but instead you can be instantly forced to bleed. When this happens, you have to bandage yourself like some games, but you only have a limited amount of bandages and therefore a limited amount of health. This is a lot better than randomly spawning health packs, in my opinion.
- The game is very good looking. Self explanitory, but in this particular game where it's key goal is to be realistic it does help a bit. One downside to this is that I cannot get it running smoothly on my current laptop, even at lowest settings. And it doesn't seem to make a difference going from highest to lowest.
Bad things:
- No singleplayer. Since I got the Rising Storm beta and a seperate multiplayer when I was gifted it, I assumed that the one which wasn't multiplayer would be the singleplayer, as most people would. The fact is I was wrong. The normal beta has no singleplayer, and instead has multiplayer which does nothing without the multiplayer installed, and training missions which I will talk about later.
- Jagged sprint. I think the sprint is meant to resemble someone running in real life, but I know I don't run in such a way and this feature make sprint almost unuseable. It's the same sort of thing as going between sprint and walking constantly in any other game, which doesn't work here.
- Training missions don't work. When I tried to do the training missions, I got sent to a loding screen, and then sent back to the missions page when I tried to do any mission. I'm not sure if this is a feature that doesn't work yet, but if it is meant to work it fails.
- The tank doesn't work. When i found out how bad I was at this and saw a class which let me have a tank, I instantly went to use it. But it doesn't seem to work. I spawned in and none of my HUD was there, and then I instantly died. This feature needs to be fixed if they want me playing this game more.
- Not noob friendly. While other FPS games are noob friendly (Like TF2) or have a singleplayer to get you used to the game before doing the multiplayer, this has neither. So when you are finally able to jump in a server which actually has people in it and you hear different codenames being thrown about you don't know about, you just give up. Especially when the people seem to be yelling at you for not doing their special tactic.
So, do I suggest Rising Storm to the average gamer? No. I think this is more of a game for history buffs, so that they can live their favourite historical battles and do it exactly how it was done in history. This might change when this game is fully released and out of beta, but for now I can't suggest it.

BioShock could have had a truly cohesive story, with nuance and character defined by more than stereotypes, and it would have been a much better game for it, too. If the studio had simply told their story chronologically, following the rise and fall of Rapture, the exact same narrative would make a far greater impact. Instead, BioShock reads like a political treatise.
Still, every audiolog is a treat, even if I don't know or care who is talking: they are like bonus flash fiction stories, evocative of a crumbling city's hopes. The plasmids are so delightfully whimsical, I can imagine crazed innovators making anything that came to mind in hopes of a quick buck (seriously, who decided they wanted to fling their "enemies" into the air using a genetically-induced tornado?). The insanities of the major and minor characters are frequently tragic, portraying humans as everything from simply human to grotesquely inhumane.
Instead of having a coherent story, BioShock paints a picture with the emotions it invokes with every texture, audiolog, jukebox tune, incongruous accent, and genetic horror. BioShock isn't so much creating Rapture as it is creating the feeling of a Rapture-like place. The only thing that would have made the picture even better would have been a good story.

I was one of the many die-hard Tropico fans who was suckered into pre-ordering this game. Big mistake. The game is buggy as hell, some things they refuse to fix. The Constitution options for immigration? Forget about it. They don't make a lick of difference. I can't recommend this title, despite it being somewhat enjoyable to play. The cheeky story and humor are there, but, if you're looking for an experience as deep and challenging as Tropico 4, you will be disappointed.
Unfortunately, as with many games of recent issue, this game suffers from dumbing down for console play. Lots of things that experienced Tropico players know and rely on to really add depth to the game are gone. The most useful overlays, such as occupancy, profitability, employment level, newspaper, television, and rado station types... all gone in favor of being able to play the game on limited hardware with just a few buttons. In fact, radio stations are gone altogether. You cannot directly set wages at buildings anymore, in favor of a "budget" system that supposedly sets wages, but in reality allows you NO control over wages to properly prioritize your economy. Rents and entry fees on homes and service buildings also gone, in favor of a simple button saying "Tourists Only". You can see these glaring oversimplifications everywhere you turn.
The campaign is far too easy, and I was able to complete it in about 20 hours with no failures, really. The dynasty system seems pointless and can be ignored without affecting gameplay in any way. In short, Tropico 5 is to Tropico 4 as the Texas flag is to the US flag... a dumbed down, easy reader version of the original.
Also, I got the "Big Cheese" DLC as part of my pre-order for free, and this is a good thing, because I would have been really upset if I had paid for it. All it adds is a singlee building, the creamery, and ONE, count em ONE mission... which is 100% more missions than the game came with outside the original campaign.
Look, I'm not a console player. I don't like console games, because I prefer something a bit deeper. That said, there are some console-type titles I have enjoyed and do enjoy playing. If this is the future of the game industry, then there are some pretty dark times ahead. I'll be putting this back on the shelf and playing user content in T4 instead.

Morphopolis is one of those little gems you only find every once and a while.
The quaint, relaxing and rather beautiful soundtrack does wonders to match with the utterly gorgeous visuals. The game is a gorgeous conglomeration of different puzzles, stitched together to make a wonderful seamless whole. Sometimes the way to progress is not immediately obvious and that is what adds to the level of difficulty, and maybe once or twice a patch of annoying.
Beginning your journey as an aphid grub, you find the puzzles that need solving and then find the parts within the environment around you to help you progress. Whether it would be a disguise to scare a beetle off, legs or antennae to fix the next bug body in which you will inhabit to the next level.
With the game only having 5 fairly short chapters to it, it does make for a rather short play, without much replay value. Be that as it may, it still gives you a solid 2 to 3 hours at the minimum of play.
I never once found myself wanting to put this down as the combo of the amazing soundtrack, visuals and just the layout of each level made me want to progress and become the bug God(ess). That also being said, the ending was quite brief, aside from the 'Bug God' achievement popping up and the screen slowly fading to black, I wouldn't have really expected it to stop there, in fact I was waiting for the level section to return for me to select the next level, but such didn't happen.
None the less, if you're in the mood for a slow paced, chill, relaxing and utterly gorgeous game with some decently difficult puzzles, this is for you.

This game makes for a great city builder with a comic twist. Previous Tropico titles were also very fun and time-consuming, but with the new edicts, tweaked economy and the added eras, this game has evolved quite well. Though it takes a while even for the somewhat experienced Tropico player to get into it, it's well worth it.
The colonial era is an enjoyable starting position where you focus on raw materials before becoming an industrial powerhouse. Previous titles always made you start with minimun buildings in 1950, but this gives your island nation a colonial tradition as well. New military buildings and modes allow you to repel rebel attacks and fight off foreign invasions.
Multiplayer is fun! Co-op or fight your friends is great, but as both cities reach around a 1,000 population, connection issues are immenent. This still needs fixing, but overall, multiplayer is pretty great!
So far, I have played several sandbox games with varying settings and one multiplayer game with a friend. I have listed several pro's and cons below:
Pro's:
Colonial Start - Great feel and well suited to the game. Every island in the caribbean has an extensive colonial history. Glad Tropico is now one of them :) You can already experience 15k + profits with every freighter which will allow easy and fast industrialization in the next era.
Resource and Manufacture Diversity - New minerals and raw resources, more factory goods and more production cycles, with the opportunity to elaborate and initiate new production cycles: Coal to Oil, Oil to Pharmeceuticals; Cocoa, sugar and milk to chocolate milk, etc.
Trading System - Profit from extra trading deals for your resources and manufacture. A big plus as this can sometimes lead to incredible boosts to economy. Though these offers appear and disappear over time, it's worth checking your trade tab every few months.
Elaborate Tourism - A diversity in the amount of tourists reflects in the many hotels that one can build. Different buildings add to appeal for different types of tourists. You'll decide to place buildings in particular places that will increase effectiveness of buildings: Haciendas and historical inns near colonial buildings; economy hotels and cabana villages near your entertainment hotspots; country hotels and cabins in the middle of nowhere, etc.
Cons:
Limited Ruling Options - In previous titles you could choose several ways to rule. Background info for your character could make a great difference. I feel with the constitution options this has actually been limited if you want to make most out of your island. When encountering different constitution choices, there three options, but it two are opposites of each other and the third a more-or-less neutral stance on the subject. I personally feel this limits options.
Traffic - With more teamsters in each era, traffic becomes a total nightmare in Modern Times. Any junction, even three way junctions, already halts most traffic. Even if you have more than enough teamsters, goods sometimes don't reach buildings for some time, even if your road layout is quite good. Hopefully they will add future options to add rotundas, yielding signs, trafficlights etc to aid traffic flow.
Music - All music has become instrumental. Whilst that is not per sé a bad thing, I do feel Tropico loses it's Hispanic touch in that sense. Tropico 3 and 4 both had excellent OSTs, whilst I feel that Tropico 5's soundtrack is a bit more repetitive and just not quite as fun. Best soundtrack is still Tropico 3.

Have you ever played monster hunter series with friends? Have you played Left for Dead with friends? I have to say that Evolve is like a mixture of those games.
It has a unique concept of 4v1 pvp.
4 Hunters VS 1 Badass Monster.
4 First Person View VS  1 Third Person View
THE HUNTERS
As the hunter, well obviously you hunt! You hunt down this 1 specific brain powered clever monster.
Each hunter has a specific role that is vital in order to take down this one beast. Medic, support, assault and trapper.
Track the monster down as fast as you can, and never ever give him a chance to get fat (and by fat i mean evolve to stage 3), cause he'll bring hell down on you.
THE MONSTER
There are two ways to win as the monster. Kill all the hunter using your monstrosity, or destroy the generator that the hunters protecting with your monstrosity as well.
Early in the game you must get as far away from the hunter and devour the many wildlife that you can get your hands on in order to evolve and get strong enough so you can face your opponent and take down that generator.
*It has a quite nice graphics. (it might still be tough for a wooden pc)
*Decent map size: Not to big not to small, evens the odds. It gives chance for the hunter to catch up with the monster and for the monster to run around. To scale lets just say it's like playing chase in the school.
*Hostile Environment: Man eating plant, giant crocodile creature in a puddle of mud, scared birds, scavengers. This things actually provides variation of situation depending on how the match is played.
*Balance & Competitive: The game is well balanced, The monster is defeatable even at their final stage, just need a good coordinated teamwork. A clever monster vs a well coordinated team is the key to a fierce yet awesome match.
*You obtain upgrades/improvement (such as more damage, more jetpack fuel, etc.) after each match. Personally i think this could ruin the balance in the future. bigger lvl player will surely dominate. But on the other hand, without this the game might just be too dull and repetitive, this gives a meaning to level up. well people have their preferences
*Price? Personally i think its too costly. But is it worth it? Keep in mind that this is a multiplayer based game, you need other player to play as well. usually less people are willing to pay for an expensive game, but looking at how the game is developed so far, i will have to recommend you to try it..

LIMBO is a game for people who really wish to please cultural gatekeepers who don't even like the video games medium to begin with. One thing gamers in general need to understand is that presentation=/= content. The first thing you see when you start the game up is the minimalist gothic art style and the first thing most players will wonder is where the game is going to go with this aesthetic. The answer is nowhere, because the presentation is the full extent of the actual "narrative" content. From the beginning you have a hodge podge of haunting purgatory imagery including giant spiders, brain slugs and killer children in the spirit of Lord of the Flies. You also have your dead children strewn about for easy dark and mature points. This goes on for about a third of the game or about 1 hour before the game swiftly drops the whole aesthetic for generic industrial environments with little to no narrative significance of any sort. The rest of the game consists of challenge rooms which resemble Aperture Science testing chambers with dim lighting.
The actual gameplay consists of generic puzzle platforming with trial and error gameplay. Trial and error gameplay can certainly be valid when it comes to precise and engaging platforming challenges, so long as the player can inform and prepare themselves ahead of time for the challenges. Most of the game though is punking the player with gory deaths, which still isn't a big deal because this game has no consequences for failure. The actual meat of the game starting from the industrial setting onward is box physics puzzles, of the Half-Life 2 variety. If when you played that part where you had to place cinderblocks at the end of a wooden plank to create a seesaw you thought "I want to play a whole game built around this" then this is the game for you.
Most of the puzzles are actually built around the loose physics engine, and the puzzles are less challenging to solve as they are hard to execute. Most of this comes from it being difficult to get the janky physics to do what you want, so the game is only hard so far as it can be difficult to get the physics to behave how you want them to. Curiously, the boy character is also subject to the spazzy physics, so deaths in which the player is likely supposed to feel disquieted are more unintentionally humorous as death by tragic purgatory metaphor may result in the boy character doing cartwheels.
This game doesn't merit being called pretentious, since pretension implies that there was an actual attempt at depth. This game is a generic flash platformer with a gothic aesthetic that runs for some time until it suddenly ends, complete with a "I wonder what it all means ;^)" ending. The gameplay isn't notable in any way either, and feels a bit amateur. All in all I can't recommend this game on any level, not even on sale, since there is a plethora of interesting games to find on steam both indie and professional which actually remember what the point of a game is.
To end this review on a positive note, I recommend you buy Abe's Oddysee in place of this game. It is a much more engaging, fun and challenging puzzle platformer, with actually palpable themes and a narrative.
If there is any reason why games are still not considered a serious art form, it is because junk like this are considered to be accomplishments in the medium.

Outstanding game. After around 70 hours, I feel I have made enough successful towns to start checking out some mods (I like to throughly beat a game before modding). So the vanilla experience is really good, don't get me wrong... with one exception. If you can get your population to around 100-130 people, the difficulty drops off pretty significantly. Those first couple of years, you have to really pay attention to the timing of your new houses. Build houses too fast, everyone gets their own house, nobody is boning. Build houses too slow, the young, horny folk don't have any love nests to make babies in. If you build your new houses all at once, an interesting thing can happen where all of your children are born really close together, then they all stop having new children at the same time, then all die at around the same time and it's a catastophe. After you hit the point where you have enough people to kind of smooth out those big gains and losses, it becomes a game of slow, metered expansion, with relatively low threat (though I have had really bad luck sometimes, like tornado tears through your farmland at the same time your livestock pens develop an infestation and such).
Overall, great game, and I'm sure mods will give me at least another 70 hours of enjoyment on it. If you buy it, trust that you will have no freaking idea why your first couple of towns fail. It's the roguelike of sim-cities. You learn by killing whole populations lol.

negative
- Lots of user interaction design errors & hitches. e.g. Trying to select an object by standing close to it is almost impossible.

(e.g. first puzzle is the 'queen problem' in chess. It was original when the 7th guest did it in the 90's, but after the sheer number of games that did the same..not so much).
- a great deal of the art budget is wasted on characters that don't add to immersion OR the story. (e.g. whitechapel area)
- the game cheats a bit on the story: you might hear back about stuff that happened 'while you were not watching', without giving out any clues to it (e.g. prison scene).
- the game may force you to do incredibly stupid things (like give a certain person the object he desires), without even acknowledging / lampshading the fact that it's out of character. (same location)
- most or all characters are charicatures or stereotypes. Protagonists don't undergo any form of change or seem fazed by anything they face.
- the game has not been playtested very thoroughly. There are blatent errors in continuity, such as suddenly knowing the name of 'the killers', after deducting where one of them works.
- the game makes weird assumptions about the world (e.g. that a rope used to lower coffins into graves would be frayed only on one side AND that this is the only place you'd expect a rope frayed on only one side to be found).
- some characters (especially heads, like the children from the intro), suffer tremendously from the uncanny valley syndrome. (Bad voice acting added in the mix there make these kids horrific to watch :X). A few more polygons would have helped.

The level design is horrible, especially at the end, where 5 'sponteous ladders' are found (boxes and sacks stacked 4 or 5 meters in just so a way that a creature without legs to speak of can walk up it) and bring you to terminator2-look-a-like iron smelter, with an iron grate walkway with added twists and turns, hanging just a few meters above a sea of molten metal. A modern point-and-click adventure in the Arthur Conan Doyle's "Sherlock Holmes" universe. "The Testament of Sherlock Holmes" is a dark, sometimes gory investigation into a criminal conspiracy that threatens the British crown in Victorian England.
Graphics are decent but clearly outdated. They do a good job at letting Victorian London come to life before you, though, and the locations are beautifully designed.
Controls can make or break and adventure game (see: Grim Fandango), but in the case of "The Testament" they are not an issue since you can choose from 3 different control schemes: classic fixed-angle point-and-click, third-person free-roaming and first-person free-roaming (first-person shooter style). At any time you can use Homes' special ability to help point out interactive elements in the environment.
Puzzles are the core of any adventure game and there are some good ones in "The Testament". Others feel too difficult and lack proper instructions. Sometimes objects become clickable only once an event has been triggered, requiring you to search locations again after you've already searched them, but it's not a big hassle. Some of the more difficult puzzles can be skipped, but it will cost you the achievement, which is fair.
Story is the frame within which the puzzles are set. "The Testament" does a decent job at presenting you with an increasingly threatening conspiracy while keeping the main villain disclosed until the end of the game. As the story progresses, Holmes himself becomes a suspect and the game does a good job at depicting Watson's increasing doubts about the integrity of his old friend. In general, the interactions between Holmes and Watson are very well done and often provide comic relief in an otherwise dark and serious narrative. The writing displays some weaknesses and certain turns of event come too suddenly and inexplicably. The story does keep you hooked, though, as you will want to find out who's behind it all and how Holmes himself might be implicated.
This is definitely a highlight for adventure fans, particularly, of course, for fans of Doyle's Sherlock Holmes. At 11 hours, the game is of very decent length for an adventure game, too.

I've played all the modern Frogwares Sherlock games, and Testament is... this is a bad game. It's just a bad game.
Investigations are poor, with absolutely ludicrous pixel hunting. The sixth sense ability is supposed to assist you in locating interactive hotspots, but it only seems to work if an object is in a direct line of vision, which means if an object is obscured on your screen, it won't show up, leading you to do the ALWAYS FUN GAMEPLAY MECHANIC of running around a room in circles trying to find the one item necessary to trigger the next cutscene.
You do a lot of pointless stuff in this game, that is supposed to reflect poorly on Holmes' credibility, but feels instead like story padding. Whitechapel feels practically like running errands. Back and forth and back and forth. In the prison, back and forth and back and forth. Backtracking is nothing new to adventure games but because every area of the game is its own chapter, you're not backtracking to other locations, you're backtracking within the same location, which just adds to the tedium.
The story wants you to take itself seriously but yikes. (SPOILERS!)
There are times when the story in this game felt sillier than the Cthulhu game, but at least the Cthulhu game knew it was camp! There's always been ridiculous elements to Sherlock Holmes cases, but this game wants you to believe it's the darkest and grimest game yet-- but it's so goofy!!
Maybe the engine just doesn't hold up anymore. Or maybe Sherlock Holmes needs to shed the current construct of puzzles and busywork. Perhaps a game more along the lines of Walking Dead/Gone Home but with a detective/invstigation slant? All I know is the gameplay of Testament is flat out bad and the story doesn't save it, and I enjoyed it far less than Awakened, Nemesis, and Jack the Ripper.
