So after a five day binge play of the BioShock franchise, here are my thoughts about the game that started it all.
For those who live under rocks, this game started two 'kinda big' controversies. One being the idiotic 'this disk will self destruct' one time instal that the original PC version came with, and the second being that the game was overtly pro-Communism and and anti-Libertarian. Before I get into the right/wrong for this game, let me address both the reasons for uproar. Firstly, video game companies have proven to be nothing but greedy a-holes that we enjoy licking. Born of the mentality that when you buy a game, it's not your property, it still belongs to the game company, we've been gifted with same day DLC, on disk DLC, the war on Game Stop, and still paying $60+ for digital titles. This was one of the first attempts to wrestle ownership of a game away from you and keep it firmly in 2K's hands, and you just pay for the privilege. Kinda funny for a game that seems to extol the virtues of the Communist manifesto that nothing belongs to the individual, to actually do just that! Clever marketing maybe? Anyway, as to the second bit of trouble, the game does go out of it's way to show that the Libertarian idea of free markets and minimal government involvement leads to mass suffering.... until you reach the end of the game. No spoilers, but as the game goes above and beyond in blaming the "Great Chain" for Rapture's destruction, it turns out to be nothing more than a clever plot device. So for all the sore fanny it caused, like most outrage in the media, it was started by people that didn't care enough to investigate the entire title to discover there wasn't any outrage at all. Surprise surprise.
RIGHT: BioShock does one thing, and does it incredibly well. This spans for all three titles not just the first. And that one thing is: MOOD. From the second you step into Rapture you are wrapped into a mood of decay and despair so vivid you can almost smell the water damage, and follows you to the very end. BioShock singularly gives this a second helping that the other titles sadly discarded by making the characters look..... surreal. Everything has a 1940's taste and even the characters seem to be odd glassy caricature out of a pulp comic book. Like Half Life, the graphical limitations of the time add a stylized feeling that actually feed into the immersion rather than detracted from it. The second thing these games do, is mess with your emotions. This references to the "controversy" over the games political undertow, but the game rapidly changes pace making you unsure what to think or believe till the very end. Like I say with any game, all the graphics in the world can't save a game that doesn't have a good plot, and BioShock keeps you tied in knots non-stop. The mapping is set up wonderfully for PC FPS players, controls are simple though there is a bit of a learning curve with Weapon/Plasmid combo for the mouse, it will become second nature in no time. You can add on to both your plasmids and weapons, changing effects and visuals letting you customize your combat style and type of play. The voice acting is top notch, again adding to that mood and immersion, the Splicer's vocal taunts are haunting and Big Daddy whale calls will make your flesh crawl. Another incredibly well done feature is the Big Daddy itself. Every area has a certain amount of Big Daddy - Little Sister combos lurching around collecting ADAM, and it is imperative that you defeat them if you want to upgrade your plasmids. But BioShock doesn't just hand them over, oh hell no. You are going to fight and die over and over to get that ADAM, because the Big Daddy's only purpose is to mangle you quickly and without mercy. There are two types: The Bouncer who uses only physical attacks, and Rosie who carries a rivet gun and fires mines. Though toward the end of the game you get use to the combat patterns and have a big enough arsenal that the Big Daddy only becomes moderately dangerous, through the first half of the game these things are ridiculously hard and actually prove a great challenge.
WRONG: Some of this I hate to even complain about considering this is a launch title for the franchise, and naturally a proving ground for certain bugs to get fixed and concepts worked out. However, I have a few bones to pick that kept me on the fence for a while. First and foremost, is enemy type. When you first run into the Splicers, they are creepy and horrible, but after the thousandth time you've blown away a male Splicer, their creepiness has long since worn off. Even the Big Daddy loses some of its intimidation by the end of the game and you realize you feel the same playing the final level of Bioshock as you do the final level of COD. It's just a target, remove it, continue on. This game is badly in need of skins for the enemies as well as attack patterns, to give it just a bit more flavor. Secondly is the hacking. Starting the game, I loved to hack things! The pipe and water flow hack was fun and challenging, but by the end of the game I was dreading it and going out of my way to find auto hacks just so I could push ahead. This could have been fixed by adding different hacks for different objects. A hack for vending machines, a hack for security bots, and a hack for vaults. There are too many plasmids that are just, for lack of better terms, worthless. They're great to look at, some have very interesting visuals, but ultimately are just not usable. You will use the Electric plasmid because of it's ability to stun Splicers, Bots, and even the Bid Daddy. You might also take Fire plasmid, but even that loses a lot of its punch toward the end of the game due to the fact that it has little to no effect on Bots, Big Daddy, and even the Splicers just seem to shrug it off. The rest are just gimmicks that work okay or not at all, but wont save you during a fight. Another thing that bothered me was at the end of the game when you dressed in the Big Daddy suit, your hands don't change to give you the feeling that you're in the suit! For a game that goes so far to set a mood, it was kind of a big 'oops' not make this one small visual correct for that scene. And lastly, screw the limited wallet. It's a moronic gimmick to force you spend cash and limit your ability to make pit stops to top off ammunition, rather than just remove that ability all together to make a supply pinch.
That aside, BioShock is a fantastic game that has aged well and has plenty of replay value with multiple endings and plenty of hidden items to keep you playing. The story alone is reason enough to grab this title, as it will have direct effect on both of the sequels, adding to their depth and understanding.

I played this game, and I enjoyed it, but I did not like the narrator at all; very much recommended.
It's thought-provoking and insightful.
At best, it is a person's interpretation of another person's journey.
The game attempts to emulate (or speculate) the experience of being a "reclusive," "lonely," (narrator's opinion) game developer by the name of Cuda, who seems to be coming unhinged by crippling alienation and the inability to go on trying to create games.
The narrator (Davey) makes it his mission to make sure that this socially challenged friend's work is "put out there" and Davey appoints himself captain of the mission of showing Cuda's games to as many people as he can, thereby finding significance himself--and loving it. His excuse is, he wants to help Cuda out of an alarmingly unstable mental state, as is his interpretation of the games.
The
is entirely composed of Cuda's games, chained together in chronological sequence, and peppered with Davey's interpretations/introductions of them--he speaks for Cuda a lot.
The game is charming, at first glance, as it seems to be a fun sampling of Cuda's "unfinished" and "abandoned" games (I feel it necessary to point out that the narrator's sweeping speculation is the only explanation we get--Cuda did not even know this game was being made).
I get the impression that Davey is fascinated by Cuda (in fact, he plainly says this, in so many words), almost as if Cuda were an alien or some foreign entity that needed a translator.

It wouldn't be right to give this game a rating out of ten, it's not that kind of product, it's too much of a personal endeavour on the developer's part. Like 'The Stanley Parable' this is quite conceptual - it's a game about making games, and about the creative process in general. However, strictly speaking, it's more of a journey than an out-and-out 'game' in the strictest sense of the word. It's a journey through someone's mind, a view behind the curtain, a glimpse at the cogs and gears working their way through different avenues and different possibilities. Ultimately though, this game is - for me- about the idea of meaning: what we mean to others(and vice versa), why we seek to apply a meaning to things, and how much that meaning matters to us. This game probably won't be for everyone (what game is?), but if you play it and come with an open mind, you won't be disappointed.

Short Version: Tropico is a great game. I fully recommend it.
Long Version: I joined the series with Tropico 4, which is very similar to this fifth installment, but much easier, so if you have the money, paying for the most modern, challenging one is your best bet. The game is simple in paper: Become Royal Governor of a British Colony, declare independence, and build your small nation throughout history. The 4 eras (Colonial, World Wars, Cold War, and Modern) will force you to change your play style all the time, and the new constitution allows you to replay as a different kind of Presidente (Pro Tip: Try being democratic. You won't get to publicly execute journalists or pesky protestors for "violations of human rights" (whatever that means...), but it will make it more challenging). Also, live each era to its fullest, so you can plan ahead. Your nation might be bustling with trade with your preffered superpower in the Cold War, but once the Soviets fall, you better adapt your commercial strategy quickly, or else you'll go back to being a third world hell-hole faster that you can say "WHY DON'T YOU BUY MY CRAP ANYMORE?". Hell, maybe I am just bad at strategy games (I am not. Dare you to a round of Civ V if you don't believe me), but the game is challenging for me on easy, as your need to change strategies will ♥♥♥♥ you up bad unless you plannes ahead for 5 years or so (5 year plan? Get it? 'Cause communist dictatorship is an option?). People are much harder to please, especially because the Constitution may divide them (the religious might favor you for all the churches you gave them, but half may hate you for not being a theocracy). The era specific random events ("The Soviets have asked us to stash some humanitarian aid that 'has been nowhere near Cuba'" (later) "GOOD GOD! THEY WERE NUKES! WHAT DO WE DO? A) Keep them B) GIve them to the USA C) Hide them, return them to the USSR when possible." This allows you to ideologically ally with one, while maintaining peace with the other superpower), various play styles (Constitution options) and development plans (Will Tropico be an industrial nation? A farming paradise (Thank Presidente for the 'buy organic craze!')? A vacational hotspot?) will give you countless replay options and entertainment.
P.S. The Nazis invaded once, and our armies destroyed each other. One Panzer with a smoking engine survived. It killed me. 100/10

Oh, how much there is to talk about with this gem.
This game has everything a zombie game could offer. You don't play as the badass protagonist who can mow through countless zombies because they are immune. You play as a nobody, an average Joe who happened to live in the wrong place- Muldraugh, or West Point.
Scavenging is realistic as every plausible shelf, drawer, closet, etc has some form of loot in it (actually, some don't and some houses are already looted. Also, the loot is random) and to add to the realism, the loot doesn't respawn, meaning if you run out of food because you ate all of it, you'll have to resort to farming.
Eventually, the water and electricity will run out/shut off so to get water you'll have to create rain collectors or make a well. However, electricity is gone so you can't use ovens to cook food... Meaning you'll have to farm.
The multiplayer beta branch is out now, and it is simply awesome. Me and my friend(s) have had a wonderful experience creating a fort, fortifying it and while guns/ammo are rare, we scavenged and managed to wipe out entire hordes.
NPCs are a planned feature and were -sort of- in the game before, as well as a mini story, with the main characters 'Kate' and 'Baldspot'. These have been removed (only temporarily, don't worry) and will be revamped and placed back into the game, even better this time- NPCs can become friends/enemies with you, will join you in your base, scavenge, etc and the story will be in-depth and beautiful.
Now while this game is utterly fantastic there are a couple noticible things which while I don't mind, some might not appreciate.
Firstly, on public servers, because loot doesn't respawn, if the server is really popular everyone will start fighting over food, etc and no one will get to find weapons. This isn't really a problem because the server owner can just do a world reset and the loss of weapons and food will encourage teamwork. However, some won't like this, and to you guys- stick to singleplayer or small, private 4 player servers. A quick note, in the current stages the multiplayer servers can handle up to 32 players, but this is changeable. Hopefully the development team will add more complex server options -there are currently very basic options- such as respawning loot every couple real-time hours, or every time the server restarts, etc.
The updates, while amazing, take time to release. A LONG TIME.
You see, the game has been out/in development since -roughly- 2011. 2-3 years later, they're only just adding multiplayer, a key asset to a zombie game. I haven't really been affected by this as I only recently purchased the game but I can see why some wood be annoyed. But as I briefly mentioned previously, every major update adds something new, something fresh to the game. I hear they're adding bunnies soon which will eat your planted carrots. ♥♥♥♥ yeah.
I rate this game 9/10. While absolutely incredible, and one of my favourite games of ALL TIME, the dev stages are slow.
But despite this, knowing how awesome the devs are, as the game grows in popularity, the devs will quicken the pace (but hopefully not lower the quality).
Please note that the game is currently in early access.

I've bought & played a lot of Telltale games & this one is about average in overall quality.  It has it's moments, but it also does some pretty annoying things from time to time & suffers from some performance issues & janky animations.
-Good Story
-Plot Twists
-Great Voice Acting
-Player Choice Interaction
-Encourages Multiple Playthroughs
-Choices don't really matter
-Janky Animations & Transitions
-Blatent Advertising
-Game is Short
The story involves you playing as Bruce Wayne being involved in a conspiracy from his parents past.  You have to choose when to play as Bruce & when to play as Batman & choices will affect certain peoples oppinions of you later on in the game, or at least give the illusion of it.  Most of the choices resolve in the same or similar outcome.  As you play through the story you'll unlock codex entries for characters, & certain areas in Gotham City.  Other than that, there's not really much more I can say without spoiling it.  It's a Telltale game, afterall & their games are 90% story.
The game has 5 chapters total, which all vary in length.  You choose dialog options with the A/B/X/Y buttons & use them combined with the joystick for QTE segments that usually involve dodging or attacking enemies.  You also set up ambushes in augmented reality that perfectly simulate what you are trying to do before hand.  Then there are basic puzzles that involve solving crime scenes & linking events within the scenes with eachother to paint a picture of what happened.  These are all set in stone, & you can't really get different pictures from mix/matching the moments.  Then there's the character opinions of you which basically are slight changes in the overall story.  If you beat up criminals or impale them, certain characters will resent Batman & if you insult them or ignore them as Bruce they'll resent him.  Overall, I've not really seen much changes in outcomes either way.  It's still the basic Interactive Movie set up that all Telltale games have been using since day one.
The game also has some scenes which you can only experience in multiple playthroughs.  When you choose between playing as Bruce or Batman changes the scenerio & dialog considerably & in order to experience everything you will need to play the game at least twice.  In the end, though, the outcome is still pretty much the same.  It's just another way of obtaining it.
The game also does some blatant advertising after each chapter, which is kind of annoying.  "GO BUY COMICS!" is basically what it's saying & it says it every time you complete a chapter.
The game is also fairly short.  I managed to beat it in just over 7 hours.  Not bad but also not as long as other games from Telltale for the same price.  It took me almost twice as long for Tales From the Borderlands, so this one being about half the length is kind of a shame.
Overall, the game is good & cutscenes are done very well.  The game does stutter from time to time & has janky animations in some cutscenes but nothing that ruins the overall game experience.  If you are thinking of picking this one up I'd say it's recommendable, just don't be too upset if the game uses some familiar faces in ways that you weren't expecting.  The game is trying to tell a new story in an alternate universe with Batman & it does a good job of it, but it does overuse some familiar faces in ways that are kind of jarring.  If you can get past that, then by all means try this one out.

I haven't played a zombie survival game quite like this. There is a constant sense of dread and fear that I don't really feel in many other games, which is probably a weird thing to put as a positive point, but trying to survive and thrive with these constant overbearing themes is quite the experience.
The field of vision system works great, in that even though it's third person you can only see zombies etc that are in the direction you are facing, making some night walks particularly tense when you can hear a zombie creeping up behind you, and turn around to see it biting your arm and making the next few hours a horrible struggle to try and stem the infection (which is pretty much hopeless, I find).

The feeling of isolation the game brings isn't even lost in the (currently very beta) multiplayer - constantly losing sight of each other in the same way as zombies made for many scary moments when we couldn't find each other. It just shows that games don't need cutting edge visuals to deliver the most authentic experience, for example Silent Hill 1 is still probably the scariest game I have ever played.
There is still a lot more to the game I haven't even tried, such as the crafting and more advanced cooking, mainly because I'm too busy being paranoid about making sure all my lights are off and curtains are closed. A favourite of mine is peering out of the curtains and accidentally locking eyes with a zombie outside, who will proceed to thump his head against your window until the dull thuds drive you insane enough to go deal with it yourself. Which you should do - it turns out they do break the windows eventually, as I so unfortunately discovered.
All in all, even in the early access state it's in the game is a great experience. I'm looking forward to seeing what's going to be added. A tenner for a game is never really a bad deal, and if you can pick it up in a sale, then it's a no-brainer. As you will soon be when the massive undead hordes get chased from the cities into your sleepy suburb. Good luck.

---Alpha Review---
*Take this review with a grain of salt* since things will change when beta/release happens
Reviewing after 3hours of play. roughly 2hours Monster, 1 hour as Trapper only.
Okay so this is Evolve as other people have mentioned it is a 4v1 Player vs Monster(Player) action game.
the Monster is supposed to evolve and evade the hunters till level 3 and then either KILL all the hunters or Destroy the Power Generator (As Monster i won Twice Killing all humans, and 3 times destroying power relay).
humans are supposed to track, hunter, and kill the monster before level 3 if possible if not they have to defend the power relay which at that point the monster usually is really hard to kill unless u got a good group of humans.
Now Reviewing the 2 Chars ive used Monster, and trapper.
Monsters get 3 points every level to spend into abilitys and these are mentioned below
Goliath Abilities: Rock Throw, Charge, Leap Slam, Firebreath. (After watching other monsters use firebreath i feel it is not needed and wasted points)
I focused on the main aspect the Monster should be doing. SNEAKING And hunting.
so i invested 2 into leap slam for extra distance, and 1 into charge. then 2 into charge 1 leap.
At Max evolution i just throw 3 points into rock throw.
Until ur level 3 hunting the Hunters is really not a smart idea. At level 2 the Monster can deal signifigant damage and possibly kill off 1-2 hunters before retreating if hes bold enough (or when you get traped it will happen).
I really enjoyed the movement of the Monster and it felt very fluid and everything about it is nice.
Crouching to move sliently and not leave footsteps. was my favorite aspect.
Overall the Hunters have the advantage 2/3rds of the game. It takes a smart monster to evade them. usually a good team of hunters will always be on your back. leaving you only a small time to eat and then evolve after like 5mins. level 3 evolution usually takes me 15mins since game start.
I hope more people try to get good at the monster. currently im 6-0 with the monster. (im pretty good at hiding, sneaking, and when traped knowing when to attack and when to move, evading most of the damage till the trap ends.)
I feel a good monster atm will overpower any good human team after level 1. (Level 2 Monsters become bulletproof taking signifitantly less damage, doubles the Hp of the monster, and has better armor and deals Really nice damage enabling some earily kills if your more offensive).
Now with the Trapper:
The Trapper is unique as its the unit that can keep the monster in a closed area and can track it with the pet Daisy. Daisy is pretty good overall but i think she needs track a bit better. its easy to lose the scent from the monster if they know what to do.
I feel the harpoons are good but some be buffed a bit. (little bit longer range). its really easy to break them as the monster. (leapslam or charge can get you out pretty easily) or climing up a cliff to disable it.)
But its fun setting traps against an unsuspecting monster and while your team starts fighting u rotate to where hes gonna run to. then ARENA TRAP.
trapping you all in and you can deal some sigfigant damage.
I have not tried the other classes yet but i think if i were to play one it would be the assault as i find his abilities the best suited for me outside trapper.
Overall for First Impressions i am surprised how smooth it ran with my Graphics card. but i do get Weird Frame drops from time to time. cant wait for the full optimized game/drivers for it. It ran beautifully with an alpha and i didnt find any Real major bugs or grips about it.
i also like that it has like 3 playable maps. which are all pretty balanced and nice. (one seems to favor the monster, one the humans and one is even.)
Cant wait to play more of it.
My only Real Con atm is that its gonna be a full priced 60$ Game :P
From what ive experianced i would rate this as a 30-40$ Game. The Music is nice, the gameplay is nice. But it needs fine tuning (its an alpha i know so not a con in my book).
Overall would like to see at least 6-9 Playable maps and some other things.
Since this is only a multiplayer alpha i can see that they really didnt scrimp.
hopefully in the beta phase we'll see the single player aspect that will also POP.
But overall i hope they keep the quaility going for the multiplayer.
TLDR:  I really enjoyed it, Good Overall, Worth 30-40$ ATM in my eyes, Would recommend other people to try it.

What we have here is Edge of Space. Edge of space is a really interesting game, it plays differently from Terraria and starbound, it's truly a breath of fresh air for the genre. The weapon focus is more on guns at the moment, although they told me they are to add melee weapons in at a future time. As for graphics, the graphics are amazing and have a interesting feel, actually kinda throws me back to the days of the SNES, kinda breaking away from that pixel feel but also sticking to it. As for the music the music makes me feel a lot of things it's ambient and interesting it's kinda sad but in a good way. Point is, It's a fun game really, the level design is interesting and there are many canverns and areas to explore. The game is challenging as a rhino trying to climb a tree made of tomato skin, it takes some getting used to. It's a little slow at first but once you figure it out, it's awesome. Outstanding game. After around 70 hours, I feel I have made enough successful towns to start checking out some mods (I like to throughly beat a game before modding). So the vanilla experience is really good, don't get me wrong... with one exception. If you can get your population to around 100-130 people, the difficulty drops off pretty significantly. Those first couple of years, you have to really pay attention to the timing of your new houses. Build houses too fast, everyone gets their own house, nobody is boning. Build houses too slow, the young, horny folk don't have any love nests to make babies in. If you build your new houses all at once, an interesting thing can happen where all of your children are born really close together, then they all stop having new children at the same time, then all die at around the same time and it's a catastophe. After you hit the point where you have enough people to kind of smooth out those big gains and losses, it becomes a game of slow, metered expansion, with relatively low threat (though I have had really bad luck sometimes, like tornado tears through your farmland at the same time your livestock pens develop an infestation and such).
Overall, great game, and I'm sure mods will give me at least another 70 hours of enjoyment on it. If you buy it, trust that you will have no freaking idea why your first couple of towns fail. It's the roguelike of sim-cities. You learn by killing whole populations lol.

This is a really great game, especially considering it was almost completely made by one person. The only drawback to it is that it lacks an endgame; once your town is not in danger of starving/freezing/dying the only thing left to do is grow bigger, which can be too easy, in a rather dull way.
